CubeSats, which were developed at educational institutions, often exhibit low mission success rates because of their limited design and system engineering experience. To address this issue, this study proposes a mission assurance framework that integrates system complexity evaluation with component importance analysis using the design structure matrix. Within this framework, system configuration and dependencies among components visualized through design structure matrix (DSM) and complexity calculations, previously performed manually, are automated. In addition, functions and components are categorized according to mission success levels, enabling a quantitative assessment of each component's contribution to overall mission success. This dual approach not only reduces system complexity but also improves the distribution of critical functions across components, thereby mitigating the risk of single-point failures and enhancing system robustness. The proposed method was validated through a case study involving the BIRDS bus developed at the Kyushu Institute of Technology. The results demonstrate that DSM-based system reconfiguration can reduce system complexity by more than 80% at the highest mission success level while improving the distribution of critical functions. This framework provides an effective tool for assessing design validity from multiple perspectives during the early development phase prior to the preliminary design review. This approach is expected to increase the reliability and mission success rates of student CubeSat projects.
Keywords CubeSats · Complexity · Design structure matrix · System design · Satellite

CubeSats are a class of standardized nanosatellites defined by a unit size of approximately $ 1 0 \times1 0 \times1 1. 3 5 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ with a mass of up to 2 kg as specified in the CubeSat Design Specification by California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly) [1]. These base units, known as "1U," can be modularly combined to form larger satellite platforms, such as 3U, 6U, or 12U, depending on mission requirements. Originally developed to provide academic institutions with a low-cost, accessible platform for hands-on space engineering education and basic research, CubeSats have rapidly evolved to support a wide range of scientific, commercial,

and governmental applications. Compared with traditional satellite missions, their compact form factor, reduced component count, use of the commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) component, and simplified systems engineering process contribute to lower development costs and shorter timelines. Since the first CubeSats were launched in 2003 [2], CubeSat technology has gained significant traction beyond academia. According to the Nanosats Database, annual CubeSat launches have exceeded 100 since 2014 and reached 390 in 2023 [3]. Despite this rapid expansion, educational institutions continue to play a pivotal role in CubeSat development.

However, achieving full mission success remains a persistent challenge in academic CubeSat projects. According to Swartwout, approximately 8% of academic CubeSats launched between 2018 and 2023 failed during initial operations, and nearly half accomplished only partial mission objectives [4]. One contributing factor is the lack of comprehensive mission assurance frameworks that are tailored to the needs of student-led or novice teams [5]. Mission assurance encompasses systematic processes for identifying, evaluating, and mitigating technical and programmatic
risks across all mission phases from early design to on-orbit operation [6].

Space system engineering and space product assurance are supported by the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook [7], the European Cooperation for Space Standardization (ECSS) standards used by ESA [8], and the JAXA System Design Standard [9]. These documents outline structured practices for requirement definition, validation, reliability assessment, and risk analysis. However, these agency-level frameworks are designed for projects that require larger scale and high assurance. Therefore, tailoring is necessary to match the CubeSat development style, which is characterized by limited resources and short development timelines. This need for tailoring is also recognized in documents, such as the JAXA System Design Standard [9] and the ESA ECSS IOD CubeSat guidelines [10, 11].

Several studies have explored satellite system engineering methods with a focus on risk management for CubeSat. For instance, Cech proposed a risk management framework for nanosatellites that covers the design phase through operation and incorporates the results of FMECA based on a case study using VZLUSAT-1 [12]. Also, Mancinelli examined a method for prioritizing risks by calculating the risk priority number (RPN) and representing each failure mode as a code in the early stage of CubeSat design [13]. In addition, Brumbaugh suggested an approach for ranking failure modes in CubeSats [14, 15]. However, they did not address how to modify the design specifically on the basis of risk assessment. Moreover, Radu proposed a system engineering method for reliability, availability, maintainability, and safety (RAMS) analysis, which aims to minimize risk, although it does not include a direct method for implementing design changes [16]. Furthermore, Nejad introduced a framework called simulation-based probabilistic risk assessment (SIMPRA), which evaluates risks and supports design improvement [17]. Since a satellite is essentially a singleitem system, conventional reliability calculations cannot be directly applied. To address this limitation, Sahara proposed a method for quantitatively evaluating satellite architectures and developed a formulation for calculating satellite system complexity [18, 19]. His study also demonstrated a significant correlation between system complexity and mission success rates and helped clarify design policy guidelines [18]. Also, Ishii applied the same formulation to quantify satellite system complexity [20].

The challenge of time-consuming calculations was identified in the process of evaluating satellite system complexity. Specifically, the calculation requires counting the number of blocks and arrows in the system block diagram, which must be repeated each time the design is modified. To address this issue, this research introduces the design structure matrix (DSM). The DSM is a systems engineering tool that represents a system as a matrix, clarifying the interrelationships

and dependencies between each component and function. The DSM concept was first developed by Professor Don Steward at California State University [21]. Since then, it has been widely applied across various fields, from home appliances to semiconductors and is not limited to specific industrial products. For example, Sawai demonstrated a method to improve the modularity of robotic arms by incorporating customer requirements into the DSM framework [22]. In addition, Luh described a DSM-based approach that clusters components on the basis of connection strength derived from graph theory to support future product variety [23]. Furthermore, AlGeddawy and Maaskant analyzed the relationships between components and sought to enhance product modularity for electrical kettles and airplane wings by modifying the clustering structure [24, 25].

Numerous studies have explored the application of DSMs to spacecraft, such as CubeSats. For example, Ibrahim applied the DSM to the i-CanSat picosatellite training kit and NEXUS CubeSat and analyzed the dependencies of components [26]. In addition, Chitsaz evaluated four components of CubeSat with respect to the four kinds of information and clarified the depth of interaction between them for design assurance [27]. As described above, although research results have been produced that have created and analyzed DSM models of CubeSats, they do not provide any concrete guidance on how to make design changes.

Building on prior studies, this research proposes a novel mission assurance framework that places system complexity at its core, with the DSM serving as the primary analytical tool. Unlike previous studies that have focused primarily on visualizing dependencies or assessing risks without offering actionable design guidance, this framework introduces a structured, iterative methodology for analyzing and optimizing satellite system architectures. By modeling subsystem interactions through the DSM, quantifying architectural complexity, and linking these metrics directly to design modification strategies, the proposed approach enables a proactive, data-driven pathway for improving mission reliability.

This study reformulated the existing complexity calculation workflow into a DSM-based representation to enable reproducible and consistent evaluation of system complexity during iterative architecture updates. In addition, in-house software was developed to compute the complexity directly from the DSM, eliminating the manual counting and pathfinding required in the conventional method. Finally, the resulting complexity metrics were incorporated into the repeatable mission assurance framework, demonstrating that they can guide specific architecture modifications. The validity of the approach was confirmed using the CubeSat architecture examined in this paper. The key novelty of this study lies in its integration of system analysis, complexity evaluation, and design refinement within a unified

framework. By providing a repeatable and scalable approach to complexity-informed design decision-making, this work offers a practical tool for strengthening mission assurance and improving the success rates of CubeSat missions.

The structure of the paper is as follows: Chapter 2 introduces the design structure matrix. Chapter 3 describes the method used to calculate the satellite system complexity using the DSM. Chapter 4 presents a case study in which the BIRDS CubeSat platform is used to demonstrate the application and effectiveness of the method. Chapters 5 and 6 discuss the results and offer concluding remarks.

section: 2 Introduction of the design structure matrix
section_key: 2 introduction of the design structure matrix
text: The DSM is a network modeling tool that represents the components forming a system and their interactions, thereby clarifying the system architecture [21]. It maps the interrelationships among N system elements as an $ N\times N $ square matrix with identical element labels in both the rows and the columns. When creating a DSM, the system components are listed in rows and columns. A cell at row i and column j indicates that the component j output something to component i. Therefore, the matrix columns represent the providing (output) side, whereas the rows correspond to the receiving (input) side. This DSM definition is similar to the adjacency matrix of an interaction graph. The adjacency matrix represents the presence or the absence of connections among components by assigning a binary value of "1" for presence and "0" for absence. The DSM is based on the same structure as an adjacency matrix, but it can be scaled to include additional information such as weight dependency by assigning numeric values or by coloring cells.

section: 2 Introduction of the design structure matrix
section_key: 2 introduction of the design structure matrix
text: The most common method for analyzing a DSM is clustering, which groups components based on the number and strength of their interactions by rearranging the rows and columns of the matrix [21]. The purpose of clustering is to improve the ease and efficiency of system integration by placing components with common suppliers, shared interfaces, or complex interconnections into the same group.

section: 2 Introduction of the design structure matrix
section_key: 2 introduction of the design structure matrix
text: Consistent with system architecture principles established in previous studies, priority is given to identifying highly independent modules that exhibit many internal interactions and few external ones [21]. This leads to the fundamental question: "How can we allocate parts to groups so as to minimize interactions between groups?" [21].

text: Figure 1 shows a weighted directed graph along with its corresponding DSM. In this example, the system consists of six components, forming a $ 6\times 6 $ matrix. The value in the cells in the DSM indicates the number of signal lines between each component. The order of the columns corresponds to the rows, with each cell in the matrix representing a connection from "Component i" to "Component j." For example, in the right diagram in Fig. 1, the cell at Row 6, Column 5 represents the connection from Component E to Component F, as indicated by the yellow arrow. Moreover, the values in the cells at Row 1, Column 3, and Row 3, Column 1 are identical, indicating that the function lines between Component A and Component C are bidirectional. The cells within the same row and column reflect the respective values of their corresponding components.

section: 2 Introduction of the design structure matrix

text: In addition, the background colors in the DSM indicate the subsystem clustering of the components. For example, Components A, B, and C are grouped into Subsystem 1 (SubSys-1), and their corresponding cells in the DSM are shaded blue, matching the color used in a weighted directed graph. Similarly, Subsystem 2 (SubSys-2), which consists of Components D, E, and F, is represented in red. Accordingly, the DSM cells depicting interactions among these components are also colored red. Cells with a white background indicate interface functions between components belonging to different subsystems.

text: The advantage of the DSM is its flexibility in accommodating system design changes. Figure 2 shows a DSM in which the design has been modified by replacing the components that constitute the subsystem shown in the left diagram. In the modified design, Components A and C have been relocated to SubSys-2, whereas Components D and F have been transferred to SubSys-1. Furthermore, it is possible to delete a component from the system by erasing the row and the column corresponding to the target component.

section: 3 DSM-based calculation for satellite system complexity
section_key: 3 dsm based calculation for satellite system complexity
text: The complexity of the target subsystem is calculated again when the system design changes. The entire system's complexity is subsequently calculated again with the new value. These values are estimated by counting the blocks and arrows from the weighted directed graph using the conventional method. Therefore, it takes considerable time to repeatedly apply the design change, modify the weighted directed graph, count the number of blocks and arrows, calculate the complexity, and compare the result with the previous answer. This research utilized the DSM to automate these sequences. This chapter shows the flow of calculating the complexity of the satellite system using the DSM step by step using an original DSM.

For example, component B has no connections to other components within SubSys-1, indicating that it is independent of the group formed by components A and C. As a result, the variable $ p_{1} $ is equal to two. This value can be estimated using Dijkstra algorithm, which is commonly employed in graph theory to compute shortest paths [29]. In this study, the algorithm is applied to each subsystem-level DSM to evaluate reachability among components and to determine, for each component, the set of components that can be reached from it via a directed path. These sets are then combined by taking their union, and whenever at least one directed path exists between two components in either direction, they are classified into the same group. Finally, the remaining groups are counted, and this number is defined as p, the number of independent functional groups.

text: On the basis of these results, optimal system designs with reduced complexity can be explored by iteratively modifying the DSM, such as by replacing, removing, or adding rows and columns, to minimize overall complexity. However, exhaustively simulating all possible configurations remains computationally intensive. For example, dividing 50 components into six groups results in approximately $ 9. 6 \times1 0^{5} $ possible combinations, and this number increases drastically to approximately $ 7. 6 \times1 0^{9} $ when the number of components reaches 100. The primary variable influencing system complexity represents the number of components. In Eq. (1), f is squared, so its contribution to subsystem complexity increases quadratically with f. Therefore, reducing the number of components is a key strategy for minimizing complexity.

section: 3 DSM-based calculation for satellite system complexity
section_key: 3 dsm based calculation for satellite system complexity
text: Nonetheless, because system functions are defined by design requirements, they must be preserved. To address this, functions can be reassigned to other parts of the system, allowing for the removal of associated components. While this approach simplifies the system architecture, it results in the concentration of multiple functions within fewer components, thereby increasing their criticality. As a result, the failure of a single component may lead to greater systemwide consequences. Thus, reducing system complexity does not necessarily guarantee higher mission success. A careful

section: 3 DSM-based calculation for satellite system complexity
section_key: 3 dsm based calculation for satellite system complexity
text: trade-off must be made between the probability of failure and the severity of its potential impact.

This chapter presents a case study of a mission assurance framework designed for use in the early stages of CubeSat development to evaluate the validity of system designs. In the proposed framework, the required functions and the associated importance of components are mapped on the DSM under progressively defined mission success levels to identify systematic bottlenecks and design imbalances as a first step. On the basis of this original DSM, DSMs are generated to correspond with each defined mission success level, and the complexity of each is calculated. The results are then plotted by success level, enabling visualization of the relationship between mission achievement and system complexity. This enables a candidate quantitative evaluation of design sufficiency at each level.

To reduce system complexity, the DSM structure is refined by addressing system imbalances. Specifically, clusters are reorganized, and interfaces are simplified through operations such as merging, splitting, and reordering rows and columns. Complexity is recalculated after each

modification to assess its impact. The objective is to derive a configuration that minimizes overall system complexity while preserving the functionality necessary to meet mission requirements. This framework is intended for application before the preliminary design review (PDR) phase, when the system configuration is nearly finalized. Introducing the method at this stage helps prevent rework in later phases, contributing to shorter development timelines and lower project costs.

section: 4.2 Introduction of the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 2 introduction of the birds bus system
text: This section introduces the BIRDS CubeSat project and its system, followed by the results of a related case study. The Kyushu Institute of Technology (Kyutech) launched the BIRDS program in 2015 to support countries with limited prior experience in CubeSat development [33, 34]. Between 2015 and 2023, a total of 17 CubeSats were developed across six generations, with an additional CubeSat project scheduled for 2025 [35-39]. The primary objective of the program is to enhance the technical capabilities of participating graduate students in CubeSat design and development while also cultivating skills in communication and project management. As part of the initiative, Kyutech accepts three students from each participating country as master's degree candidates. As a result, all phases of the CubeSat project, including mission planning, design, testing, and satellite operation, must be completed within a 2-year period.

section: 4.2 Introduction of the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 2 introduction of the birds bus system
text: To address the challenges of limited time and resources, the BIRDS standard bus system was introduced during the BIRDS-3 project [37, 40]. This standardized platform consists of seven internal boards, including the battery, and six external boards, including the antenna panel, as shown in Fig. 8. It promotes efficiency by enabling knowledge transfer and preserving lessons learned and best practices from earlier generations. It streamlines the design process and helps prevent the recurrence of previously encountered issues. The BIRDS platform has since been used in numerous CubeSat missions and has accumulated extensive flight heritage. It has also been updated to support CubeSats intended for scientific missions, reflecting the expanding goals of the program [41-44]. In addition, it was used for some educational CubeSats by outside users, such as SaganSat, LignoSat, and several CubeSats developed at the Chiba Institute of Technology [45-47].

section: 4.2 Introduction of the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 2 introduction of the birds bus system
text: Figure 9 illustrates the satellite system block diagram using the BIRDS bus system. The green background color shows each printed circuit board. The BIRDS bus system comprises four PIC microcontrollers sold by Microchip Technology as microcontroller units (MCUs): Main PIC, COM PIC, Reset PIC, and FAB PIC. Main PIC is responsible for executing mission operation commands and collecting housekeeping (HK) data. These data reflect the satellite's

section: 4.2 Introduction of the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 2 introduction of the birds bus system
text: Fig. 8 BIRDS standardized platform inside SaganSat [45]

section: 4.2 Introduction of the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 2 introduction of the birds bus system
text: health status and include parameters such as battery voltage, battery current, power line voltages and currents, and satellite time. COM PIC manages communication with the transceiver. It receives uplink commands from the GS and forwards mission and HK data received from the Main PIC to the transceiver. The Reset PIC monitors satellite time and can initiate a system reboot, including a self-reset function. FAB PIC records the status of the battery and solar cells. The system includes four flash memory units with distinct roles. The main flash memory stores HK data and scheduled commands. Shared flash memory 1 is used for data exchange between the Main PIC and the COM PIC. Shared flash memory 2 facilitates data transfer between the Main PIC and the mission payload. The COM flash memory is dedicated to downlink operations; it allows data to be preloaded before the satellite enters an operational zone, thereby enabling efficient data transmission during limited communication windows.

section: 4.2 Introduction of the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 2 introduction of the birds bus system
text: The communication system (COM), operating in the UHF band, integrates both transmitter and receiver functions. It receives signals from the ground station and transmits downlink data accordingly. Deployment switches are included to keep the satellite powered off while it remains inside the deployment pod. Once released into space, the system is automatically activated. The kill switch is designed to sever the connection between the solar cells and the battery, halting the charging process. Once the battery is depleted, this mechanism ensures that the satellite remains permanently powered off.

section: 4.2 Introduction of the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 2 introduction of the birds bus system
text: For the case study, the mission payload was assumed to include a camera module (CAM) and an attitude determination and control system (ADCS) as shown in Fig. 9. The camera module consists of a camera, an MCU to process commands, flash memory for storing image data, and a power switch that controls the module's power supply. This

text: power switch is controlled by the Main PIC. The ADCS unit comprises an MCU, a gyroscope, a magnetometer, an actuator, and a dedicated power switch. Its primary function is to orient the satellite so that the camera lens can be directed toward the Earth.

section: 4.2 Introduction of the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 2 introduction of the birds bus system
text: In this case study, the four mission success levels were defined as listed in Table 2. In addition, a different color is assigned to each mission success level. The minimum success level is the transmission of a continuous wave (CW) signal. When the satellite is powered on, it transmits CW signals periodically. The reception of this signal is considered confirmation that the satellite is operational. The second success level is achieved when the satellite successfully downlinks complete HK data. The third level involves capturing images and transmitting the full-image data. At this level, the satellite takes photographs at random, and the image data are fully downlinked. The highest success level includes successful attitude control of the satellite, enabling

section: 4.2 Introduction of the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 2 introduction of the birds bus system
text: it to capture and downlink images of the Earth with intentional pointing accuracy.

This limitation is due to the inability of the DSM to capture interactions that extend beyond the boundaries of the satellite system. To address this, a ground segment (GS), consisting of a personal computer and a radio unit, was introduced to model the influence of external systems separately.

section: 4.3 Applying the mission assurance framework to the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 3 applying the mission assurance framework to the birds bus system
text: The visualization indicates that a substantial number of components and functions are required even to achieve the minimum mission success level. This finding suggests an imbalance in the distribution of functional requirements across components, revealing potential inefficiencies in the

section: 4.3 Applying the mission assurance framework to the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 3 applying the mission assurance framework to the birds bus system
text: current system architecture. These imbalanced elements can be classified into three groups. Group 1 involves the dispersion of functions. In this case, functions required for the same mission success level are located outside of their respective clusters and are scattered across interface points. Reducing the number of such interface functions can help lower the overall system complexity. Group 2 is characterized by large clusters containing many components and functions, which results in high degrees of cohesion and coupling. To reduce these values, the cluster should be subdivided appropriately, considering the number of subsystems involved since the number of subsystems also contributes to overall satellite system complexity. Group 3 includes components that serve multiple functions associated with different mission success levels. Reassigning these functions to separate components reduces the number of critical functions tied to the lowest success level, thereby increasing tolerance for partial failure. In this case study, Groups 2 and 3 overlap.

section: 4.3 Applying the mission assurance framework to the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 3 applying the mission assurance framework to the birds bus system
text: To address the functional imbalances identified in the original system architecture, design modifications were applied to the BIRDS bus system. For example, the cluster associated with the OBC and EPS was larger than any other group. To reduce its size, it was reclassified as Group 3, and selected components were reassigned to other groups. In addition, the Reset PIC was responsible for functions distributed across several levels, as shown in Group 2. To resolve this, its role was transferred to either the Main PIC or the COM PIC. On the basis of these two design considerations, a new board known as the COM board was developed, and the task of controlling power to the UHF module was assigned to the COM PIC. These modifications aimed to redistribute system functions, simplify interconnections, and reduce clustering intensity, thereby improving system modularity and lowering overall complexity.

section: 4.3 Applying the mission assurance framework to the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 3 applying the mission assurance framework to the birds bus system
text: Figure 11 presents the DSM after these modifications, and Fig. 12 illustrates the updated system block diagram. The revised DSM clearly shows enhanced clustering, reflecting a more logical grouping of functions and a reduced number of unnecessary interconnections. Group 1, corresponding to the FAB subsystem, includes current sensors for each external panel. By relocating these sensors to the respective external panels, clustering improved. Group 3 involves power distribution. In the current design, power from the battery and solar panels is first distributed into five lines and then further divided among subsystems and mission boards.

section: 4.3 Applying the mission assurance framework to the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 3 applying the mission assurance framework to the birds bus system
text: To simplify this, the updated design introduces a shared main power line connected to all units while maintaining individual power switches for each subsystem or mission board. Group 2 highlights the large cluster involving FAB, OBC, and EPS. These units are responsible for storing HK data, executing mission operation commands, maintaining the 24-h reset timer, and handling communication with the

section: 4.3 Applying the mission assurance framework to the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 3 applying the mission assurance framework to the birds bus system
text: ground station. The FAB board also includes switch circuits, such as DepSW-1 through DepSW-4, and a kill switch, which are required for compliance with satellite release safety reviews [48]. In the revised BIRDS bus system, these functionalities are grouped into a dedicated subsystem to form a single cohesive cluster.

section: 4.3 Applying the mission assurance framework to the BIRDS bus system
section_key: 4 3 applying the mission assurance framework to the birds bus system
text: The Reset PIC, which previously handled timekeeping and triggered a reboot every 24 h, was removed. Its function was reassigned to the COM PIC, which now activates and begins CW transmission immediately after satellite deployment. It also controls the power switches for the bus system, including the FAB PIC and Main PIC. In the prior configuration, the FAB PIC collected HK data, and the Main PIC stored it. In the updated design, these tasks are assigned solely to the FAB PIC for clearer role separation. The main flash memory, previously connected to the Main PIC, was relocated to the FAB PIC and can now be accessed by the COM PIC via a multiplexer. This flash memory is referred to as FAB flash memory. As a result, only the FAB PIC and COM PIC are required to downlink HK data, whereas the Main PIC is activated exclusively for mission operations. In the event of a multiplexer malfunction, the COM PIC would no longer be able to access the FAB flash memory, preventing the achievement of mission success at Level 2. However, this failure does not impact the criteria for minimum mission success. The Main PIC communicates with mission boards and the COM PIC using the CPLD, and the forwarding mission operation commands components, such as ADCS MCU and CAM MCU. This function is equivalent to the "Mission Boss" role in the current system. The Main PIC retains its own flash memory, which is used to transfer mission data from the payload side to the bus system.

This study proposed a DSM-based mission assurance framework specifically designed for academic CubeSats and demonstrated its effectiveness through a case study involving the BIRDS bus system. Unlike traditional complexity evaluation methods that rely on manually analyzing system block diagrams, the proposed framework allows for faster and more consistent assessment by utilizing the DSM. In addition to enabling quantitative evaluation, the framework

facilitates architectural optimization through DSM reconfiguration. Design improvements can be achieved by modifying the DSM rows and columns through merging, deletion, and reassignment, all while preserving critical mission functionality. In the BIRDS CubeSat case study, the DSM effectively revealed and resolved structural inefficiencies, such as disorganized interface functions, oversized clusters, and overlapping functional dependencies, across different mission success levels.

A key feature of the framework is the integration of mission success criteria into DSM analysis. The components were color-coded on the basis of their contribution to specific mission levels, allowing users to visualize critical architectural patterns and prioritize design changes accordingly.
Fig.12 System block diagram for the satellite system using the revised BIRDS bus system
Fig.13 Comparison of satellite system complexity before and after design modification across mission success levels.

However, important limitations were identified. Minimizing cohesion can encourage splitting functions into smaller clusters, which increases the number of interface functions and therefore raises coupling between subsystems. In contrast, minimizing coupling generally drives the design toward fewer interfaces, which increases cohesion by forming larger and more tightly connected clusters. For this reason, these two objectives should be balanced in DSM-based reconfiguration.

As the number of components increases, the computational burden increases rapidly, making it impractical to evaluate all possible configurations in large systems. In addition, even if exhaustive enumeration were computationally feasible, minimizing the proposed complexity metric alone would not necessarily yield the overall best design. For example, removing redundancy solely to reduce the complexity score could introduce a single point of failure and thereby conflict with mission-assurance requirements. In addition, extensive redundancy schemes commonly used in larger satellites are often infeasible for CubeSats due to size and resource constraints, and introducing redundancy can increase the computed satellite system complexity.

On this trade-off between adding redundancy and performing more extensive testing, Bouwmeester compared full subsystem redundancy with allocating comparable project resources to testing, and reported that improved

testing generally provides a greater reliability benefit for typical CubeSat mission durations, whereas redundancy may become advantageous primarily for very long missions [49]. This study contributes to improving testability and reliability by reducing system complexity.

In this study, the proposed complexity metric is used as a system-architecture-level indicator of the satellite's ability to achieve its intended mission functions as designed. This metric is complementary to conventional reliability and risk assessments based on component failure probabilities. Therefore, design decisions should consider both the complexity-based assessment and traditional risk measures, such as the risk priority number derived from failure probability, failure impact, and failure detectability. Although reducing the number of components and consolidating functions may lower the computed complexity, such changes can increase the consequences of malfunctions and potentially raise overall risk. For this reason, the DSM designer should examine changes in the risk matrix alongside changes in the complexity metrics. This study addressed this trade-off by calculating complexity separately for each mission success level.

Thus, the framework is most useful when applied to support design refinements and to serve as one guideline for determining system architecture. Following DSM-based reconfiguration, the system complexity was reduced across all mission success levels. The most notable improvement was observed at Level 4, where the complexity decreased by more than 80 percent. These findings indicate that the proposed framework can identify problematic areas and support concrete design actions to improve mission reliability.

Academic CubeSat missions have expanded rapidly in recent years. However, many of these projects continue to face low mission success rates. Owing to the rapid and cost-effective nature of CubeSat development, incorporating complex systems is often impractical, as they require considerable time and effort to analyze, detect, and test all potential failure modes. Therefore, satellite systems should be designed with simplicity as a guiding principle, and this simplicity should be quantitatively evaluated.

introduced the use of the DSM in the complexity evaluation process, developed a program to automate this process, visualized the importance of a component in the DSM by coloring, and optimized the satellite system through a case study based on the BIRDS bus system.

Although previous studies have proposed equations for assessing satellite system complexity, challenges remain. In particular, recalculating complexity after each design change is time-consuming because it depends heavily on system block diagrams. To overcome this limitation, this study

The program was validated by comparing its output with manual calculations. A case study using the BIRDS bus system demonstrated the practical application and effectiveness of the proposed approach. DSM analysis successfully identified and addressed structural complexity within the BIRDS platform, leading to an improved system design. A comparison between the original and updated systems confirmed a reduction in overall complexity. This case study highlights that DSM-based analysis can effectively detect structural inefficiencies and support meaningful design improvements while preserving mission functionality.

Several directions for future work are identified. First, the increasing adoption of artificial intelligence in system engineering provides an opportunity to enhance this framework. AI could be used to automate DSM-based optimization and generate innovative system architectures aligned with the complexity-reduction strategy presented in this research. Second, further validation through real-world implementation is needed. The Cucket Project at Kyutech, initiated in 2024, involves undergraduate students in the development of CubeSats and rockets [50]. This program could be used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in a practical academic environment. Such a demonstration would help assess the framework's effectiveness and explore its applicability beyond satellite systems. Moreover, explicitly representing redundancy in the criticality-level assignment is a promising direction for future work. For example, the failure of the solar cells on a single external panel may not affect mission success, and the minimum mission level can still be achieved. However, if two external panels fail simultaneously, the minimum mission level may no longer be satisfied. To extend the capability of the framework, k-out-of-n availability will be incorporated to identify the minimum required subset of redundant components for each mission success level. Lastly, the DSM model will be expanded to include mechanical and thermal information in addition to the electrical and communication connections considered in this case study. This expansion is expected to improve the adaptability of the framework to a wider range of systems and to better support discussions on more comprehensive mission assurance.

text: step in this method, the values in the DSM are converted into binary form, either "1" or "0". These binary values indicate the presence or absence of a functional relationship. Specifically, "1" represents the existence of a function, corresponding to a "true" response to the question of whether a function exists, whereas "0" indicates its absence, or "false". If a numerical value is entered into a cell, it signifies that a function exists, and the cell is assigned a value of "1". Conversely, if no function is present, the cell is assigned a value of "0". In addition, all diagonal cells, denoted as $ a_{ii} $ , are also assigned a value of "1", indicating that each component has a function associated with itself. This plays an important role in connecting the input and output features to identify functional reachability. This step is equivalent to adding the identity matrix to the original binary matrix. It is represented by the matrix P in Fig. 15.

Abstract—The growing adoption of nanosatellites has significantly expanded access to space-based experimentation and education. However, early-stage CubeSat design and mission conceptualization remain challenging for students and first-time developers because of fragmented tools and steep learning curves. This paper presents NanoSatPlay, an AI-enabled, browser-based platform that unifies CubeSat design, configuration, orbit visualization, and intelligent design guidance within a single interactive environment. The system integrates a visual component-based satellite designer, a real-time three-dimensional orbit simulator, and a generative AI assistant that provides subsystem-level feedback and contextual learning support. By lowering technical barriers and emphasizing visual and experiential learning, NanoSatPlay enables rapid prototyping, systems-level understanding, and effective STEM education. The architecture, core features, and educational benefits of the platform are discussed, demonstrating its potential to democratize nanosatellite engineering.
Keywords—AI, CubeSat, NanoSat, Engineering Education, STEM, AI in Design, Orbit Simulation, Integrated Development Environment (IDE), Space Technology.

CubeSats have reduced the cost and complexity of space access through standardized form factors, enabling widespread academic and educational participation. Despite these advances, CubeSat education typically relies on multiple disconnected tools for design, simulation, and analysis, limiting systems-level learning $ ^{[10]} $ Mastery of software often outweighs understanding of engineering principles. Recent developments in generative artificial intelligence provide opportunities to simplify this workflow through adaptive guidance and integrated reasoning. NanoSatPlay addresses this need by offering a unified, web-based platform focused on accessibility, visual interaction, and AI-assisted learning.
NanoSatPlay is implemented as a platform-independent web application. The front end is built using React and Next.js, with Three.js enabling interactive 3D visualization $ ^{[10]} $ .
Fig. 1. High-level architecture of the NanoSatPlay platform, showing the interconnected core modules.

AI-driven analysis and recommendations are powered by a Genkitbased backend. The system integrates four core modules: a CubeSat Designer, an Orbit Simulator, AI Design Assistant and AI enabled learning/assessment. All modules share a common data model, allowing real-time propagation of design changes across visualization, simulation, and AI feedback layers.

The CubeSat Designer offers a component-driven 3D interface for satellite assembly. Users select a standard CubeSat form factor (e.g., 1U or 3U) and populate it using a predefined library of subsystems including solar panels, batteries, antennas, sensors, and onboard electronics $ ^{[5]} $ . The system continuously updates mass and power budgets and verifies compliance with platform constraints. This immediate feedback supports rapid experimentation while reinforcing key engineering trade-offs $ ^{[6]} $ .

The AI Design Assistant evaluates mission objectives and system configurations to assess feasibility and identify subsystem-level issues. Feedback is structured across major subsystems, including power, communication, and payload.
The assistant also recommends design improvements and connects users to relevant learning resources, enabling just-in-time, contextual instruction.
Fig. 2. The visual interface of the CubeSat Designer module developed.

section: C. Orbit Simulation and Mission Visualization
section_key: c orbit simulation and mission visualization
text: The Orbit Simulator provides real-time visualization of CubeSat motion around Earth. Users define key orbital parameters such as altitude and inclination and observe their effects on satellite trajectories through an interactive 3D environment. An AI-assisted visualization layer supplements the simulation by generating concise mission descriptions and representative imagery, translating orbital mechanics concepts into intuitive visual form.

By consolidating design, simulation, and guidance into a single browser-based tool, NanoSatPlay significantly lowers barriers to CubeSat education. The integrated workflow encourages systems thinking by making subsystem interactions immediately visible. Rapid iteration further accelerates experiential learning in classroom and remote settings.
The benefits of an integrated platform become clear when compared to the traditional, disjointed toolchain commonly used in CubeSat development. Table I provides a direct comparison of key features.

The platform is built for rapid prototyping. Figure 6 shows the iterative CubeSat design improvement with the help of AI Design Assistant reduces time, cost and improves efficiency in launching to space. A student can conceptualize a mission, assemble a preliminary design, simulate its orbit, and get AI feedback in a single session. This ability to quickly iterate and test ideas is a powerful learning tool that encourages experimentation and reinforces concepts through trial and error.

section_key: c contextual and on demand learning
text: The AI Assistant and integrated tutorials provide knowledge at the moment of need. Instead of requiring students to front-load vast amounts of theoretical knowledge, NanoSatPlay allows them to learn in context. The interactive Tutorials consist of Rich and Interactive Tutorials designed and developed by the Subject Matter Experts. It covers learning for Beginner, Intermediate and Advance topics. For example, if a user's design for an imaging mission lacks

section_key: c contextual and on demand learning
text: a sufficiently high-data-rate antenna, the AI can explain the issue and suggest relevant components and tutorials on communication systems.

While the NanoSatPlay Orbit Simulator uses optimized trigonometric calculations for a fluid, real-time 3D visualization suitable for web browsers, its conceptual foundation is rooted in the core principles of astrodynamics. A high-fidelity simulation of a CubeSat's orbit is governed by the two-body problem, which is derived from Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation and his Second Law of Motion. The fundamental vector differential equation of motion is:
$$ \mathrm {d} ^ {2} \mathbf {r} / \mathrm {d t} ^ {2} = - \left(\mathrm {G} ^ {*} \mathrm {M} / \mathrm {r} ^ {3}\right) ^ {*} \mathbf {r} $$
r is the position vector of the CubeSat relative to the Earth's center of mass, r is the magnitude of the position vector r. -
G is the universal Grav, constant $ \approx 6. 6 7 4 \times1 0^{-1 1} \mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{kg}^{2}。 $
M is the mass of the Earth $ (\approx 5.972\times 10^{24}\mathrm{kg}) $

This equation states that the satellite's acceleration (the second derivative of its position, $ \mathrm{d}^{2}\mathbf{r} / \mathrm{d}t^{2} $ ) is directly proportional to its position vector and inversely proportional to the cube of its distance from the Earth's center.

NanoSatPlay demonstrates how AI-enabled web platforms can streamline nanosatellite education by unifying design, simulation, and intelligent assistance. The platform enables rapid conceptualization while promoting practical understanding of space systems engineering. Future work will expand subsystem fidelity and mission-level analysis capabilities.

Architecture variability modeling
Architecture generation
Product line engineering

The design of a Cyber-Physical System (CPS) presents significant challenges due to a vast configuration space and intensive dependencies among subsystems. Each subsystem requires careful selection and precise sizing of components from diverse hardware product lines to meet specific functional and performance requirements. This complexity increases as designers must balance objectives and constraints while accounting for the cascading effects of decisions across interconnected subsystems, highlighting how a small change in one area can greatly affect the overall system function and performance. However, there is limited research developing an automated model-based framework with the aim to address both challenges at once: architecture variability modeling and design evaluation of a CPS. Therefore, we propose a framework that integrates a novel variability-aware modeling methodology using the function-to-form concept, i.e., Architecture Design Space Graph (ADSG), with a numerical domain-dependency modeling named Multidisciplinary Design Optimization (MDO). The functional framework is then demonstrated through a use case of CubeSat design process, including the automated generation of architecture instances and numerical design space exploration. The framework has the potential to be implemented to other CPS as it provides generic building blocks in the form of an architecture modeler, generator, translator, and optimizer by leveraging the combination of ADSG and MDO.

The design process of a Cyber-Physical System (CPS) comprises three phases: conceptual, preliminary, and detailed. During the conceptual phase, the Top Level Requirements (TLRs) of CPS are defined, covering system objectives, structural limits, constraints of electrical properties, as well as the concept of operations in which the system is expected to function. In brief, this phase has a purpose to identify highlevel functional requirements (Chudoba and Heinze, 2010). Once the conceptual design phase has been conducted, the preliminary design phase is the continuation where the architecture of the CPS is defined. The system architecture describes the components that build the system and how these components interact to each other, fulfill the functional requirements, and consequently achieve the system's objectives (Crawley et al., 2015). This phase also includes the activity to quantitatively predict the system's size and performance. Subsequently, the engineers specify the more accurate design, a ready-to-manufacture system, and simulate the real behavior of CPS during the detailed design phase. However, the scope of our research is in the conceptual and preliminary design phase.

The conceptual and preliminary design phases are responsible for up to 70% of the total cost in a design process (Camarda et al., 2010). This is due to the presence of a multi-stage and multi-disciplinary nature in both phases. The multi-stage nature of the process covers the definition of high-level CPS requirements (i.e., functional and non-functional), derivation and selection of functional architectures, until low-level early evaluation of numerical properties (Neureiter and Binder, 2022). Moreover, the process is iterative, i.e., not sequential, which makes the design duration uncertain. On the other hand, the CPS design process is multi-discipline that means it features numerous subsystems and components with various of functionalities with tight cyber and physical dependencies.

The multi-disciplinary characteristic is rooted from variability of CPS architecture that can be categorized into several groups. Based on the existing literature, the variability spread over the subsystem functionalities, components selection, and their operational concepts: physical, cyber, contextual, and temporal (Arrieta et al., 2015; Krüger et al., 2017). On the physical aspect, components may vary in shapes, weights, materials, and mechanical interfaces. The cyber variability is

addressed to variation in power, memory, software modules, control logic, and scheduling strategies. The contextual aspect covers how systems adapt differently under a dynamic operational environment and user scenarios (Wijaya et al., 2025). Meanwhile, the temporal variability is defined as the change of CPS configurations over its runtime. Another classification of CPS variability includes cardinality attribute, topology, and type (Behjati et al., 2013). These taxonomies reinforce the position CPS as a variability-intensive system not only at component level, but also the interconnections and non-linearity between its features. Despite the vast types of variability, the current research focuses on functional and component aspects of CPSs.

To manage functional and component variability during the CPSs' conceptual and preliminary design process, some efforts have been identified. Addressing both cyber and physical variability, several studies describe modeling and simulation research on various CPS, such as automotive (Suri et al., 2021) and industrial robot digital twin (Zhang et al., 2023). For physical variability, some research were conducted with use cases in stereoscopic camera (Leserf et al., 2015), space robotic system (Chhaniyara et al., 2011), and CubeSat (Spangelo et al., 2013). They model the variability of mechanical elements and their interactions during operation. On a higher or architectural level, the CPS variability were also shown in designing a CubeSat by incorporating modeling of components, subsystems, and parametric properties (Nardi et al., 2025). They implement various ways of modeling the CPS architectures, which converge around the use of a model-based approach.

Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE), instead of documentbased, has emerged as an effective methodology to describe and validate a system, particularly the functional and component variability of CPS (Friedenthal et al., 2007; Forlingieri, 2022). It facilitates the traceability of system requirements during its entire design phases. Moreover, its link with Product Line Engineering (PLE) is proven to be beneficial in terms of project delivery duration and cost minimization (Carroll and Malins, 2016; Hause and Hummell, 2019; Chalé Góngora et al., 2014). Although the known advantages, the model-based approach requires extensions to automatically generate valid architectures (i.e., dependencies between functions and components) and evaluate their numerical properties during preliminary design phase (Weilkiens et al., 2025; Epp et al., 2024). Multiple studies have been performed in this area, such as by extending the model-based approach capability with constraint programming of components (Kerzhner and Paredis, 2010), multi-objective optimization (Leserf et al., 2019), and evolutionary algorithm for optimization (Arifin et al., 2018) (see Table 1 for more details).

From those studies, we identify two challenges in designing CPS with extensive variability on using a model-based approach: managing functional & components variability in a CPS architecture (Challenge 1) and modeling the sizing variability of CPS components (Challenge 2). Those 2 challenges will be elaborated in Section 2. In Section 3, we show the related work in this research area and propose our research contributions. The contributions are translated from the challenges and related work aforementioned. In summary, they are threefold: (1) Development of function-to-form concept using Architecture Design Space Graph (ADSG) to manage CPS architecture variability (addressing Challenge 1); (2) Modeling of numerical evaluation based on domain-dependency concept using Multidisciplinary Design Optimization (MDO) for CPS component sizing (addressing Challenge 2); and (3) Use case of CubeSat design that comprises architecture variability and sizing models. The first two contributions are linked to form an automated model-based framework, which is demonstrated through the third contribution. Afterwards, the methodologies and tools for the framework are explained in Section 4. Section 5 demonstrates the third contribution thoroughly via case studies. Section 6 and discuss generalizability and threat to validity of our contributions. Section 7 and describe potential research directions and conclude our research.

section_key: 2 challenges in designing cyber physical systems
text: As aforementioned, the complexity of the CPS design process presents 2 challenges on managing and modeling variability that are explained further in the following paragraphs.

section_key: 2 challenges in designing cyber physical systems
text: Challenge 1 is managing functional & components variability in a CPS architecture. One of the core challenges in CPS design is mapping functional requirements to appropriate components among several alternatives. This variability in function-to-form mapping provides design flexibility but also creates a complex design landscape. These challenges fall under categories of variability of topology and cardinality types in physical and cyber levels (Arrieta et al., 2015). Selecting a component in a CPS architecture involves evaluating a range of tradeoffs, such as functional compatibility with other components of the same subsystem or with other subsystems. For example, in autonomous vehicles, multiple sensor types (e.g., LIDAR, radar, cameras) can be used for fulfilling the same architectural function, which is obstacle detection (D'Ambrosio and Soremekun, 2017). On the other hand, each has distinct attributes for power consumption, data processing needs, and environmental adaptability that might or might not work alongside other components.

section_key: 2 challenges in designing cyber physical systems
text: The requirements for functional and component compatibility make the design choices during the conceptual and preliminary design phases critical. A single change, such as selecting a higher-power camera, can induce changes to the selection of the embedded processor, data bus, power management unit, and even the physical part of the architecture. These ripple effects of component selection are especially pronounced in systems with tight constraints on energy, thermal loads, or physical space (e.g. drones, medical implants, or smart industrial controllers) (Klesh et al., 2012; Bradley and Atkins, 2015). This highlights the need for a systematic and automated methodology to appropriately select components that fulfill functional requirements, thus forming fully worked CPS architectures.

section_key: 2 challenges in designing cyber physical systems
text: Once the appropriate components corresponding to functional requirements are selected, Challenge 2 arises: modeling the sizing variability of CPS components. CPS design often involves custom-sized components that belong to continuous or parametric product lines. Unlike purely discrete configurations, many hardware elements are particularly sized and optimized according to the specific performance requirements. Examples of structurally variable components in CPS include motors with adjustable casing dimensions, shaft diameters, and coil winding configurations; batteries with different cell capacities; heat exchangers with scalable surface area, fin density, and internal channel geometries; antennas with configurable apertures and curvature profiles; and solar panels with variable panel areas and layered material density.

section_key: 2 challenges in designing cyber physical systems
text: All of these continuous component properties/attributes influence and are influenced by other parts of the CPS. Selecting a larger battery to support extended operation increases system mass, requiring a stronger chassis and more powerful motors, which then feed back into energy demand and heat generation. These decisions are tightly coupled and often governed by non-linear constraints and governing equations, making manual exploration or decoupled analytic analysis inadequate.

section_key: 2 challenges in designing cyber physical systems
text: parametric dependencies require an integrated numerical modeling and optimization methodology that can handle multi-discipline evaluation. The failure to model these aspects would impact on designing a suboptimal CPS. Therefore, a methodology to thoroughly explore the numerical design space is required.
In relation to both challenges, we present related work to identify their similarities and differences to current work. We selected the

papers by the common denominators among them, which are proposing the use of a model-based approach to handle architecture variability for CPS during conceptual and/or preliminary design phases (Challenge 1). The aim is to assess their capability on generated or configured CPS architectures in an automated way. Besides that, they integrated extension tools on top of the model-based framework to evaluate and explore the performances of their respective CPS with subject to variability (Challenge 2). Table 1 describes the comparison into several main categories: how did they formalize CPS using a model-based

approach, what variability types were handled, what the capabilities of extension tools are, their configurability and use cases. This list of papers is by no means exhaustive, as we sampled from some papers that are representative in this domain and cover a wide range of CPS use cases.

The first category is the formalization of CPS using a model-based approach. It is highly dependent on the modeling objectives. Therefore, we put two sub-categories here, whether they developed the models using function-to-form and/or requirements formalization. Function-to-form is an approach where functions of a system are mapped into its logical or physical fulfillment (Bussemaker et al., 2020). On the other hand, requirements formalization is a building block in MBSE to make stakeholder requirements traceable until product specifications (Henderson and Salado, 2021; Vidal and Villota, 2018). From these references, we found that requirements formalization is a common practice in this research area. Meanwhile, the function-to-form concept is still rarely developed, where there are only a few papers built their model based on this concept (Chhaniyara et al., 2011; Parant et al., 2023).

As one of our focuses, we observed that variability types might fall under multiple classifications in existing literature. Hence, we classify them into three sub-categories: CPS-wise, modeling level, and discrete/continuous. CPS-wise sub-category is to identify the variability present in CPS as a real product [Arrieta et al., 2015]. These papers also present variability in modeling level: parametric, component, architecture levels, or a combination of them. Parametric variability means numerical attributes of a CPS are varied [Balestrini-Robinson et al., 2015; Spyropoulos and Baras, 2013]. Component variability model choices for different components, but within the same product lines [Kerzhner and Paredis, 2010; Arifin et al., 2018]. Architecture variability facilitates different logical and/or physical fulfillment from cardinality of functional requirements. An example for architecture variability is a function to "provide power" that can be fulfilled by either a battery, a solar panel, or both.

We also assessed the capabilities of extension tools to numerically evaluate the variability of CPS, e.g., design space exploration and its trade-off study. This assessment covers types of numerical evaluation, domain-dependency, and optimization types. Numerical evaluation describes the types of numerical models that were built in extension tools, e.g., a class of analytical equations. It is also to identify what models are used for, for example, the component sizing, constraint aggregation, or multi-physics simulation. Meanwhile, the domain-dependency subcategory asks whether formulation of a numerical model affects the behavior of others and vice versa; whether variables are shared among blocks in both directions. We also looked for optimization types that were used in each existing work. Configurability and use cases are also important aspects of a model-based approach and its extension tools. In this case, we translate configurability into a question of "Is the framework capable of automatically generating valid architectures?" It means whether the framework has the capability to automatically prune invalid configurations with subject to variability at architecture level. As listed in Table 1, there is a limited methodology for this purpose.

Based on the list of related work and research challenges, we propose the research contributions of this paper as follows. The processes of Contribution 1 and 2 are then wrapped as an automated model-based framework for evaluating variability in CPS. Here, the "automated" means the framework is able to generate valid CPS architectures and evaluate their numerical performances automatically.

- Development of function-to-form concept using ADSG to manage CPS architecture variability (Contribution 1, to address Challenge 1). By utilizing Architecture Design and Optimization Reasoning Environment (ADORE) as an architecture modeler and generator (see Section 4), it enables automated generation of valid architecture instances to increase the configurability degree of

CPS modeling (Bussemaker et al., 2020, 2023). This contribution also accommodates broader implementation of CPS variability, such as at parametric, component, and architecture levels. This contribution is decomposed into an architecture modeler and generator (see Section 4).

- Modeling of numerical evaluation based on the domain-dependency concept using MDO (Contribution 2, to address Challenge 2). As an extension to Contribution 1, we model a two-way numerical coupling between subsystems, which is barely developed in the literature that we studied in Table 1 (Martins and Lambe, 2013). Two-way coupling means properties of Subsystem A have direct influences on properties of Subsystem B and vice versa. We leverage a Python package for MDO by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) called OpenMDAO (Gray et al., 2019). Through this model, the numerical exploration in the design space is done unbiased, without missing any valid architectures. In the context of an automated framework, this contribution is positioned as an architecture optimizer (see Section 4).

- A use case of our framework for CubeSat design that handles architecture variability and sizing models (Contribution 3). Through this case, we demonstrate that the framework is able to manage both physical and cyber parts of CubeSat variability and evaluate the numerical properties. As shown in Table 1, only one study addresses both cyber and physical parts of CubeSat (Nardi et al., 2025), let alone its numerical evaluation.

Despite the aforementioned contributions, our study has some limitations compared to the related work. Formalization of requirements is outside the scope of this paper as we focus on developing a modelbased of CPS by a function-to-form approach. Besides that, we perform a single-objective optimization for design space exploration in the extension tool. Many advanced works have been implementing multi-objective optimization and evolutionary algorithms (Arifin et al., 2018).

In this section, we explain in detail how Contribution 1 and 2 are translated into an automated model-based framework for managing and evaluating CPS variability. As shown in Fig.1, the framework consists of four building blocks: architecture modeler, generator, translator, and optimizer. All blocks are built by following a model-based approach, i.e., defining a component and its attributes as a model that is reused, and the associated attributes can be extracted. The architecture modeler and generator are the embodiment of Contribution 1, while the architecture optimizer delivers the purposes of Contribution 2. Between each building block, there is an intermediate input/output that is produced in either an automated way or manual by the users based on the predecessor block. The definition of an automated framework here is the production of all intermediate inputs/outputs that are automated, following the manually pre-constructed building blocks, leveraging a model-based transformation approach. The automated and manual inputs/outputs generation are denoted by the symbols of computers and human respectively in Fig.1. As an instance, the List of Functions, Components, QOIs need to be provided in a manual way by some experts. The Architecture Sizing Models require some modeling efforts by users before they can be executed automatically by computer. Meanwhile, the rest of the inputs/outputs are able to be entirely generated by computer, as they are the parts of the added value of the proposed framework which is the automation aspect. The methodologies and tools for all building blocks are discussed in the following subsections.

To address the first contribution, we leverage ADSG as a variabilityaware formalism to model the CPS architecture through the functionto-form concept. ADSG provides a graph-based approach that directly
Fig. 1. Workflow of the automated framework with the respective tools and running examples.

represents variability and captures the intricate dependencies characteristic of CPS architecture that has been successfully applied in fields such as aeronautics (Bussemaker et al., 2021). The ADSG formalism maps functions (FUN) and components (COMP) as nodes, with edges representing (possibly many-to-many) fulfillment relationships between them. This structure allows each function to be fulfilled by a single or multiple different components, and components to fulfill multiple functions, accurately reflecting the layered variability and dependencies in CPS architecture. In Fig. 2(a), Component 2 fulfills both Function 1 and Function 2, and acts as an input model from Component 4. Components (COMP) are further described by instances (INST), allowing for multiple instances of the same component within the architecture. Quantities of Interest (QOI) represent critical parameters that guide the optimization in the later phase 2(b). These include optimization objectives (OBJ), such as mass or manufacturing cost of a CPS, as well as attributes (ATTR) and design variables (DV).

The implementation of ADSG as a methodology is in ADORE, a webbased design space modeler. $ ^{1} $ The lists of FUNs, COMPs, QOIs, and their dependencies form a structured variability-intensive architecture called architecture design space (Fig. 2(a)). The system identification activities of collecting feasible functions & components, also decomposing & connecting them, are done manually beforehand by the users. The architecture design space is an output of the architecture modeler and will be processed further using the architecture generator.

The architecture generator plays a role in automated reasoning of the CPS architecture design space (Contribution 1). It uses the ADSG design space to filter out infeasible configurations and generate valid architecture instances only (Crawley et al., 2015; Haberfellner et al., 2019; Madni and Madni, 2018). By transforming the ADSG design space into a mixed-integer mathematical problem, the generator can produce fully configured architectures based on specific engineering choices, providing flexibility in the design process (Bussemaker et al., 2024). The core task of the generator is to solve the architecture satisfiability problem, which involves matching system functions with suitable components while adhering to predefined constraints that meet functional requirements. This process ensures that only valid and feasible architectural configurations are considered.
ADORE, as a tool for generating architecture, is capable to automatically reason about the relations between nodes and edges in the

architecture design space. For reasoning the function-to-form mapping, it follows the OR and XOR logical relations. Taking same approach as in software product lines (SPL) implementation, OR means selecting one or more alternatives of form and XOR implies on selecting only one form (She et al., 2011). As illustrated in Fig. 2, the task of ADORE is solving the XOR decision from Function 1 to Component 1 and Component 2 (modeled through direct links), also to solve the OR choice between Component 2 and Component 3 for Function 2 (modeled through both direct links and MULTI for multi-fulfillment). Once all decisions have been reasoned, the architecture design space results in 12 unique architecture instances. For instance, Fig. 3 illustrates two generated architecture instances from the previously introduced architecture design space. Afterwards, each architecture instance is automatically encoded into a design vector, which consists of integers for component selections and real numbers for QOIs.

The architecture translator is a crucial building block to enable the automated aspect of the proposed framework. It creates connections between the architecture generator and the architecture optimizer. From the architecture generator, it takes an architecture instance, derived from the ADSG, and translates it into detailed sizing models composed of multiple CPS sizing modules. The architecture translator leverages a model-to-model transformation principle (Bussemaker et al., 2022). The translation is achieved through the Class Factory Evaluator (CFE) tool (Bussemaker et al., 2023). The CFE maps the components and their numerical attributes in the architecture instances into sizing models. This process ensures that the selected components and their parameters by the architecture generator are linked to corresponding sizing equations and metrics into architecture optimizer.

In this process by CFE, each ADSG component (COMP) is mapped to an MDO class. At the same time, their CPS parameters are converted into MDO design variables. Certain quantities of interest (QOI) instantiated from the ADSG, such as mass, power, and other performance metrics, are designated as optimization objectives (OBJ), guiding the MDO process towards achieving the best possible configuration. In parallel, functional requirements and compatibility constraints, defined within the ADSG, are translated into design constraints within the MDO model. These constraints ensure that all functional and compatibility requirements are met throughout the optimization process. By aligning the architecture with the MDO framework in this structured manner, the architecture translator provides a clear path for performing detailed optimization, capturing the interactions between various components and their parameters, and enabling a robust, optimized CPS design.

The architecture optimizer has a purpose to optimizing the component parameters within architecture instances, which belongs to Contribution 2. This involves balancing multiple, often conflicting CPS performance requirements—such as minimizing power consumption, reducing mass, and maximizing data throughput. The optimizer transforms preliminary architecture instances into fully sized architectures by leveraging sizing models that calculate component dimensions. The sizing models need to be coded manually with the appropriate functions' names and inputs/outputs definition, so that they can make automated links with the architecture translator, as well as produce architecture trade space.

CPS design optimization problems are inherently multidisciplinary as explained in Section 1, due to the interactions between subsystems like power, thermal, structural, and communication. This makes the problem particularly suited for MDO methodology, which provides an integrated approach for solving tightly dependent disciplines or domains (i.e., CPS subsystems in this case) to optimize a system (Martins and Lambe, 2013). In the context of CPS design, MDO is used to evaluate the design space as a whole. Each sizing model of the

CPS component is linked through design variables and constraints that form the broader optimization problem (Martins and Ning, 2021). The formulation of the MDO problem is often represented via eXtended Design Structure Matrix (XDSM), as seen in Fig. 4 $ ^{2} $ (Lambe and Martins, 2012). This diagram serves as a visual representation of an MDO problem formulation involving multiple disciplines (e.g., Discipline1 and Discipline2), objective function $ (f) $ , constraints (e.g., $ g_{1} $ and $ g_{2} $ ), and design variables (e.g., x and $ z_{1} $ ).

This MDO problem can be solved using various tools, such as an open-source Python package called OpenMDAO (Gray et al., 2019). The optimization process within OpenMDAO from that example is to find the optimal values for the design variables that minimize the objective function while satisfying the constraints of the system. Gradient-based methods are commonly used to solve such optimization problems, as they allow efficient exploration of a continuous design space. The result are fully sized and optimized CPS architectures in a single trade space for properties comparison.
