The Apollo 11 lunar descent [1] highlighted the critical role of fault-tolerant real-time software in spaceflight. When the Apollo Guidance Computer encountered 1201 and 1202 alarms - signals of "executive overflow" from excessive processing demands - it employed priority scheduling to perform a soft reboot. This mechanism shed nonessential tasks while preserving guidance and control functions, enabling the mission to continue safely. Far from a

simple safe mode, this was a purposeful, real-time recovery strategy engineered for survival. Today's CubeSats, with their increasing autonomy and mission complexity, demand similarly robust approaches, which MBSE can help systematically design and verify.

Over time, various models have emerged in software engineering to guide the planning, implementation, and testing of software systems. The origins of the waterfall model can be traced back to 1970, when it was introduced by Winston W. Royce [2]. In the following decades, the linear execution of the System Development Life Cycle became increasingly popular. Even in its original conception, the weaknesses of late-stage testing and potential approaches to mitigate these issues were already discussed. The model is divided into the following phases:
1. Requirements Analysis and Specification
2. Design
3. Implementation and Unit Testing
4. Integration and System Testing
5. Operation and Maintenance
This approach to software development is strictly linear, with all specifications and requirements fixed from the outset. Only limited adjustments are possible in later stages of the process.

Due to rapidly changing requirements and shorter development cycles, agile approaches have emerged and have since become established in many industries. Whether Extreme Programming [3], Feature-Driven Development [4], Dynamic Systems Development [5], or Adaptive Software Development [6], all are founded on the twelve principles of the Agile Manifesto [7] introduced in 2001. These principles emphasize delivering value to the customer through iterative development, close collaboration, and the ability to adapt quickly to change. They also stress the importance of delivering working software frequently, ensuring that stakeholders can review progress and provide feedback at regular intervals. The core purpose of agile methods is to create flexible, customer-focused processes that respond effectively to evolving needs, enabling teams to deliver high-quality software in a timely and sustainable manner.

The UWE-5 is a CubeSat project whose objective is the demonstration of a K-/KA-band communications payload. The development teams are comprised of three different working groups at different universities, namely the Embedded Systems and Sensors for Earth Observation (ESSEO) group at the Julius-Maximilians- Universität Würzburg, the Satellite Communications and Radar Systems chair at the Julius-Maximilians- Universität Würzburg, and the Electronic Systems and Sensors chair at Brandenburgische Technische Universität Cottbus. The mission consists of two 3U CubeSats operating in Low Earth Orbit. The project is supported by the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and estimated to launch in 2027.
The UWE-5 satellites can be considered real-time systems. According to [8]

"A real-time computer system is a computer system where the correctness of the system behaviour depends not only on the logical results of the computations but also on the physical time when these results are produced"

Real-time computer systems are found inside bigger systems, called real-time systems, whose state changes as a function of time. The moment in time at which a result must be completed by the real-time computer system is called a deadline. If the real-time system can tolerate missing deadlines, that is, if the result of the computer is

still useful after the time limit, then the deadline is considered "soft", and otherwise it is considered "firm". When a catastrophic consequence can result from missing a deadline, then the deadline is considered "hard". Therefore, a real-time computer system is referred to as a hard real-time computer system or safety critical real-time computer system if it must meet at least one hard deadline. The spacecraft software must deal with real-world devices such as sensors and actuators in a parallel fashion [9]. This is the reason why a concurrent program design, which can be achieved by using a Real Time Operating System, makes the flight software faithfully represent the nature of the system.

However, the concurrent execution paradigm comes with relevant problems and debugging challenges, as it is not as straightforward to analyse compared to simpler sequential code execution. Moreover, since spacecraft are exposed to the harsh space environment, they often fall into unexpected scenarios that threaten mission success. Therefore, Fault Detection, Isolation and Recovery (FDIR) mechanisms are designed and employed to mitigate the potential risks and ensure that the system fulfils its purpose.

section_key: 2 model based systems engineering for cubesats
text: In the context of the CubeSat project, the stakeholders are the various developer groups responsible for developing the different subsystems, writing the application code and designing the hardware. Particular attention is paid to the interfaces between the hardware and software, and to communication between the subsystems. The system's complexity arises from the required fault tolerance and the large number of processes that communicate with each other and control actions and reactions.

The reliability of the UWE-5 CubeSat depends on a well-structured software architecture that ensures efficient interaction between subsystems, robust task execution, and fault tolerance under resource constraints. This chapter outlines the design principles and mechanisms that enable these goals.
The system model of the UWE-5 project represents a complex interaction between two satellites, external applications, and internal subsystems (see Fig. 1).
Fig. 1 UWE-5 System Model Diagram

The project comprises at least five distinct systems and seven subsystems within the satellite, all of which must communicate with one another. The software architecture of each subsystem is uniform and independent of the underlying hardware. Fig. 2 illustrates

the system model of the onboard computer as an example. A shared library, KronOS, serves as middleware between the RTOS and the process logic. The interfaces between software layers are defined through well-specified APIs, and all available hardware interfaces are documented. Each subsystem is further divided into modules, where each module is dedicated to a specific task and provides an API to other software modules. The modules within the KronOS library are optional and can be included or excluded depending on system requirements. The system diagram clearly conveys which functionalities are enabled and available within the satellite's subsystems, without requiring a detailed examination of their internal implementations.
Fig. 2 UWE-5 System Model Diagram

Building upon the modular architecture and clearly defined interfaces, the execution logic is organized to ensure that critical functions are processed reliably and without interference from lower-priority operations. This is achieved through a structured task hierarchy, implemented using three priority levels, designed to balance system complexity with robust execution:

Tasks in this category are essential for the continuous and safe operation of the CubeSat. They must always run. If a task in this group fails, a backup strategy is immediately triggered to prevent cascading failures in interconnected subsystems. This strategy involves a redundant system operating in either hot or cold standby mode, which temporarily takes over until the primary system is fully restored.

This is the default priority level. Tasks in this group handle operations that are important for the standard functioning of the CubeSat and may impact other (sub)systems. In the event of a failure, the fallback strategy is a controlled shutdown and restart of the affected task.

Tasks at this level are non-critical and can be executed at any time. They have no direct impact on other (sub)systems. If a failure occurs, the task is terminated without being restarted. The corresponding backup strategy is a graceful exit only.

To keep the system manageable and maintain effective load balancing, no additional priority levels are introduced. While this model does not rely on formal schedulability analysis, it is conceptually aligned with the notion of robust priority assignment as defined in realtime systems literature [12]. Such policies aim to ensure that systems remain schedulable even under increased interference or degraded conditions - an essential consideration for fault-tolerant CubeSat software operating under constrained resources.

section_key: 3 2 real time capabilities and freertos integration
text: A Real-Time Operating System provides the deterministic behaviour that a critical system requires to meet hard deadlines. The design philosophy behind the UWE-5 embedded software strives to achieve welldefined layers that perform functionalities and/or services to the other layers. The mission code layer is separated from the RTOS layer using an Operating System Abstraction Layer (OSAL), which is composed of the well-known POSIX threading APIs (pthreads) [13]. A special layer, called the KronOS Task-Manager, extends the FreeRTOS scheduler with functionality for dynamic resource allocation, load balancing, and fault management. This component makes use of the POSIX interfaces for task management purposes and employs the useful mechanisms that FreeRTOS offers for detecting issues related to memory usage and erroneous conditions that could lead the system into a faulty state. At the bottom are the hardware platforms that run the software stack of the UWE-5 project. The Windows PC is used for direct interaction from the developers to the rest of the systems, the MSP430F5438A is the microcontroller of the On-Board Computer, and the ATSAMV71Q20CB is the microcontroller of the Attitude and Orbit Determination System. Fig. 3 shows the interactions between the KronOS software layers.

section_key: 3 2 real time capabilities and freertos integration
text: Fig. 3 KronOS Software Layers

Dynamic resources in the system include task-specific stack memory, available power from the EPS, and processor time. Each task receives its stack from a statically allocated heap managed by FreeRTOS. Power availability and power consumption are monitored to ensure stable operation. Processing time must be efficiently distributed to meet real-time requirements. The central component for managing these resources is the Task-Manager. By monitoring system conditions, the Task-Manager ensures safe and efficient use of memory, power, and compute time. In case of anomalies, it triggers appropriate fault-handling mechanisms to maintain system stability.

Before a new task can be created, the system must be in a stable state. The required stack size is specified during task creation by the initiating process. This value is typically an estimate based on prior testing, with an added safety margin. The decision process for task creation is shown in Fig. 4. There are three possible outcomes:
1. Sufficient resources are available - the task is scheduled immediately.
2. Insufficient resources - the system attempts to free memory and processing capacity by terminating lower-priority tasks.

3. Insufficient resources with no lower-priority tasks available - if the new task is non-critical, it is rejected. If it is critical and still cannot be scheduled, the system enters a non-runnable state. This scenario must be avoided through proper system design and testing to ensure that all critical tasks remain within the system's resource limits.
This resource-aware scheduling mechanism ensures that the system remains operational even under high load, while prioritizing critical tasks and preventing resource exhaustion.
Fig. 4 Load-Balancer flow during task

To incorporate power consumption into the loadbalancing process, the Task Manager receives regular external reports from the EPS. These reports include key parameters such as the current state of charge, overall power consumption, and charging current of the batteries. Within the Task Manager, trigger points are defined to respond to critical EPS values. These include short-term power consumption peaks as well as long-term, predictable events, such as estimated remaining operational time at current consumption rates. If a trigger point indicates a lack of power while only critical tasks are running, the system initiates a controlled shutdown to conserve energy. If non-critical tasks are still active, these are first moved to the suspended state before more drastic action is taken. Once sufficient power becomes available again, previously suspended tasks are resumed automatically. This mechanism, shown in Fig. 5, ensures that energy-critical situations are handled gracefully, maintaining essential system functionality while preventing instability.
Fig. 5 Load-Balancer flow during EPS report
Fault management is divided into two categories:
on components. These faults must be addressed both in software - using fault-tolerant algorithms - and in hardware - through the implementation of redundancy.
Hard faults are permanent hardware errors that may result from environmental influences or excessive stress

Soft faults, in contrast, are non-permanent and can be detected by monitoring system behaviour. Typical examples include memory corruption, stack overflows deadlocks, floating-point exceptions, and communication failures. An essential mechanism for handling such faults is the use of hardware watchdogs.

In the context of the UWE-5 project, both external hardware watchdogs on the processor boards and internal watchdogs built into the processors are employed. According to [14] a watchdog timeout should result in a hardware reset to ensure that the processor is correctly reinitialized. A simple program counter reset may not fully reinitialize the processor, potentially leaving the system in an unstable state. Therefore, both internal and external watchdogs must be served with regular heartbeat signals. The timeout duration must be configured appropriately for the system and use case. In the event of a timeout, the watchdog must bring the system back into a stable state and retain information useful for debugging the root cause of the failure. All watchdog-related tasks are handled by a dedicated Watchdog-Task, which is assigned the highest priority in the system.

In addition, each task is assigned an individual timeout that serves as an internal task watchdog. If a task stalls or becomes unresponsive, it is terminated by a dedicated health-check task (Fig. 6) and the allocated resources are released in a controlled manner.

The term Verification and Validation (V&V) in the context of software and system development refers to a structured process that ensures correctness, completeness, and compliance throughout the entire lifecycle. According to [15] it is defined as:

"The process of determining whether the requirements for a system or component are complete and correct, the products of each development phase fulfil the requirements or conditions imposed by the previous phase, and the final system or component complies with specified requirements."

Verification ensures that the system is being built correctly, i.e., each step of development meets its intended design and technical specifications. Validation, in contrast, ensures that the right system is being built one that meets the user needs and operational requirements.

The goal of verification is to detect design errors as early as possible during system development. In this context, the focus lies on ensuring design correctness and compliance with the specification. Within the RT-Thread framework, task scheduling and synchronization follow the POSIX threading model, where the execution of software is no longer defined by a simple linear main loop. Since only one thread can be executed at a time, the RTOS is responsible for managing processor time allocation and performing context switches as necessary. Consequently, the software design must be inherently thread-safe. MBSE provides a structured means to model such thread-safe architectures at the design stage. For instance, the transmitter module of the KronOS system (see Fig. 7) represents a critical component that can be invoked concurrently by multiple threads. To minimize memory usage, shared resources such as the transmission buffer must be protected by mutual exclusion mechanisms (mutexes). This ensures that multiple threads can interact with shared resources without leading to race conditions or data corruption. Previous work has shown that mutex scheduling under RT-Thread is effective in ensuring sequential and mutually exclusive access to shared resources, preventing issues such as data inconsistency and deadlocks [16]. A particular challenge arises in processes whose correctness can be compromised by context switches. The encoding and transmission of messages are such examples. To reduce memory requirements, messages are divided into smaller segments, which are encoded and transmitted sequentially until the complete message is delivered. If this sequence is interrupted and not protected by a mutex, message segments may become interleaved, resulting in undecodable or corrupted transmissions. To mitigate this risk, the communication channel must be locked for exclusive access by the active thread before transmission begins, thereby preserving message integrity.

Thus, a key benefit of MBSE lies in its ability to identify, at an early stage, which components of a system are vulnerable to concurrency issues such as thread preemption or interrupt handling. By employing formal verification within MBSE models, potential hazards can be detected more effectively during the design phase, significantly reducing debugging complexity in later implementation stages. This proactive approach not only increases system reliability but also shortens development cycles by addressing concurrency-related risks before they manifest in deployed software.
Fig. 7 Thread-safe Transmitter data flow

The Simulation-Driven Validation Tests are intended to validate the correct implementation of the system model and to reveal potential bugs and vulnerabilities in the design. A distinction is made between HIL and SIL tests. HIL tests aim to validate the integration of a system on actual hardware. Three types of test scenarios have been defined and conducted for the validation of failsafe mechanisms.

section: 1. Watchdog Response to Deadlock and Missed Heartbeats
section_key: 1 watchdog response to deadlock and missed heartbeats
text: To evaluate the watchdog implementation, a KronOS instance with a dedicated watchdog task is executed on the OBC. The OBC incorporates two external watchdogs with a timeout of 1.6~seconds, enabling hot-swapping to a redundant processor or power source. In parallel, the internal software

section: 1. Watchdog Response to Deadlock and Missed Heartbeats
section_key: 1 watchdog response to deadlock and missed heartbeats
text: watchdog of the MSP430 is configured with a timeout of 1~second. During testing, a deliberate deadlock is introduced in a secondary task. This condition consistently causes the software watchdog to trigger after the 1-second timeout, initiating a soft reset of the processor. The experiment thereby validates that deadlocks are reliably detected and resolved through the watchdog mechanism, ensuring bounded-time recovery and system availability.

section: 2. Fault injection (soft faults) to observe system response
section_key: 2 fault injection soft faults to observe system response
text: Tasks are created sequentially to deliberately trigger a stack overflow, a floating-point exception, and a null pointer exception. Each injected fault can lead to unpredictable behaviour. A commonly observed symptom during testing is that a task becomes unresponsive and fails to execute further code. Nevertheless, the scheduler continues to allocate CPU time to the task, potentially blocking other tasks. In all tested cases, the faulty tasks are cleaned up by the task timeout mechanism (see Fig. 6), and the resources are released. Depending on the affected priority, the appropriate recovery strategy is executed.

section: 3. Fault tolerance in handling of corrupted or incomplete messages
section_key: 3 fault tolerance in handling of corrupted or incomplete messages
text: An additional task simulates the reception of incorrectly encoded messages to evaluate the fault tolerance of the decoder. The experiment demonstrates that partially received or malformed messages are reliably discarded after a defined timeout. This timeout is configured according to the maximum transmission rate of the hardware channel and the maximum message length. By enforcing these bounds, the receiver buffer is freed in time to prevent denial-of-service conditions caused by buffer overflows.

The results demonstrate that combining Model-Based Systems Engineering with simulation-driven validation provides a systematic way to design and test fault-tolerant real-time software for CubeSats. Formal modelling exposes concurrency risks such as race conditions early in the development process, while SIL and HIL experiments confirm that watchdogs, fault injection handling, and message validation mechanisms can reliably recover from deadlocks, runtime faults, and corrupted inputs. Together, these techniques reduce reliance on late-stage debugging and instead enable
preventive fault management under strict memory and processing constraints.

These findings highlight that real-time resilience cannot be guaranteed by scheduling mechanisms alone. Additional layers of fault prevention and recovery are required to ensure continuous operation. MBSE contributes by clarifying complex task interactions and making these critical mechanisms traceable and verifiable at the design stage. This structured approach shows that reliability in nanosatellite software can be achieved without sacrificing modularity or maintainability, even under highly constrained conditions.

At the same time, the effectiveness of MBSE is bounded by the quality of the models. Poorly specified or incomplete models will not yield better implementations than conventional ad hoc approaches. Moreover, issues can only be identified if they are explicitly represented in the models, and if complexity is abstracted to a level that remains comprehensible for all stakeholders. Thus, while MBSE improves transparency and reduces integration risks, it does not replace engineering judgment.

Future work will focus on characterizing and mitigating new concurrency issues that arise from multithreading and unpredictable runtime behaviour. The framework will be applied to systems of higher complexity with additional subsystems to evaluate scalability. Finally, accumulated experience will be distilled into best practices and documentation of common pitfalls, providing practical guidance for future CubeSat and small satellite developments.

section: AI4CE - Building the infrastructure for AI-supported CubeSat generation > Abstract
section_key: ai4ce building the infrastructure for ai supported cubesat generation / abstract
text: Designing CubeSats increasingly requires navigating a rapidly growing, combinatorial design space created by standardised, commercial off-the-shelf components (COTS). AI4CE is an open-source project at the Technical University Darmstadt in cooperation with Parametry.ai that operationalises bottom-up system generation for CubeSats. In this paper, an initial architecture is described, together with a curated component database (108 parts across 23 component types in 8 sub-systems) and a set of evaluation functions by which component-, sub-system-, and system-level performances are scored in mission context. All entries in the component database are transcribed from manufacturer data sheets mapped by hand to a list of supported parameter names and SI units, since automated scraping was not found reliable. Four generation methods — random, brute-force, genetic optimiser, and deep reinforcement learning (DRL) — are integrated into a unified pipeline with consistent constraint handling, result storage, and comparison tooling. Source code and artefacts are made available at https://ai4ce.space.

Abstract—This work presents a tool based on Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) for automating the process of budget calculation - mass, volume, power, and energy - for CubeSat nanosatellites based on user input which can be iteratively finetuned to fit the CubeSat limitations. CubeSat is a standard that defines nanosatellites with a base unit (1U) measuring 10x10x10 and a maximum weight of up to 2 kg per 1U. They are cost-effective due to their use of commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) components. This modularity provides flexibility on component selection to conform to the standard constraints that are forced by budget calculation. Modularity is fundamental in systems engineering design, which adopts a holistic approach to create systems by integrating various components and considering their interactions. CubeSat follows this approach. Object Process Methodology (OPM) and Systems Modeling Language (SysML) are popular modeling languages for systems engineering. This work benefits from MBSE for nanosatellite budget calculation. Specifically, it uses OPM to conceptually model it, applies OPM's computational capabilities on the produced model to calculate its budgets using OPM's coding capabilities, and eventually visually simulates the model by OPM's execution feature.

CubeSats are a class of nanosatellite which were first developed in the late '90s and have become popular since the early 2000. CubeSats initial purpose was totally educational, but very soon it has become an industrial asset with a few thousands in orbit [1].

CubeSats design have to follow guidelines that are dictated by the standardization described in CubeSat Standards Rev. 14.1 [2]. According to this standard, a CubeSat adopts a standard size and form factor, with a unit defined as 'U'. This standard describes a range of 1U-12U CubeSats, where a 1U CubeSat is a 10 cm cube and a mass of up to 2 kg.
CubeSats missions are far from recording a great success,

as Venturini et al. [3] clearly articulated, "Amidst all the hype one fact tends to get overlooked: CubeSats do not have a great record of mission success." Specifically, they attribute CubeSat mission failures to the conceptual phase. Furthermore, the use of commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) products, design discrepancies, and insufficient testing are among the causes of CubeSat failures.

As CubeSats are modular in their nature, they are composed of many subsystems which are actually built using COTS products, and as such there would be many possible combinations of those products to build the underlying nanosatellite, and hence it is essential to examine these proposed options compliance with the CubeSat budget constraints: mass, volume, power, etc.

Due to its modular structure, a systems engineering approach for designing it is of significant importance, and a ModelBased Systems Engineering (MBSE) option is even much helpful when it comes to breaking down a complex system into smaller manageable parts and dealing with complexity. This approach fits CubeSat usage of COTS and make it easier to customize the underlying system.

Object-Process Methodology OPM ISO 19450 [4], [5], [6] is a model-based systems engineering (MBSE) approach and language that has many features which make it an ideal platform for developing a full-fledged solution to provide automation capabilities and overcome barriers set up traditional approaches that cause, as mentioned, failures. Specifically, OPM provides a succinct graphical notation for a minimal set of universal things—objects and processes—for modeling systems of all kinds in a single diagram kind, which translate on the fly to a subset of natural language. OPM has been extended with computational capabilities that can be attached to the modeled processes. Not only this but OPM has simulation feature that allows the visual execution of the underlying model including interaction with the modeler. In this work, we present an OPM-based budget calculation system model, which caters to process automation, making budget calculating and other related processes explicit, understandable, and usable by the community. In particular, this automation could be useful for rapidly screening combinations of candidate components and then using that screen to increase one's chances of selecting reliable, compatible components from which to build the nanosatellite.
In this section, we briefly describe the two topics needed to deeply understand this work: CubeSat budget calculating process and OPM as the modeling language and methodology applied to this process.
Figure 1: OPM entities: object (left), process (middle), and object states (right)—deployed, undeployed

Object Process Methodology (OPM) [5], [6] is a holistic conceptual modeling language and methodology for the design and development of complex systems. Applications of OPM range from satellite control software [7] to large, complex sociotechnical systems [8]. OPM basics are defined by ISO 19450, providing practitioners with a normative reference document that is common to all OPM users and enabling anyone to read and understand OPM models.

OPM captures and integrates the functional, structural, and procedural aspects of a system in a single unifying model, which is bimodal: models are expressed by both a graphical modality and a textual modality, catering to humans' dual channel processing [9]. The intuitive graphics is translated on the fly to a subset of natural language.

The graphical view consists of a set of hierarchically organized, interconnected, and cross-validated Object-Process Diagrams (OPDs). Each OPD combines all the structural and procedural system aspects and refines and extends the OPD at the level above it to add more details, providing for an inherent mechanism for complexity management and reduction. The hierarchical tree structure of the OPDs caters to a top-down approach: modeling the underlying system starts with a high-level, abstract OPD at level 0, called the System Diagram (SD), and more refined OPDs gradually expose finer details using refinement-abstraction mechanisms that include in-zooming (out-zooming) and unfolding (folding).

Figure 1 shows the only three OPM entities: a process (ellipse), an object (rectangle), and object state ("ountangle"). The same compact set of model elements, which includes entities (object, process, and state) and links between them, is the same throughout the entire OPD hierarchy, making all the OPDs self-similar in terms of the minimal set of concepts (and symbols) they use.

A subset of English (and of many other natural languages), called Object-Process Language (OPL), is a structured textual specification language that is generated on the fly in response to each modeler's semantically meaningful graphic operation. Figure 4 shows the textual representation of the model graphically described in Figure 5. For example, the last line describes the relation between the main process, Budget Calculating, and the out objects. The OPL sentence "Budget Calculating yields Component Selection, Height Budget, Mass Budget ..." states that the main process changes the Component Selection object and writes results into Height Budget, Mass Budget and others.

Objects and processes are called OPM things. Rectangles representing physical objects are shaded to distinguish them from informatical objects. Processes transform objects by creating them, consuming them, or changing their state. By OPM convention, process names use the gerund form, and thing (object, process) names are capitalized, while state names are not. Structural and procedural links graphically
Figure 2: Structural links - aggregation, exhibition, generalization, classification, and tagged links.

define relations among entities (objects, processes, and object states). Structural links, shown in Figure 2, connect objects to objects or processes to processes to describe the static-structural model aspects. The figure is a screenshot of OPCloud, a cloud-based OPM modeling platform [10], [11] showing the possible structural links when attempting to connect two objects, each with the OPL sentence which would be generated as a result of selecting that link. Procedural links, shown in Figure 3, are between an object and a process, and they are used to model the dynamic-procedural system aspects, explicating causalities within the system [12].

OPM copes with complexity via detail-level decomposition rather than aspect-oriented decomposition, which is the common way to handle complexity in other conceptual modeling languages [5]. OPM with its one kind of diagram that uses a small set of about 20 OPM elements, along with the parallel textual modality, makes it easy to create models and check them on the fly.

In OPM, refinement is conveniently and intuitively represented graphically by in-zooming, providing the capability to select a process and specify or inspect its constituent subprocesses. Unfolding is the second major refinement mechanism, where a specific object exposes its constituent refineables, i.e., parts, features (attributes and operations), specializations, and instances. Thus, the hierarchically organized set of OPDs are derived from each other in a tree structure using one of the following refinement-abstraction mechanisms: (1) unfolding and folding of structural hierarchies of things, primarily objects, (2) zooming into or out of the inner details of things, primarily processes, (3) state expressing and suppressing, and (4) dedicated model views—OPDs that emphasize certain aspects.

Every OPM model fact needs to be defined at least once, in any of the OPDs in the OPD set, in order for it to be true for the entire model. OPM models can be constructed using OPCloud [10], [11]the ISO 19450-compatible cloud-based software, which is preferable over the early OPM modeling software OPCAT [13], [14]. OPCloud provides an OPL specification - a description in a subset of English for the entire model or an OPL paragraph - a collection of OPL sentences for each OPD separately. It also provides built-in visual simulation engines to support model validation, verification, and testing, which is especially useful in visualizing various execution scenarios.

OPM complements the conceptual qualitative modeling by providing a quantitative counterpart. Specifically, a modeler can define an object or a process as informatical (computational) which means that an object can have a value and a process can be attached with computations. Computations could be based on predefined mathematical functions, userdefined functions in JavaScript or Python code, or external connection (e.g., MATLAB). Based on these two aspects, OPCloud allows animated execution, where the modeler can execute the model on the basis of informatical objects' values and computations attached to end processes. OPCloud provides the modeler many ways for input - values are entered directly into the objects, values are entered at the model runtime or randomly simulated according to a distribution function selected by the modeler. Not only this, but it also allows getting data from Excel and outputs data back there.

OPM's characteristics and capabilities that have been presented enable clear and concise modeling of complex processes and structures in the same and only diagram kind, facilitating cognitive integration of the system's structure and behavior.

OPM has recently provided new features that allow for better reuse of model elements. These features include stereotypes and templates. These features can give a solid basis for building different models with similar basis.

The design of a CubeSat nanosatellite involves the studying of budgets, which calculate the performance of the system in many aspects. These budgets have to follow the nanosatellite subsystems' requirements and constraints[15].

The mass budget calculates the total mass of the system while ensuring that it is within the imposed limitations. The volume budget calculates the total volume captured by the system components and makes sure it is within the allocated

volume. The power budget considers the power consumed by the potential components, the power generated by the solar panels, and the battery status. The height budget calculates the total height of the components stacked one over the other [15].

In addition to these budgets, there are many others that have to be considered to make a comprehensive estimation of the system at hand. However, this work is not meant to be comprehensive in this regard, but rather to use some of the budget calculations to demonstrate a tool that automates the process of budget calculation.

OPM has been used in many diverse domains for different purposes. Casebolt et al. [16] showed how OPM can be applied to provide a method for business processes improvement. An OPM-based executable tool, FTTell, was presented for assessing potential pediatric failure to thrive (FTT) during the perinatal stage [17]. OPM has contributed to the aircraft design domain, where an OPM model-based systems engineering (MBSE) framework for civil transport aircraft design with dynamic landing constraints was introduced [18]. Another OPM-based framework was developed as a viable alternative to traditional task analysis (TA) techniques [19]. OPM has been applied to model real-time systems [20], enterprise resource planning (ERP) [21], multi-agent systems [22], data warehouses [23], biological systems [24], and Web applications [25]. Specifically, a work by Dori et al. employed OPM to conceptually model the satellite ground control software development [7]. Particularly, they built a graphical model that provides guidelines for the control software development that helps to alleviate these problems: obsolescence, lack of desired features, and software bug fixing. It should be noted that those guidelines are presented graphically and textually, as OPM supporting tools are translating graphical facts into text.

Christina et al. [26] described a tool aiming for a system-level conceptual design of nanosatellites providing users with different background knowledge to investigate satellite concepts while giving them control over the design trade-offs. The tool is implemented in Excel and does not adopt an MBSE approach.

Concerning budget calculating, a very recent thesis by Hoxha, a Matlab-based tool was developed for automating CubeSat's budget calculation [15]. This tool's goal is to program a Matlab code that calculates budgets such as mass, volume, power, and others. It takes a user input and outputs results considering margins. As this tool is purely programmed, it suffers from many traits that our work complements. First, it does not provide a conceptual model to the user and by this it assumes that the user is an expert. Second, it is not amenable to changes as every structural and/or procedural change requires coding and this by itself is restricted to developers. Third, even for developers it is not easy as the external connection of the code requires coding that connections (e.g., Excel). Fourth, animated execution is limited to some parts of the process and meant to understand some physical behavior such as detumbling where in our work we apply animated execution to the entire budget calculating process for the sake of process comprehension and step-by-step execution. Fifth, Hoxha's approach does not adopt a system engineering approach, where ours benefits from a Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) one. Finally, as OPM's supported tool

also supports OPL, it is possible to read a description of the entire model in a natural language giving non-technical stakeholders the ability to comprehend the model without delving into syntactic and graphical notations.

Gamble et al. developed a tool for risk management for lowcost CubeSat missions. It includes an inputs page used to calculate mission risk likelihood. Outputs are presented via lists and graphical formats. The Excel software was used to create the tool as it is easily accessible and easy to understand [27].

In the context of modeling, the modeling language that comes closest to what we propose here is SysML, where a modeler can express computational aspects using the dedicated static parametric diagram. As Levi et al. stated in a recent work [28], the use of SysML requires multiple types of diagrams which cognitively burden the human inspector, who has to view, follow, and comprehend the underlying model and its simulation as it dangles from one kind of diagram to another, while in OPM the entire model including all its aspects (functional, structural, and behavioral) is based on one kind of diagram. For more on the differences between OPM and SysML, the reader can refer to a comparative study by Grobshtein et al. [29]. Furthermore, since both languages exhibit various advantages, Yariv et al. have called and proposed a way to create synergies between them [30]. This synergy allows one language (for example, OPM) to benefit from the other (for example, SysML).

section_key: 4 the opm based budget calculating system
text: The purpose of this work is two-fold: (1) formally modeling the budget calculating process, and (2) using the model to automate and facilitate this process. We adopted an OPM model-based systems engineering (MBSE) approach, since, as noted, OPM combines function, structure and behavior in a single diagram kind that uses a minimal set of universal building blocks—objects and processes—and translates on the fly to a subset of natural language. These traits help to build a formal yet simple model that can be easily understood. To attain the second goal of automating the budget calculating process, we leverage OPM's computational capabilities, which enable accepting user input, act on it computationally, and provide a desired output. In this section, we introduce the model that represents the budget calculating process with its computational part, rendering it a useful tool for automating this process.

Every OPM model starts at level 0 with a system diagram (SD) as depicted in Figure 5, which shows the main process Budget Calculating, represented by an ellipse, surrounded by the objects (rectangles) involved in this process. OPM requires that SD expresses the value of the main process to the system's beneficiary. Accordingly, the purpose of the Budget Calculating process is to change the Component Selection state from not-accepted to accepted. This benefit is expressed by the OPCloud-generated OPL sentence, shown in Figure 4, "Budget Calculating changes Component Selection from not-accepted to accepted." This object, Component Selection, starts with an initial state not-accepted as the user (builder) has not yet provided the components of the intended system. Once he or she does, and the provided components comply with the system limitations, the state of Component Selection automatically changes to accepted.
Figure 5: The system diagram of the budget calculating system showing the main process, Budget Calculating, and related objects

Nanosatellite Builder, shown in Figure 5, is an OPM agent—a person or an organization that handles the process to which it is connected. Specifically, this would be the agent who interacts with the system to provide input for the Budget Calculating process. The four objects on the left represent the output of the process, each of which will contain the budget of a different aspect of the system. It should be noted that this model is not comprehensive in this regard, but rather shows a proof-of-concept of this work main idea.

According to the methodological part of OPM, the main process in SD is enabled by an instrument whose default name is the main process name followed by "System". However, in our case, we deviate slightly from this convention and call the instrument object CubeSat Nanosatellite System as it better conveys the main process' underlying system. An instrument link is designated as a "white lollipop" as shown in Figure 5.

The Budget Calculating main process as well as the CubeSat NanoSatellite System main object can be decomposed into smaller processes and objects respectively using inzooming or unfolding mechanisms. These two techniques are the OPM's approach to managing model complexity. In-zooming refines the main process and shows its internal subprocesses while preserving order on their execution. Unfolding does the same, but it is used where order is not critical. The same rationale applies to objects. In this work, for processes, we apply in-zooming, where execution order is necessary, and unfolding, where order is not. As for objects, we apply unfolding to uncover their smaller internal parts.

Figure 9 shows the first step towards the exploration of the inner parts of the system diagram (top level) components. This diagram shows a refined Budget Calculating process with required objects, from the previous upper level, moved as well. This diagram shows that the Budget Calculating process is composed of two subprocesses: Budget Quantifying and Decision Making. The former is responsible for calculating budgets and the latter decides whether these calculated budgets comply with the predefined thresholds, and updates the Component Selection state accordingly. As the diagram shows, the upper subprocess writes (using arrowed result links) to the output objects while the lower subprocess reads (using instrument links) what has been
Figure 6: The CubeSat NanoSatellite System unfolded showing its main smaller parts
written by the upper process in order to decide about the Component Selection state.

As shown in Figure 10, the Budget Quantifying process is further refined through unfolding into four subprocesses. At the very top of this Object Process Diagram (OPD) the name of the refined process is shown, then at a lower level, its four derived subprocesses: Height Budget Calculating, Mass Budget Calculating, Volume Budget Calculating, and Power Budget Calculating. Notice that there is no predefined execution order for these subprocesses as they are independent. These subprocesses are at the end of the refinement process—they are drawn with a thin contour compared with a thick one for refined processes. Some of the objects in the higher diagram are propagated to the Budget Quantifying process unfolded diagram in Figure 10, as they continue to be relevant to the unfolded process and/or its inner subprocesses. New objects, with red contours, have been added to represent the threshold values of the different system-calculated budgets. This is an example of how OPM manages complexity—objects are added where they are relevant.

Other objects, Antenna System, TRXVU, OBC, and EPS, appear in this diagram, but they were created in different diagrams, and were brought here for their relevance to it (Figure 10). These objects compose the larger object CubeSat

NanoSatellite System from Figure 5 which was unfolded into a new diagram as shown in Figure 6. Notice that the objects in Figure 6 have a thick contour that indicates that they can be further unfolded. The Antenna System is unfolded into the diagram shown in Figure 12, the TRXVU object is unfolded and shown in Figure 7, the OBC object is shown unfolded in Figure 11, and the EPS object is unfolded into Figure 8. Notice that each of these unfolded objects is composed of other objects that represent their attributes using a special structural link called exhibition-characterization. These attributes are needed for the final calculation of the different budgets.

To recap, the diagram in Figure 10 shows all subprocesses for budgets calculating using data from the different subsystems. For example, the Mass Budget Calculating subprocess is responsible for mass calculating. This subprocess is connected to all subsystems by an instrument link (a link that implies 'requires') as it needs their mass. Every subsystem has an attribute that represents its mass. After having this input from all subsystems, the Mass Budget Calculating subprocess calculates the total mass of the nanosatellite and outputs the result into a new object called Mass Budget using a result link (there is an arrow to the direction of this object). The name of Mass Budget Calculating subprocess is followed by () to indicate that it is a computational process, which means that some computations occur within it.

Recall that the two objectives of this work are to (1) formally model the Budget Calculating system and process, and (2) use the model to automate and facilitate this process. Objective (1) has been attained: The OPM model of the Budget Calculating system faithfully represents the Budget Calculating process and the involved objects at several levels of detail, clearly explicating who the agents (actors) are, how the process unfolds, and what the role of each agent is at each stage of the process. To achieve the second goal of automating the Budget Calculating process for the benefit of any CubeSat nanosatellite builder aspiring to build one, we leverage OPM's extension MAXIM [17], [31] which augments OPM ISO 19450:2015 with the ability to infuse computations and code into the previously qualitative-only OPM model.

To help a Nanosatellite Builder find the most suitable components to build a nanosatellite, we have incorporated code into several processes in the model exploiting the new OPM computational capabilities implemented in OPCloud. Figure 13 shows a JavaScript source code snippet attached to the Mass Budget Calculating() process. As noted, the () suffix in a process name indicates that it is computational.

As Figure 10 shows, for the Mass Budget Calculating() process to execute, it requires the masses of all subsystems: Antenna System, TRXVU, OBC, and EPS. The masses are entered by the user to the appropriate attributes (objects) within each subsystem object. Specifically, each object that is designated to be involved in some computations is called a computational informatical object and assigned an alias (within {}) following its name. This alias is referenced from the code attached to the computational process. For example, the mass of the OBC object is represented by an inner attribute (object) called OBC_MASS that is aliased with OBCM. When referenced from within the code, the OPCloud system creates a name that shows the object to which it belongs and as a result, the full name is OBC_OBCM. Likewise, the other three subprocesses in Figure 10 are also attached
Figure 7: TRXVU subsystem unfolded
Figure 8: EPS subsystem unfolded
Figure 9: This diagram shows the Budget Calculating Process in-zoomed
with JavaScript code that calculates the budgets they are responsible for.

For the computational processes to perform budget calculations, the user has to enter data into the appropriate places attribute objects as shown in Figures 7,8,11,and 12. The OPM supporting tool, OPCloud, provides different ways to

enter this data. The first way of input entering is ahead-of time input which requires that the user enters the data directly into the attribute object as shown in the diagrams of this work. The second way for data entering is run-time input where the user is prompted to insert data while model execution. The third option is a simulated value, where the modeler defines the range of values to select from and the probability distribution. As for output options, the modeler can choose between outputting the results directly into attribute objects as adopted here in this work, or exporting to Excel files. These are the very basic input/output mechanisms, but there are more advanced methods, but these are beyond the scope of this work.

section_key: 5 the opm based budget calculating system evaluated
text: OPCloud, a web-based tool that implements OPM, has animated execution capabilities. As our model constitutes all needed qualitative things (conceptual objects and processes) as well as quantitative things (computational objects and processes), we can use OPCloud not only to statically model (using qualitative things) the Budget Calculating System but also to execute the model (based on the quantitative part) to obtain the sought solution, in our case, validated computed values of the different budgets of the system so that the nanosatellite builder selects the right components that fit the limitations of the underlying CubeSat nanosatellite. Furthermore, OPCloud has an animated execution feature so that the process of budget calculating is visualized by tokens, green disks sliding along the model links, to show the flow.

mation traverses the OPDs in the model's OPD tree in a depth-first fashion. Execution starts at the System Diagram as shown in Figure 14a. In this figure the main process Budget Calculating, requires two objects to start execution as shown by the two tokens come from these objects: CubeSat NanoSatellite System, and Nanosatellite Builder The CubeSat NanoSatellite System object is required as the whole system, that contains the subsystems from which the main process will take its data for calculation. The other object, Nanosatellite Builder, is also a required one, but it is captured as a human agent that is needed in the process of component selection. The execution process will start drilling down into the Budget Calculating process for executing its subprocesses as shown in Figure 14b. This OPD shows the Budget Calculating process refined into two subprocesses: Budget Quantifying, and Decision Making. In the former

we calculate the budgets of different system aspects, and in the latter we decide whether the proposed components are acceptable. The execution system further drills down into the first subprocess as shown in Figure 14c. This OPD contains all subprocesses that calculate all budgets, but this specific figure shows the execution of the Height Budget Calculating subprocess. Its tokens show the data flows into the subprocess. This data comes from the subsystems and the predefined threshold then enters the subprocess that attaches some code in JavaScript. After running this code, a result is yielded and sent to the output object as shown in 14d. Likewise, the execution system does for the next subprocess as shown in Figure 14e and continues for all other subprocesses to calculate all budgets. Once done, the system starts climbing up the OPDs back to the main System Diagram. This is shown in Figure 14f that demonstrates the results going out

the Budget Quantifying subprocesses to the output objects. Following this subprocess is the Decision Making one, that runs some code in JavaScript that considers all output objects to decide whether to accept the current configuration or not. As shown in Figure 14f, all output objects have valid result (no one has an "Error" value) so we expect the Decision Making subprocess will accept the proposed configuration as shown in Figure 14g. Notice how the tokes are sliding into the output objects, and the state of the Component Selection object is changing from not-accepted to accepted.

There are cases where the proposed components do not comply with the system limitations. To demonstrate that, we changed some of the data given to the attributes which yielded an "Error" value in the Volume Budget object and hence the Component Selection object changed to not-accepted state as shown in Figure 14h.

We have proposed a model-based approach that builds on model-based systems engineering using OPM ISO 19450 with computational extensions that are built into OPCloud. The research has achieved its two stated objectives: (1) A detailed OPM model of the budget calculating process and system was constructed, making the process clear and unambiguous; (2) Leveraging the computational capabilities of OPM, the model served as the basis for an executable budget calculating tool. Specifically, this model-based tool automates and significantly shortens the tedious process of meticulously going over a large and growing number of components that build the underlying nanosatellite, eliminating the need for sifting through a possibly long list of combinations of them.

Modeling a system conceptually and attaching necessary computations to one or a few processes is enabled by newly developed OPM computational capabilities and their implementation in OPCloud. This feature is of great importance since, as demonstrated, the code embedded in the processes is designed such that the system model can be modified and augmented without the need to alter the code. This facilitates maintaining the system coherent, consistent, and synchronized. Due to OPM's high-level conceptual modeling capabilities and lower-level computational and programming capabilities, this unique fusion of conceptual and computational modeling is made possible. Specifically, we can incorporate program code into processes of an OPM model and run the model. Whenever a computational process is encountered, the code within it is executed using the values of its input computational objects. The model-based approach to CubeSats formally explicates the Budget Calculating process and automates it, greatly alleviating the task of determining what components are the best suitable. Beyond streamlining and automating the Budget Calculating process, this work demonstrates the benefits of adopting the OPM model-based systems engineering approach to the domain of CubeSats, which include standardizing and formulating global CubeSats processes and systems, and helping CubeSat professionals navigate their way in the complex, evolving web of CubeSats design.

This paper investigates using Large Language Models (LLMs) within Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) as the basis for generative design tools for spacecraft. This study has developed tooling for automatically generating system architecture, functions, modes, and components from an initial requirement set. Specifically, a Python tool was developed to couple the Capella MBSE tool to an LLM in order to facilitate a rapid generative design process. The approach was tested by application to three system design tasks: a European Space Agency Earth observation mission, a CubeSat payload design, and a masters' degree level group design for an Earth observation spacecraft. For each, generated outputs were evaluated against those produced by technical designers. It was found that the generation of system modes and components was of good quality, providing high traceability and alignment against requirements, and also providing generated architectures that in some areas were more detailed than human-generated equivalents. Further development could provide spacecraft system engineers with an 'AI design assistant', as human input is still at the centre of the process and appears necessary to ensure a high-quality output.

MBSE is the formal application of modelling to system engineering activities (INCOSE 2007). This approach to systems engineering centres on the concept of providing a 'single source of truth' for a project, whereby all stakeholders can communicate system information. This relies on three 'pillars'; modelling language, tool, and method (Wäschle et al. 2020). The modelling language defines how the information about the system is captured in the model. The tool is the software environment in which the model is constructed and the method is the process by which the model is populated. By using these three pillars, MBSE has been demonstrated to offer a more complete, consistent, and communicable approach to systems engineering than tradition methods (Ryan, Cook, and Scott 2013).
Large Language Models; Model-based Systems Engineering; generative design; spacecraft system architectures; systems engineering

MBSE-orientated tools and methods typically do not easily allow design exploration instead being focused on precise representation of a systems baseline. This makes it difficult to explore alternative solutions, as it is time consuming to model each discrete alternative.

However, tools that allow exploration are emerging within the field (Epp et al. 2023), (Leserf, de Saqui-Sannes, and Hugues 2019),(Timperley et al. 2023),(Lu et al. 2022). The most common modelling language, SysML (version 1), has minimal support for design alternatives modelling, via the use of element generalisations and refinements. In this way the modeler can identify discrete design alternatives (Meacham, Gioulekas, and Phalp 2015). Work has been done to address this issue, mostly by researchers in the field, particularly focusing on the capability to model continuous or discontinuous parameter variation (Leserf, de Saqui-Sannes, and Hugues 2019). To support more complex forms of design variation, rule (or ontology) based methods have been developed (Halvorson et al. 2022), and while useful in their specific intended domain, they cannot be used for applications outside this without defining a new set of rules. Further to these efforts, SysML version 2 is starting to be adopted in the field and offers variability points for modelling alternative configurations and supporting trade-offs.

Large Language Models (LLM), a sub-set of the wider Natural Language Processing (NLP) field, have garnered a great deal of attention recently for their capability to respond to prompts. Successful application areas include medicine (Thirunavukarasu et al. 2023), and many more. To achieve this impressive capability and flexibility, LLM's make use of transformer models (Vaswani et al. 2017) and are trained on vast amounts of text, sourced from various books, articles and websites from across the internet.

In order to maximise the output quality of these large models, a number of techniques have been developed: Fine tuning, whereby a pre-existing LLM model may have all (full model tuning) (Zhang et al. 2024) or a subset of its parameters (parameter efficient tuning) (Lester, Al-Rfou, and Constant 2021) varied into order to maximise against some evaluation criteria. Chain of thought, has been used to improve to the reasoning capabilities of LLM's, by splitting the generation process into a number of intermediate steps (Vacareanu et al. 2024). Retrieval-Augmented Generation draws on external data to provide improved accuracy of the LLM output (Fatehkia, Lucas, and Chawla 2024). This data is typically relevant to the application domain, and may be stored in the form of a knowledge graph (Agrawal et al. 2024).
These models offer a valuable opportunity to address shortcomings in current MBSE tools, by providing free-form design exploration that has not been possible up to this point.

LLMs and NLP techniques have already been applied to MBSE in areas such as: knowledge graph generation for answering queries related to space missions; requirement management with MBSE (Riesener et al. 2021); the use of Named Entity Recognition (NER) models for SysML model element generation (Chami, Zoghbi, and Bruel 2019). This last NER based approach was able to generate actors, use cases, associations and blocks.

There are various demonstrations in literature of LLM capabilities as an initial generation tool in other domains (Blocklove et al. 2024) and other relevant studies such as (Gomez et al. 2024), (Camara et al. 2023) and (Wang et al. 2024) each exploring UML generation with LLMs, with (Wang et al. 2024) using a set of criteria to evaluate different aspects of the generated UML diagrams such as class and sequence diagrams. (Ferrari, Abualhaija, and Arora 2024) focussed on UML sequence diagram generation with evaluation focussing on completeness, correctness, adherence to the standard, understandability and terminology alignment. (Apvrille and Sultan 2024) presents a tool for LLM generation of SysML models, and for evaluation, compared the generated models to ones created by masters level students in a graded design exercise. (Luitel, Nejati, and Sabetzadeh 2024) explored
Simulink model slicing with LLMs, useful for model inspection and establishing traceability to requirements.

This study aimed to assess the capability of LLMs as a generative design tool in the MBSE context in more detail. Earth observation spacecraft architectures has been chosen as an example of a complex system design problem with some consistent examples to compare against. Specifically, the study assesses the ability of LLMs to generate functions, components and modes from system requirements, an activity that in practice typically requires a significant amount of time for a system architect to produce. This paper is organised as follows. The methodology is presented in section 2, then experiment results in section 3. The results are discussed and future work proposed in section 4 and finally conclusions are provided in section 5.

As mentioned, in this work LLMs were tested as a generative design tool within MBSE through development and application of a LLM pipeline to three MBSE problem cases. Cases include a real industry case to test real-world applicability, a comprehensive researchled case, and a broad set of undergraduate projects. In each, outputs of the LLM tool are compared to designer-created outputs.
This first section presents the tool selection and the LLM interface with the MBSE tool. The setup and execution of the design cases is then described in the next section.

The MBSE tool selected for this case study was the Eclipse Foundation's Capella tool (Eclipse 2023). Originally developed by Thales Alenia Space and PolarSys industry working group, this tool offered a powerful Python interface called Python4capella (Labs4Capella 2024). This provided the opportunity for architecture elements generated by an LLM to be fed directly into the system model in Capella. Capella was also selected as it follows the ARCADIA method (Voirin 2023) which is focussed on system architecting.

For the choice of LLM, several options were considered. There are many commercial models such as text-davinci-003 (the text generation part of chatGPT-3.5) (OpenAI 2023), available from OpenAI or OPT, developed by meta. Open source models include GPT-J, GPT-NeoX and Bloom. The number of model parameters plays a critical role in the performance of an LLM (Kandpal et al. 2023). Text-davinci-003, GPT-NeoX, OPT and Bloom all have 175 billion parameters, while GPT-J has 20 billion. For the purposes of this study, text-davinci-003 was selected as the primary LLM, due to its performance and, at the time, it offered larger token limits than other models of similar type. It was also reported to have improved zero-shot capabilities, that was felt to be particularly useful for the purposes of this study. Besides this, it offered close integration with Python and low cost. While much more capable LLMs have since been released, text-davinci-003 was still used to complete all experiments to maintain consistency and it is expected that modern LLM's would likely be just as suitable, if not more. This is discussed further in section 4.

A toolchain linking the MBSE model and the generative LLM was developed. OpenAI offers a Python API (application programming interface) to allow users to communicate with their models over the internet, thus providing a convenient means of performing

prompt engineering. Therefore, in this study Python was used as the bridge to collect outputs from the LLM and feed them directly into the Capella MBSE tool. This was implemented via a Python package, called NalMage (Neural Network-Assisted Language Modelling for Architecture Generation and Engineering), that included all necessary functions to control interaction with the LLM via OpenAI's API, and generate Capella model elements within the MBSE model, via the Python4Capella API. All interactions with the user, such as entering LLM prompts, were performed via a console within Capella. Figure 1 shows the connections between each component.

The toolchain was configured to mirror classical system architecting processes, and allow user down-selecting at each process stage. The designer inputs requirements, and prompts for the LLM to automatically produce a list of functions that meet them. The user then prompts for a grouping of the generated functions into modes, and then logical components. This process is repeated at each level of the system. See Table 1 for a list of the prompt patterns used at each of these steps, and Figure 2 for a diagrammatic process overview. The prompts in Table 1 are fairly simple and the impact of using more developed prompts is discussed later. At each stage of this process the user guided the LLM prompting via the NalMage package, see Figure 3. In so doing, the system leverages the expertise of the user to guide generation of LLM outputs. For this study, only functional requirements were considered, as it was judged that these were generally more complex to handle during the system architecting process. See section 4 for suggestions on how non-functional requirements might be handled using an LLM in future work.

The textual output of the LLM provides the basis of the elements to be added to the MBSE model in Capella. The LLM model was prompted to output lists of suggested elements in bullet point form, allowing simple string splitting, performed by the NALMAGE package, to separate individual model elements down selected by the designer. Then, these elements would be mapped by the NALMAGE package to specific MBSE model types depending on what model element the designer had specified earlier in the prompting process, shown in Figure 3. The ontology used for the text-to-MBSE model transition in this study contained three model types and one textual type; requirements (textual), functions (model type), modes (model type) and components (model type), shown in Figure 4. A feature of LLMs is that they can react to user feedback within the prompts, and so offer an opportunity to mirror the iterative nature of the systems architecting process. This has been partially reflected in this study by the inclusion of the down selection step after each model element generation stage, that ensures erroneous elements are not carried into the next prompt, but there is the potential for much more in depth user feedback mechanisms to be used. Table 2 summarises the set of design experiments performed during this study. The tool was applied to three design cases with pre-existing design solutions (which were useful for comparison), with the aim of covering a wide range of different requirement types and wordings. These included:

(1) The University of Bristol's CubeSat payload PROVE Pathfinder (Etchells et al. 2022),(Timperley and Berthoud 2022), which was selected as it already had a complete and detailed design with accessible design information, and being a CubeSat mission (i.e.: a nano-spacecraft), complemented the other two full-sized spacecraft missions.

(2) A masters' level group design brief for an Earth observation spacecraft that offered an overview of a full sized satellite design with accessible design information. This was an educational example which meant that the requirement wording was considered to be clear and consistent (for the student's benefit), offering perhaps a simpler design case.

(3) An industrial study for a European Space Agency Earth Observation (EO) mission, with more limited access to design information. This study was selected as it gives a more 'real-world' industrial example rather than educational examples. Its requirements were much more detailed than the previous two examples.

text: As described previously, experiments were run to assess the quality of generated system architectures from the LLM toolchain. The quality of the generated system architectures was assessed via a set of Key Performance Indicators (KPI's) focused on traceability and alignment. These are described in the next two sections.

An important feature of system architecture is the traceability of the design of the elements, i.e.: can these be traced back through an element's parents, through the design cycle back to the requirements? (ISO/IEC/IEEE24765:2010(E)2010). Traceability was assessed using manual ratings by two human coders, each with several years' experience in systems engineering. The ratings were out of three and performed in accordance with a predefined rule set. This rule set is presented in Table 5 and developed from definitions in (ISO/IEC/IEEE24765:2010(E)2010). Each traceability score was then aggregated to provide a mean traceability score for the entire generated architecture. The traceability of the pre-existing designs (PROVE Pathfinder, University of Bristol group design, and the Industrial EO design) was also calculated using the rule set in Table 5 to provide a comparison and contextualise the generated design traceability.

Individual alignment scores were then aggregated to calculate generation precision and recall measures. The precision was calculated as the mean alignment score of the generated elements, i.e. of those elements generated by the LLM. Recall was calculated via the mean alignment score of the pre-existing design elements, i.e. those present in pre-existing designs. Optimal alignment would then occur when each element in the generated architecture could be directly mapped to an element in the pre-existing one, and vice versa, in which case Figure 6 would be a square diagonal matrix.

To identify if the generated architectures were more or less 'specific' than the pre-existing design architecture, a further aggregation method was used, based on the root mean square of the alignment scores. In this context, specificity was defined as the level of decomposition at which each layer of the generated system architecture was modelled, vs the level for the pre-existing design. Following this, if an element in the pre-existing design was aligned with multiple elements in the generated design, such as the flight software shown in Figure 5, it could be argued that the generated design was more specific, as that element in the pre-existing could have been decomposed to match the generated elements. The root mean square based aggregation was performed by first constructing a vector, $ \vec{\nu} $ , as shown in equation (3).
$$ \vec {\nu} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \overline {{A _ {i j}}} $$

where i is the number of generated elements, j is the number of pre-existing design elements, $ \overline{A_{ij}} $ is the matrix of alignment scores between all the generated and pre-existing design elements. The vector length of $ \vec{\nu} $ (Euclidean distance) is then normalised by dividing it by the square root of the number of generated elements, thus evaluating to the Root Mean Square (RMS), see equation (4). This has been called the 'over specificity parameter', as it is influenced by the number of generated elements that are highly aligned with fewer elements in the pre-existing design (meaning they are more specific). If the two designs were perfectly aligned, then $ \overline{A_{ij}} $ was a diagonal matrix of perfect scores, then this value would be 1. The more 'over specific' the generated architecture, the higher the value of $ \sigma $
$$ O v e r S p e c i f i c i t y P a r a m e t e r = \sigma = \frac {| | \vec {\nu} | |}{\sqrt {i}} $$

This is then repeated, but instead of summing across generated elements, $ \vec{\nu} $ is calculated by summing across pre-existing design elements, to arrive at the under-specificity parameter, with similar behaviour with respect to less specific generated elements.
