This was a result of the coverage of the input requirements, which for PROVE pathfinder considered a wider range of domains/system aspects than the other experiments. This is explored in further detail in experiment 5.

Figure 8 shows alignment recall and precision scores for each experiment, as scored for both coders (hence two bars for each entry). Figure 9 shows the specification parameter values, indicating where the LLM tool over or under specified for each design task. Figure 8 shows higher precision scores (2.3/3) than recall (1.8/3), meaning that the generated elements were generally present in the pre-existing design, however there were sometimes
Figure 8. Precision and alignment scores for experiment 1, 2 & 3 (scored out of 3), for both coders.
Figure 9. Under and over specification parameters for experiments 1, 2 & 3 (smaller values show stronger similarity with the pre-existing design).
elements in the pre-existing design that are missed in the generated design. Overall while the recall scores leave room for improvement, the generated designs exhibit good precision scores.

The generated PROVE architecture was, on balance, more specific than the pre-existing design, as shown in Figure 9. Again, this is likely a result of the coverage of the requirements used for this experiment. Furthermore, the traceability and alignment of the generated functions was on average lowest across the three experiments, followed by modes then components. This could be expected, as functions are more conceptually abstract than modes or components, therefore their wording is more variable and as a result the causality between prompt wording and function wording is more difficult to train an LLM to
Figure 10. Influence of prompt pattern on traceability score.

achieve. In other words there are few names for a propulsion subsystem, but many ways to describe a function raising a spacecraft's orbit. There was a large swing in specificity for functions between experiment 1 and 2, further demonstrating how the input requirements and their coverage had a large influence on the quality of different aspects of the generated architectures.

The impact of different prompt patterns on traceability score is shown in Figure 10. See Table 3 for the different patterns tested. Figure 10 shows that the more prescriptive prompt patterns produced a higher quality output. However, the benefit of adding more tokens to the prompt, meaning using a longer prompt, reduced with increasing pattern length, leading to a diminishing returns relationship.

Figure 11 presents the changes in traceability score for the additional requirement presented in Table 4. The average traceability score was 2.59 with the new requirements, up from an average of 2.24 from experiment 2. Figure 11 shows the scores for functions, modes and components were all improved by the addition of the extra requirements, besides the number of modes scoring a traceability of 3.

This section discusses the results presented in the previous section and suggests directions for future work. Experiment 1,2&3 demonstrated that architectures of acceptable quality (where at least 2 of every 3 design elements are traceable to requirements) can be generated using the TEXT-DAVINCI-003 LLM. As previously mentioned, the main limitation of the LLM was identifying functions from requirements, as these were the most conceptually
Figure 11. Impact on traceability of additional requirements.

abstract of the architecture elements generated. However, even this level of performance appears acceptable. Given that this model was depreciated in January 2024, the output quality demonstrated in this study should be considered a baseline, with more modern LLMs likely to be able to produce better results. It is proposed that the Open LLM Leaderboard (Hugging Face 2024) may be a good starting point for selecting more up to date LLMs. Furthermore, the consistency between the results of these three design experiments indicated that this approach might be applicable to a range of Earth observation spacecraft. On top of this achieved quality, the process can be completed much more quickly than by a purely human designer, as it offers higher automation.

The total cost of running these experiments was £10.20 at the time, with 248,270 token prompts used. Assuming roughly similar token costs are maintained, this indicates that prompting cost should not be a barrier to adoption of LLMs in this area, at least for externally hosted models.

The generated architectures achieved higher precision scores than recall, indicating that while most of the elements in the generated architecture could be found in the pre-existing design (or human generated design solution), the process did not include all the same elements. This result was mirrored in the specificity parameters, with the generated output being more specific than the pre-existing design. It appears that the LLM was somewhat biased towards the information present in the requirements, rather than its wider knowledge. The reason for this was likely due to the information available to the LLM being limited to the requirement text and the text corpus it was trained on. If the LLM model were to undergo fine tuning for the spacecraft domain, it may be better able to identify necessary parts of a spacecraft not referenced in requirements (such as equipment harnesses

and fixtures). This challenge also highlights the need for human designers with domain-specific knowledge to closely guide the generation process when using an LLM in this fashion. Specifically, being able to remove irrelevant design elements suggested by the LLM is particularly useful.

The prompt patterns used (or how the LLM was prompted) have a significant impact on the quality of the generated architecture, as shown in experiment 5. The more complex patterns produced a better result. This was perhaps because they provided more tokens (meaning more information) for the LLM to generate an output closer to what the user desires. Similarly, prompting with more requirements, thus more tokens, also leads to improved traceability, as shown in experiment 5. Using longer prompts in this way may also be a usable method of combatting the lower recall scores discussed above.

If using more prompt tokens, the increase in generated architecture quality should be traded against the increased computational cost (and potentially financial cost of using an external service to support the LLM). Further to this, the apparent diminishing returns relationship produced by increasing the token count should also be considered when posing prompts.

It was important to allow the human designer to down select the suggested elements in the LLM output at each stage, as the selected elements of one stage formed the input to the next, therefore poor quality elements would have a snowball effect on the overall design. An example of this is shown in Figure 5 where 3 of 9 top level functions were not decomposed to the next level, as these were not as good quality as the other 6. As a result, human intervention in the process is still important to achieve a good generated design.

This study has focused on manually rated assessments. Though this approach was cumbersome to complete, the manual assessments benefited from the experience and detailed knowledge of the assessors. This had the drawback that the rating was sensitive to opinion and biases. As can be seen from Figures 7,8 and Table 6,the assessors had moderate agreement, particularly on alignment scores, however more assessors would have improved the robustness of these assessments.
Several recommendations for pursuing this approach to system architecting can be drawn from this study:
- Using a fine-tuned LLM is not essential to providing acceptable results (however investigating model fine-tuning offers an attractive avenue for future work).
- Expert human control over the process is important to maintain good quality output architectures.
- The prompts given to the LLM should contain as much information as possible, either in terms of design elements such as requirements or in the prompt patterns used to structure the textual input.

- The above can be supported by constructing prompts that mirror typical systems engineering analysis practice, where system components and modes are identified as groupings of functions and these steps can be performed recursively at each level of the system. This helps to enforce the interconnected relationships within the output architecture and ensure each element has traceability to requirements.
There appears to be many promising avenues for further research leading on from the findings presented here. However, one of the most immediately beneficial directions would

be the expansion of the system architecting activities addressed. For example, the inclusion of non-functional requirements will be necessary to ensure that the system not only functions as intended, but also meets the necessary quality standards. It is envisioned that typical methods of non-functional analysis, such as reliability, security or other performance aspects could be leveraged for validation of these requirements and possibly fed back straight to the LLM for correction if non-conformances are identified. For example, mission analysis requirements could be addressed through integration with orbital simulation programmes such as GMAT (NASA - GSFC Open Source Software 2024) or STK (Ansys 2024). The incorporation in the model of interactions and relationships between elements, such as inter-component communication and functional dependencies, would further enhance the completeness of the architectures.

When applied to safety-critical systems like spacecraft, this LLM based architecting method may benefit from the inclusion of fault tolerance or identification of alternative system paths (such as degraded modes of operation). While this is currently considered manual work done downstream of the architecture generation presented here and not within the scope of this study, it appears likely that these aspects could be integrated with the LLM prompts for more robust architectures from the beginning.

Addressing architecture assessment methods, future work could either include many more assessors to improve the reliability of the rating and/or it should investigate automated alternatives, for example based on cosine similarity with pre-existing designs. This would allow more rapid testing and evaluation of LLMs for design generation. Furthermore, the ontology used to formalise the LLM output into model elements suitable for an MBSE model needs to be refined. More specifically, better control over the semantics of the LLM generated elements is necessary for deep integration with MBSE formalisms seen in languages like SysML. Similarly, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) (Fatehkia, Lucas, and Chawla 2024) could be added to control this formalisation of LLM output.

The LLM capabilities could be further refined by fine tuning or training on domain-specific knowledge. This may improve its ability to handle long-tail knowledge related to the spacecraft architecting domain, such as payloads and technologies specific to satellites.

Direct user feedback mechanisms also offer the potential for improved element generation with an LLM. This work has focused on generating 'baseline' architectures, with simple down selection of LLM-generated elements to combat any errors in output. However, allowing the user to highlight errors or improvements to be made in the LLM output with further prompting would enable iterative improvements directly on the LLM's responses. Performance analysis results or even KPIs, such as the manual traceability presented here or automated KPIs, could be used as part of this feedback process. Automated KPIs typically used to evaluate text generation models do exist, such as; the Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) (Papineni et al. 2002) for assessing the quality of translations, Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (Lin 2004) for summarisation and the Flesch Reading Ease Formula for text readability (Kincaid et al. 1975) (Das and Verma 2020) to name a few. However, each of these are specialised to their particular use case and therefore a new method would need to be developed, applicable to system architecting. Finally, enabling the LLM to react to requirements mid-process could be a highly valuable capability, as mid-project requirement updates are common and lead to costly changes.

This study demonstrates the successful automated generation of spacecraft system architectures using Large Language Models. A novel generation tool has been constructed, in which designer-led prompting greatly reduces design time and effort. LLM outputs have been produced for three realistic design cases, manually rated and compared to human generated design solutions. The comparison has shown that the LLM-generated elements have high textual similarity, traceability, and alignment to pre-existing design solutions. It has been shown that functions were the most challenging element type to generate. The LLM pipeline generated a consistent and acceptable output for 3 different Earth observation spacecraft missions, but human interaction is essential to maintain the quality. Using the LLM made the design process much faster. Some variability can be expected in the output quality for non-deterministic LLMs. More tokens for prompting the LLM will lead to a better output architecture, but the increased cost of doing this should be considered. Future work is planned to develop more automated methods of assessing LLMs for this application.

The transformation and evolution of the space sector relies on technological innovation, but also on digital transformation. The increasing complexity of space systems led to the deployment of new digital solutions and methodologies such as Model-Based Systems Engineering that helps to better comprehend this complexity on an individual scale. This leads to new ways of approaching projects, such as concurrent engineering which consists in involving all project stakeholders right from the preliminary phases, using facilitating tools and methods.

At CNES, PASO (Orbital Systems Architecture Plateau) is leading space systems preliminary phases and aims at formulating missions needs and pre-sizing systems in order to conclude on their feasibility. This process is conducted accordingly to the principles of concurrent engineering, thus involving all systems architects and thematic experts from the very beginning of the projects.

The objective of this paper is to describe the approach through the prism of an electrical architect, that contributes to needs analysis, realization of power budgets, system sizing and energetic simulations through a specific use case. All this is achieved thanks to a precise workflow involving multiple digital tools, with continuity and interoperability made possible between engineers and their tools by the standardization of formats and files.

The selected use case to illustrate this paper is a 16U nanosatellite operating on low-earth orbit its mission being the 3D mapping of hot stars dynamic environment by using ultraviolet spectropolarimetry measurements from space for the first time. This mission concept has been carried out by the French laboratory LESIA

(Laboratory for Space Studiers and Astrophysics Instrumentation) with the help of CNES which is in charge of evaluating its feasibility. This use case is of particular interest as it depicts a highly agile mission causing a lot of interlocked trade-offs and architecture choices involving the electrical, thermal, communication, mechanical and AOCS subsystems. From the electrical point of view, the agility of the mission makes the sizing of solar panels and battery very tedious.

The observation consists in regular measurements of more than 40 identified stars of particular interest. These measurements will be segmented in multiple observation phases with a periodicity that relies on the star's period of revolution in order to cover the whole rotation of the star and thus perform a 3D mapping of it. It basically means that the system needs to have the same identical inertial attitude for all observations of one unique star.
Fig.1 - Hot stars 3D dynamic environment
The first system analyses concluded that the best orbit for the mission is an SSO orbit at low altitudes (between 500 and 600 km).
Fig. 2 - Payload preliminary architecture
Fig. 3 - Satellite preliminary architecture

The overall concurrent engineering approach consists in setting up a common technical reference (satellite description and mission), with the aim of producing system-level budgets (mass, power, centering/inertias, data, etc.) produced by the various subsystems experts/architects.
TwoTwo main tools are constituting the base of the process. These tools are non-compulsory but are relying on standards in order to be as interoperable as possible:
- IDM-CIC: used for system description (at system and sub-systems level) and for system basic geometry definition.
- Simu-CIC: used for mission scenario definition and ephemeris generation.

The combination of these two tools allows for a complete and comprehensive definition of the satellite and its orbital scenario (attitude over time considering the mission, the orbit, ground datalinks needs and the satellite geometry). Some other tools such as IDM-View or IDM-Plot can also be used to visualize different aspects of the system defined using the two main tools. Thanks to this complete set of concurrent engineering tools, each architect therefore works in conjunction with each other thanks to a common database, which allows various experts to carry out more precise and targeted analyses in parallel, while taking into account evolutions in all subsystems enabling everyone to analyze their impact quickly and efficiently. The whole process is organized by a concurrent engineering authority who ensures that scientific and technical objectives are met.
As an electrical architect specifically, the objective of any project preliminary phase would be:
- To define preliminary power budgets,
- To pre-size solar panels and batteries,
- To perform technological trade-offs,
- To simulate the on-board power usage.

Power simulations are a very good way to compare technologies efficiently (solar cells and battery cells for instance) and to refine the power subsystem sizing. In order to be able to perform energy balance simulations, several elements are needed:
- A model of the power sub-system: battery and solar generator assemblies, power bus topology, type of architecture, regulators, etc.
- All energy flows that leads the solar generator to generate power: solar flux, earth albedo flux, earth infrared flux.
- A power profile: the system power consumption over time.

The model is defined in the Opalis software. It is a proprietary but open tool developed by CNES that allows performing power simulations. The tool includes precise modelling of electrical architectures including batteries, solar panels, regulators and bus topologies by taking into account the specific features of each element such as losses, temperature impacts, etc. Such parameters can all be specified in the model tab of the tool.
Fig. 4 - Opalis simulation model example

The energy flows are generated by the Flows Manager plugin that is now included natively in Opalis. It takes the CCSDS-like standard files generated by Simu-CIC (orbital scenario description) as an input in order to automatically convert the ephemeris data (such as sun angles) into flows for the solar generator.
Fig. 5 - Cumulated fluxes on the solar gen. $ ( W / m^{2} ) $

The power profile is generated using IDM-CIC by adding the IDM-Power plugin to it. This plugin allows to allocate the power consumptions described in the IDM-CIC power budget to system modes. It then allows to obtain a temporal view of the system's power consumption.
Fig. 6 - Power consumption of the satellite (W)
In the end, the most common process would then be the following:
0) Preliminary work:
a. Defining every sub-system and their constituting pieces of equipment in IDM-CIC.
b. Defining the orbital scenario using Simu-CIC.
1) Attributing a consumed/dissipated power to each piece of equipment in order to obtain the global power budget of the system (including margins).
2) Converting the power budget into a power profile (system power consumption over time) using IDM-Power plugin.
3) Importing power profile into the power simulation software (Opalis).
4) Converting ephemeris into energy flows (solar flux, earth infrared flux, earth albedo flux) using the Flows Manager plugin.
5) Defining the simulation model Running energy balance simulations using Opalis

The main added value of this process is that it allows to define an adaptable and interoperable model. For instance, any change on the mission can be studied almost instantly by regenerating the corresponding ephemeris data. Another example would be that any change on the configuration or structure of the satellite (for instance amount and position of the solar panel wings) can also be compared easily.

In order to perform the electrical analyses and simulations, an orbital scenario was needed. As the mission has a lot of pointing variety over a year in order to be able to observe a vast set of stars, it means that a focus is needed to identify the worst-case observation scenario in terms of sun pointing with respect to the solar generator.
Fig. 7 - Observation plan example

Flight dynamics experts from CNES thus extracted from the global observation plan provided by the LESIA the worst case scenarios in terms of sun illumination, reducing it to a period of 48h only that could be used to size the power subsystem and still be representative of the whole mission. Two solar panels configurations were tested at first, a "back" one and a "side" one. After analysis, it turned out that the back configuration was the most adapted to the mission because simpler to design (one side must point towards cold space during observations while the opposite side must be able to point towards the Sun), and because we can obtain an observation plane that improves the received energy. This configuration will then be the only one described here.
Fig. 8 - Back configuration / Side configuration

From this configuration and this restricted 48h scenario extracted from the overall observation plan leading to known sun and earth angles with regard to solar panel axes at any time, the energy flows were generated using simu-CIC and the Opalis plugin Flows Manager. The result can be seen in Fig. 5.

The power profile is generated thanks to the IDM-Power plugin, based on the following power budget allocated to mission modes and the associated temporal scenario. Its graphic depiction can be seen in Fig. 6.

The power subsystem model was then defined in Opalis as follows:
- Solar Generator:
Solar cells selected from a list of cells
20 cells max available on each solar wing (80% filling factor)
End of life parameters considered
- Battery:
Li-ion accumulators selected from a list
End of life parameters considered
- Regulators:
O Battery charger/discharger: nonregulated architecture, battery follower power bus topology (no need identified for regulated voltage on the power bus).
o Solar regulator: Direct Energy Transfer (connection/disconnection of solar sections depending of the power needs) and MPPT (Max Power Point Tracking) regulation to be tested.
Fig. 9 - Opalis model principle
Now that a preliminary power subsystem model is defined in Opalis, all the inputs can be set up for simulations:
- Energy flows will determine the power generation capabilities of the system
- The power profile will determine the power needed by the satellite

The ultimate goal of the simulation process is to refine the power subsystem definition and to size elements (in particular cells and accumulators assemblies for solar panels and battery) in order to reach an energy balance between generation, storage and usage. To do so, S and P parameters (amount of elements in Series and Parallel) are readjusted through multiple runs of simulations, until a satisfactory equilibrium state is reached at the power subsystem level. This step is also an opportunity to carry out various trade-offs between technologies and architecture principles (type of battery/solar cell, power bus topologies, control principles, etc.).

As the mission here is a LEO mission with a lot of agility, the battery is anticipated to see a lot of charge/discharge cycles. For this kind of mission, the maximum battery depth of discharge is then normally limited to 25% in order to limit the battery capacity loss over time due to cycling. In that case, a satisfactory equilibrium for the aforementioned power subsystem would thus be defined as a battery cycling between 75% and a bit less than 100% of state of charge, meaning that the energy

production is sufficient to power the satellite as well as charging the battery during low illumination time windows, while still ensuring a sufficient margin in the eventuality of a satellite malfunction.
After a few runs of simulations by making all the parameters mentioned above vary, here is the result of a stable energy budget:
Fig. 10-Result of a stable energy subsystem simulation

These various runs of simulations and tradeoffs finally led to the following final satellite electrical architecture:
O 3G30A cells from AzurSpace,
2 wings of 20 cells each (~80% filling factor),
- Assembly per wing: 5 parallel strings of 4 cells in series for a total max production at around 44W at the end of life.
- Battery:
o Li-ion INR 18650 accumulators,
2S8P assembly (8 parallel strings of 2 accumulators in series),
Total available energy storage around 180Wh at the end of life,
160x65x40mm volume with housing margin of 10%.
- Regulators:
O Battery charger/discharger: non-regulated architecture, battery follower power bus topology (no need for regulated voltage on the power bus).

o Solar regulator: Direct Energy Transfer (connection/disconnection of solar sections depending of the power needs) system with boost regulators with no MPPT regulation for simplicity and low added value in that case.

One last thing to mention is that the minimum SOC (State Of Charge) reached during the simulation is 85% which is different from the worst acceptable value for nominal operation which is 75% as mentioned previously. This is due to the fact that the battery capacity is mainly sized for the worst discharging case which generally corresponds to the satellite going into survival mode right after an eclipse. This scenario can also be simulated by making the simulation start with an initial SOC of 85% followed by three successive orbits with no illumination that would correspond to a convergence of the satellite towards the survival mode (given by the AOCS expert), with a minimal acceptable SOC of 20% in order to keep an energy margin.
Fig. 11 - Simulation of the battery worst-case scenario

The iterative aspect of the complete workflow including the simulation methodology, coupled with the concurrent engineering process involving each subsystem expert, enables to perform several analyses, trade-off studies comparisons and sizings in parallel by taking into account every constraint and design impact easily. In the context of the satellite use case
presented in this paper, this made it possible from the electrical perspective to:
- Size the battery and solar generators (type of cells and assemblies) by taking into account worst case conditions (end of life, temperature, orbital constraints).
- Test different stars observation plans in order to validate their feasibility in terms of energy stability and potentially revise scientific ambitions and needs accordingly.
- Perform technical trade-offs like different battery/solar cells, regulator types (MPPT/DET, Buck/Boost, etc.), bus voltages, etc.
- Study architecture opportunities like adding solar cells on the main structure of the satellite in addition to the dedicated wings.
- Study the sensitiveness of the solar panels operating point in function of temperature to make sure that even in harsh temperature conditions the power supply would still be sufficient.
- Study the impact of going from a 2S8P to a 2S7P battery configuration in order to meet the need for volume reduction for accommodation purposes.

Moreover, the interoperability of the different tools and methods, made possible by the standardization of files format, is a real enabler for the concurrent engineering process by making it really easy for each subsystem expert to exchange data and to communicate through engineering models. It allows everyone to use their own dedicated and specialized tools by still ensuring compatibility with inputs/outputs of other tools, leading to a smooth workflow.

The presented use case describes the process for preliminary phases, involving the laboratory and the space agency, but it could also be implemented for phases A/B/C/D by adding a satellite manufacturer/provider in the loop as long as the files standard is still respected.

section: MASTER OF SCIENCE IN MECHANICAL ENGINEERING > Abstract
section_key: master of science in mechanical engineering / abstract
text: Cube Satellites (CubeSats) have become increasingly popular, particularly in academic settings, due to their affordability, rapid development timelines, and usefulness as platforms for student training and experimental payloads. Despite these advantages, CubeSat development presents several challenges, including limited resources such as personnel, funding, and time, as well as difficulties in maintaining comprehensive documentation and managing requirement changes. Student-led projects face additional obstacles, including inexperienced team members and high turnover rates, which can hinder effective knowledge transfer.

section: MASTER OF SCIENCE IN MECHANICAL ENGINEERING > Abstract
section_key: master of science in mechanical engineering / abstract
text: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) has emerged as a promising approach to address these challenges and improve the efficiency of CubeSat design and development. Rather than relying on documents to capture system designs, MBSE uses models to represent, analyze, and validate the design. It also emphasizes a strong systems engineering mindset, ensuring a holistic approach and that the optimal system of interest is being developed to meet the project needs. Although MBSE has been applied to satellite missions and domain-agnostic methodologies exist, significant challenges still remain in adapting it, particularly in small groups, due to the steep learning curve and resource requirements for training personnel and model development. Additionally, there is a lack of satellite-specific MBSE methodologies that define thorough steps and methods to design a satellite using MBSE.

section: MASTER OF SCIENCE IN MECHANICAL ENGINEERING > Abstract
section_key: master of science in mechanical engineering / abstract
text: This research develops an approach that integrates the Arcadia MBSE methodology with NASA's Life-Cycle and Space Mission Architecture Framework (SMAF) to create a satellite-specific methodology. The objective is to provide a structure for implementing MBSE while making the design process more effective for small, academic satellite projects. After developing an initial methodology, it was applied to the Neutron-2 (N2) CubeSat Mission to gain a better understanding and refine the approach. While the MBSE methodology offers significant advantages over document-centric engineering, challenges such as steep learning curves and complex tools must be addressed through additional tutorials and a robust library of reusable models. Additionally, dynamic simulations should be derived from the MBSE models to fully leverage digital engineering and validate the design. Future work will involve producing these comprehensive tutorials and developing the supporting simulations to validate the design, as well as implementing the methodology in a classroom setting to refine it.

While CubeSats offer easier access to space than ever before, several challenges remain in developing such complex systems. These challenges are particularly prevalent in teams with limited resources, such as those found within a university environment. By examining CubeSat teams within the University of Hawai'i at Mānoa (UHM), particularly the Hawai'i Space Flight Laboratory (HSFL) and the student aerospace program, Earth and Planetary Exploration Technology (EPET), several key challenges were identified. These challenges include poor and inconsistent documentation; a lack of requirements definition and traceability; defining and developing the payload, operations plan, and software late in the design phase; and not holding formal design reviews.

Poor documentation is a common challenge among small teams. In complex designs, such as satellites, the number of documents grows rapidly as the design develops. As the design evolves, these documents must be continuously updated, a task that can easily become overwhelming for a small team. Additionally, it has been observed that UHM teams often struggle to define requirements from the top-level down to the subsystems early in the design process and to track them throughout development for validation.

Requirements derive from the customer's needs, and without proper tracking and validation throughout the life-cycle, it cannot be known if the resulting system truly meets those needs. Additionally, if customers' needs change throughout the project, an understanding of how those changes affect lower-level requirements needs to be tracked.

Another lesson learned from previous missions is that the payload, mission operations, and software need to be defined and initiated much earlier in the design process. It is common for engineers to want to dive directly into hardware development. While hardware is a critical aspect of the design, the payload, operations, and software requirements should drive the satellite design. The payload defines the purpose of the satellite; by understanding it early, the most optimal satellite bus to support it can be developed. Furthermore, what ultimately matters is the satellite's functionality, driven by its software and operations. Rather than defining physical components first and forcing the software and systems to conform to the hardware, the software and operations should be determined early and guide the overall system design.

The final challenge identified is the lack of formal design reviews. Streamlining the design process by skipping formal reviews may appear to accelerate progress, but it often leads to missed errors and misalignment with stakeholder expectations. Without these reviews, critical mistakes may go unnoticed, and stakeholders lose the opportunity to confirm that the system under development truly meets their needs. Ultimately, this can result in delays later during integration and testing when these issues are finally discovered.

Student-led missions often face the same issues discussed above, along with additional obstacles such as a lack of experience and frequent turnover. Many university students involved in CubeSat projects lack significant experience in designing, integrating, testing, and operating spacecraft. Some may even lack proper engineering design experience, depending on their class standing and university program. While the goal of these student

projects is to provide them with the experiences needed for the workforce, completing a satellite mission with no prior experience and within a rapid time frame can be a daunting challenge. While mentors ideally should be guiding them through the process, their resources are often stretched and may not be as accessible as desired. Additionally, student teams experience frequent turnover as students can graduate or leave the team due to a heavy course load. This, combined with poor documentation, leads to a loss of knowledge and often to the rework of design elements.

Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) offers a valuable solution to these issues. Rather than using a document-centric approach, MBSE employs models to capture the system's design, focusing on a holistic systems engineering mindset. MBSE methods emphasize deriving requirements early from customers' needs and tracking them throughout the life-cycle. It emphasizes reusability, meaning the models created during previous missions can be reused and serve as a starting point for new missions, which could be particularly valuable for inexperienced student teams. MBSE can also greatly aid in documentation, creating a single source of knowledge within models that can then be populated to deliverables. Lastly, the overarching goal of any student project is to train and prepare students for the professional world after graduation and to create the next generation of engineers and researchers. According to the 2035 Systems Engineering Vision by the International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE), "the future of systems engineering is model-based" [1]. By training students in the art of systems engineering and systems thinking along with the current and future methods, the next generation of engineers will be better equipped for success.

section: List of Acronyms > 1.2 Current Applications of MBSE for Academic CubeSats
section_key: list of acronyms / 1 2 current applications of mbse for academic cubesats
text: While MBSE offers a promising solution to several challenges, it is not widely used among small CubeSat development teams. Currently, MBSE is utilized by major companies and government laboratories, including NASA [2], the Department of Defense (DOD) [3], and Boeing [4]. One of the significant challenges when implementing MBSE is the resource requirements, particularly in terms of cost and time, often related to training and adoption [5]. To train the necessary personnel in using the MBSE approach and its associated tools, a significant amount of time and, therefore, money must be invested. Typically, the team has ongoing projects that they need to manage while being onboarded to MBSE, making it even more challenging. Since it takes time to learn and implement MBSE, the benefits of it aren't typically recognized at first. Because university groups usually lack both personnel and funding, implementing MBSE in academic settings poses a greater challenge than in larger companies or organizations.

section: List of Acronyms > 1.2 Current Applications of MBSE for Academic CubeSats
section_key: list of acronyms / 1 2 current applications of mbse for academic cubesats
text: INCOSE has pushed a CubeSat Reference Model (CSRM) that provides Systems Modeling Language (SysML) templates for defining the logical architecture of a CubeSat [6]. Kaslow et al. have focused on expanding the CSRM beyond a logical architecture to an entire mission architecture [7]. Gregory et al. examined the use of the CSRM in conjunction with the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook [8]. Micavapilli and Lavanga, Amato, and Gonzalez et al. have all applied Arcadia/Capella to CubeSat missions [9-11]. While these applications of MBSE to satellite projects have shown promise, they primarily focus on the preliminary design phases and do not present a CubeSat-specific MBSE methodology. Although several general, domain-agnostic MBSE methodologies exist, there remains a lack of a detailed, satellite-oriented process that outlines the steps required to design a satellite along with the methods to complete each step using MBSE.

section: List of Acronyms > 1.2 Current Applications of MBSE for Academic CubeSats
section_key: list of acronyms / 1 2 current applications of mbse for academic cubesats
text: Figure 1.1: Elements to implement MBSE in an academic setting.

This research aims to provide a methodology, comprising processes and methods, to educate students in MBSE and utilize it to enhance the design efficiency of small satellites. Specifically, linking the Arcadia methodology, a general MBSE methodology, to NASA's Space Mission Architecture Framework within the context of an academic project represents a new avenue of research. This thesis proposes that establishing a detailed MBSE methodology that integrates SMAF and Arcadia across the design life-cycle can make the use of MBSE more practical and accessible for small team satellite missions. In essence, this research customizes the existing MBSE methodology, Arcadia, for CubeSat development by integrating it with NASA's SMAF and Life-Cycle Framework. Figure 1.1 highlights the elements that were identified as needed to implement MBSE in an academic setting with the foundation being the Methodology that is the focus of this thesis.

The SmallSat MBSE Methodology is being developed for application within an academic setting, specifically at the UHM. Within UHM, the primary users will be the Hawai'i Space Flight Laboratory, the Vertically Integrated Projects (VIP) Aerospace Technologies Course, and the EPET student program. HSFL comprises both professional engineers and students, whereas the EPET and VIP programs primarily consist of engineering and science students along with faculty and staff advisors. As such, the methodology must accommodate a range of experience levels. While its primary intended environment is a university, this methodology can also be applied to other small teams.
The research objectives are outlined below.
1. Develop a maintainable MBSE methodology specific to designing CubeSats within small teams.

(a) Integrate the Arcadia Methodology, NASA's Mission Life-Cycle, and NASA's Space Mission Architecture Framework together into a methodology that can reduce time and mission risk of a university design project.
2. Implement and refine the methodology for a specific example mission, Neutron-2 (Work in Progress (WIP)).
3. Understand how the proposed MBSE Methodology can be implemented into the four- semester EPET program at UHM, starting the design process at the beginning of the program (WIP).
4. Develop thorough documentation and tutorials for implementing this methodology, along with reference models that ease the reusability for future missions (WIP).

This chapter aims to provide the background information necessary to understand the context and methodology described in Chapter 3. This includes a description of CubeSats, systems engineering, model-based systems engineering, the systems modeling language, Arcadia and Capella, NASA's Space Mission Architecture, NASA's Project Life-Cycle, and current applications of MBSE for academic CubeSats.

Sending something to space might seem like an unattainable goal for most universities. However, with the growing popularity of small satellites, as seen in Figure 2.1, this ambition has become more realistic. Small satellites are defined as any satellite that is under 180 kg in mass [12]. This can be further categorized into different types, including mini-, micro-, nano-, pico-, and femto-satellites. See Table 2.1 for the exact specifications of these categories. Cube Satellites, or CubeSats, are a form factor for satellites that can fall within the micro- or nano-satellite range. There are several different sizes of CubeSats, but their standard form factors are composed of units, where 1 unit, or 1U, is approximately a 100 x 100 x 113.5 mm cube with a mass of 2 kg [13]. These cube units are then configured to make larger sizes, such as 2U, 3U, and larger. Figure 2.2 illustrates some standard
Figure 2.1: Quantity of nanosatellite launches per year since 1998 [15].
sizes of CubeSats, and Figure 2.3 shows Neutron-1 (3U) and the Hyperspectral Thermal Imager (HyTI) (6U), both CubeSats developed by HSFL.

Due to CubeSats' small size, the time and money required to develop and operate them are significantly less than those for larger satellites, making them more attractive to amateurs and university groups that may lack resources. On average, CubeSats take less than 2 years to develop, and they tend to be secondary payloads on launches; therefore, the launch cost is significantly lower [14]. Due to their lower cost, CubeSats are seen as an excellent option for testing experimental instruments and technologies, collecting scientific data, and training students in satellite development and operations.

Systems engineering is a holistic approach that encompasses the technical and managerial efforts required to address the customer's needs, expectations, and constraints, and to create and support a solution throughout its life-cycle. It focuses on integrating all of the disciplines and subsystems to create an overall successful System of Interest (SOI) [16]. In a satellite, there are several different subsystems. The systems engineer's job is to ensure that all subsystems and components work together correctly to create the most successful satellite, not just an optimal subsystem. Various models have been established for system development, such as the Waterfall, Spiral, and V-models. The former two
Figure 2.3: Neutron-1, left, a 3U CubeSat and HyTI, right, a 6U CubeSat. Both were developed at HSFL.
are primarily used for software development, while the V-model is extensively applied to systems engineering [17]. Figure 2.4 illustrates the V-Model diagram.

Traditionally, systems engineering is document-centric, utilizing documents to manage the entire system. With complex systems, such as satellites, this documentation can easily become overwhelming in both quantity and the maintenance required to keep them up to date with the current design. MBSE is an alternative method that is model-centric and further described below.

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3 Model-Based Systems Engineering
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 model based systems engineering
text: Models, as defined by INCOSE, are essential tools that serve as simplified representations of concepts, phenomena, structures, or systems. They may take various forms, including graphical, mathematical, physical, or logical depictions, all aimed at facilitating understanding, aiding decision-making, and enabling "what-if" analyses [18]. By

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3 Model-Based Systems Engineering
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 model based systems engineering
text: Figure 2.4: The V-Model is a widely used system development model used in systems engineering.

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3 Model-Based Systems Engineering
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 model based systems engineering
text: simplifying reality and focusing on key drivers and components, models allow engineers to examine, control, and predict events more efficiently. Modeling is particularly valuable in managing complex systems, as it helps anticipate and verify solutions and their associated costs before physical implementation [19].

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3 Model-Based Systems Engineering
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 model based systems engineering
text: MBSE extends this approach by applying models to support requirements, analysis, design, implementation, and verification throughout the system's life-cycle [18]. In recent years, the use of MBSE has gained popularity, highlighting its many benefits for designing complex systems [20]. These benefits include improved communication across interdisciplinary teams, increased efficiency in the design process, better risk management, and lower costs by identifying potential issues early, as well as enhanced documentation. MBSE also supports defining strong requirements early that meet the mission's needs

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3 Model-Based Systems Engineering
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 model based systems engineering
text: Figure 2.5: Pillars of MBSE.

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3 Model-Based Systems Engineering
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 model based systems engineering
text: and improve requirement traceability and validation throughout the system's design and integration [21].

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3 Model-Based Systems Engineering
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 model based systems engineering
text: In addition to these general advantages, MBSE will play a crucial role in student projects. It will not only train students in widely adopted industry design methods but also facilitate knowledge transfer, which can be a challenge for student teams that experience frequent turnover. Moreover, by reusing elements of models from previous missions, students with limited experience in satellite design would have a strong foundation for their own projects, helping them succeed within short development timelines.

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3 Model-Based Systems Engineering
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 model based systems engineering
text: Three pillars of MBSE need to be considered during implementation: methodology, language, and tools. One of the most popular modeling languages is the SysML, which is discussed in more detail below. Examples of MBSE tools include Cameo and Rhapsody, which implement SysML but do not prescribe a specific methodology; however, the method most often used with SysML is the Object-Oriented Systems Engineering Method (OOSEM) [22]. Figure 2.5 provides an overview of the relationship between methodology, language, and tool, along with examples of each.

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3.1 Systems Modeling Language
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 1 systems modeling language
text: The most common modeling language that is used for MBSE is the Systems Modeling Language. It is a language derived from the Unified Modeling Language (UML), which is a software modeling language [23]. Although SysML is very popular, it is purely a language, not a methodology or tool. There are several methodologies, with the OOSEM being the most popular [22]. Additionally, several tools are available, such as Cameo and Rhapsody; however, SysML is not a complete solution on its own.

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3.2 Arcadia and Capella
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 2 arcadia and capella
text: When examining the three MBSE pillars with respect to Capella and Arcadia, Capella is the tool in which the models are developed, and Arcadia is the implementation methodology and the language, as shown in Figure 2.6. The Arcadia method, also known as the ARChitecture and Design Integrated Approach, is intended to provide structure and define a loose process for creating models of complex systems. The Arcadia methodology is broken down into four main layers: Operational Analysis (OA), System Analysis (SA), Logical Architecture (LA), and Physical Architecture (PA). Each layer addresses the requirements and identifies the necessary actions, entities, or system components required to meet them, utilizing several diagrams (models) to illustrate this. By the end of each layer, multiple viewpoints and an architecture are defined, elaborating on the design of the mission and the SOI [24], [25].

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3.2 Arcadia and Capella
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 2 arcadia and capella
text: In the Operational Analysis, the needs of stakeholders are examined. Defining these early in the design process ensures that later stages of design fully align with the overall mission goals. The System Analysis then considers the system of interest as a "black box," focusing on what the system must achieve without delving into how these objectives or functions will be implemented. The Logical Architecture expands on this, treating

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3.2 Arcadia and Capella
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 2 arcadia and capella
text: Figure 2.6: Pillars of MBSE with respect to Arcadia and Capella.

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3.2 Arcadia and Capella
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 2 arcadia and capella
text: Figure 2.7: The four layers of the Arcadia Methodology [26].

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3.2 Arcadia and Capella
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 2 arcadia and capella
text: the system as a "white box" to define the necessary subsystems, logical components, and their logical functions that will meet the functional requirements. Lastly, the Physical Architecture specifies the actual physical components and how they will be integrated. At the Logical and Physical layers, supporting simulations can be performed, and their results fed into the Arcadia/Capella models to validate that all requirements are being met. This four-layer process is illustrated in Figure 2.7.

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3.2 Arcadia and Capella
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 2 arcadia and capella
text: Often, engineers jump into system design without fully understanding what the system must achieve to meet stakeholder needs or even what those needs are. By defining the operational and system requirements early and understanding how these goals can be addressed broadly, teams can improve communication with the stakeholders and reduce design changes later in the process. Within each of these four layers of the Arcadia methodology, several diagrams or models are created to capture these needs and their solutions. Each Arcadia layer has a series of diagrams created using the Arcadia language. The diagrams between the layers are similar but are tailored to provide the appropriate information for the intended goal of that layer.

section: List of Acronyms > 2.3.2 Arcadia and Capella
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 3 2 arcadia and capella
text: Arcadia and Capella were chosen for this research for several reasons. Firstly, Arcadia and Capella offer a complete solution for implementing MBSE, whereas SysML is purely a language, and then a tool and methodology need to be chosen separately. Additionally, Arcadia was developed from SysML. SysML, derived from a software modeling language, was found to be less intuitive for engineers without a software engineering background. Therefore, the creators of Arcadia took SysML, simplified it even further, and changed the language to be more intuitive to all, especially systems engineers. Because of this, Arcadia is said to be an easier stepping stone to learning MBSE compared to SysML [19], [25]. The last driving factor for choosing the Arcadia and Capella solution is that Capella is open source, which is an important factor when working with many students and having limited funds.

section: List of Acronyms > 2.4 NASA's Space Mission Architecture Framework
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 4 nasa s space mission architecture framework
text: An architecture describes how a system is structured and the guidelines needed to implement it [16]. An architecture framework establishes standard conventions, principles, and methods to describe system architectures, ensuring they are developed consistently

section: List of Acronyms > 2.4 NASA's Space Mission Architecture Framework
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 4 nasa s space mission architecture framework
text: and understood across a particular domain or community of stakeholders [16]. There are several different architecture frameworks, such as the Department of Defense Architecture Framework (DoDAF) [27] and NASA's Space Mission Architecture Framework (SMAF) [28].

section: List of Acronyms > 2.4 NASA's Space Mission Architecture Framework
section_key: list of acronyms / 2 4 nasa s space mission architecture framework
text: For this research, the NASA SMAF was chosen because it is specifically intended to guide teams in achieving a satellite mission's full capabilities. It applies to uncrewed space missions focused on either scientific research or technological advancements, which meet the needs of the UHM projects. To acquire these capabilities, the architecture encompasses the formulation of the mission idea, bringing it to life, as well as the design, build, integration, testing, and operation of the mission. The architecture categorizes stakeholders, participants, viewpoints, and view products, as shown in Figure 2.8. It also defines what is expected for each view product and the project milestone at which each product should be produced [28].

section_key: list of acronyms / 2 5 project life cycle
text: A project life-cycle is a key component in the development of a satellite mission. NASA defines it as a framework that organizes all necessary project activities into distinct phases. Transitions between phases are marked by KDPs. This phased approach helps make the project more manageable by structuring progress and reviews. The NASA Project Life-Cycle was chosen for this research because it closely aligns with NASA's SMAF, identifying the phases in which the view products need to be developed. Since this research focuses on the design of a satellite, it only covers Pre-Phase A through Phase C. Below is a list of each phase, as described by NASA [29]. Figures 2.9 and 2.10 illustrate the life-cycle and the corresponding view products that should be delivered at each KDP [29]. Appendix F illustrates a more detailed version of the NASA Project Life-Cycle.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology
text: This chapter presents the proposed SmallSat MBSE Methodology developed in this research. It adapts the Arcadia layers, methods, and process steps to align with NASA's Life-Cycle Phases and describes how Capella models can be used to capture the Space Mission Architecture Framework view products. Figure 3.1 shows the overview of the methodology. Figures 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, and 3.5 each use Capella logical architecture diagrams to capture the methodology of each phase, including the process steps, the method to complete the steps, and the SMAF view products that the steps can populate. The subsequent tables, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, and 3.4, were derived from these Capella diagrams by creating tables within the tool and exporting them as CSV files. This demonstrates how model data can be exported into a more readable format for stakeholder communication. Each subsequent section explores the individual Life-Cycle Phases and the methodological steps required to complete them. These steps were derived by tailoring the general Arcadia MBSE procedure for application to a satellite mission. It is important to note that this research focuses on academic CubeSat applications; therefore, the Robotic Mission profile

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.1 Methodology Step PA.1: Define Mission Customers
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 1 methodology step pa 1 define mission customers
text: The first step within this process is to define the customers of the mission. Stakeholders are defined as organizations, companies, people, or objects that have any stake or impact on the mission. In comparison, a customer is defined as any stakeholder that receives a product or service from the mission [16]. For the full definition of a customer, see Appendix A. For example, a launch provider would be a stakeholder but not a customer. A specific scientist or science community would be a customer for a science payload. It is crucial to

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.1 Methodology Step PA.1: Define Mission Customers
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 1 methodology step pa 1 define mission customers
text: understand who the customers are, as their needs will drive the mission, whereas the needs of non-customer stakeholders will likely not drive the mission but rather define constraints.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.1 Methodology Step PA.1: Define Mission Customers
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 1 methodology step pa 1 define mission customers
text: To define the customers, an Operational Entity Breakdown Diagram (OEBD) will be used. All customers can be defined by creating Operational Entities and Actors. If customers are included among other stakeholders, this should be captured using the "Contained in" feature. The focus of this step is to specifically define customers, as the next several steps focus on understanding their needs and why this mission is essential. However, non-customer stakeholders can be defined at this step if they are known. If they are not known, they can be defined as they are realized. This may include anyone developing the SOI, any supporting entities, or the relevant environment. However, do not define the SOI or make any design decisions at this time. For example, defining a satellite launch provider implies that the mission will involve a space-based system rather than a ground-based or near-space system. This should be avoided, as design decisions should not be made before the customer's needs are defined, which is the goal of the Operational Analysis. This means that the SOI should also not be defined at this stage. Capella will automatically generate a SOI entity when the System Analysis begins, but before then, the SOI should not be considered. If non-customer stakeholders are defined, it is recommended to have a specific OEBD to illustrate the customers, as this is the primary objective of this step. The information defined in this step will be used to populate the Stakeholder Expectations SMAF View Product.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.1 Methodology Step PA.1: Define Mission Customers
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 1 methodology step pa 1 define mission customers
text: When defining different types of stakeholders (e.g., customers, environment, and support), the Property Value Management Tool (PVMT) add-on should be used to assign each entity a type. PVMT allows Capella users to define custom properties that can be associated with model elements. This tool is applied throughout the methodology to enable

section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 1 methodology step pa 1 define mission customers
text: referencing specific model elements and their properties via Python scripts, which can then be used for analysis or propagated into design view products.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.2 Methodology Step PA.2: Define the Customer's Needs
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 2 methodology step pa 2 define the customer s needs
text: After defining the customers, it is vital to identify their needs, goals, and objectives for the project or mission. The customer's needs will drive the mission, making it essential for engineers to spend time identifying and understanding these needs.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.2 Methodology Step PA.2: Define the Customer's Needs
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 2 methodology step pa 2 define the customer s needs
text: To capture the customers' needs, goals, and objectives in Capella, an OCB should be used. The entities captured in the OEBD should be added to the OCB diagram. If noncustomer entities are defined, it is recommended to have a customer-specific OCB and/or represent the different types of entity elements in a different color, ideally using the PVMT add-on tool. The PVMT tool allows for the element block style to be edited based on the properties (i.e. block color, block outline color, line color). Unfortunately, this block style defined by the properties does not apply to select diagrams, including the OCB; therefore, this visual differentiation will need to be manually changed if desired.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.2 Methodology Step PA.2: Define the Customer's Needs
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 2 methodology step pa 2 define the customer s needs
text: Once the entities are in the OCB, the entities' capability needs should be captured as operational capabilities. The customer's capability needs should be the focus of this step; however, other capabilities can also be captured. To complete this diagram, thorough conversations should be had with the customers so that their needs can be thoroughly fleshed out and understood. These diagrams should not be created by a single person, but rather in a collaborative work session where everyone is involved and aims to be on the same page. If a need can be broken down into smaller needs, for instance, if needs A, B, and C feed into a larger need Z, they should all be captured using capability extensions. The focus of this step should be the customer's root needs, not what they want the system to do. For example, the customer may wish to improve radiation models in space. Therefore, a system

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.2 Methodology Step PA.2: Define the Customer's Needs
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 2 methodology step pa 2 define the customer s needs
text: of interest will need to collect neutron count data in space. The former should be defined as the customers' needs, not the latter. In later steps, the type of data required to complete their needs will be determined; however, this step should capture the root of what they want to achieve. The content defined in this step will be used to populate several view products, including the Stakeholder Expectations Document, the Science Traceability Matrix, and the Science or Technology Concept Document.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.3 Methodology Step PA.3: Understand the Customer Needs
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 3 methodology step pa 3 understand the customer needs
text: After identifying the customer's needs, they must be understood. As engineers, it's easy to jump into designing and building the system. However, it is critical to understand the customers' needs to know if the correct system is being designed and built. Having a deep understanding of their needs and why they are important will also be essential to deriving requirements. Commonly, customers may not fully understand their own needs, or they aren't being understood correctly by the engineers. By asking questions to ensure the engineering team understands the customer's needs and why they are necessary, it can also help further define the customer's root needs and ensure that everyone has a shared understanding. Due to this, Methodology Steps PA.2 and PA.3 often will loop back and forth as the project capabilities or needs are better understood and defined.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.3 Methodology Step PA.3: Understand the Customer Needs
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 3 methodology step pa 3 understand the customer needs

While doing this, additional entities will likely need to be defined, such as the environment. Functions, functional interactions, and chains can then be used to show the phenomena or

section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 3 methodology step pa 3 understand the customer needs
text: - Define where/how collections OR demonstrations need to occur: Are there specific orbits, locations, or altitudes that the data collections or demonstrations must occur in? This may need to be its own OAB that captures the specifics of the data collections that the customer needs to collect. This information should be used to populate the Science Concept or Technology Concept View Product.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.3 Methodology Step PA.3: Understand the Customer Needs
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 3 methodology step pa 3 understand the customer needs
text: - Define the risk associated with the science collection or technology demonstration: This can be done by using the PVMT add-on and assigning a risk property to Operational Functions that pose a risk to the mission. The risk can then be further defined in the summary or description of the function. Two properties can be assigned to all functions that pose a risk: probability and consequence. These properties should be defined using PVMT and ideally change the background color of risk functions. This information should be used to populate the Science Concept or Technology Concept View Product and the Technical Risk Analysis View Product.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.3 Methodology Step PA.3: Understand the Customer Needs
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 3 methodology step pa 3 understand the customer needs
text: - Define the necessary data: This should be done by using the CDB and capturing the necessary data to complete the customer's needs. It may be unknown at this point whether the data is measured or calculated, as that can come from the design, which is completed in later phases. However, if it is known, it can be captured by using the PVMT add-on. The information captured in the CDB should populate the Science Concept or Technology Concept View Product and Science Traceability Matrix View Product.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.3 Methodology Step PA.3: Understand the Customer Needs
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 3 methodology step pa 3 understand the customer needs
text: This list of steps does not need to be done in the order listed above, but should all be captured by the end of the Operational Analysis. Additionally, if the payload is predefined for the mission and the objectives are being tailored around it, then it can be defined during this phase. This should be done using a different Capella Library and defining the Logical and Physical Architecture of the payload. This is not included in the methodology, but is something that can be considered.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.3 Methodology Step PA.3: Understand the Customer Needs
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 3 methodology step pa 3 understand the customer needs
text: With the completion of this step, the Operational Analysis should be complete. After defining the entities, customers, and their mission needs in the Operational Analysis, the System Analysis can be started to understand what the system needs to do to meet these needs. In the System Analysis, the SOI is treated like a black box, and by the end, it should be understood what type of system is needed by identifying what it needs to be capable of. For instance, at the end of the Operational Analysis, it may be unknown whether the payload needs to be flown on a satellite or a high-altitude balloon. System Analysis starts unbiased towards either of these options, but by identifying what the system needs to do to fulfill the customers' needs, it is realized that these needs can only be met by a satellite orbiting the Earth. This approach ensures that needs are defined first. Then a solution is designed to meet those needs, rather than defining solutions before the needs are determined, thereby creating unnecessary constraints.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.4 Methodology Step PA.4: Define the Mission Statement
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 4 methodology step pa 4 define the mission statement
text: The customer needs determined by the Operational Analysis should be used to derive the Mission Statement. The Mission Statement, as defined by University Nanosatellite Program (UNP), should be a brief statement that captures the entire purpose of the mission and is usually focused on the science or technology needs [32]. In Arcadia and Capella, this statement should be captured using the Mission element in the MCB. The

section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 4 methodology step pa 4 define the mission statement

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.5 Methodology Step PA.5: Define the Mission Objectives
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 5 methodology step pa 5 define the mission objectives
text: The mission objectives are derived from the Mission Statement and define the broad goals that the system must achieve to be successful [33]. To capture these in Capella, the System Capability model element should be used and captured in the MCB. To define them as being derived from the Mission Statement, the Capability Exploitation relationship should be established between the capabilities and the mission. The Mission Objectives will be part of the System Requirements Document SMAF View Product.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.6 Methodology Step PA.6: Define the Success Criteria
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 6 methodology step pa 6 define the success criteria
text: After capturing what is to be accomplished with the Mission Objectives, the desired performance of these accomplishments should be captured as Success Criteria (SC). These success criteria should be split into Minimum Success Criteria (MSC), which represents the minimum that must be achieved to consider the mission a success, and Full Success Criteria (FSC), which represents the entire performance that is desired to be met.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.1.6 Methodology Step PA.6: Define the Success Criteria
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 1 6 methodology step pa 6 define the success criteria
text: To capture these in Capella, the System Capability model element should be used. These system capabilities should be included in the same MCB, and the extension relationship from the Mission Objectives to the respective SC should be defined. The Success Criteria will be part of the System Requirements Document SMAF View Product.

section: Chapter 3 Proposed SmallSat Model-Based System Engineering Methodology > 3.2 Phase A: Concept and Technology Development
section_key: chapter 3 proposed smallsat model based system engineering methodology / 3 2 phase a concept and technology development
text: The second phase of the Life-Cycle, Phase A, is defined as the concept and technology development. There are two key decision points within this phase: the System Requirements Review and the Mission Design Review (MDR). For the SRR, the requirements are defined. This includes the Top-Level Mission requirements, the system requirements, and the subsystem requirements. This review continues to focus on the mission's needs, specifically what the system must do to meet the customer's needs defined in the previous phase. The MDR is an initial, top-level solution or design of the SOI. For a Robotic Mission, the NASA Life-Cycle states that the SRR and the MDR may be combined. For this methodology, we have chosen to combine the two due to their overlap with the System Analysis and Logical Architecture layers of Arcadia. For this combined review, the design team will initiate System Analysis, defining top-level mission requirements, understanding what the system must do to meet those requirements, and subsequently defining system requirements. After that is complete, the Logical Architecture layer must be initiated to dive into the subsystem requirements. Within the Logical Architecture layer, subsystems will be defined that are needed to meet the top-level and system requirements, along with the functions they must perform to meet them. As a result of this step, subsystem requirements will be derived, along with some logical design decisions that correlate with the MDR view products. Therefore, the SRR and MDR map to the System Analysis and the Logical Architecture layers of Arcadia. Note that the Logical Architecture is not yet complete at the end of this phase and will be further defined in the next one. The design-related view products needed for this combined KDP include
