text: The next section explores how MBSE extends SE principles into executable modeling frameworks, offering enhanced traceability, interdisciplinary collaboration, and system validation, all essential to the digital transformation of aerospace systems.

Requirements Engineering (RE) involves the disciplined handling of system needs, capturing, documenting, verifying, and organizing them to align with stakeholder goals throughout the development process. A requirement represents a specific function or condition that a system must fulfill in order to function properly. In contrast, the requirements specification is a structured document that consolidates individual needs and aligns them with defined quality standards. RE applies to both hardware and software systems, especially in socio-technical and cyber-physical environments, where it also considers human roles and ecological interfaces.

Figure 2.2A.1 presents a conceptual view of RE, illustrating the continuous and interconnected flow of its core processes: gathering, formalizing, assessing, and managing requirements. It summarizes the high-level lifecycle relationships among RE tasks and their evolving roles across development stages.
Figure 2.2A.1. Overview of Requirements Engineering.

Nine principles outlined by the International Requirements Engineering Board (IREB) define the foundational values of the discipline. These include value orientation, stakeholdercentric focus, shared understanding, contextual awareness, differentiation of problems, requirements & solutions, validation, requirement evolution, innovation, and the need for disciplined execution. This framework formalizes RE principles to guide practice across domains and project types.
Figure 2.2A.2. IREB Framework for Requirements Engineering.

Stakeholder engagement remains central to RE activities, drawing information from individuals, legacy documents, and interfacing systems. Figure 2.2A.3 categorizes elicitation techniques ranging from direct questioning and collaborative workshops to observation, artifact analysis, and creative methods such as prototyping and scenario modeling. It classifies elicitation methods based on stakeholder involvement and system context.
Figure 2.2A.3. Elicitation Techniques in Requirements Engineering (IREB).

A structured model for understanding user satisfaction, known as the Kano Model, segments requirements into delighters (unconscious differentiators), satisfiers (explicit desires), and dissatisfiers (basic expectations). This model informs prioritization and helps distinguish critical from value-added system features. It maps feature types to their influence on user satisfaction and product acceptance.
Figure 2.2A.4. The Kano Model for Feature Classification (IREB).

Validation mechanisms ensure that documented requirements are correct, complete, and feasible. Techniques range from formal inspections and informal walkthroughs to exploratory validation through prototypes and real-user alpha/beta testing. Effective validation reduces defects, fosters stakeholder trust, and informs downstream verification activities.

Requirements management addresses traceability, evolution, and control of requirement changes over time. Figure 2.2A.5 presents the requirements lifecycle as a state chart, highlighting transitions from elicitation through implementation and eventual retirement. It visualizes the evolution of requirements from origin to decommissioning.
Figure 2.2A.5. Requirements Lifecycle State Chart (IREB).

Clear connections between what a system must do and how it is built are essential throughout development. Traceability helps teams link original needs to the components and tests that address them. As shown in Figure 2.2A.6, this includes both forward links, from a requirement to its related design or code, and backward links, from implementation artifacts back to the stated goals. Maintaining these links allows engineers to track changes, verify coverage, and support decisions based on traceable evidence.
Figure 2.2A.6. Types of Requirements Traceability (IREB).

RE process configuration varies depending on project scale, customer involvement, and development model. Three common configurations include participatory (iterative, stakeholder-driven), contractual (formal, plan-driven), and product-oriented (agile, market-focused) processes. These options are depicted in Figure 2.2A.7. It maps process types to development contexts for tailored RE execution.
Figure 2.2A.7. Process Configuration in Requirements Engineering (IREB).

Agile Requirements Engineering adapts traditional RE practices to iterative environments by emphasizing collaboration, continuous refinement, and outcomes-driven development. Agile values, individual interaction, working systems, collaboration, and responsiveness, shift RE from upfront definition to incremental discovery. Figure 2.2A.8 illustrates the focus shift in Agile RE, aligning feature development with stakeholder value rather than fixed release metrics. It reorients RE priorities toward stakeholder-centric development cycles.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.1 MBSE Foundations and Frameworks in Aerospace
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 1 mbse foundations and frameworks in aerospace
text: Model-based systems engineering (MBSE) has been increasingly adopted in the aerospace industry as a means to address the growing complexity of modern systems. Instead of relying solely on documents, MBSE emphasizes formal modeling, grounded in systems engineering standards such as DoD Instruction 5000.88 (2020), to improve lifecycle visibility and coordination. The U.S. Department of Defense (2018) highlighted MBSE as central to its Digital Engineering Strategy, emphasizing the importance of utilizing validated digital models as a foundation for analysis and decision-making throughout development and acquisition, with subsequent studies (Wenyue et al., 2022) confirming that MBSE improved coordination and stakeholder validation in aerospace projects.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.1 MBSE Foundations and Frameworks in Aerospace
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 1 mbse foundations and frameworks in aerospace
text: One framework proposed to guide MBSE implementation is the MBSE Grid by Morkevicius et al. (2017), which organizes modeling activities to ensure traceability and model consistency. $ ^{11} $ Its structured layout has helped engineers move from ad hoc practices to more methodical approaches across project stages. Scalability remains a frequent concern. Estefan (2008) observed that not all MBSE strategies are suitable for every system size. Coordination challenges frequently arise when toolchains are mismatched, or modeling semantics are misaligned.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.1 MBSE Foundations and Frameworks in Aerospace
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 1 mbse foundations and frameworks in aerospace
text: In practical terms, MBSE has proven useful for small satellite programs. Siddique (2024) pointed out that modularity and traceability, two recurring challenges, can be more effectively managed through model-driven design, particularly when schedules are tight and multidisciplinary inputs must converge quickly. Akundi et al. nonetheless argue that widespread variation in how MBSE is defined and used. Some organizations struggle with inconsistent application usage across the entire lifecycle. Others face gaps in training or resistance to adopting the tool.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.1 MBSE Foundations and Frameworks in Aerospace
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 1 mbse foundations and frameworks in aerospace
text: For MBSE to support modern digital convergence, access to synchronized repositories and cohesive tool environments is necessary. These infrastructures enable collaboration and help maintain traceability, particularly when multiple teams work on complex, interrelated systems.

Evidence of MBSE's operational maturity can be found in several aerospace applications. One early example is the CubeSat project described by Spangelo et al. (2012), which applied SysML to support simulation-led design, requirement structuring, and conceptual traceability. Their study offered one of the initial end-to-end MBSE frameworks for small satellites,
demonstrating tangible advantages of model-driven engineering in constrained design environments.

Further insights are provided by Bruggeman and La Rocca (2023), who examined the use of MBSE in aircraft programs. Their findings emphasized the importance of digital workflow alignment, particularly in cases where evolving specifications necessitate structured updates to product models. This use of MBSE highlights how practical, domain-specific implementations are replacing earlier conceptual applications.

The Mars Ascent Vehicle project provides another example. Rountree (2022) discussed how MBSE was incorporated into propulsion and payload coordination, using model synchronization to inform test procedure development. In parallel, Bendarkar et al. (2023) explored MBSE's contribution to early regulatory validation processes, extending its use into certification and compliance efforts.

Earth observation missions have also benefited. As Denis et al. (2020) emphasize, increased design volatility and compressed lifecycles make model-centric strategies vital for managing uncertainty and reducing late-stage integration risk. Other advancements, such as machine learning-enabled autonomy, further underscore MBSE's role in anomaly detection and adaptive mission control (Ferreira et al., 2019).

Despite these gains, several limitations persist. Valerdi and Davidz (2009) pointed to difficulty in quantifying MBSE's return on investment and sustaining stakeholder alignment, especially in layered organizations. For adaptive and critical systems, such challenges highlight the need for context-specific modeling approaches. Recent work by Pratt and Dabkowski (2022) linked MBSE adoption to expectations of usability, perceived value, and organizational readiness, factors that often require deliberate training programs and strategic change leadership.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.3 Integration with Agile, Concurrent, and Cyber-Physical Development
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 3 integration with agile concurrent and cyber physical development
text: Recent shifts in aerospace system design have brought attention to Agile development, collaborative engineering, and cyber-physical integration, areas where MBSE continues to gain relevance. Krupa (2019) developed a lightweight Agile MBSE framework for early aircraft design that merges stakeholder input, iterative models, and rapid prototyping. These practices are wellsuited for high-speed aerospace programs that rely on distributed, cross-functional teams.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.3 Integration with Agile, Concurrent, and Cyber-Physical Development
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 3 integration with agile concurrent and cyber physical development
text: In a related effort, Bussemaker et al. (2023) demonstrated through the AGILE 4.0 project how MBSE can merge digital and physical elements. $ ^{12} $ Their work shows how remote teams collaborate on system models and validate them with physical prototypes, using synchronized simulations and feedback loops.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.3 Integration with Agile, Concurrent, and Cyber-Physical Development
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 3 integration with agile concurrent and cyber physical development
text: To support such integration, Shevchenko (2021) emphasized the need for MBSE workflows that adapt to shifting needs. She highlighted version control and automated validation as essential for maintaining model consistency throughout evolving project phases. In aerospace environments, where legacy systems, dispersed operations, and dynamic stakeholder inputs are common, these mechanisms provide needed stability and help sustain engineering coherence over time.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.4 Requirements Engineering and Synchronized Prioritization
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 4 requirements engineering and synchronized prioritization
text: MBSE's effectiveness is closely tied to how well it integrates requirements engineering (RE) practices. Holt et al. (2014) developed a model-based RE framework for Systems of Systems, offering scalable modeling patterns to handle variability, interface mismatches, and system dependencies. Their approach aligns with the growing interest in enhancing early lifecycle validation, particularly in high-dependency systems such as aircraft and spacecraft.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.4 Requirements Engineering and Synchronized Prioritization
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 4 requirements engineering and synchronized prioritization
text: Recent work by Washio et al. (2023) and Ji et al. (2023) demonstrates that embedding requirements prioritization directly into SysML models allows early detection of contradictions inconsistent assumptions, and traceability gaps. This model-synchronized prioritization becomes especially valuable for aerospace missions operating under uncertainty, as it provides a structured mechanism for managing trade-offs and mitigating cascading design failures.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.4 Requirements Engineering and Synchronized Prioritization
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 4 requirements engineering and synchronized prioritization
text: Fazal et al. (2024) proposed incorporating uncertainty quantification (UQ) into MBSE to address variable operational contexts and system robustness. When integrated with model-based prioritization, UQ enables designers to assign confidence weights and scenario-based risk profiles directly within the SysML environment.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.4 Requirements Engineering and Synchronized Prioritization
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 4 requirements engineering and synchronized prioritization
text: Collectively, these developments reveal that MBSE alone is insufficient without embedded RE strategies that accommodate change, prioritize critical needs, and ensure testability. This thematic interconnection prepares the foundation for the next section, which focuses on structured prioritization methods suitable for adaptive aerospace systems.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.5 MBSE Implementation in CubeSat and Small Satellite Projects
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 5 mbse implementation in cubesat and small satellite projects
text: The application of MBSE in small satellite missions, especially CubeSats, represents a critical advancement in extending model-centric engineering to resource-constrained and modular aerospace platforms. As CubeSat programs prioritize rapid development, limited volume, and multidisciplinary coordination, MBSE offers an integrated solution for managing complexity, ensuring traceability, and synchronizing design and verification workflows. The rise of small satellite platforms has fundamentally reshaped space economics and mission design agility, creating new incentives for MBSE-driven architectural planning in low-cost, rapid deployment contexts (Sweeting, 2018).

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.5 MBSE Implementation in CubeSat and Small Satellite Projects
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 5 mbse implementation in cubesat and small satellite projects
text: Spangelo et al. (2012) pioneered the use of SysML-based modeling in CubeSat mission architecture, emphasizing end-to-end requirement traceability, functional decomposition, and early validation. Their study highlighted how model-based techniques could replace fragmented documentation and encourage coherent systems thinking from mission conception through deployment.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.5 MBSE Implementation in CubeSat and Small Satellite Projects
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 5 mbse implementation in cubesat and small satellite projects
text: Cordero et al. (2022) further demonstrated MBSE's role in early-phase CubeSat design, proposing a concurrent engineering framework that integrates electrical, mechanical, and software domains. Their work underscores the significance of synchronization across modeling layers, particularly in short-cycle missions with overlapping development phases. Applying MBSE in the conceptual design phase of small satellites not only streamlines interface definition and structural abstraction but also enhances consistency across stakeholder viewpoints (Guo et al., 2018). Similarly, Malik, Topolski, and Nguyen (2025) applied MBSE to guide the lifecycle development of a LEO satellite, ensuring alignment between stakeholder needs and validation plans through model-governed workflows.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.5 MBSE Implementation in CubeSat and Small Satellite Projects
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 5 mbse implementation in cubesat and small satellite projects
text: Tailored MBSE approaches have become vital in small satellite development. Siddique (2025) analyzed MBSE adoption in small satellite missions and found that using SysML-based models significantly improves traceability, risk management, and stakeholder communication compared to traditional document-centric methods. This small-scale, fast-paced context demands flexible MBSE strategies that align modeling tools and workflows with agile team structures, precisely the kind of adaptation needed for the university-led CubeSat initiatives. NASA's Systems Engineering Handbook (2020) also supports this trajectory by encouraging model-based practices in small satellite projects, noting improvements in requirement stability, communication, and integration across subsystem teams.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.3.5 MBSE Implementation in CubeSat and Small Satellite Projects
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 5 mbse implementation in cubesat and small satellite projects
text: The collective findings confirm that MBSE is not only feasible but increasingly essential for CubeSat development. These applications provide a concrete link between digital engineering theory and small-scale aerospace practice, bridging the gap between industry-grade modeling principles and academic or low-cost mission contexts. This integration directly informs later chapters in this research, particularly the modeling strategy and validation framework applied in SidSat. Similarly, Herrera et al. (2019) presented the design and experimental testing of a 500 lbf LOX/methane engine, demonstrating the importance of model-supported workflows in propulsion system development, which parallels the traceability and validation strategies employed in SidSat.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.1 Foundations of RE in Aerospace MBSE
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 1 foundations of re in aerospace mbse
text: The successful execution of aerospace projects hinges on rigorous Requirements Engineering (RE), which governs the elicitation, validation, and management of system requirements across the lifecycle. Glinz et al. (2020) underscore that RE is not limited to capturing technical specifications, it requires sustained stakeholder engagement to align requirements with mission objectives and regulatory compliance. In dynamic aerospace environments, particularly within Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS), requirements must remain both traceable and responsive to evolving operational conditions. These demands highlight the limitations of static documentation approaches and underscore the need for flexible, model-integrated RE strategies that can support system evolution, stakeholder co-design, and early verification.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.1 Foundations of RE in Aerospace MBSE
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 1 foundations of re in aerospace mbse
text: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) augments the practice of RE by offering formal modeling techniques that reduce ambiguity and improve traceability across the design process. The integration of MBSE with RE is further advanced through domain-specific frameworks like the Requirements-Functional-Logical-Physical (RFLP) approach, which creates

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.1 Foundations of RE in Aerospace MBSE
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 1 foundations of re in aerospace mbse
text: continuity from stakeholder intent to physical implementation. Swaminathan et al. (2023) demonstrate how this framework supports multidisciplinary design optimization (MDO), ensuring that early requirement decisions are mapped across functional and logical layers in aerospace systems.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.1 Foundations of RE in Aerospace MBSE
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 1 foundations of re in aerospace mbse
text: Despite its benefits, the combination of RE and MBSE presents challenges in verification and validation (V&V). Bjarnason et al. (2014) found that companies frequently struggle to align requirements with V&V artifacts due to asynchronous documentation, communication gaps, and limited feedback loops. These gaps limit the utility of models as living documents and delay the ability to perform real-time verification during system evolution.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.1 Foundations of RE in Aerospace MBSE
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 1 foundations of re in aerospace mbse
text: To address these concerns, Wheaton and Herber (2024) introduced a digital requirements engineering architecture built on a SysML meta-model aligned with INCOSE standards. Their approach creates tighter integration between requirement specifications and modeling platforms, thereby improving lifecycle consistency and enabling early-stage validation in digital environments. This is further supported by Salado's (2021) systems-theoretic framework, which systematically maps stakeholder needs into formal system-level requirements, enhancing robustness in projects characterized by ambiguous goals and operational variability.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.2 Requirements Prioritization in Aerospace Context
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 2 requirements prioritization in aerospace context
text: Managing trade-offs among performance, cost, and risk is a persistent challenge in aerospace systems, especially when time and funding are limited. While requirement collection and modeling are foundational activities, prioritization is what often determines whether project goals remain aligned with evolving conditions. Conflicting stakeholder expectations, compressed timelines, and uncertain development paths demand more than intuitive choices.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.2 Requirements Prioritization in Aerospace Context
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 2 requirements prioritization in aerospace context
text: To address this, Khan (2006) analyzed various prioritization techniques, noting how informal methods often fall short in maintaining consistency. His review emphasized the need for transparent, reproducible strategies, such as pairwise ranking, weighted scoring, and structured matrices, that help teams separate mission-critical functions from lower-priority requests.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.2 Requirements Prioritization in Aerospace Context
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 2 requirements prioritization in aerospace context
text: For agile and iterative development, these needs become more pronounced. Racheva et al. (2010) tackled this by proposing a client-centered approach that integrates ongoing feedback into each delivery loop. Their work underscored the importance of maintaining stakeholder visibility while preserving decision traceability.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.2 Requirements Prioritization in Aerospace Context
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 2 requirements prioritization in aerospace context
text: Building on these ideas, Salado and Nilchiani (2015) introduced Adaptive Requirements Prioritization (ARP). This method adjusts requirement weights over time in response to changing mission needs, stakeholder re-evaluation, and operational shifts. Their model's ability to embed responsiveness into formal prioritization processes, while retaining audit trails, makes it especially suitable for aerospace programs with long lifecycles and complex risk profiles.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.3 Requirements Prioritization in Complex Adaptive Systems
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 3 requirements prioritization in complex adaptive systems
text: The rise of complex adaptive systems (CAS) in aerospace, including reconfigurable platforms, satellite swarms, and autonomous vehicles, adds a new layer of complexity to the prioritization of requirements. These systems are inherently dynamic, operating in environments where conditions shift rapidly and system configurations evolve in response. As a result, requirements in CAS must be designed not only to meet baseline objectives but also to adapt fluidly to external triggers, mission phase transitions, and emergent behaviors that arise from system interactions and environmental variability. Traditional static ranking or fixed requirement structures often prove inadequate under such conditions, prompting a need for responsive, contextaware prioritization frameworks.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.3 Requirements Prioritization in Complex Adaptive Systems
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 3 requirements prioritization in complex adaptive systems
text: Yang, Li, and Jin (2017) emphasized the difficulty of modeling adaptive requirements using traditional RE methods. They proposed a thematic structure that captures requirement volatility through self-adjusting models capable of reflecting system-environment interactions. Such flexibility is critical in adaptive aerospace platforms where priorities can shift mid-mission due to external cues or internal reconfiguration.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.3 Requirements Prioritization in Complex Adaptive Systems
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 3 requirements prioritization in complex adaptive systems
text: Environmental modeling plays a central role in enabling this form of adaptability. Kneer, Kamsties, and Schmid (2020) conducted a systematic review of environment modeling for adaptive systems and concluded that existing RE tools often fall short in supporting dynamic, context-sensitive requirements. This limits the ability of system architects to foresee priority shifts or update requirements models without disrupting the architecture. Siddique (2024) identifies an inflection point in requirements engineering where integration with digital models, prioritization logic, and stakeholder adaptation is essential to address volatility and emergent behavior in complex adaptive systems.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.4 Traceability, Verification, and Digital Thread Integration
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 4 traceability verification and digital thread integration
text: As requirement models grow in complexity and adaptability, particularly within aerospace applications involving Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS), maintaining traceability becomes a pivotal enabler of system verification and validation. Traceability ensures that each requirement can be consistently linked to its origin, implementation, and test artifacts, allowing engineers to monitor changes and validate conformance across the lifecycle. Bjarnason et al. (2014) highlighted recurring obstacles in aligning requirements to test artifacts, particularly in environments with evolving stakeholder goals, heterogeneous toolsets, and cross-functional dependencies. These challenges are further magnified in iterative, model-driven contexts, where requirements evolve concurrently with design updates. Without robust traceability mechanisms embedded within the

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.4 Traceability, Verification, and Digital Thread Integration
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 4 traceability verification and digital thread integration
text: modeling environment, verification strategies may diverge from system realities, increasing the risk of oversight or non-compliance during final integration and deployment.

section: Acknowledgements > 2.4.4 Traceability, Verification, and Digital Thread Integration
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 4 4 traceability verification and digital thread integration
text: To resolve these gaps, digital integration must be embedded directly within the requirements prioritization workflow. Wheaton and Herber's (2024) model supports bidirectional traceability and simulation-based verification through an INCOSE-aligned SysML framework. Their approach enables early detection of requirement conflicts and facilitates downstream validation through digital threads. This direction also reinforces the importance of aligning prioritization logic with validation processes, laying the foundation for a model-integrated digital engineering strategy, as discussed in the next section.

As the complexity of aerospace applications increases, driven by modular architectures, stakeholder diversity, and evolving mission parameters, requirements prioritization (RP) becomes an indispensable activity. Selecting the "right" set of requirements to address first affects system architecture, verification planning, and long-term adaptability. Multi-Criteria Analysis (MCA) provides a foundational decision-making framework by explicitly accommodating multiple conflicting objectives, offering practical guidance that bridges overly technical and overly simplistic approaches (Dean, 2022). However, despite the critical role of RP in systems engineering, especially under a Model-Based paradigm, existing methods often fail to address domain-specific constraints, such as limited resources, tight schedules, interdependent functionalities, and dynamic operational contexts, which are commonly encountered in small satellite missions.
A foundational survey by Khan (2006) classified RP methods into value-based, cost-benefit, stakeholder-driven, and mathematical optimization techniques. While this categorization

is comprehensive across industries, it often lacks aerospace-specific considerations such as lifecycle traceability, environmental sensitivity, and toolchain interoperability. Among the most widely used techniques, the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) stands out for its structured pairwise comparisons and decision matrices. Formalized by Saaty (2008), AHP enables prioritization based on stakeholder-assigned relative importance. Despite its clarity, AHP assumes decision independence and struggles with scalability in high-dimensional systems, issues especially relevant in aerospace, where interdependencies and trade-offs dominate. The integration of AHP for criteria weighting and simple additive weighting (SAW) for alternative ranking has demonstrated practical effectiveness in generating consistent, decision-supportive outcomes across multi-criteria problems (Cahyapratama & Sarno, 2018).

To improve AHP's adaptability, Yuen (2014) introduced Least Penalty Optimization Operators to reduce prioritization bias when stakeholder inputs are inconsistent. Although this method improves robustness, it still relies on static input assumptions and lacks the flexibility to accommodate evolving mission needs. Building on this, Salado and Nilchiani (2015) developed Adaptive Requirements Prioritization (ARP), embedding feedback loops and conflict resolution mechanisms into the process. ARP aligns well with Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS), enabling iterative re-prioritization as missions evolve, an essential feature in long-duration, modular aerospace deployments.

Other hybrid approaches extend prioritization under uncertainty. Jawale et al. (2017) incorporated fuzzy logic into AHP using cumulative voting to account for stakeholder ambiguity and incomplete preferences. Their approach enhances resilience to vagueness but can be challenging to implement in regulated environments where transparency and validation are crucial. Similarly, Groen et al. (2017) proposed the Prioritization and Requirements Elicitation Synergy

Tool and Ontology (PRESTO) framework, combining early stakeholder engagement with expert based scoring. PRESTO facilitates early consensus and reduces requirement volatility but lacks built-in support for system-level trade-offs or alignment with verification structures, necessitating integration with model-based traceability tools.

Goal alignment offers another avenue for prioritization. Elsood, Hefny, and Nasr (2014) proposed a goal-based RP method that maps requirements to high-level objectives, enhancing traceability. However, this approach may oversimplify multi-domain dependencies unless complemented by context-aware modeling frameworks such as SysML. Addressing probabilistic risk, Qazi et al. (2020) presented a decision model that uses Monte Carlo simulation and Bayesian reasoning to prioritize interdependent uncertainties. This method supports complex risk environments, common in the aerospace industry, but may be impractical in early-phase design due to its data and computational requirements.

Collectively, these methods represent a growing but uneven landscape of prioritization strategies. While the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) remains widely favored for its transparency and structured comparisons, it struggles with interconnected decisions and does not scale well for high-complexity systems. More advanced techniques offer adaptability and higher fidelity but tend to increase implementation demands, such as requiring specialized training, computational tools, or a reduction in interpretability. In response to these trade-offs, Shirin et al. (2017) proposed a "balanced control" principle in networked systems, which optimizes between strict output precision and minimal control effort. This principle serves as an apt metaphor for prioritization in aerospace, where precision must often be balanced against resource and schedule limitations. Together, these insights emphasize the ongoing need for an aerospace-oriented prioritization framework, one that supports traceable integration with MBSE environments,
manages evolving conditions, and accommodates stakeholder variation, all without compromising usability or compliance requirements.

Digital Engineering (DE) represents a foundational shift in how complex aerospace systems are conceived, developed, and sustained across their lifecycle. Originating from early computational modeling techniques such as digital circuit simulation (Kostopoulos, 1975), DE has evolved into a comprehensive engineering paradigm that integrates authoritative digital models and connected data into every phase of system development. This transformation was formally recognized in the U.S. Department of Defense's Digital Engineering Strategy (2018), which outlines five strategic goals aimed at improving engineering agility, communication, technical decision-making, lifecycle traceability, and system integration. These priorities align with the growing need for flexible, rapid-cycle, and cross-domain engineering in aerospace projects, where static, document-based processes cannot support modularity, reusability, and mission adaptability. As the scope and velocity of digital initiatives increase, scholars have also underscored the need for domain-wide clarity in defining the scope of Digital Engineering and differentiating it from overlapping fields such as Building Information Modeling (Hosseini et al., 2021). These foundational developments provide the basis for more integrated, traceable, and dynamic system development frameworks required in modern aerospace programs.
A core element of this digital transition is the emergence of what Roper (2021) defines as the Digital Trinity, an interconnected framework comprising Model-Based Systems Engineering

(MBSE), Digital Thread, and Digital Twin practices. $ ^{13} $ These three elements form the foundation for an integrated digital environment that supports real-time traceability, model continuity, and adaptive feedback loops. MBSE, in particular, serves as the semantic and structural framework of the trinity. It enables formal specification of requirements, functions, behaviors, and interfaces using modeling languages such as SysML. Bone et al. (2019) highlighted that MBSE facilitates deeper alignment between engineering disciplines by promoting early validation, executable design artifacts, and traceable verification activities, especially critical in safety- and missioncritical aerospace contexts. This emphasis on traceability and verification forms a natural continuation from the challenges discussed in Section 2.4.4, where bidirectional traceability was shown to be essential in evolving requirement models.

While MBSE provides the structural layer, Digital Thread offers longitudinal continuity by linking artifacts, decisions, and datasets across the system's lifecycle. Its purpose is to maintain data coherence and contextual traceability, from conceptual design through production, testing, and operations. Zimmerman, Gilbert, and Salvatore (2019) described the digital thread as an enabler of transparency and decision traceability, helping stakeholders identify the upstream and downstream effects of any system change. In aerospace projects where requirements evolve and stakeholder goals shift dynamically, this capability is essential. The tight coupling between MBSE and the digital thread ensures that updates in system models automatically propagate across connected artifacts, creating a synchronized engineering environment. This directly reinforces the traceability-focused modeling workflows introduced in prior systems engineering literature (McDermott et al., 2022).

The third dimension, the Digital Twin, extends the value of integrated modeling by creating a live, data-driven surrogate of the physical system. Unlike traditional simulations, which are typically one-off or static, digital twins continuously ingest sensor data and operational feedback to reflect the current state of the physical system. The digital twin paradigm proposed for future NASA and USAF programs underscores the critical need for synchronized system modeling and physics-based simulation environments (Glaessgen & Stargel, 2012). Tong, Bao, and Tao (2024) introduced the concept of Co-evolutionary Digital Twins (CoEDT), which dynamically adjust based on multi-dimensional feedback, enabling anomaly detection and adaptive planning. In practice, this means that a satellite in orbit can be monitored and analyzed via its digital twin, allowing ground operators to anticipate failures, reallocate resources, or adjust mission parameters in real-time. This real-time responsiveness is increasingly relevant in the context of complex adaptive aerospace systems, as discussed in Section 2.4.3, where mission conditions are fluid and reconfiguration may be necessary during operation.

The integration of these three components, MBSE, digital thread, and digital twin, forms a cohesive digital ecosystem where engineering becomes not just descriptive but also predictive and adaptive. As Bone et al. (2019) emphasized, such an approach transforms models into active participants in the engineering process, supporting continuous verification, stakeholder alignment, and lifecycle performance optimization. Trustworthy AI is emerging as a key enabler in digital engineering, supporting explainability and reliability in MBSE-integrated decision-making frameworks (Huang et al., 2021). However, implementing this trinity is not without challenges. The orchestration of toolchains, semantic alignment across platforms, and data synchronization remain critical barriers. These concerns are further explored in the following subsection, which addresses model integration and tool interoperability, focusing on how platforms such as Cameo,

MATLAB, STK, Excel, and Teamcenter are being interconnected to realize the full potential of digital engineering in the aerospace industry. The CREATE/ERS initiative within the U.S. Department of Defense exemplifies this potential by using virtual prototyping and resilient engineering strategies to modernize acquisition, reduce design cycle times, and strengthen digital mission readiness (Post et al., 2019).

While the original "Digital Trinity" proposed by Roper (2021) emphasized digital engineering, digital thread, and digital twin as enablers of agile, software-centric defense acquisition, this dissertation reinterprets the concept to suit the academic context of systems modeling and decision support. Specifically, the proposed Digital Trinity for this study consists of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) as the structural modeling backbone, requirements prioritization as the decision-oriented analytical layer, and digital integration as the enabling mechanism for tool interoperability and lifecycle feedback. Together, these three pillars support the development of traceable, adaptive, and value-driven systems within the aerospace domain, aligning with the objectives of digital engineering while being tailored for academic applications.

In aerospace systems, where mission conditions evolve and subsystems operate across layered physical environments, the feedback loop between simulation and design must be dynamic, executable, and continuously bidirectional. This tight feedback integration ensures that design assumptions remain validated under changing conditions and that system behaviors can be rapidly assessed against operational constraints. Building upon the model integration strategies outlined in Section 2.5.2, this section explores how lifecycle traceability and simulation-informed feedback loops collectively strengthen the implementation of the digital thread and support co-simulation practices across MBSE workflows.

Chapter 2 presented a comprehensive literature review encompassing foundational and emerging perspectives in Systems Engineering (SE), Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), requirements prioritization, and digital integration within aerospace domains. The review began with the principles and known limitations of conventional SE practices, then progressed toward the evolving capabilities of MBSE in managing complexity, interdependencies, and lifecycle alignment in adaptive, resource-constrained missions.

The analysis highlighted a persistent gap between theoretical MBSE frameworks and their real-world application, particularly in agile contexts such as CubeSat development. While MBSE enhances traceability, consistency, and stakeholder engagement, its effectiveness is limited when it is disconnected from dynamic prioritization methods and simulation-driven validation workflows. Existing prioritization strategies often remain static, lacking responsiveness to evolving mission parameters and compatibility with executable models or digital thread constructs.

These insights collectively reinforce the central research motivation: to develop a lightweight, validated prioritization framework embedded within an MBSE environment and interoperable across an integrated digital engineering toolchain. This proposed framework aims to strengthen early-phase decision-making, ensure end-to-end traceability, and improve adaptability across the aerospace system lifecycle.

The next chapter builds upon this foundation by outlining the methodological design of the proposed approach, detailing its theoretical underpinnings, integration architecture, and validation strategy. The SidSat CubeSat mission is introduced as a representative case study to demonstrate feasibility, technical rigor, and practical relevance.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.1 RESEARCH DESIGN AND FRAMEWORK
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 1 research design and framework
text: This research is positioned at the intersection of Model-Based Systems Engineering, adaptive decision-making, and digital integration, aiming to advance a scalable and interoperable approach for complex aerospace systems. It leverages SidSat, a CubeSat-class system, as a representative testbed to support broader applications across space-based assets, defense avionics, and distributed cyber-physical platforms. $ ^{15} $ While anchored in a single case study, the framework is deliberately structured to be extensible to system-of-systems architectures, autonomous platforms, and mission-critical infrastructures.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.1 RESEARCH DESIGN AND FRAMEWORK
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 1 research design and framework
text: The research framework synthesizes Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), advanced Requirements Engineering (RE), and integrated toolchains to address three core challenges: (i) lifecycle traceability and model fidelity in space system architectures, (ii) prioritization of requirements within the context of Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS), and (iii) orchestration of digital toolchains for cross-domain simulation and validation. This approach supports rigorous requirements decomposition, stakeholder-driven value analysis, executable feedback loops, and end-to-end traceability from architecture design to validation, all implemented through formal SysML modeling environments.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.1.1 Research Philosophy and Approach
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 1 1 research philosophy and approach
text: This study adopts a pragmatic research philosophy rooted in engineering problem-solving and systems thinking, integrating both qualitative and quantitative reasoning to capture design rationale, emergent behaviors, and measurable outcomes across the lifecycles of complex systems. The methodological approach follows a mixed methods engineering research design, combining formal system modeling, computational simulation, structured prioritization, and validation workflows.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 1 1 research philosophy and approach
text: From an epistemological perspective, the study aligns with constructivist systems engineering, recognizing that system boundaries, requirements, and priorities evolve in response to stakeholder feedback, environmental constraints, and operational dynamics. The application of MBSE supports systematic abstraction, interface definition, and architecture analysis, while the digital thread ensures bidirectional traceability across simulation results, requirement satisfaction, and model evolution.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 1 3 the digital trinity mbse prioritization integration framework
text: MBSE provides the structural backbone of the framework by using SysML to formally capture system abstractions, define interfaces, and support lifecycle management. Key modeling artifacts, such as Block Definition Diagrams, Internal Block Diagrams, Activity Diagrams, State Machine Diagrams, and Parametric Diagrams, are employed to support requirements decomposition, behavior modeling, verification, and validation (V&V). Relationships, including 《allocate》, 《derive》, 《refine》, 《satisfy》, and 《verify》, are systematically applied to preserve traceability and maintain alignment between design intent, stakeholder needs, and evolving constraints. These models are embedded within an architecture framework that supports structured viewpoints across functional, logical, and physical domains (Siddique, 2024).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.1.3 The Digital Trinity (MBSE-Prioritization-Integration) Framework
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 1 3 the digital trinity mbse prioritization integration framework
text: The prioritization component injects decision rationality into the development process by enabling stakeholder-driven requirement weighting and adaptive resource management. Recognizing the influence of emergence and evolving stakeholder constraints, this layer integrates Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) with value-driven design principles. Trade space analysis is supported through dynamic ranking and iterative refinement mechanisms, with rationale directly linked to SysML elements via compartments, tagged values, and callouts. This ensures that prioritization remains transparent, configurable, and responsive to feedback.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2 MODEL-BASED SYSTEMS ENGINEERING (MBSE) IMPLEMENTATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 model based systems engineering mbse implementation
text: The MBSE approach employed in this research establishes the structural and behavioral backbone of the SidSat system architecture, enabling a coherent, traceable, and simulation-ready design environment. By leveraging SysML modeling, the framework supports comprehensive lifecycle management, requirements decomposition, interface specification, and cross-domain traceability. Unlike conventional document-based practices, this model-centric methodology ensures the consistent flow of requirements, architecture logic, and simulation feedback across all development phases.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2 MODEL-BASED SYSTEMS ENGINEERING (MBSE) IMPLEMENTATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 model based systems engineering mbse implementation
text: MBSE further enables alignment with architecture frameworks, facilitates robust Verification & Validation (V&V), supports stakeholder needs analysis, and integrates effectively with system-of-systems constructs. As a foundational component of the Digital Trinity framework, it ensures that all engineering artifacts remain synchronized, testable, and adaptable, strengthening both technical rigor and mission assurance for small satellite platforms.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.1 MBSE Foundation and Rationale
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 1 mbse foundation and rationale
text: The foundation of the Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach in this study lies in its ability to replace document-centric practices with an integrated, model-centric strategy that enhances system fidelity, lifecycle traceability, and cross-domain coherence. MBSE enables the formal specification of system structure, behavior, and requirements through SysML, providing a unified architecture framework that spans stakeholders, engineering domains, and disciplines. By capturing abstractions using standardized constructs, such as blocks, value types, ports, interfaces, and constraints, MBSE supports end-to-end alignment of design intent, verification strategy, and stakeholder expectations.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.1 MBSE Foundation and Rationale
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 1 mbse foundation and rationale
text: A layered MBSE analytic environment connects modeling tools, data repositories, formalized engineering processes, and cross-functional stakeholders to downstream operational domains. At the core, model artifacts, such as mission scenarios, mission threads, and system baselines, are linked to simulation outputs and enterprise-level systems, including logistics, security management, display systems, and infrastructure planning. This environment highlights the extended role of MBSE beyond technical modeling, demonstrating how models inform systems operations, interface decisions, and lifecycle transitions. Such integration is especially important in aerospace contexts, where distributed teams, evolving requirements, and mission-critical dependencies demand a traceable, analytics-enabled engineering environment.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 1 mbse foundation and rationale
text: The MBSE paradigm is particularly suited to the challenges of small satellite development, where rapid iteration, resource constraints, and complex subsystem interdependencies require disciplined systems thinking and structured modeling. MBSE supports early identification of architectural gaps, simulation-informed decision-making, and iterative requirements

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.1 MBSE Foundation and Rationale
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 1 mbse foundation and rationale
text: A foundational method for aligning development and verification efforts in systems engineering is the V-Model. This diagrammatic approach pairs each design activity with a corresponding validation task. The left branch represents a gradual breakdown of system needs into more detailed components. In contrast, the right branch emphasizes the stepwise integration and validation of those components against the original requirements. This structured alignment supports early planning for testability and integrates effectively with MBSE concepts such as 《allocate》, 《derive》, 《refine》, 《satisfy》, and 《verify》, which maintain requirement traceability. In the case of SidSat, the V-Model emphasizes the importance of systematically representing requirements, architectures, and behavioral elements in forms that facilitate early-stage simulation and trace-driven analysis. The model's visual structure also reinforces the importance of recursive validation and integrated systems thinking in model-based projects.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.1 MBSE Foundation and Rationale
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 1 mbse foundation and rationale
text: The integration of MBSE into this research is not limited to its visual modeling features. It offers the advantage of managing the system lifecycle by linking functions, limitations, and test parameters through coherent relationships in SysML. These linked model elements become usable inputs for verification simulations, interface assessments, and iterative evaluation of requirements. Additionally, model annotations and extensions, such as compartments or tagged attributes, can capture prioritization logic and justification directly within the model, enhancing transparency and rationale traceability.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.1 MBSE Foundation and Rationale
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 1 mbse foundation and rationale
text: By establishing MBSE as a central element of the approach, this study ensures consistency with current digital engineering trends in aerospace. It promotes a modular system structure, enables coordination across system hierarchies, and facilitates integration with tools for data analysis and architectural evaluation. The continued development of INCOSE-aligned practices suggests scalability in model-based requirements handling (Wheaton & Herber, 2024). Furthermore, MBSE-supported architecture design has demonstrated improvements in interface definition and reuse efficiency, which are essential for managing risk in space systems (Stirgwolt, Mazzuchi, & Sarkani, 2022).

Within this environment, structural definitions, interface relationships, system behaviors, allocation logic, and constraint expressions are modeled using the SysML language, which supports system-level analysis and traceability for the SidSat CubeSat.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.3 SidSat Logical Architecture Modeling
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 3 sidsat logical architecture modeling
text: The architectural modeling of SidSat employs a structured, modular approach using SysML to define the system's static and dynamic aspects across multiple abstraction layers. This modeling effort emphasizes the decomposition of requirements, structural integrity, interface definition, and alignment with stakeholder objectives. The architecture features a 4U CubeSat configuration, incorporating mission-enabling subsystems such as a robotic arm and an AI/ML-based decision unit. The modeling strategy ensures lifecycle management through traceable, executable representations that evolve in tandem with mission and system constraints.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.3 SidSat Logical Architecture Modeling
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 3 sidsat logical architecture modeling
text: Block Definition Diagrams (BDDs) are used to establish the hierarchical decomposition of the satellite into its core subsystems: command and data handling (C&DH), communications, payload, attitude determination and control system (ADCS), power, structure, and thermal management. Each subsystem is represented as a block with associated value properties, constraint parameters, and ports to formalize its functional and physical roles. Interface blocks define standardized data, power, and mechanical connections, ensuring interoperability and reusability across architectural layers.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.3 SidSat Logical Architecture Modeling
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 3 sidsat logical architecture modeling
text: Internal Block Diagrams (IBDs) depict the internal configuration of each subsystem and its interconnections through standard, flow, and proxy ports. These diagrams expose data paths, signal flows, and control logic integration among components, supporting consistent architecture visualization and interface validation. Value types and signals are modeled to ensure consistency in unit definitions, parameter binding, and system integration rules. Constraints are formalized through parametric diagrams, which validate mass, volume, and power budgets by utilizing reusable constraint blocks tied to requirement elements. These constraint structures adhere to

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.3 SidSat Logical Architecture Modeling
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 3 sidsat logical architecture modeling
text: INCOSE-aligned modeling patterns, supporting simulation-informed validation and enhanced standardization (Wheaton & Herber, 2024).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.3 SidSat Logical Architecture Modeling
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 3 sidsat logical architecture modeling
text: To ensure alignment with system-of-systems engineering principles, multiple architecture viewpoints are employed to distinguish between functional, logical, and physical layers of the system, while maintaining cohesion through synchronized model relationships. Functional behaviors are systematically allocated to structural components using SysML relationships, allowing for a traceable mapping between abstract functions and tangible system elements. This allocation supports rigorous performance tracking, resource budgeting, and architecture verification. Each modeling element is embedded within a requirement-linked traceability framework that ensures full lifecycle alignment with stakeholder-derived needs, while also enabling backward and forward trace navigation.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.3 SidSat Logical Architecture Modeling
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 3 sidsat logical architecture modeling
text: The SidSat system architecture is modeled as a tightly integrated, feedback-driven construct that connects design intent, resource constraints, and verification logic into a unified SysML environment. This modeling approach supports both static integrity and dynamic evaluation, facilitating trade space analysis and digital simulation across iterative development phases. Constraint blocks, developed using reusable patterns aligned with INCOSE's modeling guidance (Wheaton & Herber, 2024), enforce compliance with mission-specific mass, volume, and power limits. Model continuity is preserved across tools via structured interfaces, parameter binding, and simulation feedback loops, ensuring the architecture serves as a high-fidelity baseline for subsequent integration, analysis, and system validation efforts.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.4 Behavioral Modeling and Traceability
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 4 behavioral modeling and traceability
text: Behavioral modeling is essential for characterizing the dynamic aspects of SidSat's operational profile. Engineers use SysML to express mission sequences, control logic, and internal state transitions within a unified modeling environment, thereby facilitating a comprehensive understanding of system behavior. This effort enhances behavioral validation under different conditions and strengthens traceability from stakeholder expectations through to system structures and functions. In model-based systems engineering, behavior models connect high-level concepts with executable operations, thereby facilitating alignment between mission intent and implementation throughout the system's lifecycle.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.4 Behavioral Modeling and Traceability
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 4 behavioral modeling and traceability
text: Activity Diagrams illustrate functional flows associated with key mission activities, including orbital insertion, deployment, robotic arm movement, and thermal management. Each activity encompasses a group of tasks or decisions, represented using control and object flows. System components are assigned to actions to retain structural linkage. Value types are used to define input and output flows, supporting unit consistency and directional clarity. These diagrams also facilitate the simulation of resource consumption, event ordering, and concurrency among subsystems.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.4 Behavioral Modeling and Traceability
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 4 behavioral modeling and traceability
text: State Machine Diagrams specify subsystem modes, transitions, and the logic associated with each state. Modules such as robotic control, data handling, and power regulation are modeled with events that trigger transitions and guards that define branching logic. Each state includes entry, ongoing, and exit operations to model time-sensitive behavior and process coordination. These diagrams are crucial for testing system performance in both expected and degraded operational modes.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.4 Behavioral Modeling and Traceability
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 4 behavioral modeling and traceability
text: Traceability is reinforced through standard SysML links, 《allocate》, 《derive》, 《refine》, 《satisfy》, and 《verify》 relationships associate requirements with behavior diagrams, 《refine》 supports decomposition of abstract goals, and 《allocate》 ties functions to physical components. These links are managed in Cameo through validation dashboards, coverage checks, and traceability matrices.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.4 Behavioral Modeling and Traceability
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 4 behavioral modeling and traceability
text: Behavioral, structural, and requirement views are integrated to increase visibility, improve coordination, and ensure validation readiness. This modeling effort contributes to maintaining digital thread alignment and promotes the inclusion of behavioral accuracy as a primary, not secondary, system concern. For the SidSat CubeSat, this behavioral modeling approach supports early fault detection, scenario-based analysis, and system responsiveness, establishing behavior modeling as a foundational component within the broader digital engineering strategy.

Parametric diagrams play a central role in validating quantitative relationships within the MBSE process. For the SidSat CubeSat, these diagrams are used to assess mass distribution, energy availability, structural margins, and timing alignment. By associating constraint equations with system elements via binding connectors, the model provides a direct mechanism for evaluating performance against mission parameters.

At the core of this validation strategy are constraint blocks, which encode reusable formulas derived from engineering principles and system-level requirements. These may include equations governing thermal limits, center of gravity location, total mass, and energy usage across various operational modes. Once connected to system blocks, they generate a logic network that mirrors real-world conditions and operational limits. Parameters are typed using standardized
value types to maintain unit coherence, and binding connectors ensure equality relationships are maintained across the model.

With this structure, system designers can test design alternatives under defined constraints. For instance, mass budgets can be checked against the launch vehicle's payload limits, or power flows can be analyzed to verify adequacy during eclipse periods. Because the model is executable, such checks are performed automatically as configurations change. This reduces the need for disconnected simulation tools and improves turnaround during iterative design. As shown in prior work (Anwar et al., 2020), this level of model integration reduces ambiguity and promotes repeatable system verification.

The validation is closely linked to requirements via SysML satisfy and verify relationships. Each constraint is associated with a requirement and executed using tools like Cameo's constraint solver. These evaluations remain current as models evolve, forming part of a continuous Digital Thread that ties together requirements, architecture, and behavior.

By embedding parametric evaluation into the system model, this method enables real-time verification, facilitates early detection of constraint issues, and promotes clear communication of design intent. For SidSat, this ensured that physical constraints, functional behavior, and system goals remained consistently aligned throughout the development process. $ ^{16} $

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.6 MBSE Tool Selection and Prioritization Framework
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 mbse tool selection and prioritization framework
text: The process of selecting and prioritizing MBSE tools requires more than an assessment of individual capabilities; it must also reflect project-specific modeling objectives, integration requirements, and prioritization strategies for requirements. Drawing from the multi-stage

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.6 MBSE Tool Selection and Prioritization Framework
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 mbse tool selection and prioritization framework
text: framework proposed by Khandoker et al. (2022), this section synthesizes a structured pathway for evaluating MBSE tools, tailored to support the research goals of model-centric system architecture, disciplined requirement flow-down, and structured tool interoperability. The following subsections map the framework's dimensions to three critical perspectives: MBSE-driven modeling fidelity (Section 3.2.6.1), requirements prioritization and verification alignment (Section 3.2.6.2), and digital integration and lifecycle interoperability (Section 3.2.6.3). Each perspective builds upon the core elements of domain-driven requirements elicitation and structured tool screening.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 1 tool selection to support mbse fidelity and formalism
text: The CubeSat case study uses a tailored version of the tool selection process introduced by Khandoker et al. (2022). This version, shown in Figure 3.4, follows a staged evaluation of MBSE tools. Each step considers how well the tool meets project-specific modeling needs and whether it can support the system over time with adequate detail and structure.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 1 tool selection to support mbse fidelity and formalism
text: The selection process begins by identifying the project's needs, which include the type of modeling involved, the level of detail required, and the expected benefits of MBSE, such as design

text: traceability or early system checks. The first filter involves scanning the available tool options, eliminating those that lack essential features or fail to fit the domain.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 1 tool selection to support mbse fidelity and formalism
text: In the second step, often referred to as "Tool Selection Specification", the focus shifts to practical screening. Each option is reviewed using a clear set of project needs. These include SysML support, language range, process coverage, plug-in availability, and license flexibility. This step helps confirm which tools are usable.

text: The third step in the original method utilizes QFD to match stakeholder needs with tool features. For the CubeSat case, this has been replaced by a weighted scoring model (WSM), which is a more suitable approach. The WSM works by assigning points to factors such as how well the tool models, how easy it is to use, whether it integrates with other tools, and how it supports testing. $ ^{17} $ These scores help sort the options based on what matters most.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.6.1 Tool Selection to Support MBSE Fidelity and Formalism
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 1 tool selection to support mbse fidelity and formalism
text: The final step utilizes a simple matrix to consolidate all the information. Earlier findings are summarized, and the best-fitting tool is selected. This four-step method supports tool selection for systems engineering in complex projects, where both modeling and domain fit are critical.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.6.1 Tool Selection to Support MBSE Fidelity and Formalism
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 1 tool selection to support mbse fidelity and formalism
text: The final screening is conducted through a structured decision matrix, resulting in the selection of an MBSE tool that meets both formal and functional expectations for domain-specific use. The overall process establishes a defensible, criteria-driven methodology for tool selection, supporting MBSE fidelity in high-stakes environments, such as aerospace system development.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.6.2 Requirements Prioritization and Verification Alignment in Tool Evaluation
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 2 requirements prioritization and verification alignment in tool evaluation
text: A key dimension of MBSE tool selection lies in the ability to support disciplined requirements prioritization and verification alignment. In complex aerospace systems, requirements are not uniformly critical; some have a greater impact on safety, mission objectives, or regulatory compliance. As such, MBSE environments must not only capture and manage

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.6.2 Requirements Prioritization and Verification Alignment in Tool Evaluation
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 2 requirements prioritization and verification alignment in tool evaluation
text: requirements but also enable analysts to systematically rank, trace, and validate them throughout the lifecycle.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.6.2 Requirements Prioritization and Verification Alignment in Tool Evaluation
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 2 requirements prioritization and verification alignment in tool evaluation
text: Within the second filtration phase of the tool selection framework (Khandoker et al., 2022), requirements-specific considerations emerge prominently. This stage evaluates whether candidate tools provide built-in prioritization mechanisms, such as weighted attributes, ranking models, or external interfacing with prioritization engines. Integration of such capabilities ensures that highpriority requirements can be explicitly modeled and monitored, enabling focused verification efforts and model-based validation. For this research, while Khandoker et al. employed a QFD mechanism for requirement-to-feature mapping, our framework substitutes a Weighted Scoring Model (WSM) to numerically represent the importance of requirements and quantify tool support across categories such as traceability, reusability, V&V compatibility, and simulation readiness.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.6.2 Requirements Prioritization and Verification Alignment in Tool Evaluation
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 2 requirements prioritization and verification alignment in tool evaluation
text: The selected MBSE tool must therefore offer capabilities to reflect the importance of requirements within the modeling process and verify their satisfaction through simulation, interface checking, or parametric validation. This includes requirement satisfaction matrices, constraint evaluations, coverage visualizations, and linkages between requirement elements and behavioral/structural models.

text: Figure 3.5 illustrates how MBSE tools must accommodate the interplay of people, processes, and products when managing requirements. The figure highlights key benefits, including simultaneous verification and validation, risk reduction, model reusability, cost efficiency, and improved communication. These elements reflect the multifaceted nature of requirements in MBSE environments, where technical, organizational, and procedural demands intersect. By embedding these dimensions into the tool evaluation framework, decision-makers can prioritize tools that support holistic requirements management rather than feature-limited implementations.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 3.2.6.2 Requirements Prioritization and Verification Alignment in Tool Evaluation
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 3 2 6 2 requirements prioritization and verification alignment in tool evaluation
text: Thus, requirements prioritization in MBSE tool selection is not limited to functional coverage, but also extends to usability in verification, model-based tracking, and digital continuity across stakeholders. This ensures that critical requirements are not only visible but also actively validated throughout the system's evolution.

text: In aerospace projects, selecting tools solely based on standalone capabilities often results in fragmented workflows and disconnected development processes. Digital integration supports efficient data exchange, behavioral simulation, and feedback loops across the system lifecycle. Therefore, MBSE tool selection must consider not only modeling formalisms but also the ability to interface with co-simulation, requirements prioritization, and analysis environments through standardized data formats and APIs.
