section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 6 4 implications limitations and future use
text: Furthermore, only one instance of each methodology was executed by a single modeler to maintain uniformity, which limits the generalizability of the findings. Collaborative modeling dynamics, model versioning, and stakeholder review cycles, critical components in real-world deployment, were not fully incorporated into this phase. These constraints must be acknowledged when extending the findings to broader MBSE implementation decisions.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 6 4 implications limitations and future use

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 6.4 IMPLICATIONS, LIMITATIONS, AND FUTURE USE
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 6 4 implications limitations and future use
text: Additionally, integration with requirements prioritization frameworks and digital twin simulation platforms remains a relevant extension. Evaluating how each methodology supports or hinders trace-driven prioritization and real-time performance validation will bridge the current gap between architecture modeling and operational decision-making (Di Maio et al., 2021). These directions will further enhance the understanding of MBSE tool-mission alignment, especially in constrained or adaptive system-of-systems contexts.

This evaluation compared two MBSE approaches, OOSEM and Arcadia, using a CubeSat system model as a test case. The analysis followed the FEMMP evaluation framework to assess the alignment of each method with aerospace project needs. OOSEM, built on SysML, provided modeling flexibility suited to iterative design and evolving system requirements. Its capability to support traceable requirement refinement during early development phases proved effective in managing architectural variability and subsystem integration. Arcadia, on the other hand, brought strength in structural consistency, using formal abstractions and viewpoint-based modeling to coordinate stakeholder roles. Its emphasis on scenario flows and function chains helped maintain clarity across engineering layers.

For SidSat, OOSEM was fully applied using Cameo Systems Modeler, enabling detailed system architecture with defined behavior models and verification relationships. Although Arcadia/Capella was initially included in the tool strategy, implementation was constrained by resource limitations, procedural restrictions, and access to the toolchain. As a result, Arcadia was applied conceptually to inform architectural comparisons but not used for full lifecycle modeling.

The comparison highlights key decision points when selecting MBSE frameworks, especially those involving system complexity, available expertise, and integration readiness. Observations from this case suggest that factors such as model scalability, validation effort, and co-simulation potential should be considered early in the selection process. Insights from this study contribute to advancing MBSE in small satellite design, with emphasis on improving traceability, enhancing digital modeling practices, and supporting future toolchain interoperability under constrained operational environments.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.1 REQUIREMENTS TRACEABILITY AND VALIDATION IN THE MBSE CONTEXT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 1 requirements traceability and validation in the mbse context
text: The foundation of effective systems engineering lies in ensuring that every design element, behavior, and simulation result can be traced directly back to verified and validated stakeholder requirements. Within the SidSat project, requirements traceability was implemented through a rigorous, end-to-end Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach using SysML artifacts in Cameo Systems Modeler. This approach enabled structured navigation between functional intent, design realization, and verification outcomes, facilitating transparency, accountability, and rapid iteration of validation.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.1 REQUIREMENTS TRACEABILITY AND VALIDATION IN THE MBSE CONTEXT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 1 requirements traceability and validation in the mbse context
text: To establish traceability, requirements were first captured, categorized, and structured within a requirements table, totaling approximately 110 discrete requirements across seven major categories: Communication, Functional, Performance, Battery Testing, Environmental, Mass Properties, Mechanical Specification, and Power Budget. These were derived from multiple authoritative sources, including the NASA CubeSat Launch Initiative (CSLI), CubeSat Design Specification (CDS), and deployment specifications such as the NanoRacks CubeSat Deployer (NRCSD). Each requirement was uniquely identified, classified, and assigned a validation status that was dynamically updated based on system performance simulations (IREB, 2020).

Due to the volume and complexity of interlinked elements, a comprehensive requirements diagram showing all relationships was not included in the written analysis; however, it remains fully accessible within the project's model repository and was instrumental in ensuring model consistency.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.1 REQUIREMENTS TRACEABILITY AND VALIDATION IN THE MBSE CONTEXT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 1 requirements traceability and validation in the mbse context
text: The validation process evolved from static parametric checks to fully automated simulation workflows. Initially, Cameo parametric diagrams were used to bind value properties (e.g., power consumption, alignment precision, mass) to requirement thresholds through constraint blocks. These expressions were evaluated manually through assigned test scenarios. As the system matured, automation was achieved by integrating the Cameo Simulation Toolkit with Excel, MATLAB, and STK. This enabled one-click simulations, where input parameters were pushed to MATLAB, orbital dynamics were evaluated in STK, and outputs were pulled back into the requirements table within Cameo (MathWorks, 2023; AGI, 2022).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.1 REQUIREMENTS TRACEABILITY AND VALIDATION IN THE MBSE CONTEXT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 1 requirements traceability and validation in the mbse context
text: Validation results were visualized using a color-coded requirement table, where green indicated successful validation (simulation output met or exceeded the requirement threshold). In contrast, red indicated failure (violations requiring redesign or parameter tuning). This feedback

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 1 requirements traceability and validation in the mbse context
text: mechanism provided rapid decision-making support, enabling continuous alignment between design intent and system behavior.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.1 REQUIREMENTS TRACEABILITY AND VALIDATION IN THE MBSE CONTEXT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 1 requirements traceability and validation in the mbse context
text: This integrated validation framework ensured that the SidSat system was not only built to meet stated requirements, but that every assumption, parameter, and behavior could be traced, verified, and updated in a closed feedback loop, meeting the foundational principles of digital engineering and providing a defensible audit trail for system readiness. The traceability structure laid out here directly supports higher-level verification and evaluation analyses in subsequent sections.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.2 TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND CROSS-PLATFORM VALIDATION CONSISTENCY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 2 toolchain integration and cross platform validation consistency
text: A core enabler of modern aerospace system development lies in the cohesive integration of modeling and simulation tools into a coherent digital engineering ecosystem. For the SidSat project, multiple tools were interconnected, including Cameo Systems Modeler, MATLAB, STK, Excel, Teamcenter, and AWS, to establish a traceable, consistent, and automated validation workflow across the system's lifecycle. This section outlines the logic behind toolchain integration and the measures taken to ensure consistency in data, behavior, and model-driven validation across platforms (Dunbar et al., 2023).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.2 TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND CROSS-PLATFORM VALIDATION CONSISTENCY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 2 toolchain integration and cross platform validation consistency
text: Toolchain integration began with the structuring of the system model in Cameo using SysML. Blocks, activities, parametrics, and requirement relationships were centrally defined in this environment. Value properties for key parameters, such as satellite mass, antenna frequency, power draw, and orbital lifetime, were bound to constraints and simulated through internal parametric models. While these models initially provided early insight into design feasibility, their full validation potential was unlocked through cross-platform interoperability with external simulation engines.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.2 TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND CROSS-PLATFORM VALIDATION CONSISTENCY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 2 toolchain integration and cross platform validation consistency
text: Cameo's Simulation Toolkit served as the central bridge, facilitating the execution of opaque behaviors (scripts) that passed user-defined inputs from Excel into MATLAB for numerical simulation and from MATLAB to STK for orbital dynamics evaluation. STK then provided output metrics, such as satellite lifetime, downlink windows, and Earth-pointing alignment precision, which were collected, exported, and reimported into Excel, and ultimately read back into Cameo for real-time validation against requirement thresholds.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.2 TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND CROSS-PLATFORM VALIDATION CONSISTENCY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 2 toolchain integration and cross platform validation consistency
text: To ensure cross-platform consistency, several safeguards were implemented:

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 2 toolchain integration and cross platform validation consistency
text: - Parameter mapping tables ensured that units, value types, and variable names remained consistent across tools.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 2 toolchain integration and cross platform validation consistency

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 2 toolchain integration and cross platform validation consistency
text: - Feedback loops were modeled within Cameo to represent the return path of simulation outputs and the resulting impact on requirement validation status.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 2 toolchain integration and cross platform validation consistency
text: - Automated update scripts in Cameo allowed the model to dynamically refresh requirement tables with the latest results from MATLAB and STK evaluations, minimizing manual input errors.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.2 TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND CROSS-PLATFORM VALIDATION CONSISTENCY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 2 toolchain integration and cross platform validation consistency
text: This integration framework not only enabled one-click simulations for system validation but also preserved semantic coherence, ensuring that what was modeled in SysML corresponded directly with what was computed in MATLAB and visualized in STK. This end-to-end pipeline was initially constructed through manual simulation stages, where inputs were provided by hand through parametric diagrams. However, over time, it matured into a fully automated validation workflow with nearly hands-free operation, scalable to larger system configurations.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.2 TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND CROSS-PLATFORM VALIDATION CONSISTENCY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 2 toolchain integration and cross platform validation consistency
text: Although formal hardware or software testing was outside the scope of this research, the toolchain integration activities conducted here represent a powerful surrogate, demonstrating that digital consistency and traceable validation can be achieved through simulation-based reasoning, parametric logic, and cross-domain tool interoperability.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.2 TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND CROSS-PLATFORM VALIDATION CONSISTENCY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 2 toolchain integration and cross platform validation consistency
text: In doing so, SidSat's development approach aligns with current aerospace industry standards for digital engineering, setting the stage for enterprise-level scalability and future work on user-facing simulation dashboards.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.3 SIMULATION I/O INTERFACES VIA EXCEL AND CSV
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 3 simulation i o interfaces via excel and csv
text: In the current setup for SidSat, Excel spreadsheets and CSV files are used to manage both simulation inputs and outputs. This strategy provides a streamlined mechanism for connecting the system model with external analysis tools, while avoiding the complexity of a full-scale graphical interface. Excel's widespread familiarity and tool compatibility make it a viable bridge for defining inputs, controlling simulations, and collecting results throughout the development cycle (OpsHub, 2025).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.3 SIMULATION I/O INTERFACES VIA EXCEL AND CSV
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 3 simulation i o interfaces via excel and csv
text: Mission-specific input parameters, such as antenna thresholds, battery duration, power margins, and orbital settings, are first recorded in structured Excel templates. These templates are then referenced by activity diagrams in Cameo using opaque behavior elements, which trigger automated execution pipelines in MATLAB and STK. Once initiated, these external tools compute the required outputs without needing further user action.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.3 SIMULATION I/O INTERFACES VIA EXCEL AND CSV
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 3 simulation i o interfaces via excel and csv
text: The simulation results, including system frequency response, position drift, and energy usage, are stored in CSV format and routed back to Excel. These updated files are then used to assess the validation status and track support requirements. Cameo references this returned data to update verification markers in requirement tables, flagging green for compliant results and red for

text: Although this mechanism still depends on file transfers between tools, it supports effective feedback loops without requiring real-time interfaces. Design teams can edit values directly in Excel and rerun simulations as needed, allowing iterative improvement without rebuilding the entire model.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 3 simulation i o interfaces via excel and csv
text: A more advanced interface with real-time control and visualization has been proposed for future phases, but is beyond the present scope. For now, the current approach strikes a balance between functionality and ease of use, enabling simulation execution, data tracing, and requirement validation without increasing modeling overhead, making it well-suited for earlystage development in constrained aerospace projects.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.4 SCENARIO-BASED SYSTEM BEHAVIOR ASSESSMENT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 4 scenario based system behavior assessment
text: In the context of SidSat, scenario-based system behavior assessment served as a vital mechanism for validating how the satellite would respond to mission-specific sequences, command inputs, environmental variations, and internal state transitions. This assessment was performed using a combination of SysML activity diagrams, state machine models, and integrated simulation workflows across multiple tools, including Cameo, MATLAB, and STK.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.4 SCENARIO-BASED SYSTEM BEHAVIOR ASSESSMENT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 4 scenario based system behavior assessment
text: Behavioral scenarios were first defined based on core mission phases: system deployment, antenna alignment, ground communication, orbital adjustment, and power management. Each of these mission threads was modeled in the form of activity diagrams, capturing functional decompositions and control flow dependencies. The diagrams were enriched with object nodes, opaque actions, and parameter sets to enable the dynamic invocation of simulation routines and the transfer of input/output data between tools.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.4 SCENARIO-BASED SYSTEM BEHAVIOR ASSESSMENT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 4 scenario based system behavior assessment
text: To complement activity-based models, state machine diagrams were created for key subsystems such as the Communication Subsystem and ADCS. These diagrams depicted various operational states, such as Idle, On, Communication, Transmit, Pointing Adjustment, and Safe Mode, along with triggers, guards, and effects that governed transitions. The modeling allowed visualization of reactive behavior in response to external events such as signal availability, orbital drift, or resource depletion.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.4 SCENARIO-BASED SYSTEM BEHAVIOR ASSESSMENT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 4 scenario based system behavior assessment
text: Each behavioral scenario was mapped to relevant system requirements to ensure traceability and measurable validation outcomes. For example, one scenario simulated antenna alignment dynamics to test compliance with the requirement that the system maintain orientation within $ \pm 0.5 $ degrees. Another scenario tested communication sequences, linking them to uplink and downlink frequency stability, and validated whether the system could maintain UHF signal transmission at 437 MHz and 437.4 MHz, respectively.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.4 SCENARIO-BASED SYSTEM BEHAVIOR ASSESSMENT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 4 scenario based system behavior assessment
text: Simulation execution involves two key pathways. Initially, input values were manually provided through parametric diagrams and executed via Cameo’s Simulation Toolkit. These values were progressively transferred to Excel-driven interfaces, enabling one-click automated simulation pipelines. Opaque behaviors within activity diagrams invoked MATLAB computations, STK orbit simulations, and requirement evaluations, with results exported to CSV and then looped back into Cameo. Output values were matched against requirement thresholds, and color-coded validations were displayed in the requirements table, green for pass, red for fail.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.4 SCENARIO-BASED SYSTEM BEHAVIOR ASSESSMENT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 4 scenario based system behavior assessment
text: This scenario-driven approach enabled validation not only of individual requirements but also of interrelated system behaviors under mission-like conditions. Multi-domain simulations effectively captured the complex interactions among structural, behavioral, and environmental elements, reflecting the dynamic nature of real-world aerospace systems (Schätz et al., 2002).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.4 SCENARIO-BASED SYSTEM BEHAVIOR ASSESSMENT
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 4 scenario based system behavior assessment
text: Scenario-based system behavior assessment thus provided a robust foundation for early validation and design iteration. It exposed timing misalignments, subsystem dependencies, and performance bottlenecks that would be difficult to detect in purely static models. By leveraging the strengths of SysML's behavioral formalisms and digital integration with simulation tools, SidSat achieved meaningful behavioral assurance prior to implementation.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.5 DIGITAL THREAD IMPLEMENTATION AND FEEDBACK LOOPS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 5 digital thread implementation and feedback loops
text: The SidSat system model employed a digital thread to coordinate simulation, validation, and design flow across all development phases (Glaessgen & Stargel, 2012). This thread supported traceable control using centralized SysML diagrams and feedback links across Cameo, MATLAB, STK, Excel, Teamcenter, and AWS (Holt & Perry, 2012). Core system functions, including parameter sweeps and simulation calls, were structured using opaque actions inside activity diagrams, with data movement handled via Excel workbooks (Siddique, 2024). Simulation results were routed back to requirements tables, which marked validation outcomes through conditional formatting (NASA, 2020). This approach replaced static review cycles with dynamic validation status updates visible to all team members (Castillo et al., 2025).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.5 DIGITAL THREAD IMPLEMENTATION AND FEEDBACK LOOPS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 5 digital thread implementation and feedback loops
text: Castillo, Reyes Garcia, and Shirin (2025) developed a similar digital twin concept for the CROME engine using real-time calibration and uncertainty modeling. Their work highlighted how test and evaluation could transition from manual checks to predictive, data-informed workflows (Shirin, 2025). That structure resembled SidSat's simulation-driven model updates, where ongoing system behavior altered the requirements baseline (Siddique, 2024). While early simulations required manual execution, process upgrades enabled automated scenario evaluations from the SysML environment (NASA, 2020). Validation now ran in parallel with model updates, improving design cycle efficiency and responsiveness (Holt & Perry, 2012).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.5 DIGITAL THREAD IMPLEMENTATION AND FEEDBACK LOOPS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 5 digital thread implementation and feedback loops
text: Feedback mechanisms also enabled fault detection across disciplines, linking model failures to both design logic and performance outputs (Castillo et al., 2025). One case involved misalignment in antenna orientation, where exceeding the $ \pm 0. 5 $ $ ^{\circ} $ margin caused a requirement check to fail and altered downstream power usage (Siddique, 2024). Tool integrations helped isolate the source of the failure by tracing outputs through multiple simulation results (Shirin, 2025). Output from STK and MATLAB was saved in CSV files, checked in Excel, and incorporated into Cameo for requirement traceability (NASA, 2020). These synchronized datasets maintained alignment across tools as changes were made (Holt & Perry, 2012).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.5 DIGITAL THREAD IMPLEMENTATION AND FEEDBACK LOOPS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 5 digital thread implementation and feedback loops
text: Despite this success, interface limitations persist. The current Excel-heavy process still requires technical knowledge and constant manual oversight (Siddique, 2024). Broader adoption would benefit from the development of a web-accessible dashboard or a lightweight interface to guide users through the toolchain without requiring in-depth training (Glaessgen & Stargel, 2012). Such an interface could make system information more visible to managers and non-technical reviewers (Shirin, 2025).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 7.5 DIGITAL THREAD IMPLEMENTATION AND FEEDBACK LOOPS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 7 5 digital thread implementation and feedback loops
text: The overall impact of the SidSat digital thread was to simplify coordination, clarify design intent, and reduce turnaround during validation (NASA, 2020). It ensured that behavioral models, simulations, and requirement mappings remained aligned through the design lifecycle (Holt & Perry, 2012). These outcomes show how digital threads, supported by structured feedback and automation, can help manage change and improve transparency in complex MBSE settings (Siddique, 2024).

Chapter 7 provided a detailed account of validation and evaluation efforts for the SidSat project, highlighting the value of integrated modeling, simulation-based assessment, and digital toolchain orchestration in supporting early-phase design verification (NASA, 2020). Each modeling and simulation activity, spanning requirement mapping to system-level validation, was integrated through a synchronized digital engineering workflow (Holt & Perry, 2012).

Section 7.1 addressed traceability by linking system requirements to structural, behavioral, and parametric elements within the SysML model environment, using visual constructs such as requirements tables and validation status indicators in Cameo (Siddique, 2024). This setup enabled automated compliance feedback and live verification alignment across structural and simulation models. The real-time linkage between validation artifacts and behavioral models helped maintain model consistency and ensure requirement satisfaction throughout updates.

Section 7.2 examined cross-platform logic validation, supported by data exchange across Cameo, MATLAB, Excel, and STK, which enables coherent simulation execution across tools with distinct modeling roles (Delligatti, 2013). Although hardware-in-the-loop testing was excluded in this phase, coordinated behavioral validation was achieved through activity diagram sequences and linked computational flows.

Section 7.3 described the temporary reliance on Excel and CSV interfaces for simulation parameter updates and results tracking, which effectively supported automation while underscoring the need for more advanced interfaces (Siddique, 2024). The proposed future direction is the development of a GUI-based solution to enhance usability, transparency, and collaborative stakeholder access.

Section 7.4 presented scenario-based validation using SysML activity and state machine diagrams, which simulated dynamic mission behaviors such as lifetime, orientation, and communication logic under representative conditions (Holt & Perry, 2012). These scenario models were traceably connected to mission requirements, enabling lifecycle feedback at both functional and behavioral levels.

Section 7.5 synthesized validation improvements resulting from digital thread alignment and structured feedback loops, which helped uncover interdependencies and parameter conflicts during early modeling (NASA, 2020). Feedback from system iterations enabled correction of inconsistencies in key design constraints such as battery sizing and orbital parameters.

Collectively, these model-based validation activities created a robust, simulation-integrated workflow for analyzing aerospace systems, reinforcing confidence in requirements coverage, system design trustworthiness, and deployment readiness (Delligatti, 2013). Lessons drawn from this implementation informed future refinement goals for broader integration and stakeholder interaction.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.1 INTEGRATED INSIGHTS FROM MBSE AND DIGITAL INTEGRATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 1 integrated insights from mbse and digital integration
text: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) was adopted in the SidSat project to address limitations inherent in conventional document-driven approaches (Estefan, 2008). By using SysML, the modeling process represented logical structures, behavioral operations, and interface definitions within a single environment, allowing for improved integration that traditional documents lacked (NASA, 2020). Constructs such as blocks, internal connections, parametric constraints, and allocations facilitated the early identification of conflicts and architectural gaps, thereby reinforcing decision-making across phases (Object Management Group, 2017).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.1 INTEGRATED INSIGHTS FROM MBSE AND DIGITAL INTEGRATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 1 integrated insights from mbse and digital integration
text: The modeling effort emphasized full traceability, mapping stakeholder inputs to system structures and performance needs. Trace links were preserved across the architecture and lifecycle stages, improving visibility and reducing missed dependencies (INCOSE, 2015). This structure supported design assessments by simulating how changes in system architecture would influence performance, control flow, and risk margins across different mission conditions (Siddique, 2024). Behavioral diagrams enhanced temporal understanding of key operations and validated the intended logic under nominal and off-nominal scenarios (Haskins, 2011).

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 1 integrated insights from mbse and digital integration
text: MBSE was further extended by integrating a synchronized digital toolchain. MATLAB and the Systems Tool Kit (STK) were configured alongside SysML to test dynamics, orbital constraints, and mission logic concurrently (MathWorks, 2023). Simulation inputs originated from requirement-derived tables, and system outputs were validated against defined criteria and linked back to the core model for traceability (Paredis et al., 2010). Iterative feedback allowed for the early resolution of model inconsistencies and operational issues.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 1 integrated insights from mbse and digital integration
text: Cameo Systems Modeler served as the central platform, enabling updates to flow consistently across logical and structural views without requiring reinitialization of simulations (NASA, 2020). Engineers could assess design margins and detect violations through interactive dashboards, facilitating effective stakeholder communication and ensuring continuity in digital verification. The use of MBSE ensured that system behavior, structure, and requirements coevolved under a unified model environment. $ ^{49} $

text: The SidSat system employed a cross-platform architecture that integrated Cameo, MATLAB, STK, Excel, Teamcenter, and AWS to facilitate efficient transitions between modeling, simulation, and validation tasks. Incompatibility across these tools, such as varying units, parameter mismatches, and version conflicts, initially hindered interoperability. These issues were addressed using predefined templates, automated scripts, and interface plugins. However, the experience emphasized the necessity for unified interface standards and consistent version management policies to ensure platform-wide stability (Dunbar et al., 2023).

Integration across engineering tools strengthened system-level analysis and streamlined data synchronization. These outcomes demonstrate the applicability of structured modeling techniques in addressing aerospace design challenges and contribute to a reusable framework for future missions.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.2 LESSONS FROM APPLYING REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization
text: The adoption of a structured prioritization approach significantly influenced the validation strategy for SidSat. Instead of applying equal weight to all requirements, a filtering and scoring system was used to identify and emphasize the most critical verification targets. Over one hundred requirements were reviewed, ranked, and narrowed using a systematic framework that improved traceability and resource deployment (Berander & Andrews, 2005). $ ^{50} $

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.2 LESSONS FROM APPLYING REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization
text: The BUIR approach: Benefit, Urgency, Impact, and Risk, served as the central prioritization model, as outlined in Chapter 3 and Sections 5.3.2 to 5.3.5. The formula applied was:

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.2 LESSONS FROM APPLYING REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.2 LESSONS FROM APPLYING REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization
text: Here, B represents the value to stakeholders, U reflects the urgency of the capability's need, I indicates the complexity of implementation, and R identifies the associated risk. Using this logic, requirements were categorized into priority tiers. The structured ranking clarified trade-offs and ensured focused effort during simulation, verification, and configuration (Beshears & Long, 2024).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.2 LESSONS FROM APPLYING REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization
text: The prioritization outcome directly informed system modeling and validation workflows. High-ranking requirements were explicitly traced to test cases and validated through integrated simulations using Cameo, MATLAB, and STK. The top-ranked requirement, PR 2.5 Operational Lifetime, scored 83.6 and was modeled to ensure system performance across a minimum 1.5-year orbital duration, incorporating lifetime degradation models within a value-based SysML structure. Similarly, FR 1.5.3 Survive, associated with extreme thermal conditions $ (-65^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ to $ +128^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ ), was validated through thermal modeling scenarios that integrated constraint equations into the parametric layer. Lastly, BTR 3.10.1 Vibration OCV was assessed through post-launch battery performance simulations, where open-circuit voltage (OCV) variations were mapped against acceptance thresholds using MATLAB-STK co-simulation. These high-priority items were each connected to their respective verification methods, enhancing model traceability and risk resilience.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.2 LESSONS FROM APPLYING REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization
text: Traceability became a defining feature of the process, as each requirement was mapped to logical behavior, design constraints, validation output, and supporting documentation. This allowed for embedded verification tracking and eliminated the need for separate audit logs. Consequently, simulation outcomes could be traced back to prioritization scores and validation assumptions (Estefan, 2008).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.2 LESSONS FROM APPLYING REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization
text: A notable observation was that certain prioritization criteria emerged only after model execution commenced. The feasibility of simulation, constraint definitions, and tool interface

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization
text: compatibility played a significant role in refining scores. Vague or qualitative requirements consumed disproportionate effort and yielded inconclusive verification. In contrast, clearly defined and high-priority ones aligned well with deterministic validation and simulation of fidelity.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.2 LESSONS FROM APPLYING REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization
text: The integration of prioritization with the overall digital engineering approach enabled early screening of infeasible or untestable conditions. Requirements that failed automated verification loops, due to conflicting values or undefined constraints, were either refined or temporarily excluded. This adaptation helped reduce wasted modeling effort and aligned resources to address the most pressing needs (Inayat et al., 2015).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.2 LESSONS FROM APPLYING REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization
text: The model environment itself was enhanced by incorporating visual validation indicators. Color-coded statuses within the Cameo SysML model conveyed the maturity of requirements: validated items were marked green, while failed ones were marked red. These graphics provided real-time feedback to engineering teams, encouraging rapid iteration and updates to meet evolving architectural demands.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.2 LESSONS FROM APPLYING REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization
text: The prioritization process also guided the decision-making process for tools. For example, Cameo was retained as the modeling platform due to its interoperability with simulation tools and support for embedded constraint evaluation. Lessons learned from simulation configuration informed modeling workflows, enabling the automation of test setup based on requirement scores.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.2 LESSONS FROM APPLYING REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 2 lessons from applying requirements prioritization
text: In conclusion, prioritization was not limited to ranking needs; it became integral to the entire model-based system engineering (MBSE) verification cycle. By aligning system validation with high-impact targets and traceable metrics, this approach increased transparency, adaptability, and system insight. When embedded within MBSE workflows, quantitative prioritization contributes to an agile, simulation-driven development environment for aerospace missions.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.3 LESSONS FROM DIGITAL TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND SCALABILITY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 3 lessons from digital toolchain integration and scalability
text: The SidSat development effort offered a unique opportunity to explore cross-platform integration within a digital engineering (DE) toolchain, combining Cameo, MATLAB, STK, Excel, Teamcenter, and AWS in a practical aerospace context (Siemens, 2022). These tools contributed at various stages of modeling, analysis, and feedback, enabling structured transitions across lifecycle phases (Madni et al., 2018). Many challenges emerged early, particularly those involving inconsistent data structures and unit misalignment across platforms (Pratt & Dabkowski, 2022). These were gradually mitigated through rule-based formatting conventions and common schema alignment (Nicolescu et al., 2018).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.3 LESSONS FROM DIGITAL TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND SCALABILITY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 3 lessons from digital toolchain integration and scalability
text: Initially, integration inconsistencies created setbacks in transferring data between SysML models and simulation environments (Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, 2020). Adjustments included refining input protocols and establishing tool-specific wrappers to normalize execution parameters (Siemens, 2022). As the configuration matured, validation routines became more predictable and reliable (Browning et al., 2022). These corrections also improved confidence in the automated test cycles driven by embedded scripts (Nicolescu et al., 2018).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.3 LESSONS FROM DIGITAL TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND SCALABILITY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 3 lessons from digital toolchain integration and scalability
text: At the outset, simulations were manually invoked, requiring direct edits to parametric diagrams and spreadsheets (Madni et al., 2018). Over time, this approach gave way to a semiautomated process where Excel served as a control interface to trigger MATLAB and STK routines (Siemens, 2022). These outputs were automatically routed back into Cameo to verify constraint compliance and populate validation indicators (Pratt & Dabkowski, 2022). Engineers then reviewed results within the model itself, identifying discrepancies and refining inputs iteratively (Nicolescu et al., 2018).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.3 LESSONS FROM DIGITAL TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND SCALABILITY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 3 lessons from digital toolchain integration and scalability
text: Constraint evaluation occurred through logic blocks in the SysML architecture, linking physical parameters with requirement thresholds (Siemens, 2022). Failures triggered visual feedback in the form of color-coded markers, prompting immediate re-examination of affected models (Pratt & Dabkowski, 2022). This closed-loop response reduced dependence on postprocessing and shortened the redesign cycle (Madni et al., 2018). Performance risks that typically appear late in development were caught earlier through simulation-driven alerts (Browning et al., 2022).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.3 LESSONS FROM DIGITAL TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND SCALABILITY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 3 lessons from digital toolchain integration and scalability
text: To support users not directly involved in modeling, a simple user interface was prototyped to centralize test initiation and simulation control (Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, 2020). Designed with accessibility in mind, the interface included dropdown menus, alerts, and run-status feedback, enabling broader participation in validation (Siemens, 2022). Stakeholders unfamiliar with modeling tools could now interpret test status without accessing backend environments (Pratt & Dabkowski, 2022). This abstraction encouraged more exhaustive review and shared accountability for system performance (Nicolescu et al., 2018).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.3 LESSONS FROM DIGITAL TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND SCALABILITY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 3 lessons from digital toolchain integration and scalability
text: All simulation files, scripts, and settings were organized in cloud-based repositories using Teamcenter and AWS S3 storage layers (Madni et al., 2018). Requirements were traceable across runs using consistent file naming conventions and change-tracked metadata (Siemens, 2022). These mechanisms helped maintain reproducibility, allowing configuration histories to be retrieved for audit or troubleshooting (Browning et al., 2022). The resulting workflow emphasized control over test integrity and lifecycle traceability (Pratt & Dabkowski, 2022).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.3 LESSONS FROM DIGITAL TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND SCALABILITY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 3 lessons from digital toolchain integration and scalability
text: A key architectural decision involved enforcing modularity, in line with MOSA principles, to avoid fragile point-to-point dependencies (Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, 2020). Each simulation unit, whether an Excel sheet, MATLAB script,

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 3 lessons from digital toolchain integration and scalability
text: or STK model, was decoupled for isolated versioning and debugging (Nicolescu et al., 2018). This allowed controlled upgrades and reusable modules across similar subsystems (Siemens, 2022). Integration testing confirmed functional continuity even as scripts and parameters evolved (Pratt & Dabkowski, 2022).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.3 LESSONS FROM DIGITAL TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION AND SCALABILITY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 3 lessons from digital toolchain integration and scalability
text: These toolchain experiences demonstrated a functioning digital thread suitable for iterative and scalable validation workflows (Madni et al., 2018). The effort validated the potential of synchronized MBSE and DE platforms to support agile design refinement (Browning et al., 2022). By using model-centric orchestration and version-controlled components, SidSat established a practical foundation for future aerospace digital twin efforts (Nicolescu et al., 2018).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.4 RECOMMENDATIONS FOR FUTURE AEROSPACE PROJECTS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 4 recommendations for future aerospace projects
text: Based on the comprehensive experience from the SidSat development, the following practical recommendations are offered:

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.4 RECOMMENDATIONS FOR FUTURE AEROSPACE PROJECTS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 4 recommendations for future aerospace projects
text: 1) Start Modeling Early: Begin SysML modeling at the concept phase to capture assumptions and iterate design logic before architectural lock-in.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 4 recommendations for future aerospace projects
text: 2) Emphasize Traceability: Link every requirement to a corresponding functional, structural, and testable element. Utilize validation tables, requirement diagrams, and trace matrices to ensure visibility.

text: 3) Prioritize Iteratively: Use adaptive prioritization frameworks that allow re-ranking based on model behavior, simulation feasibility, and tool constraints.

text: 4) Invest in Integration Automation: Automate wherever it is feasible but begin with semiautomated scripts to learn system interfaces and failure points.

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 4 recommendations for future aerospace projects
text: 5) Leverage Lightweight Tools: Do not underestimate the power of simple tools (e.g., Excel, CSV) when building complex workflows; modular design helps scale.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 8.4 RECOMMENDATIONS FOR FUTURE AEROSPACE PROJECTS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 8 4 recommendations for future aerospace projects
text: 6) Promote Cross-Disciplinary Engagement: Facilitate collaboration between system engineers, domain experts, and tool specialists to resolve integration barriers and model interpretation. Digital transformation research emphasizes the importance of cultural readiness, capability integration, and leadership vision in sustaining MBSE across enterprise contexts (Kraus et al., 2021).

The SidSat effort demonstrated the practical benefits of integrating model-based systems engineering with digital engineering workflows (Estefan, 2008). SysML-based modeling facilitated early validation, provided a clear structure, and ensured consistent traceability from requirements to test outcomes (Holt & Perry, 2012). By integrating a prioritization strategy, it was possible to focus resources on achievable, high-impact requirements while avoiding unnecessary design overhead (Berander & Andrews, 2005).

Simulation tools linked through an automated chain improved verification accuracy and supported incremental model refinement (Nicolescu et al., 2018). The approach proved suitable not only for academic CubeSat initiatives but also for broader system development efforts with similar resource and complexity constraints (Madni et al., 2018). More than just a modeling exercise, the process enabled responsive design thinking, visible progress tracking, and better alignment between models and mission goals (Browning et al., 2022). These observations provide a foundation for refining future systems through improved tool use and method discipline.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.1 SUMMARY OF RESEARCH CONTRIBUTIONS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 1 summary of research contributions
text: This research presents four key contributions to aerospace systems engineering, with emphasis on small satellite development, digital integration strategies, and requirement-driven system evolution. The research framework integrates Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), quantitative prioritization, and digital simulation workflows to support scalable, verifiable, and traceable design processes.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.1 SUMMARY OF RESEARCH CONTRIBUTIONS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 1 summary of research contributions
text: The first contribution enhances the application of MBSE in space system design through the development of comprehensive SysML models for SidSat, including Block Definition Diagrams (BDDs), Internal Block Diagrams (IBDs), Activities, State Machines, Parametrics, and Requirement Tables. These models established direct traceability between stakeholder needs and system behaviors, improving design structure, interface logic, and verification visibility across abstraction levels (Holt, 2014).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.1 SUMMARY OF RESEARCH CONTRIBUTIONS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 1 summary of research contributions
text: Second, a hybrid prioritization method was developed to address the challenge of ranking complex, interacting requirements under constraints typical of aerospace missions. This method combines filtration logic, scoring functions, and structured evaluation using tools such as AHP and decision matrices to rank over one hundred candidate requirements systematically. $ ^{51} $ The framework supports feasibility screening, captures a traceable rationale, and facilitates simulation-informed alignment with system objectives (Herrmann et al., 2010).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.1 SUMMARY OF RESEARCH CONTRIBUTIONS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 1 summary of research contributions
text: Third, the study contributes an operational digital engineering toolchain that integrates Cameo Systems Modeler with MATLAB, STK, Excel, and AWS/Teamcenter platforms. This workflow enables the structured sharing of parameters, scenario testing, and outcome validation using model-driven activity triggers, resulting in semi-automated simulation execution and test result propagation without reliance on hardware iterations (MathWorks, 2023).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.1 SUMMARY OF RESEARCH CONTRIBUTIONS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 1 summary of research contributions
text: Fourth, the SidSat case study offers a working demonstration of how integrated MBSE practices can be implemented within small-scale teams, showing a shift from isolated documents to live model coordination. It confirms that digitally connected MBSE enables early defect discovery, improves simulation configuration, and increases reuse of verified models, particularly in educational or constrained program settings (Dunbar et al., 2023).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.1 SUMMARY OF RESEARCH CONTRIBUTIONS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 1 summary of research contributions
text: In addition to its CubeSat-specific relevance, this research has broader applicability to systems such as autonomous platforms, reusable launch vehicles, and multi-domain defense networks. These domains exhibit similar system constraints, including rapid timelines and regulatory oversight, and stand to benefit from reusable modeling strategies that support simulation-backed decisions and architecture-level traceability (NASA, 2018).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.1 SUMMARY OF RESEARCH CONTRIBUTIONS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 1 summary of research contributions
text: The methods also align with industry priorities by addressing lifecycle coordination, toolchain synchronization, and risk-based requirement filtering. The ability to trace each requirement through modeling artifacts, behavior chains, and simulation feedback supports verification planning and contract deliverable consistency (INCOSE, 2015).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.1 SUMMARY OF RESEARCH CONTRIBUTIONS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 1 summary of research contributions
text: Collectively, this study delivers a repeatable and tool-agnostic systems engineering approach that supports end-to-end digital lifecycle execution. The combined use of MBSE modeling, dynamic prioritization, and simulation feedback loops supports scalable system verification and fosters resilient decision-making processes (Estefan, 2008).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.1 SUMMARY OF RESEARCH CONTRIBUTIONS
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 1 summary of research contributions
text: The research concludes with a proposed direction for future development: transitioning spreadsheet-based dashboards into fully integrated model viewers and embedding live test output within requirement views. These enhancements are intended to streamline interpretation during verification, reduce handoff ambiguity, and improve digital continuity across design iterations (Object Management Group, 2017).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.2 IMPLICATIONS FOR AEROSPACE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 2 implications for aerospace systems engineering
text: The findings presented in this study provide actionable insights for advancing aerospace and defense systems engineering, particularly in the design and validation of mission-critical architectures (Pyster & Olwell, 2013). By implementing MBSE and digital engineering principles on the SidSat project, it became evident that structured modeling processes improve system clarity, early validation, and cross-phase traceability (INCOSE, 2015). Simulation-integrated frameworks helped align requirements with subsystem behavior, enabling iterative testing within defined operational boundaries (Zimmerman et al., 2019).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.2 IMPLICATIONS FOR AEROSPACE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 2 implications for aerospace systems engineering
text: Aerospace systems developed through traditional document-based workflows often experience fragmented coordination, unclear validation logic, and extensive rework cycles (NASA, 2020). The integrated modeling and simulation approach adopted here helped mitigate such inefficiencies by offering a single, unified representation of system intent across all development stages (Object Management Group, 2017). Each requirement was contextually anchored within the model, simplifying design justification and reducing ambiguity (Holt, 2014).

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 2 implications for aerospace systems engineering
text: These methods also apply to defense domains where change propagation, audit traceability, and controlled revalidation are essential under evolving mission constraints (Department of Defense, 2018). The BUIR-based prioritization logic embedded within the model allowed system engineers to quickly filter, score, and validate high-risk requirements before downstream

text: integration (Bonnet et al., 2016). The resulting model provided a shared digital reference for design reviews and stakeholder briefings, improving cross-disciplinary collaboration (Estefan, 2008).

section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 2 implications for aerospace systems engineering

The model-centric testbed enabled the detection of infeasible constraints early in the lifecycle, thereby reducing the risk of late-stage design reversals (Teamcenter, 2022).

text: Although the primary application involved a 4U CubeSat, the framework can be generalized to avionics testing, guidance systems, and spaceborne sensor networks without architectural disruption (The Boeing Company, 2024). As the industry transitions toward digital first practices, the findings affirm the operational value of MBSE-driven verification strategies (Airbus, 2024). These methods collectively support mission assurance, cost reduction, and lifecycle continuity (Voirin, 2017).

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.3 LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 3 limitations of the study
text: While this research has made important contributions to the field, several limitations must be acknowledged to interpret its findings and identify areas for future enhancement properly.

section: Chapter 3: Methodology > 9.3 LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY
section_key: chapter 3 methodology / 9 3 limitations of the study
text: First, the modeling and validation activities were confined to simulation-based environments and virtual toolchains, without incorporating physical subsystem testing or hardware-in-the-loop experimentation (INCOSE, 2015). Although functional fidelity was verified using tools such as MATLAB, STK, and Cameo, the lack of hardware interaction limited the evaluation of environmental realism and integration performance (MathWorks, 2023).

text: These limitations are common in academic MBSE efforts and help define a path forward, emphasizing the importance of phased implementation, cross-domain validation, and extended toolchain readiness for future aerospace applications (Pyster & Olwell, 2013).
Building upon the outcomes of this investigation, several directions remain for advancing the proposed MBSE and digital engineering methods within broader aerospace contexts (NASA, 2020).

First, transitioning the framework to support hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) execution offers the potential to evaluate system behavior under real-time operational conditions (MathWorks, 2023). $ ^{52} $ This extension would require interface development with avionics components, telemetry systems, and timing protocols for ground and space communication links.

Second, the spreadsheet-based input/output interface should evolve into a platform independent digital dashboard that supports scenario configuration, test execution, and metrics visualization across distributed teams (AWS, 2023). Web-enabled dashboards with database linkage would also allow long-term storage, query-based validation, and traceability across simulation runs.
Third, the current implementation is limited to a single system; however, future research could generalize the approach for use with federated aerospace systems, such as CubeSat swarms,

hybrid UAV constellations, and launch-support architectures (Browning et al., 2022). This would require extensions to scenario logic, cross-platform data binding, and synchronization control between component systems.

Fourth, integrating natural language processing (NLP) with prioritization logic may streamline the capture of requirements from technical reports or stakeholder briefings, automating both decomposition and adaptive ranking under changing constraints (Alai, 2019). AI/ML techniques could be tested for requirement refinement, pattern detection, and scoring automation in resource-sensitive trade spaces.

Fifth, standardization and benchmarking against frameworks such as ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 and the INCOSE SE Handbook can help validate the framework's industrial readiness (INCOSE, 2015). This alignment would ensure that the approach remains compatible with existing systems engineering practices and documentation requirements.

Sixth, expanding the digital thread to support aerospace system classes beyond CubeSats, including propulsion modules, reentry systems, and avionics firmware, would allow the framework to demonstrate its modularity and domain transferability (Boeing Company, 2024). Moreover, this framework offers high potential as an instructional and workforce training tool when embedded within academic curricula or aerospace research and development (R&D) labs (Post et al., 2019).

Lastly, embedding the MBSE-based prioritization and digital validation logic directly into development lifecycles offers organizations a path to improved responsiveness, lifecycle integration, and design assurance (Object Management Group, 2017). These recommendations aim to extend the proposed model from a research demonstrator to a robust system development accelerator suitable for regulated, dynamic aerospace missions.

This effort marks the culmination of a multidisciplinary journey across the evolving domains of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), requirements prioritization, and digital integration in aerospace applications. It is the outcome of years spent refining models, developing interoperable toolchains, and analyzing system behavior, all in pursuit of a single question: how complex aerospace systems might be conceived, designed, and validated in a digitally enabled era?

This research was grounded in a practical challenge, how to manage the complexity of aerospace missions while maintaining testability, traceability, and scalability from the earliest stages. This question shaped the development of a unified methodological approach that blends Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), simulation-based validation, and intelligent requirements prioritization. Through the SidSat case study, the effort showed that even constrained, small-scale missions can benefit from professional-grade modeling techniques, cross-platform interoperability, and lifecycle validation supported by simulation and analytical logic.

Beyond technical implementation, this work represents the tension between system structure and real-world adaptability. The research was influenced by institutional barriers, scheduling gaps, and practical design limitations that mirrored the environments in which systems engineers often work. Each challenge, whether related to software, hardware, timing, or coordination, offered new insight into how digital engineering must remain flexible to succeed in operational contexts.

This work is more than a demonstration of tools or processes. It is a reflection of systems thinking itself, an attempt to navigate uncertainty while preserving clarity of purpose. Just as a satellite achieves stability through dynamic balance with its environment, so too must system engineers learn to work between abstraction and implementation. From the earliest concept
diagrams to the final orbital simulations, this work represents an intentional journey to understand, not just engineer, complex systems.

As exploration continues beyond Earth and missions become increasingly complex, frameworks that prioritize clarity, resilience, and validation will become essential. This research serves as one small but intentional contribution toward that collective effort, grounded in practice and driven by purpose.

This research has established a foundational approach that integrates Model-Based Systems Engineering, adaptive requirements prioritization, and digital toolchain connectivity within the demanding context of aerospace systems. These contributions respond directly to prevailing challenges in lifecycle modeling, traceability, and cross-domain integration, while also encouraging new pathways for sustainable, testable, and evolvable system design.

This research offers a scaffold rather than a solution, a beginning built through hands-on modeling, cross-domain simulation, and a willingness to question embedded assumptions. The methods and insights developed here are not fixed endpoints but provide a platform for continued exploration grounded in practical modeling, simulation-based validation, and critical evaluation. The process itself reflected the nature of the systems under study, defined by constraints, refined through iteration, and reinforced by multidisciplinary feedback. As aerospace systems grow in complexity, meaningful progress will depend on architectures that not only perform with technical rigor but also adapt to uncertainty, mission variability, and evolving stakeholder priorities.

section: From Concept to Capability: The Road Beyond > APPENDIX E. DIGITAL TOOLCHAIN INTEGRATION
section_key: from concept to capability the road beyond / appendix e digital toolchain integration
text: This appendix summarizes the digital toolchain configuration and integration approach applied to support model-based systems engineering activities for the SidSat mission. The core toolchain included Cameo Systems Modeler for SysML-based system architecture modeling, MATLAB for evaluating parametric constraints, STK for validating orbital scenarios, and Microsoft Excel/CSV for tracking and storing requirements data. These tools were integrated to enable synchronized data exchange, simulation-informed validation, and traceable model transformations across the system lifecycle. Although the primary integration focused on these four tools, preliminary efforts were also initiated to connect with Teamcenter and AWS for lifecycle data management and cloud-based simulation support. Additionally, an external user interface (UI) for streamlined input and output handling is currently under development to improve model accessibility and simulation control. $ ^{56} $

Leonhard Kessler $ ^{a *} $ , Vincenzo Messina $ ^{a} $ , Alessandro Golkar $ ^{a} $

$ ^{a} $ Chair of Spacecraft Systems, Department of Aerospace and Geodesy, Technical University of Munich, 85521 Ottobrunn, Germany, leonhard.kessler@tum.de, vincenzo.messina@tum.de, golkar@tum.de $ ^{*} $ Corresponding author

The evolution of CubeSats from a technical demonstrator to a reliable, low-cost platform for custom scientific and commercial missions has introduced a new era of space operations. This shift has heightened the demand for risk management, reliability, and predictable data delivery. The increasing competition in the aerospace industry has intensified the need for more efficient methods. Digital Twin presents a promising solution for streamlining the life cycle of a CubeSat, enabling accelerated development and more reliable operations. Despite its potential, limited research prevents broader application in the CubeSat sector.

This study delves into the unique and complex challenges of implementing a Digital Twin for a CubeSat, considering its short development cycles, high modularity, and limited resources. The theoretical considerations integrate insights from a comprehensive review of relevant literature and data collected through an industry survey, providing a holistic perspective on the subject matter. It offers insights into tailoring the Digital Twin process to the characteristics of CubeSats. The practical side showcases the hardware and software components utilized in the implementation, using a 6U-CubeSat as a case study. It focuses on early lifecycle data correlation of the payload power management, enhancing the understanding of the satellite's behavior and enabling early configuration optimization.

The industry survey analyzes the application of the Digital Twin in the satellite industry. It assesses the current state of implementations within the sector using a maturity model, highlighting the increasing interest in the topic and identifying the current techniques. Insights gained from the industry perspective are contextualized. This involves identifying key challenges and system requirements, emphasizing subsystem detail fidelity, and prioritizing modeling scope across the life cycle. A generic CubeSat Digital Twin framework is presented, which includes the central architecture, possible applications, and benefits for the system, enabling the application of a Digital Twin to future CubeSat missions. The focus is on understandability, effective data integration, and ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the Digital Twin. It shifts the approach from safety factor-based to instantiation-based designs, enabling informed decision-making through integrated data.

The exploration of the feasibility of practical implementation is demonstrated through the implementation of CubeSat Digital Twin in the CubeSat project of the Chair of Spacecraft Systems at the Technical University of Munich, the EventSat. This mission involves a 6U CubeSat designed to advance object detection in space using an event-based camera. The implementation strategy focuses on the power management of the satellite. It illustrates its practical application by developing a Digital Twin to mirror the satellite's behavior with an automated control loop. The system correlates real-world data with simulations and adapts the operation of the physical payload to changing parameters. This research identifies key strategies, limitations, and areas for improvement, utilizing insights obtained from industry perspectives through interviews and end-user feedback. It successfully bridges the gap between theoretical concepts and practical implementation, ensuring the effective application of Digital Twin technology in CubeSat development and operations.
Keywords: CubeSat, Digital Twin, Industry Survey, Questionnaire, Framework, Case Study

The evolution of CubeSats over the past 25 years, transitioning from technical demonstrators to capable platforms for space research, has ushered in a new era of space operations. This progress empowers an increasing number of companies, start-ups, academic

institutions, and government agencies to build and launch satellites [1]. To be successful, however, this increase in satellite launches and the growing interaction with space also comes with numerous challenges. System safety measures and subsystems are critical design criteria [2]. Technology demonstrations,

comprehensive test facilities, and enhancements in incorporating new technologies are crucial as more and more CubeSats are launched and designed to operate in Low-Earth Orbit and beyond [3]. The Digital Twin is a promising technology that supports a product throughout its lifecycle by simulating, analyzing, and optimizing its performance as a virtual representation of the physical system. It offers valuable insights into maintenance and reliability, helps maximize product performance, delivers data on new products, and enhances overall efficiency [4].

The Digital Twin concept originates from Grieves introduction of the "Mirrored Space Model" to enable product lifecycle management [5]. Defining it as comprising three elements: "real space, virtual space(s), and a linking mechanism, referred to as data and information/process connection between real space and virtual space(s)" [6]. The Digital Twin progressed from theoretical research to pragmatic implementations over the last 20 years and is currently undergoing a period of rapid development, with more than a thousand papers published per year concerning this topic [7]. In this research, various definitions have been published to represent the current state and specific domains, reflecting the progression and development of the Digital Twin concept. This has evolved into a mature, comprehensive definition applicable to multiple domains and types of Digital Twins published by the ISO/IEC organizations.

section: The Digital Twin is defined as:
section_key: the digital twin is defined as
text: "digital representation of a target entity with data connections that enable convergence between the physical and digital states at an appropriate rate of synchronization" - with two entry notes:

section: The Digital Twin is defined as:
section_key: the digital twin is defined as
text: "Note 1 to entry: Digital twin has some or all of the capabilities of connection, integration, analysis, simulation, visualization, optimization, collaboration,
Note 2 to entry: Digital twin can provide an integrated view throughout the life cycle of the target entity. " [8]

The growing interest in Digital Twins has led to the perception that the concept is inaccessible and intangible, particularly in industries like the New Space sector, due to its association with the traditional space sector. This perception is reinforced by NASA's early involvement in Digital Twin research, which proposed an ambitious concept integrating a broad range of technologies into a singular focus. Consequently, the concept is linked to complex, expensive projects [9].

Replicas of spacecraft have been used in the aerospace sector since the 1960s [10]. Starting with mock-ups of spacecraft, these replicas are used to internalize procedures before launch and to test solutions and approaches during spaceflight. This allows for problem-solving and handling unscheduled events in a safe environment without risk to human beings [10]. This approach is adopted for satellites by creating non-flight versions of satellites for testing and verifying designs with engineering models.

While Digital Twins are applied in various aerospace applications, publications often focus on specific disciplines or single-example applications [11] [12]. Notably, the space sector, particularly CubeSats, shows insufficient research on Digital Twin applications, which remain nascent, with very few implemented examples in publications [13]. However, company announcements and industry contacts suggest ongoing development in this area.

This research addresses the existing gap by conducting an industry survey to gain deeper insights into the current state-of-the-art. This is used to clarify the challenges and approaches related to Digital Twins in the space sector. As a novel contribution, a methodology for the implementation of a CubeSat Digital Twin is presented and evaluated through a practical demonstration of its application.

The paper is structured as follows: first, an industry survey assesses the maturity of the satellite industry regarding Digital Twins, highlighting current developments and challenges. Second, a framework for a CubeSat Digital Twin is introduced, outlined throughout its lifecycle, and highlighting the unique aspects of a Digital Twin for a CubeSat. Next, the framework is applied in a case study involving a 6U CubeSat currently in development at the Technical University of Munich. An outlook is given on future research work and further developments. Finally, the last section will draw some conclusions.

section: 2. Digital Twin Survey in the Space Industry
section_key: 2 digital twin survey in the space industry
text: A survey has been conducted to expand the knowledge of Digital Twins in the satellite domain. It collects insights into the conception and understanding of the Digital Twin, its usage, and its relation to CubeSats in the industry. A quantitative, fully standardized questionnaire was used for the survey. This type of questionnaire consists of closed questions or statements with predetermined answer options, allowing respondents to select the most appropriate responses. Answering this highly structured format enabled the individual to answer by self-scheduling the response time discreetly and anonymously. Beyond the research conducted through the literature review, an empirical evaluation of the topic of Digital Twins in the satellite industry through a survey provides further insights into

section: 2. Digital Twin Survey in the Space Industry
section_key: 2 digital twin survey in the space industry
text: the state-of-the-art development. Additionally, it enables gathering the challenges companies face when considering implementing a Digital Twin. This gives further insights into current projects under development in institutions that do not publish their work, which is especially the case in the private industry or projects that have not reached the stage of development that brings novelty to the field of research [14].

section: 2. Digital Twin Survey in the Space Industry
