According to the analyses discussed in the previous sections, a preliminary selection of key subsystems was
completed providing the following functional architecture of the Borealis 6U CubeSat:
- Power Subsystem: The primary power source will consist of body-mounted solar panels. This setup ensures adequate power generation to support all onboard systems.

- Communication Subsystem: Communication s/s will be based on dual UHF (TX/RX) and S-band (TX/RX) transceivers, ensuring reliable data transmission and command reception throughout the mission duration. The preferred choice according to the analysis discussed in this paper
- Propulsion Subsystem: Hall-effect thruster providing efficient orbit transfer and manoeuvring capabilities

- Attitude Determination and Control Subsystem (ADCS): The ADCS will comprise a suite of sensors, including gyroscopes, star trackers, sun sensors, and magnetometers, along with actuators such as reaction wheels and magnetorquers. This configuration ensures precise orientation control and stability.
- On-board Computer (OBC): The computing architecture will employ a SOC (System on Chip), offering robust processing power for real-time data handling and system management.
- Thermal Management: A combination of passive and active thermal management techniques will be employed to maintain optimal operating temperatures for all components.
- Data Handling: The CubeSat will feature onboard storage capabilities, allowing for the
collection and temporary storage of scientific data before transmission during communication windows. The real-time processing capability might enable on-board data handling and analysis.

- Payload: The primary scientific payload will include a fluorescence microscope and lab-on-chip with integrated sensors for studying biofilm growth and behavior, supplemented by radiation sensors and other scientific instruments for scientific payload control and.

The BOREALIS CubeSat mission represents a significant step forward in the study of live cells in space through a lab-on-chip platform and the validation of new technologies within CubeSats.

The BOREALIS CubeSat implemented MBSE with the support of Valispace, Monte Carlo analysis to select the best concept and model among the presented ones with the specific variables of utility and cost, conducted mission analysis for its specific LEO-MEO mission requirements, propulsion selected regarding mission performance and TID accumulation considering the needed propellent mass and volume.

Through the presented comprehensive system analysis, including the exploration of alternative mission concepts and the incorporation of a MBSE provided insightful results defining a preliminary mission baseline concept. Among the main highlights, we highlight how the HET propulsion alternative offers substantial benefits over the HPGP, including a lower initial orbit requirement, improved volume efficiency, and a more manageable orbit transfer time. These advantages directly address the initial challenges of the mission and align more closely with the mission's scientific and operational objectives.

The system engineering approach and tools used in this first part of the mission have been presented with detail, including the trade-space analysis and the additional quantitative analysis used to validate the model (Monte Carlo and sensitivity analysis).

The BOREALIS mission is set to have an impact beyond space applications. The in-depth study of biofilms, responsible for the majority of persistent infections, and the validation of radioprotection strategies hold promise for advancing medical diagnostics, radiation therapy, and nuclear medicine on Earth. In conclusion, BOREALIS embodies a dual purpose: ensuring human well-being and productivity in space while simultaneously enhancing the quality of life on Earth through space-induced scientific advancements.

The next steps will involve implementing the detailed design of all the subsystems, procurement activities of the main parts, payload manufacturing and testing, and maintaining close collaboration with stakeholders to ensure the mission's continued success.

Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) has received widespread adoption in the space industry, allowing engineers to develop, design and validate their activities through formal models. MBSE's perceived benefits include enhanced communication, complexity management, knowledge transfer, and improved verification capabilities through traceability. However, generic or tailored MBSE tools have not yet found such widespread adoption in small satellite missions, such as CubeSats. Drawing from a review of previous and current missions, we postulate that many MBSE tools and processes add a considerable overhead in terms of time, cost and effort to establish and maintain models. On the other hand, Document-Based Systems Engineering, often used on such projects, may suffer from inconsistency, lack of detail, and difficulty in accessing reliable and up-to-date engineering data. In this paper, we propose a concept and design for a new software tool for small spacecraft engineering, focused on engineering parameter management and sharing. This design is based on modern design and user experience principles, with a basic requirement of allowing users to access any engineering parameter within 20 seconds of having access to a web browser. The tool uses a standard block-based structure to describe the hierarchy of a space system, with modifiable parameters and content assigned to each block. This structure is stored under a version-controlled database (such as git or dolt), allowing history tracking, merging, auditing and real-time collaboration. Ready-made templates can also be used to produce aggregate values, such as mass or cost budgets. A REST API allows integration with different external tools, such as MS Excel Power Query, and an integration with an AI-based copilot is envisioned. To complement the design concept of our tool, we additionally provide User Interface mockups of key actions, as well as an early functional proof-of-concept developed with a Python backend. We use data from the POQUITO mission from the University of Luxembourg to emulate a use case in our proof-of-concept. This implementation is also released as free software to allow future users to modify and extend our tool. We conclude with a roadmap for the potential future development of the tool, with an aim of improving the engineering data management workflow for small satellite missions and surpass the limits of document-based information tracking, without the added burden of industrial modelling processes.
Keywords: cubesat, testing, design, FYS, on-board computer

One of the main disciplines of Systems Enginering is Configuration Management. As defined in the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook [1], " [Configuration Management] enables all stakeholders in the technical effort, at any given time in the life of a product, to use identical data for development activities and decision-making".

Configuration and Technical Data Management may refer to spacecraft data managed during the entire lifetime of a space project. This data is usually refined or updated from one phase to the next, while engineers might event need to consider alternative options for the product.
Technical data of a spacecraft may include product trees, equipment specifications, numerical values, emulation models, interfaces and more.
Spacecraft configuration data may come in the type of "strings" (text), numbers, hierarchies (e.g. for a product
tree), tables and more. (e.g. for a failure mode analysis).

Information about spacecraft configuration can range from between a few spreadsheets to thousands of pages of text-based documentation, depending on the size and complexity of the project. What we call "Engineering Data" may be combined with project documentation, or be stored in an independent format, in a structured manner or a domain-specific model. Kanavouras et al. [3] separate spacecraft documentation into two types:

- Text-based documentation, where text is written, usually in a rich-text format, and stored in a central repository or printed. Content is usually edited using a specific format, such as Office Open XML (used by Microsoft Word) or Markdown (used by online software).
- Model-based documentation, where system parameters and technical data are stored in a structured
Fig. 1: Example parameters of a spacecraft component [2]
format or language, specifically designed to allow description of the system.

As space projects usually involve collaboration between multiple teams and stakeholders, technical data must also be shareable between participants. This must be done so that engineering data is kept up-to-date across team members, with additional approval or authorisation pipelines when required. The process of sharing happens in one of the following ways:
- Manual file sharing, usually through e-mail or a file-sharing service
- Tool-specific collaboration tools, such as those offered by Microsoft Sharepoint, Google Workspace, or wikis. This might include real-time change tracking.
- An independent version control system with difference and author tracking

Specifically for small space missions, such as CubeSat methods with less overhead are typically used. [4] In fact, Honoré-Livermore [4] specifically identified the need to develop improved information systems for documentation and data management, specifically for CubeSat missions.
CubeSat missions specifically have employed both document-based and model-based documentation [5, 6, 7].

A noteworthy platform for document-based documentation are spreadsheets, which allow representing information in a semi-structured format, without imposing a specific arrangement on users. Spreadsheets also typically allow a range of calculations to be performed in-application,
making them convenient as a centralised source of automatically updated data and results.

Given the major time and effort required for project documentation (Sanchez-Rosado et al. [8] estimated that estimated that 12% to 35% of a software project's development time is spent on documentation), its criticality in space projects, and the wide variety of different tools available for this purpose, it is essential to investigate ways of improving documentation effectiveness, speed and correctness for space projects. Ambler [9] proposed the following formula to measure documentation effectiveness:
Potential value $ = $ Produced value $ \cdot $ C $ \cdot $ R $ \cdot $ U $ \cdot $ F $ \cdot $ T (1)
- Produced value is guesstimated by the producers of the artifact.
- C is the percentage of the artifact that is currently "correct".
- R = The chance that the artifact will be read by the intended audience.
- U = The chance that the document that is actually understood by the intended audience.
- F = The chance that the advice contained in artifact will be followed.
- $ T $ = The chance that the advice will be trusted.
Different project classes combined with inappropriate documentation or Engineering Data Management (EDM) tools can lead to significant inefficiencies in one of the above factors, for example:
- Academic/educational missions using formal MBSE tools may not have the personnel or capacity to keep engineering data up-to-date, reducing the C and T parameters.

- Academic/educational missions using a nonstructured way of storing engineering data may reduce the parameter R and the produced value of the documentation, as useful information is usually stored in unstructured folders and documents without central control, making data retrieval difficult, unreliable and slow.
- Small industrial missions may avoid the generation of documentation altogether, reducing the produced value of documentation.

While Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) is generally perceived to increase documentation consistency and verification & validation verifiability [10, 11], users have associated increased complexity and worse understandability with it [10].

MBSE users also report mixed conclusions connected to the results on development time, cost and effort [10]. This discrepancy can be explained as the overhead of implementing a new, often unknown management methodology, outweighs the potential gains, especially in smaller projects. For each system or team, there exists an ideal trade-off between Systems Engineering (SE) effort and SE benefit that optimises parameters such as development time [12].

In smaller space projects, such as CubeSat missions, the overhead added by MBSE methods is more evident, as teams prefer to work in a more agile fashion, favouring high responsiveness to change and rapid information sharing. In this case, tool selection can play an equally important role as methodology selection [13].
MBSE tools for configuration and technical data management can be separated into two categories: [3]:

- Informal, where only limited parts of a system may be modelled based on an opinionated structure defined by a tool or process. Examples include Starion Group's COMET (formerly associated with RHEA Group's CDP4 and ESA's OCDT), Valispace, Duro PDM One, ISAE Supaero's Nanospace [14] and more.
Formal MBSE methods are typically tied to the tools they use. Examples include ARCADIA/Capella [15], Papyrus, Rhapsody, CATIA, Enterprise Architect and more [10].
Developers can also choose to implement a formal or informal model-based ecosystem by manually adapting

generic, commercially available tools or Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems, such as Microsoft Sharepoint, Eclipse, Odoo or others. This approach trades a significant deployment and maintenance effort for slightly more flexibility on the model structure.

Based on the above, we claim that the development of a novel Engineering Data Management (EDM) tool, combined with a suitable data management process, can significantly reduce the organisational overhead of EDM for small satellite missions (focused on CubeSats). We will therefore present requirements, concepts and mockups for a new software tool, used to manage engineering parameters of a hierarchical space system

The rest of this work is structured as follows: In Section 2, we present the basic requirements and justification that differentiate our tool from the state of the art. In Section 3, we present the functionality and mock-ups of our tool. Finally, Section 4 shows the next steps in the tool's development. It is important to clarify that this work does not introduce a new software tool itself, but rather the concept of one, following a typicall User Interface (UI) design workflow, with our aim being to guide software development for future tools.
For the development of a prototype concept for engineering data management, we consider the following requirements and their rationale:
- RQ-1: The tool shall represent a spacecraft in a hierarchical tree-like structure of multiple entities containing multiple parameters each.

This generic requirement defines the core functionality of our tool: To store spacecraft engineering data in a hierarchical format. A tree-like structure is indeed a common method of representing a product and its details, which is already common in most EDM tools. It also allows extending functionality beyond what is offered by a grid-like data representation, as used in a spreadsheet.

Product tree structures are usually asked to represent different types of repetition or instantiation inside a product. For example, a type of fastener, electrical connector or integrated circuit may be shared across different subsystems and assemblies. While we don't specify explicitly how to handle these cases as a requirement, we note that many MBSE tools clearly differentiate between an "element template" and an "element instance" which can be repeated. However, we do note that most elements of a small spacecraft are rarely duplicated; therefore the process of instantiating an element should not require duplicate effort
to create and store a template representation for it.

text: The discussion of Developer Experience has to inadvertently focus on software development trends in the industry. For example, while an interpreted language (such as Python) is usually regarded as less performant than a compiled language (such as C++), it is more likely that engineering graduates are familiar with the former, which in turn increases the chances that they will interact with the codebase and be familiar with any errors caused.

While we intend for our concept to be usable as a centre for small spacecraft development, its functionality has to be limited in this area. To this end, we feel important to clarify features not targeted by our proposal:

- Requirement management and validation. While requirements solicitation, processing and realisability checking has already been demonstrated in low-overhead tooling [18], we prefer to keep it outside our proposed solution for an early demonstration. Space mission requirements tend to be complex and usually not unambiguously specified, making manual verification efforts overshadow many automatic works.
- Test management and Risk/failure management, on the grounds of being out-of-scope.

Following a typical UI prototyping flow, we created a set of mockups of our front-end interface, showing its main features (Figures 2 to 5). The primary tool used for this purpose was Moqups (https://moqups.com).
We furthermore developed a proof-of-concept frontend using Nuxt.js to demonstrate the applicability of a web interface for our tool, as shown in Figure 6.
In the following section we will investigate the applicability of the aforementioned requirements to our tool:
- RQ-1: The tool shall represent a spacecraft in a hierarchical tree-like structure of multiple entities containing multiple parameters each.

The hierarchy shown in Figure 2 represents a typical product tree of a satellite, showing a high-level view of subsystems that can be expanded into their child components. Note that abstract subsystems can be represented as well, such as software or trajectories. The latter example can indicatively cover values such as altitude, inclination and other trajectory parameters that are commonly requested but also frequently updated in missions.
Each "entity" can therefore represent a subsystem an assembly, or any other product within a satellite. Some additional opinionated attributes are optionally available for each entity:
- Product Name
- Image
- Links (to datasheets, engineering files, user manuals or others)
- Notes (to provide information not representable by parameters)
Each entity can be associated with many parameters of different types, as described in Section 3.2.
- RQ-2: The complete functionality of the tool shall be accessible from the web.

Our prototype tool is designed with a web-first view able to run on a local server or the cloud. We have developed a prototype front-end using Nuxt.js and Tailwind CSS, as shown in Figure 6, which has no requirements from the user's side apart from a web server, and is therefore usable by desktop and handheld devices.
- RQ-3: Stored data shall be version controlled.
Version control of data can be performed by either:
- Using a plain database and implementing versioning features on it (such as MySQL or MongoDB)
- Using a plain Version Control System (VCS) and implementing data storage features (such as Git or SVN)
- Using a tailored solution for versioned data storage (such as DVC or Dolt)
Fig. 2: Entity view mockup

While any of the above solutions will be suitable, the ideal one would combine low overhead with data storage in a human-readable format, so that project models can easily be inspected or transferred in their raw form.

Our proposed solution is to use the Git VCS, by representing each entity as a YAML file [19]. Git has been chosen thanks to its wide support, with advanced change management tools available. YAML files were chosen because they are human and machine-readable and editable, with a flexible structure and low processing overhead. By default, they also represent values on different lines, which is compatible with most Git difference viewers. A user could then also theoretically create a spacecraft model entirely by hand, by creating the appropriate YAML files, with no tool interaction required.

The concept of the "Parameter" is at the core of our proposed tool, as it is the main unit of data storage within an entity.

Parameter values are sometimes provided explicitly by developers, having been specified in requirements or extracted through manual calculation. However, parameters may also depend on other parameters or be the results of automated analysis by another tool. Our platform should be flexible enough to support different parameter sources, the following of which we have identified:
- Manual — typed by the user on the interface
- External — imported into the interface by an external tool through an API
- Calculated using an expression — for parameters that depend on other parameters or simple calculations, made through a programming or expression language, such as Lua
As the model representation of a rapidly-evolving system can rarely be absolutely correct, we can provide a
method of identifying the confidence of a parameter's correctness. This can be visualised by parameter states which follow a workflow process:
- Rejected someone has identified that the parameter is incorrect
- Pending — the parameter value has been updated, but a reviewer needs to approve it
- Approved — the parameter has been approved and is most likely correct
- Expired — a specific amount of time has passed since the parameter was last checked; a second look is needed to ensure it is not outdated.
- New Data (only for calculated parameters) — the dependents of this parameter have been updated, but this one hasn't; it is most likely incorrect.
The main aspect of parameter representation is their type, which can be a:
- Number — a simple floating point number with no limits. Can be associated with a respective unit,
using an off-the-shelf unit conversion platform to ensure API consistency.
- String — single or multi-line text. This can be used as a wildcard by users if other parameter types are not suitable.
- Enumeration one of many possible values (e.g. TRL)
- Reference to entity — this essentially allows describing interfaces between modules, by modelling "ManyToOne" relationships.
- Table — an arbitrary matrix of descendant parameter types
- Function an operator that acts on a parameter value to produce another parameter value based on simple scripts; useful to represent e.g. efficiency curves.

Finally, we define an additional "variable" modifier for parameters, in order to represent numbers which typically change over time, such as power consumption, ground station coverage and others. A time-variable parameter can generate a graph in time of this parameter's trend, and programmatically generate statistics such as min(), max(), mean(), time_low(), time_high(), and others. Time-variable parameters can be represented with one of the following ways:
- Duty cycle — by defining a minimum, maximum, and percentage duty cycle
- On/off duration — by defining a minimum, maximum, and off/on or off/total duration
- Sinusoidal — by providing the frequency, phase and amplitude of a sinusoid
- Arbitrary graph — by linearly interpolating across a periodic set of fixed points provided by the user
We note that this approach, compared to the defining just two edge values and a duty cycle, allows specifying the exact time durations of each state and can provide more flexibility in calculations.
To comply with RQ-6, plugins should be able to augment parameters by implementing any more of the above modifiers.

Through this pleiminary User Interface study, we formulated requirements for a modern Engineering Data Management tool developed for the space industry and focused on small satellite engineering. While the objective of our study was not to present a production-ready
concept, we expect that our results will be useful to developers of MBSE data management tools, with a focus on the CubeSat (and smaller) ecosystem, for both academic and industrial teams.

Future work on the tool itself includes the exploration of main features, such as entity templates, parameters dependent on state (e.g. Nominal mode vs Safe mode), automatic generation of aggregate reports (e.g. budgets) and well-defined integration and scripting capabilities. The tool also calls for at least targeted use of simple Artificial Intelligence (AI) and/or Large Language Models (LLMs), in parts such as expression generation, parameter guesstimation, image/icon generation, quick search and more. After the conceptual studies, an actual back-end and front-end implementation can commence, along with case studies in real-world usage and comparisons to other tools.

Additional steps beyond software development can include surveying satellite developers regarding their needs and preferences on EDM, with a focus on practicality and low overhead, as well as a rigorous investigation of the critical positive and negative aspects of MBSE tools [10, 11].

The SPACE4YOU (SPace Activities and CompEtences for industrY bOost in bUsiness) project aims at enhancing existing skills, and realities, but also at creating novel ideas and stimulating technological transfer between the Academia, large system integrators, and small-medium enterprises. This project promotes collaboration and open knowledge sharing to accelerate the development of forthcoming space technologies and applications, providing a common environment and shared tools and methods for designing, simulating, developing, and testing new space systems. One of the research contributions resulted in a Concurrent Model-Based approach based on digital tools for designing and developing missions and services of micro and nanosatellites.

This paper presents an innovative approach that combines the concurrent engineering paradigm with standardized calculation sheets linked to a CubeSat Technologies Database, facilitating the preliminary design process and enabling component selection based on applicable specifications and performance data of available technology. This combined concurrent design approach offers faster, more flexible, and transparent design management compared to traditional methods, simplifying the system design flow and the decision-making process in the early phases of a space mission project. This approach has been implemented and tested during several CubeSats projects, among them an in-orbit servicing cis-lunar mission and a CubeSat constellation around Bennu asteroid, emphasizing collaborative learning through concurrent design sessions, and encouraging both communication and resource sharing across different technical fields. The research team worked simultaneously tackling the various aspects of space mission design, from conceptual design up to subsystem sizing, supported by both standardized calculation sheets and CubeSat Technologies Database. The effectiveness of the new Concurrent Model-Based approach in achieving accurate and efficient results has been determined by assessing the design outcomes against appropriate figures of merit.

Therefore, this work contributes to the development of best practices and tools in space technology and system management, exploiting the results and outcomes of an innovative approach to small satellite design for space exploration, and promoting lessons learned within the space engineering community.

The increasing demand for fast, cost-effective, and innovative space missions has boosted the development of small satellites, particularly CubeSats [1]. Efficient and effective design methodologies are crucial to ensure

the success of these missions. In recent years, Concurrent Engineering (CE) and Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) [2] have become increasingly important and employed in the design of CubeSats missions [3]. Concurrent Engineering is a product development approach that aims to reduce mission design time and development costs while increasing the system development quality, by carrying out tasks in parallel with near-real-time teamwork and using modern design tools. In the design of space missions and systems, CE is mainly applied at the phase 0/A and is defined by ESA as "a systematic approach to integrated product development that emphasises meeting customer expectations. It embodies the values of cooperation, trust and team sharing so that decision-making is consensual, involving all perspectives in parallel, from the very beginning of the product life cycle" [4]. On the other hand, Model-Based Systems Engineering is a model-centric system engineering approach for representing complex systems that has recently gained attention and importance for its contribution to reducing development time and improving cost efficiency in space systems design [5]. In contrast to traditional document-centric systems engineering methods, CE and MBSE rely on computer-based tools and procedures to improve the design, development, and verification process of space systems by enabling a structured and digitally processable expression of information through digital models and tools, which are used as the primary means of information exchange.

This paper presents a novel Concurrent Model-Based approach for CubeSat mission design, developed by the STAR (Systems and Technologies for Aerospace Research) [6] research group from Politecnico di Torino (PoliTo) within the framework of the flagship project SPACE4YOU (SPace Activities and CompEtences for industrY bOost in bUsiness) [7]. As part of the Spoke 1 Industry 4.0 for sustainable mobility and aerospace of the innovation ecosystem NODES-Nord-Ovest Digitale E Sostenibile (Digital and Sustainable North-Western Italy) which involves the North-Western Italian regions of Piemonte, Valle d'Aosta and the bordering provinces of Lombardia, the SPACE4YOU project aims at enhancing existing skills, and realities, but also at creating novel ideas and fostering collaboration, knowledge sharing, and technological transfer between the Academia, large system integrators, small-medium enterprises, accelerators, and incubators within the space ecosystem. One of the objectives of the SPACE4YOU project is to accelerate the development of forthcoming space technologies and applications by providing a common environment and shared techniques, methodologies, models, procedures, and tools for the design, simulation, development, and testing of new space systems.

The Concurrent Model-Based approach combines the principles of CE and MBSE to achieve a more efficient and effective system design process for micro and nanosatellite missions and services, offering several advantages over conventional methods, including faster design processes, enhanced flexibility, and improved transparency.

This paper delves into the details of the Concurrent Model-Based approach, explaining the principles and benefits of this methodology in section 2, as well as the implementation of two specific tools. Section 3 will present the application of the approach to a specific case study through Concurrent Design Sessions. The results of the mission design and an assessment of the effectiveness of the approach used will be discussed in section 4, together with recommendations according to lessons learned and possible future implementations. Finally, conclusions on the methodology used in space missions design are given in section 5.

One of the key contributions to the SPACE4YOU project to support the design phases of space missions and systems is the Concurrent Model-Based approach, a design methodology particularly suitable for the phase 0/A [8] of a space project. This methodology combines the CE paradigm with system models and tools, aiming to improve the design process and facilitate cooperation among team members and collaboration of scientific communities. The fundamental principles of the Concurrent Model-Based approach are simultaneous system modelling and iterative design refinement: multiple teams work concurrently on various aspects of the system, using models and tools to represent their respective disciplines. This allows teams to collaborate effectively by sharing and exchanging models, ensuring consistency and alignment across the system. Parallel system development and early identification of potential issues and risks ensures a continuous refinement of the models and leads to optimized system design. Furthermore, by integrating the models early in the development process, the system compatibility can be assessed, reducing errors and minimising potential conflicts, and the verification process can begin in advance with respect to traditional methodologies.

By combining the strengths of CE and MBSE, promoting simultaneous engineering, early integration, iterative design, communication and risk management, and providing a structured framework for modelling analysis and verification, the Concurrent Model-Based approach can significantly reduce the development time of complex systems, improve their efficiency, quality, and overall performance, as well as reduce cost and risk. In addition, the constant support of the models and tools provide a clear view of design iterations, facilitating both decision-making, through a comprehensive
understanding of the system behaviour and interactions and the transition of design from one phase to the next.

In order to effectively implement the design approach, it is important to complement it with digital tools and standardized procedures: the STAR team at PoliTo focused on the development of suitable tools for the preliminary design of CubeSats, in particular a digital tool, named Small-Satellite System Design (S3D) Tool, and a comprehensive database, named CubeSat Technologies Database (CUTE-DB).

section_key: 2 1 small satellite system design s3d tool
text: The S3D Tool is intended to facilitate the design process, by performing the CubeSat subsystems sizing and evaluating the system budgets. It consists of a set of calculation sheets implemented in Microsoft Excel dedicated to the main disciplines of the preliminary design phase of a CubeSat project: Attitude Determination and Control System (ADCS), Communication System (CommSys), Electrical Power System (EPS), Propulsion System, Thermal Control System (TCS), Optical Payload, Risk, and Cost. Each discipline corresponds to a spreadsheet, which is generally organised into several sheets as in the following order: (i) Cover, (ii) Change log, which contains changes and updates to the spreadsheet, (iii) From Theory, which collects the objectives of the discipline, the theoretical definitions and equations, and typical values of specific parameters from the literature [9,10], (iv) Input, where the user can enter the inputs for that discipline, values typically coming from mission analysis and system parameters, (v) Sizing and Budget, one or more sheets are dedicated to the calculations, a table collects the outputs and some graphs give a visual representation of the results, and (vi) Constants, which contains all the constants needed for the calculations in the previous sheets.

The CUTE-DB provides immediate access to specifications and performance data of commercially

available components, supporting not only the component selection during the design process but also ensuring that CubeSat projects are based on current technological realities. The current version of the CUTE-DB is an Excel-based database, covering several CubeSat technologies such as Deployers, Structures, Command and Data Handling (C&DH) systems, EPS, ADCS, CommSys, Propulsion Systems, Navigation Systems, Optical Payloads, TCS, Docking Systems, Mechanisms, and Platforms. The first sheet gives an overview of the abovementioned technologies, highlighting their Technology Readiness Level (TRL) and the country of origin, as illustrated in Fig. 2.

Instead, the following sheets are dedicated to the different technologies listed in the following order: Deployer, Structure, C&DH, Power System Integrated, Solar Cells, Solar Array, Power Conditioning and Distribution Unit (PCDU), Batteries, ADCS Integrated, Sun Sensors, Horizon Sensors, Star Trackers, Magnetometers, Gyroscopes, Reaction Wheels, Magnetic Torquers, Transceiver, Antenna, Cold Gas Propulsion System, Chemical Propulsion System, Electrical Propulsion System, Others Propulsion System, Relative Navigation System, Absolute Navigation System, Optical Payload, Thermal Active Systems, Thermal Passive Systems, Docking Systems, Mechanisms, and Platforms. The database structure is kept consistent throughout the different sheets, where the properties of each technology and their relationships are highlighted, representing a picture of what is currently available in the market. In particular, each sheet contains the following sections: (i) Item (name, photo, brief description, reference link), (ii) Developer (company name, country of origin), (iii) Physical properties (unit, size, mass, material, other specific physical parameters), (iv) Functional properties (technology-dependent), (v) Environmental properties (survival temperatures, operational temperatures, radiation tolerance, vibration tolerance), (vi) Power

The CUTE-DB has been populated using several sources available online [11, 12], as well as official developer websites, and it is currently updated to June 2024.
Once both tools for the preliminary design of CubeSats have been developed, the Concurrent Model-Based approach has been applied to several case studies through concurrent design sessions.

The standard ESA ESTEC Concurrent Design Facility (CDF) process [4] consists of multiple sessions usually a pre-study phase, 8 sessions of 4 hours each performed over a month (2 sessions per week) and post-study activities. As per [13, 14], this process has been adapted, reducing the workflow into four, 4-hour sessions, structured as follows: (i) Session 1: Kick-off & Start of mission design - the mission objectives, study requirements and drivers are presented. A preliminary mission analysis is performed, and different Concepts of Operations (ConOps) and mission architectures are identified. In addition, a preliminary cost and risk assessment is initiated; (ii) Session 2: Mission design ConOps and mission architecture are consolidated, while the mission analysis is iterated, defining the Delta-V. The system architecture is defined, and the preliminary subsystem architectures are outlined. Cost and risk assessments are further elaborated; (iii) Session 3: System design - system and subsystem budgets are computed, and preliminary subsystems sizing is carried out; (iv) Session 4: Consolidation of baseline - finalization of the iteration(s), up to the selection of the subsystem-level components.

Each session starts with a 15-minute kick-off, in which an overview/summary of the project status is given to enable everyone to start with a clear idea of the assumptions to be used. In addition, the main objectives of the session are explained, and the main tasks are presented. The kick-off is followed by 3.5 hours of iteration work, during which the baseline study is performed, following the previously presented objectives and tasks, and the team continuously communicates, discusses, and takes decisions by consensus. Finally, the last 15 minutes of the session are dedicated to an internal presentation where each expert presents their work, the results are discussed and the next steps of the study are defined, to be carried out in the next concurrent session.

The System Engineer is the primary user of the central repository of the S3D Tool, though it is accessible to all team members. It allows automated data transfer from the other spreadsheets of the S3D Tool and enables faster validation of the sizing, budgets and design, reducing manual effort and minimizing errors.

Therefore, the Concurrent Model-Based approach and the related tools (both S3D Tool and CUTE-DB) have been implemented and tested in several case studies, including the Bennu Observer Small Satellites (BOSS) mission, the Geo-Profundo mission [13], and the Cislunar mission [15].
The BOSS mission is a feasibility study of a CubeSat mission, with the aim to conduct in-situ observations of the Bennu asteroid, a near-Earth object (NEO). The

mission goals are (i) to map the asteroid from a relatively close distance, retrieving crucial data of Bennu surface composition at high resolution, (ii) to characterize the environment in close proximity of the asteroid, and (iii) to demonstrate the utilisation of small satellite technologies in deep space.

The mission architecture is based on a motherdaughter configuration, in which the mothercraft provides the interplanetary transfer of the small satellite(s) to the asteroid, a safe deployment in the proximity of the asteroid, and relays communications to/from Earth.

By implementing the Concurrent Model-Based approach, four concurrent design sessions have been carried out. Session 1 started by presenting the mission and system drivers and constraints, followed by a brainstorming activity to identify the main challenges in a deep space mission and systems design and the potential stakeholders, which led to the definition of the mission statement and mission objectives.

The mission statement of the BOSS mission has been defined as follows: "The mission aims to develop a lowcost and fast delivery deep space mission to characterize the topography, composition and environment of the Bennu asteroid, to improve scientific knowledge about the early Solar System and contribute to planetary defence studies. The mission additionally aims to demonstrate small satellite technologies in deep space through a mother-daughter configuration.".
Several ConOps and the mission architecture have been drafted and a preliminary trajectory analysis has been carried out. In addition, preliminary cost and risk assessments have been conducted.

At the end of the concurrent study, a detailed final presentation has been conducted to review the results achieved and lessons learned have been collected, allowing for a subsequent iteration of the Concurrent Model-Based approach and the related digital tools.

To sum up, the final mission will consist of this concept of operation involving a 12U CubeSat launched on Falcon Heavy inside a mothercraft towards Bennu. After a heliocentric transfer of 2 years and 3 months, both satellites will rendezvous with the Bennu asteroid. BOSS will be deployed from the mothercraft, about 2 months after arrival, in an orbit around Bennu at approximately 1.6 to 2.1 km from the surface with a Delta-V of 1 cm/s in the Nadir direction.

The Deployment & Commissioning phase will ensure the primary systems and payload checkout followed by the instrument calibration, to go through the Remote Sensing scenario where the scientific goals will be fulfilled. During this phase, the CubeSat will communicate with ground stations using the mothership as a relay, control its attitude and trajectory autonomously, generate maps for navigation, and produce power using the solar panels. A 6-month operational terminator orbit at 1 km from the surface, followed by a lower 500 m distance 6-month extension of on-orbit operations is planned and controlled with
station-keeping manoeuvres. Finally, the BOSS satellite will be disposed with a hyperbolic scape into a heliocentric orbit.

Besides the BOSS mission, another case study for the Concurrent Model-Based approach explores the feasibility of a 6U CubeSat mission in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), named Geo-Profundo [13], designed to monitor the urban growth of the Piedmont region, in Italy, and to demonstrate technologies for future deep-space CubeSat missions.
The methodology has also been applied to the feasibility study of the in-orbit servicing of multi-purpose autonomous CubeSat inspectors in proximity of the Lunar Gateway [15].

The results of the concurrent design sessions of the BOSS mission were presented in 3.2, and now the effectiveness of the Concurrent Model-Based approach is discussed, comparing the feasibility study results obtained from the concurrent design sessions with the same study conducted with the traditional methodology.

The CE-MBSE methodology resulted in a spacecraft mass of 22.59 kg, which is approximately 15% lower than the 26.6 kg calculated using the traditional methodology. This reduction in mass is likely due to the integrated, iterative nature of the concurrent approach, allowing design teams to identify and eliminate inefficiencies earlier in the process. In contrast, the traditional method, which is typically more segmented and sequential, has less real-time feedback between subsystems, leading to an overall heavier final design.

The Delta-V budget is another critical parameter in mission design. The CE-MBSE approach produced a Delta-V budget of 1.33 m/s, nearly double the 0.68 m/s calculated using the traditional methodology. This may be due to the time allocated for the feasibility analysis, which, using the traditional methodology, allowed for more iteration and refinement in the trajectory analysis.
However, the shown results only take into account the 4 sessions results and not the post-study refinement.

The cost assessment shows a difference between the two methodologies. The CE-MBSE approach projected a total mission cost of 15 million euros, which is significantly lower than the 22 million euros estimated through the traditional approach. This cost efficiency likely stems from the concurrent design's ability to minimize redesigns, optimize resources, and reduce the need for extensive iterations across different teams. In contrast, the traditional method, with its longer timelines and potentially higher number of revisions, contributes to a higher overall cost.

The time taken to conduct the feasibility analysis is perhaps one of the most striking differences. Using the CE-MBSE methodology, the feasibility study was completed in one month, compared to the three months required when using the traditional approach. This shortened timeline reflects the enhanced collaboration and integration made possible by concurrent engineering, where multiple teams work in parallel rather than waiting for sequential handoffs.
Several lessons learned have been drawn by the firsthand experiences of the authors as well as the case studies delivered.

Firstly, the S3D Tool needs to be improved and optimised. A preliminary calculation sheet for the Optical Payload has been developed to support initial design and performance evaluations. However, this sheet needs to be updated to reflect the latest design changes and integrated into the central repository to ensure alignment with the overall system design and easy access by all team members. In addition, dedicated spreadsheets for other kinds of payloads for CubeSat missions need to be developed.

Beyond the Optical Payload, a similar calculation sheet dedicated to the Command & Data Handling (C&DH) subsystem must also be created to standardize performance calculations and requirements tracking across all key systems. This will improve the consistency and efficiency of the design process.

Additionally, alternative environments are currently under investigation to complement or replace the current tools in use. Specifically, software environments such as Comet and Matlab's System Composer are being explored for their potential to offer enhanced systems engineering capabilities, such as improved model-based design, architecture definition, and real-time collaboration features. These tools may provide additional flexibility and robustness in handling the complex integration and coordination tasks required for the mission, as well as
possible enhancements to make the methodology suitable also for the later phases of a space project.

Furthermore, a discussion on CUTE-DB is open among the research team: to optimize the database management system used in the project, other environments are being evaluated, with MySQL being a key candidate under investigation [16]. The choice of database will be crucial in managing the large amounts of data generated and processed during the design and testing phases, ensuring that information is stored, retrieved, and managed efficiently. By exploring MySQL and other database solutions, the project aims to establish a more scalable and reliable system for data management.

Finally, one of the main goals of the project is to develop and refine best practices and tools for space technology and systems management. This involves exploiting the results and outcomes of this approach to small satellite design for space exploration and promoting lessons learned within the space engineering community.

This paper highlights the significant potential of a Concurrent Model-Based approach in CubeSat mission design, highlighting the essential need for shared models and tools within the space ecosystem. By integrating the principles of Concurrent Engineering and Model-Based Systems Engineering, this methodology not only streamlines the design process but also enhances collaboration among diverse stakeholders, fostering a more efficient development environment.

The SPACE4YOU initiative serves as a prime example of how a collaborative environment not only fosters synergy but also ensures that valuable lessons learned from previous missions are effectively documented and utilized, paving the way for continuous improvement in space exploration and development. This approach accelerates innovation and promotes best practices across the space sector, reinforcing the importance of collective expertise.

In conclusion, the Concurrent Model-Based approach represents a transformative shift in CubeSat mission design, playing a crucial role in shaping the future of space exploration, enabling more efficient, innovative, and sustainable mission outcomes.

Currently, half of the satellites do not reach 20% of their expected lifetime. The possibility of recycling these "zombie satellites" (ZS) with limited capabilities would lead to an optimization of this on-orbit infrastructure, reducing unnecessary launches, and being more cost-effective, as for example, a 12U CubeSat costs around €2.5 million to manufacture and launch. In this way, it will not be necessary to launch some new satellites for these new missions, with the corresponding positive environmental and economic impact. Based on the ZS concept, this research proposed an eco-friendly satellite design and exploitation approach, centered on integrating space sustainability strategies, adopting green practices, within the NewSpace paradigm. For a complete analysis of the whole satellite life process, it is necessary to integrate eco-friendly and lean manufacturing characteristics. As a result, this concept is defined to bring together the numerous efforts for a sustainable space and considers the innovative technologies to be created for this kind of standard satellites.
To address this subject, this doctoral thesis undertakes a research study and practical experiences focused on small satellites. This Ph.D. thesis is divided into 6 parts comprising 12 chapters.

The first part contains two chapters. Chapter one, provides a general introduction to the topic of space sustainability, highlighting the importance of this Ph.D. thesis, linking it to the research objectives, and conducting a state-of-the-art study through a bibliometric analysis reviewing trends in academic literature on the development, advances, and research of space sustainability. The second chapter is focused on introducing the development of the Eco-LeanSat concept, emphasizing a sustainable approach to satellite manufacturing and the repurposing of remaining satellite capabilities after failure. This chapter addresses the evolution of smallsat capabilities, highlighting disruptive events that have facilitated access to and exploration of capabilities in space, as well as efforts made by leading space institutions to promote space sustainability strategies.

The second part of the thesis deals with proposals for reusing satellites that have experienced in-orbit failure but can still be repurposed for other purposes or complementary missions. To address this topic, this part is divided into two chapters. The third chapter presents a statistical study using the SeraData and Telastra databases and a compilation of information gathered from the web, examining the most frequent failures in smallsats, conducting an anomalies evaluation, and characterizing satellites based on the most common failures in large constellations, proposing future research in this area to consider these capabilities in satellite mission design so that a satellite, if it fails, does not become space debris but can be reused for other missions. The fourth chapter contains a study of the causes of failures arising from the space environment, analyzing the impact of indicators such as sunspots, K-index, Disturbance Storm Time (DST), Coronal Mass Ejection (CME), X-Ray, and electron and proton fluxes that can influence electrical damage to satellite components.

Taking into account the information from the second chapter, the third part of this research comprises a proposal for satellite manufacturing considering agile methodologies, Lean Six Sigma and software for Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) that optimize not only technical aspects but also administrative aspects and timelines. These studies are carried out practically in the missions of NanoSat Lab: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 and $ ^{3} $Cat-8, and in the Colombian mission $ ^{3} $ColStar. This third part contains 4 chapters. The fifth chapter presents the application of Lean Six Sigma in the $ ^{3} $Cat-8 mission, with the aim of simulating the mission using Bizagi software to identify bottlenecks and optimize mission execution in terms of time and human resources. Continuing under this optimization perspective in satellite mission design, the sixth chapter presents the preliminary design of the $ ^{3} $ColStar mission, a proposal developed by different institutions from Colombia, Spain, and Mexico, which was submitted to the $ 8^{th} $ Round KiboCUBE call granted by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) and the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA). This chapter presents the general considerations taken into account for the mission proposal, also applying

Capella's Model Based System Engineering software to improve and optimize the technical, and administrative development processes of the mission. In this line, chapter seven presents the development of algorithms for the Attitude Control System for SmallSats with Low-Thrust Propulsion Systems in the $ ^{3} $Cat-8 mission, highlighting the importance of designing sustainable missions that guarantee satellite life extension through the implementation of novel engineering proposals. Similarly, chapter eight presents the thermal analysis of the $ ^{3} $Cat-4 mission, the fourth member of UPC's NanoSat Lab CubeSat series, selected by the ESA Academy's Fly Your Satellite! program in 2017, aiming to present the results of the thermal analysis carried out for this mission, evaluating different scenarios, including the most critical cases at both high and low temperatures. The results consider different albedos and orbital parameters to establish the optimal temperatures to achieve the best mission performance within nominal temperatures and in all operational modes of the satellite. Results evaluating the thermal performance of other materials, such as Kapton, as well as the redesign of the optical properties of the satellite's solar panels, are also included.

The fourth part of the doctoral thesis includes chapter 9, which addresses legal considerations identified throughout the study to highlight key aspects for conducting sustainable missions in the future, such as regulations to be considered for reusing satellites in orbit, given that it was identified that there are currently no specific regulations for developing this type of missions, identifying a relevant consideration for future legal studies. Chapter 10 consists of future studies proposed to be developed through this proposed sustainability approach.

The fifth part of the thesis consists of the appendices of the mentioned chapters, and finally, the sixth part of the document considers the list of publications and other academic activities carried out during the doctoral study.

text: Introduction

During the fourth quarter of 2023, a record number of launches was registered for the third consecutive year, with a total of 223 attempts and 212 successful launches [1]. This increase was driven by a 50% rise in commercial launch activity compared to the previous year. The United States experienced a 33% increase in launch attempts, with China, India, and Japan also increasing their space activity. Additionally, over 2800 satellites were deployed into orbit, marking a 23% increase from 2022 and setting a record for the number of payloads launched in a year [1]. In the first quarter of 2024, 8 Extra Large Satellites (> 5000kg), 3 Very Large Satellites (3500.01 - 5000kg), 4 Large Satellites (2500.01 - 3500kg), 8 Medium Satellites (1000.01 - 2500kg), 433 Small Satellites (500.01 - 1000kg), 25 Minisatellites (100.01 - 500kg), 40 Microsatellites - Large (40.01 - 100kg), 27 Microsatellites - Small (10.01 - 40kg), 47 Nanosatellites (1 - 10kg), and 1 Picosatellite (0.1 - 0.99kg) were launched [2]. The number of satellites launched shows an exponential growth in the sector and rapid expansion in the satellite space market.

This revolution has received the name of "NewSpace," characterized by a collaborative work among diverse disciplines, the gradual implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals in the short and medium terms [3], and the accelerated progress of science and engineering benefiting from the miniaturization of technology under an efficient, low-cost [4], and quality-controlled methodology, allowing more actors to participate in the aerospace sector.

For the specific case of the satellite industry, the CubeSat standard [5] has facilitated the access to space to more public and private institutions. However, as this number grows, the number of space debris increases, and so the chances of satellite collisions [6]. According to data from the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Inter-Agency Debris Committee (IADC) with the Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines, more than 30,000 pieces of space debris have been recorded, although the number of objects larger than a centimeter in size is likely to exceed a million. As seen in Fig 1.1 [7]; many unidentified objects (UIs) are being detected and tracked through space surveillance networks [7]. The graph shows the amount of UI between the years 1960 and 2023, considering the payload launch traffic within 200 km with a perigee height [hp] less than or equal to 1750 km. Note: Consider payload launch traffic within 200 km with a perigee height (hp) less than or equal to 1750 km.

As it can be seen, a significant increase in the number of commercial satellites launched to low Earth orbits (LEO) has taken place in the last two years, the vast majority weighting between 100 and 1000 kg. Although most constellations have been launched to offer valuable and necessary telecommunications services, they will challenge long-term sustainability issues. To address this problem, numerous efforts have been made worldwide. One of them is the ESA's Clean Space initiative [8], started in 2012 to consider the environmental impact of the entire life cycle of space missions. Clean Space's activities fall into three principal areas [8] (Fig 5.2.) [8]:
- Eco-Design: addressing environmental impacts and fostering green technologies.
- Space Debris Mitigation: minimizing the production of space debris.
- On-orbit servicing/Active Debris Removal: removing spacecraft from orbit and demonstrating on-orbit

Figure 1.2: ESA's Clean Space initiative
servicing of spacecraft.

Currently, half of the satellites do not reach 20% of their expected lifetime. Recycling "zombie satellites" will optimize this on-orbit infrastructure, reducing unnecessary launches and being more cost-effective, as a 12U CubeSat costs around €2.5 million to be manufactured and launched [9]. In this way, it will not be necessary to launch so many new satellites for these new missions, with the corresponding positive environmental and economic impact. The project proposal "Second Life for Zombie Satellites (2L4ZS)" [9] was formulated to study how to recycle "zombie satellites" (i.e., partially operative satellites currently orbiting in space) to perform new missions with their remaining capabilities, how new satellites had to be designed so that they could be more easily "recycled", including all the legal implications.

2L4ZS was planned as a sustainable response to the deployment of new satellite mega-constellations (i.e. the recent launches of Starlink, OnWeb, Telesat, Kuper, etc.) [10], aiming at generating and strengthening innovative concepts related to satellite repair services on-orbit to carry out processes of reconfiguration, updating and standardization of hardware and software. Based on the "zombie satellite" concept, this research proposes the eco-friendly satellite concept, which is centered on integrated space business strategies for sustainability environmental by adopting green practices [11] within the NewSpace paradigm.

1. Durability and reliability: Benefiting from the OldSpace know-how, the product is designed and manufactured to meet the objectives for which it was created, and for this purpose, it must be designed and manufactured following quality processes that ensure its compliance. The business models depend
on reliable and high-quality space asset operation for a variety of purposes. [12]
2. Re-entry: The aim is to design structures that can remove the spacecrafts from orbit (Active Debris Removal) and demonstrate on-orbit servicing.

3. Re-use: Implies the creation of a new generation of multi-purpose satellites so that they are not limited in their capacity to develop a few tasks but can perform other activities autonomously and collaboratively with other satellites (such as services on orbit for sharing information between satellite constellations) thus optimize the use of space.

In order to develop a proposal that incorporates the eco-friendly satellite concept, it is necessary to analyze the efficiency of all the processes involved in the lifetime of the satellite (from mission planning to the end of its useful life and subsequent processes). For this reason, it is required to incorporate a lean design throughout the satellite manufacturing system to improve and optimize its production system by eliminating activities that do not generate value for the process or the customer. The concept of "lean satellites" [13] was adopted in 2014 to characterize satellites that are developed fast, and at low-cost, independently of their size and/or mass. The "lean satellite" concept is nowadays under discussion within International Academy of Astronautics (IAA) study group, and an International Organization for Standardization (ISO) working group to define the requirements a satellite must satisfy to be classified as lean, not only in terms of project cost or development time, but also in terms of project management strategy [14, 15]. The lean satellite's philosophy development is driven by fast delivery and low-cost; however, the reliability of the developed space systems should be enough to operate them in space, and achieve, at least, the mission minimum success criteria to prevent it from becoming a useless space debris [15].

text: A. First Goal: To conduct a study on satellite missions and relevant use cases that can be based on recycled "zombie satellites" (e.g. small imaging satellites without attitude control reused for IoT communications). The intention was to explore and promote this definition as a proposal for a future satellite mission standard, generating awareness to include recycling as part of the product life cycle, by incorporating it in the design of future satellite missions.

text: B. Second Goal: Characterization of the capabilities and limitations of "zombie satellite" architectures. The identification of services for the "zombie satellites" was performed across two components (type and severity of damage), through a statistical study. This led to trends associated to specific technologies or quality control processes. This exercise analyzed an extensive database of reported failures, damage, probability, time of occurrence, etc. Additionally, the causes of the most common damages incurred by satellites due to space weather were evaluated.

section: Approach to Space Sustainability > 1.2.1 On-Orbit Servicing Spacecraft
section_key: approach to space sustainability / 1 2 1 on orbit servicing spacecraft
text: For this first category, research is presented based on an extensive literature review and data analysis of the feasibility of on-orbit servicing spacecraft (OOS) to extend the operational life of satellites. The On-Orbit Servicing, Assembly and Manufacturing (OSAM) 1 spacecraft could then refuel both Sentinels as an alternative option to Landsat 72. For OSAM 1 to refuel Landsat 7, it is $261.91M cheaper than Landsat-7 replacement and the most economically viable and sustainable option, considering the information revealed by the systematic analysis of the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) satellite that the Sentinel 1A and 1B satellites orbit at approximately the same altitude as Landsat 7 (700 km), and have a collective propulsion mass (MProp) of 308 kg, which is lower than the 544 kg of Landsat 7.

section: Approach to Space Sustainability > 1.2.1 On-Orbit Servicing Spacecraft
section_key: approach to space sustainability / 1 2 1 on orbit servicing spacecraft
text: OSAM 1 will mitigate the immediate space debris problem. However, a new model of standardized cooperative satellites with pluggable external interfaces could facilitate planned and unplanned upgrades, modifications, and repairs for future missions and technology upgrades [17].

text: Another recent study highlights a geostationary satellite project called the "Recycler" [18]. that can collect cooperative satellite components. The Recycler can open a second-hand market for waste-efficient on-orbit servicing (OOS) by reusing existing hardware. This study provides a strategic analysis on how to reuse missions using an approach drawn from Game Theory. This allows a unique guidance on which aspects of the "Recycler" project should be targeted. Starting from an economic problem, the model is gradually complexified to accommodate future standard Recycler contracts [18]. A sensitivity analysis and a case study are conducted to assess the project's feasibility. It is concluded that the main obstacles of the Recycler are:

section: Approach to Space Sustainability > 1.2.3 Space Sustainability and Lean Satellite Systems Concept
section_key: approach to space sustainability / 1 2 3 space sustainability and lean satellite systems concept
text: In the category of Space Sustainability - Satellite Repair, a study is reviewed that proposes to conceptualize space orbit and radio frequency spectrum as essential commons, the governance of which requires international cooperation. In examining the possibilities and challenges of space orbit governance, the paper focuses mainly on ensuring the safety and sustainability of space through the introduction of on-orbit servicing operations (OOS) [20]. The report identifies aspects of OOS that warrant new collaborations, notably the standardization of docking and rendezvous practices that could facilitate future space activities. Recognizing the potential for future commercialization of on-orbit refueling, repair, and debris removal operations, this paper argues that standardization practices would be the first step in enhancing international cooperation and strengthening the existing regime for the peaceful use of outer space. These future collaborations and space activities are part of the topics addressed within the Chapter 9, regulatory and Legal Gaps will be considered to analyze regulatory aspects for commercializing space services or activities on orbit, which is one of the tasks the eco-friendly satellite prototype plans to perform.

section: Approach to Space Sustainability > 1.2.3 Space Sustainability and Lean Satellite Systems Concept
section_key: approach to space sustainability / 1 2 3 space sustainability and lean satellite systems concept
text: Another relevant study about the lean satellite system concept shows the monitored failures occurring during the development of the lean satellite HORYU-IV to identify the evolution of the cumulative number of failures against cumulative testing time. Moreover, the subsystems driving the failures depending on the different development phases were identified. The results showed that 1/2 to 2/3 of the failures are discovered during

section: Approach to Space Sustainability > 1.2.3 Space Sustainability and Lean Satellite Systems Concept
section_key: approach to space sustainability / 1 2 3 space sustainability and lean satellite systems concept
text: the early testing stage. Moreover, when the mean time before failure was calculated, it appeared that for any development phase considered, a new failure appears on average every 20 h of testing. Simulations were also performed, showing that for an initial testing time of 50 h, reliability after a 1-month launch could be improved by nearly six times compared to an initial testing time of 20 h. Through this work, the authors aim to provide a qualitative reference for lean satellite developers to help better manage resources to develop lean satellites following a fast delivery and low-cost philosophy while ensuring sufficient reliability to achieve minimum mission success [15].

section: Approach to Space Sustainability > 1.2.3 Space Sustainability and Lean Satellite Systems Concept
section_key: approach to space sustainability / 1 2 3 space sustainability and lean satellite systems concept
text: In the same study analyzed, Dubos [21] showed that small satellites have the highest infant mortality rate. This points out that insufficient testing is carried out prior to launch. Thus, there is a need to identify critical tests to improve lean satellites' reliability. Moreover, some studies [22] [23] [24] surveyed on-orbit failures. They identified that solar array deployment mechanisms and telemetry tracking and command (TTC) sub-system were the two main drivers of satellite infant mortality, regardless of the satellite category. To identify critical testing to carry out before launch, it is also necessary to assess the criticality of the testing depending on the considered sub-system and its impact on the lean satellite mission success [15].

section_key: approach to space sustainability / chapter 1 approach to space sustainability
text: Introduces the concept of space sustainability, highlighting the importance of this doctoral thesis, establishing connections with the research objectives, and conducting an extensive literature review using bibliometric analysis. This analysis explores trends in academic publications concerning advancements, innovations, and investigations in the field of space sustainability. In addition, the goals of the thesis are presented. Finally, the outline of the Ph.D. thesis is started.

section_key: approach to space sustainability / chapter 2 considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling
text: Shows an introduction and brief review of the Eco-LeanSat idea, stressing the importance of adopting a sustainable methodology in satellite production and repurposing the residual functionalities of satellites post-failure. This segment delves into the evolution of small satellite capabilities, spotlighting pivotal events that have eased accessibility to and exploitation of space capabilities. Additionally, it outlines endeavors undertaken by prominent space entities to advance strategies for space sustainability.

section: Approach to Space Sustainability > Chapter 3. Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment
section_key: approach to space sustainability / chapter 3 towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment
text: Presents an analytical investigation utilizing the SeraData and Telastra databases along with a compilation of web-sourced data. This study explores the most common failures observed in small satellites, conducts an assessment of anomalies, and categorizes satellites based on prevalent failures in extensive constellations. It proposes future research directions in this domain to incorporate these capabilities into satellite mission designs, ensuring that a satellite, in the event of failure, avoids contributing to space debris and can instead be repurposed for alternative missions.

section: Approach to Space Sustainability > Chapter 4. Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation
section_key: approach to space sustainability / chapter 4 statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation
text: Encompasses an examination of failure causes stemming from the space environment, scrutinizing the influence of various indicators such as sunspots, K-index, Disturbance Storm Time (DST), Coronal Mass Ejection (CME), X-Ray, electron, and proton fluxes, which have the potential to impact the electrical integrity of satellite components.

section_key: approach to space sustainability / part iii effective and sustainable advancing satellite manufacturing for a greener space environment
text: Considering the insights gleaned from the lasts chapters, the third section of this study entails a proposition for satellite production, integrating agile methodologies, Lean Six Sigma principles, and Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) software. These approaches aim to enhance not just technical elements but also administrative processes and project timelines. These methodologies are practically applied in missions conducted at the NanoSat Lab, including $ ^{3} $Cat-4 and $ ^{3} $Cat-8, as well as in the Colombian mission $ ^{3} $ColStar.

section_key: approach to space sustainability / chapter 5 integrating lean six sigma methodology for optimization satellite manufacturing process 3 cat 8 mission
text: Presents the Lean Six Sigma methodologies applied to the $ ^{3} $Cat-8 mission. The objective is to simulate the mission using Bizagi software, aiming to identify bottlenecks and enhance mission execution efficiency in terms of both time management and human resources utilization.

section_key: approach to space sustainability / chapter 6 preliminary design of satellite systems through the integration of modelbased system engineering and agile methodologies application to the 3 colstar mission
text: Describes a case study on the integration of Agile Systems Engineering methodologies in the preliminary design phase of satellite systems. Using Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), technical consistency was managed across various architectural documents, minimizing errors. The preliminary design was developed using the Arcadia Method, supported by the Capella modeling tool, enabling the digitization of the system.

section_key: approach to space sustainability / chapter 7 novel magnetic attitude control system for smallsats with low thrust propulsion systems

It emphasizes the significance of crafting sustainable missions that ensure satellite longevity by integrating innovative engineering solutions.

section: Approach to Space Sustainability > Chapter 8. $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results
section_key: approach to space sustainability / chapter 8 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results
text: Presents the thermal analysis conducted for the $ ^{3} $Cat-4 mission, which is part of the CubeSat series developed by UPC's NanoSat Lab and was selected for the ESA Academy's Fly Your Satellite! program. Its primary aim is to present the outcomes of the thermal analysis conducted for this mission, which involved assessing various scenarios, including extreme temperature conditions. The analysis takes into account different factors such as albedos and orbital parameters to determine the optimal temperatures required for optimal mission performance under standard conditions and across all satellite operational modes. Additionally, the results encompass an evaluation of the thermal behavior of alternative materials like Kapton, along with proposed modifications to enhance the optical properties of the satellite's solar panels.

It underscores the need for regulations regarding the reuse of satellites in orbit, noting that there are currently no specific guidelines for such missions. This highlights a crucial area for future legal research and consideration.
