text: With the aim of introducing the development of this Ph.D. thesis and delving into the topic of space sustainability, it was considered to present in the following chapter an exploratory study investigating a proposal for sustainable satellite manufacturing and the utilization of remaining satellite capabilities postfailure for new applications. This proposal initially identifies innovative applications of ecological design and then delves into sustainability across the satellite lifecycle supply chain, focusing on four main methods: active debris removal, transportation logistics, mission extension, and repair and construction. The chapter also examines future trends in space activities with the aim of optimizing the potential of satellites to offer new services. Additionally, it outlines a potential efficient manufacturing process that includes logistical aspects to support a more sustainable space economy. Ultimately, the chapter concludes with a technological study that tracks the evolution of Smallsats and Cubesat platforms, identifying innovative designs for a sustainable space environment.

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > Abstract
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / abstract
text: This research aims to contribute to the development of the Eco-LeanSat concept, focusing on a sustainable approach to satellite manufacturing, and the repurposing of remaining satellite capabilities after failure. Despite no longer being suitable for their original purpose, these remaining capabilities can find new applications. The study begins by identifying relevant innovative Eco-designs applications. Subsequently, it examines sustainability within the satellite lifecycle supply chain, categorizing it into four methods: 1) active debris removal (ADR), 2) transport logistics, 3) mission extension, and 4) repair and construction. Aligned with emerging trends in space activities, the study also considers future developments to maximize satellite potential to provide new services. Additionally, the research includes a description of a potential lean manufacturing process, encompassing logistic chain, to support the development of a more sustainable space economy. Finally, the study concludes with a technology survey tracing the evolution of Smallsats and Cubesat platform developments, identifying relevant innovative designs for a sustainable space environment.

text: Although most constellations have been launched to offer valuable and necessary services, they may create long-term sustainability issues. In the same way, various sustainable strategies have been developed worldwide to address short-, medium-, and long-term solutions aimed at mitigating unsustainable practices in the space sector. One example is the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space of the United Nations, which discusses matters related to space and sustainable development [23].

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > 2.1 Introduction
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / 2 1 introduction
text: Another example is NASA's sustainability report and future plans [24], which ensure adherence to the sustainability goals outlined in Executive Order 14057 and NASA policies, with a primary focus on reducing environmental risks and promoting sustainable practices throughout all stages of work [25]. NASA's sustainability route plan involves the White Sands Test Facility (WSTF), which operates an Environmental Management program. The facility prioritizes waste minimization through the promotion of recycling, reuse, and the Reuse Market Place (ReMaP) software application to divert materials away from landfills. Furthermore, the WSTF is committed to sustainable acquisition, favoring eco-friendly products and services. The Site-wide Sustainability Working Group (S2WG) actively engages employees in initiatives aimed at enhancing water and energy efficiency while meeting mission goals. The facility encourages green projects and relies on S2WG to evaluate funding proposals, encompassing categories like sustainable acquisition, waste reduction, recycling, hazardous waste management, and pollution prevention [26, 27]. These endeavors collectively reduce the facility's environmental impact and cultivate a culture of sustainability [28].

text: Involving other relevant institutions of the sector in the implementation of the strategy, the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee (IADC) "Report on the Status of the Space Debris Environment 2024" [54] underscores the importance of achieving zero debris in space through sustainable practices. Sustainability in space, defined by the United Nations as serving current requirements without jeopardizing future generations' demands, requires establishing criteria to measure a viable space environment [54]. While the report acknowledges the effectiveness of space debris mitigation guidelines, it also highlights the need for further adoption and stricter adherence to these measures. Despite efforts to slow the growth of the space debris population, the report warns of a potential doubling of orbital objects within 50 years if current trends persist. Moreover, without additional measures such as active debris removal technology, collisions among existing space debris objects could exacerbate the problem.

text: Furthermore, prestigious institutions in this field, such as the IAF Space Traffic Management Technical Committee, have conducted research into various aspects of space traffic management (STM) in order to promote safe space exploration and use while minimizing risks to people and property on Earth. This initiative, established through a collaborative effort between the IAA (International Academy of Astronautics), the IISL (International Institute of Space Law), and the IAF (International Astronautical Federation), aims to develop comprehensive recommendations on STM behaviors as well as proposals addressed to decision makers at both national and international levels [58]. The IAF STM TC's research activities cover a broad spectrum of technical challenges within the STM environment. These include operational coordination services, collision avoidance (both in orbit and during launch and reentry), frequency management and coordination, space hardware disposal, space situational awareness (SSA), space surveillance and tracking (SST), space weather (SWE), space environment management (SEM) for space debris mitigation and remediation, and space operations assurance (SOA), which combines SEM, SSA, and STM. Recent publications from the IAF STM TC emphasize the need for space object monitoring data as the cornerstone of any space traffic management system [58]. The UN Long-Term Sustainability Standards emphasize the need to gather and accurately retain orbital data as well as the development of related technologies in order to support long-term space activities. Ongoing developments in the field include implementing optical surveys in LEO, laser ranging of non-cooperative targets, developing techniques for attitude determination, implementing active LED systems for satellite identification, and addressing challenges in cis-lunar applications [58]. The goal is to identify technological advancements that increase the volume and accuracy of observations, such as ground-based laser tracking to improve ranging accuracy, passive optical systems to supplement radar visibility zones, passive RF systems to improve data timeliness, space-based measurements to collect data on small objects, and attitude motion standards to support emerging missions like active debris removal and on-orbit servicing. These efforts aim to improve STM capabilities and contribute to the long-term management of space activities [58].

text: - Manufacturing (comprising components, subsystems, and system integration): It is essential to highlight the advances made in ISO standards for small satellites. The ISO/TC20/SC14 committee [64] began efforts in 2014 to produce standards that define and regulate the use of small satellites, resulting in work item ISO/WD/20991, "Requirements for Small Spacecraft" [65]. This standard seeks to lay the groundwork for the responsible deployment and operation of tiny satellites, with a focus on sustainability and space debris mitigation. In March 2016, the study group presented a report to the IAA, concluding that small satellites should be identified by their design and management philosophy, not their size. The term "lean satellite" has been used to describe satellites that use creative, low-cost ways to enable rapid delivery with small teams. The group developed a scaling system to measure adherence to the lean satellite concept, which was tested on nearly 30 satellites worldwide [66]. In 2019, the Kyushu Institute of Technology (Kyutech), with Japanese government assistance, launched a project to standardize the CubeSat electrical interface [67]. This initiative uses the lean satellite community to get worldwide feedback and build the standard. Activities include editing drafts, coordinating with ISO/TC20/SC14, and organizing international workshops. The standard document, "Space Systems—CubeSat Interface", is currently being developed. This standard specifies the interface and the documentation required to enable integration and reduce compatibility difficulties, resulting in a substantially shorter process of selecting and testing CubeSat components.

The program emphasizes innovation and continuous enhancement to meet the ever-evolving requirements of NASA's programs and projects [77, 78].

The ESA's collaborations with industry partners revolve around the development of advanced technologies and materials specifically engineered to withstand the harsh environmental conditions of space while adhering to stringent environmental impact mitigation strategies [79,80].

text: In the Manufacturing stage, there are proposals [32] that encompass new methodologies for cost-efficiency, rapid delivery, and waste reduction. This includes the incorporation of new engineering methods and technologies like Industry 4.0 as well as space infrastructures for robotic in-orbit assembly and component manufacturing [90, 91]. Moving to the Launch stage, we find developments related to orbital transfer vehicles, in-space transportation services [92], separation systems, and cluster capabilities [93]. In the Satellite Operation stage, with a focus on sustainability, there are advancements in spacecraft docking and connection devices [94, 95] as well as for the refueling of satellites in space [96, 97]. Finally, in the Satellite Life Extension proposal stage, we consider developments in recycling space debris into raw materials and active debris removal (ADR) [98, 99, 100].

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > 2.2.6 Challenges
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / 2 2 6 challenges
text: One segment that has presented significant challenges within the supply chain is the manufacturing stage processes. Efforts to enhance reliability during this stage have led to advances in the performance of new materials, technologies, software, and more for space applications [101]. Consequently, there has been a concerted effort to improve the performance of satellite subsystems and extend their missions [102]. Over the years, the satellite industry has witnessed a significant evolution in its supply chain dynamics. Earlier, the supply chain for satellite missions was primarily characterized by long lead times, high costs, and limited suppliers [6,72]. However, with technological advances and the emergence of a more competitive space industry, supply chain management for satellites has evolved. This evolution includes streamlined manufacturing processes, improved component standardization, and the diversification of suppliers, resulting in reduced costs and increased accessibility to satellite technology [103].

text: In a sustainable approach, the evaluation of these new materials should not only encompass their performance within the satellite structure, but it should also consider their impact when used in space (e.g., for repairs or in-orbit manufacturing) or upon re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere. Additionally, the final disposal of these materials at the end of their useful life should be considered, including options for recycling or utilization in other processes [104, 105]. This holistic approach to supply chain management in the satellite industry reflects the growing awareness of environmental sustainability and the need to manage resources efficiently throughout the entire lifecycle of satellite missions [106, 107].

text: The primary hurdles for future CubeSat and small satellite technologies include coordination, data processing, propulsion, de-orbiting devices, and large deployable structures. Coordinating huge constellations of small satellites poses significant challenges, which can be solved via inter-satellite link (ISL) communications and satellite docking programs. Furthermore, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) will allow for autonomous diagnostics, on-board data processing, and constellation management, all of which improve operating efficiency. Increasing data processing and transmission capabilities necessitates the use of modern communication technologies such as Ku-band and Ka-band transmitters or laser communication, but with careful power management concerns. Furthermore, the utilization of propulsion systems, particularly those based on electricity, chemicals, or water, allows for controlled satellite movement and orbital modifications. Improvements in active and passive de-orbiting systems, such as electric and chemical propulsion, as well as passive systems like air drag augmentation devices (DADs), help to reduce the risks associated with space

However, a substantial number of launched satellites, despite the increasing volume, do not operate throughout their expected lifespans. This is often due to various reasons, such as economic constraints, mission completion, or political considerations [108, 109]. In certain instances, new satellites are launched to replace those experiencing unexpected anomalies rather than leveraging their residual capabilities.

text: Prospective initiatives ought to focus on providing comprehensive anomaly descriptions to better grasp their implications on satellite architectures. Overcoming the challenges associated with reviving failed satellites demands addressing technological, regulatory, liability, legal, and ownership barriers. The design and technology of forthcoming satellites should prioritize flexibility in both hardware and software architectures [110, 111]. Furthermore, it is crucial to heighten awareness within the industry about the economic and environmental advantages of repurposing satellites, encompassing the reduction of orbital congestion, the minimization of unnecessary launches, the mitigation of space debris, and the alleviation of ecological impacts on the planet [112]. Notably, the Eco-LeanSat proposal lays the groundwork for a potential future satellite infrastructure, facilitating the execution of reuse operations for both hardware and software. Considering the previous study of sustainable proposals for eco-design and their application in the supply chain, and with a view towards applying them to future satellites, the following chapter conducts a technology survey. This survey traces the evolution of SmallSat and CubeSat platform developments, identifying relevant innovative designs and highlighting applications oriented towards sustainable space practices.

text: (i) In 2020, the UPC Federated Satellite System (FSSCat) mission marked a significant milestone by employing AI for the first time for cloud detection. FSSCat consisted of two 6-unit CubeSats: one of them was equipped with UPC's Flexible Microwave Payload-2 (FMPL-2), featuring an L-band microwave radiometer and a GNSS reflectometer implemented in a Zynq----7045 FPGA for sea ice and soil moisture monitoring. Additionally, the second CubeSat included Cosine's HyperScout-2 visible + near-infrared + thermal infrared hyperspectral imager and included the PhiSat-1 AI board in a Movidius processor. Notably, FSSCat was the first CubeSat-based mission that contributed to the Copernicus program [161]. The application of AI in CubeSat missions has revolutionized the efficiency and accuracy of data processing. By employing AI algorithms, CubeSats can conduct real-time data analysis, make autonomous decisions, and optimize satellite operations, leading to enhanced mission performance and reduced operational costs. For the FSSCat mission, AI was utilized to select data for download based on cloud coverage, optimizing data transmission. This integration of AI in CubeSats exemplifies how advanced technologies enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of space exploration endeavors.

text: Governments, universities, and commercial companies in the space sector have been adopting new and innovative solutions to the manufacturing processes of small structures and have been proposing new payloads. For instance, Fleet Space Technologies, an Australian manufacturer, developed the first 3D-printed satellite, Alpha CubeSat, and the first 3D-printed rocket, Terran 1, which was launched on 24 March 2023 by the American company Relativity Space. The use of 3D printing enables the production of custom satellites with a general structure and system parts at a much lower cost than conventional satellites.

text: Significant innovations encompass optical and laser technology and AI; these play a crucial role in Earth observation and environmental monitoring. They improve data precision for climate monitoring, disaster detection, and resource management. These advancements also strengthen satellite communications, facilitating high-speed, low-latency transmissions, which are essential for services like Starlink's efficient high-performance satellite network. Currently, Starlink's satellite communications constellation comprises over 4000 satellites in orbit. Yet in the near future, companies such as OneWeb and Telesat plan to establish smaller constellations. Tech giants like Amazon and Samsung have also announced intentions to deploy their own constellations, consisting of 3236 and 4600 broadband satellites, respectively [162].

text: To summarize, until 2013, CubeSats were a small field dominated by academic and university projects. After 2013, mostly due to Planet and Spire Global constellations, most CubeSats shifted to the commercial sector. As of 2012, only 72 CubeSats were in orbit, and as of May 2023, more than 2100 CubeSats have been successfully deployed into orbit. Today, the communications field intends to improve the performance of 5G ecosystems and beyond through non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) based on satellite constellations [174]. Furthermore, there is a trend to develop scientific experiments and create space architectures that use reusable vehicles to access space and return to Earth, such as the Space Rider, which has been conceived to provide a space laboratory for payloads to operate in orbit for a variety of applications [175].

text: Since the introduction of the CubeSat standard, over the last two decades, technology has achieved a high level of maturity, particularly for generating high power using large, deployable solar panels, which is vital for Earth observation and communication missions. However, notable challenges persist, including the need for larger deployable structures to support advanced antennas, high-precision attitude control systems, enhanced RF inter-satellite links, flexible systems for managing diverse payloads, integration of artificial intelligence for onboard processing, and increased reliability for extended missions, including GEO and inter-planetary ones. These challenges and innovations are defining the future of CubeSats and small satellite technologies [27].

text: To secure the long-term viability of space activities in the face of the development of small satellites and CubeSats, a diversified strategy is required. First and foremost, it is critical to establish comprehensive space traffic control systems [177]. These systems would aid with monitoring and regulating the increasing number

text: of satellites in orbit, reducing the risk of collisions and assuring efficient use of orbital space. Furthermore, strong debris mitigation requirements are required to reduce the environmental impact of space activities. This is accomplished by implementing measures to reduce space debris generation, such as designing satellites for safe reentry or deploying deorbiting mechanisms, which will help to maintain orbital environments for future generations [70]. International collaboration on space policy and regulation will be critical for addressing these problems. Harmonizing standards and regulations across nations can establish a unified framework for sustainable space activities and ensure equitable access to space resources while safeguarding the Earth's environment. Also, investing in the development of technology for debris removal and satellite recycling is critical [63]. Efforts to develop and deploy spacecraft capable of actively removing debris from orbit as well as repurposing or recycling decommissioned satellites can help to reduce the environmental impact of space activities and contribute to the long-term viability of space operations.

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > Table 10.3:
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / table 10 3
text: (a) Active Debris Removal (ADR): Space debris, which includes decommissioned satellites and other fragments, presents a growing threat to the safety and functionality of operational satellites. The implementation of effective active debris removal (ADR) methods is vital for establishing and maintaining a sustainable space environment. In Table 10.3, this is categorized as Active Debris Removal (ADR)/Docking, and we delve into state-of-the-art ADR technologies and strategies, such as deorbiting with no pre-installed docking interface, capture systems with integrated propulsion, self-destructing magnetic tugboats, space transportation systems, and space debris "Gobblers", among others. This examination underscores the significance of proactive debris management for mitigating collision risks and preserving orbital space for future satellite deployments.

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > Table 10.3:
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / table 10 3
text: (b) Transport Logistics: Efficient logistics and transportation systems are important for ensuring the successful launching, deployment, and repositioning of satellites. In Table 10.1, categorized under "Management and Manufacturing Techniques", we delve into cutting-edge logistics solutions, including technologies like orbit-reconfigurable satellites, radiation-resistant components, 3D printing, and other innovative approaches. These solutions are purposefully designed to not only reduce the environmental impact of satellite launches but also to optimize satellite placement for maximum efficiency.

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > Table 10.3:
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / table 10 3
text: (c) Mission Extension: Extending the operational life of satellites is not only an economically sound approach, but it also environmentally responsible. We delve into innovative mission extension technologies, such as satellite servicing and in-orbit refueling, as sustainable methods for prolonging the lifespans of satellites and reducing the necessity for new deployments. In Table 10.2, we showcase a range of developments

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > Table 10.3:
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / table 10 3
text: (e.g., disruptive technologies, communication and data transfer advancements, and innovations in military security and intelligence surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR)). These developments encompass innovative payloads aimed at optimizing satellite performance and ensuring the continued success of missions.

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > Table 10.3:
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / table 10 3
text: (d) Repair and Construction: Satellite repair and in-orbit construction capabilities are imperative for mitigating the environmental impact caused by outdated and malfunctioning satellites. In Table 10.4, we explore the development of autonomous construction and repair techniques, encompassing on-orbit assembly and component replacement [187, 188, 189]. These approaches are instrumental for extending the operational lifespan of satellites while concurrently minimizing the generation of space debris [190].

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > Table 10.3:
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / table 10 3
text: As depicted in Figure 2.12, these parameters collectively represent a comprehensive framework for advancing the sustainability of satellite architectures. Future developments in these areas hold the promise of more reliable and environmentally friendly satellite technologies that are well-equipped to meet the growing demands for space-based services and technologies [191] .

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > 2.5 Conclusions and Future Research
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / 2 5 conclusions and future research
text: The design of an eco-friendly logistics satellite supply chain requires the collaboration of multiple stakeholders. This study has highlighted the significant technological advances within specific sections of the supply chain. For instance, in the manufacturing stage, the proposal of utilizing new materials with sustainable characteristics for space applications shows promising progress. In the launch stage, the implementation of intelligent dispenser technology enhances satellite deployment accuracy, thereby reducing the risk of mission failure. Additionally, the operation stage has witnessed the emergence of projects aimed not only at fulfilling scientific objectives but also at prolonging the satellite's lifespan. Sustainable practices such as in-orbit repair, ADR, and environmentally responsible satellite disposal methods following mission completion are proposed in this segment.

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > 2.5 Conclusions and Future Research
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / 2 5 conclusions and future research
text: Future research on this subject must consider political, legal, economic, and security consequences. The concept of a satellite "as a service", similar to a multi-owner property, offers potential to reduce the number of space assets by allowing satellite resources to be reconfigured in orbit for different customers at different times. Furthermore, the rapid evolution of on-orbit servicing (OSS) creates several obstacles and opportunities. OSS technologies such as in-space repairs, refueling, refurbishing, and service have the potential to dramatically extend satellite lifecycles while also addressing space debris concerns. For example, more than half of GEO satellites are predicted to have operational issues owing to fuel depletion, but refueling can extend their operational life, keep orbital slots, and benefit both governmental and commercial operators. Companies such as SES and Intelsat are incorporating OSS life extension capabilities into their business models, demonstrating increased customer confidence [70,192]. Recent investments have highlighted the importance of these technologies. The launch deal between SpaceLogistics and SpaceX as well as the U.S. Air Force's investment in Orbit Fab's refueling interface demonstrate the strategic value of OSS. Refueling improves mobility, allowing satellites to retain or alter orbits, respond to threats, and avoid collisions, all of which are critical for the resilience and agility of space infrastructure [192]. The rapid evolution of OSS presents numerous challenges and opportunities. Recent initiatives such as Clean Space by the ESA and collaborations on projects like Astroscale, ClearSpace, D-Orbit, and Telespazio, alongside Thales Alenia Space, demonstrate a growing commitment to advancing OSS technologies [193]. These initiatives have received funding to mature their ideas, and their results were presented in preparation of the 2022 ESA council at the ministerial level [193]. Additionally, the development of modular spacecraft designed for serviceability, including refueling and upgrades, can further extend the lifespans of satellites and improve functionality as technology evolves. This modularity reduces costs and launch weights while enabling on-orbit assembly and repair, fostering a robust secondary market for older-but-functional spacecraft. This shift towards modular and serviceable designs will likely become standard by the end of the 2020s, driven by initiatives like the U.S. Defense Innovation Unit's Modularity for Space Systems (M4SS) project [194]. Furthermore, the adoption of safety standards, exemplified by the JAXA's JERG-2-026 "SAFETY STANDARD FOR ON-ORBIT SERVICING MISSIONS" [195], underscores the importance of establishing regulatory frameworks to ensure the safe and effective operation of OSS missions. Exploring these topics in depth will provide significant insights for policymakers, legal experts, and industry professionals as they navigate the changing landscape of sustainable space logistics.

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > 2.5 Conclusions and Future Research
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / 2 5 conclusions and future research
text: The research outlines critical methods for future Eco-LeanSat designs that balance environmental responsibility and performance enhancement. Primarily, the adoption of sustainable materials and manufacturing processes assumes an important role in mitigating the ecological footprint associated with satellite production. This necessitates the sourcing of materials from renewable or recycled sources and the minimization of waste throughout the manufacturing process. To accomplish this, rigorous material testing and the establishment of regulations conducive to the integration of these novel materials into space missions are imperative. For example, the LignoSat mission [68], as mentioned in the article, employs wood in satellite construction, exemplifying an innovative approach to sustainability. Moreover, research into advancements in 3D-printing technology for satellite fabrication is underway, furthering the development of environmentally friendly satellite designs that leave no harmful particles on Earth or in space. Demonstrating the successful adoption and implementation of these materials opens the door to further exploration and study in the realm of spatial sustainability. Second, boosting energy efficiency is critical for maintaining environmental responsibility. Eco-LeanSat designs might include innovative energy management systems and energy-efficient components to reduce power usage during satellite operation. Additionally, incorporating solar panels or other renewable energy sources can help to lessen dependency on nonrenewable energy sources. Furthermore, using eco-friendly propulsion solutions, such as electric propulsion, might improve environmental sustainability.

section: Considerations for Eco-LeanSat Satellite Manufacturing and Recycling > 2.5 Conclusions and Future Research
section_key: considerations for eco leansat satellite manufacturing and recycling / 2 5 conclusions and future research
text: Considering the exploration of sustainability in space discussed in this chapter, particularly in relation to satellites, the subsequent chapter of this thesis delves into an analysis of the myriad objects comprising space debris, with a focus on disused satellites commonly abandoned in space due to various anomalies. While these satellite failures may not always result in catastrophic outcomes, certain subsystems possess potential for reuse, extending beyond their initial design, thus opening avenues for studying their potential repurposing for future purposes and missions. The primary objective of this study is to assess the feasibility of "recycling" partially failed satellites, often referred to as "Zombie Satellites," through a statistical evaluation of the severity of their anomalies and an examination of their residual capabilities and limitations. Through a comprehensive statistical analysis, anomalies are meticulously categorized based on subsystem, orbit type, occurrence date during the satellite's lifespan, and severity. Additionally, the study presents an analysis aimed at identifying failed satellites within some of the current large constellations.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > Abstract
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / abstract
text: Thousands of rockets, spaceships, and satellites have been launched, resulting in a steady increase in the number of space debris notably in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and Geostationary Orbit (GEO). Among the objects comprising space debris, defunct satellites are commonly found, which may have been abandoned in space due to various anomalies. While these satellite failures may not be catastrophic, certain subsystems could still be repurposed for alternative uses beyond their initial design. This study aims to assess the feasibility of "recycling" partially failed satellites, also known as "Zombie Satellites," by statistically evaluating the severity of their anomalies and quantifying their remaining capabilities and limitations.

section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / abstract
text: By conducting a comprehensive statistical analysis, the anomalies have been categorized based on subsystem, orbit type, occurrence date during the satellite's lifespan, and severity. Additionally, an analysis is presented to identify failed satellites from some of the current large constellations.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.1 Introduction
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 1 introduction
text: Since 1957 until the beginning of 2023, approximately 11000 small spacecrafts (between 100 g to 1000 kg), and 4900 large ones (between 1001 kg and 5000 kg) have been launched [1]. Satellite payloads are conceived and designed to fulfill a specific mission and to satisfy the requirements for several applications (e.g., communications, Earth observation, navigation, astronomy, etc.). While often the payload works for the entire lifetime of the satellite, and sometimes it even exceeds its nominal lifetime, not all missions reach the initially expected lifetime and goals. Hence, satellites can end their mission when one of the scenarios presented in the scheme of Fig.3.1 occurs.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.1 Introduction
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 1 introduction
text: The first scenario occurs when a satellite successfully achieves its initial expected goals. In such cases, the mission may be extended or terminated, leading to the decommissioning of the satellite. If the satellite is in a Low Earth Orbit (LEO), as specified by the European Cooperation for Space Standardization (ECSS) standard ECSS-U-AS-10C and ISO 24113 Fourth edition [2, 3], it is required to decay within 25 years. In the case of a GEO satellite, after decommissioning, and only if the satellite has fuel, it will be retired to a graveyard orbit to reduce any inconvenience to other operational missions. Another scenario occurs when the mission is stopped because the business model is no longer economically profitable, as it happened with the Iridium constellation, which was then used by the US DoD for military purposes [4]. The third and last case, which is the aim of this study, is when a satellite experiences unexpected failures during orbit operations

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.1 Introduction
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 1 introduction
text: affecting temporarily or permanently the capabilities of satellite subsystems, thus ending abruptly the mission for which the satellite was initially conceived.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.1 Introduction
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 1 introduction
text: In these three cases, satellites in orbit that still have operational resources and capabilities remain inoperative in space and are exposed to radiation, wasting their potential lifetime, while waiting for natural re-entry. These unused ZSs orbiting in space increase the debris population, thus increasing the risks to the space ecosystem, and even endangering other active missions [5, 6], while they could potentially be reused for other purposes. By analyzing three different databases, the main objective of this study is to perform an in-depth analysis of the taxonomy of satellite anomalies, their severity, and their impact on satellite performance. In addition, an assessment of the possibility of leveraging ZSs that have partially failed is performed.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.2 Space Debris Reduction Strategies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 2 space debris reduction strategies
text: Space debris is an increasing cause of concern. Since the beginning of the space era, thousands of rockets, spaceships, and satellites have been launched, and at least initially, no one foresaw what to do with them at the end of their useful life. As a result, the number of space debris in notably LEO [7] and GEO orbits has been steadily increasing. In the last two decades, non-deliberate fragmentations continue to occur at about 11.7 events per year as shown in Fig 3.2 [8].

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.2 Space Debris Reduction Strategies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 2 space debris reduction strategies
text: Hence, different approaches have been followed to address this situation. The most common strategies have

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.2 Space Debris Reduction Strategies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 2 space debris reduction strategies
text: focused on ensuring a natural reentry in less than 25 years or forcing the controlled re-entry of satellites by their own or external means (if they cannot re-enter by themselves) [9]. In this case, for example, the UK Space Agency, in 2021, conducted a feasibility study on how to deorbit two defunct LEO satellites that were not built with retrieval and removal mechanisms in mind by 2025 [10], proposing the development of a system with propulsion capabilities. From the outcome of this study, on 25 August 2021, the End-of-Life Services by Astroscale-demonstration (ELSA-d) was conducted to capture and remove objects in orbit [11]. This design evolved during the ELSA-m mission, a public-private partnership with the ESA and OneWeb. ELSA-m will use a magnetic capture mechanism, and therefore, it can only capture satellites equipped with a docking plate before launch.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.2 Space Debris Reduction Strategies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 2 space debris reduction strategies
text: Another proposal is the COSMIC [12] initiative which proposes a spacecraft to capture and deorbit three or four objects in a single mission for a constellation customer.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.2 Space Debris Reduction Strategies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 2 space debris reduction strategies
text: In contrast to ELSA-m, COSMIC will use a robotic arm or gripping mechanism, which would enable to capture a defunct satellite not originally built to be grabbed. Another approach that has been considered by the JAXA is to de-orbit a discarded upper stage of a rocket without a docking plate. The next launch of the Active Debris Removal by Astroscale-Japan (ADRAS-J) [13] mission was in February 2024 when Rocket Lab launched its spacecraft to inspect the spent of the upper stage ahead of a removal attempt that could take place in 2025.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.2 Space Debris Reduction Strategies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 2 space debris reduction strategies
text: In addition to developing propulsion systems to re-enter defunct satellites, another strategy focuses on refueling satellites to maintain their orbits. For example, Northrop Grumman's Mission Extension Vehicle-2 (MEV-2) [14], a satellite life extension vehicle, completed on 12 April 2021 its first docking to the Intelsat 10-02, a GEO satellite launched in 2004. The MEV was designed to dock to GEO satellites, whose fuel is nearly depleted. MEV-2 does not move the satellite into a different orbit, instead, it acts as a new engine and fuel tank to extend the spacecraft's lifetime, enabling aging GEO communication satellites to continue operations for up to five more years each. Another approach was developed by Lockheed Martin [15], who plans to launch two CubeSats to demonstrate how small satellites can be used to upgrade GEO satellites or provide life-extension services such as refueling.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.2 Space Debris Reduction Strategies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 2 space debris reduction strategies
text: Moreover, investigations have been conducted on OOS and satellite life extension. Among these proposals, DARPA Phoenix program [16], which seeks to demonstrate that a robotic servicing vehicle can perform reliable and useful operations in GEO, such as the correction of some mission-ending mechanical anomalies, assistance in orbital maneuvers, and installation of attachable payloads. Subsequently, [17] proposed a robotic spacecraft to harvest components to repair existing satellites.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.2 Space Debris Reduction Strategies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 2 space debris reduction strategies
text: These approaches have focused on cleaning the space ecosystem by de-orbiting inoperative satellites, refueling satellites to provide services, and developing robotic spacecraft to repair, move, and/or assist aging satellites [9] (Fig. 3.3). However, to the best of our knowledge, no approach has been considered to recycle satellites that have partially failed so as to provide new services by leveraging their remaining capabilities. The possibility to recycle ZSs will optimize the in orbit infrastructure, reducing unnecessary launches, thus,

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.2 Space Debris Reduction Strategies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 2 space debris reduction strategies
text: mitigating directly the debris population, and contributing to the space ecosystem protection. Therefore, this work will: 1. analyze and assess the possibility of reusing failed satellites by analyzing their anomalies' severity, status, and 2. perform a feasibility study to conduct other services, especially for Earth observation and communication purposes.

The first database is Telastra [18], which contains entries for over 1500 anomalies experienced by satellites from 1963 to 2021, mostly in GEO. Seradata database [1] provides anomalies experienced by over 1000 spacecraft in LEO, GEO, MEO, and other orbits.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.4 Anomalies evaluation criteria
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 4 anomalies evaluation criteria
text: All subsystems are responsible for a specific task on the satellite. Some of these subsystems are indispensable, while others are not, and despite being disabled, the satellite can continue partially functioning. Hence, Table 3.1 analyses the remaining satellite's capability to perform several applications in case an anomaly impacts each subsystem. Table 3.1 distinguishes three different cases:

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.4 Anomalies evaluation criteria
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 4 anomalies evaluation criteria
text: - Satellite without capabilities: Lack of, at least, one of its indispensable subsystems or components and, therefore, the satellite will not be able to perform either its initial mission or any other.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.4 Anomalies evaluation criteria
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 4 anomalies evaluation criteria
text: - Satellite with limited capabilities: The lack of certain subsystems or components implies that the satellite can operate, but with certain limitations.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.4 Anomalies evaluation criteria
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 4 anomalies evaluation criteria
text: - Satellite with full capability: Despite the lack or unavailability of certain subsystems, the satellite will continue to operate without limitations (e.g. failure is in a redundant subsystems).

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.4 Anomalies evaluation criteria
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 4 anomalies evaluation criteria
text: Communication equipment such as the antenna, duplexer, amplifiers, telemetry transmitter, command receiver, encoders, and decoders are essential for communication and controlling the satellite. Nevertheless, in case of command receivers or demodulators failures in the TRC system, the communication system (data link) can receive commands and demodulate them before being executed by the onboard computer. In case an anomaly disables the communication system, by using the telemetry link, the satellite can still perform other services such as Earth observation, space observation, meteorology, and scientific research (e.g., biology, physics). The new service will be selected according its to appropriateness requirements, such as the power needed, and the amount of ground station transmitting and receiving the data, among others. Thrusters provide a fast reaction to stabilize satellites during orbit, and may be indispensable for some specific missions. Nevertheless, a satellite with no thrusters, but with reaction wheels combined with magnetorquers may provide full attitude stabilization of the satellite. The attitude reference sensor depends on mission accuracy. For instance, Earth sensors (with an accuracy around $ 1^{\circ} $ ) may be unsuitable for space observation satellites, since they require the high accuracy achieved by star trackers. Hence, in case of a failure of some attitude sensors, since generally a satellite is equipped with more than one type, it will be assessed if the satellite has the capability for other uses. Regarding electrical power, all the subsystem equipment is essential to generate, store, and distribute the power to the entire satellite. At least one solar panel is required to generate power. Batteries may not be essential, as some satellites were operational only during sunlight after battery failure. However, this study considers the EPS as a critical subsystem to provide a continuous and reliable service. As for the thermal control system, although passive thermal stabilization may be properly achieved, a satellite without the capability to control and maintain actively its temperature exhibits important limitations for an extended life.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.1 Satellite anomalies occurrence during lifetime
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 1 satellite anomalies occurrence during lifetime
text: From the analysis conducted, in which only 55% anomalies report the failure date, 31% of the anomalies in orbit occurred during the first quarter of the nominal satellite's useful life. This result confirms the starting point of this study, since an early anomaly of the payload leads to a waste of the remaining capabilities of the satellite for the rest of the original mission lifetime. During the second, third, and fourth quarters, the probability of anomaly decreases drastically, indicating that the most critical stage is the first quarter, when the satellite must perform some crucial functions, such as deployments (solar panels, antennas, tethers, etc.), perform the initial attitude stabilization and orientation, thruster ignition to reach an accurate orbit position, etc. In addition, it can also be related to a lack of comprehensive ground tests ("infancy failures"). It must

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.2 Satellite anomalies analysis per subsystem
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 2 satellite anomalies analysis per subsystem
text: It has been found that the communications subsystem turned out to be the one with most failures:12% (Table 3.2), which is consistent with the fact that 36% of the analyzed satellites are GEO, and for telecommunication purposes. Communication anomalies include failures in the amplifier (TWTA or SSPA), channel power gain drop, the appearance of spurious signals, noise and interference, transmitter and receiver failures, and some other communication anomalies in which the component is not specified.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.2 Satellite anomalies analysis per subsystem
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 2 satellite anomalies analysis per subsystem
text: After the communications system, the ADCS presents the second largest percentage of anomalies (10%). Reference sensors (e.g., spurious inhibition and bias shift in their output voltages), and reaction wheel failures are among the most common failures.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.2 Satellite anomalies analysis per subsystem
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 2 satellite anomalies analysis per subsystem
text: The EPS and payloads are also among the subsystems with a significant anomaly percentage (8%). The solar arrays' degradation, circuit failures, and the batteries' decline to store power are the most frequent failures in the EPS. Regarding payloads, failures are directly related to the mission instrument (e.g. atomic clocks, radiometers, and cameras).

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.2 Satellite anomalies analysis per subsystem
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 2 satellite anomalies analysis per subsystem
text: Propulsion failures (4%) include thrusters and apogee kick motors (especially for GEO satellites), thrust decay, low or high impulse, burning fuel too quickly, fuel leak, low pressure in the fuel tanks, propellant lower or greater than expected, ignition delays, etc. As for the mechanisms (3%) , solar arrays and reflectors not deployed, are among the typical failures, while for TT&C the commands decoders and telemetry coders, spurious commands, and command processors are among the most common failures.

section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 2 satellite anomalies analysis per subsystem
text: Since most GEO satellites are equipped with communication payloads, and the anomalies related to these payloads have been considered part of the communication subsystem, LEO presents more payload failures than GEO, while GEO does present more failures in the communication subsystem (Fig.3.7). GEO satellites have more propulsion failures, mostly because of the apogee kick motors that need to reach a circular geosynchronous orbit, the amount of fuel, and the fuel tank environment considering the solar and cosmic radiation effects on the GEO orbit over the LEO. Computers on GEO satellites fail less than LEO ones, possibly because the former are RadHard, have redundancy, and are designed for a lifetime over 10 or 15 years.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.3 Severity of satellites' anomalies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 3 severity of satellites anomalies
text: The impact of an anomaly on a mission can vary significantly. For this analysis, the effects and severity of the anomalies were determined according to the following classification:

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.3 Severity of satellites' anomalies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 3 severity of satellites anomalies
text: - Work Around: This category encompasses the anomalies whose effects were (or were almost) negligible in the satellite. Moreover, for simplicity, it also encompasses those satellites that kept working after the occurrence of an anomaly despite some limitations. For instance, due to limited electrical power, some transponders may be switched off, limiting the service of the satellite.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.3 Severity of satellites' anomalies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 3 severity of satellites anomalies
text: - Redundant Subsystem or Component: Normally a redundant subsystem or component is used when the anomaly affects permanently or temporarily the initial system. For various factors, such as space and mass requirements, not all satellites have the possibility to have redundant component or subsystems.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.3 Severity of satellites' anomalies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 3 severity of satellites anomalies
text: - Subsystem Temporarily Disabled: The subsystem was temporarily disabled after experiencing the anomaly.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.3 Severity of satellites' anomalies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 3 severity of satellites anomalies
text: - Satellite Temporarily Disabled: The satellite was temporarily not operational after experiencing the anomaly.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.3 Severity of satellites' anomalies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 3 severity of satellites anomalies
text: - Subsystem Permanently Disabled: The subsystem was permanently disabled after experiencing an anomaly. If the disabled subsystem corresponds to the EPS or to any other crucial equipment (e.g., the command decoder, attitude control processor, etc.) with no redundancy, the satellite is considered permanently disabled. Most of the anomalies that lead to ZSs (Fig.3.1), present this type of severity.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.3 Severity of satellites' anomalies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 3 severity of satellites anomalies
text: - Satellite Permanently Disabled: This category represents the worst scenario that a given anomaly can mean to a satellite. Generally, the satellite becomes useless at this stage, and nothing can be done to get it back to life. However, in some cases, because the satellite cannot carry out the specific mission launched for, it remains abandoned although still has some capabilities to offer other services besides the one initially designed to become a ZS.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.3 Severity of satellites' anomalies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 3 severity of satellites anomalies
text: The results obtained from the analysis indicate that 24% of the anomalies in orbit led to a total loss hence, disabling permanently the satellite (Fig. 3.8), whereas 23% of the anomalies did not affect the satellite; therefore, it was able to resume the mission totally or partially. 10% of the failures disabled the satellites temporarily, 4% affected the subsystems temporarily and, 8% of the anomalies led the satellite to switch to the redundant system or component. In addition, 9% disabled permanently a subsystem, while 22% correspond to an unknown severity of unspecified anomalies.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.3 Severity of satellites' anomalies
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 3 severity of satellites anomalies
text: Throughout history, continuous improvements have been implemented to have more reliable, effective, and long-lasting systems. In Fig. 3.9, an evolution of the anomalies' severity is presented yearly. From 1963 to 1970, most of the anomalies that occurred, disabled the satellite permanently. However, from 1970 to 1986 satellites with redundant component or subsystems after an anomaly appeared (41 anomalies), increasing significantly from 1987 to 2000 (98 anomalies).

text: The lack of information on the typology of the anomaly, does not allow us to evaluate the remaining capabilities that these satellites had and that could be reused. Most LEO satellites, after experiencing a failure, cannot resume their mission and are decommissioned and abandoned rapidly before evaluating their remaining subsystems and capabilities.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.4 Characterization of ZSs
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 4 characterization of zss
text: Once the anomalies and their different impacts on the satellite have been analyzed, in this section the conditions for a satellite to be considered a ZS are discussed. Firstly, a reassessment of the impact of the anomaly on the satellite is necessary to study the feasibility of being reused. As indicated in Table 3.1, depending on the systems and equipment affected by an anomaly, it will be necessary to find out whether it is a fatal anomaly or whether the satellite, despite experiencing anomalies, continues to gather certain capabilities. Once the anomaly experienced has been evaluated as well as its effects on the systems, the next aspect to consider is the year the satellite or constellation was launched. Besides the accumulated radiation effects on the satellite after being exposed for an extended period, this is extremely important because of the technological innovation experienced in this last decade since the systems of a reused satellite must guarantee compatibility with other terrestrial and space architectures. Apart from the previous considerations, the satellite must still be orbiting in a usable orbit, not decayed, or moved to the graveyard orbit.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.4.1 ZSs in Constellations
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 4 1 zss in constellations
text: Considering that since 2013 at least 62% of satellites launched are part of constellations (5824 launches of 120 constellations versus a total of 9356 spacecraft launched in that period) [1], in most cases, of private companies, to demonstrate the presence of the so-called ZSs, this section focuses on analyzing the status of the some of the largest constellations by assessing their current active, inactive, and failed satellites. According to Seradata's database, and as reported in Table 3.3, currently, of the ten longest constellations, there are 956 inactive satellites orbiting, of which 347 and 349 correspond to Space X and Planet Labs, respectively. Considering that the hibernated satellites are already excluded, the number of failed satellites reported as compared to the number of inactive satellites appears to be low, indicating that not all failed satellites are reported, as for instance, Space X and Planet Labs, in which only 262 and 27 satellites are reported to have

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.5.4.1 ZSs in Constellations
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 5 4 1 zss in constellations
text: failed. An inactive satellite does not imply being a ZS. To affirm which inactive satellites are possible zombies, an anomaly reassessment is required to quantify the capabilities and limitations of the satellite. Hence, those inactive satellites with or over 25% capability are selected. Satellites with at least 25% the non-fatality of the anomaly is indicated, thus, it is guaranteed that at least the essential subsystems and components can still be reused. The higher this percentage, the more capabilities the satellite has, and fewer subsystems have been affected after the anomaly. In addition, it must be taken into consideration that there are inactive satellites, that unlike those ones analyzed after an in-orbit anomaly, they may have suffered unreported anomalies or been abandoned because of different causes as depicted in Fig 3.1, thus, the number of zombie inactive satellites increases significantly. Finally, to ensure the viability of those selected satellites, only those launched in 2010 onwards are selected and considered ZSs. In this regard, the analysis shows that Space X and Planet Labs constellations do have 85 and 322, respectively, inactive failed satellites with operational capabilities of more than or equal to 25%, while only 29 for ORBCOMM as indicated in Table 3.3 [1]. Unspecified anomalies in those constellations must be taken into account, as they hinder and limit the consideration and assessment of most of those satellites. As for the other constellations, such as Iridium communications and Satellogic, the non-specification and uncertainty of the anomalies' severity has totally limited the identification of those inactive satellites with remaining capabilities. Thus, besides the potential ZSs identified, Table 3.3 also reports possible ZSs, which are cases of inactive satellites with unknown remaining capabilities. Moreover, those satellites that before being decayed or moved to the graveyard orbits were possible ZSs that have also been included.
