section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.6 Conclusions
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 6 conclusions
text: The importance of satellites in daily life is out of question; hence, an increasing number of satellites are being launched to meet the needs of different users. However, of the hundreds (and in recent years, thousands) of satellites launched each year, only a few operate at the end of their expected lifetime. In some cases, satellites are decommissioned and/or abandoned for different reasons (economic, end mission, political, etc.). On some occasions, it is decided to launch new ones owing to unexpected anomalies instead of leveraging the capabilities they still have. In the analysis presented, the probability of a satellite failing in the first quarter of its life is three times larger than in the second quarter, and seven times more than in the last quarter of its life, evidencing the waste of satellites' capabilities, since not all the failures experienced during the first quarter are catastrophic and many systems can be leveraged. Most of the frequent failures correspond to crucial equipment for the satellite such as output amplifiers, reference sensors, batteries, and solar panels. Nevertheless, payload instruments, do also present a high probability of failure, leading in some extreme cases, to the end of the initial mission. During the analysis, it has been observed that some failed satellites tend to be decommissioned early, to decay (LEO orbits), to be moved to a graveyard orbit (GEO orbits), drifting completely from their orbit, instead of re-assessing the anomaly and raising the possibility of using the satellite for other purposes.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.6 Conclusions
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 6 conclusions
text: A failed satellite that has experienced a non-fatal anomaly and cannot perform the initial mission can be reused for other purposes depending on the remaining capabilities. For instance, in case of a data link

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.6 Conclusions
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 6 conclusions
text: anomaly, using the telemetry link, the satellite can still be capable to offer some low-rate applications such as: 1) the Internet of Things (IoT), by connecting low-bandwidth IoT devices in remote areas where traditional terrestrial networks are unavailable, 2) environmental monitoring, and selected remote sensing applications [26], which typically require low data rates and low-speed radios to transmit efficiently the data collected, 3) asset trackings, such as ships or cargo containers in remote areas, among others. On the other hand, assuming an anomaly in the ADCS which results in an undesired pointing, the satellite can be leveraged on applications that do not require a high pointing accuracy such as IoT devices, which do not require a high pointing precision as their antennas have a wide radiation pattern. Some failures in the storage systems may be critical to resume some services which require the processing of large data quantities; hence, the satellite may be still exploitable in those applications, but with limited data storage capability. Navigation purposes, for instance, require limited data storage as GPS and GLONASS satellites do only need to store satellite ephemeris data and clock corrections. Similarly, satellites used for weather monitoring typically only need to store images and other data related to weather patterns.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.6 Conclusions
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 6 conclusions
text: According to the authors' knowledge, this study is the first approach to how leverage failed satellites. A significant limitation encountered during this study is the number of unreported anomalies. To achieve more extensive and detailed results, a detailed description of the anomalies would be necessary for future projects so as to determine the effects of anomalies on the satellite architecture. Moreover, more research must be conducted, because bringing a ZS back to life poses multiple technology challenges, and also barriers regarding regulations, liabilities, and legal and technological aspects [27]. They may require a different frequency filling to reuse the communication devices for other purposes, a transfer of ownership, a reconfiguration, access to their operations, etc. Future designs and new technologies must ensure the flexibility of the hardware and software satellite architecture. In addition, it is essential to raise awareness in the sector about the economic and environmental impact that ZSs can provide by reducing the saturation in orbit, unnecessary launches, space debris originating, and ecological effects on the planet.

section: Towards a Second Life for Zombie Satellites: Anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment > 3.6 Conclusions
section_key: towards a second life for zombie satellites anomaly occurrence and potential recycling assessment / 3 6 conclusions
text: Given that an Eco-Lean proposal must address not only mechanical or manufacturing-related issues in orbiting satellites, but also factors that, according to the previous study, can cause severe partial or total failures in satellite systems, this thesis encompasses, in the following chapter, a statistical analysis of various space weather indicators. These indicators may be directly linked to the deterioration of spacecraft systems due to exposure to space radiation. Electrostatic discharges (ESD), single event latch-up (SEL), and single event upsets (SEU) are among the most frequent causes of reported anomalies in satellites. The aim is to quantify how concentrations and fluctuations of space radiation around Earth can damage spacecraft equipment and jeopardize mission continuity.

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > Abstract
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / abstract
text: Exposure to space radiation degrades substantially satellite systems, provoking severe partial or in some extreme cases, total failures. Electrostatic discharges (ESD), single event latch-up (SEL), and single event upsets (SEU) are among the most frequent causes of those reported satellite anomalies. The impact of space radiation dose on satellite equipment has been studied in-depth. This study conducts a statistical analysis to explore the relationships between Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) and Geostationary Orbit (GEO) satellite anomalies and particle concentrations, solar and geomagnetic activity in the period 2010-2022. Through a monthly and daily timescale analysis, the present work explores the temporal response of space disturbances on satellite systems and the periods when satellite are vulnerable to those disturbances.

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > Abstract
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / abstract
text: Keywords Satellite Anomalies, Space Radiation, Solar Activity, Geomagnetic Disturbances.

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.1 Introduction
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 1 introduction
text: Besides the technical specifications and the fulfillment of functional capabilities of electronic components, their durability, and resilience in space conditions are a major concern for the space industry. Over time, substantial evidence has been accumulated relating an important amount of satellite anomalies to space environment conditions. For example, in Telastra database [1], which lists over 1500 anomalies primarily associated with GEO satellites, sample reported failures suspected to be related to radiation effects are TDRS-1 in 1983, TDF-1 in 1989, Telecom 2A in 1994, and Thaicom-5 in 2011. More satellite failures associated to space weather have been reported on several studies such as [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Thus, understanding the space environment's effects is essential to advance towards more robust designs and operational strategies [8, 9].

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.1 Introduction
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 1 introduction
text: In this regard, several studies, mostly based on statistical analysis and primarily focused on GEO anomalies [10,11], have been carried out to figure out the temporal response of space disturbances on satellite equipment, the most susceptible periods by which the anomaly rate increases, and the effects of the different radiation particles upon several systems. For instance, [12] analyzed 95 commercial satellite anomalies in 1997-2009, obtaining a strong correlation between anomaly rate and geomagnetic activity, and interesting seasonal variations in the occurrence of GEO anomalies. Similarly, [13] investigated potential statistical correlations between electron/proton flux data and GEO satellite anomalies for the period 1986-1994, showing the susceptibility of GEO satellites to solar protons during solar maximum activity, and relativistic electrons during the minimum activity. However, the majority of research, including the aforementioned studies, consider only GEO anomalies in their analysis, which restricts our understanding to high orbits only. In

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.1 Introduction
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 1 introduction
text: addition, according to authors' knowledge, no similar analysis has been performed for anomalies that occurred in the last years, to evaluate the effectiveness and evolution of Radiation Hardened (RadHard) components. Furthermore, considering the "New Space Era" from 2013, onwards and the revolution towards small satellites (e.g. CubeSats) [14], it is critical to understand how the minimization of satellite mechanical structure and electronic components mitigates radiation exposure [15, 16]. In that regard, this study presents a statistical analysis that compares reported anomalies of LEO ( $ \leqslant $ 1000 kg) and GEO satellites ( $ \leqslant $ 5000 kg) spanning the period from 2010 to 2022 with four variables: sunspots (SS), coronal mass ejections (CME), Kp-index, and the Disturbance Storm-Time (DST). Moreover, it investigates the connection between satellite anomalies and the flux of protons, electrons, and X-ray particles. In particular, this study aims to: 1) understand the temporal response of space weather disturbances and satellite anomalies occurrence, 2) ascertain how solar and geomagnetic storms affect satellites based on their orbit, thus, LEO and GEO anomalies are analyzed separately, 3) identify susceptible periods of time when the anomaly rate fluctuates significantly, 4) determine the most suitable timescale to evaluate anomalies and space weather depending on the orbit and disturbance indicator, and 5) examine the effects on satellite systems that increasing fluxes of particles have.

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.1 Introduction
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 1 introduction
text: This manuscript is organized as follows: space radiation characteristics and their potential impact on spacecraft systems are briefly introduced in Section 4.2. Section 4.3 describes the anomalies database, the space radiation indicators used, and the methodology followed to carry out the analysis. Section 4.4 presents the results of the statistical analysis, while in Section 4.5 the results are discussed and summarized.

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.2 Space Weather Effects on Satellite Systems
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 2 space weather effects on satellite systems
text: Space weather phenomena and their related particle properties can affect different satellite systems. The primary sources of radiation in Earth's satellite orbits proceed from solar event particles (SPE particles), galactic cosmic rays (GCR), and auroral particles (mostly low-energy electrons) [17]. High-energy charged particles known as GCRs originate outside the solar system and are composed of protons, electrons, and heavy ions. GCRs and solar activity have a negative correlation, which means that, when solar activity is at its lowest and the Sun's magnetic field is weaker, more GCRs enter into the inner solar system [18]. As for solar radiation, SPEs occur when charged particles in the Sun's atmosphere are accelerated at very high velocities, escaping to the interplanetary space [19, 20]. In case those particles have enough energy to penetrate the Earth's magnetic field, they reach the Earth's magnetosphere and ionosphere surrounding mainly, the North and South poles. SPEs have a mean composition of 96.4% protons, 3.5% alpha particles, and 0.1% heavier ions [21], where the peak flow of particles with energies above 10 MeV per nucleon can surpass $ 1 0^{5} \mathrm{c m}^{-2} s^{-1} $ [22].

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.2 Space Weather Effects on Satellite Systems
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 2 space weather effects on satellite systems
text: The radiation intensity that a satellite may encounter during its lifetime depends significantly on its orbit attitude and inclination [23]. For example, orbits with low altitudes are often attained by less radiation flow due to the shielding effects of Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere thus, providing better safety for LEO satellites [23, 24, 25]. However in LEO, satellites that, for example, orbit across the inner Van Allen belt, where the Earth's magnetic field traps the high-energy protons, will still be substantially exposed to high dosages [26, 27, 28]. In addition, the radiation in orbit also varies depending on the temporal fluctuations of several space phenomena such as the regular solar cycles, sporadic solar flares, solar wind, and geomagnetic storms. Hence, the satellite subsystems may experience a variety of effects and disruptions based on the particles' characteristics (e.g. typology, energy levels) derived from those space weather events (see Fig. 4.1) [29, 30]. The main radiation effects on satellite systems as well as those particles causing them can be summarized in the following points:

text: Although satellites are conceived to operate in the space environment, some of those particles can interact with the satellites' surfaces, and damage the electronics, creating a serious damage to the system [32, 33]. Within this context, numerous subsystems and equipment in the satellite are significantly vulnerable to radiation effects [33]. For instance, solar arrays are susceptible to ultraviolet (UV) radiation, polymers are vulnerable to high-energy photons [34], and high-energy electrons may provoke severe electrical discharges. In addition, high-energy protons and ions can substantially affect sensitive electronic components by changing bits (SEU) and disabling device capabilities (Single event Latchup or Burnout, SEL or SEB, respectively) [35, 36, 37].

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.3.2 Space Radiation Indicators
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 3 2 space radiation indicators
text: On one hand, the Sun does provide most of the particle flow reaching the Earth. However, its low magnetic field during minimal sunspot number facilitates GCRs' access to the solar system. On the other hand, Earth's magnetic field is crucial to shield or trap radiation particles that can affect satellite missions. Thus, the solar cycle and geomagnetic activity play a fundamental role in the Earth's orbit radiation density and appear to be the most convenient radiation and perturbation indicators. In this regard, and following previous research, [6, 12, 42, 43], the sunspots number, CMEs linear velocity, the Kp-index, and the DST have been considered in this analysis.

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.3.2 Space Radiation Indicators
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 3 2 space radiation indicators
text: Sunspots are regions on the Sun's surface cooler than others, where the magnetic fields are so extremely strong that they keep some of the heat within the Sun from reaching the surface. The magnetic field lines near sunspots often tangle and cross, causing energy explosions and releasing a lot of radiation into space. Those explosions, also known as solar flares, are sometimes accompanied by huge bubbles of radiation and particles from the Sun that explode into space at very high speeds when the Sun's magnetic field lines suddenly reorganize [44]. Thus, sunspots are closely linked to solar activity, resulting in an important indicator to identify and interpret satellite anomalies. Sunspot data has been obtained from the Royal Observatory of Belgium website [45, 46], which provides daily sunspot activity from January 1, 1818 onwards.

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.3.2 Space Radiation Indicators
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 3 2 space radiation indicators
text: CMEs consist of the expulsion of a vast amount of plasma from the solar corona into space at speeds reaching hundreds of kilometers per second. Primarily composed of electrons and protons, these ejections also contain traces of helium, oxygen, and iron in ion form [47]. This wave of radiation and solar wind, when detached from the Sun, poses a significant risk when directed towards Earth [48]. If its magnetic field is oriented southward, it could cause significant damage to electrical circuits, transformers, and communication systems,

section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 3 2 space radiation indicators
text: as well as affect the Earth's magnetic field for a period [49]. Each CME is characterized by parameters such as the date and time of its appearance in the field of view (FOV) of the LASCO/C2 telescope and the central position angle (CPA), the latter being crucial for distinguishing between multiple simultaneous CMEs. CMEs with an apparent width of 360 degrees are marked as Halo and can be symmetric (S) or asymmetric, with brightness asymmetry (BA) or outline asymmetry (OA). Additionally, they are defined by three speeds: linear, quadratic evaluated at the time of the last measurement, and quadratic at 20 solar radii, as well as by their acceleration, which can be positive, negative, or close to zero. The mass of a CME, taken as representative when it reaches a quasi-constant value after increasing in the first few solar radii, along with the linear speed, allows for the calculation of its kinetic energy [50]. But, given that the linear velocity parameter CMEs refers to the speed at which material ejected from the Sun moves into space, this study used this parameter as a relevant comparison metric to determine the speed at which this material moves in a straight line away from the Sun. This is an essential element because it can alter how CMEs interact with the Earth's magnetosphere, thereby influencing space weather. Thus, CMEs linear velocities data during the study period were extracted from the NASA SOHO LASCO CME Catalog, Version 2 [50]. This catalog categorizes all daily CME records collected by the ESA/NASA SOHO satellite, dedicated to solar observation. The main instrument used, called LASCO, enables the observation of the solar corona [51]. The methodology adopted in the analysis was to select the record with the highest linear speed [km/s] for each day between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2022, when multiple data points were available on the same day.

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.3.2 Space Radiation Indicators
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 3 2 space radiation indicators
text: Regarding the geomagnetic activity, two variables have been used. The first one, the K-index, also known as the planetary K-index, is an indicator that quantifies the disturbances in the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field with an integer between 0 and 9, with 1 indicating low magnetic activity and 5 or more indicating a geomagnetic storm [11, 52]. The Kp-index, which is updated every three hours, is calculated by averaging the K-indices from a network of thirteen geomagnetic observatories located in mid-latitude regions. As sunspots data, the Kp-index has been acquired from the Royal Observatory of Belgium website [45] [46], covering daily Kp-Index information from January 1, 2009 onwards. As for the second indicator, unlike the Kp-index which offers general information about the geomagnetic activity, the DST assesses disturbances in the Earth's magnetic field induced by geomagnetic storms [53]. A higher negative value of the DST index indicates more severe geomagnetic disruptions [54]. This could be due to increased solar activity, such as solar flares or CME, which produce stronger solar winds, and hence cause greater disruption in the Earth's magnetic field [55]. Whereas the Kp-index provides a comprehensive assessment of geomagnetic activity on Earth, the DST differs by especially targeting disturbances induced by geomagnetic storms. DST data has been obtained from the Geomagnetic Equatorial DST index Home Page, providing information dating back to 1953 [56].

section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.3.2 Space Radiation Indicators
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 3 2 space radiation indicators
text: As mentioned before, the solar corona is primarily composed of plasma, an atmosphere of ionized gas that is not static and can even detach from the star [57]. This movement of the corona is known as solar wind, a stream of charged particles released from the Sun's upper atmosphere. This plasma consists mainly of electrons, protons, and alpha particles, with thermal energies ranging from 1.5 to 10 eV [58]. To assess the risk that particle fluxes pose to Earth, especially in a satellite environment, this study also assesses the effects that several particle fluxes such as proton, electron, and X-rays can have upon satellite equipment. The corresponding data was extracted from weekly reports in the historical repository of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Space Weather Prediction Center (NOAA), provided by the GOES-14 and GOES-15 satellites from January 1, 2010, to December 31, 2022 [59, 60]. For the analysis, protons with energy larger than 10 MeV (proton Fluence - protons/cm $ ^{2} $ -day-steradian) and electrons with energies of more than 2 MeV (Electron Fluence - electrons/cm $ ^{2} $ -day-steradian) were considered. For the X-ray analysis, the weekly report from NOAA was also utilized, specifically the section on Daily Solar Data: X-ray Background Flux, identified by a letter indicating the level of solar activity. During periods of low solar activity, such as during solar minimum, the X-ray background flux falls within the A (between $ 10^{-8} $ and $ 10^{-7} $ protons/m $ ^{2} $ ) or B (between $ 10^{-7} $ and $ 10^{-6} $ protons/m $ ^{2} $ ) range. During periods of increased activity, the background rises to approximately level C (between $ 10^{-6} $ and $ 10^{-5} $ protons/m $ ^{2} $ ). Within these ranges, a numerical value is used to specify the flux measured in watts per square meter [61].

This is consistent considering that after an injection of charged particles, they can remain on satellite orbits afterward. Hence, the effects of this radiation on satellite equipment may be not necessarily when the space weather indicators reach their peak, and failures may occur in the upcoming days, weeks, or months. section: Statistical Relationship Analysis Between LEO and GEO Satellite Anomalies and Space Radiation > 4.4.3 Orbit Inclination's Impact on Anomaly Rate
section_key: statistical relationship analysis between leo and geo satellite anomalies and space radiation / 4 4 3 orbit inclination s impact on anomaly rate
text: The Earth's magnetic field traps protons and electrons, resulting in radiation belts known as Van Allen belts. Thus, as mentioned before, the radiation density that satellites must cross during their course is significantly influenced by their orbital altitude and inclination. As for orbit altitude, by which the analysis has been simplified by categorizing LEO and GEO satellites, each satellite whose reported anomalies have been considered in this study has had its orbital inclination classified as seen in Fig. 4.9. Regarding LEO, those active satellites whose orbital inclination $ (\theta) $ were within $ 15^{\circ}-30^{\circ} $ and $ 45^{\circ}-60^{\circ} $ ranges presented slightly higher anomaly rate percentages than other ranges such as $ 0^{\circ}-15^{\circ} $ and $ 75^{\circ}-90^{\circ} $ , whereas active satellites orbiting between $ 60^{\circ}-75^{\circ} $ range presented the higher anomaly rate (22.5%) . Unlike the unexpectedly high failure rate presented in the $ 15^{\circ}-30^{\circ} $ range, the rates at $ 45^{\circ}-60^{\circ} $ and $ 60^{\circ}-75^{\circ} $ are highly consistent considering that higher electron concentrations are observed between $ 45^{\circ} $ and $ 85^{\circ} $ while for low inclination orbits $ (\theta\leqslant 30^{\circ}) $ the electron concentrations are relatively low [66]. The high anomaly rate of those satellites whose inclination ranges between $ 45^{\circ} $ and $ 60^{\circ} $ can also be directly linked with the several passes per day through the SAA, situated at 200-800 km over the Earth's surface [67]. Furthermore, as indicated in Fig 4.9, polar and near-polar orbits $ (90^{\circ}\leqslant\theta<105^{\circ}) $ also present moderately high anomaly rates, which is consistent considering that polar-orbiting satellites pass through dangerous charged particle concentrations (e.g. electrons of energy about 1 MeV) several times per day [68]. In addition, with the open magnetic field lines over the poles, polar-orbiting satellites are exposed directly to large solar proton fluxes and lower energy GCRs [69]. text: Taking into consideration the historical study of satellite evolution, which has revealed potential disruptive uses in recent years, the possibility of recycling satellites currently in orbit was subsequently evaluated through studies of causes and failures. In this third part of the Ph.D. thesis, a study is presented on how satellites can be manufactured from their initial stages with the new concept of making them more efficient and reusable, by applying agile methodologies in their development and manufacturing of systems and subsystems. text: The mission is strategically aimed at advancing scientific knowledge through innovative research endeavors, serving as a testing ground for pioneering observations of the ionosphere. Moreover, $ ^{3} $ Cat-8 is not only restricted to educational and scientific goals, but it also serves as a technological demonstration mission. The facet of the mission involves the testing and validation of various critical technologies essential for future space endeavors. From a deployable antenna systems, telemetry systems, the mission explores a wide array of cutting-edge technologies. Furthermore, it delves into evolved techniques in satellite systems, with a particular emphasis on harnessing LoRa for inter-satellite communications [24]. In doing so, $ ^{3} $ Cat-8 contributes significantly to the ongoing advancement of space technology.

section: Preliminary Design of Satellite Systems Through the Integration of Model-Based System Engineering and Agile Methodologies: Application to the $ ^{3} $ColStar Mission > Abstract
section_key: preliminary design of satellite systems through the integration of model based system engineering and agile methodologies application to the 3 colstar mission / abstract
text: This chapter presents a case study on the integration of Agile Systems Engineering methodologies in the preliminary design phase of satellite systems, focusing on the $ ^{3} $ColStar satellite mission. Through Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), technical consistency was rigorously managed across various architectural documents, ensuring coherency and minimizing errors. Furthermore, the preliminary design was developed, with the implementation of the Arcadia Method, supported by the Capella modelling tool. This allowed the digitalization of the system, which was represented by models that contain requirements, architecture, and interfaces between the different parts of the system. At the same time, the preliminary design process was streamlined and completed within an accelerated time frame of 4 months, with weekly sprints driving progress based on the scrum methodology. This case study highlights the effectiveness of Agile Systems Engineering principles to improve the team communication accuracy, communication, and efficiency of satellite systems preliminary design, providing valuable insights for future missions.

section_key: preliminary design of satellite systems through the integration of model based system engineering and agile methodologies application to the 3 colstar mission / 6 1 introduction
text: In the last decades, the field of small satellite engineering has undergone a transformative evolution, reshaping space science, communications, Earth observation, and education. This revolution has been facilitated by the widespread availability and miniaturization of low-cost electronics, coupled with increased launch opportunities [1]. What was once solely the domain of governments and large organizations has now been democratized, with small companies, universities, and even low- and middle-income countries actively participating in satellite development [2]. Despite this progress, many satellite missions continue to face challenges, including delays, budget overruns, and sub-optimal performance. In particular, university CubeSat teams, struggle with issues such as high turnover rates, knowledge management, and balancing academic coursework with project responsibilities [3,4].

The initiative was established in 2007 to realize the MBSE Vision of the "future of systems engineering is model based" to scale systems engineering by replacing document-oriented practices with models (see Fig 6.1). section: Preliminary Design of Satellite Systems Through the Integration of Model-Based System Engineering and Agile Methodologies: Application to the $ ^{3} $ColStar Mission > 6.1 Introduction
section_key: preliminary design of satellite systems through the integration of model based system engineering and agile methodologies application to the 3 colstar mission / 6 1 introduction
text: This chapter explores how an integrated approach to Agile Systems Engineering and Project Management can address the unique challenges faced by small satellite engineering teams. For instance, firstly, these missions operate in dynamic contexts where it is crucial to adhere to "frozen specifications". This ensures stability and consistency despite the quickly changing requirements due to technical breakthroughs, evolving user needs, and shifting scientific goals. Agile techniques enable adaptation to these changes through iterative development cycles and constant stakeholder interaction [26]. Additionally, small satellite projects are often limited in terms of funding, personnel resources, and timescale. Iterative planning, frequent deliverables, and prioritization are examples of agile approaches that help to improve resource allocation and maximize efficiency in managing limited resources [27, 28]. Furthermore, the complexity of integrating multiple subsystems in small satellites while maintaining compatibility, functionality, and reliability presents considerable technical obstacles. Agile Systems Engineering stresses incremental integration and continuous testing, therefore decreasing the risks involved with subsystem integration [29]. Moreover, many small satellite projects require geographically scattered teams from several locations, countries, and time zones. Agile techniques encourage good communication, collaboration technologies, and remote work practices to guarantee smooth coordination and alignment among distributed teams [30, 31]. The literature supports the efficacy of Agile Systems Engineering and Project Management in tackling these issues. Agile approaches improve flexibility, responsiveness, and adaptation in engineering projects, particularly in the aerospace and satellite sectors [32, 33]. Teams can reduce risks, expedite development timeframes, and improve overall project outcomes by implementing agile principles tailored to the unique needs of tiny satellite missions.

section: Preliminary Design of Satellite Systems Through the Integration of Model-Based System Engineering and Agile Methodologies: Application to the $ ^{3} $ColStar Mission > 6.2 The $ ^{3} $ColStar Satellite Mission
section_key: preliminary design of satellite systems through the integration of model based system engineering and agile methodologies application to the 3 colstar mission / 6 2 the 3 colstar satellite mission
text: The " $ ^{3} $ ColStar KiboCUBE Colombia" CubeSat (1U) mission emerged from the ambitious initiative to design a satellite manufactured up to 70% in Colombia. The $ ^{3} $ ColStar mission aims to produce reliable solar weather data through its primary payload and demonstrate the functionality of an IoT payload in space. This mission stands out in the literature for its unique dual-focus on solar weather monitoring and IoT integration on a small satellite platform. In contrast, existing missions in the literature often prioritize either scientific data collection or technical demonstration, rarely addressing both simultaneously. The dual-purpose approach of $ ^{3} $ ColStar offers distinct advantages by leveraging satellite resources for a diverse range of scientific and technological objectives. One of the primary scientific objectives is the study and analysis of space weather phenomena. Space weather refers to the environmental conditions in space as influenced by the Sun and the solar wind. These phenomena, including solar flares and cosmic rays, can have significant effects on satellite operations, GPS systems, and even terrestrial power grids. In Colombia, studying space weather is particularly crucial due to the country's geographical location near the equator. This region is more susceptible to variations in the Earth's magnetic field, which can affect communication and navigation systems. By advancing our understanding of space weather, the $ ^{3} $ ColStar mission aims to improve the resilience and reliability of these critical systems in Colombia and similar regions [38]. Furthermore, the $ ^{3} $ ColStar mission includes a secondary IoT payload aimed at providing internet access to remote areas where connectivity is scarce. This objective is critical for enhancing internet usage across the majority of regions in Colombia, promoting digital inclusion, and supporting the socio-economic development of underserved communities. Additionally, the mission seeks to develop and integrate locally manufactured space components and subsystems, such as the structure, EPS (Electrical Power System), OBC (On-Board Computer), ADCS (Attitude Determination and Control System), and electronics. These advancements not only contribute to scientific knowledge but also foster technological innovation and collaboration among Colombian academia, industry, and government.

text: Equipped with two payloads, this CubeSat will contribute to scientific and technological advancements. Its primary payload features the MiniPIX TPX3 SPACE [44] sensor device, featuring a compact radiation camera tailored specifically for space missions. Designed to fit in the CubeSat 1U platform, this device enables advanced particle tracking with minimal power consumption and weight. Its capabilities are crucial to monitor particles generated by solar storms and mitigate potential damage to critical infrastructure, such as power lines, internet networks, and satellites [44]. Provided by ADVACAM, the device ensures precise particle characterization and real-time analysis, thus enhancing the scientific objectives of the mission [43].

section: Preliminary Design of Satellite Systems Through the Integration of Model-Based System Engineering and Agile Methodologies: Application to the $ ^{3} $ColStar Mission > 6.2.2 $ ^{3} $ColStar Main Requirements
section_key: preliminary design of satellite systems through the integration of model based system engineering and agile methodologies application to the 3 colstar mission / 6 2 2 3 colstar main requirements
text: The $ ^{3} $ColStar mission criteria were designed to outline both the overarching needs and specific requirements that must be fulfilled for the mission to be successful. Needs refer to the broad, high-level objectives that the mission aims to achieve, such as advancing scientific research, fostering technological innovation, and creating social impact. Requirements, on the other hand, are the detailed, quantifiable conditions and specifications derived from these needs, which guide the design, development, operation, and evaluation of the satellite. For instance, one of the needs is to enhance Colombia's expertise in space technology. Corresponding requirements include the development and integration of locally manufactured space components and subsystems, such as the structure, EPS, OBC, ADCS, and electronics. Another need is to foster collaboration among academia, industry, and government. The requirements to meet this need involve involving 13 institutions and ensuring effective communication and collaboration among stakeholders through regular meetings, shared documentation, and coordinated project timelines. Additionally, the need to provide educational and social benefits is translated into requirements like deploying IoT connection points in remote areas and engaging with schools to use mission results for educational purposes. By clearly defining these needs and translating them into specific, measurable requirements, the $ ^{3} $ColStar mission ensures that every aspect of the mission is aligned with its high-level objectives and can be systematically designed, developed, and evaluated for success. The most relevant requirements are described in Table 10.5 (Appendix 10.4.1).

section: Preliminary Design of Satellite Systems Through the Integration of Model-Based System Engineering and Agile Methodologies: Application to the $ ^{3} $ColStar Mission > 6.2.3 Preliminary Design
section_key: preliminary design of satellite systems through the integration of model based system engineering and agile methodologies application to the 3 colstar mission / 6 2 3 preliminary design
text: The preliminary design process for each subsystem of the satellite platform followed a systematic approach aligned with mission requirements. This method ensured that each subsystem was designed to meet specific functional and performance criteria outlined in the mission objectives. While actual manufacturing of all subsystems has not yet commenced, rigorous design activities were undertaken to establish the foundation for future development and integration. This included an integrated yet individually focused subsystem design approach, fostering collaboration among subsystems. Additionally, weekly meetings were held with all subsystem teams to address cross-functional issues and ensure cohesive problem-solving across all parts involved. Regarding the comparison with concurrent methodologies, the approach chosen for the preliminary design phase prioritized sequential development to ensure thorough validation and alignment with mission specifications. This decision aimed to facilitate detailed analysis and verification of each subsystem's functionality before advancing to the next phase. While concurrent methodologies may offer advantages in terms of parallel development and accelerated integration, the selected approach was deemed suitable for ensuring comprehensive validation and minimizing risks associated with subsystem interaction and

text: performance. Additionally, the design activities were monitored and controlled by MBSE, providing detailed development information for each subsystem. System Engineering control was made easier throughout the design phase thanks to good documentation and configuration management procedures. Progress on each subsystem's design was constantly documented and updated, ensuring that all stakeholders had access to the most recent information via a common online repository. This method reduces the risks associated with potential discrepancies and promotes efficient integration efforts once subsystem manufacturing and assembly begin.

section: Preliminary Design of Satellite Systems Through the Integration of Model-Based System Engineering and Agile Methodologies: Application to the $ ^{3} $ColStar Mission > 6.2.3.2 Thermal Subsystem
section_key: preliminary design of satellite systems through the integration of model based system engineering and agile methodologies application to the 3 colstar mission / 6 2 3 2 thermal subsystem
text: The thermal design of a satellite is crucial for ensuring the health and longevity of a spacecraft in Earth's orbit. The objectives of the Thermal Subsystem are to analyze the thermal space environment specific to the CubeSat's orbit and identify potential thermal challenges, and to establish survivability and operational temperature limits for every component of the CubeSat [56]. This approach ensures that the CubeSat can withstand the extreme temperature fluctuations experienced in space and maintain optimal operating conditions for its components. In order to conduct a preliminary analysis of the thermal subsystem, a thermal model was developed using the lumped parameter method. This model employed a MATLAB algorithm to estimate radiative heat loads, including solar, terrestrial infrared and albedo radiation. This approach considers the entire satellite as a lumped, isothermal system (represented by a single node) with an effective mass and heat capacity. The equations can be found in Appendix 10.4.3 (Eqns. 10.1 and 10.2).

text: The OBC's ability to withstand single-particle inversions and other radiation-induced flaws is crucial. It uses error detection and correction (EDAC) techniques like as memory scrubbing and parity checks, as well as hardware solutions like Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR) and watchdog timers [67]. Backup systems or components provide redundancy, while radiation-hardened parts lessen the likelihood of errors. These safeguards are complemented by software mitigation strategies such as checkpointing and rollback, as well as voting algorithms. Real-time error correction algorithms and hardware are used, and automatic system reconfiguration switches to backup systems or alternate modes when problems are discovered. These solutions ensure that the OBC can successfully regulate and reduce the effects of single-particle inversions, allowing satellites to operate reliably in the hostile space environment [68].

text: The ADCS module seeks is in charge of the attitude and orientation control for the CubeSat, hence meeting a variety of operational requirements. These consist of spinning control to reduce orbital disturbances, pointing control for efficient communication with the IoT payload, and detumbling control to manage high rotational speeds after deployment. The performance of the ADCS is not heavily taxed by the space weather sensor, but the IoT payload requires accurate pointing control in order to communicate. The main goal of environment survival is energy production, which calls for deployable solar panels that need pointing control. However, because of the CubeSat's small size, there are few issues about gravity gradient torque or solar pressure. Figure. 6.8(a) shows the centralized architecture, where OBC is in charge of ADCS execution. Fig. 6.8(b) presents the distributed architecture, where a spacialized controller will be in charge of the ADCS execution, both MCU or FPGA technologic choises will be considered.

text: The ADVACAM detector [44] will be used for monitoring cosmic weather. This technology provides timely warnings against increased solar activity, which can pose risks to the health of astronauts and disrupt the functionality of sensitive onboard electronics in satellites and spacecraft. The MiniPIX TPX3 SPACE particle [44] counting camera builds upon technology originally developed for basic particle physics research at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN. This lightweight device, weighing just a few tens of grams, can distinguish the type of each individual particle, as well as its energy and direction.

text: Several methods have been proposed for the design of CubeSats. Probably the most well known are systems engineering and Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE). Before detailing our specific methodology, this section presents a brief overview of existing methods that have served as inspiration for the $ ^{3} $ColStar KiboCUBE Agile Methodology Implementation such as the V-Model and Digital Engineering. Subsequently, we delve into the Arcadia Method and Capella modeling tool, emphasizing their role in our approach.

text: For the last mentioned part, we will delineate the systems engineering design processes utilized for the mission. This includes elements discussed in previous chapters, such as a thorough definition of stakeholder needs and technical requirements (Section 6.2), crucial for guiding the satellite's development. The logical decomposition of the system will be clearly articulated, elucidating how the satellite's subsystems were identified and structured to align with mission objectives. Furthermore, we will present the design solutions adopted for each subsystem, demonstrating how they were derived from the requirements and integrated into the overall satellite architecture. These aspects will be explored within the framework of Capella and Arcadia methodologies, ensuring a systematic and comprehensive examination of the satellite's preliminary design phase.

Given the multi-disciplinary nature of space assets planning, design, implementation and operation, systems engineering is a holistic and integrative discipline aimed at balancing different professional efforts to produce a coherent system [80]. section: Preliminary Design of Satellite Systems Through the Integration of Model-Based System Engineering and Agile Methodologies: Application to the $ ^{3} $ColStar Mission > 6.3.1.2 The V-Model.
section_key: preliminary design of satellite systems through the integration of model based system engineering and agile methodologies application to the 3 colstar mission / 6 3 1 2 the v model
text: The systems engineering "V" model, a.k.a., the V-model, has been widely used in the aerospace and defense industries [81]. It is called V-model because the activities are presented by using a "V" letter metaphor. The left part of the "V" is for the specification activities that go from high level specifications and designs to more detailed and granular ones; there there are the implementation tasks (represented by the foundation of the "V" letter base); and finally the are the testing activities represented by the right part of the "V" letter, that go from more granular tests (e.g., unit level tests) to high level ones (e.g., acceptance tests). The V-model is a systems development process with a heavy a-priori specification and design stage (similarly to the NASA systems engineering); it is also known as the validation-and-verification model.

text: It is a cross-disciplinary field that takes advantage of digital tool and processes for the design, development and production of engineering products across the project lifecycle [2]. The main purpose of digital engineering is to improve the efficiency and accuracy of the engineering process, along with reduced project risk. Digital engineering is conceived under the perspective that systems engineering needs to evolve based on current situations such as: (i) systems are becoming increasingly complicated and interconnected; (ii) resources reduction in projects; (iii) project complexity is increasing; (iv) some current practices are not sustainable.

text: Therefore, digital engineering aims at effectively managing complexity, reduce cost and schedule, and improve productivity via the integration of processes, digital tools and techniques within the systems development life-cycle [2].

section: Preliminary Design of Satellite Systems Through the Integration of Model-Based System Engineering and Agile Methodologies: Application to the $ ^{3} $ColStar Mission > 6.3.1.4 Model Based Systems Engineering
section_key: preliminary design of satellite systems through the integration of model based system engineering and agile methodologies application to the 3 colstar mission / 6 3 1 4 model based systems engineering
text: MBSE is an approach that uses digital models of the system and its engineering aspects as the main way to share and manage information, feedback, and requirements, instead of relying on documents. It covers the whole process of creating, communicating, and ensuring that all the digital models that describe a system are consistent from the conceptual design phase through the later phases of the life cycle, such as the requirements definition, design, analysis, and verification and validation activities [82]. MBSE is based on modeling languages and methods such as the Systems Modeling Language (SysML) [83], which is used in tools like Cameo Systems modeler [84], MagicDraw [85, 86] or the Arcadia method [11], used in Capella [87]. MBSE allows to represent and communicate the structural, functional and dynamic aspects of a complex system and aims to improve the efficiency, quality and traceability of the systems engineering process, as well as to facilitate collaboration between the different actors involved [88].

text: Arcadia enables a thorough modeling of complex systems in the Architecture Engineering context, across multiple levels of abstraction. It is founded on a hierarchical framework that first defines the problem space at the top level, and later defines proposed solutions that traverse the system's various elements. It is bolstered by a viewpoint-centric approach that underscores the need to integrate the many views that are vital to the system's design. It is further reinforced by its support for a thorough trade-off analysis that allows decisions at all levels of architectural design [11, 87, 89].

text: Concerning, the implementation and testing stages of the $ ^{3} $ColStar project, the development team will adopt a Scrum-inspired methodology, tailored to suit their specific needs. This approach, depicted in Figure 6.16(a), differed slightly from the original Scrum framework. Sprints will be conducted on a weekly basis, with each team maintaining its own product backlog. Additionally, weekly scrum meetings will be held within each team to ensure effective communication and progress tracking. The framework is displayed in Figure 6.16(b) and two parallel processes are shown. In reality, each sub-team or subsystem will operate with its own independent backlog and follows a distinct scrum process, unlike the typical software development approach where there is a single backlog for the whole team. This, and the focus on MBSE, will allow us working in an Agile way and implementing changes quickly [97]. The independent operation of subsystem teams, each with its own backlog and distinct scrum process, is managed to ensure the consistency and benefits of the MBSE approach. In the $ ^{3} $ColStar mission, this is achieved through integration and coordination practices verified

text: Using MBSE allows for a systematic and integration of various technical, operational, and design aspects, resulting in a more comprehensive conception of the $ ^{3} $ ColStar mission. MBSE facilitated the early identification of key requirements, efficient risk management, and the optimization of system performance. Using MBSE allowed for a systematic and integration of various technical, operational, and design aspects, resulting in a more comprehensive conception of the $ ^{3} $ ColStar mission. Specifically, MBSE facilitated the early identification of key requirements, efficient risk management, and optimization of overall system performance. The application of the Capella tool and Arcadia method enabled us to ensure that all subsystem designs were integrated and traceable back to the mission's high-level requirements. Throughout the preliminary design phase, the use of a unified model helped maintain consistency across all subsystems. Changes in one subsystem's design were reflected in the overall model, allowing for continuous verification and validation of the system's coherence. This integration was further supported by weekly meetings and coordination practices that addressed cross-functional issues, ensuring alignment with the mission objectives and design requirements. Additionally, the integration of Capella revealed that we could avoid design rework, streamlining the process and completing this initial phase in a shorter timeframe than anticipated. MBSE systematically captured and managed stakeholder expectations and technical requirements, decomposing them into functional, logical, and physical architectures. This structured approach provided clear traceability from requirements to design solutions, ensuring that every aspect of the mission was meticulously planned and validated. By adopting

text: The application of the Arcadia method for the Preliminary Design of the $ ^{3} $ColStar mission enabled the completion of this process within a remarkable timeframe of just 4 months, facilitated by weekly general sprints. This timeframe compares favorably with the recommendations provided in the Space project management- Project planning and implementation (ECSS-M-ST-10C Rev. 1) [34], and NASA Procedural Requirements (NPR) [35], which suggest a duration of 1 to 6 months for similar processes. The utilization of this methodology in other 1U CubeSat missions has demonstrated improved conceptualization, enhanced communication between subsystems, and technical precision, thereby minimizing errors in mission development [106]. It is worth noting that having a framework process as Arcadia allowed each subsystem team to make progress individually and integrate each team result easily. In the case of the $ ^{3} $ColStar mission, our goal is to allow collaboration among different universities and organizations, particularly because each has different core competencies and resources, and the organizations do not have members with the same skills. Therefore, we assigned subsystems to universities/organizations based on their capabilities/skills/resources/knowledge. Thus, using Arcadia and MBSE allowed us to have a way to centralize the design decisions and progress.

text: Furthermore, the incorporation of Capella into our approach provided a means to achieve technical consistency through digitalized processes, aligning with the principles of agile methodology. The implementation of Capella facilitated the creation of a Shared system model with multiple views, connected to discipline models, thereby formalizing aspects of systems engineering through model-based systems engineering (MBSE). It is crucial to note that MBSE does not replace traditional systems engineering, but rather complements it with rigorous methods and tools, ensuring coherency within the model and managing technical consistency across various architectural documents.

text: In summary, in this paper we described our experience of integrating agile systems engineering principles, the Arcadia methodology, and the Capella tool in the preliminary design of the $ ^{3} $ColStar satellite mission. With the presented approach we were able to expedite the design process and enhance the accuracy, communication, and efficiency of mission development, setting a precedent for future CubeSat missions and beyond. It is worth noting that We did not conduct a comparative study of the presented approach versus a traditional one, because of the budget constraints and the burden that implies having two different teams working with different approaches. However, future work could be devoted to have more evidence regarding the implications of using agile methods for space systems engineering.

text: Based on the analysis conducted in the chapter 3 addressing satellite subsystems prone to failures, it was decided to undertake a detailed examination of the ADCS and Thermal subsystems. Concerning the ADCS subsystem specifically, a segment of this exploration will be outlined in the forthcoming chapter, which centers around an analysis of one of the satellite subsystems as observed during the $ ^{3} $Cat-8 mission. As a doctoral student, I had the privilege of participating in this mission. Collaborating with the entire ADCS team, our focus was on developing a linear magnetic attitude control algorithm customized for a six-unit CubeSat. This algorithm incorporated a low-thrust electrical propulsion system for orbital maneuvering, and we assessed its efficacy. This investigation not only highlights the importance and practicality of sustainable proposals by integrating a trusther for exploring novel activities in orbit for smallsats and optimizing a satellite's capabilities to extend its operational lifespan but also emphasizes their technical feasibility, a perspective enriched by practical involvement in satellite missions.

text: Several actuator options exist and have been studied, the most popular being the reaction wheels, magnetic torquers and reaction control thrusters [10]. These three types of actuators are significantly different from each other, each one having its own advantages and disadvantages. The actuators for a satellite must be selected according to the mission. The parameters that usually influence the selection are the physical dimensions of the spacecraft, the disturbances that it will encounter in orbit, the orbital altitude, the spacecraft's payload, and the pointing requirements. Other actuator options such as solar radiation pressure control panels and sails [11][12], moving masses [13] or aerodynamic control surfaces [14] can also be used, although they have only been tested as technology demonstrators or in larger missions, thus they are not considered in our case.

section: Novel Magnetic Attitude Control System for SmallSats with Low-Thrust Propulsion Systems > 7.3 Actuators modeling

text: From all the actuator options, the ones selected for the $ ^{3} $Cat-8 mission are magnetorquers, one per axis (total of three) and a reaction wheel aligned with the Z-axis not used in the TVP mode, but in the Sun pointing one (not described in this study). The selection of these actuators is based on volume considerations, as they can be fit in a small volume unlike reaction wheels, or thrusters. Moreover, they do not consume a lot of power, and they can actuate against continuous loads such as the thruster firing with an offset with respect to the satellite's center of mass. Looking into other actuator options, the reaction control thrusters are not suitable for the mission, since they are typically used in larger satellites, as they can create significantly larger torques than the magnetorquers or the reaction wheels.

text: The temporal extension of the simulations is 24 h., to avoid false positives that could appear for short simulation times, especially if they are of less than one orbit. Albeit in an uncontrolled case the spacecraft will usually become ungoverned in a short time span, with marginal control it can appear as stable during the first orbits or hours. Figure 7.5 shows the comparison between a controlled (Fig 7.5(a)), and an uncontrolled situation (Fig 7.5(b)). For the latter case, the TVP controller is capable of overcoming the disturbances, but after around 4 hours, stability is lost and the spacecraft is no longer pointing along the desired vector, with the controller unable to regain authority. Therefore we consider that in this case, the control system is not able to maintain the attitude. A minimum simulation time is required to avoid false positives and accurately assess the capability of the control system. Figure 7.5(a) shows a clearly controlled case, with the spacecraft correctly oriented throughout the whole simulation.

text: A series of simulations has been conducted for different thrust offset angles, magnetorquers' saturation, and thrust magnitude. For a given thrust and a set of combinations of offset angle and saturation, a region with control and a region without can be expected. The border between these regions is considered marginal control. It gives the absolute minimum saturation the magnetorquers will need to reach in order to be capable of controlling the spacecraft when the thrust has a certain offset angle. From this border, it is possible to define additional regions for different Control Margin of Safety (CMoS). This value refers to the additional control that the magnetorquers will have to counter perturbations, including the thrust-induced moment. At first glance, the system seems capable to control the spacecraft in TVP mode, and the spacecraft's attitude is as expected, with the vectorial components of the quaternion constant and equal to zero, and the scalar component at one, that is, the identity quaternion, as shown in Eqn. 7.19.

text: However, knowing that the thrust is on the order of $ 1 0^{-4} $ N, and that the induced torque is on the order of $ 1 0^{-6} $ N $ \cdot $ m, the actual disturbances and actuation torques must also be analyzed. Figure 7.6 shows both the disturbance torque $ \overrightarrow{D} $ , and the control torque $ \overrightarrow{L} $ . It can be seen that the control torque counteracts the effects of the disturbances generated by the thruster and the environment, applying a torque of equal magnitude and opposite sense. The thrust disturbance is an order of magnitude larger than the environmental disturbances, and it mainly affects the Y axis of the spacecraft, given the symmetries involved (very low misalignment of $ CoM_{y} $ ).

section: Novel Magnetic Attitude Control System for SmallSats with Low-Thrust Propulsion Systems > 7.5.1 TVP mode controller performance
section_key: novel magnetic attitude control system for smallsats with low thrust propulsion systems / 7 5 1 tvp mode controller performance
text: It is important to note that at most two magnetorquers are producing torque at any given moment. The share of actuation is determined by the control algorithm. Along the orbit, there are points where the Earth's magnetic field is aligned with the magnetorquer that is commanded to produce the required control torque, and in those cases, the spacecraft would be unable to control itself. However, it was found that these alignments occur twice per orbit, and were sufficiently short for the control system not to lose the required pointing. For larger disturbance torques, and lower saturation, the deviation from the desired attitude may be larger than the required one, and other means of control should be used instead, such as reaction wheels.

text: Finally, in addition to the pointing accuracy, it is important to assess the spacecraft's angular velocity. Figure 7.7 shows the small amplitude oscillations suffered by the satellite in TVP mode. An initial peak can be observed at the start of the simulation, which corresponds to the initial induced rate by the thruster. However, the magnitude of this peak is sufficiently low, and it is rapidly controlled, and reduced. Overall, the rate around the Y axis is the highest one, with peaks up to $ 2\cdot10^{-6} $ rad/s. It is, nevertheless, well within margins, and at the same order of magnitude as that of the other axes' rates.

Albeit the propulsion system has an already fixed thrust of 140 $ \mu\mathrm{N} $ , the precise location of the spacecraft's center of mass and the offset angle of the thruster have still some uncertainty. section_key: novel magnetic attitude control system for smallsats with low thrust propulsion systems / 7 6 conclusions
text: In this study the capabilities of a magnetic control for a 6U CubeSat with a thruster have been presented, including a thrust misalignment. The control was achieved solely by magnetic actuators. It has been shown that the satellite can maintain the desired orientation with sufficiently low angular rates, needed during the orbital raising maneuver.

section: Novel Magnetic Attitude Control System for SmallSats with Low-Thrust Propulsion Systems > 7.6 Conclusions
section_key: novel magnetic attitude control system for smallsats with low thrust propulsion systems / 7 6 conclusions
text: This study has defined a new configuration of control stability with linear attitude dynamics for a satellite with a thruster, based on a control algorithm using quaternion and angular velocity feedback. The structure ensures the management of the satellite's misalignment by the desired control towards the reference quaternion and therefore, it has the best attitude determination accuracy with a wide margin of security for the attitude control.

text: Building upon the comprehensive analysis initiated in Chapters 3 and 4, which explored satellite subsystems vulnerable to failures, and furthering the study of the preceding chapters aimed at enhancing manufacturing and design in new satellite missions, the following chapter specifically concentrates on Thermal Analysis throughout nanosatellite missions. The subsequent chapter presents the outcomes of the investigation carried out during the $ ^{3} $Cat-4 mission.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > Abstract
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / abstract
text: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 is the fourth member of the CubeSat series of UPC's NanoSat Lab, selected by the ESA Academy's Fly Your Satellite! program in 2017. This mission aims at demonstrating the capabilities of nano-satellites, and in particular those based in the 1-Unit CubeSat standard, for challenging Earth Observation (EO) using Global Navigation Satellite System - Reflectometry (GNSS-R) and L-band microwave radiometry, as well as for Automatic Identification Systems (AIS). The following study presents the results of the thermal analysis carried out for this mission, evaluating different scenarios, including the most critical cases at both high and low temperatures. The results consider different albedos and orbital parameters in order to establish the optimal temperatures to achieve the best mission performance within the nominal temperatures, and in all operational modes of the satellite. Simulation results are included considering the thermal performance of other materials, such as Kapton, as well as the redesign of the optical properties of the satellite's solar panels. The correlation with the thermal model and the TVAC test campaign was conducted at the ESA ESEC-GALAXIA facilities in Belgium.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.1 Introduction
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 1 introduction
text: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 (Fig. 8.1) [1] is the fourth mission of Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (UPC) NanoSat Lab's CubeSat series, and aims at demonstrating the capabilities of nano-satellites, particularly those adhering to the 1-Unit CubeSat standard, for some Earth Observation (EO) applications using Global Navigation Satellite System - Reflectometry (GNSS-R), L-band microwave radiometry, as well as Automatic Identification Systems (AIS).

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.1 Introduction
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 1 introduction
text: The mission has three key objectives. Firstly, it serves as an educational platform, involving graduate and undergraduate students who have actively contributed to the development, implementation, and validation of the subsystems, as well as conducting mission analysis and test campaigns. Secondly, it serves as a technology demonstration, featuring the Flexible Microwave Payload (FMPL-1), which integrates three EO instruments in a single one, and showcases the feasibility of the deployment of the payload antenna. Lastly, the mission facilitates scientific experiments, including assessing GNSS-R observables' sensitivity at different frequency bands, evaluating ionospheric corrections' impact, exploring GNSS-R applications for soil moisture and vegetation biomass inference, investigating RFI detection and mitigation techniques, and creating RFI maps. Accepted into the European Space Agency (ESA) Academy's "Fly Your Satellite!" program, the $ ^{3} $ Cat-4 mission represents an exciting opportunity for advancement in space education, training, research and technology development [1].

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.1 Introduction
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 1 introduction
text: CubeSat is the generic name for a type of nanosatellites, which in its elementary form (1U =1 unit) has the shape of a 10 cm side cube, which weighs less than 2 kg [2], and are typically constructed with commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) components making it possible to design and produce performance satellites at a low cost [3]. The original objective of the CubeSat standard was to enable university students to design, build, test, and operate an artificial satellite in space during their University studies [4], thanks to the simplification of the satellite structure and its interface with the deployer.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.2 Analysis assumptions
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 2 analysis assumptions
text: The $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis aims to verify that all the spacecraft components operate within their operational temperature range throughout all mission phases. To develop an accurate model, the following approach has been proposed. First, an isothermal solid cube was used as the base model. Subsequently, models incorporating thermal radiation as the primary mode of heat transfer were utilized to provide more precise results. Finally, models incorporating both conduction and radiation as the primary modes of heat transfer were employed to adequately characterize the spacecraft, and verify the thermal requirements of each component.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.2 Analysis assumptions
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 2 analysis assumptions
text: The main objective of the isothermal analyses is to identify a passive thermal control method that ensures the spacecraft's temperature remains within the desired range. An additional objective is to estimate the spacecraft's behavior in space conditions in order to gather information for the TVAC test. In this case, considering the limitations imposed by the manufacturer, the evaluated technique involves the use of various materials on the spacecraft's surface.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.2 Analysis assumptions
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 2 analysis assumptions
text: Regarding the radiation analysis, their objective is to validate the thermal model of the spacecraft. The analyses presented in this study demonstrate the completed development stage of the "radiation model" for $ ^{3} $Cat-4. These analyses have provided valuable insights into the current state of the model, and the performance has been verified under various heating conditions.

section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 3 1 1 external heating environment
text: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 satellite is expected to be launched aboard the maiden flight of the Ariane 6 launcher to achieve a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) [15]. Table 8.5 (right column) presents the orbital parameters for the most challenging external heating environment, as analyzed in this document (unless stated otherwise).

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.3.1.1 External Heating Environment
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 3 1 1 external heating environment
text: The beta angle of the orbit, which represents the angle between the orbiting object and the Sun, has been utilized to determine the hot and cold scenarios, indicating the effective solar incidence at each specific time. While the beta angle is generally assumed to be constant, it may experience slight variations throughout the year due to the solar analemma [16]. These variations can affect the duration or even the absence of shadows during an orbit. Consequently, orbits with the shortest or non-existent eclipses and those with the longest eclipse durations define the extreme conditions for the hottest and coldest scenarios.

text: The maximum and minimum solar flux values in this table correspond to the winter and summer solstices, respectively. In terms of Earth's albedo, the extreme values shown in the table represent the fraction of incident sunlight reflected by clouds (maximum albedo), and by an ocean or forest (minimum albedo). For Earth's infrared (IR) emitted radiation, the extreme cases consider the Earth as a black body at 260 K and 240 K for maximum and minimum values, respectively.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.3.1.1 External Heating Environment
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 3 1 1 external heating environment
text: The perigee height is also analyzed from a thermal perspective, and the most restrictive altitude of 650 km (adapted for the Ariane 6 launch) is considered. This choice was made in response to the consideration of envelope launchers and keeping other options open. The decision to retain the old altitude from the Vega rocket was intentional, as it provides a more conservative approach, ensuring that the thermal analysis encompasses a broader range of potential scenarios. Higher altitudes generally correspond to larger distances from the Earth, and cooler conditions, making this height the most limiting situation for this orbit.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.3.1.1 External Heating Environment
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 3 1 1 external heating environment
text: The duration of the eclipses can significantly impact the satellite's maximum and minimum temperatures during an orbit. For the orbit inclination presented in Table 8.5, the most extreme cases, specifically the shortest and longest eclipse times, have been considered. To determine these cases, the orbit beta angle $ (\beta) $ has been defined as the minimum angle between the orbit plane, and the solar vector. Lower $ \beta $ angles correspond to longer eclipses, resulting in colder conditions.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.3.1.1 External Heating Environment
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 3 1 1 external heating environment
text: The calculation procedure outlined in NMEA AIVDM message format [19], has been followed to obtain the expected orbit $ \beta $ angle during the launch year. For the cold case, the beta angle is $ 0^{\circ} $ , as the longest eclipse occurs when the orbit plane aligns with the Sun vector. Conversely, for the hot case, the shortest eclipse occurs when the $ \beta $ angle is closest to $ \pm 90^{\circ} $ , indicating no eclipse and maximal solar incidence. Applying the same procedure, the expected maximum beta angle is $ 85.5^{\circ} $

text: It should be noted that the values presented as extreme in Table 8.4 are unlikely to occur. These values are intended to encompass the hottest and coldest potential heating environments that the spacecraft may encounter. However, for the analysis the non-extreme parameters listed in the table were used, since they pose more realistic environments.

text: Other aspects were considered, such as the time step at which the orbit is divided. The orbital period is 5776 seconds, but it was not feasible to simulate every second. Therefore, various parameters needed to be adjusted to determine the time step for the orbit. Given that the simulation covered 7 complete orbits, a balance between resolution and optimal execution time was achieved.

After several weeks of testing optimal results were achieved with an error of less than 0.01% in just 30 minutes.

text: To verify that the added changes did not excessively deviate from the isometric cube analysis, the results of the previous and the current version were compared. The difference between the temperature values is taken as the reference. The same SSO orbit is used (for this case, the Sun Safe mode with 2.5 $ ^{\circ} $ /s in the Z axis of rotation was simulated). The considered criteria takes 10 $ ^{\circ} $ C as the maximum deviation in temperature for subsystems or components that have not been modified in the new model.
