section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.4.1 Heater Duty Cycle Trade-off Analysis Results

text: The heater is activated if it is required to maintain the battery temperature within an appropriate range. It consists of a resistor placed between the batteries that dissipates 2.9 W. The resistor was placed in contact with the batteries using epoxy adhesive. During the simulations, various hysteresis temperatures (i.e., the temperature difference between the start and end points of a thermal process or cycle) were considered.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.4.3 Final Simulation Results
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 4 3 final simulation results
text: The comprehensive simulations conducted to evaluate the spacecraft's operability under extreme thermal conditions have provided crucial insights, particularly regarding the EPS batteries. In the coldest scenarios, the batteries were found to be substantially below their minimum design temperature for charging, with a deviation of up to $ 2 6 \mathrm{~} ^ {\circ} \mathrm{C} $ from the design threshold. Conversely, in the hottest scenarios, temperatures exceeded the maximum design limit by $ 5.5 \mathrm{~} ^ {\circ} \mathrm{C} $ . To counter these extremes, the EPS heater needs to be operational across all scenarios, with its duty cycle varying between 6 to $ 30 \% $ , influenced by the satellite mode and rotation (see Table 10.9).

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.4.3 Final Simulation Results
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 4 3 final simulation results
text: The NADS system sheath case, another component under scrutiny, is expected to operate below its designated temperature range. Remarkably, it showed no material degradation even at -100 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ , validating its use in such extreme conditions.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.4.3 Final Simulation Results
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 4 3 final simulation results
text: In scenarios involving the satellite in stowed and detumbling configurations, lower temperatures are anticipated due to reduced power dissipation and diminished solar flux exposure. These colder conditions are manageable by slightly increasing the heater's duty cycles, approximately by 10%. Since these configurations are transient, lasting a few days at most, emphasis should be placed on adjustments for the nominal modes.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.4.3 Final Simulation Results
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 4 3 final simulation results
text: Regarding the hot case scenarios, the thermal management strategy has been effective, requiring no significant additional actions. The strategic application of gold paint on most satellite surfaces and white AZ-2000-IECW paint on the +X/-X faces sufficiently prevents overheating. In extreme cases without rotation, the maximum temperature surpasses the design limits by only 5.4 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ , a scenario deemed improbable based on ADCS simulations.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.4.3 Final Simulation Results
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 4 3 final simulation results
text: Overall, the thermal management approach is advantageous, primarily in preventing component overheating, which poses a greater risk than overcooling. The satellite's design, which lacks active cooling mechanisms and depends on subsystem shutdown for temperature control, aligns poorly with continuous operational needs. Consequently, the recalibration of the heater's ON/OFF margins, ensuring the satellite maintains a positive power budget even in the coldest projected scenarios. This approach balances the need to avoid battery overcooling with the imperative to maintain satellite functionality and power efficiency. For the current power budget, the heater ON/OFF temperature that allows generating power for all the cold scenarios is 4 to 5 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ (Table 10.9). With this heater activation temperature, the minimum predicted battery temperature is around $ 0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}. $

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.1 Test Overview
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 1 test overview
text: Once the results were validated by the expert support team from ESA, the $ ^{3} $Cat-4 environmental test campaign in the thermal-vacuum chamber at the CubeSat Support Facilities (CSF) at ESEC-GALAXIA facilities (Belgium) was prepared. The entire procedure for this test is documented in the " $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Test Specifications and Test Procedures Full Assembly Verification Environmental Test Campaign - Thermal and Vacuum Testing" [23], prepared by $ ^{3} $Cat-4 team with the support of ESA ESTEC Thermal Control Section (TEC-MTT) for use with CubeSat Systems, which combines a tailored version of the ECSS standards with lessons learned from past CubeSat projects.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.1 Test Overview
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 1 test overview
text: All the test descriptions include the requirements that have to be verified in order to determine if the test results are satisfactory. It also outlined the test specifications and requirements that define the conditions under which the test should be conducted and a detailed schedule of the test organization [23].

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.1 Test Overview
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 1 test overview
text: The TVAC test consists in putting the satellite under thermal stress, in both operative and non-operative hot and cold temperatures. During and after the test, its expected functionalities are checked to assess if the temperature variation inflicts damage or malfunction in the system. The main objective of the thermal vacuum testing is to study and ensure the temperature ranges with which the $ ^{3} $Cat-4 nanosatellite will confront in its operation, in both hot and cold cases. To test this temperature ranges, two different types of thermal cycles are applied to the spacecraft [23].

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.2 TVAC test campaign flowgraph
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 2 tvac test campaign flowgraph
text: The initial stage consists on performing a set of tests to ensure the health of the satellite, and also provide a baseline to refer on during the TVAC testing. During this phase, the spacecraft is unpacked and prepared for functional testing within a cleanroom environment, ensuring readiness for the initial Reduced Functional Test (RFT). The test organization involves the mission team, including the test supervisor, hardware and software responsible individuals, facility operators, and necessary ESA Academy staff. The stage lasts for 3 hours and consists of two phases: equipment and personnel arrival at the testing facilities, followed by spacecraft unpacking and hardware setup for functional testing. Figure 8.7 [23] shows the spacecraft is positioned in the vertical MGSE for this test.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.3 DUT Thermocouple (TC) placement:
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 3 dut thermocouple tc placement
text: The Thermal Reference Point (TRP) is a parameter utilized during the TVAC test campaign. It serves as a reference for controlling the temperature during the test execution, as it provides essential data to regulate the spacecraft's temperature. The position of the thermocouples (TC) is determined based on the TRP location, and such as it is less influenced by heating parts such as the heaters placed on the batteries. It has the fastest response to the change in temperatures and allows the operator to control the environment in a safer manner.

section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 4 1 bake out
text: The bake-out programmed for this test lasts up to 25 hours at a temperature of $ 5 0 \mathrm{~} ^ {\circ} \mathrm{C} $ . The bake-out time includes the hot non-operational cycle of 4 hours. The required pressure must be below $ 1 0^{-5} $ hPa or mB. It will be the first part of the TVAC test.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.4.2 Test Levels and Conditions
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 4 2 test levels and conditions
text: Furthermore, the temperature rate of change is determined based on the thermal analyses, considering the worst-case scenario with the highest thermal gradients. The temperature rate of change is set at 0.25 K/min, which complies with the facility's specifications. The maximum temperature rate of change expected in orbit is 1 K/min.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.4.2 Test Levels and Conditions
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 4 2 test levels and conditions
text: The dwell time criteria is set to a minimum of 2 hours. This conservative value allows sufficient time for all internal components to stabilize at the required temperature. For ambient, operational, and non-operational cycles, the stability criteria for all subsystems is a maximum rate of change of 1 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{h} $ . During the thermal balance test, the criteria is 0.5 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / 4 \mathrm{~h} $

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.4.2 Test Levels and Conditions
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 4 2 test levels and conditions
text: The TRP is placed on top of the structure's rails, and the difference in temperature between the batteries and the structure is almost $ + 1 \mathrm{~^\circ C} $ $ (4 2. 5 \mathrm{~^\circ C} $ at the batteries and $ 4 3. 2 \mathrm{~^\circ C} $ at the structure), as per the current thermal simulations. However, although this is the expected behaviour in flight, during TVAC testing all of the sides of the S/C will be at similar environmental conditions, thus this gradient may be lower and/or negligible. For this reason, it is not considered for the Test Specification value. Therefore, the maximum operational temperature will be $ 4 5 \mathrm{~^\circ C} $ $ [- 0 \mathrm{~^\circ C} / + 4 \mathrm{~^\circ C} ] $

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.4.2 Test Levels and Conditions
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 4 2 test levels and conditions
text: A thermal gradient may exist between the batteries and the external TRP. For this reason, especially in hot cases, the maximum operational temperature may be revised during the test, with close inspection when performing the first ambient plateau after TVAC closure. The TRP temperature can be modified to ensure that the batteries do not exceed their maximum temperature rating of 45 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ . It is important to note that, as the batteries will not be charged at the maximum operational temperature, there is an extra safety margin for them, as the discharge temperature rate goes up to $ 60^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ .

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.5 Test Campaign Results
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 5 test campaign results
text: In preparation for the TVAC Test Campaign, the System Level Environmental Test Campaign was conducted, encompassing the successful completion of both the Mission and Vibrations Tests. These tests have effectively ensured the spacecraft's preparedness for its designated mission. Furthermore, the thermal behavior of the spacecraft was thoroughly validated by exposing its components and subsystems to the predicted in-orbit environment. The test setup employed a fully radiative configuration, incorporating a PA12 isolating basket and suspension through Dyneema wires, as shown in Fig. 8.12.

text: Furthermore, in line with operational safety protocols, the ZADS was manually disconnected by the external Electrical Ground Support Equipment when temperatures drop below -20 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ . This temperature threshold aligns with its. Operational Qualification Temperature [24].

section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 5 1 test execution

section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 5 1 test execution
text: Additionally, extended-duration thermal balance cases were implemented to enhance our comprehension of the satellite's behavior over prolonged periods.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.5.1 Test Execution
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 5 1 test execution
text: All phases of the thermal balance test complied with the 0.5K/4h criterion. Although some phases did not exactly meet the predefined targets, the overall test requirements were fully satisfied, as evidenced by the successful completion of the third hot operational cycle. These thermal balance phases primarily served to collect data on the S/C thermal behavior, demonstrating its ability to maintain stable conditions over extended periods. The temperature profile for the entire Hot Thermal Balance test is depicted in Fig. 8.14.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.5.1 Test Execution
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 5 1 test execution
text: It was noted that the heater power dissipation exceeded the initial expectations. To accommodate cold cases (Fig. 8.15) and achieve the lower qualification temperatures, hysteresis temperatures were adjusted, resulting in a decrease to $ [-1 6^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / -1 5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}] $

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.5.1 Test Execution
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 5 1 test execution
text: After initiating the hot switch-on, the spacecraft's temperature was gradually reduced below 15 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ in two controlled steps to avoid exceeding the minimum non-operational temperature limits, reaching -18.5 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ . The TRP was then stabilized with minimal temperature variation before initiating a cold switch-on, ensuring battery safety. Post-switch-on checks revealed a 'Cold Batteries' error due to temperatures below 0 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ leading to an update in the EPS configuration for future cases. Heater activation at below 5 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ resulted in a rapid temperature rise in the EPS and batteries compared to the rest of the spacecraft.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.5.5.1 Test Execution
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 5 5 1 test execution
text: Subsequent modifications to the COMMS configuration and a weekend-long thermal balance test were conducted, including a scenario with the TRP set at -8.5 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ , resulting in 100% heater duty cycle. This was followed by another thermal balance with TRP at 4 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ , reflecting more realistic orbital conditions, where battery temperatures were maintained above the threshold. Unexpected transitions to survival mode due to EPS errors provided additional data. A hot dissipation case was also simulated, with adjustments in the COMMS duty cycle and spacecraft modes, though interrupted by another EPS error. Despite these challenges, a partial thermal balance was achieved. The overall high dissipation thermal balance sequence and subsequent health checks yielded positive results.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.6 Conclusions
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 6 conclusions
text: A comprehensive thermal analysis was conducted for the $ ^{3} $Cat-4 1U CubeSat, prompted by design modifications and alterations in the orbital parameters. The updated thermal model was rigorously validated against prior results, ensuring its accuracy and reliability. To safeguard the thermal and power budgets within prescribed limits, an in-depth study of the heater and external coatings was undertaken. The outcomes of this study provided assurance that the spacecraft's thermal and power profiles remained well within the defined boundaries. The Thermal Vacuum (TVAC) test campaign served as a critical phase in the validation process, specifically attesting to the heater's performance. Overall, the TVAC test campaign demonstrated the spacecraft's resilience and capability to withstand the anticipated temperature variations, affirming its readiness for the demanding conditions of space. These findings collectively contribute to the confidence in the thermal robustness of the satellite in its intended operational environment.

section: $ ^{3} $Cat-4 Thermal Analysis and Thermal Vacuum Test Campaign Results > 8.6 Conclusions
section_key: 3 cat 4 thermal analysis and thermal vacuum test campaign results / 8 6 conclusions
text: The previous chapters have established criteria for evaluating the remaining capabilities of satellites after subsystem failures, highlighting the possibility of reusing those with non-critical anomalies, especially "zombie satellites" (ZS), which still retain operational subsystems. This reuse could enhance orbital infrastructure and reduce space debris. However, progress toward eco-lean designs faces technological, legal, and regulatory challenges. Therefore, the next section of the thesis focuses on legal issues, exploring a more sustainable management and development of space resources.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > Abstract
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / abstract
text: Recycling abandoned or partially failed satellites, also known as zombie satellites (ZSs), is an emerging concept that can significantly reduce the number of satellites to be launched, and ultimately the amount of space junk. By assessing and leveraging the remaining capabilities of those satellites, they can be repurposed for missions beyond the initial one. This work conducts an operability assessment of satellite recycling by exploiting their remaining subsystems and equipment for Telecommunications and Earth Observation applications. Besides, to ensure that those satellites can be used for different purposes, several regulatory and legal aspects have to be tackled. Finally, with the goal of incorporating recycling into satellite design, various standardization approaches are discussed for future satellite missions.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > Abstract
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / abstract
text: Keywords Space Debris, Space Regulations, Recyclable Satellites, Satellite Standardization.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.1 Introduction
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 1 introduction
text: Since 1957 thousands of satellites have been launched for space exploration, or to provide different types of services such as communications, Earth observation (EO), navigation, etc. However, space activity has also had some negative effects. A widespread concern is related to the increase of non-operational space-based objects. Millions of smaller pieces of space debris are orbiting at very high velocities, thus endangering significantly current and future space missions [1, 2, 3].

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.1 Introduction
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 1 introduction
text: Space debris include upper stages of rockets, debris fragments due to collisions, accidental or intentional explosions, debris from propellants, and deterioration of materials due to extreme space weather conditions [4]. In addition, an important percentage of space debris is formed by non-operational satellites that have partially or totally failed or that have been abandoned due to different causes [5]. Hence, different approaches have been proposed and, in some cases developed, to mitigate the risks associated to space debris, so as to continue using space in a sustainable way.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.1 Introduction
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 1 introduction
text: To authors' knowledge, so far all the approaches have focused on cleaning the space ecosystem by de-orbiting inoperative satellites [6], refueling satellites [7], and developing robotic spacecrafts to repair, move, and assist these defunct or handicapped satellites [8]. Unlike these previous procedures, considering that satellites' failures may not be catastrophic, and still, some of the subsystems may still be usable for other purposes, a novel alternative will consist of recycling those satellites for other purposes, thus reducing the orbit saturation, the number of launches, the amount of space debris, and other environmental effects on the planet [5][9]. In a prior work carried out by the authors [10], it was concluded that the probability of a satellite failing in the first quarter of its life is three times larger than in the second quarter, and seven times larger than in the last quarter of its life. This is an evidence of the waste of satellites' capabilities, since not all the failures experienced during the first quarter are catastrophic, and many systems can still be leveraged. Moreover, it

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.1 Introduction
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 1 introduction
text: has been observed that, instead of re-assessing in depth the anomaly, and studying the possibility to reuse it for other purposes, some failed satellites tend to be decommissioned early [11], to decay (LEO orbits), to be moved to a graveyard orbit (GEO orbits), or drift completely from their orbit. However, reusing and bringing a satellite back is not simple and poses several challenges and complications. Thus, this chapter aims to study and summarize the technological capabilities and limitations of those ZSs, as well as to expose regulatory gaps, liabilities, and some legal barriers.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.1 Introduction
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 1 introduction
text: This chapter is structured in four sections. The first one presents a characterization of zombie satellites (ZS) and their peculiarities. The second section is focused on the analysis of the operational capabilities of ZSs reused for telecommunications and EO purposes. The third section explains the main laws, and regulations that a ZS will be subjected to, in case to be recycled. In the fourth section, several measures and initiatives are proposed to enhance and adapt the conception and design of future satellites to raise the attainability so that they can be reused and leveraged more easily.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.2 Characterization of ZSs
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 2 characterization of zss
text: Not all satellites orbiting around are operational. There are satellites orbiting with some of their subsystems turned off to mitigate radiation effects [12], so they can replace other satellites in case of anomaly [13]. These satellites are expected to operate at some point in their lifetime, and they serve as a backup alternative to guarantee service continuity (e.g. GPS, broadcasting) [14]. However, unlike the previous case in which satellites are in reserve and totally serviceable, there are many "zombie satellites" (ZSs) orbiting, that have been abandoned after an anomaly occurrence, or that have not achieved the expected profitability [15]. Hence, a ZS fulfills that: 1) it is declared as non-operational, 2) it is moving into an orbit from which it is still possible to carry out some specific missions, and 3) its essential subsystems such as Electrical Power System (EPS), Telemetry, Tracking, and Command (TT&C), and communications (COMM) still have the capability to perform their functions.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.2 Characterization of ZSs
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 2 characterization of zss
text: In a previous work [10], the current ten largest constellations were analyzed using Seradata [16] and Telastra [17] databases. It was determined that around 956 inactive satellites are orbiting, from which it was estimated that 347 and 349 correspond to Space X and Planet Labs, respectively. Since an inactive satellite does not imply being a ZS, a reassessment was carried out in [10] to quantify the capabilities and limitations of the satellites, and from those launched after 2010, it was concluded that Space X and Planet constellations had around 85 and 322 ZSs, respectively, and ORBCOMM constellation 29. Although the study was constrained by the unreported anomalies and lack of description of those reported, the results aforementioned extracted from [10] evidence the existence of a large number of ZSs.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.3 Operational Assessment of ZSs
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 3 operational assessment of zss
text: The concept of recycling a satellite is an innovative idea that has become more visible because of the non-negligible and increasing number of inoperative satellites, the increasing number of satellite launches, and the appearance of new user demands [5]. Hence, besides the identification of possible ZSs, an important analysis must still be conducted regarding the possibilities, barriers, challenges, and limitations of recycling a ZS from the operational, and regulatory perspectives. As stated previously, in order to leverage a failed satellite, the failures that occurred must not be catastrophic, that is, independently from the mission, the satellites should still preserve some essential subsystems and equipment [9,10]. Firstly, the satellite must be capable to establish communications with the corresponding ground station. In line with the remaining communication equipment requirements, the satellite will be reused for some specific missions. Secondly, all the equipment responsible for the generation, storage, and distribution of power is also essential. In addition, the onboard computer and data-handling systems are fundamental, and a software reconfiguration must be carried out before the operation of the ZS [18]. Propulsion equipment (e.g., thrusters) may not be necessary for some missions [19], whilst for ADCS, attitude sensors, processors, and torques are mandatory in order to control the orientation and stabilize the satellite [20]. Besides the essential systems indicated, the mission for which the ZSs will be used determines which additional systems and equipment the satellite must include to perform and achieve the desired goals.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.3 Operational Assessment of ZSs
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 3 operational assessment of zss
text: In this regard, it should be noted that most of the current ZS identified in [10] are small satellites belonging to constellations such as Planet Labs (3U CubeSats) and Starlink (microsatellites). Therefore, due to volume limitations, they are not usually equipped with redundant diversified payloads. This implies an important constraint to reuse those satellites for missions that require specific payloads. Hence, the vast majority of ZSs

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.3 Operational Assessment of ZSs
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 3 operational assessment of zss
text: that experienced anomalies can only be used for limited communications purposes. With the aim of extending the variety of missions that ZSs can cover, and therefore increasing the feasibility of satellite recycling, section 9.5) presents several conceptions and design proposals for the standardization of future small satellites. Once the resulting capabilities of the ZS are assessed, certain requirements, conditions, and requisites must be assessed in accordance with the mission to be performed.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.3.1 ZSs for Communication Purposes
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 3 1 zss for communication purposes
text: As for a ZS intended to be reused for communications, several aspects must be considered. If the ZS still has the communications capability in both links (high data rate for downlink and low date rate for TT&C), as in the case of satellites abandoned because of poor business profitability [21] [22] [23], a variety of communications applications can be covered with no restrictions. However, most communications satellites tend to experience failures in their high-capacity transponders [9] [10] [24] [25] [26], and afterwards, they are reported as permanently disabled satellites without assessing the remaining capacities of the Telemetry, Tracking, and Command (TT&C) channel. The TT&C link establishes the communications between the spacecraft and the ground control segment, and is responsible for receiving telecommands (controlling the modes of operation, configuring devices and subsystems, fixing software (SW) and firmware (FW) errors, among others), and for transmitting telemetry (housekeeping, attitude, and payload data) [27]. Although generally, TT&C links operate at the S-band [28], and have limited data rates as compared to Ka/Ku band links, since the ZSs identified in [10] are LEO constellations several low-speed communications services requiring low-power transmission can still be performed. Among those communications, Internet of Things (IoT) technology stands out currently as one of the most captivating technologies whose services can be performed by ZSs with no capability in their high-rate channel. Besides leveraging low-rate channels, IoT systems do not require as high pointing accuracy as other satellite applications (e.g. EO, astronomy), thus, raising the likelihood of leveraging those ZSs presenting anomalies in some of their ADCS equipment.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.3.1 ZSs for Communication Purposes
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 3 1 zss for communication purposes
text: Limited visibility between LEO satellites and ground stations has always limited low latency requirements [29]. Thus, in addition, to expanding the ground station network in designated areas of interest, inter-satellite links (ISL) represent an optimal alternative to handle those data traffic restrictions [30]. In this regard, abandoned satellites with remaining communications capabilities can constitute an opportunity to extend the satellite network, by leveraging the different satellite links to connect to other satellites. In addition, with a dense satellite network, capacity is increased significantly because of the frequency reuse, hence increasing communications throughput in a more profitable manner. It should be noted that the "high and low-speed link" terms are used when the communication is with the ground segment when the signal must cross long distances going through different atmospheric conditions and phenomena [31]. Thus, besides the high speed that a Ka/Ku link presents, the S-band, generally used for TT&C links [32], can provide high enough speed connectivity for inter-satellite links [33].

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.3.2 ZSs for EO and Navigation Systems
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 3 2 zss for eo and navigation systems
text: The initial conception and design of the satellite may imply certain limitations to reuse it for uses such as Earth observation or navigation purposes. For instance, a satellite initially intended exclusively for telecommunication purposes, whose payload will consist of transponders, cannot be easily reused for EO. In general, only satellites initially conceived for remote sensing purposes and equipped with the appropriate instrument could perform certain EO missions. A notable exception are the receivers of signals of Opportunity (SoOp) in which the receiver collects typically navigation and communications signals after they cross the atmosphere or reflect on the Earth's surface. A major example is the NASA SMAP mission [34], in which the radar receiver was tuned at GPS L2-band after the radar transmitter failed [35]. In this way, a GNSS-R instrument with a very large antenna was opportunistically created. This approach could possibly be extended to other communication missions, as power amplifiers are what typically fail in transponder systems, as concluded in [9, 10].

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.3.2 ZSs for EO and Navigation Systems
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 3 2 zss for eo and navigation systems
text: Although attitude determination and control are essential for all spacecraft to guarantee the solar panel orientation and communication links, they are highly decisive for EO purposes considering the strict high-pointing accuracy required so the space-borne EO instruments can point to the desired scanning area. Thus, besides the specific EO payload, an assessment of ADCS is extremely necessary for those ZSs intended for EO. Remote sensing applications typically require low data rates and low-speed radios to transmit the data collected [36], thus, as in some communications applications, ZSs with remaining capabilities in the low-rate channels can still be leveraged in those applications.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.3.2 ZSs for EO and Navigation Systems
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 3 2 zss for eo and navigation systems
text: Certain errors in the command and data handling system (CDHS) may not be fatal, allowing the satellite to continue operating in certain ways. On the one hand, if a ZS's EO payload processors fail, the ZS can still be used for other low-data applications (like communications or navigation), since those processors are in charge of reducing the amount of data in the downlink by performing data processing operations like compression and discarding uninteresting data, among other procedures [37]. On the other hand, the possibility of storage system failures is greatly increased by the susceptibility of certain volatile memories (such as SRAMs and SDRAMs) to single-event upsets (SEUs) and multiple-bit upsets (MBUs), as well as the vulnerability of some controllers of specific SD card models to single event functional interrupts (SEFIs) [37]. Anomalies in storage systems could be crucial for applications that require processing large amounts of data; therefore, the satellite could still be useful in those applications, but with restricted data storage capacity. For example, GPS and GLONASS satellites only need to store satellite ephemeris data and clock corrections, so their data storage requirements for navigation purposes are minimal [38].

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.3.3 On-Board Reconfiguration of ZS
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 3 3 on board reconfiguration of zs
text: The unattainability of physical upgrades or repairs after a satellite is launched has increased the demand for self-repair, upgrade, and reconfiguration capabilities on board. Satellites with those aptitudes can handle software (SW) and hardware (HW) failures, and have the flexibility to change mission goals and service requirements to some extent. Precisely, those latter vantages are pivotal to ZSs, facilitating the required service changes and operations adaptability.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.3.3 On-Board Reconfiguration of ZS
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 3 3 on board reconfiguration of zs
text: While reconfigurable technology on the ground is more advanced, in-orbit reconfiguration strategies have only started emerging and evolving significantly in this last decade, and in consequence, most of the traditional satellites display a lack of adaptability and can only perform specific missions. This poor flexibility challenges the reuse of ZSs, thus, wasting satellite resources. Nevertheless, with the arrival of the "New Space Era" and as versatile satellites become more necessary, small satellite conceivement has evolved towards more reconfigurable implementations in several subsystems: in the OBC, TT&C [39, 40], attitude control unit (ACU) [41, 42, 43], power control unit (PCU) [44], and radio frequency equipment [45], among others [46].

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.3.3 On-Board Reconfiguration of ZS
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 3 3 on board reconfiguration of zs
text: Small satellites' On-Board Computer (OBC) and Data Handling (DH) systems have been traditionally equipped with microcontrollers and Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA) due to their high processing capabilities, low cost, design flexibility, and different peripherals connection [47]. FPGAs can be fully reconfigured, and currently, FPGAs also support partial runtime reconfiguration (RTR), such as Virtex/E/II/II Pro/4 families from Xilinx [48], and ispXPGA families from Lattice Semiconductors [49], in which only a part of the system is reconfigured while the rest of the system is not interrupted [50]. The reconfiguration process is frequently accomplished through memory rewriting or command adjustment techniques. Whereas the former is based on rewriting the OBS's processing carrying certain risks, the latter modifies the spacecraft's operational parameters in response to commands from the ground. Hence, once the operational requirements of the new mission are established and considering a ZS with reconfiguration capabilities, in order to initiate the ZS operation, the ground station must encrypt and transmit the desired operational instructions ("bitstreams") to the ZS [51].

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.4 Regulations and Legal Constraints
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 4 regulations and legal constraints
text: Recycled ZSs, like any regular satellite, are subject to a series of space legislations, and regulations, as well as certain operational specifications, established at international, national, and regional levels. Because of the variability of regulatory gaps among states, and jurisdictions, for simplicity, this section addresses some of the measures and actions to be considered for ZSs in accordance to the treaties and principles of space law established by the UN [52], and the ITU regulations [53].

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.4.1 UN Space Law concerning ZSs
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 4 1 un space law concerning zss
text: International space law regulates the conduct of space activities. Its main framework is based on five specific international treaties, known as the "five United Nations treaties on outer space". Among the five treaties, the "Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space" [52][54] and "Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects" [52] [55], which entered into force in 1976 and 1972, respectively, underscore as they contain certain articles that concern satellite recycling. Regarding the former, Article IV specifies the parameters required in order to register any space object and asserts that from time to time, this information must be updated, if the case arises. Besides the status and orbital parameters

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.4.1 UN Space Law concerning ZSs
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 4 1 un space law concerning zss
text: such as nodal period, perigee, and apogee, the mission of the space object is among the requested data. Thus, UN registration must be updated if, for instance, a ZS with propulsion capabilities has changed its orbital position to perform a newly designed mission. Furthermore, the General Assembly resolution 62/101 recommends the provision of information related to the change of supervision of a space object, which is a major point considering the ownership and operational transfers that ZS may experience. Nevertheless, and according to the authors' knowledge, there is no specific international system by which a space object owned by an entity domiciled in the initial State of the registry can be transferred to another one domiciled in a foreign State, and currently, those operations are carried out informally between countries without any internationally agreed provisions. The "Liability Convention" [52] [55], tackles the liabilities for damage caused by space objects, whether such activities are carried on by governmental agencies or by non-governmental entities. Considering the potential responsibilities that may be transferred during a ZS acquisition, all parties involved in the process should take those liability principles into account. Aside from the treaties mentioned, the UN establishes five more principles, among them, those related to television broadcasting and remote sensing [56] [52]. Regarding the former, ZSs may provide limited capability and reliability for services without interruption and with high quality such as broadcasting, whilst the latter, as stated in section 9.3), the probabilities depend on the available ZS's EO payloads. Thus, for ZSs repurposed for EO uses, remote sensing principles should be taken into consideration. Specifically, evident principles such as entering consultations with a state whose territory is sensed (Principle XIII), and protecting Earth natural's environment (Principle X), among others.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.4.2 Regulatory Approach for ZS
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 4 2 regulatory approach for zs
text: The type of link (uplink, downlink, ISL, etc.), coverage (land, maritime, global, etc.), earth station (fixed, mobile, ESV, etc.), and use (communications, EO, etc.) may lead to necessary changes of parameters, such as the orbital position or frequency band in order to fulfill the new desired service.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.4.2 Regulatory Approach for ZS
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 4 2 regulatory approach for zs
text: Radio-frequency spectrum and orbits are finite resources, thus necessitating international cooperation and coordination among governments and satellite operators to ensure equitable access, and avoid harmful interference during their operations. Depending on the desired band, the concerned entities should have to pursue different procedures. For instance, in case a ZS requires an allocation in a non-planned band not subjected to the coordination procedure set out in the ITU RR [53], the corresponding operator should apply for the assignment in the desired band by submitting a new API (Advance Publication Information) to the national administration, where the application is filed on a first-come-first-served basis. The ITU-BR notifies the frequency assignment (Article 11), and records it in the Master International Frequency Register (MIFR). On the contrary, if the ZS operator seeks to operate in a planned band, it should submit the necessary requirements, then the assignments are set through public conferences, and finally registered in the MIFR [57].

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.4.2 Regulatory Approach for ZS
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 4 2 regulatory approach for zs
text: Besides the worldwide regulations mentioned, it is crucial to acknowledge the regulations variability among nations and jurisdictions. Indeed, with the rapidly growing small satellite sector, governmental agencies in several countries have begun to develop more flexible and adapted licensing procedures, guiding small satellite operators through the regulatory process. Thus, in the case of the US, for example, if an entity wishes to reuse any of the 322 ZS's from Planet Labs [10] for Earth Observation, it must encounter several national agencies such as the FCC to assign frequencies for use by non-governmental satellite operators, NTIA to handle the frequencies for federal use, NOAA to issue licenses for non-federal remote sensing operations, among others [58]. Hence, all those identified ZSs, besides fulfilling the international regulations, must be subjected to regional and national agreements and guidelines.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.4.2 Regulatory Approach for ZS
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 4 2 regulatory approach for zs
text: Space insurance management is also a fundamental step in the recycling process to cover the damages that may occur. Thus, to define the liability among the different entities, a technical assessment (evaluation of its health, critical systems, and ongoing operational capabilities) must be conducted before considering the reuse of the ZS [59, 60, 61, 62].

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.5 Standardization of Future Satellites
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 5 standardization of future satellites
text: Currently, leveraging failed satellites is hampered by some major barriers. On the one hand, many satellites suffer from anomalies in essential subsystems and equipment (OBC, EPS, and TT&C) which disables completely the satellite, and prevents any possible reuse. On the other hand, having satellites initially conceived to perform only a specific mission, limits their capability to be reused for other missions (see section

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.5 Standardization of Future Satellites
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 5 standardization of future satellites
text: 9. 3.2). To overcome those handicaps, the aim is to include "recycling" as part of the satellite design, by means of novel autonomous, modular, and standardized satellite architectures to facilitate satellite reuse and application flexibility, with the corresponding positive environmental and economic impact.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.5 Standardization of Future Satellites
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 5 standardization of future satellites
text: Enhancing satellite resilience and reliability in front of an anomaly occurrence is critical to define standardization solutions for future satellite manufacturing. Traditionally, reliability has been achieved by applying redundancy to full subsystems or specific components, in which for instance, two identical units are interconnected with the remaining system in a way that either one can fulfill the required functionality (cross-strapping) [63, 64]. Redundancy has been a crucial advance in large satellite design to extend satellites' lifetime and improve resilience [10], however, within the limited volume of the rapidly emerging nanosatellites, such techniques are restrained. Still, related approaches have been proposed and conceived for CubeSats. For the Delfi-C3 CubeSat launched in 2008, Delft University of Technology proposed a non-identical backup system for the acquisition and transmission of data from of one its demonstration payloads [65][66], whilst for Delfi-n3Xt launched in 2013, to avoid single-point-of-failure (SPOF) risks, a design philosophy based on the onboard computer, radio transceivers, and parts of the electrical power subsystem redundancy was proposed [66][67]. Although those approaches demonstrate redundancy affordability even in small satellites, further investigations must be conducted to discern the feasibility of such strategies to improve reliability.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.5 Standardization of Future Satellites
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 5 standardization of future satellites
text: Besides implementing systems' redundancy to remedy in-orbit failures and extend lifetime in case of anomaly occurrence, standardization must also guarantee the leverage of the preserved satellite subsystems and equipment. Thus, decentralized architectures are decisive to bypass the tight integration and successive failures of satellite equipment. Numerous satellites have already been conceived based on a decentralized and distributed philosophy, such as the Aalborg University AAUSAT3 [68], launched in 2013, in which each subsystem has sufficient processing power and data storage to fulfill its internal needs, and the IRAZU CubeSat [69], launched in 2018, in which each subsystem has its own microprocessor connected to the bus, which reflects that in some cases, decentralization is strongly associated with redundancy.

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.5 Standardization of Future Satellites
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 5 standardization of future satellites
text: Robotic spacecraft for in-orbit services (IOS) represents another important advance to extend the satellite's life by refueling, maneuver assistance, and repair. In February 2020, the Mission Extension Vehicle-1 (MEV-1) by Northrop Grumman [70], conducted the first satellite servicing operation, in which it controlled the orbit of Intelsat 901 by using its own thrusters and fuel supply, unlocking a new course of action to mitigate space debris and limit new satellite launches. To facilitate those operations in the future, satellite modularity and versatility are crucial. By decomposing systems and components into independent parts, comprising a set of standardized components, and linking subsystems via standardized interfaces, satellite architecture must become highly flexible, permitting the extraction and substitution of damaged components by IOS. Indeed, future docking modules would have also to be standardized alongside with satellite standardization [71].

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.5 Standardization of Future Satellites
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 5 standardization of future satellites
text: Reconfigurability and autonomy also play a fundamental role in defining satellite standardization. As exposed in section 3.3, due to operational limitations, ZS may have to be repurposed for another mission different than the initial one. This requires reconfigurable systems that can change physical connections, and perform software upgrades according to new mission requirements. In order to increase satellites' functional lifespan in-orbit reconfiguration is crucial to 1) the adaptability of mission objectives enabling the satellite to switch between roles [72, 73], 2) satellite orbit or orientation adjustment to cover the desired areas or pointing to other satellites (ISL), and 3) ensuring diagnostics and remedial actions in response of anomalies [74]. In-orbit reconfiguration, especially when integrated with artificial intelligence and robotics advancements [75], increases significantly the operational versatility of satellite missions [76] and promises enhanced cost-effectiveness and adaptability for future satellites missions [77].

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.6 Conclusions
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 6 conclusions
text: Despite still having enough capacity to be recycled for other purposes, hundreds of satellites have been moved to a graveyard orbit (GEO) or re-entered the atmosphere (LEO) due to partial failures or low profitability. With the arrival of the "New Space Era" in 2013, thousands of satellites are being launched annually, and the current number of abandoned satellites with still some capacity is increasing exponentially, with the corresponding economic and ecological effects. This study has outlined the features of these satellites (ZS) and provides an operational evaluation that relies on a ZS's residual capabilities to carry out specific tasks, with an emphasis on telecommunication, EO, and navigation applications. In addition, it briefly analyzes the international regulatory gaps and space laws that ZSs will encounter to be legally recycled, underscoring the lack of standardized regulatory procedures for the emerging small satellites. Acknowledging the flexibility of

section: Operational and Regulatory Assessment for Satellites Recycling > 9.6 Conclusions
section_key: operational and regulatory assessment for satellites recycling / 9 6 conclusions
text: future satellites is crucial in order to facilitate ZSs reuse, this manuscript also discusses some design and conception strategies to achieve the required adaptability and versatility.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: This study provides a comprehensive insight into the development of sustainable practices within the satellite technology sector. By introducing the concept of Eco-LeanSat, the foundations are laid for integrating sustainability into satellite manufacturing and reuse processes.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: Efforts to promote a sustainable orbital environment require collaboration to establish standards in space debris maintenance, manufacturing, and management. The proposal to integrate "Life Extension" into the satellite manufacturing logistics underscores the importance of sustainability throughout the satellite's lifecycle. This approach, supported by technical recommendations and a comprehensive action plan, establishes a clear path to mitigate waste production in key orbits in the coming years. Policy evolution, platform improvements, development of disposal services, and enhanced space operations form the basis for proactive measures aimed at ensuring the sustainability of space missions.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: Acknowledging the collective efforts of organizations such as UNOOSA, ESA, NASA, and JAXA, the study emphasizes the importance of addressing challenges within the supply chain. By advocating for a holistic approach in evaluating environmentally responsible materials and disposal practices, it promotes more sustainable manufacturing processes and end-of-life satellite management.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: Furthermore, exploring potential actions with existing space debris, such as the reuse of failed satellites and in-orbit recycling, reveals promising avenues to mitigate space debris challenges. Identifying comprehensive descriptions of anomalies, technological advancements, regulatory considerations, and industry awareness are highlighted as crucial factors for realizing the economic and environmental benefits of satellite reuse.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: In the chapters of this thesis, sustainable proposals have been addressed, and evaluation criteria have been established to assess the residual capabilities of satellites after failures in specific subsystems, classifying them into null, limited, and full capacities. This provides a framework for understanding the potential for satellite reuse based on their remaining functionalities. Additionally, a significant proportion of anomalies that do not result in the permanent loss of the satellite have been identified, suggesting the opportunity to reuse these assets instead of prematurely decommissioning them. The concept of "zombie satellites" (ZS), which may still have operational subsystems, is emphasized. By characterizing ZS and exploring possibilities for their reuse, this study proposes an innovative approach to optimize orbital infrastructure and mitigate space debris. The reuse of partially damaged satellites could contribute to the sustainability of the space ecosystem by reducing unnecessary launches and optimizing resource utilization. Consequently, parameters have been proposed to consider for future eco-lean designs in satellites, which would enable more efficient and sustainable operation in space.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: Additionally, the causes of these orbit failures caused by space radiation have been considered, which can help strengthen materials and operational processes with satellites in space with the aim of prolonging their lifespan. These results examined the relationship between space weather and anomalies observed in small satellites in LEO and GEO, with a particular emphasis on solar and geomagnetic activity. The analysis results showed that solar activity is critical for spacecraft anomalies. However, contrary to what is generally believed, increases in anomaly rates do not necessarily coincide with peaks in solar activity or during ascending phases.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: This is consistent with the fact that during periods of low sunspot count, cosmic ray particles enter the inner solar system, and the density of relativistic particles tends to increase substantially.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: When exploring the time lag of solar activity on satellite systems, in some cases, there was more solar activity in the month before the month of the anomaly occurrence, indicating a non-instantaneous radiation effect on spacecraft. Additionally, considering that single-event effects tend to occur instantaneously or can be regarded as such, whereas total dose effects take from months to years, this could suggest that anomalies in LEO are closely associated with single-event effects, whereas anomalies in GEO are related to total dose effects.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: The outcomes of this analysis may aid in defining operational strategies (e.g., by switching off some vulnerable systems and reserve mode, among others) to minimize radiation effects on spacecraft systems. Future research should delve deeper into several directions. On one hand, it is decisive to advance in monitoring, characterizing, and predicting radiation levels by using, for instance, physics-based, machine-learning models, and real-time satellite observations. On the other hand, it is crucial to investigate new alternative radiation-hardened and tolerant systems and to assess the robustness of satellite materials.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: In terms of design, considering missions that are not only effective in operation and sustainability but also in design, this thesis explored the study of the application of agile methodologies, confirming the efficient use of resources and responding quickly to changes in requirements and the environment that are aspects that future missions in small satellites will face in the present and in coming years. From this perspective, the application in missions containing a sustainable perspective, the study of the $ ^{3} $ Cat-8 mission presents a linear magnetic attitude control algorithm for a six-unit CubeSat, with a low-thrust electrical propulsion system for orbital raising, and evaluates the controller's performance underscores the important role played by CubeSats in the rapid expansion of the space sector, particularly in cost-effective access to space and fostering innovative science and technology missions. Through partnerships with research institutions and companies, missions like $ ^{3} $ Cat-8 from the UPC NanoSat Lab aim to expand the boundaries of ionospheric research and technology demonstration while addressing the urgent need for sustainable space practices. By exploring the novel concept of integrating propulsion systems into small satellites, the $ ^{3} $ Cat-8 mission pioneers a multipurpose approach to satellite functionality in orbit, aiming to contribute to the reduction of space debris and promote a more sustainable space environment.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: Challenges posed by emerging technologies, such as the novel electrospray thruster developed by IENAI SPACE for the $ ^{3} $Cat-8 mission, highlight the need for advanced control methodologies like the one proposed in this study. By addressing these challenges and refining control strategies based on quaternion attitude kinematics and Euler rotation equations, future nanosatellite missions can enhance their capabilities and ensure mission success.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: The detailed analysis of spacecraft dimensions, mass properties, thruster models, and control modes presented in this study provides valuable insights for CubeSat mission design and operation. Additionally, the discussion on actuator modeling, focusing on the selection and sizing of magnetorquers, offers critical considerations for optimizing ADCS. This research contributes to the ongoing advancement of CubeSat technology and its application in future CubeSat missions to achieve new proposals in technological innovation while promoting sustainability in space. Consequently, the thermal analysis conducted for the $ ^{3} $ Cat-4 mission has provided invaluable insights into the thermal behavior of the spacecraft under various operational conditions. Through the use of modeling techniques and simulations, a comprehensive assessment of the satellite's thermal performance has been achieved. This analysis has not only identified passive thermal control methods but has also devised effective strategies to maintain the spacecraft temperature within the desired range throughout all mission phases. These findings are crucial to ensuring optimal functionality and longevity of the satellite hardware components.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: The TVAC testing campaign has provided essential validation, affirming the thermal resilience of the spacecraft and its ability to withstand anticipated temperature variations. Integrating the results of TVAC testing with thermal analysis has instilled confidence in the satellite's thermal capability, validating its readiness for the demanding operational environment of space. Looking ahead, the insights gained from this thermal analysis will play a crucial role in guiding the design and implementation of thermal control systems for future nanosatellite missions.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: Despite the potential benefits of recycling partially used satellites (ZS) or implementing eco-lean satellites, several challenges persist, including technological, legal, and regulatory considerations. From a legal perspective, although many of these satellites could be recycled for other purposes, hundreds of them have

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: been displaced to graveyard orbits (GEO) or re-entered the atmosphere (LEO) due to partial failures or low profitability. With the advent of the "New Space Age" in 2013, the annual launch of thousands of satellites is contributing to an exponential increase in the number of abandoned satellites that still have some capacity, with significant economic and sustainable effects.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: However, activities such as reusing satellites from different nationalities or owners, conducting manufacturing or repair operations in orbit, among others, present international and legal regulatory gaps in space laws, making it challenging to legally recycle ZS. Therefore, it is essential to develop standardized regulatory procedures for emerging small satellites, addressing these aspects from design and operation perspectives, with multipurpose and sustainable proposals in mind. Recognizing the flexibility of future satellites is crucial to facilitate their reuse, which involves generating design and conception strategies that ensure the adaptability and versatility required.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: The doctoral thesis highlights the urgent need for sustainable practices in space missions and presents a roadmap comprising various strategies and initiatives aimed at achieving this goal. Continued research, collaboration, and innovation are urged to further advance sustainability in satellite manufacturing and refurbishment, considering the broad implications of political, legal, economic, and security aspects.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.1 Ph.D. Conclusions
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 1 ph d conclusions
text: Embracing the concept of satellites "as a service" and leveraging the rapid development of services in orbit emerge as fundamental strategies to extend satellite lifecycles and mitigate concerns about space debris, ensuring a sustainable future for space exploration and technology. Further research is warranted to address these challenges fully and fully capitalize on the opportunities presented by satellite recycling, which will be described in the following chapter. Overall, this study underscores the importance of innovative approaches to space debris management and advocates for a more sustainable use of space resources to ensure the long-term viability of space activities.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.2 Future Research Lines
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 2 future research lines
text: This Section provides a few ideas to follow-up on the work presented in this thesis.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.2 Future Research Lines
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 2 future research lines
text: - Continued research, collaboration, and innovation to further advance sustainability in satellite manufacturing and repurposing while considering the broader implications of political, legal, economic, and security aspects.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.2 Future Research Lines
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 2 future research lines
text: - According to the author understanding, this study represents the first attempt to address the utilization of failed satellites. A significant limitation identified during this research is the lack of reports on a significant number of anomalies. To achieve more comprehensive and detailed results, future projects would require a detailed description of these anomalies to determine their impact on the satellite's architecture. Additionally, further research is imperative as reviving a failed satellite poses various technological challenges, as well as barriers related to regulation, responsibility, and legal and technological aspects.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.2 Future Research Lines
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 2 future research lines
text: - Future designs and new technologies must ensure the flexibility of both hardware and software satellite architectures. Therefore, studies aimed at facilitating this adaptation in future designs should be continued.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.2 Future Research Lines
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 2 future research lines
text: - Is essential to raise awareness within the sector about the economic and environmental impact that ZSs can have by reducing orbital congestion, unnecessary launches, space debris generation, and ecological effects on the planet.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.2 Future Research Lines
section_key: conclusions future research lines / 10 2 future research lines
text: - Future research should focus on advancing monitoring, characterizing, and predicting radiation levels using methods such as physics-based models, machine learning, and real-time satellite observations. Additionally, it is vital to explore innovative radiation-hardened and tolerant systems and evaluate the durability of satellite materials.

section: Conclusions Future research lines > 10.2 Future Research Lines

text: - In order to fully demonstrate the benefits of applying lean six sigma in a space project, it is suggested to conduct a study that applies lean six sigma with complementary software tools such as Bizagi or Capella in MBSE for all stages of development of an entire satellite and evaluate its impact, since in this study it was only applied in a preliminary design stage and a period of development.

text: The governing equation for this problem can be derived by performing an energy balance on the satellite, considering the incident solar $ \dot{Q}_{s} $ , albedo $ \dot{Q}_{a} $ , and Earth infrared $ \dot{Q}_{e} $ radiation loads, as well as the radiation exchange with deep space.

Nanosatellites, as a standardized Space research project with fast and cost-effective development possibilities, have enabled universities in a growing number of emerging countries to develop a wide range of space missions in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). This paper aims to contribute to research efforts to improve the success of university nanosatellite missions using Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) to facilitate the initial project management and design phases. The proposed model-based approach is the result of experience gained from the MASAT1 project, a Moroccan university nanosatellite, and it is based on an architectural framework that allows the system to be described via a set of views. The management and design process is based on a reference framework based on existing standards such as ESA's European Cooperation for Spatial Standardization (ECSS). The choice fell on the Systems Modeling Language (SysML) for the MBSE implementation with the future goal of developing executable SysML Modeling approaches.
Keywords CubeSat·Nanosatellite·MBSE·Management·SysML·Modeling

Space may be the main symbol of technological progress in our modern society as it offers opportunities for the development of a nation's intellectual, technological, and economic capital. This is an area that has long been inaccessible to countries and organizations with limited budgets or little experience in space technology. The advent of the CubeSat standard and the rise of microelectronics and COTS (Commercial Off-The-Shelf) components have democratized the space field by allowing academics around the world to develop space missions that are less costly in terms of budget, design time, and human and technological resources [1]. About 80 countries

participated in the launch of 2286 nanosatellites via 18 different launchers until May 23, 2023, and more than 2080 are expected to be launched between 2022 and 2027 [2]. However, even if universities are one of the main actors with 488 missions developed by 192 academic programs until 2018, the early failure rate of these missions is around 40% [3] [4]. One reason for such low reliability can be the traditional project management and design procedures following the approach of Document-Based Systems Engineering (DBSE) based on space industry standards such as European Cooperation on Space Standardization (ECSS), which are usually over-specified for nanosatellite projects.

The combination of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and Systems Modeling Language (SysML) emerged as an alternative management and design approach that improves mission reliability by focusing on the engineering aspects of projects. MBSE is an engineering approach defined as the formal application of modeling to support system requirements, analysis, design, and verification activities, starting at the conceptual design phase, and continuing through the development and life cycle phases [5]. Typical advantages of MBSE are that it provides better traceability, design consistency,
quality improvement, and reduced document management overhead.
Several research results provide fundamental methods for supporting the development of nanosatellites using MBSE with SysML as a modeling tool:

- For several years, the Space Systems Working Group (SSWG) of the International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE) has been initiating a project to develop Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) for CubeSat designers and developers [6-8].

- The work of NASA systems engineers as part of the Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) Convergence and Modernization Initiative (MIAMI) provides a vision and strategic bridge to the future of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) at NASA through 2029 [9].

- Guo et al. [10] developed an MBSE framework to support DelFFi nanosatellite mission development. SysML has been used only for specification and requirements documentation creation. The parametric model is then simulated into an executable model in Simulink to verify the DelFFi system configuration and compliance with system requirements.

In this context, Sidi Mohammad ben Abdullah University of Fes is currently developing its first MASAT1 nanosatellite project to acquire space engineering technology and basic knowledge. However, with our limited resources, we encountered great difficulty in getting the project off to a good start, as most of the documentation and articles available cover the technical aspects of a CubeSat mission [11] and few articles detail the preparation and early phase management of a university nanosatellite mission. Indeed, the development of a CubeSat in an academic context often involves working outside support structures such as space agencies or industrialists who can rely on full-time staff and proven project management techniques, among other things.

This paper aims to build on the work of the cited article to provide a detailed, easy-to-understand, and effective Model-Based Systems Engineering for those wishing to launch a CubeSat project, including the initial phases of
preparation, management, and analysis, tailored for university projects carried out by cohorts of students.
This paper is organized into two main parts:

- The first part presents traditional systems engineering practices of DBSE to adjust standards such as ECSS, and the standard Project Breakdown Structure used for the management of space projects and the design process. A proposed MBSE framework model for adapting this PBS standard to a student-driving nanosatellite project management and design process is then described.
- The second part describes the MBSE Framework approach applied to the mission analysis phase of the MASAT1 Project.

The aim of using MBSE for a nanosatellite project is to create a model framework or repository that can be used by university teams (with limited resources) wishing to design CubeSat or Nanosatellite projects. This type of formal modeling application will guide them through the entire nanosatellite mission design and management process (mission analysis, system design verification, and validation).
Implementation of MBSE is enabled by
- A graphical modeling language that defines diagrams and a set of possible relationships between them to represent elements.
- An engineering methodology adopted by systems engineers to build the system model.
- A SysML modeling toolset. As can be seen from Table 1, many tools are available at varying costs and usability. We used No Magic MagicDraw modeler with SysML and Cameo Simulation toolkit plugin.

As a graphical modeling language, we use SysML (System Modeling Language), as it is particularly recommended for systems engineering. It's an extension of the Unified Modeling Language (UML) and provides nine types of
