University groups are especially a large contributor in the overall number of launches of yearly CubeSats. As of 27 July 2021, there have been 68 CubeSat launches with 40 of them being from university groups (about 58 percent of launches) in the year of 2021; university groups have consistently maintained plurality on total launches [6]. This showcases directly how many university-based CubeSat projects occurred or potentially may occur if trends continue onward into the future. However, this presents its own challenges.

The motivation of this article is to improve the success rate of CubeSat missions from university groups by providing readily available and usable tools for university teams. To further reinforce the need to improve the success rate, the following data is presented in Figure 7 which showcases the total successes and failures of CubeSats from universities for the given time periods [10]. The data provided is categorized by six different mission success statuses of unknown, launch fail, dead on arrival (DOA), early loss, partial mission, and full mission.
Mission Status for University- Class Missions (2002-2009)
Mission Status for University- Class Missions (2010-2017)
Figure 7. Mission status of CubeSat university-class missions provided by Swartwout [10].

As seen in the preceding Figure 7, university CubeSat mission failure rates have increased while partial and full mission success rates have decreased in conjunction with the increasing number of missions as seen in Figure 6. However, Swartwout notes that the highest number of failures originate from "regular independent" groups with a failure rate of 65 percent at the time of data gathering in 2017 [10]. These "regular independent" groups have fewer than four missions performed nor are designated as a national center for spacecraft development by its government.

The issue present is that many of the growing number of university groups producing CubeSats lack the resources, training, experience, or methodology to reliably give assurance to their missions. The majority of the work is often performed by untrained students that are unfamiliar with the aspects of CubeSat development (e.g., system engineering, design methods, and testing). The SeaLion team also faced these issues as well.

To address some of these issues, SeaLion team members sought to simplify the development process by providing readily available and learnable system engineering approaches and tools. These provided approaches and tools include factors such as planning, documentation, project management, and simplifying the process. This is important since special attention should be given to systems engineering and information exchange for multidisciplinary teams [11]. To showcase these factor's importance, a survey of forty CubeSat groups on how to set up CubeSat projects, conducted by the University of Bristol, emphasized the following relevant lessons learned [12]:
- Planning: Make efforts to "spend a lot of time in the planning stage".
- Documentation/Project Management: Groups should have "good documentation of requirements, work done and work to do".
- Simplicity: Simplify anything you possibly can to increase confidence in success.
The developed mission architecture and associated findings will emphasize the aforementioned points to further the SeaLion CubeSat's development.

The goal of the SeaLion CubeSat mission architecture was to capture the data structures and expected behaviors for the development of the flight software. The data structures and expected behaviors were captured in such a way that can unambiguously understood well enough to be implemented, as well as provide full traceability and rationale for architectural elements with minimal configuration management overhead [13]. Thus, the SeaLion CubeSat mission architecture had to achieve the following:
- Ensure templates only contain formatting data (this includes not storing boilerplate text in templates);
- Ensure models are the authoritative source of truth for all artifact content (e.g., artifact structure, meta-data, boilerplate, commentary, discussion, diagrams, tables, etc.);
- Models should persist on the local filesystem;
- Documents should be in plain text as to be compatible with modern distributed version control system (e.g., Git) and for ease of use;
- Documents should be able to persist alongside code and communicate to one another;
- Documents should be model-based as to have a separation of concerns between content and formatting as well as be both human and machine readable for querying and generating views.

A MBSE approach was adopted by the SeaLion CubeSat mission architecture team since it provided benefits such as reducing the ambiguity that usually comes with using informal language to specify systems or its various aspects. It also minimized the duplication of content that tends to accumulate in a document-based system engineering approach.

Proper adoption of a MBSE approach also includes the selection of the modeling language and modeling tool. Considerations when selecting the modeling language and tool was overhead incurred from training the team, the technical overhead of setting up modeling tools and future adaptability. Refer to Table 1 for modeling language down selection overview. In addition, the SeaLion CubeSat mission architecture team eventually decided to adopt a docs-as-code approach to further enhance the MBSE approach to achieve the listed goals shown above.

As noted before, attention should be given for planning, documentation, project management, and simplifying the process. Special emphasis should be given to systems engineering and information exchange [11].

Traditional approaches use documents as their authoritative source of truth for conducting system engineering activities [1]. Information in a traditional systems engineering approach today is mostly captured informally. For example, this causes disadvantages such as information not being authored based on a methodology, spontaneously and infrequently integrated, not properly configuration managed, not properly changed managed, and not effectively shared with stakeholders [14]. These documents often do not have a living relationship with other documents or to other corresponding elements; thus, changes to one document require manual changes to other documents [15]. Document-based approaches can exacerbate problems since it lacks point-to-point communication channels as well as lacking methods to enforce consistency [16].

In contrast, a MBSE approach captures information in a highly structured modeling language, authored based on a methodology, configuration managed in a common tool, highly integrated, traceable to its provenance, and sharing with stakeholders. Models provide the following key advantages over document-based approaches [15]:
- Information is readily communicated and shared within the project.
- Changes are easily accommodated.
- Traceability is automated.
To showcase the benefits, an architecture process of 4858 information element transfers was performed. It noted that all of these transfers were performed manually with non-

MBSE approaches; however, 13% of these transfers were automated with MBSE with the potential of up to 81% should it be used for trade study and peer review tasks [17]. The SeaLion mission architecture team seeks to take advantage of these efficiency gains that MBSE can achieve. Space projects have been taking advantage of MBSE such as the ExoMars mission, Euclid, Galileo, and nanosatellite programs [18-20]. CubeSat projects have also been using MBSE and have shown to "hold promise of reducing the burden of system engineering tasks" [21] and can "promote uniformity and consistency across future CubeSat models" [21]. These attributes are important to reduce workload among team members and to facilitate new team members as they join future projects. Facilitation of new members is especially useful for universities since students are not available long term due to events such as graduation.

Documents-as-code (Docs-as-code) refers to a philosophy that team members should be writing documentation with the same tools as code [22]. This allows for documentation to be updated seamlessly without additional work with document tools (doctools). The code tools would include version control (e.g., Git), issues trackers, code tools (e.g., Visual Studio Code), etc. To do so would mean that writers would follow the same workflows as the development team and they would be integrated into the product team. A stated result would be to enable "a culture where writers and developers both feel ownership of documentation, and work together to make it as good as possible" [22]. The SeaLion team taking advantage of the aforementioned philosophy would realize the benefits of utilizing the same principles and practices used to manage software, using modern version control tools (e.g., Git), for the configuration management of mission and flight software architecture documentation, and captured in a model-based approach [22]. In addition, these models can be stored and used persistently on a local file system without the use of cloud based services. Proprietary services are not required to generate documentation, modify documentation, or modify models. Similar approaches have been seen in Structurizr [23] and F Prime Prime (FPP) [24]. FPP is based on F Prime which is an open-source software framework developed by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory [25]; it is a modeldriven approach for producing flight software code that can be compiled directly onto flight hardware. While docs-as-code has precedent, the methodologies noted are not easily accessible to those without a sufficient background in programming.

The languages considered were SysML V1 [26], SysML V2 [27], PlantUML [28], and the Mach 30 modeling language (M30ML) [29] with the mission architecture team conducting a trade study to determine the most suitable one. The down selection criteria that the SeaLion CubeSat mission architecture team has taken into consideration is shown in Table 1.

M30ML was chosen for its lightweight human and machine-readable textual syntax, file-based model interchange support (for persisting models directly on the local filesystem), ability to generate both textual and graphical views, and relatively minimal overhead with modern doctools [29]. The lightweight textual syntax and minimal overhead is especially important for for a team that has very minimal experience working with such tools. Other candidate modeling languages lacked in many regards compared to M30ML in these criteria and thus, M30ML was selected. SysML v2 had a good number of characteristics that M30ML had; however, the lack of minimal overhead with modern doctools prevented its adoption. At the time of publication of this article, the current state-of-the-art MBSE languages (e.g., SysML v2) have not prescribed an approach for file-based model interchange for persisting models on the local filesystem. SysML v1 has XML Metadata Interchange (XMI) as a file-based interchange but it can only handle graphical views and not textual views. Adapting other MBSE languages would take significant work to adopt a docs-as-code approach in their current states.

M30ML was developed using the Ontological Modeling Language (OML) as its basis. OML is a language that enables defining systems engineering vocabularies and using them to describe systems [30]. OML, inspired by Web Ontology Language 2 (OWL2) and the Semantic Web Rule Language (SWRL), is meant to be a more gentler and more disciplined method of the aforementioned standard for use in systems engineering [30]. OWL2 does not conform easily to individual modeling rules without tooling support; thus, OML was created. OML is a tool to improve the speed of modeling and the quality of models while in a more concise and human-friendly high-level external representation [31]. However, more recently, M30ML's development has been moved from OML to LinkML since it uses a lighter weight toolchain and YAML-based syntax [32].

M30ML is a language for modeling an architecture with YAML-based modeling. YAML as a file type is a highly structured, machine queryable, human readable, lightweight, and line-oriented markup language. This makes it ideal for document generation use cases as well as use with version control tools such as Git. The simple line by line structure as shown in Figure 8 exemplifies its simplicity. Users are readily able to read, interpret, and edit documents using the YAML file format so as long they are taught what each line element is. Doctools such as asciidoctor and bibtex were made compatible with minimal technical overhead which was taken advantage of for the submission to the AIAA SciTech 2023 Forum [4]. M30ML also provided modeling elements familiar in agile software development, such as stakeholder needs, user stories, data structures, and with relationship elements for defining traceability between modeling elements [29].

The implementation of M30ML serves as the basis for SeaLion mission architecture. Presented here are the various elements, components, and products generated that is stored on the SeaLion-mission-architecture GitHub page [13]. At the time of publication of this article, the implementation of the SeaLion mission architecture was performed to the prior mission parameters where the SeaLion CubeSat was designed for a short lifespan compared to now greatly extended planned lifespan. Since the mission parameters was changed rather recently prior to publication, the architecture had yet to be updated for them.

The SeaLion mission architecture is organized into two main folders of architecture and of components [13]. Architecture contains the references, stakeholder needs, user stories, and data structures shown in Figure 9. Components, as the name implies, contains the components and subcomponents of the CubeSat. For the focus of this article, the architecture folder is the primary concern. Components is currently a work in progress at time of publication of this article and will be addressed with future required work. For the mission architecture shown in Figure 9, generally data structures are derived from user stories. Furthermore, user stories are subsequently derived from stakeholder needs with their respective references.

The development of SeaLion's mission architecture is guided by a series of stakeholder needs [33]. After SeaLion's project methodology documentation is committed to using M30ML based on YAML modeling tools, the first step is to identify all stakeholder needs. The two primary stakeholders of SeaLion are ODU and the USCGA. Their respective needs are classified from primary, secondary, and tertiary based on mission importance.

Stakeholder YAML files are stored in the '1-StakeholderNeeds' folder shown in Figure 11. Each file is numbered with a X.X number format with the first number designating if it is primary, secondary, or tertiary and the second number denoting a place within a list of that class (e.g., 1.1 would indicate primary stakeholder need 1). In addition, the letter associated (e.g., A1, B1, C1, etc.) in the filename would also signify if it's a primary, secondary, or tertiary stakeholder need. Each YAML file contains an id number, name, statement, and derived-from field shown in Figure 12. Note the reference YAML file that has filed in the derived From field that serves as the basis for the stakeholder need. While not all stakeholder needs have it filled, it is available to be used as needed. Figure 11 showcases all the YAML files stored in the stakeholders file folder.

Once the SeaLion mission architecture's stakeholder needs are identified and recorded, the stakeholder needs are then used to identify a series of user stories which then lead to design decisions captured in data structure and activity definitions [34]. These user stories are written from the perspective of the ground operator which would be a student from ODU who monitors and controls the functions of the SeaLion CubeSat. User story YAML files are stored in the '2-UserStories' folder shown in Figure 14. These files are all given an ID number in no particular order of importance. See the following Figure 14 for the user story YAML file structure.

As an example, the second user story desire is to "verify that satellite is operating nominally" [13]. Its full statement, derived from the actor, behavior, and rationale, would read "as a Ground Station Operator I want to view satellite beacon data (alternating between health and mission data), received via UHF so that I can verify that satellite is operating nominally" [34]. Its associated YAML file named '2-ViewBeaconData.yaml' is presented in Figure 15. Note that this user story is derived from stakeholder needs A1, A3, A5, B1, B2, C1, C2, and C3 which are stakeholder needs mentioned in the prior section detailing stakeholder needs. Additionally, the example statement is cut-off in Figure 15 for readability. It should read in full as "View satellite beacon data (health or mission data) to verify that state vector correspond with expected orbit profile and/or to validate that a mission mode was successful". This satellite beacon data, transmitted via UHF, is used to validate that any and all functions of the satellite are operating nominally or as planned in respect to their payloads hence the large derived-from list in the associated YAML file.

As noted multiple times throughout this article, there have been a number of figures and tables generated from the YAML files placed within the SeaLion mission architecture GitHub repository. Many of the figures are UML diagrams that are auto-generated artifacts rendered from the M30ML modeling language and formatted using the Liquid template language. This is how the docs-as-code approach is implemented. YAML code files are used to generate documents for information sharing between group members. This means that any changes made to the SeaLion mission architecture model can immediately be used to generate new documents. Whether it be diagrams, tables, or text, continuous updating is ensured that any changes affecting dependencies within the mission architecture are kept in sync. YAML files are automatically processed using templates language (e.g., Jinja2) via a build shell script. This also means that content of the model and formatting of documents are decoupled. The model is formatting-agnostic for documentation purposes as this is handled by the template language. A conference proceeding manuscript presented in AIAA SciTech 2023 was created purely by a docs-as-code format [4]. The team used a LaTeX template to automatically format the manuscript to the conference guidelines and subsequently inject items such as the generated diagrams, tables, and references directly into the manuscript.

The implementation of M30ML for components, at the time of this article's publication, is currently in the process of integrating content information into the model. A brief description of current component implementation into the SeaLion model is provided. However, the model content mentioned herein is subjected to change.

The current SeaLion mission architecture repository, at time of article publication, for components is "structured as a Distributed OSHW Framework (DOF)—component for defining the contents of the Mission concept of operations (ConOps) as a collection of nested subcomponents, component interfaces, and component functions for generating bill of materials (BOMs) and assembly instructions for the SeaLion CubeSat" [13]. The DOF pillars are based on Open Source Hardware (OSHW) principals [29]. The implementation methodology presented herein is an extension of M30ML specifically for the use of modeling a CubeSat design.

The SeaLion mission architecture repository has a components folder dedicated to its namesake. Inside the components folder of the repository are two subfolders; one labeled with 'sealion-cubesat' and another labeled with 'sealion-ground-station'. Each of those folders would contain a components folder and subsequently those individual labeled components can have their own components folder. Thus, a chain of components and subcomponents can be created as illustrated in Figure 21. A parts YAML file in each components folder details what the subcomponents would be. Implementation of the overall mission architecture has been successful for the original mission profile. Future work includes adapting the mission architecture to the new mission profile from the launch delay. For example, it has spawned a trade study for rechargeable batteries and solar panels. However, the original mission architecture does not require any extensive reworking since many attributes are similar. The mission architecture requires only a few sessions between team members to make adaptations. All documentation would be automatically updated to reflect these changes per the docs-as-code approach which will eliminate additional work in that category.

Extensions to the DOF data model are also under development for enabling additional use cases, such as the N2 chart, for CubeSat systems engineering [33]. This extended data model would serve as a self-describing specification that new CubeSat projects could adopt for their own CubeSat missions, whereby the SeaLion mission would serve as the first reference implementation. Additionally, training material will be developed around this new data model in efforts to help guide incoming CubeSat developers. Multiple team members of the SeaLion mission have been able to quickly learn the methodology of using the docs-as-code approach within a short training session with an experienced member. However, a fully realized tutorial would be beneficial to allow for self-learning. Current guides are lists of definitions and format guides rather than a step-by-step tutorial on using the approach, which has caused confusion among members that attempted to learn the material by themselves.

Additionally, observations from the implementation of the docs-as-code approach noted that an effective communication plan between team members is key to the overall effectiveness of the mission architecture. Team members focused on specific parts of the CubeSat's development (e.g., structure, payload, etc.) are required to add all necessary content to the architecture. If team members are unavailable due to other more important obligations (e.g., university courses), it can cause considerable delays in the architecture's completion. The SeaLion mission architecture team necessitated frequent meetings with individual team members to gather the necessary content for the architecture to capture

all legacy work. Legacy work refers to design decisions made prior to the architecture model's introduction. In an ideal case, a mission architecture would be formatted prior to any major design decision so that all team members can work directly on the architecture model rather than adapting legacy work to the model.

The SeaLion mission architecture team used MBSE with a docs-as-code approach to the SeaLion project. This was performed in an effort to reduce the friction and disconnect associated with traditional systems engineering for CubeSat developers. This is particularly important when CubeSat projects are growing more numerous with many of their respective team members being new to space systems development. The methodology presented herein has accomplished the ability to create individual elements of the architecture in an human readable code that is also easy to make revisions to and persists on a local file system. Even for those who are unfamiliar with coding software or methodology. Thus, minimal training is required for usage. The mission architecture presented captures the necessary information required of its original mission profile while also generating documents for easy presentation as well. Further work is required to create tutorials to train new users in a self-learning environment. Other future work includes the components implementation to facilitate interfaces and junctions for proper component relationships and planning, DOF data model extensions, and adaption to the new mission profile. Additionally, new users to this methodology should establish an effective team communication plan at the beginning of a project in order to prevent delays or rework in the creation of a mission architecture.

Abstract—The benefits of using Model-based System Engineering (MBSE) approaches for the development of projects go beyond just replacing document-centric methods. MBSE is expected to aid in the ability to manage complexity and capture knowledge. By using MBSE approaches on CubeSats this paper aims to address notions of traceability and how system models can be used to verify the fulfillment of requirements. This work is carried out in Papyrus, an open-source model-based engineering tool, and builds on existing studies regarding CubeSats system models. The development of these sorts of models can benefit future CubeSat developers by reducing design time and cost. These models can also be used in an academic setting to facilitate learning about CubeSats and their design process. In this paper, a CubeSat power subsystem SysML model is presented, while the notion of traceability is introduced by the creation of a specific profile for model assumptions and a java code that allows visualizing the impacts of the change of one or more parameters of the CubeSat model. The model proposed in this paper contains key information about a system, such as requirements, structure, behavior, and analysis. This model-based approach for CubeSat subsystems helps to visualize and understand what is needed for the design of a CubeSat power subsystem, while guaranteeing that the designers are clearly aware of which requirements are being met and which are not.
Index Terms—MBSE, CubeSat, Traceability, Power Subsystem, Papyrus.

The new space age [1] is characterized by an increased access to space. This has been made possible by new: launch service providers, launch vehicles, space systems technologies, and international partnerships. CubeSats have as well played a major role [2], they were first proposed in order to help students gain satellite engineering experience, without their traditionally high costs to build and launch [3]. The reduced cost of CubeSats encouraged a "democratization" of space, and their use has now spread to applications such as alternative platforms for experiments and laboratories, affordable technology demonstrators and proof-of-concept platforms, payloads outside of Earth orbit, and so on [4]. Throughout the last couple of decades there has been a rapid rise in the use of CubeSats [5], increasing to hundreds per year. CubeSats are highly versatile platforms that can be used for different mission objectives. This versatility, plus accessibility, standardization, entrepreneurship, technology, and community [2], has enabled its worldwide adoption.

For over 10 years, the INCOSE Space Systems Working Group (SSWG) Challenge Team has conducted research into the applicability of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) to build a CubeSat design model [6]. This team has focused on the elaboration of a sufficiently complete CubeSat System Reference Model (CSRM) that can be adapted to any CubeSat project and so far more than 20 research papers have been published by this working group [7]

Although the concept and design stage account for only roughly 15% of the total mission cost, they commit 70-80% of the life-cycle cost [8], [9]. The study of MBSE approaches for the design of CubeSats could help lower the time and effort behind its development. Therefore, the current paper aims to expand on the previous work done within the SSWG, while proposing a modeling methodology for a MBSE approach to CubeSat design, to guarantee traceability early from the conceptual stage. The traceability enabled by data integration can contribute to automating the design optimization of CubeSats and allow for the early detection of potential design errors.
For this purpose, the current paper:
- proposes additional concepts that can be added to the existing model,
- illustrates with an example of the application of the proposed modeling methodology for a CubeSat power subsystem in the open-source MBSE tool Papyrus, and
- presents an automatic requirement verification approach from system model data with a java code.

This paper is organized as follows. After the introduction, Section II briefly presents CubeSats, their MBSE modeling, and state-of-the-art traceability methods. Section III then presents the proposed methodology to elaborate the new model, as well as the taken architectural decisions. This section also presents the traceability aspects of the model, and its implementation is discussed. The results of this model and its traceability implementation are analyzed and discussed in the fourth section. Section V concludes the paper with an outlook for future work perspectives.
CubeSats are a type of nanosatellite that must respect certain specifications regarding attributes such as shape and size [10]. They are usually launched as secondary payloads, taking
advantage of piggyback launch capabilities, and they stand out as companies are able to mass-produce their components and offer them as components off-the-shelf (COTS) [11].

Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) can be defined as "the formalized application of modeling to support system requirements, design, analysis, verification, and validation activities beginning in the conceptual design phase and continuing throughout development and later life cycle phases" [12]. MBSE is part of a long-term trend toward model-centric approaches in order to replace document-centric approaches. The application of MBSE is expected to provide the following benefits [12], [13]:
- Enhance productivity and quality,
- Increase ability to manage system complexity,
- Improve ability to teach and learn systems engineering fundamentals, and
- Enhance knowledge capture,
- Provide improved communications among the system development team.

In order to achieve these goals, the MBSE Initiative was launched at the INCOSE International Workshop in 2007. This initiative creates Challenge or Activity Teams that promote the research of specialized areas of MBSE-related development activity or work on specific challenge problems. These Challenge Teams include, in particular, the Space Systems Working Group.

The INCOSE Space Systems Working Group (SSWG) created the CubeSat System Reference Model (CSRM) based on SysML (System Modeling Language). SysML is a graphical modeling language, that enables to visualize and communicate essential aspects of a system's design, such as structure, behavior, requirements, and parameters [14]. SysML proposes the following diagrams to visualize and communicate these aspects: Requirement Diagram, Behavior Diagrams (Activity, Sequence, State Machine, and Use Case Diagram), and Structure Diagrams (Block Definition, Internal Block, Parametric, and Package Diagram).

Over the years SSWG members have actively covered different aspects of the model. The CubeSat case study objectives and the basis of the model framework were presented in [15]. A way to extend the CSRM was shown by demonstrating the ability to model behaviors and scenarios using simulation tools such as Matlab [16]. An eight-step methodology for defining the behaviors of CubeSats was published in [17]. It starts with mission requirements and ends with providing a functional architecture modeled as an activity hierarchy. The integration of this methodology in the CubeSat System Reference Model is fully justified considering that it provides the following advantages as pointed out in [17]:
- A repeatable and generalized method for CubeSat development, and
- A method including standard systems engineering practices (top-down approach, requirement definition and analysis, functional analysis, and use case realization).

A topic that is rarely associated with MBSE in the literature concerns technical measures [18]. Technical measures can be used to determine if the technical solution will meet stakeholder needs, provide early indications if the development effort is not progressing as needed to meet key milestones, predict the likelihood of the delivered solution meeting performance requirements, monitor high-risk items, and assess the effectiveness of risk mitigation actions [18], [19].

In recent years the Space Systems Working Group published two papers [20], [21] about the CSRM application and possible opportunities to extend this model. In addition, two theses on CubeSat model development were published [22], [23]. Even though the models proposed in these theses are not 100% in line with the SSWG CSRM model, they provide an alternative view and a contribution to the practical implementation of the model.

Traceability can be defined as the quality of having an origin or course of development that may be found or followed [24]. SysML proposes some basic elements to ensure a sort of requirement traceability [25]:
- Requirement ID,
- Requirement relationships (satisfy, verify, trace, etc.), and
- The possibility to customize SysML for specific domains using profiles and stereotype definition.
Unfortunately, the basic requirement attributes and relationships present two majors drawbacks:
- A limited coverage of the various traceable aspects of the requirements, and
- A fully manual set-up and update procedure.
An example of this limited coverage can be the absence of information on the author of a requirement, the update dates, eventual documentation/standards associated with a requirement, etc.

In order to solve these problems, a SysML-based approach was proposed to enhance requirements traceability in SysML model diagrams and generate trace links at different levels of granularity in [24]. This approach is based on two elements: a SysML profile for expanding requirements definition and traceability, and an algorithm allowing trace generation. This profile includes the following elements for requirement traceability: type, status, source, stakeholder, etc.

An alternative approach based on the Design Structure Matrices (DSM) usage was presented in [26]. They present an algorithm and a tool to extract data from the output model files and obtain either a requirement DSM, function DSM, or component DSM, or alternatively a multidomain matrix that includes all relations between the requirements, functions, and components.
Illustrated with a CubeSat power subsystem model, this section presents how modeling can be realized to provide better traceability and ease of reproduction (the model can

be found here $ ^{1} $ ). For the purposes of this study, the actual implementation of the model was done in Papyrus [27] based on SSWG work cited before. One of the goals was to incorporate traceability improvements into the model, meaning a visualization of the impacts of parameter changes on other parameter values and related requirements.

1) Papyrus: is an industrial-grade, open-source ModelBased Engineering tool that allows the creation of customized profiles, where the user has the possibility to create models from specifications [28]. Papyrus provides the following advantages/capabilities [28]:
- Papyrus can be used as an Eclipse plugin, which allows us to extend the functionality of Papyrus by installing other Eclipse plugins,

- Papyrus supports two kinds of editors (diagrams and tables) and allows to have a combination of these representations in a single project (this allows to have multiple representations of the same type or create a completely new representation),

- The tool supports the creation of profiles that can be applied to other parts of a model using the stereotypes created in these profiles (stereotypes that allow to add constraints, properties, etc., and to customize the model for a specific domain), and
- With Moka (Eclipse plugin) models can be executed using a rich and extensible animation and simulation framework.

Papyrus-made models can be also used as a base for developing data extraction tools, such as the one presented in [26] based on TTool system models. As mentioned above, Papyrus is industrial-grade open-source software, and another benefit of this is that it enables the modeling effort to be more accessible.

2) Model Landing Page: When starting to model, it was decided to create a landing page with the help of a package diagram, to provide an overview of the subsystem. Our power subsystem model landing page (see Fig. 1) is composed of the following fundamental aspects of the model: requirements, structure, behavior, and analysis. It is an adaptation of the 10 different categories that the CSRM presents [20]. Each of these parts is discussed in more detail in the following sections.

3) Requirements Development: Requirements play a major role in systems engineering [9], as they: form the basis of system validation and stakeholder acceptance, act as a reference for integration and verification activities, and serve as a means of communication between the technical staff, management finance department, and the stakeholder community.

The model requirements package accessible through the landing page is divided into two main parts: Assumptions and Requirements. In the case of the Cubesat power subsystem that serves as an illustration of how this methodology could be applied to other subsystems, the assumptions concern the
Fig.1. Model landing page

power budget parameters on which the design team will not have a direct impact (such as the radius of the Earth, that is assumed to be equal to 6378 km). Generally, these values are fixed by external constraints/forces, or constitute an initial assumption and will therefore only be changed by the project team/customer if it has been demonstrated that it is not viable.
The identification of requirements is crucial throughout the entire life cycle of a system. For a subsystem, we propose to consider the following kind of requirements:

- The "general" requirements can be traced back to CubeSat standard specifications, such as the standard requirements applicable to CubeSats from 1U to 12U format. These requirements can be obtained by consulting documents maintained by, among others, California Polytechnic State University Aerospace Engineering members. These documents can be found in [29]. These requirements notably may have an impact on the components that can be selected.
- The "mission-specific" requirements consist of requirements specific to the mission in question and which may have an impact on the specificities/customization of a CubeSat.

4) Structure Development: The power subsystem presents three main parts: the power generation, power storage, and power supply control parts; plus the bus. Fig. 2 shows the block definition diagram (BDD) of this subsystem for an architecture based on solar energy as an energy source. In addition, the use of an internal block diagram (IBD) is recommended to specify interactions that occur on an internal level of the subsystem. IBD enables to convey additional information that BDD can't convey such as the connections among part properties and reference properties; the types of matter, energy, or data that flow across the connections; and the services that are provided and required across the connections [14].

5) Behavior Development: The behavior of a subsystem can be described in different ways and SysML provides several diagram types to be able to visualize these different descriptions: use case, activity, sequence, and state machine diagrams [14]:
Fig. 2. Power subsystem structure

- Use Case Diagram (UCD): used to express information about the services your subsystem provides, the stakeholders who require those services, and the subsystem components which provide these services.

- Activity Diagrams (AD): used to express sequences of behaviors and event occurrences over time. This kind of diagram is particularly adapted to expressing the flow of objects-matter, energy, or data-through a behavior, with a focus on how the objects can be accessed and modified in an execution of that behavior during system operation

- Sequences Diagram (SD): used to express sequences of behaviors and event occurrences over time as an AD. This sort of diagram is a good choice for specifying a behavior when you want the focus to be on how the parts of a block interact with one another via operation calls and asynchronous signals that can have an emergent behavior.

- State Machine Diagram (SMD): used to tackle the same goal as SD and AD but this kind of diagram focuses attention on how a structure within a system changes state in response to event occurrences over time

In the case of the power subsystem model, a UCD was constructed (Fig.3), as well as an SD so as to specify functions of the UCD if necessary. It can be seen that the power subsystem's main use case is generalized in two more concrete cases which are: "generate electric power" and "control". This last use case itself specified with other functions: "store power", "distribute power" and "protection". These different use cases can then be observed in different situations using sequence diagrams. For example, the manage energy use case may mean charging or discharging the battery and these cases can be realized in different conditions. Fig. 4 shows the battery in sunlight time. In this paper only nominal behavior is shown as in [30] without loss of complexity, mission modes are not discussed in this paper. However, the methodology presented here can be extended to take mission modes into account by creating complementary behavioral diagrams for the concerned
modes.

6) Analysis Development: This part presents how the proposed modeling approach addresses system analysis, which should facilitate decision-making regarding system components selection/design and performance. For the power subsystem this includes the power budget and the following diagrams were used:
- A BDD containing constraint blocks that allows defining the different relationships present in the budget, and
- A parametric diagram (PAR) that allows displaying the bindings between constraint parameters in different constraint expressions to create a composite system of equations [14].

The power budget must be met to ensure that the consumed power does not exceed the produced power by the CubeSat [31], which is essential for mission success. The BDD of this budget (see Fig. 5) shows the different constraints and the associated parameters that will be used to build the associated PAR. This PAR is linked to the power budget block and shows the power budget like a "black box", with the constraint relationships inside the block.

SysML is a general-purpose modeling language that is intended to support a wide range of domains [25]. SysML includes its own extension mechanisms in order to extend existing SysML concepts (e.g. Requirements) with additional properties and constraints. These mechanisms are called stereotypes and are grouped in profiles, which are therefore particular packages used to customize to specific application domains. For example, a profile to improve traceability in SysML model is presented in [24]. For the case study of the power subsystem, the construction of profiles can be useful in the following cases:
- The improvement of information traceability by creating profile-specific properties. These properties will then be identifiable, and their changes and impacts visualized.
Fig. 3. Power subsystem UCD
Fig. 4. Battery discharging sequence diagram
- The generation of a sort of library with typical CubeSat components with their parameters to promote its reusability throughout different system models.

For our model, an assumptions profile was created and applied in order to include assumptions. This profile allows the java script presented in this paper to distinguish assumptions from other elements of the model and treat them appropriately. An assumption is composed of two elements: the parameter name for which a value is assumed, and a constraint with the assumed value ("Parameter name = assumed value"). Thanks to this assumption format, the code is able to impose this value on the specified parameter and take it into account during the subsystem analysis. This profile has been used to specify the assumed value of each parameter listed in Table II. More generally, this profile is useful to set the values that are external to the project. For example, in our case, the radius of the Earth or its standard gravitational parameter. Finally, this profile can
allow teams in the future to reuse previous models easier as they wouldn't need to guess what assumptions were made, and what their value was.
For the case study of the power subsystem, the following objectives were defined:
- Provide requirement "usual" traceability, and

- Provide parameter impact traceability and visualization. "Usual" traceability implies traceability achieved using only Papyrus tools. SysML proposes some elements to ensure this traceability aspect (see Section II) and also profile creation allows to improve this part. For example, [32] proposes a profile based on questions to obtain all information necessary for this first traceability aspect. In the case of the power subsystem model, the choice was made not to carry out a traceability-oriented profile, favoring the creation of a simple profile for the assumptions so that they are well handled by the code.

In the here presented model for the power subsystem, a choice was made to limit the sort of diagrams used, for example, AD and SMD were not used, as for the purposes of our analysis they were not essential. Nevertheless, the model proposes a concise and understandable view of a CubeSat power subsystem. The main objectives were to:
- Obtain an overview of the power subsystem requirements and assumptions used in the power budget (achieved through the Requirement Diagram and assumption profile),
- Obtain a visualization of the power subsystem, its components, and its main parameters (achieved using a BDD),
- Show the component interactions (achieved using an IBD),
- Obtain an analysis of the CubeSat power subsystem through the power budget and observe the roles of the different parameters (achieved using a Constraint BDD and a PAR),
- Visualize power subsystem functions and their allocation to system components (with a UCD), and
- Show the time sequence of the main functions (through an SD).

The model can be found in the project repository $ ^{2} $ . This model in combination with the Java script is used for traceability and visualization of "non-usual" aspects. The model presented in this paper can be considered as a good starting point for users wishing to design a CubeSat power subsystem and have traceability throughout its parameters. One of the advantages of the model proposed in this paper is that it was constructed using Papyrus which is an open-source software. This means it can easily be reproduced by those who wish to use it and adapt it to their own needs. Besides, guidelines are suggested in order to increase the verifiability of requirements using a traceability process. This model-based approach for CubeSat subsystems helps to
visualize and understand what the structure of a CubeSat power subsystem is, as well as its functions.

The Java code discussed in this paper has the potential to improve traceability throughout models made using the Papyrus Eclipse's plugin with SysML 1.6. In this paper, an example application is presented that uses the proposed assumption profile and follows the guidelines proposed in section IV to create the model elements. The code allows the visualization of the impacts of the different parameters of the model when their values are changed and whether the different model constraints are respected or not following these changes.

While this paper provides good insights into how CubeSats subsystems can be modeled in Papyrus and introduces notions of verifiability, it also paves the way for future work perspectives in this domain. For instance, the development of reusable standard profiles for all CubeSat components for all subsystems, and requirement types. These profiles could then be used by anyone wishing to design a new CubeSat, potentially making the modeling process less time-consuming and improving the adoption of such models in organizations. Indeed, if such profiles were available and used, it would mean that models would present standardized components, associated parameters, and their notations. Secondly, the Java code can be further developed for it to work with more complex SysML models (a complete CubeSat model for example) and to visualize changes directly in the model after its execution. When the MBSE modeling framework and traceability analysis will be at a stage mature enough to aid in the development of CubeSats, a quantitative benefit study could be performed in order to assess key performance indicators such as cost and time. Currently, the expansion of the model to cover other subsystems is in progress.

This article presents the systematic design process for a low-cost 6U CubeSat platform, drawing on the experience of the highly motivated Pluto team. The team's success in a national academic CubeSat design competition led to the establishment of a space startup and the decision to develop a 6U platform. The primary motivation for writing this research is to increase access to space and space services by helping startups _especially in underdeveloped countries, design and build a CubeSat with the least cost and effort in the shortest possible time. In the design process, simplicity, reliability, and the possibility of reproduction at the lowest possible cost have been prioritized. Aligned with ECSS standards tailored for CubeSats, the design method parameters of the 6U platform are thoroughly examined. The article highlights the development of a state machine and the justification of design requirements through standard methods and tracking them using RTM and RVTM tables. Effective interface control while using COTS components is emphasized to reduce costs by approximately 50% while ensuring quality and meeting space environment requirements. The architecture of the Pluto platform, comprising entirely of commercial components, is showcased, providing insights into its system characteristics. This systematic design underscores the importance of modularity, affordability, and utilization of COTS components. By sharing their experiences, the Pluto team aims to support space industry startups and inspire innovative CubeSat projects.
Keywords CubeSat·Small satellite·System engineering·COTS·Off the shelf·Platform

Modern CubeSats are a special class of nanosatellite. The size of one-unit (1U) CubeSat is $ 1 0 \mathrm{c m} \times 1 0 \mathrm{c m} \times 1 1 \mathrm{c m} $ CubeSats can be composed of several combinations of the 1U to form up to 6U or even more [1]. Initially, CubeSats were developed in universities for elementary applications only. Due to the advancement of technology, especially in the production of small, light, and high-efficiency electronic components, it became possible to using CubeSats in more complicated missions like Scientific research or proof of technology which is going to be used on large satellites;

these researches still primarily done in universities. In the last decade, CubeSats are being produced for industrial purposes and in a highly competitive commercial sector. According to a Statistical Overview in 2020, about 56% of CubeSats are developed by small companies [2]. In fact, in 2003, only six CubeSats were launched, and all of them were made by universities. Whereas, in 2018, about 150 of the 240 CubeSats made by companies were developed [2]. Recently, CubeSats are even used for deep space exploration; their small size and weight enables CubeSats to "piggyback" on rocket launches and accompany orbiters travelling to Moon and Mars [3]. Thanks to CubeSats, many major universities now have a space program. But it is not just major universities; smaller universities, high schools, and middle schools have also been able to start CubeSat programs of their own [4]. CubeSats have made space accessible for small companies, students, and small institutions underdeveloped countries. According to ECSS standards, Iran space agency decided to hold a design competition for designing a 3_U CubeSat. Pluto team

has earned first place in both the detailed design and engineering model phase; after that, the Pluto team decided to start its start-up and build a 6_U platform; this paper will review the design of a low-cost 6U CubeSat Platform done Based on Pluto Experience. In 2012, an 8 kg 6U CubeSat was designed which was capable of performing Earth Observation missions equivalent to those of current 50-150 kg microsatellites. Based on this research, a constellation of 35 6U CubeSats would have approximately the exact launch cost as the five RapidEye satellite constellations. The data downlinked by the 6U CubeSat constellation would be of much higher temporal resolution since the constellation could contain seven planes of five spacecraft each, compared with a single plane of five spacecraft for the RapidEye constellation [5]. Therefore, CubeSats could be a solution for the enormous costs of space programs, and they can make space accessible for more people. From the beginning of CubeSats, engineers have tried to come up with cheaper and faster ways to make them. Scientists have been trying to produce CubeSats by 3-D printers and COTS components and engage students in the designing process to prepare them for future works [1,6]. In 2018, Sua Song design a 3U CubeSat Platform to service 1U payloads, and he reduce the time required to prepare a satellite from 1 year to several months [7]. In 2018, Madry proposed using commercial off-the-shelf components that have not been spaceflight eligible in CubeSats [8]. In 2019, Western University designed a 2U cube satellite to facilitate the learning of aerospace students and to be prepared for future projects [9]. In 2019, the University of Manitoba designed a CubeSat and used a new method of satellite design with a creative management approach to improving access to space for smaller organizations and for educational purposes [6]. In 2020, a new modular structure was proposed by N. Zosimovych to help students and Startups building a low-cost CubeSat structure [1]. In order to increase the speed of production and the possibility of adaptation to new production methods, in 2020, Espalin proposed the method of using 3D printers to build CubeSat's subsystem [10].

CubeSats are gradually doing the same operations that large satellites used to do, helping to make space accessible and benefit everyone from satellite services. Large and small companies are being attracted to the CubeSats market, but for start-ups, there are two main steps with a cheap and reliable CubeSat which is designed in a short time. First: understanding the design framework and the necessary requirements. Second: interfaces Control and provide cheap and reliable components. In sections one and two, a review of the minimum requirements, necessary documentation, and a sample of System architecture based on Pluto team experience for design a CubeSat platform in the shortest possible time is given. In sections three and four, few tables are presented to control the interfaces and a review of the prevalence of the use of off-the-shelf parts. Finally, in section five, Pluto

platform specifications are shown. Also, a technical budget and a minimum of common electrical interfaces have been proposed, which can help minimize the cost and time of the design and production process and simplify the selection of parts from existing commercial components.

In budgeting, it can be seen that the power and ADCS subsystem's weight is slightly higher than expected due to the use of commercial solar panels and homemade magnetorquers. If there is a need to reduce weight in structure using a 3D printer instead of aluminum and CNC machines is highly recommended. For tracing and verifying the requirements six parameters are regarded, the functional structure, validation phase, test description, the necessary physical structure in the related subsystem, the physical interface structure, and the description of the verification method. In Pluto, all components are selected as commercial components. Therefore, redundancy is considered for single-point failures in sensors and OBC boards. There are two CDH boards as cold redundant and an FPGA used as supervisor. All sensors and ODS are integrated into the ADCS board. The processing budget of the main board is considered in such a way that it can support all subsystem algorithms to manage their tasks and permit engineers to make some changes in future works. Interface control has been done at three levels_launcher and space environment and between subsystem components, all the engineers of all subsystems review these documents through the design and building phases. Subsystem interfaces are divided into sections of electrical, data, mechanical, and thermal. Mechanical interfaces include all the details of the subsystems simulated in the structural software model, Compliance with the mass and volume budget, Location of the element, Material of fittings and alloy used in fittings, requires spacer and if necessary, mention the required distance to other parts. The selection of the general specifications of the satellite is based on statistical studies on the platforms available in the market and the system requirements. The Pluto platform subsystems are EPS, ADCS, ODS, STR, TCS, TTC, and CDH. Payload interfaces are CAN, SPI, RS422/UART, maximum Payload mass could be up to 8 kg, Spacecraft mass is about 4 kg, and Satellite power is 6.4 Watt EOL (nadir) and 13W at EOL (sun pointing). In ADCS subsystem Accuracy is better than 3 deg, Knowledge better than 2 deg, Stability better than 0.42 deg/s, the link margin is 3 dB at a 5 deg elevation angle and data rates are VHF downlink equals to 9600 bps, UHF uplink is the same, S-band downlink is 4 Mbps.

Satellite subsystems are as follows: Power, attitude determination and control, orbit determination, structure, thermal control, command and data handling, communications. With the advancement of technology, CubeSats have become able to perform more complex missions, and designers are moving towards using 6-U platforms. Pluto's team chose 6U platform against 3U because they can provide enough power for telecommunication and Remote Sensing missions without using deployable solar panels and accept the related costs and risks, but just by orienting towards the sun and designing a suitable mode manager. Moreover, the 6-U platform offers more space to place more accurate Earth Observation (EO) components, precision position determination and servo mechanisms, extra batteries for IoT missions, or test multiple Space Science payloads simultaneously on a single platform. It is noticeable that although the 6-U platforms provide about twice as much space and power for the payload, its costs are about 1.5 times. Therefore, the budget table is related to a 6-U platform.

The mass budget intended for the ADSC subsystem is about 200 g more than usual, which is due to the use of homemade magnetorquers. The requirements are the do's and don'ts that, if met, can ensure that the purpose of the mission is satisfied. The European space agency has recommended a way to publish the requirements on the ECSS-E-ST-10C document. This document recommends first writing requirements based on the space environment, the purpose of the mission, and the lessons learned from previous CubeSats. Next, the sentences should review, then the importance of having those requirements is examined in the structure of RTM and finally published [13]. In other words, the requirements allocated to the system elements and their interfaces are traceable to the customer's requirements baseline [14]. Researchers have associated the waterfall methodology with "requirement freezing" early in the development life cycle, making the project inflexible and unable to respond to changing requirements or use cases. Also, high costs and efforts seem to be a major downside to the waterfall design process [15]. The goal here is to speed up the design process, so the minimum requirements for a platform are mentioned here to facilitate the selection among off-the-shelf components. Developing the correct requirements will lead us to choose the COTS in the right way. We need to achieve a specification tree base on the subsystem requirements. The requirements that are presented here are based on the experience of the Pluto team, CubeSats standards, review of documents from other satellites, and the statistical study to obtain the interfaces and the technical budget required to support the maximum range of payloads (the most crucial factor in designing a platform is
to be able to service the broadest possible range of payloads with different purposes and different interfaces).
1. The satellite platform should be designed to fit the dimensions of a six-unit cubic satellite.
2. The weight of the satellite platform, including all subsystems (Empty bus mass), should be a maximum of 6000 g.
3. The satellite must serve a payload with a weight of up to 8000 g.
4. The satellite must serve a payload with a volume of up to three units.
5. The satellite must communicate with the payload by CAN, SPI, RS422/UART ports.
6. The lifetime of satellites and their subsystems must be specified—at least 1 year.

7. The satellite must withstand the environmental conditions of its entire life cycle and carry out its mission according to the scenario correctly. (Includes radiation effects, effects of thermal changes, outgassing effects.)
8. The health signal must be defined for all subsystems.
9. All subsystems must follow the technical budget.
10. The possibility of failure of the satellite mission must be minimized.
11. The dimensions of the satellite boards should be maximum of $ 9 6 \times9 6 \times1 5 $ mm.
12. Satellite design strategy should be based on hardware redundancy. Hardware redundancy should not interfere with the mission.
13. The satellite must be equipped with a ground tester.
14. The satellite must be able to be stored for up to a year.
15. The list of sensitive items at the time of storage must be defined.
16. Critical parts should be inspected after storage.
17. Fault tree analysis (FTA) for the entire satellite must be performed.

18. If possible, a reliability analysis should be performed for the satellite. Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) and failure mode, effects, and criticality analysis (FMECA) should be performed.
19. The radio silence must be observed for 45 min.
20. Deployable elements must be activated after 30 min from separation.

Recently, in some projects, such as the Manitoba Sat-1, changeable requirements have been set, and Agile methodologies have been used to encourage designer creativity [6]. Although this is creative, if a team do not have enough design experience, for example, as a start-up or student team in underdeveloped countries which want to enter the field of space technology by using the advantage of low-cost CubeSats, the project can be led to technical problems or can be very time-consuming. In this project, a small number of system requirements are introduced as unchangeable requirements, and other requirements can be marked with a TBD, which are just a recommendation and can be changed based on design options. Since several requirements are changeable and denoted by TBD or TBR, it is necessary for the system engineer and project manager to be aware of the workflow of the subsystems to make sure that all members are aware of any changes in the requirements, especially interface requirements. A traditional approach is project control by the manager. One new approach presented in Manitobasat-1 Provides visibility to invisible work and guidance in the Agile philosophy and methods. The ManitobaSat-1 team uses Playbook's Kanban user interface to track the tasks performed by every team member and the team as a whole [6]. The suggestion of this research and what has followed in designing the Pluto platform is that the ICD and RTM documents should be read and updated by the subsystem's engineers every week, and every subsystem had a particular color to make his/her notifications on it. Lead system engineer declares the changes to all members weekly.

RTM:Requirements are verified by one or a combination of these methods: design review, testing, inspection, or analysis methods [16]. are used to formulate subsystem requirements. Subsystem requirements drive the design to the product tree.

section: 2.3 Verification and Justification Plan and a Way for Tracing the Requirements
section_key: 2 3 verification and justification plan and a way for tracing the requirements
text: Having a plan to justify the design and verifying is crucial because most CubeSats teams are start-ups, or student teams cannot withstand failure and will soon go bankrupt or frustrated. More than 1000 CubeSats launched, they still achieve less than 50% rate of successful missions, which is caused mainly by poor V&V processes. It should be pointed out that 50% of the CubeSat-based missions fail, and inexperienced teams develop 70% of them [17]. V&V - processes are crucial to all space missions to be successful & usually demanding time and money, which is incompatible with the U class development philosophy," faster and cheaper" [18]. There are two general ways to increase the chances of success of CubeSats. First: presents the CubeSat Reference Model—CRM—The goal of the CRM is to facilitate the design, verification, and validation of a CubeSat project using SysML [17]. This method is cheap and not very time-consuming. The Pluto team used SysML to develop a sequence diagram and the state machine and software. Other studies, [19, 20], focus on Model-Driven Engineering, aiming to automate the V&V of onboard embedded software. (Activity of space product V&V where different models are specified for the space mission, like Mockups, Engineering Model, Qualification Model, Flight Model, etc.) building all these models is costly, so in designing the Pluto platform, only the engineering model was developed. One way to justify a design is to justify the requirements and ensure that they are met. Justifying the requirements and ensuring that they are met is a cheap and necessary way to increase the CubeSat chances of success. In designing the Pluto platform, Table 3 has been used to justify the design and ensure that the requirements are met, in addition to compiling the state machine and building the engineering model.

As seen in the functional structure, the satellite has four operating phases and ten operating modes. Each mode also has several use cases that are called or not called depending on the conditions of entering the mode. These conditions will be described in the CONOPS and sequence diagram. These phases, modes, and use cases are defined to cover all the operational requirements of a platform in the simplest way. It is noticeable that the mission mode is defined according to the type of payload and is not described here.
Test phase In this phase, the satellite is integrated, and tests at the levels determined according to the model philosophy are applied to the system or subsystems.
Pre-launch phase This phase begins with completing the Test phase and includes storage modes, transferring, troubleshooting.

Storage mode In storage mode, the storage conditions of the satellite up to the subsystem level will be described. These conditions can include environmental conditions such as humidity or the need for a cleanroom or subsystem conditions such as battery charge level.

Transfer to launcher mode During the satellite transportation, packing conditions, possible required covers, and environmental conditions like humidity percentage or any necessary protection should be described.

Troubleshooting mode In this mode, the satellite is installed inside the pod in the launcher and once all the subsystems are activated and then deactivated, moreover the telecommunication link is established and tested, and then the battery will be 100% charged. By removing the RBF switch, the satellite will be ready to launch.
Initiate the mission_ nominal operation.
Launch phase This phase includes two modes of separation and deploying the antenna.

Release mode In this mode, the satellite exits from the pod then the Power distribution board is turned on by the switch at the end of the structure. Then CDH board is turned on and receives the first health signal from the subsystems.
Bootup & antenna development mode In this mode, the deployable antennas will extend after 30 min then the satellite will pass the time required for the radio silence.

Nominal operation phase Most of the satellite life will be spent in this phase. Nominal operations and safe modes are defined in this phase. Generally, after this phase, the satellite will enter the death phase.

Detumbling & Lost Satellite mode In this mode, magnetic torquers reduce the angular velocity created during injection in orbit. Also, if the satellite is lost, the mode manager will enter this mode to turn on the beacon signal (including health signals and position data). Health signals include: solar cell voltages, currents, temperatures, battery capacity, and satellite angular rates, subsystems health signals [16].

Standby mode After reducing the satellite's Angular velocity (to about 0.003 rad per second), CubeSat will orient towards the earth with an accuracy of three degrees (TBC). Calibration will also be performed in this mode. Collecting health data and being ready to receive signals from the ground station are also functions of this mode.
Mission mode: depending on payload.
Safe mode In this mode, three failures are defined to respond to three major types of failures.

One_increase the charge level is defined to recover batteries when the battery charge level reaches less than 30%. The health data collection loop is active in this mode, but the positioning will be done only through the propagator algorithm, not GPS.

Two_critical charge level Defined for the survival of the satellite and the chance of recovery if the charge level is less than 10% (TBC). In this mode, only the power generation and distribution system and the main processor will be working.

Three_Subsystem isolation If an error is detected in a use case by the FDIR algorithm, the system isolates the relevant section and converts the isolation information into a ready-to send packet to the ground station. Then switch to detumbling mode (lost-use case) and Waiting for the ground station order.

In addition to developing the functional structure, the CONOPS should be written to facilitate developing satellite software and mode management. The mission CONOPS also serves as an outline for identifying the relevancy between phases and modes [11]. The CONOPS formed for the Pluto platform is shown in Fig. 3. The necessary conditions for the transition between modes, which are summarily shown in Fig. 3, are described in Table 4.

As shown in the functional structure tree of detumbling use case of Detumbling & Lost mode in Fig. 4, each phase contains several modes. Moreover, each mode contains some use cases, including a description of the activities required to fulfill the mode's goal. A use case description must include entry conditions, exit conditions, active subsystems at that use case, and the purpose for which the use case is defined [21]. After entering a mode, the system enters one of the use cases of that mode based on the entry conditions. For example, the Pluto platform's Detumbling/Lost Satellite mode includes two use cases (Detumbling and Lost).

State machine: Now that the functional scenario is fully defined, this scenario can be implemented as a state machine. A functional state machine is a model that describes the behavior of a system by tracking the system's "mode state" [22]. MATLAB software has been used to develop the state machine of the Pluto platform. In each state, the necessary algorithms are called based on the scenario (and the use case) and put the system components in a predefined state. A table of coding is used to define the states of the components in each use case. These codes are then will apply to the state machine as a command. For example, a sensor can have both read and unread states, or a board can be in standby or operating modes (as can be seen in Table 5). To manage the System, the states of each component and all the algorithms should be defined in the state machine.

section_key: 3 use of off the shelf parts
text: As the demand for CubeSats increases, several companies offer ready-made parts for making CubeSats [23-27]. These parts can be easily assembled, but these parts are costly (Up to ten times a piece with the same performance but without a flight heritage), and it is not possible to supply them for student-teams or in developing countries. In addition, the suppliers of these parts are limited companies that have already launched satellites and have been able to validate the parts by flight heritage. As mentioned, the main reason for the growth of the CubeSats was the low final price compared to the large satellites. By advancing technology that caused reduced size and increased the quality
