section: ABSTRACT > 6.3.2 Tool Robustness and Variable Management
section_key: abstract / 6 3 2 tool robustness and variable management
text: The CubeSat Conceptual Design Tool was designed to have a long operational life cycle, meaning the tool can function and evolve over the years as CubeSats and the needs of their developers evolve. To enable this, the Design Options within the Assumption File of this tool are designed to easily be changed as technology matures over time, with a simple modification to a CSV file. Also, the Subsystem Design Modules were implemented so they run largely independent from each other, containing their own GUI, running their own calculations, and outputting their own results. Such an architecture allows for the tool to be gradually built and upgraded one subsystem at a time, improving the long-term sustainability of the tool.

section: ABSTRACT > 6.3.2 Tool Robustness and Variable Management
section_key: abstract / 6 3 2 tool robustness and variable management
text: However, there is one major weakness in that life-cycle plan, and that is managing the parameters that are utilized by the tool. While parameters are owned by a single Subsystem Design Module, they can be used by any other subsystem. This is a major feature of the tool, allowing design analysis utilizing a wide range of parameters from all subsystems, but it presents a problem during the piece-wise development of the tool. For example, modifications to one module changing or removing a variable can

section: ABSTRACT > 6.3.2 Tool Robustness and Variable Management
section_key: abstract / 6 3 2 tool robustness and variable management
text: break another module that relies on that variable. Furthermore, one subsystem's developer may realize they need a parameter from an already developed subsystem, but that subsystem was not developed to provide said parameter.

section: ABSTRACT > 6.3.2 Tool Robustness and Variable Management
section_key: abstract / 6 3 2 tool robustness and variable management
text: It is therefore critical for the parameters used by Subsystem Design Modules and their relationships with other parameters to be actively coordinated during the Conceptual Design Tool's development and sustainment. In order to do this, an interface control document (ICD) should be created, listing all available parameters in the tool for each subsystem, alongside what values they require for development or require them for use. Preferably, this document would be largely completed before all the remaining modules are created, so that future subsystem developers know what parameters they may need to include. However, this would require a multidisciplinary effort to gather the key parameters needed, and would not be a comprehensive list, as individual subsystems would not know all the parameters they use until their developed. An ICD containing the relationships between all of the parameters used by the Conceptual Design Tool is a major step towards building a stable, sustainable tool.

section: ABSTRACT > 6.3.2 Tool Robustness and Variable Management
section_key: abstract / 6 3 2 tool robustness and variable management
text: Another important aspect of building robustness into the tool is validating the values being input by the user. Currently, input validation only exists in a few places in the tool, mainly in the form of ensuring the user has made a selection where one is required. However, it has been found that Tkinter has validation attributes available for their data entry widgets that allows the program to check whether the entered values fit within predefined parameters, including numerical ranges and data types [41]. Implementing data entry validation for the current EPS Design Module and with all future subsystems should be completed to ensure the tool is usable even with imperfect users who are likely to mistype something while inputting large amounts of data.

section: ABSTRACT > 6.3.2 Tool Robustness and Variable Management
section_key: abstract / 6 3 2 tool robustness and variable management
text: Furthermore, there are changes that can be made to how data is read into the tool and how variables are assigned to be written out of it. Currently, this is done in a

section: ABSTRACT > 6.3.2 Tool Robustness and Variable Management
section_key: abstract / 6 3 2 tool robustness and variable management
text: location-driven manner, meaning that the locations of variables in the CSVs have to be permanently coded into the Subsystem Design Module. However, this is a delicate approach, and one that is readily broken if changes are made to the tool's code or the Assumption File for that module. A better way to access variables from the CSVs would be to use a name-driven look up method, where the tool looks for the variable's name in the CSV file and then assigns the variable to the adjacent data. This method is an improvement over a location-driven process because it allows for modifications to be made to an Assumptions File or a Subsystem Design Module without errors being introduced causing the wrong values to be read into one or more variables. This also makes adding to or modifying the parameters used in a subsystem significantly easier. Fortunately, the Assumption Files already contain the variable names for each parameter, and these are already read into the tool as well. Therefore, it is only a minor change to make the variable assignments based on a name-driven approach rather than using a specific location of an array that is coded into the tool. All future Subsystem Design Modules should follow this adaptable name-driven approach to reading and writing data to the CSVs rather than the inflexible location-driven approach.

Currently, the results of the design process are only available in the form of a CSV with the Output File. This makes it hard for a user to easily view their results, check their validity, and possibly iterate on the process to get a different design. To this point, creating a GUI-based results dashboard within the Conceptual Design Tool is highly desired. Such a feature would expedite the user's analysis of the results and could even provide an indication of whether the design is a valid result for a CubeSat.

One potential implementation of a results dashboard would be a pop-up window that appears after the tool runs. It could show the main takeaway results from the tool on one tab, with a more detailed breakdown of results by subsystem available in other tabs.

It could also highlight any values that were assumed when the tool ran because the user did not know them when inputting data. This would let user knows where there is uncertainty in the state of the design. It would also be important that the dashboard provides some interpretation of the results for the user, as they may not know what values are valid or feasible for their design. One way to do this could be by comparing certain resulting design values to preset limits for the estimated CubeSat size that the user chose in the Main GUI.

A potential long-term expansion for the dashboard development effort would be to integrate recommended COTS components for the CubeSat into the viewing of the results. This would require databases of CubeSat components for different subsystems and their specifications to be accessible to the Conceptual Design Tool. At the conclusion of the tool running, the components that fit the resulting design parameters would be selected from the component databases and presented to the user within the dashboard as possible options for them to use for their CubeSat.

Similar to the Conceptual Design Tool, the CubeSat Model requires continued development for the remaining subsystems. This work is mostly adding the packages for each subsystems parameters to be stored in and creating the tables to transfer data into those parameters. However, there is also room for the CubeSat Model to be further developed by potentially developing the requirements package and relating some requirements to results from the Conceptual Design Tool.

It also may be beneficial for a CPCL team member to work on the customization of the CubeSat Model so that the elements of the model fit to their specific CubeSat development process and organizational structure. Eventually, it may even be preferable to split off most of the modeling work from the CubeSat Conceptual Design Tool itself. The CubeSat Model could then be used and maintained by its primary users, while the
CubeSat Conceptual Design Tool would be the focus developers who specialize in conceptual design.

With many subsystems remaining to be developed, the Subsystem Design Module validation testing will only get more challenging as users have to include more comprehensive test cases that cover all available subsystems. Therefore, a set of universal test cases, that cover the inputs and outputs for every subsystem, would greatly assist future validation campaigns, especially if they could be automatically ran through a test script rather than physically entered into the tool. However, it is recognized that such automation may not be possible under the existing software architecture.

Furthermore, validation should be done on regarding the accessibility of the tool to CubeSat developers. Specifically, this should entail testing the comprehension of instructions available within the CubeSat Conceptual Design Tool and outside of it by users of differing technical backgrounds. It is important that the operation of the tool can be communicated to both experienced CubeSat developers and new users without institutional knowledge for support. Validating the accessibility of the tool should be an ongoing priority.

text: An ever-existent force is the growth and development of technology done to either improve an already existing system or to improve the standards of human life. In the past half century there have been leaps and bounds in technology improvement, as well as the standards of living, specifically because of the design and development of spacecraft. The continued growth and innovation have introduced boundless potential for engineering and science in the technological age. Though the usage of conventional spacecraft requires up to 15 years of development and operate for nearly the same amount of time (Larson and Wertz), this limits the frequency to which spacecraft can aid in the improvement of technology.

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > CHAPTER 1-INTRODUCTION
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / chapter 1 introduction
text: However, a new age satellite is the CubeSat. A satellite roughly 10 x 10 x 10 $ cm^{3} $ referred to as a 1U CubeSat. CubeSats, which fall under the nanosatellite class, often operate in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), conducting missions of all kinds from simple Earth imaging missions to RaInCube's precipitation profiling of Earth in 2018 (Peral et al.). Initially developed and designed by California Polytechnic State University San Luis Obispo (CPSLO) and Stanford University in 1999 (Chin et al.; Helvajian and Janson). These nanosatellites have become the cornerstone for universities to enable their students to obtain hands on experience with satellite development and testing. Simultaneously, CubeSats are also used in the Aerospace industry as testing equipment and sometimes as support vehicles for space missions, such as the Mars Cube One (MarCO) satellites used by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) in 2018 (Asmar and Matousek).

text: Meanwhile, within the International Council on Systems Engineering's (INCOSE) Space Systems Working Group (SSWG), the development of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) for CubeSat architecture has been in the works for nearly a decade now. The SSWG has published multiple articles on the physical and behavioral segments of CubeSats and their modeling within the MBSE program Systems Modeling Language (SysML) (Spangelo et al.; Kaslow et al.). However, these articles are limited in their actualization and usage due to their lack application to a non-hypothetical CubeSat project.

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > Literature Review
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / literature review
text: Though some publications provide information on the design and development of CubeSats and the application of systems engineering, a majority focus on the reliability of CubeSats and how to improve it (Nieto-Peroy and Emami; Venturini et al.; Ancheta). While some look into the statistical analysis behind CubeSat flight history (Toorian et al.; Villela et al.) and the areas to which reliability and missions correlate.

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > Literature Review
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / literature review
text: In some ways like the articles and publications mentioned above, this paper seeks to applied systems engineering methods to a CubeSat. The intention is to create a standardized model, similar to the SSWG's but applied to a non-hypothetical project that seeks to improve upon a technology. This standardized model, created with MBSE

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > Literature Review
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / literature review
text: methodologies and software, will be designed to improve the reliability of CubeSats throughout their development, design, and mission operations.

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > Research Objectives
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / research objectives
text: In support of technology development, this paper aims to achieve the following research objectives using CubeSats.

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > Research Objectives
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / research objectives
text: Objective 1: Create a standardized systems engineering model for CubeSat designers and developers as a basis to construct their satellites from. Currently, there has been little implementation of MBSE in existing CubeSat projects. This is similar to the SSWG research groups goal, who have been investigating for several years to determine the efficacy of MBSE in CubeSat development (Kaslow et al.; Spangelo et al.). The later sections of this paper are to demonstrate the usage of MBSE with the CubeSat design process from beginning stages of requirements development to the operation of the CubeSat in LEO.

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > Research Objectives
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / research objectives
text: Objective 2: Improve the success rate of CubeSats from academia and the viability of their usage in technology demonstration for industry. From 2002 to 2018 there have been over 850 CubeSats launched with only 29% of them being from academia. Furthermore, only about 240 CubeSats have been used in technology development and demonstration without even considering the success in their missions (Villela et al.). The standardization of CubeSat design and decision making including the integration and verification and validation (V&V) explained throughout this paper are intended to increase the usage rate of academic CubeSats in technology development while also decreasing the mortality rate.

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > Research Objectives
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / research objectives
text: Objective 3: Detail the usage of the standardized model in an actual technology development and demonstration project. The demonstration of the model in a CubeSat project that involves technology development is the paramount to proving the efficacy of CubeSats developed by academia as viable options for the mutual benefit of industry and universities. The later sections of the paper describe the process by which the MBSE model was used in a collaboration project between California State Polytechnic University of Pomona's (CPP) Aerospace Engineering department, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), and the United States Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL). Project Development and Support

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > Research Objectives
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / research objectives
text: The collaboration project above involves the design and development of a 3U CubeSat, by CPP students and staff. This CubeSat will incorporate a new thermal technology, proposed by several JPL technologists, and will be manufactured using additive manufacturing techniques on several of the CubeSat subsystems using AFRL facilities. The complexity of the project required the usage of systems engineering methodologies to address requirements tracking and documentation, subsystem designs, and system operational parameters including the life cycle of the CubeSat. To obtain concise data and design parameters and decisions, MBSE was a necessary practice for the project.

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > Research Objectives
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / research objectives
text: The usage of MBSE was welcomed by both the CPP team and the JPL advisors because of the simplicity of documentation and hierarchical needs as well as the operations and parametric analysis conducted within it. The CubeSat model became one of the backbones for the project as it gave direct context to constraints and design decisions needed to be carried out by the CPP team. The model's fidelity increased with

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > Research Objectives
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / research objectives
text: the assistance of the JPL advisors as it was tailored to the specific needs for the CubeSat project. The enthusiasm from the collaborators bolstered the potential of it from being a single project to a multi-project program, as such the need for a documented model that is easily modifiable for changing project goals is needed for the CubeSat Technology Exploration Program (CubeSTEP) to continue in the coming years.

text: Satellite development is an extremely complex process involving design, testing, manufacturing, and operations of the satellite. These projects involve countless numbers of personnel and work hours to ensure the successful development of the project from conceptual phases well into flight and operations finally ending in disposal and end of life modes. There are many different approaches to the life cycle of a project by various organizations as shown in Figure 2 below from Visualizing Project Management (Forsberg et al.). However, to fully encompass all aspects of a satellite's development process systems engineering is required to lead the way of successful projects.

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > CHAPTER 2-SATELLITE DEVELOPMENT
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / chapter 2 satellite development
text: Acting as the cornerstone of any project, systems engineering encompasses all stages of the design process from requirements development to architecture design and the eventual operations, maintenance, and disposal phases. Since the conception of spacecraft design, systems engineering has been an integral part of the design approach for these highly complex systems. Though industry has only steadily increased the implementation and usage of systems engineering in projects. However, it was originally used as a method of documentation for various project aspects such as design changes, testing plans, and review reports. With the increasing complexity of satellites and all supporting infrastructure and information, systems engineering became the go-to method of interconnection and integration of all parts of a project. The ability to define, design, and document all parts and decisions within a project has led to reduced costs, better scheduling, and increased reliability (Hirshorn).

text: launch vehicles, and even with other satellites. As such, spacecraft are considered a part of a system of systems, Figure 3, sfurther increasing the complexity of their design and functions. In both Spacecraft Systems Engineering (Fortescue

However, even these systems engineering methodologies are becoming impractical as spacecraft become increasingly unwieldy and complex in their system of systems for standard methods of approach, let alone are even less applicable for CubeSat missions.

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > CHAPTER 2-SATELLITE DEVELOPMENT
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / chapter 2 satellite development
text: Spacecraft design and development came from humble origins as did all engineering fields. Originally done with paper and pen methods for design and development, this often led to thousands of documents. These files were extremely difficult to track and ensure that they were up to date with the latest versions of a system's design. Due to this unmanageable practice, systems engineering took the stage to ensure the organization of a project's documents were orderly as well as distributed properly, becoming key in the flow of information on project details. Being the keystone of information for a project, systems engineering relies heavily on keeping up to date information, documentation of design changes, as well as managing integration and interconnection control throughout the system (Fortescue et al.).

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > CHAPTER 2-SATELLITE DEVELOPMENT
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / chapter 2 satellite development
text: Once the digital age began, systems practices became even more robust and prominent in projects. Digitizing the efforts of systems engineers and their tasks has significantly increase the efficiency and efficacy of their work. Digital documents and databases enable massive amounts of information to be stored, recorded, and kept with minimal additional work. However, even with the use of computers ensuring the distribution of up-to-date information is bulky and can often be misinterpreted when not

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > CHAPTER 2-SATELLITE DEVELOPMENT
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / chapter 2 satellite development
text: conveyed properly. To address the document-based information exchange in systems engineering, MBSE was developed introduced by INCOSE. With the creation of MBSE, direct interaction between teams and engineers on project became simple with models providing immediate updates to changes in design to all members working on a system. As MBSE has grown over the past two decades, it has become incredibly useful in providing system simulation and testing opportunities on designs before manufacturing even begins, significantly reducing costs and time associated with the design cycles.

section: In Partial Fulfillment Of the Requirements for the Degree Master of Science > CHAPTER 2-SATELLITE DEVELOPMENT
section_key: in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree master of science / chapter 2 satellite development
text: MBSE's influence is sweeping across industry with many organizations switching from the digital format of systems engineering to MBSE. With the trend of MBSE, it will likely become the most integral part of a system design regardless of the industry or size of project. It’s usage in nano-satellite development is inevitable, becoming one of the major reasons why INCOSE and many other organizations are putting focus into developing systems engineering practices for CubeSats (Spangelo et al.; Kaslow et al.; Schultz et al.; Bajaj et al.; Ancheta). Thus, a practical model of a CubeSat, developed alongside the beginning of an actual mission, is paramount to the future of MBSE and small satellite development.

The development of a systems architecture for CubeSats using MBSE methodologies is essential to the improvement of design and reliability of CubeSats in the future. To achieve this, the MBSE program Cameo Enterprise Architecture (CEA) from No Magic at Dassault Systemes is used to design the model-based design of the satellite and its supporting elements. The application of this software and a supporting add-on called SysML from No Magic is described in the remaining sections of the paper.

Due to the limitations of time, personnel, access to the SysML software capabilities, this constrained the level of fidelity of the designed CubeSat model. As such the model diagrams described in the remaining sections are based on the availability of the resources at hand as well as the knowledge of the software acquired during its development. Thus, the scope of the model was restricted to high and medium level modeling where overall system properties and elements like requirements development as well as the detailed subsystem design were implemented. However, intricate modeling of component interconnections and detailed software processing and sequencing was limited.

text: After the CubeSat's requirements development was completed and thoroughly modeled within the SysML software, the design for the various subsystem component diagrams were begun. Describing the necessary components of a satellite is difficult when there are thousands of parts involved, as such SysML allows modelers to succinctly define the number of components involved in each subsystem. Using Block Definition Diagrams (BDDs), construction of a CubeSat's flight structure and all major components are displayed in the simple diagram form of Figure 12. Each item displayed has associated values next to them denoting the number of required elements per system. As an example, the Solar Array in the Power Subsystem block shows a $ [1\dots^{*}]$ next to it, this tells the modeler and engineers that the system requires a minimum of 1 solar array panel but can have any larger number onboard shown by the asterisk.

text: One of the strongest capabilities of MBSE is being able to conduct mathematical analysis within the software or call upon external software for analysis results and reports. SysML offers these features through external software integration features as well as the Parametric diagrams. The parametric diagrams allow the software to conduct analysis on any constraint that is denoted within a block. Figure 26 shows a simplified mass budget analysis for CubeSTEP. Within the CubeSat Total Mass block an equation is stated for the mass calculation. text: However, the drawbacks of conducting analyses within SysML is the lack of complex mathematical formulas since constraints are limited to basic mathematical symbols. SysML makes up for this with its capability of integration with external software, such as MATLAB, STK, Python, and more. The ability to call functions and simulations from these more robust analytical software and use the resulting information in SysML enables the modelers and engineering teams to conduct larger scale simulations of a CubeSat's performance as well as tracking for data validation and requirements compliance.

Addressing the low reliability of CubeSat missions, specifically ones from academia, is of key concern to this project. Due to the lack of systems engineering practices and reliability assessment and analyses seen in academic projects, the quality assurance of the mission and its success rates have suffered. As such, initialize the failure determination and analysis within the model is investigated below.
CubeSat Failure Modes

Applying the block definition diagrams, failure modes of a satellite are created by displaying the failure constraints causing a mission failure. As shown in Figure 28, each failure mode is then correlated to a respective activity block, linked to one of the activity diagrams discussed earlier. These failure modes violate the connected activity thus causing either partial or total mission failure state for the CubeSat. The failure state is then connected to Figure 25 CubeSTEP Operational States Powered On block's failure detection block.
Figure 28 CubeSat Mission Failure Modes

The creation of the constraints above allows for the user to generate parametric diagrams for each of the failures to conduct the analyses necessary for determining the system reliability. Using additional features of SysML Parametric diagrams enables the automatic generation of Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) tables as needed. The failure rate values determined through FMEA are then used in the failure analyses used to determine the most at-risk components and where to focus efforts on risk reduction.

text: Using the minimum cut set found above, several methods of risk management are to be used. These include the following methods:

text: These failure analysis methods provide the engineers and development team with insightful information on the high-risk areas of a design and where to focus efforts to improve the system reliability before operations.

This paper presents the design approach of a CubeSat using model-based systems engineering methods and software. The generalized form of a CubeSat's system modeling is elaborated on to provide future CubeSat developers with a basis to begin their work from. Having a standardized formulation for the design and development of CubeSats, specifically through the generalized model designed here, will lead to greater reliability and performance of the satellites in the future of all form factors.

The implementation of the CubeSat model described above to CPP's CubeSTEP, adds to the viability of the model's usage in CubeSat design. Having the CubeSTEP design team use portions of the model, such as the requirements listing, behavioral sequences, and preliminary calculations used by the structures, thermal, and systems engineering teams reveals the importance of having a system model capable of providing team members with information when necessary. Beyond the design team's usage of the model, our stakeholders from NASA JPL and US AFRL were able to convey the mission objectives and correlate any specific requirements needed. The verification and satisfaction of their needs was presented to them through the requirements tables and listings described within this paper.

To further increase the viability and capability of the CubeSat model, a larger team of model-based systems engineers and satellite design team members will be required to increase the fidelity of the models presented in this paper. It is recommended that future teams focus on the interconnections between system models, the integration of analytical and simulation software, the analysis diagram development of reliability

analyses, and the simulation of behavioral components within the CubeSat model using SysML's diagram simulation capabilities. The future developers to the generalized model should continually reference and contact the SSWG group at INCOSE because of the incredible work they are doing. Even if the information gleamed from them is aimed at theoretical missions the information displayed in their models helped me understand the innerworkings of both the software itself and some subsystems that I did not know much about. However, the team should not be focused on their work too much because of the theoretical design methods. Specifications of the mission at hand must always take precedent and should be the first things considered when using the generalized model.

There are several resources for future teams to research to aid in the development of the CubeSat model. These include NoMagic's SysML documentation, INCOSE's SysML workshops and lectures, as well as INCOSE's SSWG team who continually provide yearly or bi-yearly updates on their efforts in theoretical CubeSat modeling.

From complex to complicated: development of a Model Based Systems Engineering and cyber security approach for a quantum key distribution nanosatellite.
Douglas McNeil $ ^{a} $ , Colin Aitken $ ^{a} $ , Cassandra Mercury $ ^{a} $ , Sonali Mohapatra $ ^{a} $ , Hazel Jeffrey $ ^{a} $ , Daniel Oi $ ^{a} $

$ ^{a} $ Craft Prospect Ltd, Suite 12, Fairfield, 1048 Govan Road, Glasgow, UK, G51 4XS, Email: info@craftprospect.com $ ^{b} $ University of Strathclyde, 16 Richmond Street, Glasgow G1 1XQ, Email: daniel.oi@strath.ac.uk

Current global security systems are built on the premise that mathematical complexity and limitations of processing power are sufficient to protect data. With the emergence of quantum computing these assumptions are now being challenged. Space based Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is a method of encryption key delivery offering significant benefits over ground-based counterparts in terms of range and coverage. Additionally, the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers increases in efficiency through cloud avoidance. For an AI enabled nanosatellite for QKD, design engineers must trade the often-conflicting requirements of space, cybersecurity, AI and quantum to progress the design from the complex to the merely complicated. The Responsive Operations for Key Services (ROKS) mission aims to provide QKD services which augment larger scale QKD efforts. The onboarding of AI to detect and avoid cloud has a significant impact on the concept of operations, moving to significant levels of autonomy. In systems engineering terms, added to the design burden of implementing an emerging technology such as QKD, the established principles of operation are also being challenged. Additionally, as nanosatellites have rarely been deployed as nodes in a secure network to date, the project requires the synthesising of different security standards and approaches into a coherent framework. For the programme significant consideration is given to project lifecycle. In the initial phases agile principles are employed, allowing for experimentation in design. With increasing knowledge of the problem space, there is a reduction in the uncertainty in design elements, leading to a transition from an agile based lifecycle to the waterfall-based methods more suitable for Flight Model implementation. Underpinning the project is a Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach. Enterprise Architect was selected as the MBSE tool of choice during blue sky design stages, allowing a smooth transition from capability level considerations to systems and subsystems design. The Zachman framework offers a consistent, but potentially over flexible, approach to model development. MBSE offers a clear methodology for integrating the model with external simulation tools to provide on ground verification of platform behaviours and porting design effort to support new mission concepts. The application of flexibility in lifecycle management, sound security principles and a model-based approach to technical development has proven to be a highly effective approach in increasing our understanding of complex systems allowing for complicated, but mature, designs to be defined.

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is an emerging field within cyber security which can serve to supplement increased assured demand or as a replacement for existing public key infrastructure. In traditional methodologies encryption is managed by the sharing of keys which with a powerful enough processing capability can be compromised. This is particularly relevant with the emergence of quantum computers, offering the potential to solve complex mathematical functions far more efficiently than existing computing methods. QKD exchanges keys in a way which protects key transfer using fundamental laws of physics, and therefore would be impervious to direct quantum computer enabled brute force attack. QKD distributes secret keys in a way that cannot be effectively intercepted, copied or measured, without leaving obvious signs of observation. Such
systems provide the security of knowing that any eavesdropping on the key transfer stage of communications can be immediately detected and addressed.

Due to the losses experienced in optical fibres in ground based QKD networks and line of sight limitations (50-100km before another node is required), space represents an excellent, global, and highly scalable mechanism for the distribution of secure keys. Nowadays, nations are engaged in a Quantum Space Race determined to be the first to industrialise QKD using satellites [1].

The 'Augmented Quantum Key Distribution (AQKD) satellite service uses nanosatellites (particularly CubeSats) to deliver cryptographic keys and related services for fractions of the cost of traditional satellite constellations. The initial service implementation is based on a technology demonstration through the 'Responsive Operations for Key Services' (ROKS) satellite to be launched in 2022. This AQKD service, rather than compete with large service providers, will aim to augment these larger networks. The service will support the emergence of terrestrial and satellite-based quantum key security systems. The use of nanosatellites provides rapid deployment and smoothens the demand, enabling low-cost and reliable services for consumers, investors, and partners alike. These small satellites have the potential to serve in establishing strategic nodes for global communications across countries, continents, and isolated regions.

This paper discussed the design of the ROKS demonstration mission. This mission operates at the intersection of Artificial Intelligence (AI), quantum technologies, space and cyber security and as such presents a unique and complex case with regards to systems engineering. To address this focus was placed on a structured approached based on Model Based Systems Engineering. This allows the translation of the design from 'blue sky' concept to implemented subsystems. These subsystems represent a departure from current design principles within the space sector, and as such can be used as a yardstick for other emerging capabilities.

Currently secure data transfer is managed using techniques such as Public Key Infrastructure. While this has been a useful technology to this point, it is at risk of becoming obsolete based on the processing power afforded by quantum computers. Compounding this is the problem of forwards security. Data which retains value into the future (e.g. health records) are vulnerable to attacks where information is recorded and unencrypted
when processing power allows. The above issue leads to problems in sectors which are heavily reliant secure data.
Based on the above there are a number of sectors which need to be considering the challenges of quantum supremacy now, so as to be prepared for obsolescence. Sectors which may be vulnerable are:
- Security and Defence
- Oil and Gas
- Healthcare
- Governmental communications
- Telecoms
- Cloud Computing
- Utilities and critical infrastructure
- Internet of Things
- Aviation and maritime
- Finance

There are few examples of the role out of genuinely novel capabilities since nanosatellites have reached the maturity levels required to support the deployment of emerging technologies. QKD is uniquely suitable given requirements around global coverage, rapid revisit, Service Level Agreement based delivery and limitation in fibre-based delivery. As such nanosatellites offer several niche benefits when considered as an augmentation strategy for larger space or ground based networks, namely:
- Smoothing of demand where networks experience elevated key requests.
- Gap filling capacity where infrastructure is unavailable or not yet deployed.
- Alternate key channels where customers have bespoke security requirements.
- Key delivery to locations outside of existing infrastructure.
- Additional delivery opportunities to overcome cloud cover constraints.
- Redundancy in case of failure/attack of standard network.
- Highly miniaturised systems capable of integration of secure nodes onto space assets.

If the engineering challenges of miniaturisation, trust, security and operational efficiency can be solved there is a significant opportunity for nanosatellite delivered QKD. These challenges have impacted considerably on the architectural design of the ROKS mission.

Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) facilitates model driven, as opposed to document driven projects. For the ROKS project the Enterprise Architect MBSE tool was selected due to it extension packages for Enterprise Architecture alongside SysML functions. In order to support the Model Based approach the Zachman Framework for Enterprise Architecture was selected to structure development. This allowed for the project to begin by answering high level questions around the business case for QKD as a nascent market, before flowing business considerations into the systems design itself through various levels of instantiation.

Through the tool traceability is managed, ensuring requirement flow down from capability level to subsystem level. An example of business level activity is given in Fig. 1. where the tool has been used to map stakeholders within the QKD domain and segment these into 'types' such as end users.
Fig. 1. Stakeholder mapping in Enterprise Architect

The use of Enterprise Architect supports design decomposition. The models' behavioural views enforce an approach which considers the structural and behavioural architectural elements in parallel. This ensures equal focus is placed on the functional (e.g. software) as well as physical (e.g. hardware) design.

Through the use of MBSE approaches the complexity associated with the development of a multifaceted satellite-based service was managed and the effort associated with doing so was reduced.

The fundamental architectural design for the design of the Quantum Systems was where to draw the 'red / black' boundary. This essentially defines which system elements are treated as trusted systems and which are untrusted, a concept particularly acute in the context of QKD. While the temptation may be to draw this boundary somewhere within the ground segment, essentially treating the entire space-based system as trusted, the boundary for the ROKS system was defined between the platform and payload. This allows the use of untrusted 3rd party avionics (e.g. an 'Off The Shelf' satellite bus) but also means that the payload itself can be deployed on platforms such as High Altitude Pseudo Satellites (HAPS) and also as a secondary payload on a separate satellite platform. To implement this, significant consideration was given to the Payload Computer subsystem, which acts as a gatekeeper between the secure payload elements and the untrusted platform avionics.

Critical to this unit is the selection of hardware to ensure standard attack vectors through the platform can be addressed. Further to this key management principles common to existing infrastructure must be replicated (e.g. isolated key storage).

A second key architectural consideration regards the hosting of autonomous functions. These functions, at their most basic, allow for target selection on orbit (e.g. if target A is cloud covered, task the platform to point to the lower priority target B). Here neural networks are deployed on standard space-based hardware which can detect and geolocate cloud using a low performance imager. Due to the decision to develop the payload in isolation from the platform this functionality must be payload hosted. This creates a situation where a payload must task the platform avionics (i.e. the main On Board Computer - OBC). This is a significant deviation from traditional operational concepts where a primary schedule is followed and is hosted on the main OBC.
Fig. 4. Cloud Detection Using the Craft Prospect Forwards Looking Imager.

Any system is only as secure as its least secure element. This means that to deliver a space based cyber security service, best practice must be always maintained. Early work revealed that there was no one size fits all' open set of standards for space based cyber security services. Based on significant desk-based research and work with security orientated partners an approach which combined a number of separate standards into a bespoke framework was defined. Examples of standards which were incorporated includes ISO:27001 [2] for general company system and facility security, CCSDS [3] for space specific considerations, ETSI developments towards a standard suite for QKD [4] systems and even British Standards around Automotive and Control Systems for device level considerations [5].
This consolidation of requirements ensures that security concepts are flown into the design at all levels and a comprehensive approach is taken.

The above concepts have all informed the design of a satellite for demonstration of AI enabled QKD for nanosatellite. This platform is based on the purchase of a Commercial Off The Shelf (COTS) nanosatellite platform, with a payload consisting of a number of key subsystems. These subsystems are:
- A bespoke CubeSat compliant telescope designed specifically for optical communications applications (in partnership with Fraunhofer UK).
- An optical beam steering subsystem capable of correcting the beam direction beyond the limitation of the CubeSat Attitude Control subsystem.
- A QKD source capable of supporting a number of Weak Coherent Pulse protocols (in this case BB84) [6].
- Low power real time AI, implemented on the Craft Prospect Forwards Looking Imager product. This hosts cloud detection algorithms for informing satellite operations.
- Secure Assured Computing, managing the red / black interface and hosting assured autonomous computing.
At the time of authorship, the Flight Model platform is in development, with launch set for late 2022.
Fig. 5. Cartoon Showing the ROKS Platform Subsystems

This paper proposes high-level approaches for the model-based design and implementation of a secure AI enabled satellite for the provision of QKD. While the approach has shown considerable value in progressing the design to flight model implementation there are some

core lessons learned. While the use of Model Based Systems Engineering has been a significant success, the implementation of the Zachman Framework was noted to create a number of arbitrary tasks which did not influence the design process. Here more flexibility in deployment, or potentially consideration of more widely used frameworks (such as TOGAF [7]) may have improved design efficiency.

In terms of the approach to security, engagement with partner organisations early in the programme has aided with knowledge transfer and ensure a comprehensive framework has been defined. This has informed not only system requirements, but also company operations and general cyber security approaches. This approach could be further refined towards a baseline for future space based cyber security services.

In terms of autonomy, the complexity of autonomous operations is aided by a MBSE approach which focused on the function of the system. By focusing on the functional architecture early in the project the operation of autonomous elements could be understood, and its impact on other subsystems defined. This has allowed the definition and implementation of a novel approach to cloud detection which allows for targeted downlink of optical communications data based on local weather conditions.
The above has facilitated the development of a mission concept and requisite subsystems for QKD demonstration from nanosatellite.

Abstract—The International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE) Space System Working Group (SSWG) has created the CubeSat System Reference Model (CSRM), a representation of the logical architecture of a CubeSat system, intended to be used by system architects and engineers as a starting point as they develop the physical architecture of the Space and Ground segments of the CubeSat mission of interest to them.

The CSRM is based on Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) principles, is System Modeling Language (SysML) compliant, is hosted in a graphical modeling tool, and is intended to foster completeness and economies of scale associated with reusability. The CSRM has been vetted by System Engineering professionals and has been introduced to the CubeSat mission development team community with favorable results. The CSRM has been submitted to the Object Management Group (OMG) as a CubeSat specification, and is being evaluated for that role.

Mission Engineering, a concept where the mission itself is looked at as a system is being explored as a means to maintain balance between the spacecraft system, operations (including ground systems), and the mission (the integration of needed capabilities). Now opportunities exist to extend the already-developed CSRM to enable the application of Mission Engineering to modeling a complete CubeSat mission. This paper presents the challenges and approach that the INCOSE SSWG will address, including a path for extension of the CRSM for use in exploring its applicability to the Mission Engineering concept, and capturing the Mission as a Model to create a unifying environment for universities to build on each other's successes as they learn to design for Space.

The International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE) Space Systems Working Group (SSWG) has been focused on the design and development of the CubeSat System Reference Model (CSRM) since 2014. [1] - [6] That effort was successfully completed in 2020. The CSRM has been submitted to the Object Management Group (OMG) as a CubeSat specification, and is being evaluated for that role. The SSWG plans on exploring how the approaches and methodologies used in the development of the CSRM can be applied to the realm of Mission Engineering. The team will identify possible follow-on capabilities for the SSWG during 2021-2022, with the goal of selecting the appropriate way ahead and presenting its results to the IEEE Aerospace Conference at Big Sky in March 2022.
The 2021 IEEE Aerospace Conference provides an ideal opportunity for the SSWG to present its ideas to the IEEE for its comments and feedback. Recommendations for further work are encouraged.
This paper provides the following:
- An overview of the CSRM
- A definition of Mission Engineering to guide the application of the CSRM
- A discussion of the CSRM as a tool for Mission Engineering
- A discussion of our approach to extending the CSRM in support of Mission Engineering
- Anticipated path forward.

The INCOSE Systems Engineering Body of Knowledge (SEBoK) defines Mission Engineering as "the application of systems engineering to the planning, analysis, and designing of missions where the mission is the system of interest" [7]. It goes on to say that Mission Engineering "analyzes the mission goals and threads, analyzes the available as well as emerging operational and system capabilities, and designs a mission architecture to achieve the mission goal." The SEBoK also identifies the main activities of Mission Engineering which are discussed below.

Mission Capability Analysis and Definition. The problem scenario is analyzed to determine what capabilities are required and to develop a Concept of Operations (ConOps) for the mission. A capability is defined as the ability to complete a task or execute a course of action under specified conditions and level of performance [8]. A ConOps covers a series of connected operations to be carried out simultaneously or in succession [7]. It is written from the operator's perspective.

Mission Thread Definition. The end-to-end set of operational activities are analyzed. This starts with modeling operational activities, their sequencing, and the information flows between them. References [9-11] provide a good discussion of mission threads.
Tradeoff Analysis. Alternatives for accomplishing the mission are developed and trade studies are conducted to determine the best alternative given resources and time available.

Mission Architecting. An operational architecture is developed describing the capabilities, operational activities, operational nodes, and other relevant elements to model the mission. Wertz et al. [12] identify elements associated with a space mission architecture to include the space segment, ground segment, mission operations, launch segment, orbit, end user, and command, control, and communications architecture.

Requirements Engineering. The functional and nonfunctional requirements are determined from the capability analysis, ConOps, and mission threads. The requirements are allocated to the operational nodes.

Interoperability Analysis. Operational interoperability describes the ability of the systems to coordinate their activities to support completion of the mission thread. Technical interoperability describes the ability of the systems to exchange data with considerations for the timeliness and quality of the data. Interoperability between systems completing the mission must occur at both the operational and technical levels. Giachetti et al. [10] provide a good discussion of interoperability analysis as it applies to mission-oriented System of Systems Engineering (SoSE).

Mission-oriented System of Systems (SoS) Implementation Mission engineering is closely associated with SoS because most missions are accomplished through the coordination and interoperability of multiple systems. The mission-oriented SoS is implemented through designing and developing new systems, modifying existing systems, and/or modifying doctrine, policies, procedures, and other nonmateriel means to help achieve the mission. Ideally the mission-oriented SoS could be rapidly conceived, assembled, and deployed to react to a rapidly changing environment. However, there are many challenges associated with the engineering of a SoS.
The INCOSE SoS Primer describes major challenges associated with a SoS [13]:
- Each constituent system is independent and makes decisions or upgrades without considering the rest of the SoS if their own goals conflict with SoS goals.
- Constituent systems may withdraw from the SoS if their own goals conflict with SoS goals.

- The SoS itself is commonly large-scale and usually highly complex. It is difficult to produce accurate predictive models of all emergent behaviors, and so global SoS performance is difficult to design.
- Testing and verifying upgrades to a SoS is difficult and expensive due to scale, complexity and constant evolution.
- The Primer characterizes a SoS as having:
- Multiple levels of stakeholders with mixed and possibly competing interests.
- Multiple and possible contradictory, objectives and purpose.
- Disparate management structure with no clear accountability.
- Multiple lifecycles with elements being implemented asynchronously.
- Multiple owners making individual resourcing decisions.
- These aspects of a SoS create challenges that cannot be met by a traditional systems engineering approach. To address this challenge, 7 core elements of SoSE have been developed [13, 14]:
- Understanding SoS capability objectives.
- Understanding constituent systems and their relationships.
- Assessing SoS performance against capability objectives.
- Developing, evolving, and maintaining a SoS architecture.
- Monitoring and assessing the impact of changes on the SoS performance.
- Addressing requirements and solution options.
- Orchestrating upgrades.
Chen and Unewisse [14] recognize that these 7 core elements represent part of what is required, but there are still a range
of outstanding challenges that remain for SoSE to include managing the complexity and monitoring the well-being of a SoS.
Mission Verification and Validation. Includes verification that the system as delivered satisfies the requirements and validates that the system fulfills the mission purpose and stakeholder needs.

text: Mission-oriented System of Systems (SoS) Implementation. The challenges associated with SoS and SoSE were discussed in the previous section. Applying an MBSE approach to SoSE creates even more challenges. Chen and Unewisse [14] state that incorporating MBSE into SoSE practice is shown to be a necessary, albeit challenging, step in developing practical approaches to SoSE. They go on to say it will require improvements and extensions of MBSE concepts, processes and tools in order to adequately and successfully address SoS challenges and issues. There are some examples of efforts to provide a solution to this problem. For example, Chen and Unewisse identify activity areas within SoSE that could be supported by MBSE. Williamson [16] provides a conceptual model for applying MBSE to SoS. While there is much progress being made in this area, there are still challenges to be addressed. As such, how the CSRM would address this is another area that requires much further research.

INCOSE is an international organization founded to develop, disseminate, enable, promote, and advance systems engineering and systems approaches.
OMG is an international technology standards consortium consisting of vendors, end-users, academic institutions, and government agencies.

Utilizing Model-Based System Engineering, the INCOSE Space Systems Working Group created the CubeSat System Reference Model as a logical architecture that developers can use in the creation of their own mission-specific CubeSats, and to also act as a repository for system engineering artifacts. While the CSRM has tremendous utility in the development of a system, more work needs to be done in properly modelling the mission in its entirety (e.g., creation of metrics that allow for the evaluation of alternatives, mission utility, etc.). This is precisely where the methodologies used in the development of the CSRM could be applied towards system-of-systems approach to mission integration and management. The SSWG is in the early stages of a study that will explore the feasibility of extending the CSRM into the realm of Mission Engineering.

As part of this study, the SSWG is soliciting input from stakeholders on possible methodologies, conceptual frameworks, evaluation criteria, or any other strategies that we should consider during this early stage of our work. We intend to provide updates and gather further feedback per our previously described Path Forward.
