Several simulations have been conducted to assess the goodness of the selected architectures and their ranking. For the one here presented, the Guidance Navigation and Control (GNC), the Propulsion, the Electric Power Subsystem (EPS) and the Telemetry Tracking and Command (TT&C) subsystems have been considered, each one characterized by several decisions and alternatives which can be consulted in the decision trees in Appendix A; small satellites technologies have been explored and markers have been assigned to them. Four functionalities are used for this simulation:
- F1 = Perform continuous imaging of a debris.
- F2 = Execute relative manoeuvres.
- F3 = Transmit large data files to ground.
- F4 = Execute transfer to operative orbit.

F1 and F2 are contemporary, and more importance is assigned to them with respect to F3 and F4, therefore $ v_{imp}=[0100] $ . The Sparsity Factor is set to 1 and the Weighted Sum Method (WSM) has been used to solve the decision matrices.

The results related to the Level 1 architectures selection are reported in Fig. 24. The horizontal axis reports a four-digit number indicating the architecture: the first digit is the alternative of the first decision, the second digit is the alternative of the second decision and so on up to the fourth first level decision. The diagram reports the ranked J values of each architecture, computed as the average between the two Performance Scores values. The diagram in Fig. 25 reports the same ranking values sorted from the highest to the lowest.

The tool output after Step 5 is reported in Fig. 26 and the updated sorting in Fig. 27. Eight Final Proposed Architectures are downselected, while the remaining ones have zero values because of their inability to satisfy

all the functionalities markers. The best L1 architecture suggested by the tool is the one with indexes 1-1-2-1 composed by 3-axis stabilization, chemical propulsion, solar panels + batteries and high gain antenna; the selected Level 1 architecture is coherent with what expected by functionalities.

The proposed overall architecture is coherent with the requests and the tool provides reliable results, embracing a casuistry rather than a specific mission. As the number of input functionalities is increased, the tool can converge to precise needs of a particular scenario, getting a "tailored" output for it. A limit is related to the substantial solutions changing with the tool-embedded tree markers, therefore requiring a refinement to cover more system aspects associating precise meanings to them. The best

way to exploit such preliminary version of the tool is to associate it to some quantitative analysis and architecture design. The MBSE environment should also be targeted to exploit all the outputs, as it improves the system thinking providing a natural terrain to experiment with functional analysis having a set of selected components.

The research conducted for this work set out to improve small satellites design lifecycle using an MBSE solution to assess benefits and limits, associated to a decision-making tool for preliminary architecture automated selection. The precise syntax and semantics of the ARCADIA language, merged with the Capella tool, allow to express complex concepts and articulated architectures of a small satellite in a concise and intuitive way, coherently with all systems engineering practices, also providing strong basis for the on-board software development. The methodology accompanies systems engineers in their definition from the very high-level mission objectives up to the components definition, guaranteeing consistency among levels and providing a clear vision of the entire system to any involved team member and/or stakeholder. An extension of MBSE has also been discussed by introducing a decision-making algorithm for the selection of one or more preliminary architectures, intended to be used in the feasibility study of small satellites missions when it is difficult to reduce the number of design alternatives due to the highly qualitative domain. The tool has been validated and results are promising, highlighting its ability to skim the architectures basing on the inputs provided.

The work related to the MBSE approach presents some limitations that can also be interpreted as future works. Firstly, the study excluded the parameterization of the whole architecture model and a consequent interface with an analytical and numerical tool to run simulations. The nearest ARCADIA concept to such parametrization is the adoption of Class diagrams to model quantities exchanged between elements and to have a data repository too. Interfacing Capella with other engineering software could further enhance the overall system design and team working, moving toward a digital twin. In parallel, a formalization of the presented AIV/AIT plan modeling in terms of syntax, semantics and dedicated diagrams within the tool represents an open point for a research study.

The prototype version of the decision-making tool opens the road to many future developments. Firstly, the embedded decision tree can be improved increasing its details and revising the assigned markers using data mining techniques that exploit a statistical set of data built up from the literature information on past concluded space missions, addressing a more precise markers matrices filling. Also, new blocks can be introduced to the current algorithm such as a cross-relation block to

evaluate how the selection of a particular component influences the others, being careful to not stiffen the tool introducing too much constraining conditions. Other interesting developments concern the introduction of sizing blocks which implement mission analysis and basic computations of subsystems parameters to get as output a preliminary quantitative sizing too. Such blocks could be used to add some more decision-making conditions expanding the components selection to an available catalogue, leading to a more complete output.

Although MBSE still has many social hurdles to overcome, the authors expect a gradual awareness from the space community about the benefits a system design lifecycle can gain from it, as demonstrated in this work. Interfacing MBSE solutions with intelligent tools such as the prototype one developed for this paper represents a way to overcome the stringent requirements asked by the new complex space systems and to face up the less relaxed mission development times required by the incoming New Space Economy.

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > ABSTRACT
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / abstract
text: While Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) improves the ambiguity problem of the conventional document-based way, it brings management complexity. Faced with the complexity, one of the core issues that companies care about is how to effectively evaluate, predict, and manage it in the early system design stage. The inaccuracy of contemporary complexity measurement approaches still exits due to the inconsistency between the actual design process in physical space and the theoretical simulation in virtual space. Digital Twin (DT) provides a promising way to alleviate the problem by bridging the physical space and virtual space. Aiming to integrate DT with MBSE for the system design complexity analysis and prediction, based on previous work, an integration framework named System Design Digital Twin in 5 Dimensions was introduced from a knowledge perspective. The framework provides services for design complexity measurement, effort estimation, and change propagation prediction. Then, to represent the system design digital twin in a unified way, a modeling profile is constructed through SysML stereotypes. The modeling profile includes System design digital model in virtual space profile, system services profile, relationships profile and digital twin data profile. Finally, the system design of a cube-satellite space mission demonstrates the proposed unfiled modeling approach.

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 1. Introduction
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 1 introduction
text: The development of a complex product such as a vehicle, an airplane, or a satellite has evolved to employ a system engineering methodology. In the conventional Document-Based Systems Engineering (DBSE), designers share information and design intent through a set of documents, such as requirements spreadsheets, interface definition diagrams, and design specifications. However, DBSE shows limitations, where the growth in system complexity has increased the risk to unacceptable levels. Ambiguity tends to arise when designers scatter information throughout a disjointed set of documents [1]. As a result, designers from different disciplines have to spend a lot of time understanding the design intent and avoiding ambiguity.

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 1. Introduction
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 1 introduction
text: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) improves on DBSE by formalizing the application of modeling to support requirements analysis, function analysis, and design synthesis [2]. Use of MBSE follows the traditional "Vee" model, while this paper focuses on system decomposition and definition, that is, the left part of the "Vee" model, which is the system design (SD) [3]. Researchers have proposed promising MBSE methodologies like Harmony Systems Engineering [4], Object Process Methodology (OPM) [5], Vitech MBSE [6], and System Modeling Methodology [7]. Although using unified languages, such as SysML [8] and OPL [5], the methodologies can specify the system

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 1. Introduction
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 1 introduction
text: model iteratively. It is still time-consuming for designers to implement them. In other words, MBSE brings complexity management issues while improving the ambiguity problem [2]. Because the existence of factors like uncertain design information, the coupling of design functions, and changes in design status has increased the complexity, controlling the progress of the MBSE process becomes difficult, and product development time exceeds expectations.

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 1. Introduction
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 1 introduction
text: Faced with this complexity, one of the core issues that companies care about is how to effectively evaluate, predict, and manage it in the early SD stage. For this reason, different researchers have proposed various methods, such as information entropy theory [9], computational complexity theory [10], and axiomatic design [11], and Bashir-Zhang-Thomson (BZT) method [12]. However, these methods still have inaccurate problems. For example, the information entropy theory is suitable for unpredictable system behavior, but the ability to accurately display the complexity changes is insufficient [13]. The information axiom in the axiomatic design can evaluate design complexity through achieving functional probability, but it rarely focuses on the design process [3]. While the BZT method can simulate the academic workload of design under different scenarios, it lacks consideration of the impact of actual engineering changes on complexity [14]. The main reason for such drawbacks is that the actual design process in physical space is inconsistent with the theoretical simulation in virtual space.

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 1. Introduction
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 1 introduction
text: The emergence of Digital Twin (DT) provides an effective way to solve the problem of inaccurate complexity prediction by bridging the physical space and the virtual space [15-17]. The concept of DT can date back to Grieves's presentation about Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) in 2003 [18], and it becomes more mature and specific until 2011. Gartner continuously lists DT as the current top strategic technology development direction in 2016, 2017, and 2018. DT is defined as a digital replica of a system and maintained as a virtual equivalent throughout the physical product's lifespan, which ensures consistency between the ideal model and the actual state by providing smart and real-time services [19-21].

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 1. Introduction
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 1 introduction
text: Significant researches have proven the significance of the integration of DT and MBSE. For example, Bachelor et al. present how DT changes how the MBSE process is managed, overcoming the issues associated with federated IT infrastructures, and tools integration [22]. Thomas et al. propose a holistic system lifecycle engineering approach that can close the loop between system architectures and DTs [23]. Erikstad et al. propose a set of reusable design patterns for DTs, which can be applied to different classes of SD and operation problems [24]. Schluse et al. describe an experimental DT for the gap between the first systems engineering steps, and the various algorithms simulation technology can offer [25].

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 1. Introduction
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 1 introduction
text: However, seldom researches focus on integrating DT with MBSE for the SD complexity analysis and prediction. As SD can be viewed as the supply and demand of knowledge between designers and product functions, from a knowledge perspective, this paper firstly introduces a framework for integrating DT with MBSE called System Design Digital Twin in 5 Dimensions (SDDT5D). The frame provides services for design complexity measurement, effort estimation, and change propagation prediction. Then, to represent the system design digital twin in a unified way, a modeling profile is constructed through SysML stereotypes. The system model reduces ambiguity through unifying system requirements, functions, and structures and behaviors. Finally, the SD of a Radio Aurora Explorer mission demonstrates the proposed method.

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 2. A knowledge-based system design
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 2 a knowledge based system design
text: In SD, the product can be represented by decomposed requirements and functions, which are then assigned to different designers responsible for designing detailed behaviors states, and structures to accomplish the functions, as displayed in Fig.1. Under a knowledge perspective, SD of a complex product can be viewed as a knowledge intensive process that a product is the embodiment of knowledge, functions are the requirements of knowledge; behaviors, states and structures are the application of knowledge; designers are the providers of knowledge. As a result, the essence of SD is integrating multiple knowledge domains from corresponding designers to achieve the

section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 2 a knowledge based system design
text: According to the knowledge-based SD presented in Fig.1, functions of a product and the capability of designers should be mapped into different types of knowledge items, respectively. Achieving SD within the stipulated time relies on the matching degree between the required knowledge of decomposed functions and the level of designers' ability to master each type of knowledge domain. Decisive steps of the knowledge-based SD are functional decomposition and knowledge specification for purposes and designers.

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 2.1. Functional decomposition
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 2 1 functional decomposition
text: Functions refer to the input-output relationships of materials, energy, and signals in the product. A function is usually expressed by "verb + noun", such as "determine the attitude", "store electrical energy", etc. A function tree diagram can be used to develop a graphical representation of the functional decomposition [26]. The decomposition starts from the most abstract function, and by answering "how to implement this function?", an abstract function expands into multiple sub-functions to form a "tree".

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 2.1. Functional decomposition
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 2 1 functional decomposition
text: There are many approaches to build a function tree diagram. One of the most used methods is the Function Analysis System Technique (FAST) proposed by Bytheway [27]. Through FAST, Fig. 2 shows a function tree diagram with 36 functions of SD of a Radio Aurora Explorer (RAX) mission. According to FAST's functional decomposition criteria, when a function is simple enough to map to existing or commercially available components or subsystems, the decomposition can stop. For example, "Function 3-Convert solar energy into electricity" in Fig. 2 is at the end level as a solar wing can accomplish it. The benefit of utilizing a function tree diagram is that a function is independent of the product structure to represent the essence of a product before the embodiment of a design concept is achieved, which allows one to get an estimate of the design effort earlier in SD.

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 2.2. Mapping functions to knowledge space
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 2 2 mapping functions to knowledge space
text: In knowledge-based SD, knowledge is the link between product functions and the design team. The decomposed functions and their integration are achieved through the expertise of designers. Zhang defines technical knowledge as the professional skills used by designers in design activities that can be acquired through professional learning or actual product development. Technical knowledge is divided into general knowledge (GK) and product knowledge (PK) [29].

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 2.2. Mapping functions to knowledge space
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 2 2 mapping functions to knowledge space
text: (1) GK is defined as the skills in a particular domain, which can be acquired through formal education, structured study, or systematic training. It determines the capability of a designer to be component at certain functions.

section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 2.2. Mapping functions to knowledge space

text: (2) PK is defined as the comprehension of the specific product to be designed, which is mostly developed from prior experience in similar projects. Designers with good PK are aware of interdependent activities besides their tasks and can accomplish integration from functions to the parent function.

section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 2 2 mapping functions to knowledge space
text: Accordingly, a function is developed by GK, and sub-functions are integrated by PK. We use a scale to map a function into knowledge space to evaluate the required knowledge items in designing a specific function. Based on the study by Zhang and Thomson [26], we use knowledge magnitude to indicate the importance of a certain knowledge item to the function development, where a higher value indicates a severer requirement. All knowledge items should be limited to the same scale range, expressed by [0, r] $ (r\in N+) $ . The most common situation is that $ r=2 $ , where a higher value typically means less uncertainty and higher knowledge requirement; on the contrary, if the magnitude of a knowledge item is 0, it is not important for the development of the function. text: SDS is the core enabler in $ \mathrm{S D D T}_{5 \mathrm{D}} $ , which can provide intelligent execution, precise estimation, and reliable control for the SD. The services are necessarily a series of mathematical models that integrate tracking, evaluation, optimization, and estimate algorithms. Analysis approaches in virtual space can be performed by specific services using real data from physical space. As illustrated in Table 3, three kinds of services are discussed in detail in Section 4.

text: DTD acts as the driving force of $ \mathrm{S D D T}_{5 \mathrm{D}} $ , including data from physical entities, virtual models, and services, and the data regularly update with changes in real-time status. Because both $ \mathrm{S D}_{\mathrm{P S}} $ and $ \mathrm{S D D M}_{\mathrm{V S}} $ come down to the design object (i.e., the product), designers, and design activities, data in DTD can be classified into the product data, the designer data, and the design activity data, as listed in Table 4.

text: The role of DTD has two aspects. It provides data for early-stage predetermination of design states, such as the complexity measurement of the design, the estimation of required design effort, and the prediction of the change propagation. For another, it provides data for realtime tracking of design states, such as completed design tasks, designer workload, and rest effort of the design.

text: System design in the framework (Fig. 4) is an iterative optimization process. The system design digital model represents information of design objects, designers, and design activities from the design team. With the development of the system, the digital model information becomes complete. Moreover, through system services, the actual system design process can be optimized. For example, managers can more accurately identify the knowledge requirement of functions and designate more capable designers on crucial functions. section: Unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge-based system design > 5. Case study and discussion
section_key: unified modeling for digital twin of a knowledge based system design / 5 case study and discussion
text: To assess the proposed method's practical usability, two students (Group A) and two experienced managers (Group B) were asked to participate in an experiment about estimating the total effort of the RAX CubeSate system design. The two students having the SysML knowledge background used the proposed unified models to represnt the system design, while the two managers in Group B used a traditional document-based approach, such as the requirements specification by Microsoft Word and the interface definition document by Microsoft Excel, to specify the system design. The student group spent about 48 h in modeling the system model by the $ \mathrm{SDDT}_{5 \mathrm{D}} $ modeling profile and spend 4 more hours in getting the correct total effort. Compared with students, managers in Group B spend less time in specifying the systems, about 24 h. However, the two managers used more time, about 10 h, in getting the correct total effort as they wasted more time in understanding the ambiguity issues. Although the students spent more time in modeling the system model, they saved more time in analyzing the design complexity. Moreover, the unified model can be reused in a more detailed stage to avoid the ambiguity between the understandings of different designers.

For example, Table 9 lists ten different scenarios for simulating the change of RAX system design. The simulation case includes all 36 functions, ten kinds of knowledge, and multiple interfaces of all RAX system designs, assuming that function 17 has been changed. Among them, scenario 1 is the basic scenario; for scenario 2, only the affected functions are simulated; then, two new random functions are added to the list of changed functions (scenario 3); then, with different knowledge vectors 1 and 2 random interfaces for simulation (scenario 4 to 10). The primary purpose of these scenarios is to cover many possible examples of function change propagation: addition/deletion of functions, addition/removal of knowledge items, and modification of interfaces. text: This work was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 51905493, and No. 51775517), the Shanghai Key Lab of Advanced Manufacturing Environment (No. KT20190603).
, Hao Li, Xiaoyu Wen,
- Integrating digital twin (DT) with model-based systems engineering (MBSE) for the system design complexity analysis and prediction.
- A system design digital twin in 5 dimensions $ \mathrm{S D D T}_{5 \mathrm{D}} $ framework is introduced, which is able to map the actual system design process into the corresponding virtual space.
- The core concepts and relationships of $ \mathrm{S D D T}_{5 \mathrm{D}} $ are customized by a SysML profile that keeps every view of the system digital model unified.
- The system model reduces ambiguity through unifying system requirements, functions, and structures and behaviors.

While Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) improves the ambiguity problem of the conventional document-based way, it brings management complexity. Faced with the complexity, one of the core issues that companies care about is how to effectively evaluate, predict, and manage it in the early system design stage. The inaccuracy of contemporary complexity measurement approaches still exits due to the inconsistency between the actual design process in physical space and the theoretical simulation in virtual space. Digital Twin (DT) provides a promising way to alleviate the problem by bridging the physical space and virtual space. Aiming to integrate DT with MBSE for the system design complexity analysis and prediction, based on previous work, an integration framework named System Design Digital Twin in 5 Dimensions was introduced from a knowledge perspective. The framework provides services for design complexity measurement, effort estimation, and change propagation prediction. Then, to represent the system design digital twin in a unified way, a modeling profile is constructed through SysML stereotypes. The modeling profile includes System design digital model in virtual space profile, system services profile, relationships profile and digital
twin data profile. Finally, the system design of a cube-satellite space mission demonstrates the proposed unfiled modeling approach.
Keywords
Model-based systems engineering; Digital twin; System design; Unified modeling; Systems modeling language

The development of a complex product such as a vehicle, an airplane, or a satellite has evolved to employ a system engineering methodology. In the conventional Document-Based Systems Engineering (DBSE), designers share information and design intent through a set of documents, such as requirements spreadsheets, interface definition diagrams, and design specifications. However, DBSE shows limitations, where the growth in system complexity has increased the risk to unacceptable levels. Ambiguity tends to arise when designers scatter information throughout a disjointed set of documents [1]. As a result, designers from different disciplines have to spend a lot of time understanding the design intent and avoiding ambiguity.

Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) improves on DBSE by formalizing the application of modeling to support requirements analysis, function analysis, and design synthesis [2]. Use of MBSE follows the traditional "Vee" model, while this paper focuses on system decomposition and definition, that is, the left part of the "Vee" model, which is the system design (SD) [3]. Researchers have proposed promising MBSE methodologies like Harmony Systems Engineering [4], Object Process Methodology (OPM) [5], Vitech MBSE [6], and System Modeling Methodology [7]. Although using unified languages, such as SysML [8] and OPL [5], the methodologies can specify the system model iteratively. It is still time-consuming for designers to implement them. In other words, MBSE brings complexity management issues while improving the ambiguity problem [2]. Because the existence of factors like uncertain design information, the coupling of design functions, and changes in design status has increased the complexity, controlling the progress of the MBSE process becomes difficult, and product development time exceeds expectations.

Faced with this complexity, one of the core issues that companies care about is how to effectively evaluate, predict, and manage it in the early SD stage. For this reason, different researchers have proposed various methods, such as information entropy theory [9],

computational complexity theory [10], and axiomatic design [11], and Bashir-Zhang-Thomson (BZT) method [12]. However, these methods still have inaccurate problems. For example, the information entropy theory is suitable for unpredictable system behavior, but the ability to accurately display the complexity changes is insufficient [13]. The information axiom in the axiomatic design can evaluate design complexity through achieving functional probability, but it rarely focuses on the design process [3]. While the BZT method can simulate the academic workload of design under different scenarios, it lacks consideration of the impact of actual engineering changes on complexity [14]. The main reason for such drawbacks is that the actual design process in physical space is inconsistent with the theoretical simulation in virtual space.

The emergence of Digital Twin (DT) provides an effective way to solve the problem of inaccurate complexity prediction by bridging the physical space and the virtual space [15], [16], [17]. The concept of DT can date back to Grieves's presentation about Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) in 2003 [18], and it becomes more mature and specific until 2011. Gartner continuously lists DT as the current top strategic technology development direction in 2016, 2017, and 2018. DT is defined as a digital replica of a system and maintained as a virtual equivalent throughout the physical product's lifespan, which ensures consistency between the ideal model and the actual state by providing smart and real-time services [19], [20], [21].

Significant researches have proven the significance of the integration of DT and MBSE. For example, Bachelor etal. present how DT changes how the MBSE process is managed, overcoming the issues associated with federated IT infrastructures, and tools integration [22]. Thomas etal. propose a holistic system lifecycle engineering approach that can close the loop between system architectures and DTs [23]. Erikstad etal. propose a set of reusable design patterns for DTs, which can be applied to different classes of SD and operation problems [24]. Schluse etal. describe an experimental DT for the gap between the first systems engineering steps, and the various algorithms simulation technology can offer [25].

However, seldom researches focus on integrating DT with MBSE for the SD complexity analysis and prediction. As SD can be viewed as the supply and demand of knowledge between designers and product functions, from a knowledge perspective, this paper firstly introduces a framework for integrating DT with MBSE called System Design Digital Twin in 5 Dimensions (SDDT5D). The frame provides services for design complexity measurement, effort estimation, and change propagation prediction. Then, to represent the system design digital twin in a unified way, a modeling profile is constructed through SysML stereotypes. The system model reduces ambiguity through unifying system requirements, functions, and structures and behaviors. Finally, the SD of a Radio Aurora Explorer mission demonstrates the proposed method.

In SD, the product can be represented by decomposed requirements and functions, which are then assigned to different designers responsible for designing detailed behaviors states, and structures to accomplish the functions, as displayed in Fig.1. Under a knowledge perspective, SD of a complex product can be viewed as a knowledge-intensive process that a product is the embodiment of knowledge, functions are the requirements of knowledge; behaviors, states and structures are the application of knowledge; designers are the providers of knowledge. As a result, the essence of SD is integrating multiple knowledge domains from corresponding designers to achieve the desired functions.

According to the knowledge-based SD presented in Fig.1, functions of a product and the capability of designers should be mapped into different types of knowledge items, respectively. Achieving SD within the stipulated time relies on the matching degree between the required knowledge of decomposed functions and the level of designers' ability to master each type of knowledge domain. Decisive steps of the knowledge-based SD are functional decomposition and knowledge specification for purposes and designers.

Functions refer to the input-output relationships of materials, energy, and signals in the product. A function is usually expressed by "verb+noun", such as "determine the attitude", "store electrical energy", etc. A function tree diagram can be used to develop a graphical representation of the functional decomposition [26]. The decomposition starts from the most
abstract function, and by answering "how to implement this function?", an abstract function expands into multiple sub-functions to form a "tree".

There are many approaches to build a function tree diagram. One of the most used methods is the Function Analysis System Technique (FAST) proposed by Bytheway [27]. Through FAST, Fig.2 shows a function tree diagram with 36 functions of SD of a Radio Aurora Explorer (RAX) mission. According to FAST's functional decomposition criteria, when a function is simple enough to map to existing or commercially available components or subsystems, the decomposition can stop. For example, "Function 3-Convert solar energy into electricity" in Fig.2 is at the end level as a solar wing can accomplish it. The benefit of utilizing a function tree diagram is that a function is independent of the product structure to represent the essence of a product before the embodiment of a design concept is achieved, which allows one to get an estimate of the design effort earlier in SD.

In knowledge-based SD, knowledge is the link between product functions and the design team. The decomposed functions and their integration are achieved through the expertise of designers. Zhang defines technical knowledge as the professional skills used by designers in design activities that can be acquired through professional learning or actual product development. Technical knowledge is divided into general knowledge (GK) and product knowledge (PK) [29].

(1) GK is defined as the skills in a particular domain, which can be acquired through formal education, structured study, or systematic training. It determines the capability of a designer to be component at certain functions.

(2) PK is defined as the comprehension of the specific product to be designed, which is mostly developed from prior experience in similar projects. Designers with good PK are aware of interdependent activities besides their tasks and can accomplish integration from functions to the parent function.

Accordingly, a function is developed by GK, and sub-functions are integrated by PK. We use a scale to map a function into knowledge space to evaluate the required knowledge items in designing a specific function. Based on the study by Zhang and Thomson [26], we use knowledge magnitude to indicate the importance of a certain knowledge item to the function development, where a higher value indicates a severer requirement. All knowledge items should be limited to the same scale range, expressed by $ [0,r] $ $ (r\in N+) $ . The most common situation is that $ r=2 $ , where a higher value typically means less uncertainty and higher knowledge requirement; on the contrary, if the magnitude of a knowledge item is 0, it is not important for the development of the function. Correspondingly, a designer's capability for applying GK is defined with the magnitude: novice (numerical value=0), ordinary (numerical value=1) and expert (numerical value=2). The knowledge-based SD in Section2 establishes a theoretical basis for the operation of a system design digital twin. According to the research from Tao, a complete digital twin framework should include five components: the physical entity in physical space, the virtual entity in virtual space, services for analyzing the entity, digital twin data from the entity, and connections between them [30]. Following the same structure, for a knowledge-based SD, the corresponding digital twin framework, named System Design Digital Twin in 5 Dimensions $ \mathrm{(SDDT_{5D})} $ , is consists of five similar components, as illustrated in Fig.4.

text: $ \mathrm{S D}_{\mathrm{P S}} $ is the actual SD process of a product itself. In physical space, decomposed functions of the specific design object are assigned to designers. Designers with technical knowledge can develop the assigned function through sequential design tasks in a design activity. Therefore, main components of $ \mathrm{S D}_{\mathrm{P S}} $ are the design object, designers, and design activities.

section: 3.2. System design digital model in virtual space (SDDM $ _{VS} $ )

text: As digital twin (DT) is defined as a real mapping of an entity in real word in the product life cycle, an $ \mathrm{S D D M_{V S}} $ is a digital twin of $ \mathrm{S D_{P S}} $ , which mirrors the life of an actual SD process and its characteristics. Therefore, an $ \mathrm{S D D M_{V S}} $ includes digital models of the design object (i.e., the function DT), designers (i.e., the designer DT), and design activities (i.e., the design activity DT).

SDS is the core enabler in $ \mathrm{S D D T}_{5 \mathrm{D}} $ , which can provide intelligent execution, precise estimation, and reliable control for the SD. The services are necessarily a series of mathematical models that integrate tracking, evaluation, optimization, and estimate algorithms. Analysis approaches in virtual space can be performed by specific services using real data from physical space. As illustrated in Table3, three kinds of services are discussed in detail in Section4.

Table row. Column 1: Design change propagation prediction; Column 2: Change propagation paths in the function tree are identified, and change propagation probabilities are predicted..

DTD acts as the driving force of $ \mathrm{S D D T}_{5 \mathrm{D}} $ , including data from physical entities, virtual models, and services, and the data regularly update with changes in real-time status. Because both $ \mathrm{S D}_{P S} $ and $ \mathrm{S D D M}_{V S} $ come down to the design object (i.e., the product), designers, and design activities, data in DTD can be classified into the product data, the designer data, and the design activity data, as listed in Table4.
Table 4. Data type in DTD.
Table row. Column 1: Data type; Column 2: Content.

Table row. Column 1: Product data; Column 2: This refers to the functional requirements and their relationships, such as the decomposition, interaction, and integration of functions, which reflects the complexity of the design process..
Table row. Column 1: Designer data; Column 2: This refers to the design capabilities possessed by designers, which can be quantified by knowledge vectors..
Table row. Column 1: Design activity data; Column 2: This includes data from technical development, consultation between designers, and data exchange between functions..

The role of DTD has two aspects. It provides data for early-stage predetermination of design states, such as the complexity measurement of the design, the estimation of required design effort, and the prediction of the change propagation. For another, it provides data for real-time tracking of design states, such as completed design tasks, designer workload, and rest effort of the design.

CN plays as an intermedium for connecting the above four components so that the digital twin can carry out real-time and efficient information transmission, and thereby ensuring the interaction and iterative optimization between the physical space and virtual space.
$$ \mathrm {S D D T} _ {5 \mathrm {D}} = \left\{\mathrm {S D} _ {\mathrm {P S}}, \mathrm {S D D M} _ {\mathrm {V S}}, \mathrm {S D S}, \mathrm {D T D}, \mathrm {C N} \right\} $$

In summary, Formula (1) expresses $ \mathrm{S D D T}_{5 \mathrm{D}} $ $ \mathrm{S D}_{\mathrm{P S}} $ and CN are out of the scope of the research as $ \mathrm{S D}_{\mathrm{P S}} $ is an objective reality, and CN mostly relies on the quality of the hardware, so the focus of this article is $ \mathrm{S D D M}_{\mathrm{V S}} $ , SDS, DTD, and the unified modeling approach for them [28].

System design in the framework (Fig.4) is an iterative optimization process. The system design digital model represents information of design objects, designers, and design activities from the design team. With the development of the system, the digital model information becomes complete. Moreover, through system services, the actual system design process can be optimized. For example, managers can more accurately identify the knowledge requirement of functions and designate more capable designers on crucial functions. Details of System Design Digital Model in Virtual Space, Designer DT, Design activity DT, System Design Services and their relationships are illustrated in [28].

SysML is used for modeling the unified model of $ \mathrm{S D D M_{V S}} $ , SDS, and DTD, because it has been designed to enable extensions that support specialized concepts by its extension mechanism, called stereotyping [8]. Stereotypes are organized into a profile. SysML itself is defined as a UML profile.

Stereotypes are used for customizing core concepts of System Design Digital Twin in 5 Dimensions (SDDT $ _{5D} $ ). A $ SDDT_{5D} $ modeling profile is constructed, as displayed in Fig.6, where mappings and decomposition relationships, etc. constitute the relationship profile; the function DT, designer DT, and design activity DT profiles form the $ SDDM_{VS} $ profile. The product data, designer data, and design activity data profiles constitute the DTD profile. The design complexity measurement, effort estimation, and change propagation prediction profiles constitute the SDS profile.

The $ \mathrm{SDDM_{V S}} $ profile includes definitions of functions, interfaces, designers, and design activities. As illustrated in Fig.9, a function stereotype is generated from a Block. It contains attributes and parameters, such as the decomposition level, required knowledge vector, development complexity, consumed effort, and change probability. A function can be a child function, a parent function, or a peer function; their relationships are specified by «decomposed to», «integrate to» and «peer to». Additionally, an interface consists of a connector (named Interface_connector) and two ports (named Interface_Port). An Interface_connector extends from the Connector and inherits from the Block; an Interface_Port inherits from the ProxyPort.

A designer stereotype is defined by inheriting from the Block. Two attributes of a designer stereotype are provided, the ability_GK represents the designer's ability of general knowledge, and the ability_PK refers to the designer's ability of product knowledge. Moreover, a designer is classified into a junior designer, an intermediate designer, or a senior designer based on the ability_GK and ability_PK, as illustrated in Fig.10.

A DTD profile includes the product data stereotype, designer data stereotype, and design activity data stereotype. These are defined by inheriting from the Block, specifying values and parameters, and creating new data types. For example, in Fig.12, ProductData is a kind of Block, and it has attributes like required knowledge vectors mapped from functions, total complexity (C_Total), total effort (E_Total), number of designers (NoD) and information quality (IQ), etc. In a similar approach, DesignerData, like the ability of function development (AFD) and functional integration (AFI) and the DesignActivityData, can be defined.

System design of space mission is challenging as functions are coupled and constrained by the limited available commodities. Furthermore, additional complexities arise because designers describe the system in a document-based way. Radio Aurora Explorer (RAX) is a standard mission in the aerospace field. The primary objective of the mission is to study the formation of magnetic field-aligned plasma irregularities (FAI). Based on a RAX CubeSat project, in 2012, the SSWG (Space Systems Working Group) of INCOSE demonstrated the feasibility of the MBSD approach in reality, where SysML could formally specify every aspect of a system [31]. Accordingly, in the following section, the modeling approach proposed in this paper is applied to the system design of a virtual RAX CubeSat mission.

Necessary information has been given, for example, the decomposed functions are revealed in Fig.2, the required knowledge is provided in Table2, and the interfaces among functions are shown in Fig.11 in [28]. Besides, the quantitative aspects of designers and design activities are required, which are shown in Table6. To model the amount of effort needed, we make the following assumptions: the AFD value in the designer data based on the ratio of junior, intermediate, and senior designers is 2:5:3. Each designer is assigned a function development

task, so the NoD value is 1 for 36. TriangularD (40,64,50) is selected as the triangle distribution in the design activity data, and the information receiving and preparation time are set to 2h, respectively. Furthermore, function 16 $ \left( \mathrm{F}_{1 6} \right) $ is the key function because it has the most interfaces, and function 17 $ \left( \mathrm{F}_{1 7} \right) $ is selected as the changed function.

It can be seen from Table7 that the total complexity (C_Total) is 195, and the total effort (E_Total) is approximately 4819h. Based on the estimated design effort, managers can use the trade-off analysis by setting SysML models' different values to optimize the design progress. For example, based on the result, managers can more accurately identify the knowledge requirement of functions and designate more capable designers on key functions.

To assess the proposed method's practical usability, two students (Group A) and two experienced managers (Group B) were asked to participate in an experiment about estimating the total effort of the RAX CubeSate system design. The two students having the SysML knowledge background used the proposed unified models to represnt the system design, while the two managers in Group B used a traditional document-based approach, such as the requirements specification by Microsoft Word and the interface definition document by Microsoft Excel, to specify the system design. The student group spent about 48h in modeling the system model by the $ \mathrm{SDDT}_{5 \mathrm{D}} $ modeling profile and spend 4 more hours in getting the correct total effort. Compared with students, managers in Group B spend less time in specifying the systems, about 24h. However, the two managers used more time, about 10h, in getting the correct total effort as they wasted more time in understanding the ambiguity issues. Although the students spent more time in modeling the system model, they saved more time in analyzing the design complexity. Moreover, the unified model can be reused in a more detailed stage to avoid the ambiguity between the understandings of different designers.

Additionally, the effort required to develop the key function $ F_{1 6} $ is about 303h, accounting for 6.29% of the total effort, which can prove that this function is one of the core functions. The information transfer effort $ ( E_{tansfer-F16} ) $ required during the development of $ F_{1 6} $ is 60h, and the knowledge consultation effort of it $ ( E_{Consult-F16} ) $ is about 29h.

According to the prediction, the manager can decide whether to change the corresponding design parameters. A significant function of the established unified model is that it can simulate different scenarios by conveniently changing different parameters in the SysML parameter diagram, thereby helping the designer to determine critical functions and interfaces in the early design stage. For example, Table9 lists ten different scenarios for simulating the change of RAX system design. The simulation case includes all 36 functions, ten kinds of knowledge, and multiple interfaces of all RAX system designs, assuming that function 17 has been changed. Among them, scenario 1 is the basic scenario; for scenario 2, only the affected functions are simulated; then, two new random functions are added to the list of changed functions (scenario 3); then, with different knowledge vectors 1 and 2 random interfaces for simulation (scenario 4 to 10). The primary purpose of these scenarios is to cover many possible examples of function change propagation: addition/deletion of functions, addition/removal of knowledge items, and modification of interfaces. Simulation results show that additional work is required if there are any changes in the design, as shown in Fig.19.

However, designers criticized the intensive manual work required for building a model. In reality, designers were unwilling to spend so much time in creating SysML diagrams. More importantly, an experienced manager said that they preferred making decisions by referencing similar cases of a previous design or believing their experience. They suggested a few improvement ideas for future work, such as linking the model to available information databases, and building ontologies for common cases to reuse or reference them rather than creating new ones.

Leading MBSE methodologies like Harmony SE, OOSEM, SA, etc., improve upon traditional DBSE by formalizing the application of modeling to support requirements analysis, function analysis, and design synthesis. However, one of the core issues that companies care about is how to effectively evaluate, predict, and manage the complexity of a complex project in the early SD stage. The existing methods still have the problem of inaccuracy. The main reason is that the actual SD in a physical space is inconsistent with the theoretical simulation of the virtual space. The emergence of digital twins (DT) has provided an effective way to provide intelligent, efficient, and real-time services for SD to ensure the consistency between the virtual model and
the physical state. In order to integrate DT with MBSE to help project managers understand the design complexity in early stage:

(1) According to a knowledge-based SD theory, a System Design Digital Twin in 5 Dimensions （ $ \mathrm{SDDT}_{5\mathrm{D}} $ ）framework is introduced, which can map the actual SD process into the corresponding virtual space.
(2) The core concepts and relationships of $ \mathrm{SDDT}_{5 \mathrm{D}} $ are customized by a SysML profile that keeps every view of the digital system model unified.

Although SysML modeling tools, such as Magicdraw, enable designers to create and document a system model, many designers in China find it unacceptable to spend too much time in learning such a graphical modeling language without appropriate patterns. Besides, it is difficult for the machine to understand the semantics of the SysML diagrams. In the future, we will carry out in-depth research on:
(1) Linking available information databases to create reusable cases and appropriate pattern, and
(2) Represent systems design information to be both user-understandable and machine-readable.

As systems grow in complexity, Systems Engineers have embraced Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) to tackle this complexity. The Systems Modeling Language (SysML) is the most commonly used language by the Systems Engineers to implement MBSE. SysML can highly express conceptual models, but struggles to demonstrate executable models. In order to perform requirements/behavior verifications, systems engineers/designers mostly use separate simulation tools. Hence, the efficiency of the systems engineering process is often reduced due to the isolated and consecutive use of both SysML modeling tool and other simulation tools, for example defining simulation inputs to each simulation tool separately. Hence, Executable SysML is the next logical step towards achieving true MBSE support for all Systems Engineering activities in the life cycle phases- system requirements, analysis, design, implementation, integration, verification, transition, validation, acceptance testing, training and maintenance. Therefore, various research efforts are being conducted to develop executable SysML Modeling approaches. This thesis paper develops a SysML Executable Modeling Methodology (SEMM), which is demonstrated by modeling a CubeSat based Space Situational Awareness (SSA) system in SysML. The SysML SSA-CubeSat System model is made executable by integrating with Commercial-Off-The-Shelf (COTS) simulation software, namely - Systems Tool Kit (STK) and MATLAB, following the approaches defined in the SEMM.

Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) focuses on formalized application of modeling to support systems engineering artifacts development from the conceptual design phase throughout the end of the system of interest (SOI) lifecycle(Hart, 2015). The term MBSE was first Introduced by Dr. Wayne Wymore at the University of Arizona in his book Model Based Systems Engineering in 1993 (Wymore, 1993). Systems engineers are in an era of increasing complexity of modern systems (Calvano & John, 2004). In order to manage the complexity, Model Based Systems Engineering is the proposed solution by the researchers(French, 2015; Alvarez, 2016).

From the Table 1.1, it is apparent that, OOSEM/SysML have the more tool support than any other MBSE methodologies developed. SysML has emerged as the de facto standard system modeling language for MBSE (Delligatti, 2014).

MBSE is advancing in a way that intends to combine modeling with its natural next step simulation, to support the definition of system requirements, system design, system analysis, and system verification and validation. Therefore, SysML needs to be an executable language in order to directly support system system's lifecycle activities (Nikolaidou et al., 2010). Model is the physical, mathematical or logical illustration of a system, process or phenomenon (DoD Modeling and Simulation (MCS) Glossary, 1998). For example, a static model of a car. On the other hand, Simulation is the execution of a model over time. For example, simulating movement of a car. So, a SysML model can be made executable by enabling simulation capability into it.
Various schemes have been proposed to make SysML executable. Kaslow et al. used ModelCenter (a COTS software from Phoenix Integration) to integrate the analytical

(MATLAB) and simulation (STK) models with the CubeSat Reference Model(CRM)(D. Kaslow et al., 2014). Kapos et al. demonstrated how to develop executable SysML Models with Query/View/Transformation Language(Kapos et al., 2014). Discrete Event System Specification(DEVS) formalism was used to integrate simulation capabilities into SysML models(Nikolaidou et al., 2010). Maheshwari et al. created executable agent based models using SysML. The simulation for the generated SysML models was translated and executed in MATLAB by a custom framework called Discrete Agent Framework (DAF)(Maheshwari et al., 2015). Batarseh et al. used Atlas Transformation Language to translate SysML model into Arena models to enable execution (Batarseh & McGinnis, 2012). Aforementioned papers were able to make the SysML model executable with the aid of either transformation languages namely QVT, ATLAS, DEVS, DAF or separate software suites i.e. ModelCenter.

Karban et al. proposed a new Executable System Engineering Method(ESEM) for SysML Modeling using Cameo Simulation Tookit (CST) by Nomagic Inc(Karban, Jankevičius, et al., 2016).CST uses foundational UML(fUML) as a foundation to plug additional standard engines(Ciccozzi et al., 2019). Amissah et al. presented an executable language that re-factors the SysML language schema and introduced an equivalent textual syntax for model specification in conjunction with the existing graphical syntax(Amissah et al., 2018).

All the attempts described above in order to develop Executable SysML model have gaps in their methodology. Most of the approaches require substantial transformation of the SysML model to fit within an execution environment. Some of the approaches use another commercial software in order to integrate SysML model to other analytical/simulation tools. Apart from Karban's paper, none of the above executable SysML approaches developed a

reusable, standard methodology/framework for executable modeling. Although Karban at el. presented a well-formed 8-step methodology for executable modeling, it lacks the integration capability with other COTS analytical/simulation software (e.g. STK/MATLAB). Therefore, there exists a need for a developing a SysML Executable Modeling Methodology which can mitigate above mentioned challenges.
The objectives of this thesis paper are as follows.
I. Developing a theoretical approach for enabling execution of models described in SysML.
II. Modeling of a CubeSat based Space Situational Awareness system in SysML by incorporating the systems engineering artifacts.
III. Applying the developed SysML executable modeling methodology to integrate system analysis/simulation and requirements verification into the model.

Hence, a six step System Executable Modeling Methodology (SEMM) was developed. Then, a CubeSat-SSA SysML Model was built in Cameo Systems Modeler (N. M. Inc, n.d.). Finally, the model was integrated with MATLAB and Systems Tool Kit (A. G. Inc, 2013) to incorporate simulation and requirements verification capability into the model.

CHAPTER I provides background and problem statement of the thesis paper. CHAPTER II contains literature review on SysML, related research and space situational awareness. CHAPTER III describes the SysML Executable Modeling Methodology (SEMM) and its implementation. CHAPTER IV shows the SysML CubeSat-SSA system model built by applying the SEMM. CHAPTER IV also showed three illustrative examples to demonstrate
the integration of COTS simulation tools with the SysML Model. CHAPTER V includes the overall summary of the thesis work and future research expansions.
The assumptions/Limitations of this research include:
1) The only MBSE model language considered is SysML,
2) The software implementing this approach is not verified or validated for general application,
3) The only sensor platform considered for this SSA system is a CubeSat
4) The only sensor considered for this SSA System is optical sensor
5) The SSA System architectures considered are homogeneous

6) The only system analysis performed is effectiveness analysis, which evaluates three Measures of Effectiveness-SSA Relevance, Access and Conjunction Analysis. The MOEs are selected based on the frequently used parameters defined in the recently developed SSA research papers.

In recent years, Systems Modeling Language has emerged as the most popular tool for implementing systems engineering process(Peak et al., 2007; Sage & Lynch, 1998). According to Friedenthal, Moore, and Steiner(2009), "SysML is a general-purpose graphical modeling language that supports the analysis, specification, design, verification, and validation for complex systems" (Friedenthal et al., n.d.). section: ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS > 2.3.1 What is Space Situational Awareness?
section_key: acknowledgements / 2 3 1 what is space situational awareness
text: Space Situational Awareness is the ability to observe, understand and predict the physical location and behavior of natural and manmade objects in orbit around the earth (Space Situational Awareness, n.d.). Space traffic (both physical and informational) are increasing at an exponential rate. Since the start of space exploration in 1957, about 5500 rockets have been launched into earth orbit, resulting in approximately 5000 satellites and 23000 debris still in space(esa, n.d.). SSA can deliver knowledge of potential threats posed to both space assets and Earth by adversaries and environments, including space weather, space debris, uncontrolled space-crafts and space weapons(Gasparini & Miranda, 2010; Kennewell & Vo, 2013). To alleviate the threats posed by these space hazards, SSA systems could detect potential collisions in advance and avoid potential accidents by enacting effective maneuver protocols(Jayaweera et al., 2011; National Research on Space Debris, Safety of Space Objects with Nuclear Power Sources on Board and Problems Relating to Their Collision with Space Debris, 2009; Neff, 2016).

text: Small satellites generally refer to a class of spacecraft that are also termed as nanosatellites or CubeSats. CubeSats have shown promise as potentially reliable and low cost means of conducting space research. This is facilitated due to a defined and standardized spacecraft envelope which also allows commercial off the shelf (COTS) components and instruments to be assembled onto the CubeSat (Swartwout, 2013).

The following steps describe the procedure to implement the SEMM for any system of interest (SOI). For this thesis paper, a CubeSat-SSA system has been chosen as the SOI.
1. Step 1: Model Organization
2. Step 2: Defining Stakeholder Needs/System Requirements/Use Cases/Concept of Operations(ConOps)/MOEs
3. Step 3: Modeling System Architecture (Physical/Logical)/Internal Structure/Subsystem Communication
4. Step 4: Specify System Behavior Modeling and Analysis Context
5. Step 5: Integration with the COTS Analysis/ Simulation tools
6. Step 6: Run Analysis/Simulation

I. SysML Requirement Diagram: A requirement diagram represents text-based requirements and their relationships with other requirements and/or model elements, and test cases to support requirements traceability. Relationship types between requirements to requirements or other elements are containment, derive, refine, satisfy, verify and trace. Requirements table is another form of requirement diagram, which can import or export the requirements to and from an Excel sheet.

II. SysML Block Definition Diagram: Block Definition Diagram (BDD) characterizes structural elements called blocks. BDD is principally useful for representing hierarchical compositions, relationships, behavior features and classifications. A block can have different stereotypes depending on the usage. For example, System Context stereotype is frequently used for defining context of a simulation to be executed.

III. SysML Internal Block Diagram: Internal Block Diagram (IBD) represents interconnection, interfaces and ports between the parts of a block. Signals can be sent from one port to another port through connectors to depict the transfer of data between the parts.
IV. SysML Use Case Diagram: Use Case Diagram describes the relationship between the system functions and actors to visualize the use case scenarios and/or operations concepts.

V. SysML Activity Diagram: An activity diagram is used to model different types of system/component behavior with the aid of flow of inputs, outputs and control. An activity diagram also shows how the actions transform the inputs to outputs. It can be drawn using actions, controls, data flows and swim lanes. Different types of action
performs different functions. For example, opaque action supports different scripting languages in order to implement the defined behavior.

VI. SysML Sequence Diagram: Sequence Diagram shows interactions through the sequence of messages exchanged between systems, parts or components. Sequence diagram can be generated automatically by making the model executable. Most commonly used diagram elements are lifelines, gate, synchronous message, asynchronous message, return message and activation options.

VII. SysML State Machine Diagram: State Machine Diagram represents behavior of a model entity through its transitions between states triggered by events/signals/values. States can have defined Behaviors for any Activities: Entry, Exit, or Do Activity. Transition between states can be triggered through guards too.

VIII. SysML Parametric Diagram: Parametric diagram represents constraints or equations to support engineering analysis, evaluation of mathematical expressions (for example, $ \mathrm{F=m^{*}a} $ ) and binding equivalent parameters. A Parametric diagram includes the usage of a constraint block to constrain the properties of another block. Constrained properties normally have simple value types that can also convey units, quantity kinds, and probability distributions.

IX. SysML Package Diagram: Package Diagram represents the organization of a system model in terms of packages that also serve as containers/folders that contain model elements. Package Diagram also help in systematic model navigation. It is a good practice to organize the model elements according to the four pillars of SysML - Requirements, Structure, Behavior and Parametric.

From the previous section, it is possible to integrate various COTS tools with the system model. For the scope of this thesis paper, Cameo Systems Modeler (CSM) with Cameo Simulation Toolkit (CST) plugin from Nomagic was used to create the system model(Cameo Systems Modeler, n.d.). Moreover, MATLAB and Systems Tool Kit (STK) were two other COTS simulation tools being integrated with the system model to make it executable(A. G. Inc, 2013).

CSM is a COTS multi-platform collaborative MBSE environment, which delivers intelligence, robustness and creativity to define, track and visualize all aspects of systems in the most standard-compliant SysML models and diagrams (Cameo Systems Modeler, n.d.). In this thesis paper, the version for the CSM is 19.0 SP1 enterprise edition and operating system is Windows 10. The reasons for choosing CSM are as follows- most widely used SysML tool in the industry, ADSL lab have the commercial license for CSM and CSM comes with Cameo Simulation Toolkit (CST) plugin. CSM's User Interface (UI) consists of Main Menu, Main Toolbars, Model Browser, Diagram Pane, Diagram Palette and Quick Properties Panel (Figure 3.3). The main menu located at the top of the modeling tool window contains the following elements: File, Edit, View, Layout, Diagrams, Options, Tools, Analyze, Collaborate, Window and Help. CSM has two types of toolbars- Main toolbars and Diagram toolbars. Model Browser provides a visual representation of the hierarchy of modeled elements in a hierarchy and they can be compressed and/or expanded.
Figure 3.3: Layout of the CSM User Interface (UI)

Diagram palette contains different model/diagram elements. User can drag and drop these palette elements to the diagram pane. CST is a plugin attached to the CSM in order to provide extendable model execution framework based on OMG fUML standards. fUML stands for Foundational Subset for Executable UML Models(Seidewitz & Tatibouet, 2015). fUML designates a basic virtual machine for the Unified Modeling Language, and the specific abstractions supported, facilitating acquiescent models to be transformed into various executable forms for verification, integration and deployment. CST plugin is helpful for validating system behavior and model checking by executing, animating and debugging SysML diagrams, which are made executable. CST is capable of performing activity execution, state machine execution, parametric execution, multiple action language support, model debugging, UI prototyping etc. Figure 3.4 shows the CST sessions tab.
Figure 3.4: Sessions Tab in CST

CST creates simulation sessions when the model is being simulated. Active elements are the elements a simulation session is currently executing (denoted by red by default). Once active elements has been simulated, they are called visited element (denoted by green by default). Orange color denotes last visited element by default. An example is shown in the Figure 3.5.
Figure 3.5: Different colors denoting active, visited and last visited elements

CST also has a simulation console pane, which shows simulation information during a model simulation (Figure 3.6). Simulation console can be used to take input from the user and display the simulation results.
Figure 3.6: Runtime Information of CST

The Variables pane shows the structure of an executing model and the runtime values during the model simulation. The pane consists of two columns - name and value. The name column depicts the context and structural features of the simulated model whereas value column represents the runtime values of those elements in the name column. Runtime values are editable if they are of the following types- Boolean, Integer, Real and String.

MATLAB is a multi-paradigm computing environment and programming language developed by Mathworks. With the aid of MATLAB, a user can analyze data, develop algorithms and construct models and applications. Moreover, MATLAB is one of the supported scripting languages by CSM. MATLAB supports interface to various COTS simulation tools such as STK to serve as a communication bridge between analytical and visualization engines.

STK is a physics based 3D modeling, simulation and visualization tool used by engineers, space mission analysts, space operators and decision makers in order to model and simulate complex land, sea, air or space systems. STK supports a wide variety of environments, objects, sensors, constraints, utilities and tools, visualization, reports and graphs and other extended capabilities. STK also provides supports for modeling Space Situational Awareness (SSA) capabilities and scenarios through AdvCat analysis, access calculations software suite etc. STK also comes with STK integration plugin, which can be used to provide interface with other
applications such as MATLAB and Excel. For this thesis paper, STK 11.2 was used to simulate a simple SSA scenario. An example debris cloud generated by STK is shown in Figure 3.7.
Figure 3.7: A STK 3D model showing debris cloud

section_key: acknowledgements / 3 3 cubesat ssa system model by semm
text: In this section, a detail description about the SEMM steps will be discussed by constructing the CubeSat-SSA system model. In this thesis, paper, Parametric and sequence diagrams were not used hence excluded from the framework.

The Model is organized by the package names according to the four pillars of SysML (Requirements, Structure, Behavior and Parametric). For this thesis paper, the Parametrics package was excluded, as there was no use of Parametric diagram in this particular model.

SysML Requirements diagram falls under Requirements package. SysML Block Definition Diagram and SysML Internal Block Diagram reside inside Structure Package. All the behavior diagrams (SysML Activity Diagram and SysML State Machine Diagram) used in the model being placed inside Behavior Package. Further package decomposition was used for organization of the model elements inside these three major packages (Requirements, Structure and Behavior). A package groups blocks, packages and other model elements together. The packages can have dependency, generalization, realize, containment, and association relationships. Following procedures were used in CSM to add a new package in the model- Right click in the Model under containment tree, Select Create Element and Select Package as the element type.

STK_Relevance's classifier behavior used a MATLAB function script, which automated and modified the SSA relevance function defined in a previous research. In that research work, authors used SSA relevance measures of effectiveness for comparing SSA system architectures using a network of CubeSats(Chandra et al., 2018). However, the authors were forced to run the MATLAB script independently due to the non-executable nature of the model they defined.

The final step of the SEMM was to run Analysis/Simulation from the CubeSat-SSA system Model. Each of the three scenarios defined using system context and associated behavior diagrams were run using Cameo Simulation Toolkit. An important note to consider before running the scenario was to make sure the simulation was run with context. The following procedures were followed to run with system context-
- Selecting the System context of interest
- Right clicking and selecting simulation
- After that clicking the run(Figure 3.27)

SysML Requirement Diagram represented the operational requirements for CubeSat-SSA system (Figure 4.2). One of the requirements had satisfy relationship with a parameter namely coverage percentage. Later in the modeling work, executable modeling approach facilitated automatic requirements verification in order to verify that particular requirement.
Figure 4.2: Operational Requirements for CubeSat-SSA System

The model also contain concept of operations for CubeSats and use cases for CubeSat-SSA system under behavior package. SysML state machine diagram pictured the Concept of Operations and use cases were captured using SysML use case diagram. SysML Block Definition Diagrams represented the physical architecture of the model. SSA Domain comprises of Artificial Space Objects, Natural Space Objects, Orbital Debris and Space Weather. CubeSat SSA System Architecture falls under Artificial Space Objects. CubeSat-SSA System Architecture consists of Space Segment, SSA Command and Data Centre, Command and Data Centre Sevices, Transport, Launch and Deployment Services and GPS. Space segment and SSA Command and Data Centre were further decomposed into subsystems. CubeSats alongside their orbits have one to many relationships with the space
segment (1...*), which indicates multiplicity. Figure 4.5 through 4.11 shows the CubeSat-SSA system architecture.
Figure 4.5: SSA Domain
Figure 4.6: CubeSat SSA System Architecture
A CubeSat includes SSA Mission Payload, Communication Subsystem, Power Subsystem, Propulsion Subsystem, Command and Data Handling Subsystem, Attitude Determination and
Control Subsystem, and Structures and Mechanisms Subsystem. Optical sensor, Camera. Image processor and GPS Receiver and Antenna are part of SSA Mission Payload.
Figure 4.7: Space Segment
Figure 4.8: SSA Mission Payload
Attitude Determination and Control Subsystem consists of Software, Actuator, Sensor and Shared Processor/Memory. SSA Command and Data Center comprises of Plan and Schedule

Subsystem, CubeSat Command Subsystem, Space-Ground Communication Subsystem, Ground Equipment Control Subsystem, Network Subsystem, Facilities Subsystem, SSA Data Processing Subsystem and SSA Data Dissemination Subsystem.
Figure 4.9: Attitude Determination and Control Subsystem
Figure 4.10: SSA Command and Data Center (SCDC)

SysML Internal Block Definition Diagram in Figure 4.11 shows the simple representation of the command, data and power flowing between various CubeSat Subsystems and SCDC. Commands are sent from SCDC to the CubeSats in the space. CubeSats track objects, collect SSA data through SSA mission payload, and send information back to the SCDC for analysis.

section: ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS > Scenario 1: Access to Space Objects
section_key: acknowledgements / scenario 1 access to space objects
text: The scenario utilizes co-simulation in STK to visualize the scenario and calculate the results. In this scenario, an observation satellite (CubeSat) tracks 10 unknown objects. A pointing sensor is attached to the observation satellite, namely ADSLSat. Random creation of the unknown objects is based on the following assumptions- radius of earth is 6371 km, low earth orbit range from 100 to 2000 km, minimum semi major axis is 6471 km and maximum semi major axis is 8371 km. The scenario return the access values (access start times and access stop times) for each of the unknown object. When the scenario is simulated, the pointing sensor points to the closest unknown object it has access. The scenario can be run/reset/closed solely from SysML model without opening the STK application. Moreover, STK returns access values to the SysML model through CST console via MATLAB programming interface (Figure 4.12). Code snippets for scenario 1 is attached in the Appendix section. Scenario start time and stop time were chosen arbitrarily.
