text: While reviewed reliability assessment methods specifically aimed at reducing complexity and cost to make them more accessible for student-based development teams, they can be considered as the simplified versions of the commercially applied techniques, that usually incorporate multiple risk assessment methods, e.g. the PRA methodology, making them less practical for the projects with a limited budget. The simplifications make the analysis less complex and time consuming; this, however, comes with a price: only a relatively small number of reliability analysis aspects can be covered, which may increase the probability of the unforeseen behavior during testing or even in-orbit operation. This concern is inherent to all reviewed methodologies in the previous sections. The methodology presented in this thesis work is expected to cope with this issue as it attempts to cover multiple aspects of system reliability analysis, utilize both functional and physical architectures and provide basis for both qualitative and quantitative analysis, while still being rather accessible for a practical application at the universities, by deploying the benefits of MBSE. These benefits, however, can be obtained only if the reliability analysis and system design are integrated into a single model. Using SysML for reliability analysis only may become very time consuming, even assuming the engineer already has experience with SysML. This is because a number of system design elements will still have to be modeled first prior to developing a reliability model.

section_key: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of master of science in aerospace engineering at the delft university of technology to be defended publicly on friday december 11 2020 at 09 30 am / background information on space environment
text: The major contributor to variety of events that occur in our solar system is the sun, which has a core temperature of 15,7 million Kelvin, a surface temperature of 6000 Kelvin and 1 million degrees Kelvin in the sun's atmosphere (corona). The temperatures of such a high magnitude cause all of the sun material to be in plasma state. Some of this plasma is injected into space, which is called solar wind, that mainly consists of protons and electrons with densities of 5 particles per $ cm^{3} $ and average velocities of 300 km/s, also carrying the sun's magnetic field with it. The solar wind may interact with the sun's magnetic field resulting in mass ejections of higher density and the velocities of several times higher above the average. This is called coronal mass ejections (CMEs). The CMEs often reach the near-Earth space environment which typically happens once in several days.

section: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of Master of Science in Aerospace Engineering at the Delft University of Technology, to be defended publicly on Friday December 11, 2020 at 09:30 AM. > Background information on space environment
section_key: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of master of science in aerospace engineering at the delft university of technology to be defended publicly on friday december 11 2020 at 09 30 am / background information on space environment
text: Another anomaly that can be related to CMEs is the solar flares, which are massive explosions near the sun's surface producing a high energy radiation that results in even higher velocity particles compared to the CMEs. Both phenomena may thus result in arrival of high-energy protons at near-Earth space, which is called the solar proton events. Such events may cause the interaction of the high-energy particles with the Earth's magnetic field and induce variations in plasma densities and the Earth's magnetic field strength and orientation in the near-Earth space and the upper atmosphere. This phenomenon is called the geomagnetic activity. A particular case of the geomagnetic activity is the geomagnetic storm, a period of intensive magnetic field strengths and injection of high-energy plasma into the Earth's magnetic field (magnetosphere). Inside the magnetosphere high-energy charged particles are aligned across the Earth's magnetic field lines and constitute the Van Allen radiation belts that occur form 1500 km altitude to approximately 6 Earth radii. The Van Allen radiation belts (Figure A-1) are known to threaten the satellites mostly in medium Earth orbit (MEO) but also in low Earth orbit (LEO) with high inclinations, and geostationary orbits (GEO) [11]. Besides, due to the fact that the Earth's dipolar field is shifted relative to the Earth's center, the Van Allen belts can reach relatively low altitudes up to 200 km in the region of the eastern coast of South America, which is called the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA) (Figure A-2). text: On 8 august 1989 ESA launched a star mapping mission, called HIPPARCOS whose final destination was a $ 1 2^{0} $ W geostationary position but due to a failure of its apogee motor the satellite couldn't come any further than the initial geostationary transfer orbit (GTO). The corresponding radiation environment containing the high-energy particles that can travel through spacecraft material and cause various anomalies such as decreased power production by solar arrays, electronic failures and amplification of background noise in sensors [1], highly exceeded the design specifications of HIPPARCOS. When the high-energy particles impact the spacecraft material also both the surface and internal charging may occur, not only resulting in degradation of electronics over time but also in instantaneous electrostatic discharges [11]. In addition, a major solar event of March 1991 caused the enhancement of radiation flux in the Van Allen belts. The subsequent increase in background noise in the instruments could be immediately addressed to this phenomenon [12].

text: The ESD is an arc discharge that arises as a result of a charge buildup on a satellite surface or between its internal hardware components (when a spacecraft travels through the ionized atmosphere it can develop an induced charge of thousands of Volts [1]). The most common cause of internal charging is the penetration by the high-energy electrons (> 10keV) which then localize around insulating materials such as wiring insulation and circuit boards. When a certain threshold of electrical potential between the internal components has been reached an ESD may occur in electric and electronic parts. The charge buildup rate depends on the specific location of a spacecraft in space environment while the electric potential that is required to produce an arc depends on the used materials and a relative position of the conductors [11].

text: A representative case of this phenomenon is the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System (TDRS-1) designed by NASA to provide communications and high data-rate transmissions for low Earth-orbiting satellites. The TDRS-1 was launched from the space shuttle in Aril, 1983 but due to a failure of the shuttle's second stage thruster the satellite had to make use of its own power source to reach the GEO with $ 0^{\circ} $ inclination. During the transfer orbit, various anomalies have been observed in the Attitude Control System (ACS). The reason behind these anomalies was the state changes in the Random Access Memory (RAM) in the ACS. A number of these anomalies were considered as mission-threatening, requiring an extensive intervention by ground control. This unusual behavior in memory equipment is typically referred to as Single Event Upsets (SEU) [16].

text: SEU is an anomalous change in the state of a memory device. While the ESD's occur after a gradual charge buildup, the single event upsets are caused by impact of one or several high-energy particles (protons and electrons of > 2MeV) into vulnerable (sub)system components, immediately resulting in an operational anomaly [11].

text: An example of an SEU is a "bit flip" when the solid state memory devices suddenly gain charge after being impacted. This may negatively influence the system software and hardware. Another example is a single-event latch up (SEL) when a subsystem hangs or crashes. Under these conditions the affected subsystem may even pull an excessive current from the EPS and drastically reduce the available electrical power for all other subsystems, also called single-event burnout (SEB) [11].

The spikes in SEUs are associated with solar events that occurred in August, September and October of 1989 [16].

text: The earlier mentioned space environmental effects are well-known but still pose a threat to space missions as they are difficult to be completely accounted for during the (sub)system design due to the limited mission budgets. On the other hand, there exist various ground testing facilities that help to simulate the dynamic space environment and its appropriate effects. However, in a variety of cases design errors have become the main reason of mission failures when the space environmental conditions didn't exceed the design specifications [11]. It becomes clear when the example below is considered.

text: The STRV 1-C and STRV 1-D, the Space Technology and research Vehicles were the microsatellites launched on November 16, 2000 to test the influence of the radiation environment on the state-of the-art materials and components in geosynchronous transfer orbit. Two weeks after the launch the STRV-1C experienced control problems and a couple of days later the STRV-1D showed the same symptoms prior to the final loss of contact with a ground station [18].

section_key: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of master of science in aerospace engineering at the delft university of technology to be defended publicly on friday december 11 2020 at 09 30 am / insufficient design
text: Failure analysis has led to the conclusion that a software design error was culprit which sent a continuous current to latching relays (these are the bi-stable relays that are switched by a short current pulse after which they retain their last position when the current is switched off, instead of being hold in their position by a continuous current) of the radio frequency distribution unit instead of a short pulse. Because of the continuous current a thermal damage to relays insulation material between coils occurred leading to a short circuit, thereby disabling the main receiver [19]. There was no possibility to activate the redundant receiver as the corresponding trip switch couldn't be switched on from the ground because it was meant to be communicated through the main receiver. This means that both satellites finally couldn't receive any ground command, including recovery commands.

section: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of Master of Science in Aerospace Engineering at the Delft University of Technology, to be defended publicly on Friday December 11, 2020 at 09:30 AM. > Insufficient design
section_key: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of master of science in aerospace engineering at the delft university of technology to be defended publicly on friday december 11 2020 at 09 30 am / insufficient design
text: In this example two design flaws were responsible for the irretrievable failure of the satellites. A software design error was the primary reason, providing a continuous current to the latching relays instead of a pulsed signal. The secondary reason was a badly thought out redundancy: the activation of the redundant receiver from the ground couldn't be achieved because the corresponding trip switch could only be communicated through the main receiver.

text: On February $ 1 7^{\mathrm{th}} $ Jaxa (a Japan's space agency) has launched an X-ray satellite observatory to explore the nature of super-massive black holes, also attempting to retrieve the origin of the dark matter [20]. Within a month after the satellite has reached the orbit, contact with it was lost during its maneuvering into a position for examining an active galaxy cluster. The investigation has concluded that a software error and a control command mistakenly sent by the ground operators, activated the angular motion on the wrong moment which moved the satellite into uncontrolled spin. The angular velocity exceeded the design specification of the mechanical attachment of the solar panels leading to their break off, leaving the satellite subsystems and instruments without power [21].

text: The problem started when the ACS (attitude control system) suddenly reported that the satellite was spinning while it wasn't. To "counteract" the mistakenly interpreted spin, ground operators activated the reaction wheel. At the same moment, the magnetic torque operated by the ACS was malfunctioning which led to a further spin up of the reaction wheel. Besides, also the star tracker data was lost, otherwise the ground controllers would have probably been reported on time about the unintended spinning. When the ACS went in a safe mode and a problem became clear, operators activated the thrusters to compensate for a spin but due to the incorrect thruster parameters the rotation velocity has become even higher causing the solar panels to break off [22].

text: The purpose of this subsection was to get an indication of which satellite subsystem contributes to the most fatal failures of the Earth orbiting satellites. When comparing the results of different studies it becomes obvious that despite the differences in considered mass ranges, amount of data and time span, the electric power subsystem appears to have the highest share in fatal mission failures. It will further be used as a sample subsystem for the sake of risk analysis in the course of this report (starting from Chapter 2). The reason for this among other things is a comprehensive amount of data on failure descriptions for this subsystem which can be used to create an extensive failure mode specification.

text: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) and Failure Mode and Effects Criticality Analysis (FMECA) A FMEA is an analytical and structured method to determine system's failure modes and their effect on system's performance. Besides, this method also provides possibilities for risk mitigation and management [10]. FMEA identifies potential hazards during the system's early design stages which helps to prevent design flaws in later stages, where applying changes can be very costly. FMECA extends FMEA by adding a criticality factor estimating the severity of each failure. The methods are considered to be qualitative, however the outcome of performed analysis can result in quantitative figures such as risk priority numbers. section_key: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of master of science in aerospace engineering at the delft university of technology to be defended publicly on friday december 11 2020 at 09 30 am / hazard and operability hazop
text: This method has in general a lot of similarities with the previously described FME(C)A. It identifies deviations in operation of a system, and their initiating events that can result in undesirable consequences. Also, it helps to determine actions for the purpose of risk mitigation [27]. This method uses a set of guidewords (e.g., none, reverse, less of, more of, as well as, part of, sooner than, later than, etc.) to examine each system element or each task and activity of a human operator. The input model to start the analysis is a physical component diagram or a task diagram [32]. Based on this diagram a brainstorm session takes place where different specialists use their experience and imagination to systematically determine all possible scenarios in which hazard of failure might occur.

section_key: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of master of science in aerospace engineering at the delft university of technology to be defended publicly on friday december 11 2020 at 09 30 am / hazard and operability hazop
text: HAZOP can be best applied to systems in which human operation plays a major role or to systems for which the potential hazards are difficult to detect and quantify. The drawback of this method is its inability to account for the cognitive ability of a human that could lead to an unsafe action. Besides, performing the analysis in different organizations for the same system can provide different results. Also, the interaction between the system or process components is not being taken into account. Finally, the analysis can be expensive and time consuming [31].

text: Both methods are uniform for predicting the reliability of electronic parts and systems. A basic difference between both methods is the amount of information needed to apply them. PCA typically requires part quantities, quality levels and the operational environment, when the accurate design data and component specifications are not determined in the early design process. So it requires a minimal amount of information and is thus useful in the early design stages. The formula which is used in PCA is just the summation of the base failure rates of all components in the system, based on the generic failure rate tables and environmental quality factors, which makes this method less accurate compared to PSA. The PSA requires a greater amount of information and is applied later in the design process when a detailed parts lists and actual operating conditions such as environment, temperature, voltage, current, power levels, etc. are known [35], [36], [37].

The blocks that represent the system components, can be connected in series or parallel configuration. Parallel connection is used to show the redundancy. text: Event tree is a graphic representation of the potential events that can occur in a system. ETA usually starts with a diagram (Event Sequence Diagram - see Figure A-13) in which a top event (i.e., a specific failure) is being captured on the left side. Then, it identifies the corresponding chain events and their consequences until the end state is reached on the right side of the diagram, which provides a specific scenario. Each event can be true or false depending on a system's current state. The possible consequences of the initiating event are considered and the outcomes are analyzed to estimate their potential results. This process stops when the end state is reached, showing the potential final result caused by the initial event. Event trees are useful for analyzing systems with sequential operations and transitions, as proceeding from the beginning towards the end of the diagram the events are advancing in time. The final goal of an event tree is to estimate the probability of each scenario [10], [42].

text: There exist two general software reliability models. The first model, which is sometimes called a "defect density" model attempts to predict software reliability based on the design parameters, while the second model, a "software reliability growth model", is meant to deal with the software test data. It models how the system reliability changes over time during testing process, as when the failures are discovered, the bugs can be repaired, thereby increasing the total software reliability [46], [47].

section: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of Master of Science in Aerospace Engineering at the Delft University of Technology, to be defended publicly on Friday December 11, 2020 at 09:30 AM. > Software Reliability Growth Modeling
section_key: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of master of science in aerospace engineering at the delft university of technology to be defended publicly on friday december 11 2020 at 09 30 am / software reliability growth modeling
text: The basic principle of the growth model is to develop a statistical relation between the defect detection data and some existing functions (e.g., an exponential function). The growth models are basically the statistical interpolation of defect detection data by mathematical functions. When the correlation matches, the basic function can be applied to predict future behavior of the software. By correlating the reliability growth with such function, it becomes possible to predict reliability at a future point in time. General software reliability growth models include a parameter which is related to a number of bugs. Applying this parameter in combination with an actual number of bugs found, the amount of faults in the remaining code can be estimated [46], [47].

text: The growth models can be divided in two main types: concave and S-shaped (see Figure A-15). The common thing about these models is their asymptotic behavior: a fault detection rate decreases as the number of defects found and repaired, increases. This behavior is caused by two major factors: 1) repair and new functionality may contribute to the new defects; 2) each time a bug is repaired, the total amount of bugs also decreases until a certain constant value due to the first factor.

text: The CSRM is a method developed by NASA to model and identify software-related risks thereby accounting for potential faults and failures that have been identified in the previous space missions. The main focus lies on the software risks at the functional level based on various PRA (Probabilistic Risk Assessment - see subsection A2.2.5) techniques which help to identify and evaluate operational mission scenarios. This forms a further basis for developing risk models and the corresponding quantitative analysis in relation to the mission-critical and safety-critical system functions. The key feature of CSRM is a software functional decomposition to differentiate its functions, control and safety actions for identifying both "unconditional" and "conditional" software failures. text: The advantage of CSRM is that it can be applied at different system development stages, such as the specification and design levels. At the specification level CSRM's input will be the top-level system specification and generic data to obtain the preliminary software risk identification and its potential contribution to system performance. When the system design has been advanced to the more detailed level and more design data is available a design-level CSRM analysis can be performed. Another advantage of CSRM is that it can be integrated with other risk analysis methods.

section_key: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of master of science in aerospace engineering at the delft university of technology to be defended publicly on friday december 11 2020 at 09 30 am / a2 2 5 pra probabilistic risk assessment
text: PRA originates from the aerospace industry and is being nowadays applied within various technical economic and social disciplines. It is not a single method but a methodology comprising a variety of coherent risk assessment methods (a number of which is described in the preceding subsections), each having its specific application. A PRA generally leads to a risk curve and the corresponding uncertainties as a final result. The risk curve can reflect on different parameters but typically compares the frequency of exceeding a consequence value versus the consequence values. When the risk assessment is qualitative a two-dimensional probability versus consequence matrix can be constructed. PRA can be used for internal (e.g., hardware and software failures, operator error, etc.) and external (e.g., space environment) initiating events [50], [51].

For this reason, PRA is vastly incorporated in NASA's risk management approach. The method can be applied to reveal risks and hazards during the design, operation and maintenance, thereby improving all RAMS (Reliability, Availability, Maintainability and Safety) aspects [50], [51].

text: A typical PRA process consists of the following steps:

section: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of Master of Science in Aerospace Engineering at the Delft University of Technology, to be defended publicly on Friday December 11, 2020 at 09:30 AM. > A2.2.5 (PRA) Probabilistic Risk Assessment
section_key: in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of master of science in aerospace engineering at the delft university of technology to be defended publicly on friday december 11 2020 at 09 30 am / a2 2 5 pra probabilistic risk assessment
text: First, the purpose of risk assessment has to be defined together with the undesirable consequences for a project or mission failure. The next step encompasses the comprehensive system study based on its design and the operations it is made for. After no more doubts exist on how a system is designed and what it has to do, the analysis has to take place on what can go wrong and the corresponding initiating events have to identified. For this purpose, the methods like FMEA and MLD can be applied. The accident scenarios can for example be modelled using ETA and ESD, while different triggers that cause system failures can be estimated using FTA. The probability of occurrence of each end state can be calculated and summed up. After the risk probabilities are estimated, the uncertainty and sensitivity (i.e., the relation between input changes and analysis results) analyses have to be performed. For the uncertainty analysis the probabilistic methods like Monte Carlo simulation can be applied [50], [51].

Model-Based Systems Design (MBSD) formalizes the application of system modeling. However, it is still difficult for designers to implement MBSD in practice. One of the challenges is to make the field of design more unified, as different MBSD methodologies focus on specific areas, and various designers from different areas use ambiguous terms. Moreover, the failure of some products originates in undiscovered couplings of functions in the design stage. Axiomatic Design (AD) provides a scientific foundation for system design. In order to reduce ambiguity and alleviate functional couplings, this paper integrates AD with the MBSD and proposes a unified systems design approach, called Axiomatic Model-Based Systems Design (A-MBSD). A-MBSD uses four pillars: (a) the fundamental framework of AD; (b) the Independence Axiom; (c) a new behavior domain (BD); and (d) an A-MBSD modeling profile. Finally, the design of a Forest Fire Satellite Monitoring and Control System demonstrates that the proposed approach can improve unity and alleviate the coupling of functions in a system design.

The development of a large-scale product such as an automobile, a satellite, or an airplane has evolved to employ a systems engineering methodology, in which systems design (SD) performs a crucial role through the explicit representations of system requirements and overall solutions that have a profound influence on subsequent integration, verification, validation, and operation. A general SD process includes three iterative activities: requirements analysis, function analysis, and design synthesis. $ ^{1} $

In the conventional Document-Based Systems Design (DBSD) process, designers share information and design intent through a set of documents, $ ^{2} $ such as requirements specifications, interface definition documents, N-squared charts, and SD specifications. However, DBSD shows limitations, where the growth in system complexity has increased the risk to unacceptable levels. Ambiguity tends to arise when information is scattered throughout a disjointed set of text documents, spreadsheets, and diagrams.

Model-Based Systems Design (MBSD) improves upon DBSD by formalizing the application of modeling to support requirements analysis, function analysis, and design synthesis. $ ^{3} $ Application of Model-based

Systems Engineering (MBSE) follows traditional "Vee" model, while this paper focuses on system decomposition and definition, that is, the left part of "Vee" model, which is MBSD. $ ^{4} $ Researchers have proposed many MBSD methodologies. Popular ones include Harmony Systems Engineering, $ ^{5} $ Object Process Methodology (OPM), $ ^{6,7} $ Vitech MBSE, $ ^{8} $ Object-Oriented Systems Engineering Methodology (OOSEM), $ ^{9} $ System Modeling Methodology (SYSMOD), $ ^{10} $ and State Analysis (SA). $ ^{11} $ Table 1 compares these methods by listing their core ideas, modeling languages, supporting tools, advantages, and limitations.

Although several of the previously listed MBSD methodologies focus on using unified languages, such as SysML $ ^{12} $ and OPL, $ ^{6} $ throughout the product development life cycle, and they are able to specify the SD through the language iteratively, it is still a challenge for designers to implement them in a unified way. This is in large part because most designers from different areas create products intuitively, and use ambiguous terms based on their experience, which leads to unnecessary iterations. $ ^{13} $

Although partitioning criteria in OOSEM can increase cohesion and reduce couplings by refactoring common functionality and partitioning comments, it falls to the experience of designers to determine what other characteristics a good design should have. Therefore, one challenge for SD is how to make it in a more unified way in order to alleviate misunderstanding among various design teams.

To complement contemporary MBSD methods by reducing ambiguity and alleviating functional couplings, this paper provides an analysis technique that integrates MBSD with Axiomatic Design (AD) from two perspectives: $ ^{14} $
1. The fundamental framework of AD is used within the context of MBSD.
2. Behavior analysis and unified modeling technology of MBSD are introduced to enhance AD.

AD was developed to become a commonly applied engineering design theory, and Kulak et al $ ^{15} $ provided an overview during a 20-year period (1990-2010) from the type of axiom, application area, method,

and evaluation type. The findings of this study indicated that AD was used mainly in the areas of product (42%) and software design (23%), while it was used in systems design only 19% of the time. Over the past few years, AD has played a larger role in SD where growth in system complexity has increased risk to unacceptable levels. Hong and Park $ ^{16} $ proposed a collaborative design process for large-scale systems by admonishing designers to maintain the independence of functional elements using the Independence Axiom. Hehenberger et al $ ^{17} $ presented a hierarchical design process for mechatronic systems that integrates AD principles with systems design. Wang et al $ ^{4} $ proposed a semantic model for axiomatic systems design.

The key concepts and theories of AD can be related to MBSD from four pillars: first, an AD process provides a framework for MBSD by organizing information into four design domains, that is, customer, functional, physical, and process; $ ^{14} $ second, functional couplings that hinder the SD process $ ^{18} $ can be identified by the Independence Axiom of AD; third, behavior analysis of MBSD can bridge the functional and physical domains (PDs) $ ^{19} $ so as to analyze the relationships between functions and structures, and help designers establish the design matrix to apply the independence axiom; fourth, MBSD's model-based
technology can unify representations of different AD design domains as to reduce ambiguous representations.

However, research and applications of AD and MBSD are relatively independent. For AD, although much attention is paid to product design, manufacturing SD, material processing, and decisions during design, $ ^{20} $ there is less research on effectively integrating AD with model-based technology and SD. In terms of MBSD, advanced modeling languages and integration between a system model and domain-specific models are research hotspots. $ ^{21,22} $

In order to integrate MBSD with AD, this paper gives a unified engineering systems design approach called Axiomatic ModelBased Systems Design (A-MBSD), which introduces the result of behavior analysis as a new domain (behavior domain [BD]) into AD and constructs a top-down system decomposition process called Requirements- Functions -Behaviors-Structures (RFBS). In addition, to represent the system model in a unified way, an A-MBSD modeling profile is constructed through SysML stereotypes.
In short, A-MBSD improves MBSD by incorporating AD.
1. The new BD of A-MBSD increases the reliability of the design matrix by bridging the functional and PDs.
2. The system model of A-MBSD reduces ambiguity through unifying system requirements, functions, and structures.
3. The RFBS framework enables designers to document and manage design information from high abstract levels to more detailed levels.
4. A-MBSD is tool independent and places emphasis on specifying decomposing, and allocating functional requirements (FRs).
5. The Independence Axiom of AD is used to help designers make correct decisions by identifying the coupling of functions at an early stage.

Finally, the proposed method is demonstrated by the design of a Forest Fire Satellite Monitoring and Control System (FFSMCS), which shows that the method can improve design unity and alleviate unnecessary, nonintrinsic couplings during SD.
AD is a design methodology created by Suh. $ ^{2 3} $ AD is built on three core methods: design domains, a zigzag process, and design axioms.

1. Design domains. AD consists of four domains: customer, functional, physical, and process, as displayed in Figure 1. They are represented by Customer Needs (CNs), FRs, Design Parameters (DPs), and Process Variants (PVs).

2. A zigzag process. The mapping between adjacent domains is accomplished by top-down zigzag decomposition, which is called the requirements flow-down in systems engineering. There are two kinds of mapping relationships between two domains: (a) mapping at the same level, and (b) mapping between two different levels.

Because adjusting one DP affects one FR, the design matrix is diagonal and the design is an ideal design.

Although AD can improve SD, inaccuracy in the design matrix tends to arise when a function of a complex product involves various DPs. $ ^{17} $ For example, complex functional influences among a satellite and its monitoring system, navigation system, and ground control station can be accurately specified only after designers analyze their activities, interactions, and other behaviors. this issue by introducing behavior analysis into AD and constructing an RFBS decomposition process. The difference between behavior analysis and conventional Function-Behavior-Structure (FBS) is discussed in Section 2.2.

Rosenman and Gero $ ^{24} $ proposed the FBS framework for representing the design process. Then, Gero and Kannengiesser $ ^{25} $ formally defined core concepts of FBS: (a) Functions describe design objectives; (b) Behaviors describe actions of components that realize objectives; (c) Structures describe the components and their relationships. Katehi et al $ ^{26} $ provided another definition: "FBS relates the components (structures) in a system to their purpose (function) in the system and the mechanisms that enable them to perform their functions (behavior)." Katehi also stated that the FBS framework is suited for representing SD because SD involves specifying functions, identifying corresponding components and their relationships, and describing how they work together to fulfill original requirements.

A-MBSD is based on the FBS framework where functions are not allocated to structures directly. In FBS, when a design starts, a function is analyzed first by the behaviors to identify alternative solutions. van Beek et al $ ^{27} $ applied FBS in the conceptual design of mechatronic systems by automatically generating a Design Structure Matrix (DSM) from FBS. Couturier et al $ ^{28} $ proposed an FBS-based model for analyzing consequences of design decisions in mechatronic systems engineering. Hamraz et al $ ^{29,30} $ integrated FBS with change management technology for predicting multidomain change propagation risks.

However, behavior modeling methods of the above FBS-based studies show limitations. First, behaviors are only described by verb-object structures, and relationships in FBS are represented by simple binary relations. For example, the BD in Ref. 27 does not illustrate complex interactions between different actions; Refs. 29 and 30 do not distinguish behaviors that relate functions to structures, every function of a diesel engine is enabled by some mechanical, electronic, and thermal behavior of components. Designers thus need rich experience to understand how the behavior of elements in the

system structure enables the realization of their functions. However, designers always skip this analysis and map system functions directly into DPs when structures that fulfill a behavior are well-developed according to previous design experience. For example, a design matrix of AD is constructed based upon the assumption that the functional domain is directly mapped into the PD. Although Song and Lin $ ^{19} $ have introduced behaviors into AD, the method only describes a behavior by use of a simple natural language. According to Suh $ ^{31} $ and Henley, $ ^{32} $ in such situation, designers have to identify function couplings by a predefined design matrix, which leads to inconsistency between the matrix and reality.

A-MBSD complies with the FBS framework. In A-MBSD, modeling the BD requires representing actions of a behavior, as well as specifying how these actions are executed for realizing functions. In addition, the structure is treated as a set of DPs. Therefore, although definitions of functions, behaviors, and structures of the proposed RFBS are same as FBS, RFBS of A-MBSD has three additional positive characteristics.

1. More refined mapping mechanism. The design process based on FBS is a top-down process, in which decomposed functions are mapped to behaviors and structures. The foundation of the RFBS-based process is a "Z" form decomposition, in which after functions are mapped to behaviors and structures, the design goes back into the function domain (FD) for the next iteration. In the next iteration, more detailed behaviors enable the designer to analyze how structures accomplish abstract functions. Thus, functional couplings can be identified at an early stage.

2. Emphasis on CNs. A SD starts from analyzing requirements, which examines, evaluates, and translates external inputs into a set of functional and performance requirements. $ ^{33} $ In addition, as the number of customer requirements becomes larger, designers should explicitly capture them in a representation of the FD. $ ^{34} $ So, it is important to clearly classify different CNs and formally define FRs.

3. A different process of modeling behaviors, which is similar to the behavior modeling approach of OOSEM. Compared with FBS behaviors in RFBS are dynamic processes that are represented by the exchange of information, material, and energy between components carrying out actions, message transfer, and state changes. RFBS not only helps designers understand relationships between functions and structures and build the design matrix, but it also enables them to analyze the hierarchical and internal structure of the system.
A-MBSD is a top-down, iterative process as shown in Figure 3, and it consists of a SD process and a domain-specific design process. The SD is composed of three phases: system requirements analysis,
FIGURE 3 A-MBSD framework

system function analysis and allocation, and design synthesis. It differs from a general SD process by organizing information into AD design domains. SysML is used to build the requirement, function, behavior, and structure models that constitute a unified system model.

SD starts by analyzing requirements, which analyzes the provided mission and creates a customer domain (CD). Designers then translate CNs into a set of functional, performance requirements, and constraints. The result of this phase is represented in a FD by specifying FRs, which are also inputs to the subsequent phase.

In system function analysis and allocation, first, a designer defines use cases (UCs) according to FRs. Then, the designer analyzes these UCs through an action response, message transfer, and state change to create a BD shown by the dashed ellipse in Figure 3. Based on the behavior, the designer decomposes functions and defines the functional architecture. Thus, elaborated functions bridge the gap between the abstract set of FRs and the detailed set of DPs. For example, functions of a ground station communicating with a satellite are realized by a series of activities like receiving, analyzing, and sending commands. In the next iteration, these activities are further decomposed and allocated to specific components. Exchange of information, material, and energy between components carrying out these activities specifies interfaces between the components. The result of this phase is the input for the subsequent phase.

Introducing the independence axiom into the design synthesis is the unique aspect of the A-MBSE. Design synthesis starts by applying the Independence Axiom. Before defining alternative solutions, a designer can identify functional couplings by the design matrix that represents the realizing relationships between FRs and DPs. Only designs conforming to the Independence Axiom can be considered as alternatives. The designer then selects the optimal solutions with corresponding DPs as the final system architecture, which is the structure model (S model) in the PD. In this paper, DPs represent the Design Parameters, which are the elements in the PD that are chosen to satisfy the FRs. According to the definition in AD, both variables and their associated components at any level of aggregation are called DPs. The scale of DPs is very wide, including systems, subsystems, components, or variables.

Accordingly, A-MBSD enables designers to connect the FD with the PD by analyzing behaviors and building the design matrix rather than being based only on experience; this is illustrated in Section 3.2.

In a specific decomposition level, first, the FD is mapped into the BD rather than the PD directly, and then FRs are analyzed by activities interactions, and other behaviors to be allocated to components that have DPs. Figure 4 gives the new mapping process called RFBS, which is from CNs in the requirement domain, FRs in the functional domain, behavior elements (BEs) in the BD to DPs in the physical/structure domain.

In order to analyze the relationships between FRs and DPs and help designers establish the design matrix to apply the independence axiom, a BD is introduced. The new BD consists of BEs that include UCs for describing system services and actions as well as messages
FIGURE 4 Mapping process of A-MBSD

between components parameterized by DPs. Figure 5 illustrates how to use these BEs to explain FRs and allocate them to DPs, whereas in MBSD, functions are allocated to components by "swim lines" in activity diagrams or by executing the functions allocated to a given block. $ ^{14} $ First, designers represent FRs at different levels of abstraction by UCs or actions. While UCs are generally used to represent functions at the top level, actions are created when the functions are decomposed into more detailed levels.

Second, activity diagrams enable designers to specify how actions are executed to realize corresponding UCs. The partition of activities can allocate actions into different parameterized components. In addition, these actions are treated as input FRs for the next iteration.

Third, sequence diagrams are created based on activity diagrams for generating the internal structure of the system in which interfaces are captured by the messages transferred between parameterized components.

Figure 6 shows how the RFBS mapping process enables designers to build the SD matrix [A] and apply the Independence Axiom to identify the coupling of the design. Relationships between FRs and BEs constitute the function-behavior matrix [B], and the relationships between BEs and DPs constitute the behavior-structure matrix [C], where together they constitute a composite design matrix.
The logical OR operation is used to obtain the SD matrix [A] as shown by the new system equation (2). Equation (3) shows its corresponding extension where {BE} denotes a vector composed of BEs.
Designers judge if a current design complies with the Independence Axiom by the form of the SD matrix [A].

1. When [A] is diagonal, the design is said to be ideal; thus, designers further decompose DPs and FRs, and initiate the next iteration.

2. When [A] is triangular, the design is said to be decoupled. Designers should realign DPs to obtain independent FRs. For example, the design matrix shown in Figure 6 is decoupled as changes of DP2 affect both FR1 and FR2 after DP1 is specified. FRs are independent of each other when DP2 is achieved before DP1.
3. The design is coupled in other situations. Designers have to reselect DPs in order to remove the impacts that DPs have on different FRs until FRs stay independent from each other.

In fact, SysML is defined as a UML profile.
Stereotypes are used for customizing core concepts of AD. An AMBSD Modeling Profile is constructed as shown in Figure 7, where the

The former is provided by a customer directly and the latter is a requirement translated from a CN for designers understanding. section: 5 A-MBSD IS USED TO SPECIFY A SATELLITE SYSTEM DESIGN FOR OBSERVING FOREST FIRES
section_key: 5 a mbsd is used to specify a satellite system design for observing forest fires
text: The FireSAT mission was aimed at observing forest fires $ ^{35} $ and has been adopted as a standard study case for understanding the space SD process. Based on the FireSAT project, in 2011, the SSWG (Space Systems Working Group) of INCOSE demonstrated the feasibility of the MBSD approach in reality, where SysML could formally specify every aspect of a system through a CubeSat project. $ ^{36} $ Accordingly, in the following sections, the A-MBSD is applied to the SD of a virtual FireSAT mission.

section: 5 A-MBSD IS USED TO SPECIFY A SATELLITE SYSTEM DESIGN FOR OBSERVING FOREST FIRES
section_key: 5 a mbsd is used to specify a satellite system design for observing forest fires
text: FIGURE 16 Top level FRs of FFSMCS

Forest fires cause serious harm every year to both the environment and people's daily lives. An assumed FireSAT project, called FFSMCS, is aimed at monitoring daily forest fires and informing local forestry departments of these fires to be able to control them in time.

The overall mission of the FFSMCS is described as: "Because forest fires cause dramatic harm to local people's safety of life and wealth, and seriously impact the development of local tourism and business, it is necessary to build a system for effectively observing and controlling potential forest fires. The system should satisfy the following requirements: a local forestry department can afford it; information about a forest fire such as its location, diffusion situation, and duration that are collected by the system should be available for the local forestry department, managers of the forest region, and firefighters; data formats of the above information should be readable by users without special training; and the system should enable users to respond effectively to any change in the forest fire."

Although a conventional MBSD approach can specify components and parameters realizing functions of the mission by iterative processes, function analysis resulting in unsatisfactory requirements due to the omission of potential relationships between functions, behaviors, components, and requirements should be determined. Especially when functions are coupled, designers have to reselect DPs, and even reanalyze FRs, which dramatically increases iteration times and obstructs development efficiency. The proposed A-MBSD is thus applied to the FFSMCS to illustrate how the RFBS documents SD information explicitly helping designers to make decisions through building design matrixes and using the Independence Axiom.

The behavior analysis aims at helping designers build the design matrix to identify the coupling of functions. It can be seen in Figure 18 that BE1 needs information from DP2 and DP3, which means that BEs are not independent. Accordingly, the components of DP2 for sending commands are specified first, then, components of DP3 for generating navigation signals, and components of DP1 for monitoring forest fires can be designed. As a result, the functions of specified components are not coupled with unspecified ones. For example, interfaces of DP1 responsible for receiving commands sent by DP2 should be specified after the corresponding interfaces for sending such commands are designed.

The sequence diagram that enables designers to identify interfaces is created based on the activity diagram of BE1. The SysML block definition diagram and internal block diagram are then used to specify the hierarchical and internal structure of PD1. In this way, after every DP is represented, a unified system model of FFSMCS can be created. Due to this paper's limitation, it is not discussed here.

The FFSMCS is a large-scale engineering system that involves multiple disciplines, for example, mechanical, electronics, and software engineering, and consists of various subsystems and components. The SD of the FFSMCS plays a significant role for subsequent detailed design, system integration, manufacturing, and implementation. Conventional mission analysis and SD of a satellite system is a document-oriented process, where informal representations can lead to inconsistent information, which can increase iteration times and obstruct development

efficiency dramatically. In contrast to a system model that does not apply the proposed functional analysis, the return on investment of using A-MBSD is obvious since changes due to coupled functions can be identified at an early stage and impacted structures, behaviors and requirements can be traced clearly. Otherwise, the change effort is huge when couplings are identified during detailed design because then designers have to reselect DPs, and even reanalyze FRs.

A-MBSD represents the system model of the FFSMCS from requirement, functional, behavioral, and physical perspectives in a unified way. The zigzag mappings of RFBS enable designers to analyze and decompose the functions of the FFSMCS and manage the abstract levels of the SD.

In a specific iteration, designers can document system, hierarchical and internal structures, construct the design matrix through analyzing system functions and behaviors, and identify functional couplings by the Independence Axiom. In addition, designers can navigate impacted DPs and CNs due to the coupling of functions through the RFBS model.

However, designers have criticized the intensive manual work required for building the system model. In reality, designers were unwilling to spend too much time in learning SysML. In addition, experienced designers have said that they would not select a design that is largely based on the degree of independence and coupling among requirements and solutions, and that they preferred referencing similar design cases or cases from their experience. On the other hand, they suggested a few improvement ideas for future work, such as linking the model to available information databases and building AD ontologies for common cases in order to reuse or reference them rather than creating new ones.

Leading MBSD methodologies like Harmony SE, OOSEM, SA, etc., improve upon traditional DBSD by formalizing the application of modeling to support requirements analysis, function analysis, and design synthesis. However, different MBSD methodologies focus on specific areas, and various designers from different areas use ambiguous terms. Moreover, failure of some products originated in undiscovered couplings of functions in the design stage. In order to implement MBSD in a more unified way by reducing ambiguity and alleviating functional couplings:

1. Based on the axiomatic SD, this paper proposes a unified MBSD approach, called A-MBSD, that is not only able to represent a system's static structure, but is also able to allocate functions to the structure by observing dynamic behaviors.
2. The RFBS framework introduces a new BD into AD for bridging abstract functions and more detailed design solutions.
3. The core concepts and relationships of AD are customized by a SysML profile (ie, an A-MBSD profile) that keeps every view of the system model unified.

Although SysML modeling tools, such as Magicdraw, enable designers to create and document a system model, many designers in China find it unacceptable to spend too much time in learning such a graphical modeling language without appropriate patterns. In addition, when the number of models increases greatly, it is hard to respond to design changes. In the future, we will carry out in-depth research on:
1. Linking available information databases to the A-MBSD to create reusable cases and appropriate pattern, and
2. Managing design change to predict change impact using the AMBSD approach.

This paper will review the technical outcomes of a unique two-semester graduate-level Small Satellite Systems Design Course, offered under a collaboration between North Carolina A&T, Old Dominion University, Georgia Tech and Florida Institute of Technology, with additional faculty support from Hampton University and NASA Langley Research Center. The course provided students with skills that are relevant to present day satellite design while fostering an open-ended mission design assignment that is relevant to the support of Earth observation using systems of small satellites. Major outcomes of this course include that the students have the experience of working in multi-disciplinary, multi-university teams, practicing critical thinking skills, and managing the design of complex systems. In addition, the course was developed around utilizing Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) practices and tools throughout the design life-cycle while utilizing a common design language, Systems Modelling Language (SysML). The approach started with a mission idea and proceeded to a feasible concept that included requirements development and management, concept modeling and performance simulation, and prototype building using low-cost additive manufacturing techniques, ending with a "Shark-tank" style presentation.

Systems Engineering projects are interdisciplinary in nature and require efficient and effective management throughout the project life cycle. This two-semester graduate-level course was a collaborative offering between North Carolina A&T, Old Dominion University, Georgia Tech, and Florida Institute of Technology, and was facilitated by The National Institute of Aerospace. With support from Hampton University and NASA Langley, this course offered participating students a unique opportunity to employ a Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach to the design of a small satellite. The faculty initially formed four teams, intentionally pairing students from different universities and disciplinary backgrounds to expose them to some of the inherent challenges of collaborating with team members from a geographical distance. The teams were given a set of customer requirements and one of four different global target regions. Then, with as few limitations as possible, were set free to design a satellite system to fulfill these requirements as interpreted by each team.

The first class was a traditional face-to-face meeting to allow for as many members as possible to establish an in person connection with their teammates. The teams were chosen by the faculty to ensure an even distribution of students from different institutions with different discipline backgrounds would be on each team. Doing so meant students would have to work with students at other institutions that varied significantly with size and demographic distinctions. Through the initial meeting, web conferencing and cloud-based collaboration tools were researched and voted on using a decision matrix to identify the tools that would best serve the needs of the class throughout the duration of the course. This served as both an icebreaker and a team building exercise as each group was given a certain set of tools to look up and present to the rest of the class, with the decision matrix being a focal point for

determining the desired attributes and their values. The course was delivered via interactive web conferencing and utilized a cloud-based collaborative tool for the class as whole as well as for individual teams. Each class meeting provided students with a seminar-styled series of lectures given by different professors and scientists with expertise in the various topics relevant to the project.

During the first semester each of the four teams, Chesapeake BaySAT, Polar (ICE) $ ^{3} $ , SPACE GOAT, and BioScope, held virtual meetings as needed to plan, research, design, and prepare the required presentations. The design process and procedure followed the methods outlined in the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook [NASA/SP 2007-6105], as well as the text Space Mission Engineering: The New SMAD. Teams learned and utilized MBSE tools like Visual Paradigm, Modelio, and Magic Draw to structure and organize their projects using SysML/ UML2 syntax and semantics. Emphasis was placed on trade studies for decision making and all aspects of mission architecture were addressed including con-ops, orbital design and analysis, performance metrics, data budgets, cost, testing, scheduling, sub-systems integration, and preliminary risk assessment. There were three major presentations given to a panel of faculty members and guest experts, each followed by technical questions and feedback: a Mission Concept Review (MCR), a Preliminary Design Review (PDR), and a Critical Design Review (CDR). The result was four unique mission concepts that were feasible and developed enough to present to a customer, the faculty, for selection. As there were intentionally no financial limitations imposed for this semester, the proposed budgets for the mission concepts ranged from approximately $1 Million to $2.65 Million.

The second semester began with a major de-scoping of the first semester results with the goal of launching a reasonably priced payload, with the same initial customer requirements, as a balloon satellite to an altitude of 30 kilometers targeting the geographical region of the Chesapeake Bay. The teams were reorganized into two teams and used the concept of ThinSat/XinaBox technology as a starting point for the re-design. Utilizing the MBSE methods learned in semester one, the missions were de-scoped and re-framed. Once the designs were completed, the remainder of the semester was spent acquiring and assembling the satellites for launch.

Chesapeake Bay SAT chose to focus on improving upon the currently established state of the art values for the spatial and temporal resolutions of current similar science missions. These values are taken to be 375m/pixel for spatial resolution and 2 passes/day for temporal resolution. They also sought to incorporate as much value into the design as possible by incorporating multiple areas of observation into the functionality of the satellite.

section: Primary Objective and Mission Concept Overview
section_key: primary objective and mission concept overview
text: Chesapeake Bay SAT's primary mission objective was to collect measurements on the Chesapeake Bay's phytoplankton levels to understand its ecological health. This will be done through launching and establishing a constellation of three CubeSats for a one-year mission, collecting data in all four seasons. This constellation of three will be launched at evenly spaced intervals and will follow an identical orbital path. The constellation concept will provide a temporal resolution of 5 passes/day. Each 6U satellite in the constellation will utilize deployable solar arrays and a battery for power, and carry a scientific payload of:

text: This mission configuration improves upon the spatial resolution by a factor of 10 and the temporal resolution by a factor of 2.5.

The mission will utilize the orbital parameters listed in the table below. This orbit provides 100% coverage of the Chesapeake Bay twice a day 70% of the year. With orbital drift, there are three periods during the year in which coverage is reduced. This drift is not tethered to seasonal change and coverage reduction can reduced through pointing. An additional advantage of this orbit is the shared inclination with the International Space Station. This allows for numerous launch opportunities for orbit insertion as a secondary payload with an ISS resupply mission. Team Polar (Ice) $ ^{3} $ focused on the improvement of spatial and temporal resolutions using COTS parts to reduce mission cost as well as added functionality. The added functionality was chosen to maximize the scientific value of the mission due to the seasonal conditions of the assigned region of the Beaufort Sea.

Polar $ \{Ice \} ^ {3} $ had a primary mission objective to image chlorophyll and measure sea surface temperatures in the Beaufort Sea; this area includes Prudhoe Bay and Mackenzie Bay. The secondary science mission is to track ice changes in the target region since the Beaufort Sea is frozen from late October to May, resulting in chlorophyll only being present in the summer months. The Pine Island Glacier has also been identified as a region of interest. The team began with a performance objective to produce images that have a spatial and temporal resolution that is at least three times greater than the images that are currently available to researchers; these values would be better than 125 m/pixel for spatial resolution and 6 per day for temporal resolution.

This mission will utilize two 6U CubeSats. The result will be a lower cost mission that utilizes COTS products to produce the images with the expected improvements. Each satellite will use a battery and fixed solar panels for power. The scientific payload for each satellite includes:
- A Visual and Near IR imager- the Hyperscout by Cosine
- A Longwave IR Imager- the Tau2 640 by FLIR with a 50mm lens

These instruments have spatial resolutions of 72m/pixel for the VNIR, and 183 m/pixel for the LWIR, which represents an improvement of approximately 5 times the current standard. Additionally, the constellation configuration provides a temporal resolution of 8 passes/day, an improvement by a factor of 4.

The final orbit was selected based on the access it provided to the target region and the frequency of visitation. Four ground stations were identified for the downlink of data. Team SPACE GOAT focused on minimizing cost using COTS parts, in order to demonstrate the versatility and value in developing CubeSat missions.

The primary mission of SPACE GOAT was to detect, monitor, and report microscopic algae (phytoplankton) and macroscopic algae (seaweed) growth rates in the exclusive economic zone of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago and surrounding areas via Chl-a and SST. Additionally, the mission will demonstrate improvement of algae monitoring capabilities (spatial/temporal resolution) over currently available resolutions. Additionally, SPACE GOAT intended to detect, monitor, and report microscopic algae (phytoplankton) and macroscopic algae
(seaweed) growth rates in the exclusive economic zones of other countries and unclaimed high seas via Chl-a and SST.

The SPACE GOAT mission included a constellation of three 6U CubeSats in a circular orbit with an offset of $ 60^{\circ} $ between the Right Ascension of the Ascending Node (RAAN) of each satellite. Together they will observe ocean color and sea surface temperature of the primary region of Trinidad and Tobago as well as other secondary regions of scientific interest along the satellites orbital path. Along with fixed solar panels and a battery for power, each satellite would be have a payload including:
- Chameleon Multispectral linescan Imager by Space Advisory Company.
- Flir Tau2 640 Thermal Infrared Imager w/ 100mm lens.
This configuration provides spatial resolutions of 19m/pixel and 84.5 m/pixel respectively at an altitude of 500 km. This represents an improvement of the current standard by a factor of 19.

Team BioScope chose to include additional functionality to the required mission objectives. These two areas of added functionality include incorporating the ability to process the multi-spectral images for multiple scientific purposes and the orbital design to offer several secondary regions of scientific interest.

BioScope's primary objective was to monitor ocean color through the detection and quantification of Chl-a specifically in (but not limited to) the region of the South West African Coast with a design that improves upon the current SOA capabilities in either spatial resolution, temporal resolution, or both.

The BioScope Mission consists of a train of 2 satellites in a circular orbit about the earth at an inclination of $ 7 0^{\circ} $ and an altitude of 422km. Together they will observe ocean color, SST, and provide access to a wide range of scientific data and images appealing to the science community as well as the private sector. Each satellite has a 6U CubeSat structure housing state of the art imagers with fixed solar panels and battery.
- Sat 1 includes a Headwall Photonics VNIR hyperspectral push-broom imager and TIR sensor.
- Sat 2 includes a Headwall Photonics SWIR hyperspectral push-broom imager and TIR sensor.

This configuration provides a spatial resolution of 38m/pixel for the VNIR instrument, 42m/pixel for the SWIR, and 301m/pixel for the TIR @ 422m. This is an improvement of the current standard by more than a factor of 8.

Secondary Objectives

Bioscope's concept for secondary mission objectives provides maximum flexibility to our customer. This concept takes full advantage of the chosen Headwall Photonics, Inc. VNIR and SWIR hyperspectral imagers. Utilizing pushbroom continuous scan imagers, BioScope would be able to collect full spectrum images from which any wavelength of interest or combination of wavelengths can be extracted and viewed in post processing. This flexibility affords the customer the ability and opportunity to mitigate mission costs with the marketability of additional data and imagery that will appeal to a wide range of additional customers in the science community, both in official environmental agencies as well as in the private sector.

Some examples of additional objectives that could be marketed to additional customers include specific harmful bacterial and algal blooms, coastal water health (in the 20-30m depth range), oil spill detection and monitoring, natural gas and petroleum seepage, monitoring and mapping micro-plastics in the oceans, mineral mapping, vegetation and forest health, drought monitoring, mapping burned regions, and many more. The details regarding image type and bandwidths required for each of these examples were provided in BioScope's presentations and formal reports. The versatility of the Headwall imagers and the software that accompanies them makes this approach to secondary objectives feasible.

The orbit of the BioScope mission was designed to balance spatial resolution (primary), temporal resolution (secondary), orbital lifetime (both for longevity of image collection, and passive deorbit within a responsible period), day and night coverage of the target region of scientific interest, and access to secondary regions of scientific interest.

section: E. Concept of Operations and other Mission Design Elements
section_key: e concept of operations and other mission design elements
text: All four teams presented a mature concept of operations as well as equipment selection for the Avionics, Communications, and Data Handling subsystems to support their mission design. Equipment selection for these subsystems were specific to each teams' scientific instruments chosen and their mission objectives. Teams justified the choices for these subsystem components by considering their system's demand for data, file size, image quality, transmission opportunity and cost, and the feasibility of data compression and on-board processing. After each "Shark-Tank" style presentation, teams were questioned and pushed for clarification in all areas of their design. The final presentation of the first semester was the Critical Design Review (CDR). In this presentation teams were required to demonstrate the continuity of their project design management through the MBSE methods learned, with a focus on subsystems integration. Also required by the course instructors was a preliminary risk analysis. Some methods used were Fault Tree Analysis and the Risk Assessment Matrix. Figure 7 is an example of one team's ConOps illustration.

Over winter break, representatives from each team attended a workshop hosted by XinaBox, a South African company dedicated to making science affordable and accessible using modular scientific sensors sized for FlatSat applications. This was the starting point for the second semester with the goal of having an operational system that would be launched. The XinaBox kits are designed for simple science and weather experiments, which require customization to achieve the primary objective of ocean color observation. The class makeup of this semester changed somewhat due to scheduling conflicts. The remaining students from GT, ODU, and NC A&T were reorganized into two teams and instructed to de-scope the mission designs from semester one. The new scope limited the missions to a high-altitude balloon launch versus the low earth orbits previously planned for by each team; additionally a major reduction in cost was mandated to make the launch feasible and attainable in the semester time frame. The new teams, ICE $ ^{2} $ BayBSAT and BioGOAT, were faced with the challenge of reducing cost while maintaining as much of the primary and secondary objectives from the model missions of the first semester. This prompted new payload instrument selections and a re-design of the subsystems. The new target region for both teams was assigned as the Chesapeake Bay and the design altitude for the balloon is 30 km. At each presentation the teams used their previously established MBSE derived project management framework to incorporate the de-scoping parameters. The satellite systems related lectures and instruction continued throughout the course, but more time was devoted to planning and managing the de-scoping of the missions.

At the start of the de-scoping process, funding was still to be determined. This affected the re-design process and resulted in an evolution of the design over the course of the semester. The new BalloonSat concept enabled an immediate reduction in cost as the lower altitude of 30 km allowed for less expensive imagers to achieve comparable spatial resolutions. A few weeks into the second semester NC A&T, ODU, and GA Tech each committed an amount of $500 to the project, which prompted further mission concept changes as a ballpark budget emerged. An example of these concept changes is that both teams originally had the goal of including the secondary objective of sensing Sea Surface Temperature (SST), but ultimately eliminated this capability from their mission concepts. Additionally, both teams made multiple iterations of budget reductions and submitted them to course instructors to facilitate the securing of further funding. The final word on funding came on April 25 with additional contributions from the National Institute of Aerospace and Science and Technology Corporation (STC) of Hampton, VA totaling $1500. This process created a time delay for the ordering of equipment and, consequentially, has delayed the launch tentatively until later in May.

ICE $ ^{2} $ BayBSAT's primary focus for the de-scoping was cost reduction, which required a simplification of mission objectives. The new mission concept is to employ two small visual imagers: one RGB camera and a second without an infrared filter. These images will be processed after retrieval to provide the required scientific information on chlorophyll-a in the Chesapeake Bay by calculating the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) for each
pixel. The NDVI ratio emphasizes photosynthesis while filtering out solar glare and values can range from -1 to 1. High photosynthesis activity corresponds to an NDVI value between 0.1 and 0.9.

The housekeeping processes will be controlled with a raspberry pi3 B+ and supported by XinaBox x-chip sensors. The main housing for the payload will be a Styrofoam container. To reduce the tendency of the payload to spin, a tethering system will be employed (as shown in Figure 12) [1] utilizing four booms and eight securing lines. A 3D printed housing will be used to contain the XinaBox chips and raspberry pi3 B+ (Figure 13).
-8MP Images will be produced with 11 m/pixel Spatial Resolution.
ICE $ ^{2} $ BayBSAT will use a SPOT Trace backup GPS system to increase the chances of recovery.

BioGOAT's new mission concept focused on balancing the lower cost with the original concept of providing added functionality from the BioScope first semester design. The payload will include a MAPIR VNIR Imager that will provide images with 3 bands of information in the 850nm (NIR), 550nm (Green), and 475nm (Blue) ranges. Also included in the payload will be a First-Person View camera. BioGOAT's BalloonSat will be able to determine altitude by sensing atmospheric pressure as well as direction, with an additional sensor that will serve as a digital compass. The mission will be controlled by a raspberry pi3 and supported with XinaBox sensors. Images will be transmitted at regular intervals during the mission, while images taken between transmission will be processed on recovery. The main housing will be a 3D printed chassis (Figure 14) with Styrofoam panels for insulation.

BioGOAT has decided to attempt to steer the parachute towards shore if the flight simulation predicts an ocean touchdown. The concept was inspired by the work the University of Missouri has done in the area of steerable parachutes for cargo delivery [2]. This required a custom designed cruciform style parachute, and a pair of linear actuators. For simplicity, the actuators selected include built-in PID controllers. The original idea included a custom Autonomous Guidance algorithm to guide the parachute towards one of a few predetermined GPS locations. The time delay in funding has reduced the plan to guiding the parachute back to shore, making use of the digital compass XinaBox add-on chip. This goal is completely dependent on time and will be attempted once the data handling and

communications functionality of the primary mission goals has been assured. Figures 15(a), 15(b), and 15(c) illustrate the rigging configurations for this concept. By applying this concept to BioGOAT's BalloonSat system configuration it is estimated that BioGOAT could potentially autonomously steer the parachute back to shore if it reaches a steerable altitude of between 6,000 and 10,000 ft (depending on wind velocities) no more than 3.34 miles or 5.57 miles, respectively, away from shore.

section: V. Avionics and Onboard Computing Systems
section_key: v avionics and onboard computing systems
text: The myriad of computing solutions available to handle data and communication processing needs meant that there was a variety of options for teams to choose from during both semesters of the class. The Onboard Computing System (OBC) can be based on custom-built hardware and software or use Commercial off the Shelf (COTS) components or any mixture of the two. What became readily apparent to all the groups is that a sizeable gap in price, performance, and capability existed between some of the more enterprise grade custom solutions and their COTS/hobbyist counterparts. This was in part due to the significant advancements in computational power as a result of the boom in mobile computing, the push for the Internet of Things (IoT) and hobbyist processing power coupled with a significant decrease in hardware pricing.

section: V. Avionics and Onboard Computing Systems
section_key: v avionics and onboard computing systems
text: An example of how pronounced this differential was exhibited by the BioScope/BioGoat selection presented as a part of their final design review of the first semester. The ISIS OBC (Figure 18(a)) which cost $5,600 featured several space hardened and redundant onboard components that were specifically designed and built to withstand the severe environment to be encountered in space. The manufacturer had been in business for decades as a supplier to the space industry and supported multiple real-time operating systems specifically designed for space flight. In contrast, the BeagleBoard BeagleBone (Figure 18(b)) which cost $50 had double the processing power, double the data storage, and eight times the amount of RAM available for running applications (Figure 19). With a cost differential so pronounced, justifying the significantly higher cost which in turn would lower the overall risk tolerance of the mission while sacrificing performance characteristics often made choosing the more expensive platform an indefensible position. This phenomenon presented itself for multiple avionics and OBCs offerings that were evaluated by the groups throughout the course.

This multi-University course in Small Satellite Systems Design was a unique and rewarding experience as a graduate student. The scope of the course was broad and yet it provided a detailed exposure to nearly all aspects of the design of small satellite systems. Utilizing the project management approach of Model Based Systems Engineering provided students with valuable real-world knowledge and experience that will be useful in both the research and corporate environments. The multi-University and multi-disciplinary aspects of this course highlighted the usefulness of the MBSE approach as most engineering projects are multi-disciplinary in nature and modern technology makes communicating with experts around the world nearly effortless.

Students provided some feedback on this course at the end of the second semester. The main suggestion was to have the funding amount and process defined at the beginning of the build semester. This would allow teams to be more productive during the build semester, and requiring only one design process with a well-defined scope and budget. It would also allow time for purchasing parts with longer lead times and allow them to budget time for more testing. Another possibility would be to only have one team during the build semester to allow for more cooperative work on the various subsystems.
