The Mode management architecture style (Figure 12) restricts the set of actions which can be executed (i.e., enabled actions) based on a set of modes. It consists of one coordinator of type Mode Manager, n parameter components of type B1 and k parameter components of type B2. Each B2 component triggers the transition of the Mode Manager to a specific mode. B1 components have actions that should be enabled in specific mode(s) of the Mode Manager. Mode Manager has one control location for each mode, one port type toMode with cardinality k and k port types inMode with cardinality 1. Each toMode port is connected with the changeMode port of a dedicated B2 component.

B1 has k port types modeBegin with cardinality mc[0,1]. In other words, a component instance of B1 might have any number of port instances of modeBegin from 0 to k. B1 has also a modeEnd port type with cardinality k. m[i]b stands for "mode i begin" and indicates that an action that is enabled in mode i has begun its execution. The m[i]e ports stand for "mode i end" and indicate that an action that is enabled in mode i has ended. Such ports are
Figure 11: Application of an Action flow architecture

exported as modeEnd in the interface of the B1 components. Each inMode port instance of the Mode Manager must be connected with the corresponding m[i]b port instances of all B1 components through an n-ary connector, where a different multiplicity in the interval [1,n] is considered for each port instance.
Figure 12: Architecture diagram of the Mode management style (component behavior is shown for k=3)

This architecture style enforces sets of properties of the P3.1 pattern that refer to states of the same state-set. According to each such property, "the main specification shall begin only if a state is observed". The style is parameterized by setting k equal to the number of states in the state-set. To identify instances of m[i]b ports, we use a new symbol enforce_beg(M), which is evaluated as follows:
- if $M = M1$ or $M = M2$, enforce_beg(M)=beg(M)
- if $M = M3$, in which case $beg(M) = obs(s2)$, enforce_beg(M) is the beg of each action that triggers state s2;

these actions are found in conceptual model by backward tracing the relationships action $ \xrightarrow{generates} $ event $ \xrightarrow{sets} $ state. The second evaluation case reflects that the restriction of being in a state can only be ensured by restricting the event of entering in that state. Operands of type B1 are the components having the ports mapped to the m[i]b ports. The changeMode port type is mapped to the ports of the occ of each event that sets the state. Operands of type B2 are the components having these ports. After having applied a mode management architecture, each "virtual port" assigned to the obs of the represented states is replaced by an inMode[i] port of the Mode Manager.

The Mode management style is also used in combination with the Event monitoring style to enforce the P2.1 pattern. Specifically, we apply the Mode management after having applied the Event monitoring, by mapping the m[i]b port type to the port of the event monitoring coordinator that observes the event.

In general, the enforcement of liveness properties requires additional assumptions of fair execution scheduling. Furthermore, in order to guarantee the preservation of liveness properties by architecture composition, one has to verify the architectures' pair-wise non-interference [5].

However, liveness properties of the patterns P1.2 and P2.2, can, indeed, be enforced by the bipartite connectors' simplification of the Event monitoring architecture style. Let us consider the safety property "the main specification begins atomically upon the occurrence of event e", formulated as follows:
$$ P 1. 2 ^ {\prime}: \mathrm {b e t w e e n o c c} (\mathrm {e}) \mathrm {a n d} \mathbf {X} o c c (\mathrm {e}), b e g (\mathrm {M}) \mathrm {e x i s t s}. ^ {6} $$
It can be easily shown that P1.2 is implied by P1.2', which can be enforced by the bipartite connectors' simplification if the assumptions for its application hold (cf Section 4.4.3).

Another way to indirectly enforce P1.2 through the Event monitoring architecture style is by considering the following safety property: "after an occurrence of event e, another such event does not occur before the beginning of the main specification", formulated as follows:
$$ P 1. 2": \text {b e t w e e n o c c (e) a n d o c c (e)}, b e g (\mathrm {M}) \text {e x i s t s.} ^ {7} $$
It can be easily shown that P1.2", which is enforceable by the Event monitoring architecture style, implies P1.2, if it can be verified or assumed that occ(e) occurs infinitely often:
$$ P 1. 2. a s m: \mathrm {g l o b a l l y}, o c c (\mathrm {e}) \mathrm {r e s p o n d s t o} o c c (\mathrm {e}) $$

Finding the suitable approach for enforcing a given property involves a decision-making process. Algorithm 1 introduces such a process for properties of the P1.1 pattern. The first conditional (line 1) checks whether the bipartite connector simplification can be applied, the second conditional (line 3) checks whether Event monitoring is necessary, and the else statement (line 6) is reached if the property should be verified, through inspection or model checking.
Algorithm 1 Decision-making process for the P1.1 pattern
Require: occ(e), beg(M)
Ensure: P1.1 is either enforced or should be verified
1: if occ(e) is allocated to a different atomic component than beg(M) then
2: P1.1 is enforced by the bipartite connectors' simplification of the Event monitoring style
3: else if occ(e) is allocated to the same atomic component with beg(M) and P1.1 does not hold by inspection then
4: P1.1 is enforced by the Event monitoring style
5: else
6: P1.1 should be verified
7: end if

The direct or indirect enforcement of the P1.2 pattern is guided by the process shown in Algorithm 2. The flow takes into account the architecture that enforces P1.1, if such an architecture has been applied. The decision of the flow is either that the P1.2 property has been enforced by the architecture, or that it has to be verified through model checking. Similar processes are followed for the remaining patterns.
Algorithm 2 Decision-making process for the P1.2 pattern
Require: the applied architecture that enforces P1.1, if any
Ensure: P1.2 is either enforced or has to be verified through model checking
1: if the Event monitoring style has been applied and the P1.2.asm is verified then
2: P1.2 is enforced by the Event monitoring style
3: else if the bipartite connectors' simplification has been applied then
4: P1.2 is enforced by the the bipartite connectors' simplification
5: else
6: P1.2 has to be verified through model checking
7: end if

The RERD tool supports the requirement specification, property derivation, architecture instantiation and property enforcement, i.e. the steps 1, 3, 4 and 5 of the model-based process, whereas in step 6 the D-Finder tool is used and the nuXmv model checker [21], if there is need for verifying CTL properties. For step 1, the Requirements Engineer selects among the predefined boilerplate clauses and then inserts in each placeholder a textual description referring to a uniquely identified concept. The concept can be selected from the previously defined concepts (search support is provided) or if a new concept is needed it is entered along with its relationships. The conceptual model is stored, shared and is accessed through an underlying ontology architecture, whose design does not need to be known to the Requirement Engineer (the concept classes in Figure 7 suffice for specifying requirements).

Figure 18 shows the Requirement Editing screen of the RERD tool. The upper part of the screen allows selecting among the available boilerplate clauses, which are displayed in separate tables. In the middle part, requirements are shown in an editable form, that is, their placeholders and additional information for the requirement (e.g. id, category) can be filled in this panel. The lower part of the screen is used for browsing and searching requirements that match string(s) given in a search box. The table displays the requirements returned by each search (all requirements match an empty string), with buttons attached to each row for editing/deleting them.

The RERD tool also stores the user-defined values for the symbols used in patterns. Specifically, the System Software Engineer assigns ports to the symbols that are necessary for the properties of the specified requirements. These symbols may be reused in more than one property. Hence, when the Verification Engineer uses the tool during the property derivation (step 3), the necessary properties are automatically created by retrieving the values of symbols.

For architecture instantiation and property enforcement (steps 4 and 5), the System Software Engineer can choose among the available architecture styles and parameterize them for creating architectures that enforce a set of properties. The architectures are then automatically applied to their operand components and the design model is updated as appropriate.

DesignBIP [54] is a web-based graphical editing tool, which can be used for the specification of BIP models and BIP architectures. The tool can assist the creation of the initial design model in step 1. Moreover, it allows for the creation of new architecture styles to be integrated in the RERD tool, whenever RERD is extended with new boilerplates (and enforcement opportunities).

The D-Finder tool [11] is used by the Verification Engineer for verifying the deadlock-freedom of the design model (step 6). D-Finder is capable of analyzing very large BIP models using compositional verification on an overapproximated set of reachable states. For model checking CTL properties, the BIP model has to be transformed with the BIP-to-NuSMV tool into the input language of the nuXmv model checker.

The CubETH nanosatellite [70] is comprised of: the electrical power subsystem (EPS), the command and data management subsystem (CDMS), the telecommunication subsystem (COM), the attitude determination and control subsystem (ADCS) and the payload (PL). Our early validation study is focused on the software for the following subcomponents of the CDMS subsystem (cf. AppendixB.1): 1) the CDMS status that resets internal and external watchdogs; 2) the Payload that is in charge of payload operations; 3) three Housekeeping components that recover engineering data from the EPS, PL and COM subsystems; 4) the CDMS Housekeeping which is internal to the CDMS; 5) the I2C_sat that implements the $ I^{2} C $ bus protocol; 6) the Flash memory management that implements a non-volatile flash memory and its read-write protocol; 7) the s3_5, s3_6, s15_1 and s15_2 services that activate or deactivate the housekeeping component actions; 8) the Error Logging that implements a shared RAM region. The case study comprises 38 requirements, from which 57 properties were derived. The complete BIP model can be found in AppendixB.5.

Combined application of architectures can generate deadlocks. We verified the deadlock-freedom of the design model using the D-Finder tool [11]. D-Finder's compositional analysis is sound, but incomplete: due to the employed over-approximation of reachable states, it can produce false positives, i.e., potential deadlock states that are in fact unreachable in the concrete system. However, our design model was found to be deadlock-free without any potential deadlocks. Thus, no additional reachability analysis was needed. The verification of deadlock-freedom was completed in 12 seconds, for our model consisting of 46 atomic components and 155 connectors.

The key advantage of our architecture-based approach is that the burden of verification is shifted from the final design to architectures, which are considerably smaller in size and can be reused. In particular, we managed to enforce 47 out of 57 derived properties using our simple architecture styles. The remaining 10 derived properties were verified by inspection and 4 fairness assumptions were left for verification using the nuXmv model checker.

Table 13 summarizes the duration of each process step for the input of the problem size shown in each row; the three roles of the process were performed by an engineer who was fully familiar with the process's tool support. The property derivation and property enforcement steps are not shown, since they are fully automated and the time needed was negligible. We note that the time spent is not evenly distributed across the steps and it tends to be less towards the end of the process. Also, it is essential to clarify for the shown times that the architecture styles had already been configured in the RERD tool and the input forms for the style parameters had been defined. This takes 1-2 hours per style. Much greater effort was needed, though, to create the taxonomy of our architecture styles which took about 1
man-month. However, this taxonomy serves as a knowledge base in abstract form that we have acquired, and which can be also reused to build other models of satellite on-board software.

section: 6.2. Telecommand Management of an earth observation satellite
section_key: 6 2 telecommand management of an earth observation satellite
text: In a second case study, our model-based approach was also applied to an extract of 29 software requirements for the Telecommand Management function of a low orbit earth observation satellite. The requirements and the BIP model of this study cannot be disclosed, due to confidentiality liability terms. We derived 58 properties from the requirements and 34 (58%) of them were eventually enforced through architectures.

section: 6.2. Telecommand Management of an earth observation satellite
section_key: 6 2 telecommand management of an earth observation satellite
text: More specifically, during this case study we identified the need for and formulated an architecture style for Priority Management [56]. In overall, the integrated architectures were 10 Action Flows, 3 Mutual Exclusion Management, 13 Mode management and 1 Priority Management. The number of components in the BIP model was 25.

The applicability of our approach in an industrial context depends on a number of factors that we discuss henceforward. First, we assume the availability of a conceptual model like the one depicted in Figure 8. Such a model represents the structural elements and their conceptual constraints comprising the problem domain [31]; its adequacy and completeness determines the range of available concepts and relationships for the boilerplate attributes, the initial design, and the property derivation steps. We consider that conceptual modeling is performed by the Requirement Engineers in cooperation with the domain experts in charge of system design. This activity also includes capturing the domain assumptions, i.e., common and often tacit knowledge for the problem domain, and in spite of the system under design [49, 44]. The so-called domain knowledge (cf. Section 4) may concern with standardized protocols, services, libraries or physical laws, and can provide additional semantic information about the nature of the concepts in question. This information is essential, in order to conclude e.g. that certain events or data ranges that respect the conceptual model syntactically, are not relevant semantically. Some assumptions may be related to physics, e.g. "mass cannot be negative", and some assumptions may be mission-specific, e.g. "the temperature within the orbiting range of the spacecraft cannot rise above N degrees". Elicitation of domain knowledge, as a collaborative effort, could be facilitated by the use of templates for each ontology class [3].

The conceptual model and all assumptions related to domain knowledge are encoded into domain-specific and system-specific ontologies, which are accessed through the RERD tool. New concepts may be created from within the tool and the user is notified for violations of constraints related to the model integrity (e.g. undefined relationships). The model quality (syntactic, semantic, pragmatic) [43,41] is a responsibility of the Requirement Engineers, who should aim for models that can be reused to significant extent in multiple projects. Certainly, the reusability depends on the abstraction level of design, since the requirements are usually specified at different abstraction levels along the development lifecycle (for space systems we have the spacecraft, avionics and software levels) and a conceptual model is pertinent only to a specific level [46]. The aforementioned problems and the right ontology in relation to our model-based design process need to be further researched in future work.

A second important issue is the expressiveness of the boilerplate language, and whether it can be sufficient for specifying the full range of requirement types found in the design of, say, space systems. This of course depends on the expressiveness of the property patterns, and on the analyzability of BIP models with extended semantics for the various property types, because correctness-by-construction does not vanish the need for a posteriori verification. The structure of the boilerplate language in Section 4.1 resembles that of RSL in the CESAR reference technology platform [2]. We currently support fewer templates than RSL for the prefix, main and suffix clauses, but this set of

templates was sufficient for expressing the requirements of the case studies. Moreover, the RERD tool was designed such that new templates may be added; the only prerequisite is that the additional templates must be associated with property patterns, as in Table 7. The adopted framework of patterns from [27] is well-established and stems from industrially-relevant studies, but it only covers functional property specifications. We certainly foresee the need for boilerplates with templates for non-functional aspects, which call for support by e.g. timing patterns [68] and probabilistic patterns [34]. Here, it is worth to note:

- the extension of BIP [62] that allows specifying probabilistic aspects of BIP components, while providing a stochastic semantics for the parallel composition of components through interactions and priorities;

- the RT-BIP extension for modeling timing constraints as a timed automaton, and a real-time engine for computing the schedules meeting the timing constraints, given the underlying platform's real-time clock [1].

ing the schedules meeting the timing constraints, given the underlying platform's real-time clock [1]. These extensions are accompanied by advanced verification tools, some of which implement scalable compositional verification techniques [67].

However, a matter of vital importance is how expressive can be a boilerplate language with a controlled vocabulary for the attributes with respect to today's industrial practice of natural language specifications. The loss of expressiveness is inevitable, though necessary to avoid ambiguity; the true question is whether it is still possible and whether we really need to cover the same system aspects with those in today's specifications. This question also matters for languages like EARS [50, 51], which insist on natural language specifications using a fixed set of structural rules (though the EARS-CTRL analysis works with a user-defined glossary of terms). From our experience with the case studies, which were based on natural language requirements, we believe that only a subset of them needs to be validated. This set includes requirements that are suspected for consistency issues and have to be established or checked with respect to the system's structure and behavior. The Requirement Engineers tend to classify the requirements in project documentation into categories (e.g. at the software level of space systems there are various classes of interface requirements, performance requirements, functional requirements and design/construction requirements). Any boilerplate language is considered adequate only if it can express all representative forms of natural language requirements that need to be validated, for all categories of requirements in project documentation (e.g. the design/construction requirements is not necessary to be expressed using boilerplates). This may imply changes to the scope of individual requirements (e.g. a natural language requirement may be broken into multiple boilerplate requirements). To this end, the RERD tool displays the set of applicable boilerplates, for each category of requirements found in a user-defined catalogue of categories (Figure 18).

Our emphasis lies on precisely capturing the requirements by properties whichideally—can be enforced through BIP architectures or—if not enforced—could be verified. As we aim to a semi-automated formalization of requirements, we are intentionally limited to specific types of requirements and templates. Our approach can accommodate additional templates for requirement boilerplates, provided that they are associated with property patterns, for which it is known how they can be enforced or verified.

The applicability of the correctness-by-construction approach throughout our model-based process depends on a library of BIP architecture styles for enforcing a worthwhile set of properties in the different categories of requirements. We have implicitly adopted the commonly accepted perception that the requirement specification and the system's architectural design are in some sense intertwined [72, 63]. While specifying system requirements, the Requirement Engineers have in mind the overall structure of the system under design (functional and physical architecture inputs shown in Figure 6), whereas a significant part of their specifications comes from adapting requirements found in previous projects. Our notion of architecture styles provides the means to formally capture common solutions to recurring design problems in an abstract and reusable form. This certainly incurs a non-negligible investment cost towards developing adequate and organized libraries of architecture styles, especially since the set of property patterns that they can enforce has to be precisely defined. The set of styles in this article was derived by identifying commonalities in the base of natural language requirements of the case studies. Additional effort is required to this respect, whereas a recent research work opens prospects for defining styles which enforce quantitative properties [66].

Another important issue is the scalability and the effort needed for applying our model-based process. Indicative figures for problems of the size of our case studies have been previously mentioned. We acknowledge that in industrial problems of moderate size additional challenges may arise. More specifically, it may be trickier to identify and uniquely determine—on a team basis—the concepts for specifying requirements, as well as to verify properties against a large-scale design model. The a posteriori verification with model checking does not scale well and it can be rendered infeasible for large-scale models. With the architecture-based design a key advantage is, in particular, that the burden

of verification is shifted from the final design to architectures, which can be reused. Moreover, as was illustrated in the case studies, the verification of deadlock freedom—which is essential when combining architectures—with the compositional approach of D-Finder is very fast. However, when a non-enforceable property is not verified in Step 6 of our process, identifying a relevant sub-model for corrective action is complex. An important issue is how to present the resulting BIP model to engineers in a cognisable manner. In any case, the complexity of locating a design error is not inherent to the process proposed in the present paper: it arises for any design process involving verification. In that sense, our proposal, improves the current state of practice by reducing the number of properties that must be verified. Although additional techniques could be applied to better identify the source of an error, such as fault localisation [76] and reduction [61] techniques for BIP models, or analysis techniques similar to that used for the cone-of-influence reduction [26] $ ^{9} $ , we consider this direction as out of scope of the present paper and leave it for future research.

We presented a model-based approach for the formalization of system requirements, and their early validation with respect to system design. Our model-based process constitutes a novel approach built on top of correctness-by- construction techniques, which open a new perspective in the field. The incrementally built design model in BIP provides evidence of design correctness and consistency or else it can guide the revision of requirements. It can also form a baseline for formal refinement [40] towards introducing requirements/properties at a lower design abstraction level, while ensuring that the already established requirements and properties are preserved. Significant challenges remain to be addressed, if our approach is to be adopted in a realistic industrial context. However, although difficulties remain, which might be addressed in future work, the process presented in the paper is an advance towards reducing the validation testing during the late stages of development.

text: Awele Ifeyinwa Anyanhun was born in Benin City, Nigeria. She received her Diploma in Computer Engineering, Bachelors of Engineering degree in Electrical/Electronic Engineering, and her Masters of Engineering degree in Electronics and Telecommunications from the University of Benin in 1999, 2005 and 2010 respectively. She worked as a lecturer in the Electrical Engineering Department at the University of Benin from 2009 to 2013.

section: has met the dissertation requirements of North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University
section_key: has met the dissertation requirements of north carolina agricultural and technical state university
text: She began her doctoral studies in Electrical and Systems Engineering at the North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University in 2014. She was a Samuel Langley program fellow from 2015 until her graduation. She received a a mini-research grant award from the Graduate Student Advisory Council at North Carolina A&T State University. She pursued her research in the areas of Inter-Satellite Communication for Small Satellite Systems and Model-Based Systems Engineering under the direction of Dr. William W. Edmonson during which time she interned at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, NASA Station, Pasadena, California.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > Abstract
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / abstract
text: Small satellite systems are fast becoming very attractive for space science exploration especially in low earth orbit due to their more cost-effective benefits. However, the constraints placed on these satellites in terms of their form factor, mass and power requirements, limit their usefulness and effectiveness for highly complex missions. Furthermore, the limited capability of the communication system of these satellites remains the most significant hurdle to their optimal utilization. Confronted with these challenges, our goal is to develop a system architectural model based on model-based systems engineering (MBSE) approach and principles, that can be used to capture, analyze and describe the communication system design equipped with inter-satellite communication capability for high-speed data relay. In this dissertation, we develop a high-level system architectural model for inter-satellite communication among a constellation of small satellites utilizing a hybrid visible light and X-band communication system. First, a model-based architectural framework is developed for defining the behavioral and structural aspects of an ISC system architecture to ensure a rigorous architectural design process is adhered to. Second, a domain-specific profile that extends the Systems Modeling Language (SysML) is developed for enabling the capture of ISC system domain information with a higher degree of precision, leaving less room for interpretation. Third, a high-level system architecture model is developed consisting of a conceptual phase design model capturing the concept of operations for the proposed ISC system; a system-level requirements model defining unambiguous, consistent, attainable and verifiable ISC system requirements that are located in the central model repository. Finally, following the definition of ISC system requirements, the high-level system architecture model is developed; the communication system model is defined for the communication-oriented layers (physical, data-link and network layers) of the Open System Interconnection (OSI) reference model. The developed system architecture model captures the system behavior, structure and parametric. The high-level architecture model lays the groundwork for our future work which entails the development of models for the detailed design phase of the design life-cycle.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > Introduction

text: There is an emerging trend towards the use of small spacecraft to perform science, surveillance and engineering demonstration mission [120]. This emerging trend is due largely, to a growing interest among the science community in using distributed systems of small satellites to enhance observations for earth and space science [85]. The concept of deploying multiple small spacecraft with inter-satellite communication (ISC) capabilities is a step towards realizing the potentials previously accomplished by larger monolithic spacecraft. Inter-satellite communication between formation flying small spacecraft in low earth orbit (LEO) can be realized using visible light communication (VLC) [6]. However, it is not technically wise nor economically practical to build a communication system without first creating a system architectural model that when implemented will not violate the size, mass, and power (SMaP) constraints of the small spacecraft. Standardized CubeSats have strict size, power and mass constraints due to their form factor [105].

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / introduction
text: Defining a systems architecture is a critical step in the development of any complex system. System Architecture - depending on the context in which it is used, refers to either the Architecture of a System - i.e a model used to describe or analyze a system or System Architecting - the method or process used to build the architecture of a system. The purpose of system architecture activities is to define a comprehensive solution based on principles, concepts, and properties logically related, and consistent with each other [11]. This process helps to describe consistently and design efficiently complex systems. Systems architecting is a response to the conceptual and practical difficulties associated with the description and design of complex systems [53]; failure to accurately define a systems architecture prior to build often results in unwanted emergent system characteristics that will impact system cost significantly.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > Introduction

Currently, visible light communications for space systems is a new and emerging trend necessitating the need to develop a system architecture that can adequately define the structure, properties, behavior, relationships (between elements) and multiple views of the system. Developing a comprehensive system model that captures the systems architecture will provide stakeholders with the ability to visualize the entire system, assess different options and communicate designs more clearly before taking on risks - (technical, financial, or otherwise) of actual construction.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / introduction
text: This research presents a System Architecture Model for an inter-satellite communication system between small satellite systems utilizing visible light communications and radio frequency communications based on a model-based systems engineering approach. In particular, this research focuses on four phases of the system development life-cycle; these phases include the Conceptual Design Phase, Requirements Analysis Phase, High-Level Architecture Phase and a subset of the Detailed Design Phase. Furthermore, given the complex nature of the communication system to be developed, a model based inter-satellite communication architectural framework (ISC-AF) is developed. This framework can be regarded as a set of guidelines, patterns or rules used to delineate the architecture of an ISC system; It specifies the way and manner in which the fundamental organization of the ISC system architecture can be presented. Accordingly, a domain specific (DS) profile is also created to support high-level abstractions of the system architecture and enable reusability by transforming system concepts into a collection of self-contained modules.

VLC technology is an emerging green technology in the field of wireless communication using visible light. It is a subset of optical wireless Communication (OWC) and as a communication medium, uses the visible light portion of the electromagnetic spectrum (750THz) or 400nm to (428 THz) or 700nm for transmission. LEDs are used as transmitters in this communication technology while photodiodes or image sensors are used as receivers. VLC technology opens the door for many new applications to be realized because

Substantive work has been done in capturing the Open System Interconnection (OSI) physical layer design of a VLC system for ISC in [6] [4] [5]. This work demonstrates the feasibility of implementing VLC for communication among small satellites using LEDs as portrayed in Figure 1. However, a systematic and rigorous approach has not been taken in developing a comprehensive architecture for an inter-satellite communication system between small satellites that can utilize visible light via LEDs, and that can be analyzed and assessed for implementation.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 2.1 Systems Engineering Principles
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 2 1 systems engineering principles
text: Systems Engineering (SE) is an interdisciplinary field that emerged as an effective way to manage complexity and change in systems. System engineering is considered a process necessary to successfully design and operate a complex system. It is based on a holistic perspective of problems and design. It focuses on customer needs and required functionality [79]. Systems engineering involves system specification, development and verification activities. It provides system-level oversight during the development of a complex system and hence is distinct from discipline-specific engineering. A key point to note is that despite the fact that systems engineering may define requirements allocated to these specific engineering disciplines, It does not specify the design or technology used within them except, perhaps at a high level. Systems engineering is defined in the Systems Engineering Book of Knowledge (SEBOK) [11] as an "interdisciplinary approach and means to enable the realization of successful (engineered) systems [32]. It focuses on holistically and concurrently understanding stakeholder needs, exploring opportunities, documenting requirements and synthesizing, verifying, validating and evolving solutions while considering the complete problem. SE concentrates on defining and documenting system requirements in the early development phase, preparation of the system design, and the verification of the system. The holistic approach used by SE as against specific disciplines also involves obtaining solutions to problems that emerge only as a result of the newly developed system [132]. The SE perspective is based on systems thinking.

text: 2. 1.1 Systems Thinking Systems thinking is a unique perspective on reality - a perspective that sharpens the awareness of wholes and how the parts within those wholes interrelate. When a system is considered as a combination of system elements, systems thinking acknowledges

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 2.1 Systems Engineering Principles

text: the primacy of the whole (system) and the primacy of the relation of the interrelationships of the system elements to the whole [70]. Systems thinking is an essential skill set shared with many disciplines and provides a vital intellectual underpinning for systems engineering. It uses models to make sense of complex problems. According to [69], Systems thinking enables a system engineer look at problems from different viewpoints. It is considered a skill set that enables a better understanding of the deep roots of complex system behavior to better predict and adjust their outcomes. Since uncertainty is an inevitable attribute of a complex system, system thinking provides a platform that enables system engineers deal with uncertainty in complex systems. In [10] systems thinking is defined as a system in itself. They describe system thinking as a "system of thinking." Systems thinking is a necessity for everyone in a decision making role. The term systems thinking was coined by Barry Richmond in 1981 [104].

text: 2. 1.3 Systems Engineering Process The systems engineering process (SEP) is a comprehensive, iterative and recursive problem-solving process that includes both management and technical processes. A process is defined as a logical sequence of tasks performed to achieve a particular objective. This life cycle process is achieved by applying a set of life-cycle building blocks which are the fundamental building blocks for engineering any kind of complex system

Some common life-cycle process models include the Vee, spiral [119], incremental [40] and hybrid [40] life-cycle models.

text: 2. 1.4 System Related Concepts In systems engineering, a System can be broadly defined as an integrated set of elements that accomplish a defined objective. It comprises of system elements, interconnections (interactions) between elements and an external system boundary. From a systems engineering perspective, A system is said to result from a deliberate design and must be managerially and operationally independent. The international standard organization ISO 15288 -systems and software engineering life cycle processes [1] defines a system as "a combination of interacting elements organized to achieve one or more stated purposes. The INCOSE definition of a system is taken directly from this standard. The United States Department of Defense (DoD) also define a system as a "functionally, physically and or behaviorally related group of regularly interacting or interdependent elements; that group of elements forming a unified whole. Elements are the building blocks of systems, and they can comprise of hardware, software, personnel,

text: policies, facilities documents, and databases. In the systems engineering domain, a system is also defined as one that delivers an operational capability. A system can be divided into a hierarchy of sets of elements that include subsystems, components, subcomponents and parts. Some system related concepts include:

text: 2. 1.4.1 System-of-Interest (SoI) At a conceptual level, a system can be considered as a System of Interest (SOI). The International Council for Systems Engineering (INCOSE) [32] defines a system of interest as "The system whose life cycle is under consideration. According to [131], an SOI is defined as "the system consisting of a mission system and its support system(s) assigned to perform a specific objective. Furthermore, ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 [1] takes a hierarchical view by describing it as "the top system in the system structure which also consists of lower-level systems. Hitchins in [76] provides a definition by stating that a system of interest "contains intra-connected subsystems which are systems in their own right existing within their own environment."

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 2.1 Systems Engineering Principles
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 2 1 systems engineering principles
text: 2. 1.4.2 System-of-Systems (SOS) Another system related concept is the emerging system-of-systems concept which is defined as the large-scale integration of many independent, self-contained systems in order to satisfy a global need. A system of systems is defined by INCOSE as an interoperating collection of components systems that produce results unachievable by the individual systems alone. In the US Department of Defense DoD guidelines, a system of systems (SoS) is defined as "A set or arrangement of systems that result when independent and useful systems are integrated into a larger system that delivers unique capabilities. The generalization relationship exists between a system and a SoS according to the US DoD definition. This relationship is elaborated by the statement "although a system-of-systems is a system, not all systems are system-of-systems." [18] Also a SoS can be described as the bringing together of a set of systems to perform a specific task or group of tasks that can not be performed by each individual system on its own [1].

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 2.2 Model Based Systems Engineering
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 2 2 model based systems engineering
text: The concept of applying a model-based approach to the practice of Systems Engineering (SE) brought about the advent of model-based systems engineering. The growing complexity in all areas of system development has increased the need for the systems engineering discipline; however, in order to be effective, systems engineering must provide an organized, repeatable, iterative and convergent approach to developing complex systems [80]. An apt and simplified definition of SE given in [38] states that "Systems Engineering can be defined as the practice of engineering from the systems viewpoint ". Extending this definition, we can define MBSE as the practice of engineering from a systems viewpoint using models. MBSE has as its main artifact a system model that contains all relevant information required to completely and consistently describe, verify and validate a system. This system model which can be better qualified as computer-interpretable models as stated in [103] forms the distinguishable difference between the document-centric approach and model-centric approach to the practice of systems engineering.

text: As accurately stated in [62], to get a good understanding of MBSE, one must of necessity have a good and unambiguous definition of systems engineering. Based on the definition of SE by INCOSE, the realization of successful systems should be the expected outcome. INCOSE goes further to define MBSE as "The formalized application of modeling to support system requirements, design, analysis, verification & validation activities beginning in the conceptual design phase and continuing throughout development and later life cycle phases ". Paraphrasing the above definition to concisely capture our expectation, we define MBSE as the "Formalized application of modeling to enable the realization of successful systems ". The benefits of implementing an MBSE approach in either defining an Architectural Framework (AF) or in the development of successful systems include the realization of a model that comprises a coherent and consistent set of views that reflect multiple viewpoints of the system [62]. Other benefits associated with the application of effective MBSE include: automatic generation and maintenance of system documents, complexity control, and management, consistency of information, inherent traceability, simpler access to information, improved communication regarding language, concept and terminology and increased

text: 2. 2.1 MBSE Methodology A modeling methodology refers to a documented set of design tasks that are performed in order to create a system model. In [45], a comprehensive survey of MBSE methodologies is provided. The author defines a methodology as a collection of related processes, methods and tools [86]. Considering modeling methods span all stages of the systems engineering life cycle and, not all stages are necessary for every project, modeling methods will need to be tailored to meet specific needs [35]. A modeling methodology is necessary for guiding the development of a system model by providing a roadmap (set of design tasks) for all team members to ensure that consistency, guidance, and fidelity is built into the system model. Examples of MBSE methodology include The "INCOSE Object-Oriented Systems Engineering Method and "IBM Rational Unified Process for Systems Engineering."

text: 2. 3.2 Defense Based Architectural Frameworks Defense-based AF are designed to support defense operations and activities. The most common defense-based AF is the United State Department of Defense AF (DoDAF) [127]. The DoDAF provides a foundational framework for developing and characterizing architecture descriptions. DoDAF incorporates three views: Operational View (OV), Systems and Services View (SV), and Technical Standards View (TV). These views are depicted in Figure 13 and provide the basis for deriving measures of performance and interoperability. The command, control, communication and computer Intelligence Surveillance and Reconnaissance (C4ISR) defense group first adopted the idea of implementing an AF for their activities. Other defense organizations around the world have also adopted the defense based AF paradigm and have developed their standards. Other defense-based AFs include The UK Ministry of defense (MODAF) standard [87], NATO defense standard (NAF) [93], AGATE AF from France, Canada's DNDAF, MDAF from Italy and ADOAF from Australia.

text: 2. 3.3 Enterprise Architectural Framework The Open Group Architectural Framework (TOGAF) [126] is an enterprise based architectural framework developed by the Open Group. It is a proven enterprise architecture methodology and framework used by the world's leading organizations to improve business efficiency. TOGAF represents a set of supporting resources for developing an Enterprise Architecture.As an architecture standard, it also ensures consistent standards, methods, and communication among enterprise architecture professionals. The Zachman AF [138] is an enterprise framework invented by John Zachman in 1980. The framework borrows from business design principles in architecture and manufacturing and provides a way of viewing an enterprise and its information systems from different perspectives, showing how the components of the enterprise are related. The Zachman framework provides a means of classifying an organization's architecture [78].

The ESA-AF introduces new concepts, viewpoints, and views for the representation of European and space-specific characteristics and provides an infrastructure for methodology evolution which supports feedback from the European space industry.

text: 2. 3.6 MBSE - Based Architectural Framework Architectures and Architectural Frameworks are now considered to be fundamental to model-based systems engineering. An MBSE - based Architectural Framework (MBSE-based AF) describes from an MBSE perspective, the conventions, principles, and practices for the description of architectures established within a specific domain. An Architectural Framework based on an MBSE approach is defined as a set of one or more Viewpoint and an Ontology and is used to structure an architecture from the point of view of a specific industry, Stakeholder Role set, or Organization [62]. The MBSE-based AF is designed to meet the Needs defined by one or more Architectural Framework Concern and is created such that it complies with industry standards. Based on the work done in [62], an MBSE-based AF is made up of a number of Viewpoints that define the information that can be presented; the framework

text: 2. 3.6.1 Viewpoint Viewpoint modeling is an effective approach for dealing with the inherent complexity of systems. A Viewpoint Provides the framework for defining the content and structure of a view. The content and structure of a Viewpoint use the concepts and terms from the Ontology via one or more Viewpoint Element that make up the Viewpoint. It defines the perspective from which a View is taken. It also represents the vantage point that determines what is depicted in a given View. Each Viewpoint is defined so that it meets the needs defined by one or more Viewpoint Concern. A Viewpoint defines the information that can be presented; it is a definition of what can be produced when an Architecture is based on an Architectural Framework.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 2.3 Architectural Frameworks

text: 2. 3.6.2 Views A View can be described as the representation of a system architecture from the perspective of a defined Viewpoint. It corresponds to the visualization of part of the architecture of a system that conforms to the structure and content defined in a Viewpoint. A View is made up of one or more View Element. It is an artifact, produced as part of an architecture and it describes an aspect of that architecture. If the architecture is created using an architectural framework, then every View will conform to a Viewpoint in the architectural framework.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 2.3 Architectural Frameworks

text: 2. 3.6.3 Perspective A Perspective is used as the organizational schema for Views with a common purpose. It represents a collection of one or more View (and hence also one or more defining Viewpoint) that are related by their purpose. That is, one or more View which address the same architectural needs, rather than being related in some other way, such as by mode of visualization.

text: Small Satellites Systems (SmSS) are artificial satellites with an overall mass of 180kg and below. These class of satellites are divided into six sub-groups: mini-satellites (100- 180kg), micro-satellites (10-100kg), nano-satellites (1-10kg), pico-satellites (0.01-1kg) and femto-satellites (0.001-0.01kg) [81] as shown in Table 5. A subclass of the nano-satellite sub-group known as CubeSats has become the most popular group class of small satellites in recent times due to various advantages they offer such as their standardized specifications. CubeSats are standardized satellites with a fixed size and form factor of One Unit (i.e. "1U"), measuring 10 x 10 x 10cm extend-able to larger sizes of 1.5U, 2U, 3U, 6U, 12U, and 27U [81]. Figure 15 depicts the skeleton chassis for various CubeSat sizes. Due to low cost and rapid development times associated with these group of satellites, as technological advancements increase, these satellites will become endowed with the ability and potential to overcome their Size Mass and Power (SMaP) limitations. A major reason for the great advancements already recorded with small satellite technology is due to an increasing number of countries becoming space-faring nations.

text: 2. 4.3 Open System Interconnection (OSI) Reference Model The Open System Interconnection (OSI) reference model [2] defines a layered approach for data communication

text: between communication systems without regard for the internal structure implemented by the communication systems. As a conceptual framework, It aids in enabling understanding of the complex interactions which occur within a communication network. The layer-based OSI model partitions the communication system network architecture into seven layers which, from top to bottom are the Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data-link and Physical layers respectively. The OSI model implements protocols (i.e. a set of rules that govern data communication) used in the exchange of data between communication systems in a network. Each layer provides services to the layer above it and receives services from the layer below it.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 3.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 3 1 introduction
text: Developing an architectural framework for the definition of an inter-satellite communication system architecture is a desirable starting point for this research because an architectural framework is essential for the successful design and implementation of any system. For the system architecture to be useful, it is crucial that a rigorous architectural design process is adhered to, and this can only be realized when the architecture conforms to a well defined architectural framework. A well defined architectural framework represents an embodiment of a minimum set of guidelines, practices, and requirements for artifacts that describe a system's architecture and support the definition of architectures. Defining architectural frameworks for the development of system architectures has become a fundamental part of systems engineering practice. There is a utility to defining and implementing a model-centric approach based on MBSE as it enables the development of a framework essential for the realization of robust system architectures which meet the needs of stakeholders and customers.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 3.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 3 1 introduction
text: The objective of this chapter is to present a model-based systems engineering (MBSE) architectural framework design for defining small-satellite systems inter-satellite communication (SmSS-ISC) architectures. The framework is shown as a model comprising of a set of views which conform to viewpoints to which an ISC system architecture must conform. Section 3.1 introduces the concept of an MBSE architectural framework and the inherent value in developing a framework on which system architectures can be based. In Section 3.2, the ISC-AF for ISC system architectures is described. A summary of the chapter is presented in Section 3.3.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 3.2 MBSE Based Architectural Framework Development
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 3 2 mbse based architectural framework development
text: The value of initiating the system design process with the development of a framework is embodied in the many benefits with which an MBSE based approach impacts the system design process. Firstly, utilizing models in the development of an architectural framework aid in complexity management because models can be measured and controlled. The ability to automatically measure the outputs of a model and thereby control its results enables the management of the model's complexity and hence that of the developed architectural framework. In particular, the use of a model results in ensuring consistent and coherent information across the whole architectural framework. Utilization of a coherent and consistent model provides improved communication by way of defining an Ontology that defines all related and relevant concepts and terminology used as the basis for all views that make up the model. Consequently, all knowledge about the architectural framework is represented coherently by the model ensuring consistency and traceability between model elements and guaranteeing simpler access to information for users of the framework.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 3.2 MBSE Based Architectural Framework Development
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 3 2 mbse based architectural framework development
text: A well defined architectural framework must allow for the definition of architectures that model both the behavioral and structural aspects of a system thereby establishing the value of the framework and its impact on the system architecture. Guidelines established in [62] and are adhered to in this research work buttress the fact that an architectural framework must be defined regarding a series of Viewpoints and have pre-defined set of rules that are defined to ensure consistency.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 3.3 ISC Architectural Framework for Small Satellite Systems
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 3 3 isc architectural framework for small satellite systems
text: The Inter-Satellite Communication - Architectural Framework (ISC-AF) for Small Satellite Systems can be regarded as a set of guidelines, patterns or rules that delineate the architecture of an ISC system. The ISC-AF specifies the way and manner in which the fundamental organization of the ISC system architecture can be presented. Given that this research is focused on an MBSE approach towards the development of an ISC system, though there exist a varied number of architectural framework definitions in literature, the definition and viewpoints that best characterize

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 3.3 ISC Architectural Framework for Small Satellite Systems
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 3 3 isc architectural framework for small satellite systems
text: We define the ISC architectural framework as a set of Viewpoints and an Ontology constrained by well defined rules that ensure consistency across the framework spectrum. The ISC-AF provides the structure necessary for describing ISC system architectures.This structure allows ISC system architectures be defined in a way that models both the structural aspects and behavioral aspects of every system being represented by the architecture. An Ontology is essential whenever a framework is defined in terms of a set of viewpoints; it serves as an element of the architectural framework that defines all the concepts and terms that relate to any architecture structured according to the architectural framework. Consequently, our ISC-AF is essentially made up of five viewpoints that conform to our defined ontology. Viewpoints provide conventions, and languages for constructing, presenting and analyzing views. These viewpoints depicted on the block definition diagram (bdd) in Figure 18 are defined in a systematic manner to ensure that they conform to the ISC-AF ontology. The viewpoints used to define the architectural framework are represented using the following views:

text: 3. 3.6 Chapter Summary An architectural framework establish the basis for creating, interpreting and analyzing architectures within a domain. In this chapter we presented an architectural framework design for Inter-Satellite Communication (ISC) between Small Satellite Systems (SmSS) based on an MBSE approach. The Systems Modeling Language (SysML) was used as the modeling tool to aid in the development process. The architectural framework (AF) designed provides a standard framework for modeling an ISC system architecture. The AF enables the representation of an ISC system architecture based on viewpoints which are realized by a set of views. The AF is presented as a set of views conforming to viewpoints which focus on specific concerns regarding the ISC-AF. The defined ISC-AF ontology enforces consistency and rigor in the system architectures that are defined based on the ISC-AF.The ISC-AF views are represented using bdds and use case diagrams.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 4.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 4 1 introduction
text: Communication between stakeholders, system engineers, and design teams can be particularly challenging due to gaps in knowledge, vocabulary and understanding [23]. Employing the use of modeling languages to capture system design improves communication through better presentation and increased information consistency. Towards this end, a SysML profile for modeling an ISC system architectures is created. The profile models common system concepts that capture the structure, requirements, behavior and parametric information of an ISC system. Through increased traceability and integration, the profile allows for greater consistency between VLC information and system design information and will aid in communicating this information to stakeholders and project teams. The profile specifies common terminology for core communication concepts; key benefits of extending UML/SysML for defining a domain-specific profile include The ability to capture information with a higher degree of precision, leaving less room for interpretation.

text: Section 4.1 gives an overview of domain-specific profiling in the context of model-based systems engineering. Next, in Section 4.2 we establish the requirements that the developed profile must satisfy to be considered a valid domain-specific profile. In Section 4.4, the domain-specific profile designed for the ISC domain is presented. The profile defines domain-specific stereotypes for capturing ISC system requirements, structure, behavior and system constraints. Conformance of the profile to the stated requirements is discussed in Section 4.5 while the chapter is summarized in Section 4.6.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 4.2 MBSE & Domain Specific Profiles
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 4 2 mbse domain specific profiles
text: SysML is a general-purpose graphical modeling language used to support the practice of system modeling [51]. The capabilities of SysML are augmented by providing better semantics with which to represent and capture concepts relevant to the domain of interest when a domain-specific profile is defined. The SysML meta-model is used as the foundation for defining Domain Specific Languages (DSL) [75]. A SysML profile is developed by extending the SysML meta-model and introducing domain-specific concepts into it in the form of stereotypes. A stereotype represents an extension to the SysML/UML meta-classes and may be parametrized with properties known as tagged values. A stereotype may also contain constraints written in object constraint language (OCL) specifying the structure and/or behavior restrictions of a stereotype in a well-formed model [73]. In the context of MBSE, a model representing a system and its environment is a basis of communication among stakeholders from different domains [31], hence creating models customized for a specific domain of interest will lead to enhanced communication and understanding between stakeholders and system developers while supporting the description of static and dynamic aspects of the system. Creating a domain-specific profile is the first step towards creating models that support efficient information sharing. Shown in Figure 28 is the high-level diagram of the domain-specific profile package.

text: 4. 3.2 Profile Requirements for Behavior Constructs The primary task of the physical layer of the VLC ISL system is consolidating the hardware requirements of a VLC network to enable the successful transmission of data. The physical layer is the first and lowest layer of the seven-layer OSI model; It provides the optical wireless link for transmitting data between satellites and also performs services requested by the data link layer of the VLC system. The VLC ISL system physical layer is responsible for the wireless optical relay of data using the visible light band. The system ensures data to be transmitted is converted into an optical signal and transmitted via the LED-Array front-end. The system also ensures that data/commands are received via its receiver front-end after which the data goes through several processes at the physical layer before the data is retrieved and forwarded to higher layers. The following requirements are proposed to support the modeling of these tasks:

text: 4. 3.4 Profile Requirements for Link Budget Modeling The major constraint that exists in a communication system is that of the link budget. A link budget is a method used to quantify the link performance and by extension the overall system performance for a telecommunication system. For a VLC link to exist between multiple small satellites, the received power at any given satellite must be higher than the minimum received signal after path loss has been subtracted. The performance and reliability of a VLC network for space communication hinges on the system's link budget. Hence modeling of the link budget constraint is important. text: An overview of the VLC System Domain-Specific Profile Package is presented in this section. The profile package consists of the sub-packages: VLC Model Library, VLC Stereotypes Package and the VLC Customization Model Package. Contained within the profile model library are domain-specific ValueTypes; the system consists of value properties that are typed by specific ValueTypes contained in the model library. The stereotype package holds all domain-specific stereotypes (VLC system stereotypes) which are extended from the UML and SysML meta-classes. A VLC stereotype specializes a SysML stereotype. These stereotypes are created within a special kind of package called a profile, and they are used as the customization target when creating customization model elements.

text: 4. 4.2 Stereotypes that Support Modeling the Systems Behavior In order to create domain specific VL-ISC system behavior models, stereotypes that support the systems dynamic behavior such as States, Actions, etc. have been defined in the profile. These system behavior stereotypes describe certain behavioral aspects of the VLC system. Overall, the profile defines a total of ten (10) behavior stereotypes that support system behavior modeling; these stereotypes are outlined in Table. 10. Some examples of stereotypes needed to support system behavior modeling are portrayed in Figure 33 and Figure 34. The stereotypes defined include- TransmitSignalAction and ReceiverSignalEvent stereotypes, EncapsulationAction and DecapsulationAction stereotypes, and the TransponderState stereotype. The TransmitSignalAction stereotype represents an action that creates an outgoing signal while the ReceiveSignalEvent stereotype represents an action that consumes an incoming signal. Shown in Table 11 are a subset of the DS SysML Profile behavior stereotypes.

text: 4. 4.3 Stereotypes that Support Modeling the Systems Structure Shown in Table.12 are a subset of stereotypes that support the modeling of the VLC system structure. The stereotypes presented in our proposed profile include the following: the LayerType stereotype, this stereotype represents a defined layer such as the Physical or Data Link layer of the OSI model or any other communication reference model. The TransponderModel Stereotype which is also defined in the profile represents a certain make of transponder e.g. a VL Hybrid transponder. We also defined the TransmitterModel and ReceiverModel stereotypes. This stereotypes represent a certain specific make or model of transmitter and receiver which may be custom built based on a specific design for a particular mission. The OSILayer stereotype supports the modeling of specific layers as structural elements representing a domain of interest during system design.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 4.5 Conformance to Profile Modeling Requirements
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 4 5 conformance to profile modeling requirements
text: The VL-ISC System DS-Profile conforms to and satisfies all modeling requirements listed in section 3. The profile provides various structural stereotypes which are used in modeling the structure of the system. When these stereotypes are instantiated in the model, the modeler is able to input the various characteristics of the specified stereotype. Shown in Figure 35 is an example of the TransmitterModel stereotype, when this stereotype is instantiated by the system designer, he is able to include certain model specific characteristics of the TransmitterModel such as the Name, brand, dimensions and certain instance specific characteristics. From the table for structural stereotypes it can be observed that the profile satisfies all the language structural requirements because it provides specific stereotypes for the modeling of both functional and non-functional VL-ISC system requirements. The profile also satisfies the listed requirements needed to support the modeling of the system behavior. Specified in the DS-Profile are various behavioral stereotypes that can be used to model certain aspects of the system behavior as shown in Table.11 and Figure 33 and Figure 34. The profile satisfies the VLC system requirements and link budget constraint requirements as shown in Table.8 and Table.14. The creation of a DS-Profile for a VL-ISC System is an iterative and ongoing process subject to updates as the VLC system design matures. The profile does not need to provide specific constructs to capture model elements for which SysML semantics is sufficient.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 4.6 Chapter Summary
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 4 6 chapter summary
text: Presented in this chapter is a Domain Specific Profile developed in other to support the modeling of an Inter-satellite Communication System utilizing visible light communication via LEDs. The DS-Profile is created using both UML and SysML metamodels which imports in order to extend the modeling language for the ISC domain. Also enumerated in this chapter are sets of requirements which the profile must and does satisfy in order to support the modeling of the ISC system's Requirements, Structure, Behavior and parametric information. The DS-Profile satisfies the stated profile requirements and is capable of supporting an ISC system design

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 1 introduction
text: In this chapter, we present the conceptual design model for an inter-satellite communication system to be utilized for three formation-flying small satellites in low-earth orbit. The conceptual model is developed during the concept engineering phase of system design. The design artifact produced during this phase is referred to as the Concept of Operations. In this Section, we briefly reiterate the benefits of applying MBSE principles to the system design effort and present the MBSE life-cycle V-model. This chapter we address the first life-cycle building block - Concept Engineering. Next, we introduce the term - concept engineering and give a brief background on model-based concept development in Section 5.1. Section 5.2 is devoted to describing the concept of operations model which entails outlining the mission description. The project scope activities which include scope definition, stakeholder need analysis, defining mission goals and system context are described in Section 5.3. In Section 5.4, we present the operational concept model for the ISC system, design drivers in the form of identified constraints are also presented. Section 5.6 outlines the ConOps maturation phases while the chapter summary is presented in Section 5.7.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 1 introduction
text: 5. 1.1 Model based Systems Engineering MBSE formalizes the practice of systems development through the use of models [49]; It enhances the ability to capture, analyze, share and manage the information associated with the complete specification of a system. The principles of model-based systems engineering provide the framework needed to select a set of interrelated models to help characterize and analyze a system and document the design, acquisition and sustainment process. The models created provide increased ability to manage system complexity by enabling the system model to be viewed from multiple perspectives and to analyze the impact of

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 1 introduction
text: changes. Models can be validated, queried, reasoned about, and used to create documentation and operational artifacts. The selection and use of common models throughout and across a systems life cycle will help to improve communications between stakeholders, system engineers, and developers by providing a common ground for discussion [49] [80]. The successful implementation of MBSE across a wide range of systems engineering problems proves there are significant benefits to be derived from the use of models as the basis for systems engineering [114].

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 1 introduction
text: 5. 1.2 MBSE Life-Cycle Model A system life-cycle model can be described as a view of a system that addresses all phases of its existence from the system conception phase through design and development, production, maintenance, retirement/system phase-out, and disposal [97]. All Systems Engineering models and processes are organized around the concept of a system life-cycle model. The V-Model (Verification & Validation) shown in Figure 36 is a graphical representation of the life cycle processes that can be applied to the development of a complex system based on MBSE principles. Each phase of the systems design life-cycle is modeled, and the models which act as the primary data source are centrally stored in a model repository. Each life-cycle phase is iterative, and as modifications/updates are made to the systems design, the ability to effect these changes and measure their impact across the system's life-cycle is considered facile.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.2 Concept Engineering
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 2 concept engineering
text: The term Concept Engineering was first used by the authors of [77] to describe the activities performed in the early phase of a complex systems life cycle. In various sectors such as defense, aerospace, and automotive industries, different terminology exists which describe the life-cycle phase, crucial activities performed during this phase and expected outcomes. The Department of Defense (DoD) description of concept engineering as stated in [19] describes it as the phase of systems engineering life-cycle prior to requirements elicitation, system architecting and design, during which the developer "rapidly elucidate the needs, explore solutions, develop a concept of operations and derive requirements for material solutions." In the Space and Aerospace industry, the term "Concept and Technology Development " is used to describe the set of activities that are performed during the early phase of the system life-cycle [91]. In the Systems Engineering Book of Knowledge (SEBoK) [13], "Conceptual Design " is the term used to describe the early phase of systems engineering activities.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.2 Concept Engineering
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 2 concept engineering
text: A key deliverable from the concept engineering phase of the system life-cycle process is the Concept of Operations (ConOps) document. A CONOPS (document) as defined by INCOSE in [32] "is a document (model) produced early in the requirements definition process to describe what the system will do and why, It should also define critical, top-level performance requirements or objectives ". A ConOps describes the desires, operational need and user expectations of the proposed system without requiring it to be stated in a formal way or requiring the provision of a testable specification. This document (model) bridges the gap between all stakeholders by communicating to them an agreed upon perspective of the operational boundaries, the measures of effectiveness, standards of acceptance and system design. Shown in Table. 15 are various organizational standards that have defined guidelines for the development of a ConOps.
