section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.2 Concept Engineering
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 2 concept engineering
text: 5. 2.1 Model Based System Concept Development Model-based system concept development is an approach to system concept development in which models are used to capture the concept development phase activities of a proposed system. System concepts consist of two perspectives [134]: a concept of operations (ConOps) perspective and an operational concept (OpsCon) perspective. In systems engineering practice, these two perspectives have traditionally been captured using textual documents. This traditional approach suffers from: a lack of precision in describing system characteristics and operational scenarios, inconsistencies between related documents whose information are used in the preparation of the ConOps and difficulty in maintaining synchronization and consistency between stakeholder requirements and system level requirements. This limitation often result in inefficiencies and quality issues that only become apparent during integration and testing [33] phase. Deploying MBSE at the system concept level will enable the systems engineering team to make one complete model of the system, making it possible to trace (verify) the system design back to the stakeholder needs and goals.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.2 Concept Engineering
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 2 concept engineering
text: A model based Concept of Operations (ConOps) can be defined as a model produced early in the requirement definition process which describes what the system will do and why. It clearly defines the needs of the stakeholders and the operational boundaries of the high-level system design. Deploying MBSE at the system concept level enables the systems engineering team make one complete model of the system thereby making it possible to trace (verify) the system design back to the stakeholder needs and goals.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.2 Concept Engineering
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 2 concept engineering
text: In the practice of MBSE it is vital that the modeling activities support the who systems engineering life cycle, this will inevitably include the concept development phase hence this research work aims to capture the system concept development phase using a model-based approach. Modeling the concept development phase improves communication between stakeholders as it enables the visualization of proposed solutions and the processes required to achieve expected system capability. A key benefit of conceptual development modeling as stated in [66] is that it keeps the focus on the concept alone and aids in answering the question "Why am I developing this system?". The ConOps model captures the systems operational scenarios (OpsCon) as a black box; It provides an efficient way to explore, update, and communicate system aspects to the stakeholders while significantly reducing or eliminating dependence on textual documents. Furthermore, explicit traceability between elements of the ConOps is achieved enabling better assessments of the impacts due to changes.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.3 Concept of Operations Model
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 3 concept of operations model
text: A Concept of Operations is defined by the INCOSE in [58] as a document (model) produced early in the requirements definition process to describe what the system will do and why. A ConOps is necessary in order to capture all required information needed for the development of system requirements and the design of the system; It places the high-level needs in context leading to a description of the systems operational usage during various mission phases in order to meet stakeholder expectations. A ConOps is treated as a living document (model), subject to changes and updates as appropriate.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.3 Concept of Operations Model
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 3 concept of operations model
text: 5. 3.1 Mission Description Outlined in this ConOps model is the baseline strategy for relay communications between three formation flying spacecraft deployed in low earth orbit. The network of spacecraft comprises two (2) CubeSats (6U) and One (1) SmallSat. Shown in Figure 37 is a view of the conceptual design while Fig. 38 captures corresponding access time data modeled using the System Tool kit (STK) [54]. The CubeSats will orbit in equatorial low earth orbits (LEO) while the SmallSat will be deployed in a sun-synchronous low earth orbit at a slightly higher altitude than the CubeSats. The satellites will be piggyback aboard a launch vehicle which will assist the CubeSats in achieving orbital insertion. They will utilize their RF-band full duplex links for initial communication with Earth prior to orbital insertion. Once the CubeSats and SmallSat have achieved orbital insertion, the VL transponder will be activated, and they will utilize VL-band full duplex links for communication. Commands will be uplinked to the two formation flying CubeSats via the SmallSat Orbiter orbiting in a sun synchronous orbit. The ISC system will consist of a Hybrid ISC VLX Transponder system capable of full-duplex communication employing the use of either Visible Light (utilizing LEDs) or RF (utilizing X-band) Inter-Satellites Links (ISLs).

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.4 Project Scope
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 4 project scope
text: The scope definition process provides a crucial foundation for writing proper system requirements which is vital to building a successful system. Scope defining activities are concerned mainly with exclusively capturing externally visible system properties. The ability to define the system scope clearly will directly impact positively the quality of system requirements written. Scoping activities prevent the capturing of incorrect requirements and avoid the omission of key requirements [134].

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.4 Project Scope
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 4 project scope
text: Applying an MBSE approach to the project scoping process does not change the activities performed or deliverables produced during this phase of concept development. However, the significant difference in employing a model-based approach is in the primary artifact produced which is a system model [114]. The activity diagram depicted in Figure 39 outlines the major activities involved in the project scope definition process. The scope definition action flows into a fork node and is split into multiple concurrent actions using as depicted in the figure. The set of activities that ensue and define the project scope include defining the stakeholder needs, outlining the goals of the project which meet the stakeholder needs; delineating objectives that are specific, concrete, measurable and are associated to goals; developing operational concept along with stating any constraints and assumptions associated with the proposed project.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.5 System Effectiveness Measures
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 5 system effectiveness measures
text: Defining the system scope represents the starting point for determining effectiveness measures [55]. Measures of Effectiveness (MOE) and Measures of Performance (MOP) represent two effectiveness measurements utilized in systems engineering for tracking important and essential performance parameters. Measure of Effectiveness are a measure of how well an operational task is accomplished through using a system, it represents the operational measures of success that are closely related to the achievement of the mission or operational objectives being evaluated. They reflect mission level performance requirements [128] [106]. In [94], MOEs are referred to as measures designed to correspond to accomplishment of mission objectives and achievement of desired results. An MOE can represent an aggregation of MOPs implying that MOEs may be further decomposed into Measures of Performance (MOP). Measure of Performance is the measure that characterizes physical or functional attributes relating to the system operation, measured or estimated under specified testing and/or operational environment conditions. They are derived from dimensional parameters. The MOPs are used to determine whether the system meets performance requirements necessary to satisfy the MOE.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.5 System Effectiveness Measures
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 5 system effectiveness measures
text: Measures of Effectiveness provide quantifiable benchmarks against which the system concept and implementation can be compared. Choosing incorrect MOEs will result in a system that does not meet customer expectations [55]. The author in [122] suggested that Measures of Effectiveness are required to answer the question "Does this system meet my need?" and defined MOE as "standards against which the capability of a solution to meet the needs of a problem may be judged." MOEs can be captured using a parametric diagram. Figure 44 depicts a parametric diagram modeled to capture a high-level MOE. The diagram shows the relationship between the high-level MOE - Communication System Effectiveness, and the lower-level MOEs - Probability of Continuous Connectivity, Data Security, Robustness and Resilience. Furthermore, the MOPs aggregated to form some of the lower-level MOEs are also captured in the parametric model.

text: The proposed VLX communication system consists of a Hybrid Visible Light (via LEDs) and RF (X-Band) Transponder capable of providing communication services via Inter-Satellite Links. The VLX system will be capable of delivering high data rates (Gbits) as well as near real-time data from the satellite payload. The system as a whole provides a long life-time capability guarantee due to the durability and reliability of light emitting diodes.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 5.6 Operation Concept Model
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 5 6 operation concept model
text: The orbiting SmallSat will communicate primarily with the formation flying CubeSats via the Visible Light (VL-Band) full duplex links. The CubeSats once deployed and in orbit will communicate and relay payload and engineering data via their VL-band inter-satellite links to the SmallSat for onward relay to earth. The communication system shall employ the use of Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) for the transmitter optical frontEnd. Stringent quality of services requirements necessitate a robust relay communication system design that will exhibit single fault tolerance; hence the ISC system RF (X-band) full-duplex communication link system will fulfill the role of an ancillary communication system reserved as a back-up system in the case of a fault or failure of the primary VL-ISL.

text: 5. 6.1 System Context and Boundary Definition The system context establishes the framework within which the system-of-interest will operate. The objective of the system context definition process is meant to focus attention on external factors that need to considered when developing the system requirements. It portrays all external entities that will interact with the system thereby helping to describe the black box functional view and define the system boundary. Defining the system boundary helps identify what is external and internal to the system-of-interest and is used as a communication tool early in the system conceptual design to get an agreement on the scope of the system requirements. The system context model is one of the most crucial parts of the system model as it captures the system's relationship with its environment while also capturing its interfaces with external systems. A simplified view of the system context modeled using a use case diagram is shown in Figure 46 [133].

text: 5. 6.2 Identify External Interfaces Identifying and defining all external interfaces during the concept definition phase aids in risk assessment and eliminates the need for costly system modifications due to bad interface assumptions. A system is especially vulnerable at its interfaces, therefore it is extremely critical to identify external interfaces with other systems early to reduce system development cost. Identifying these external interfaces early equate to identifying key drivers for the system that must be addressed in the requirements model. text: 5. 6.3 Use Case Operational Scenarios Defined stakeholder use cases are developed using behavioral diagrams to produce high-level system scenarios. In [14], operational scenarios are described as a set of dynamic exchanges between functions that allow the system to achieve a mission or service. Operational scenarios are pivotal to operational concept development as they enable visualization and promote understanding of how the system is supposed to react under various nominal, alt-nominal and off-nominal usage. The sequence diagram is used to highlight operational scenarios; these scenarios provide the basis for generating comprehensive system requirements. Key system features can be omitted during system design if this phase of OpsCon development is not adequately captured in the system concept model. During operational scenario development, scenarios are broadly classified into two (2) groups: Nominal ("Sunny Day") scenarios and Off-Nominal ("Rainy Day") scenarios. A collection of nominal and non-nominal scenarios provides a more complete description of a system and is, therefore, more useful in analysis

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 6.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 6 1 introduction
text: The ability to accurately define and capture requirements for a complex system is arguably the most important factor in determining the success or failure of the finished system. This assertion is made based on the direct impact a well articulated and structured requirements specification has on the quality of the finished product and every phase of the system's life-cycle. System requirements are used to specify particular conditions or capabilities that must be satisfied by the developed system; they are also used to specify essential performance conditions which the system must achieve. According to [11], system requirements are all of the requirements at the system level that describe the functions which the system should fulfill to satisfy stakeholder needs and requirements. They constitute a collection of needs expressed by stakeholders stating specific constraints under which the system must operate [118]. Requirements engineering constitutes the branch of system engineering that bridges the gap between the informal world of stakeholder needs and the formal world of system behavior [129].

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 6.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 6 1 introduction
text: Requirements specification is the product of the requirements engineering phase. The system requirements specification is the by-product of this phase and plays a critical role in the overall systems engineering process; the specification forms the basis for system architecture design activities, and system integration and verification activities. They represent the reference point for validation and stakeholder acceptance and provide a means of communication between members of the design and development team [11].

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 6.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 6 1 introduction
text: Current practices in requirements engineering involve the capture and documentation of requirements largely in textual format. This method of requirement specification documentation is fraught with numerous challenges such as inconsistencies and difficulty in maintaining synchronization between stakeholder requirements and system level requirements. Configuration

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 6.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 6 1 introduction
text: management becomes a herculean task in the face of multiple versions of textual specifications. This limitation often result in inefficiencies and quality issues that only become apparent during the integration and testing phase [33]. The limitations encountered with text-only requirement specification documentation can be addressed by utilizing a model-based approach to requirements engineering. Model-based requirements engineering entails the development of a requirements model that captures the requirements on all levels of the requirement hierarchy and the relationships that exist between them [51]. The model becomes the "single source of truth" and forms the basis of all generated requirement artifacts. The requirements model is stored in a central repository alongside the models relating to other phases of the system design life-cycle.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 6.1 Introduction

Section 6.1 outlines the characteristics of good requirements and the sentence structures required for capturing good textual requirements. The concept of model-based requirements engineering is addressed in section 6.2, and this concept forms the basis for the ISC requirements engineering analysis which is described in Section 6.3. The chapter is summarized in Section 6.4.

text: The term Requirements Engineering (RE) is used to describe the set of activities that translate stakeholder needs into engineered requirements. Requirements engineering is defined in [37] as the "subset of systems engineering concerned with discovering, developing, tracing, analyzing, qualifying, communicating and managing the requirements that define the system at successive levels of abstraction." RE plays a crucial role in every phase of the system development life-cycle.

Key RE activities include requirements elicitation, requirement analysis, requirement specification, requirement verification, validation and

text: 6. 2.1 Requirements Requirements capture the desired capability of a system. The International Council of Systems Engineering (INCOSE) defines a requirement as "A statement that identifies a system, product or process, operational or functional, or design characteristic or constraint, which is unambiguous, clear, unique, consistent, stand-alone and verifiable, and is deemed necessary for stakeholder acceptability [32]." Systems are designed and built to meet the requirements of stakeholders; consequently, as stated in [63], requirements are a property of a system that is either needed or wanted by a stakeholder. Requirements can be classified based on the "Type" or Level of "Abstraction" [111]. Classification according to Type

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 6.2 Requirements Engineering
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 6 2 requirements engineering
text: of Requirement refers to the nature of the requirement i.e business requirements, functional requirements, non-functional requirements (performance, interface, operational, usability etc.); classifying requirements according to Levels of Abstraction refers to defining requirements based on the specific levels to which they belong within the requirement definition process. Examples of defining requirements based on levels of abstraction include stakeholder, system, subsystem and component level requirements.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 6.2 Requirements Engineering

text: 6. 2.2 Characteristics of Good Requirements The importance of developing a good requirement specification cannot be over-emphasized, primarily because requirements form the basis for the development of any given project or system. A system is constructed so that the requirements can be met. Poorly captured requirements make it impossible to satisfy the need of the stakeholders. Well-articulated requirements enable the management of risks from the earliest possible point in development [37]. Requirements can be classified as either good (well written) or bad (poorly written) requirements. Characteristics of good requirements based on [74], [107] and [28] [36] include:

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 6.2 Requirements Engineering

text: a) Necessary: The system to be built should be incapable of functioning in the desired way without the specific requirement. A requirement is not necessary if it can not be traced back to a high-level requirement or need.

text: d) Complete: The stated requirement must be descriptive enough to stand alone.

text: e) Singular: The requirement statement must include only one requirement statement, be concise and clear.

text: f) Verifiable: A stated requirement is verifiable if it states something that can be verified by examination, test, analysis or demonstration.

text: g) Attainable: The stated requirement must be achievable and must be technically feasible within cost, schedule, legal, and safety constraints.

text: Two rules are defined by INCOSE to guide the construction of requirement statement structures. The first states that "the statements must be a single sentence, implying that each requirement should express a single thought in a simple manner." The second rule states that "each requirement statement should be as short as possible." Defined in [107] are three simple sentence structure types used in defining the structure of requirement statements.

text: The Systems Modeling Language (SysML) is a general-purpose graphical modeling language designed for engineering applications. Textual requirements can be captured in SysML using requirement tables, matrices and diagrams. As a modeling language, SysML provides graphical representations for the effective modeling of a system's requirements and offers the benefit of verification and validation of the system by allowing system model elements be traced to system requirements [9]. A behavioral model which represents the captured requirements can then be verified through model execution and formal analysis [40].

text: 6. 3.1 Requirements Table In SysML, requirements and their relationships can be represented using requirements tables. This form of representation outlines the various requirements of a system, its relationships and properties in a tabular format. A standard requirements table includes properties to specify the Requirements Unique Identifier which holds a property used to identify a particular requirement, the Requirements Name and Requirements Text which holds the detailed requirements text in separate columns. Depicted in Table 21 is an example of a standard SysML requirements table representation used in detailing the various system requirements, their attributes and relationships.

text: The ISC stakeholder requirements result in one or more corresponding system-level requirements. These requirements are captured at a finer level of granularity as decomposition is performed capturing more detailed interfaces, functions and performance expectations of the VLX communication system. The captured system-level requirements represent atomic, unambiguous feasible, understandable, verifiable and correctly derived statements of the VLX

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 6.4 ISC Requirements Engineering
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 6 4 isc requirements engineering
text: communication system properties. The identified stakeholder use cases are utilized as the organizational schema for the stakeholder requirements and all subsequent lower-level derived requirements. All requirement analysis activities are performed based on the characterized use cases of the proposed communication system. The main focus of the ISC requirements engineering phase is on the functional, performance and interface requirements of the communication system. These requirements do not capture the internal structure or technology of the system but are rather captured as "black box" requirements. The various requirement views used in portraying the requirements were developed in [7] and conform to the architectural framework for defining ISC system architectures. The views conforming to the architectural framework viewpoints include the: Requirement Description View, Requirement Context View and Requirement Traceability View.

text: 6. 4.1 General Requirements Analysis The stakeholder general requirements refer to requirements that are not captured under any specific use case but are necessary for the proper functioning of the system. The stakeholder general requirements portrayed in Figure 66 refer to requirements concerned with the overall system and are needed for the system to operate as required. The captured general requirements are statements of expected system property or usage and they focus on the general features required by the stakeholders and specify the capabilities the system must satisfy and key performance conditions which they expect the system to achieve. The system-level general requirements are derived from these requirements.

text: 6. 4.3 Perform Ranging Service Use Case Requirements Analysis The Requirement Context View depicting the refinement of stakeholder requirements the perform ranging use case is portrayed in Figure 72. Depicting requirements in this form aids in identifying and giving insight into the interactions between requirements and stakeholder use cases and the consequences of these interactions. The stakeholder ranging requirements indicate the need for the communication system to perform ranging services on its inter-satellite links. The ability of the VLX communication system to achieve this capability is vital to the implementation of inter-satellite communication between small satellite systems (SmSS). text: 6. 4.5 ISC Requirements Glossary Developing a requirements glossary for terms specific to the domain-of-interest is an essential and critical activity during the requirements engineering phase of system development. The ISC Requirements Glossary serves to provide definitions of terms used in the requirements specification document for the Data Relay, Ranging and Timing Service system use cases. A properly prepared requirements glossary ensures that all stakeholders, systems engineers and system designers understand what is meant by the terminology, acronyms, and phrases that are present in the requirements specifications. Using the same words consistently when writing requirements helps reduce ambiguity and facilitates a clear understanding of the meaning and import of each requirement statement. The ISC Requirement Glossary portrayed in Table. 26 is a living document that is constantly being updated with new words, phrases and acronyms defined in the requirements specifications. This continuous process endeavors to reduce ambiguity with regards to each requirement statement.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 1 introduction
text: In this chapter, we develop the high-level ISC system architecture. We describe the application of MBSE principles to the creation of artifacts that describe the system-of-interest from an architectural perspective. It describes and outlines the high-level system architectural model developed for the communication-oriented layers of a satellite communication system based on the Open System Interconnection (OSI) reference model. The system model captures the behavior, structure and parametric at a high level of abstraction. It forms the basis for the subsequent step of detailed design modeling. The conceptual design model, system requirements specification and the architectural framework to which the system architecture conforms lay the ground work for the developed ISC model.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 1 introduction
text: A system architectural model represents an abstract, conceptualization-oriented and global view of the proposed system [12]. The development of a systems architecture involves defining key aspects of the proposed system; the developed architectural model provides an effective way to understand, manage and overcome the challenges which system complexity introduces to the system design process. The architecture of a system can be represented in many ways through the use of models and modeling languages [97].

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 1 introduction
text: When using a model-based approach, the modeling language is used to define the requirements architecture, system design and system architecture based on a referenced methodology. Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) provides a structured approach for the development of system models; Its current focus is on the use of architecture models (functional architecture and physical architecture) as a basis for the development of physical system models and operational system models.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.1 Introduction
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 1 introduction
text: 7. 1.1 Overview The rest of the chapter is organized as follows. In Section 7.1, we present the intermediate communication system structure based on the OSI reference model and present the abstraction levels for the ISC model. In Section 7.2, the high-level ISC domain architecture is presented; Executable models are developed to analyze the high-level system behavior and consequent high-level architecture design. For the next layer of system abstraction that exposes finer granularity of the system, we present in Section 7.3 the black box model for the communication system subsystems. We summarize this chapter in Section 7.4.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.2 Small Satellite Systems
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 2 small satellite systems
text: Formation-flying missions are typically more cost effective in the long term due to the economies of scale enabled by large production runs of small satellites, the adaptability of the system and the ability to reduce launch costs through use of smaller secondary launch opportunities [139]. Developing ISC capabilities between CubeSats and SmallSats will enable more complex space mission be accomplished at a fraction of the cost of deploying large monolithic satellites for similar space missions. ISC provides support for high data transmission and data-rate capacity, real-time data delivery and interoperability among satellites within a given network [101].

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.2 Small Satellite Systems
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 2 small satellite systems
text: The need for Inter-Satellite Communication (ISC) between Small Satellite Systems (SmSS) necessitates the need for the development of a satellite communication system architecture with ISC capability. However, limiting constraints imposed on their form factor, power and mass requirements limit their applicability for most advanced missions. ISC between SmSS operating in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) will enable autonomous transfer of data between satellites thereby eliminating the need for extensive ground-based relay system. CubeSats capability to engage in formation flying activities is limited by the capabilities of the on-board communication subsystem. Depicted in Figure 78 is the architectural layout for small-satellite systems showing its various subsystem and payload types. The classification of the communication links of the subsystem fall into two categories: 1) satellite-to-ground links and 2) Inter-satellite links.

text: 7. 2.1 OSI Framework for ISC Inter-Satellite Communication for Small-Satellite Systems (SmSS) is based on the network and protocol layering concepts of the OSI reference model [123]. The Open System Interconnection (OSI) reference model [2] defines a layered approach for data communication between communication systems; It implements protocols (i.e a set of rules that govern data communication) used in the exchange of data between communication systems in a network. The OSI model modular approach permits the communication process to be decomposed into a more tractable process which can be handled in a flexible and scalable manner. In [101], an extensive survey on ISC for SmSS based on the OSI model framework was discussed. Satellites which implement ISC can be characterized as either an End System or an Intermediate System [46] based on their specific roles in the communication process.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.2 Small Satellite Systems
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 2 small satellite systems
text: 7. 2.1.1 End systems: End systems are communication systems involved in the end-to-end (source-to-destination) data communication exchange. These communication systems specifically implement protocols on all seven layers of the OSI model as shown in Figure 79. Data to be transmitted usually originates from an end system and they are the final recipients of transmitted data.

text: 7. 2.1.2 Intermediate Systems: Intermediate systems are communication systems that utilize only a subset of the OSI model layers (protocol stack) in executing their communication services. The communication systems implement the subset of the protocol stack corresponding to the communication-oriented layers of the OSI model.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.2 Small Satellite Systems

text: The Physical, Data-link and Network layers constitute the communication-oriented layers of the OSI model as shown in Figure 80; these layers are also known as the network support layers. They are responsible for ensuring the smooth transition of error-free data from a source satellite to a destination satellite or ground station. This research work is focused on communication within these three layers.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.2 Small Satellite Systems
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 2 small satellite systems
text: In [26] modeling on higher levels of abstraction is seen to offer the advantage of providing greater support for high complexity system designs. The ISC system for small satellites is regarded as a complex system based on the required functionality of providing reliable space-based communication between satellites which it has to implement. A correct and consistent system model for ISC is modeled at varying levels of abstraction by applying an MBSE approach. This approach aids in harnessing complexity by initially hiding details that are not relevant during the high-level design and elaborating them as we progress to finer levels of system granularity. In dealing with complexity, the ISC system is modeled at varying levels of decomposition where each level corresponds to a valid viewpoint of the overall system as shown in Figure 81. The high-level ISC system is decomposed into individual communication system (subsystems). The communication subsystem can be considered as a system itself and further decomposed into subsystems (OSI layers) which are the main building blocks of the communication system.

text: 7. 3.1.2 Transmit & Receive Use Case Functional Flow The black box activity diagram shown in Figure 83 describes the transmit & receive use case functional flow. The high-level activity diagram aims to identify the various flows of behavior of the system; It depicts the functions the ISC system performs as it executes the system use cases by capturing the functional flow information. text: The system behavior captured in the use case activity diagram begins with the initialize dataflow function by the actor (comm.sw) on the receipt of a data input parameter. The fork node duplicates the control flow coming from the initialize dataflow action unto two parallel flows in which the LoS Check action is performed in one flow and a detect incoming signal action in the parallel flow. On completion of these actions, a decision node is reached in each case. The presence of a direct LoS configuration will cause the guard condition $ [LoS=true] $ to execute. Control flows to another fork node from which the two system functions select channel and process data are performed simultaneously. On completion of both actions a send signal action - "data signal" portrays the transmission of the data signal. In the case of the second parallel flow, if the guard condition [successful] is true a ready to receive action is performed after which the system begins receiving the incoming data signal. The receipt of the data signal by the receiving satellite is depicted on the activity diagram by the accept signal event - "receiving data signal"; the signal

text: 7. 3.1.4 Transmit & Receive Use Case State Machine The System Communication View shown in Figure 86 defines the high-level state-based behavior of the ISC system and its system elements. This view is realized using a state machine diagram. The state machine shows the ISC system states and the events that trigger transitions from one state to another. A state describes

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.3 ISC High-Level System Model
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 3 isc high level system model
text: the happenings in a system at any given time. The ISC system state machine consists of a composite state. The communicating state is a concurrent composite state as can be seen from the figure. A composite state allows states to be modeled that have internal behavior that can be further decomposed into states themselves [62]. The communicating composite state has an entry behavior - "dataflow" which triggers the transmitting and receiving states concurrently implying each CubeSat or SmallSat is capable of full-duplex communication. The transmitting and receiving states transition to the standby state when the event transmit/receive complete are triggered. When an event instance is dispatched, the state machine responds by performing actions [110]. The transmitting and receiving states once initialized enter into the standby state. The transition triggered by the event data_available has a guard link established = yes. This means that the transition can only fire if the guard link established evaluates to true.

text: 7. 3.2.1 ISC High-Level Architecture (BDD) The System Connectivity View shown in Figure 87 is used to capture the high-level ISC structure. This view is realized using a bdd. The bdd portrays the systems structure and its relationship with the main system elements. Stereotyped blocks which represent design-time specification of the system [40] are used to represent both the ISC system and the system elements. The ISC system is seen to be composed of three VLX communication systems. The composition relationship existing between the ISC system and the VLX communication system indicates that the VLX communication system has a single composite owner which is the ISC system. A composite relationship also exists between the ISC system and the ISC link illustrating that all ISLs are owned at a high-level by the inter-satellite communication system. Also modeled is an aggregation relationship between the ISC system and the Data system element. This relationship signifies that the communication system shares part ownership of the Data with other satellite subsystems such as the Command & Data Handler (C&DH) Subsystem which processes and stores the data. The Data model element is seen to be composed of the command data, engineering or housekeeping data and payload data. Video, image, voice or text data-types which are all a subtype of the more general payload data class.

At this level of system decomposition, the internal parts of the system up to the subsystem level are exposed and the interactions between these subsystems can be mapped to the subsystems that perform them. text: 7. 4.1.4 VLX System State-Based Analysis The System Communication View depicted in Figure 94, Figure 95 and Figure 96 represent executable state machines built for the transmitData behavior of the communication subsystems. The state machines captured represent the network layer, Data-link layer and physical layer subsystems of the VLX Communication system. They capture the states of each subsystem and are strongly connected to the system interface and sequence diagrams.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.4 Communication Subsystem Model
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 4 communication subsystem model
text: The NL Encapsulation state machine consists of five states: sensing, routing, addressing, forwarding and standby. The state machine shown in Figure 94 depicts the various states the

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.4 Communication Subsystem Model
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 4 communication subsystem model
text: communication system transitions through as it executes the NL Encapsulation behavior. The state machine begins by executing the do activity of the sensing state. The receipt of the segment_available signal causes the state machine to transition from the sensing state to the routing state; while in the routing state, the system appends the necessary routing information to the received segment. Transition of the state machine to the addressing state occurs once the routing info has been successfully appended. From the addressing state the system transitions through the remaining states in the state machine. Once the packet has been forwarded, the state machine transitions to the standby state.

text: The DL Encapsulation state machine consists of eight states: sensing, multiplexing, time_stamping, encoding, randomizing, synchronizing, forwarding and standby. The state machine shown in Figure 95 depicts the various states the communication system transitions through as it executes the DL Encapsulation behavior. On receipt of the packet from the network layer, the system transitions to the multiplexing state from the sensing state; it then proceeds to perform the do activity - "DL_timeStamping" once it transitions to the time stamping state. The completion

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.4 Communication Subsystem Model
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 4 communication subsystem model
text: of the do activity generates the time stamped signal which causes the state machine to transition to the encoding state. From the encoding state the system transitions through the randomizing, synchronizing and forwarding states as it executes the system function of - "transmitData". Once the packet has been encapsulated, the resulting frame is forwarded to the physical layer and the state machine transitions to the standby state.

text: The PL Encapsulation state machine consists of six states: sensing, encoding, modulating, pulse shaping, forwarding and standby. The state machine shown in Figure 96 depicts the various states the communication system transitions through as it executes the PL Encapsulation behavior. On receipt of the frame from the data link layer, the system transitions to the encoding state were the subsystem proceeds to perform the do activity - encoding. The completion of the do activity generates the encoded_frame signal which causes the state machine to transition to the modulating state. From the modulating state the system transitions through the remaining states in the state machine. Once the signal has been transmitted, the state machine goes into the standby state.

text: 7. 4.2.4 VLX Communication Parametric Diagram The VLX system parametric diagram shown in Figure 100 portrays the mathematical relationships that represent certain performance constraints imposed on the system. The constraint properties of the VLX system are specified in the constraints compartment of the VLX communication system Block and these constraint properties are typed by constraint blocks. The constraint blocks depicted in the diagram are used to constrain the properties of the VLX communication system block. Some system level constraints properties defined at this stage of system design include the TID constraint property which is typed by the Total Ionizing Dose constraint block; this constraint precisely defines and constrains the Total Ionizing Dose (TID) levels to which the VLX communication system must be designed to withstand. The Life Time constraint property typed by the Design Lifetime constraint block constrains the life time of the communication system to be developed. This performance constrain implies that the VLX system must be capable of working without faults for a minimum of three (3) years.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 7.5 Chapter Summary
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 7 5 chapter summary
text: The work presented in this paper outlines the high-level architectural model for a small satellite communication system to be utilized for ISC. Employing MBSE principles and approach to the design, provides a systematic way of dealing with system complexity while ensuring consistency, precision and traceability of the system design. MBSE also provides a means of verifying and validating the developed system model. The modeled communication system architecture corresponds to the three lower layers of the OSI reference model. The system design artifacts which make up the system model were derived from the use case functional analysis and architecture design phases. The modeled views conform to the prescribed views outlined for an ISC system model based on an ISC architectural framework. The systems modeling language (SysML) was used as the modeling language to aid in the design process.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 8.1 Conclusion
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 8 1 conclusion
text: This dissertation presents an MBSE high-level system architecture model for an inter-satellite communication system for a constellation of small satellite systems. The goal of this work is to develop a system architecture model for a hybrid visible-light and RF (VLX) communication system that will form the basis for the detailed design model as well as physical system models and operating models.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 8.1 Conclusion
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 8 1 conclusion
text: An architectural framework for inter-satellite communication (ISC) between small satellites constitutes the first contribution of this research work. The framework addressed the need for a model-based SE architectural framework that can be used as a basis for ISC system architecture design which we have not found in literature. This framework specifies the way and manner in which the fundamental organization of an ISC system architecture can be presented. The framework will be applied to develop the proposed system architecture model for a VLC system for ISC.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 8.1 Conclusion
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 8 1 conclusion
text: The proposed domain-specific SysML profile which will be employed to support the VLC system modeling activities establishes the second contribution of this research work. The profile enables the modeling of common system concepts specific to VLC which is the domain of interest. Applying the profile for the development of a system model will allow for greater consistency between VLC domain information and the system design information. This profile facilitates the capture of design information with a higher degree of precision.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 8.1 Conclusion
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 8 1 conclusion
text: The final contribution of this dissertation is the development of the high-level architectural model for an inter-satellite communication system that will utilize visible-light and radio frequency (X-Band) communication. This contribution is presented in Chapters 5-7. In Chapter 5, the development of a model-based Concept of Operations model for the proposed system is presented. The model-based ConOps serves as the starting point of the system requirement analysis and system

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 8.1 Conclusion
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 8 1 conclusion
text: design phases. Capturing system concepts in a model-based way makes it possible to have a central model with systems engineering artifacts from the various design life-cycle phases. The created conceptual model is representative of the most abstract description of how the (mission) tasks will be conducted when the system is available. In Chapter 6, we presented the requirements engineering phase activities and outcomes of the system design life-cycle based on the operational concept activities performed in Chapter 5. The requirements engineering model is located in the central model repository alongside other system design artifacts. The captured ISC requirements specification consists of unambiguous, consistent, attainable and verifiable system requirements that form the foundation for the high-level architecture design. The proposed high-level system architecture model was presented in Chapter 7. The system-level model corresponds to and is representative of the lower three layers of the OSI reference model framework. The high-level architecture model features a modular design, allowing for the separation of concerns, and utilizing the benefits of abstraction modeling. This high-level communication system model captures the desired system architecture for the proposed VLX communication system and provides the basis for predictable systems engineering by providing a view of system-wide impacts of the given architectural choice.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 8.1 Conclusion
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 8 1 conclusion
text: The system model which is verified via model execution fosters confidence in the correctness of the model and the system architecture which it represents. It aids in managing system complexity and risk, and allows for the visualization of the entire communication system at a high-level. A key benefit of the ISC system architecture model is the resulting consistent and coherent views that exist across the whole system architecture and the inherent traceability between all system artifacts across the system design life-cycle.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 8.2 Future Work
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 8 2 future work
text: This research presented the development of a High-level system architecture model for ISC between small satellites in the context of model-based systems engineering. Emanating from the groundwork laid in this research are several areas of possible extension and future direction in the context of architecting small satellite systems based on MBSE principles.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 8.2 Future Work
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 8 2 future work
text: 8. 2.1 Develop the Subsystem Architecture An important area for future work extension is the development of the ISC subsystem-level architecture. Modeling the Physical, Data-link, and Network Layer Subsystem architectures will provide system designers with a comprehensive system architecture model that can be employed directly in developing a prototype for the ISC system. The physical layer subsystem model will enable us capture the physical architecture of the ISC system which entails the hardware components and the corresponding connections between them. Furthermore, modeling the physical layer will involve developing a parametric model that can be used to constrain the system. Adding constraints to the system model will ensure that the system design cannot be altered during the design or development process.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 8.2 Future Work
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 8 2 future work
text: 8. 2.2 Application to other Small Satellite Subsystems The concept of operations model developed for the small satellite communication system can be extended to capture the necessary information for the development of all onboard subsystems of the SmallSat and CubeSats. Operational concept models detailing the operational scenarios as each subsystem performs their various operations should be addressed. Further work should investigate extending the framework for all subsystems of the satellite as specified in the SmSS taxonomy depicted in Chapter 7, Figure. 78. This Framework will enable the development of the architectures of the various subsystems.

section: CHAPTER 7. High-Level ISC Architecture Design 140 > 8.2 Future Work
section_key: chapter 7 high level isc architecture design 140 / 8 2 future work
text: 8. 2.3 Application to Architecting System of Systems Models The architectural framework and domain-specific profile developed for the communication system can be extended and developed into a generic model-based architectural framework for the description of architectures established within the system of systems (SoS) domain. The resulting framework can be tailored to specific SoS for which a domain-specific profile can also be developed. This concept will facilitate quick design and development of system models. Furthermore, the step-by-step process of developing a model-based concept of operations, operational concept, requirement specification and high-level architecture can be applied as a generic step-by-step process for the development of SoS model-based system architecture models.

Rebekah A. Austin, Vanderbilt University
Nagabhushan Mahadevan, Vanderbilt University
Arthur F. Witulski, PhD, Vanderbilt University
John Evans, PhD, NASA
Key Words: COTS, CubeSat, Goal Structuring Notation, Radiation Hardness Assurance, Fault Models, Bayesian Networks

Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) electronics are used in satellites that span the size, cost, and acceptable risk spectrum. At one extreme the CubeSat, a platform originally created for university-based spacecraft design, is often constructed only from COTS electronics. At the other extreme, even highbudget NASA spacecraft use COTS electronics in non-mission critical circuits, especially when no radiation-hardened alternatives exist or the radiation-hardened parts do not meet the system requirements. There is significant uncertainty in the radiation test results of COTS electronics; hence additional means of assessing risk and radiation hardness are needed. In this work we construct a fault-propagation model of a CubeSat payload in a SysML platform, and then develop a Bayesian network from the fault model of the system. The sensitivity of the system to variations in component radiation response can be evaluated quantitatively, within the limits of the assumptions and available data. This sensitivity study then informs the structure and content of the overall radiation-reliability assurance case.

Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) electronic parts are being used in satellites because radiation hardened components may not meet mission performance requirements and may not be at the state-of-the-art [1]. Inclusion of COTS parts in a satellite requires careful consideration of how the part will respond to the space radiation environment. One common method for evaluation of the radiation-reliability of parts is lot testing. For COTS parts, it is often difficult or impossible to secure parts from a single "lot." Manufacturers may not make available information about the wafer lot and packaging facility. Thus, parts with the same part number could come from multiple wafers and parts from the same wafer could be packaged at multiple assembly sites. If "lot" testing is not possible, a larger amount of variability must be assumed for part radiation test results. This paper describes a model-based approach for how a system can be evaluated for sensitivity to the part radiation response variability, without
using conventional lot testing or relying on radiation-hardened components.

Figure 1- Model-Based Assurance Case + (MBAC+) process diagram. The modeling languages in the circles connect the engineering disciplines in the rectangles and enable an integrated modeling approach to radiation hardness assurance.

An existing CubeSat science payload was selected as an example for this study. The payload was designed to record the number of radiation-induced single event upsets (SEUs), a bit flip in the memory, in a commercial 28nm static random access memory (SRAM) in low-Earth orbit for 1 year. In order to accomplish the mission objective, the surrounding electronics must tolerate the space radiation environment for the duration of the mission. The approach described in the paper involves 1) creating a System Modeling Language (SysML) model of the CubeSat payload, 2) adding radiation-induced fault-propagation models accounting for impact on expected functionality, and 3) constructing a Bayesian

network model from the fault model that evaluates the system performance ("correctness" and "availability" of SRAM) based on probabilistic dependency between the radiation environment, component health and functionality. Finally, the insights and results from the Bayesian analysis are then incorporated into a Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) assurance case. The assurance case for the radiation-tolerance of the payload was developed according to the NASA Reliability and Maintainability (R&M) Standard [2]. A software tool based on the Web-based Generic Modeling Environment (WebGME) [3] serves as the modeling framework for the SysML functional requirement model, the system architecture model, the fault propagation model, and the GSN model.

section: 2 INTEGRATED APPROACH TO SYSTEM SENSITIVITY OF RADIATION-INDUCED FAULTS
section_key: 2 integrated approach to system sensitivity of radiation induced faults
text: NASA is creating a Model-Based Mission Assurance (MBMA) paradigm to incorporate reliability into the Model-Base System Engineering (MBSE) paradigm. This work uses the Model-Based Assurance Case + (MBAC+) process and the System Engineering and Assurance Models (SEAM) tool set to support the modeling activities of requirements, design, and reliability engineering [4]. In Figure 1, the integrated approach is presented. Goals derived from mission objectives and environment and how they are met in the system design are captured in System Modeling Language (SysML) functional decomposition and block diagram models. The graphical argument that the goals lead to a reliable system is done using the Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) standard. While the SysML and GSN models are linked in the SEAM tool set, the underlying fault propagation model is used to construct the Bayesian network model. The Bayesian network model is then used to study the sensitivity of the design to radiation which supports the evidence for the goals that argue for the radiation reliability of the system. These three modeling standards and the process of creating and linking them form the MBAC+ process.

The SysML model of the CubeSat payload is constructed from the SysML models of the individual parts. The parts are connected together to describe the energy and signal flow throughout the system, as well as the propagation of faults. Figure 2 shows a simplified system model of the CubeSat

experiment board that includes just power bus, load switch, linear regulator, microcontroller, and the SRAM. The power ports and their associated connections are in black, while the signal ports and their associated connections are in green.

text: The internals of the component models include fault models that capture the component faults induced by radiation effects such as total-ionizing dose (TID), single-event latch-up (SEL), and single-event transients (SET), which are described in [5], and the propagation of the fault effects both within the component and across the system. The model describes root cause of the fault (failure modes such as TID, SEL, SET), the resulting effects such as anomalies, functionality degradation, and any mitigation response to anomalies. The model also describes the fault-effects propagating into and out of the component using labeled edges connected to the ports.

section: 2.3 Construction of Bayesian Net from System Fault Model
section_key: 2 3 construction of bayesian net from system fault model
text: The nodes and edges in the Bayesian network structure are identified by traversing all the fault paths in the system model. The nodes include faults, functional effects, mitigation functions, and observable anomalous conditions captured in the system fault model. Edges are added between the nodes if a fault path or functional dependency is identified. The structure is refined by grouping the radiation-induced failure modes as environment nodes. Also, wherever possible, anomalies, degradation, and mitigation responses are abstracted into component nodes whose states correspond to the health of the component or functionality of the component. The graph is further simplified based on expert knowledge. Figure 5 shows the refined Bayesian net for the load switch SRAM system for the best and worst case environments.

section: 2.3 Construction of Bayesian Net from System Fault Model
section_key: 2 3 construction of bayesian net from system fault model
text: Top-level nodes are introduced to capture the mission operation time as well as the mission environment. These nodes influence the nodes related to radiation effects (TID, SEL). The states of these nodes represent the probability of the presence of a fault (SEL) or the strength of the radiation effect (TID). Because TID is an effects that builds up over time while SEL is a random, temporary effect, that is affected by the location of the experiment in its orbit, this network shows the sensitivity of the system at a particular time and place in the system's life cycle.

section: 2.3 Construction of Bayesian Net from System Fault Model
section_key: 2 3 construction of bayesian net from system fault model
text: The nodes bearing the component names, LoadSwitch, Microcontroller, LinearRegulator, and SRAM, reflect the health and performance of these components. The states in these nodes correspond to the correct or incorrect operation of the component. In the case of the SRAM, the "correct operation" and "incorrect operation" states represents whether the SRAM experiment correctly captured the SEU that occurred during a five minute experiment. The "unavailable" state represents the cases when SRAM is not available for operation either because of system reset related to mitigation or malfunctioning of other components.

section: 2.4 Revision of GSN Assurance Case from Bayesian Analysis
section_key: 2 4 revision of gsn assurance case from bayesian analysis
text: The Bayesian model evaluates the impact of the radiation environment on the performance (availability and correctness) of the CubeSat payload. It assesses the performance degradation of individual components in the context of radiation environment as well as impact of degradation of other components. For instance, the node related to LoadSwitch performance takes into account radiation effects as well as faults on control lines from the microcontroller. Likewise, the performance of the linear regulator to supply correct input voltage to the SRAM is affected by radiation faults internal and externally on the control lines from the microcontroller. Finally, the SRAM correctness and availability for the mission experiment depends on the radiation level and performance of microcontroller and the linear regulator.

section: 2.4 Revision of GSN Assurance Case from Bayesian Analysis
section_key: 2 4 revision of gsn assurance case from bayesian analysis
text: The conditional probability tables for each node in the Bayesian network model take into account the impact of radiation as well as the impact of "degraded" performance of related components in the system. The Bayesian network sensitivity analysis helps reveal the relative strength of parameters in the conditional probability table to influence the target nodes like the system operation or performance of a specific component. This could be useful in performing more directed testing and design changes to improve the overall system performance.

The integrated approach presented in this paper creates a system level radiation-induced fault model from the fault model of individual parts, taking into account functionality degradation and mitigation measures. The fault model helps create the structure of both the GSN assurance case model and

the Bayesian network model by identifying the possible fault paths and related effects on functionality. The results from the Bayesian network analysis are useful in understanding the sensitivity of system performance to radiation effects in specific parts, thereby providing additional information to prioritize parts testing, adjust radiation margins, and update the design to add radiation-effects mitigation.

This approach does require a significant modeling effort upfront to create the libraries necessary for this analysis, but subsequent designs should see this modeling effort decrease. The results of the sensitivity analysis are only as good as the data used to create the distributions. This process is still being researched, including how to map test results to discrete Bayesian nets.

The presented modeling approach shows how the radiation reliability of the individual parts can be evaluated at a system-level and how to quantify the reliability of the system based on the system design, not just the reliability of the individual parts. This approach also allows us to see the system sensitivity to uncertainty in our radiation characterization tests and thus helping to determine which part populations should be better understood to increase the reliability of our system.
