This paper presents the development of a general automated process using multibody dynamics software (RecurDyn), to efficiently take a detailed hinge assembly model and simulate its range of motion while retrieving stiffness information for all degrees of freedom and use that data to define a simple but accurate, nonlinear point-to-point force for use in a solar array assembly model. A vertical software application is presented that characterizes and simplifies the hinge model and allows the simplified model to be integrated easily into a solar array system model. The flexible hinges connect nonlinear flexible body representations of the solar panels in an array. The example application is the simulation of CubeSat structures, which are typically large compared to the spacecraft body. The utility of the vertical application is demonstrated through the successful simulation of the e-Hawk solar array (MMA Design). The described techniques and vertical application can also be applied to a wide range of deployable space structures.

Modeling the nonlinear dynamics of spacecraft structures during and post deployment is critical for mitigating risk during spacecraft development. Reducing the difficulty and time required to develop simulations for characterizing the dynamics of deployable structures is beneficial to spacecraft developers. This is especially true for the developers of smaller spacecraft such as small sats, cubesats, and microsats because as deployable structures, primarily the solar arrays, are relatively large compared to the size of the spacecraft body. This paper presents the development of a general automated process using multibody dynamics software (RecurDyn), to efficiently take a detailed hinge assembly model and simulate its range of motion while retrieving stiffness information for all degrees of freedom and use that data to define a simple but accurate, nonlinear point-to-point force for use in the solar array assembly model. Included in the paper will be data from the simulation of the e-Hawk solar array (MMA Design). The e-Hawk deployable CubeSat solar array is a high performance power harvesting system designed for use on 6U and larger platforms. Simulations for a deployed cubesat solar array model, based on the e-Hawk, were used to determine the maximum tumbling rates that can be tolerated before the solar array becomes unstable, meaning the hinge forces can't keep components in contact with bump stops. Simulating the nonlinear dynamics of the e-Hawk, a commercially available deployable solar array, demonstrates the utility and benefits that can be achieved from the automated modeling process described in subsequent sections of this paper.

There is high value in time, money and most importantly safety and reliability in simulating the nonlinear dynamics of stowing, deploying, and performance of deployable space structures, especially given the profound limitations of physical testing. Dynamic simulation mitigates the risk of developing new deployable space structures, including solar arrays, by predicting transient motions and loads during stowage, deployment, and mission-related maneuvers [1,2]. Dynamic simulation can also be used to assess the efficacy of using motion control to lessen the effect of accelerations on the response of the space structure [3].

One of the earliest investigations that recognized the potential of multibody dynamics software for analyzing the dynamics of spacecraft solar arrays was accomplished by Young and Pack $ ^{4} $ . Since this study, the application of multibody dynamics software to analyze spacecraft structures has been somewhat limited. In 1996 Tadikonda et. al. $ ^{5} $ simulated the deployment of a flexible spacecraft structure using a multibody dynamics approach. Banerjee $ ^{6} $ presents an overview of the early application of multibody dynamics analysis for spacecraft structures. More recently Sinn and Vasile $ ^{7} $ modeled biologically inspired smart space structures using a multibody dynamics code developed by the authors. The structure under study was a multi-cell inflatable structure. The use of multibody dynamic analysis to predict the behavivior of spacecraft structures has been somewhat limited due to the availability of commercial software that can accurately predict both rigid and flexible body behavior. The focus of the study presented in this paper is deployable solar arrays for cubesats, but the application of multibody dynamics software for analyzing spacecraft structures has broader applications.
Figure 1. Example Cubesat with Deployed Solar Arrays

MotionPort LLC has successfully demonstrated the benefits of simulation for large solar arrays in the 300 kW class as described in ref [1]. There is also an ongoing need for better understanding the behavior of relatively large deployable space structures that are used with smaller spacecraft, such as the cubesat configuration shown in fig. 1 [8]. Additionally, design tools for developers of these spacecraft must include dynamic simulation capabilities in order to increase deployment reliability and predictability. The dynamic behavior of deployable space structures for smallsats is significant because the mass of each structure is relatively large compared to the overall mass of the smallsat.

In addition, there is substantial interest in the aerospace community in reducing the difficulty and required time to develop simulation models for characterizing the dynamics of smallsat structures. Past efforts improved the efficiency of modeling split-tube (or roll-out) solar arrays as summarized in the technical paper referenced in [2]. A key modeling issue with solar arrays comprised of stiff panels is to properly represent the stiffness and stored energy of the hinge assemblies (typically including a spring) that are used to connect and deploy the panels. The hinge assemblies may be comprised of parts with highly variable and complex geometry. The proper modeling of such assemblies would typically require two detailed finite element meshes of the two halves of the hinge geometry. The simulation of the solar array assembly with meshes for the panels as well as all of the connections could require significant computer resources and time. A method to represent the connections simply and accurately is highly desirable in order to have fast run times for the solar array simulation. The simplification of the hinges is especially important because the solar panels need to be represented as nonlinear flexible bodies in order to account for the stiffness and momentum effects of the panels as they are deployed and also as the spacecraft is rotated.

There is an ongoing need for a better understanding of the behavior of relatively large deployable structures that are attached to relatively small spacecraft bodies. The overall goal of the work described in this paper is to create a vertical software application using multibody dynamics software to improve model creation and reduce the run time of simulations. To achieve this goal two objectives were met. The first is the development of a general automated process to efficiently take a detailed hinge assembly model and simulate its range of motion while retrieving stiffness information for all degrees of freedom and convert that data to define a simple but accurate nonlinear point-to-point force for use in the solar array assembly model. The second objective is the development and simulation of a high-

fidelity system-level model of the deployment dynamics of a commercial deployable solar array that was designed for use with a 6U cubesat. The deployed cubesat solar array model will also undergo simulated tests to determine the maximum tumbling rates that can be tolerated before the deployed solar array configuration becomes unstable (hinge forces can't keep components in contact with bump stops). The development of the vertical software application is described in detail below.

section: III. Vertical Software Application for Hinge Simulation
section_key: iii vertical software application for hinge simulation
text: A. Motivation for a computationally efficient hinge model.

section: III. Vertical Software Application for Hinge Simulation
section_key: iii vertical software application for hinge simulation
text: The e-HaWK deployable CubeSat solar array is a high performance power harvesting system designed to fit 6U and larger spacecraft platforms. The deployable is designed as a two wing system, symmetric around the center of the spacecraft as shown below in Figure 2. Each wing is a tri-fold design where three panels stow within each other with the center main panel on top and the two side panels folded underneath.

section: III. Vertical Software Application for Hinge Simulation
section_key: iii vertical software application for hinge simulation
text: The solar array substrates use a unique morphing panel technology which enables the solar array to stow in a flat condition and then "morph" into a V-panel configuration for higher deployed stiffness. Panel-to-panel hinges group each morphing panel together allowing them to fold at $ 1 8 0^{\circ} $ . Panel-to-panel kinetics are actuated by a multifunctional torsion spring hinge mechanism which spans between two hinge locations mounted at the inflection point on each substrate.

section: III. Vertical Software Application for Hinge Simulation
section_key: iii vertical software application for hinge simulation
text: Figure 2. The e-HaWK Deployable CubeSat Solar Array from MMA Design

section: III. Vertical Software Application for Hinge Simulation
section_key: iii vertical software application for hinge simulation
text: The torsion springs are designed to handle $ 2 7 0^{\circ} $ of rotation so that the end of travel force is not zero, but rather $ 1 / 3 \cdot\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{starting force}} $ This is done to preload each panel hinge into a hard stop to increase deployed stiffness. Root wing hinges operate in a similar fashion, but use coil springs and only displace through $ 9 0^{\circ} $ of rotation. The Preload force assumption is identical to the panel-to-panel hinges in that $ 1 / 3 \cdot\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{starting force}} $ remains in the root hinge components to effectively preload the mechanism for high deployed stiffness.

section: III. Vertical Software Application for Hinge Simulation
section_key: iii vertical software application for hinge simulation
text: The system's launch restraint is a highly effective mechanism that engages the edges of the solar array stack and by using a mechanical lever arm morphs the V-panel into a flat configuration and presses against the spacecraft bus. The

section: III. Vertical Software Application for Hinge Simulation
section_key: iii vertical software application for hinge simulation
text: lever arm when rotated down into a locked position mates with the melt rod assembly. The melt rod assembly holds the stowed solar array in place and releases it on command from the end user.

The two types of hinges, one with embedded torsion springs and one without, used in the subject solar array are shown in fig. 3. The vertical development simplifies the hinge model and automates the hinge simulation tasks. The simplification is done for each hinge type using the same function. First a detailed model of the hinge assembly will be constructed, using finite element meshes to define portions of the hinge components as flexible, and including any necessary contacts between those components. The vertical application then presents a dialog to the user to enable him or her to set-up the model quickly for stiffness testing. The application then carries out a series of automated simulations to test the stiffness of the hinge and also rotates the hinge 90 degrees to capture the same information with the hinge in the vertical orientation. Once the simulations are done the vertical application will sort through the output data to calculate the hinge's stiffness for each DOF, and that information will be used to define a RecurDyn userfunction Screw force entity that is an efficient point-to-point force. The formulation of the Screw force will perform interpolation between the horizontal and vertical hinge positions to determine the hinge stiffnesses throughout the range of motion of the hinge.
a) Hinge with embedded springs
b) Hinge without springs
Figure 3. Hinge types used in the e-Hawk solar array

The RecurDyn multibody dynamics software allows the use of both flexible and rigid bodies within a model, which allows hinge behavior to be predicted accurately. To prepare the hinge model to be characterized automatically within the vertical software application the hinge should be modeled beforehand with meshed flexible bodies representing the areas where deflection is expected to occur. The flexible bodies are connected to a rigid body that will serve as a stable base for applying constraints and forces. The hinge is modeled in the horizontal position. Reference markers are created beforehand at key locations in the model to make the model setup easier to perform using the vertical application. Figure 4 shows an example of a mesh used for the flexible bodies of a rotational hinge. A marker is created at the location of the hinge pivot center. This marker serves as the reference frame when applying the forces and torques to the action side of the hinge.
Figure 4. Meshed flexible bodies and reference marker used to orient applied forces and torques.

The vertical application is executed through three tasks. These are 1) the Run Hinge Simulation task, 2) the Review Hinge Simulation Results task, and 3) the Create Simplified Hinge Force task. Each task is executed through a dialog box. When the user executes the Run Hinge Simulation task the dialog box shown in fig. 5 is displayed. The dialog allows the user to define the base and action bodies as well as specify which simulations, to run. The user can also specify the peak force or torque applied for each simulation. The Set Up and Run button commands the vertical application to run the simulations specified by the user. For each simulation, the force(s) or torque(s) will be applied with magnitudes that vary between the positive and negative values of the max force or torque specified in the dialog box. The general pattern of an applied force is shown in fig. 6. For each direction that a force or torque is applied the simulation is run with the hinge in both the horizontal and vertical position, as shown in fig. 7. During the simulation the displacement of the action side of the hinge is predicted and force vs. displacement or torque vs. rotation information is stored as a spline in the hinge model database.
Figure 5. Dialog box for Run Hinge Simulation task.
Figure 6. General pattern of force or torque applied to action side of hinge
Figure 7: Two hinge positions used in each simulation.
Figure 8. Example of hinge characterization data

The spline information can be displayed using the Review Hinge Simulation task. This opens a dialog box that allows the user to display a graph of any of the simulations that were run previously, as well as the animation results. An example of torque vs. rotation data is shown in fig. 8.

The final task is the Create Simplified Hinge force in System Model task. This task allows the user to command the vertical development application to integrate the hinge characterization simulation data into a system level model. To execute the task, the Create Simplified Hinge Force icon is chosen from the ribbon menu in RecurDyn. When the user clicks on this icon, the dialog shown at right in Figure 9 is displayed. The dialog enables the user to easily select from the modeling window the bodies that will connect to the simplified hinge force, as well as the locations of those connections and intended orientations of the hinge halves.

When the user clicks on the Apply button, the vertical application will create a new subsystem within the system level model that contains the simplified hinge force, as shown below in Figure 10. The subsystem, shown in Figure 11, will contain a base and action dummy body that are connected with a RecurDyn Screw Force, which can exert forces or torques from one body to another in all six degrees of freedom, with each force or torque being defined by an expression. The vertical application will align the subsystem with the base marker selected by the user, and the action dummy body within the subsystem will be oriented to align with the action marker selected by the user. A fixed joint will be created between the base body in the system level model and the base dummy body within the subsystem, as well as between the action body in the system level model and the action dummy body within the subsystem. The subsystem can be exported to a file which can be stored and imported into a different model. This capability allows the user to develop a library of hinges.
Figure 9. Create Simplified Hinge Force (Subsystem) in Model.
Figure 10. Subsystem added to model.
Figure 11. Contents of subsystem.

The expressions controlling the component forces and torques of the screw force were formulated to simulate the reaction force of the hinge, based on the hinge characterization simulations. The formulation enforces radial behavior so that both x- and y-axis translation are considered simultaneously and not independently when calculating the reaction forces. (The same consideration is made for x- and y-axis rotation.) This is needed because a gap typically exists between hinge components, allowing for free movement of the components before any deflection begins. To demonstrate this, in Figure 12 below, a translational force of constant magnitude but rotating direction is applied to the action body shown in red, in order to take the action body through its path of free motion. With a non-radial formulation, the path of motion is erroneously square and overestimates the amount of gap at the diagonal positions. But with the radial formulation, the path of motion is correctly circular in shape.
Figure 12. Importance of radial formulation for modeling a gap between parts.
The formulation also performs interpolation of the hinge stiffness when the hinge is between the horizontal and vertical positions tested.

section: IV. Integration of Simplified Hinge Model into the e-Hawk System Model
section_key: iv integration of simplified hinge model into the e hawk system model
text: A system level model of the e-HaWK solar array was constructed in RecurDyn. This model was used to characterize the deployment process and evaluate the sensitivity of the design to various input parameters. This process was broken up into the following steps; 1) flexible body representation of the solar panels, 2) storage, 3) deployment characterization, and 4) simulation trials. A mesh based upon shell elements was made to represent the solar panels of the solar array. This mesh accounts for the frame geometry, solar cells, and mounting considerations. The solar array substrates use a unique morphing panel technology which enables the solar array to stow in a flat condition then "morph" into a V-panel configuration for higher deployed stiffness. Accurate simulation of deployment required starting the simulation from its prestressed state. This was the stowed configuration. The deployment event was simulated and evaluated to determine the ability of the model to accurately characterize the deployment process. Once deployed, additional dynamic events are evaluated. A series of 11 trials were simulated to assess the overall predicted behavior of the solar wing representation.

section: A. Flexible Body Representation of the Solar Panels
section_key: a flexible body representation of the solar panels
text: The first step in the development of the system level model was to make a flexible body representation of the solar panels. One wing of the solar array consists of 3 panels as seen previously in fig. 2. The two side panels are identical and are represented using a single mesh. A second mesh was made for the center panel which has a slightly different geometry from the side panels. The mesh consists of a single layer of shell elements as seen in Figure 13. The mesh takes into consideration the frame geometry and solar cells by applying different material properties to the frame, the solar cells, and the region where these two overlap.

section: A. Flexible Body Representation of the Solar Panels
section_key: a flexible body representation of the solar panels
text: Figure 13. Rigid body representation (left) and flexible body representation (right) of the side panel

section: A. Flexible Body Representation of the Solar Panels
section_key: a flexible body representation of the solar panels
text: The panel mesh was fixed to the hinges using RecurDyn Force Distributing Rigid (FDR) elements (equivalent to Nastran RBE2 elements) using the nodes immediately surrounding the hinge. This was then tested using a 1g drop test to determine the viability of the mesh and the attachment to the hinge. The hinges were fixed to ground and the panel dropped 20 degrees before impacting the bump stops. The first impact with the bump stops is shown in Figure 14. In this image it can be seen that the majority of the stress is distributed through the frame as expected. Stress concentrations occur near the hinges where the load is being applied and in the middle where the frame narrows to a small cross section. This was determined to be an acceptable mesh for the system level model.

section: A. Flexible Body Representation of the Solar Panels
section_key: a flexible body representation of the solar panels
text: Figure 14. Peak stresses during initial impact with the bump stops during a 1g drop test. Stress units are lbf/in $ ^{2} $

During actual operation, the solar array is stored in a prestressed state. Two launch bars flatten the v-shaped panels until an electronic melt wire releases the system. Accurate characterization of the deployment process requires that the solar array starts in this prestressed state. This was achieved in two steps. First, the system was folded with all contacts inactive. Second, the contacts were activated and the system was given time to settle. The stored solar array with the panels in a prestressed state can be seen in Figure 15.
Figure 15. The prestressed state of the stored solar array panels. Stress units are Ibf/in $ ^{2} $

With the solar array stored in a prestressed state the model was ready to simulate deployment in a zero-g environment. There were three main impacts during the deployment process. First, the root hinge impacted the bump stops as the center panel extended to 90 degrees. Second, the panel-to-panel hinges on the right hand side impacted the bump stops as the right panel extended to 180 degrees as seen on the left side of Figure 4. Finally, the panel-to-panel hinges on the left hand side impacted the bump stops as the left panel extended to 180 degrees as seen on the right side of fig. 16.
Figure 16. Panel-to-panel hinge hard stop impact during solar array deployment. Stress units are lbf/in $ ^{2} $

This process can also be visualized using the position data of the revolute joints at the hinges as seen in fig.17. In the first 0.5 seconds some instability can be seen as the panels release from their prestressed state and begin to unfold. After approximately 1 second the center panel has extended 90 degrees and the root hinges impact the bump stops. Very little vibration is seen as the panel-to-panel hinges impact the bump stops. The solar array is fully deployed in 1.9 seconds and after 2.6 seconds the residual motion in the material has dampened out. The amount of vibration at impact is highly dependent upon the damping parameter at the contact. If necessary, this parameter can be adjusted to match results in a validation study.
Figure 17. Angular position of hinge action body during deployment.

Additional simulations can be performed in a fully deployed condition to further characterize potential dynamic events for the solar array. Information on characterization parameters such as linear and angular acceleration and fundamental frequency are obtained easily from the simulations. Figures 18-21 show examples of data that is obtained for these parameters from the simulations. Figure 18 shows the linear acceleration. It is of interest to note the maximum thrust force that can be applied before the wing decouples from the hard stops. The moment the wing decouples from the hard stops is measured by tracking when the contact force between the hard stops drops to 0. Results from a gradually increasing linear acceleration are shown in fig. 21. The wing decoupled from the hard stop at a linear acceleration of $ 2 6. 5 \mathrm{~ i n / s^{2}} $ . This corresponds to a 6.0 lb. thrust force.
Figure 18. Linear acceleration of the deployed solar panel.

Figure 19 shows the force on the hinge during changes in angular acceleration. In fig. 19 the angular acceleration is ramped up quickly to keep the angular velocity negligible. The results from a ramped up angular velocity applied at the center of mass can be seen in fig. 22. The side panel decoupled from the hard stop at an angular acceleration of 11.8 rad/s^2.
Figure 19. Hinge contact force during changes in angular acceleration.

The fundamental frequency of the system is evaluated using the model by applying a small simulated force at the corner of one of the panels. This force was released instantaneously and the position of the node at the corner where the force was applied is tracked over time. Figure 20 shows this test performed with hinges that were artificially locked in one orientation. An FFT is obtained from the data to gather frequency information as seen in Fig. 21. In this case, the FFT shows a fundamental frequency at 5.5 Hz.
Figure 20. Time history of the solar panel after a small force impulse is applied.
Figure 21. FFTcreated plot from the data presented in fig. 20.

In order to capture the effect of the hinges, this same test was applied with hinges that were free to rotate. This necessitated using a smaller force to avoid complete decoupling of the hard stops. The results of this test are shown in fig. 22. This test resulted in a fundamental frequency of approximately 3 Hz. However, this motion dampened fast enough that only one period could be evaluated.
Figure 22. Response of a freely rotating hinge to an applied impulse force.

A set of 11 trials was run to evaluate the sensitivity of the model to various input factors. The five input factors that were evaluated are root spring stiffness, panel-panel spring stiffness, side panel substrate modulus, center panel substrate modulus, and solar array add-on mass. Parameters were adjusted by 20% from the nominal value. The study was conducted with the intention of being used to develop physical test to validate the performance of the simulations. A summary of the results can be seen in Table 1.

A strong correlation was found between the input parameters and the time to deploy, the maximum tumbling with instability, and the maximum input thrust. Increasing the spring stiffness tends to decrease time to deploy and increases stability while deployed while increasing the solar array add-on mass increased the time to deploy and decreased stability while deployed. However, trial 1 seems to be an outlier to these trends. Examining the simulation results for this case reveals an oscillation in the residual stresses of the left panel that is timed in such a way that the deployment of the left panel is delayed.

A vertical application that runs within the RecurDyn multibody dynamics software package which automates the development of hinge models has been presented. The simplification of a hinge with complex geometry to a single nonlinear component allows a nonlinear finite element representation to be used for each of the solar panels while maintaining a reasonable simulation time. Accurately modeling the dynamic behavior of deployable spacecraft structures, such as solar arrays is important for reducing risk during spacecraft development. The application is useful for spacecraft designers as it reduces model development time as well as simulation run time. The vertical application will be especially useful to developers of CubeSat as the solar arrays are large compared to the spacecraft body. The utility of the vertical application is demonstrated through the development of a deployment simulation and post deployment characterization of the e-Hawk solar array. In addition, a deployable space structure of any size can be simulated using the above tools and techniques.

text: Eds.: Azad M. Madni, Barry Boehm Daniel A. Erwin, Roger Ghanem; University of Southern California Marilee J. Wheaton, The Aerospace Corporation Redondo Beach, CA, March 23-25, 2017

As Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) continues to mature and becomes part of space engineering practice, the concept of a Reference Model becomes increasingly important. The CubeSat Reference Model (CRM) is an example of a reference model that is being developed by the INCOSE Space Systems Working Group (SSWG). The intent of the model is to facilitate the design, verification and validation of CubeSat design. The CRM is being developed with sufficient flexibility to support customization for specific CubeSat missions by mission-specific CubeSat teams. This paper presents the key elements of the CRM developed using MBSE practices. It presents different views of the model along with a validation and verification approach. Further research is needed into how best to augment with other models to facilitate CubeSat test and evaluation.
Keywords: verification; validation; CubeSat; Reference Model; MBSE

A CubeSat is a low-cost standardized nanosatellite. It originated from the CubeSat Project which was established in 1999 by California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly), San Luis Obispo and Stanford University's Space and Systems Development Laboratory (SSDL). The CubeSat Project was established for the university community to design, build, and launch satellites using mostly off-the-shelf components. The basic CubeSat unit is 10x10x10 centimeters with a mass of about 1.3 kilograms. This cubic unit is referred to as 1U. CubeSat units can be joined to form a larger satellite. One-, two-, and three-unit (1U, 2U, and 3U) CubeSats have been the most common configurations so far. They are typically launched as secondary payloads or deployed from the International Space Station.

Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) is a key recent practice to advance the systems engineering discipline [1]. The International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE) established the MBSE Initiative [2] to promote, advance, and institutionalize the practice of MBSE. As part of this effort, since 2011 the INCOSE Space Systems Working Group (SSWG) Challenge Team has been investigating the applicability of MBSE for designing CubeSats. The SSWG team comprises academics (including faculty and students), practitioners (including engineers and software developers from NASA centers and industry), and representatives of commercial tool vendors.
The goals of the MBSE Challenge Project are to:
- Demonstrate Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) methodology as applied to a CubeSat mission;
- Provide a CubeSat Reference Model (CRM) for CubeSat teams to use as the starting point for developing mission-specific CubeSat models; and
- Develop the CRM as an Object Management Group (OMG) specification.
Central to this MBSE work is the creation of a CubeSat Reference Model (CRM). A generic reference

model in MBSE is a conceptual framework based on a domain-specific ontology. It consists of an interlinked set of concepts produced by a body of subject matter experts with the express purpose of fostering clear communications within collaborative teams of stakeholders. A reference model embodies the set of core concepts (including goals) that engineers can use for various purposes such as verification and validation, and test and evaluation. An apt analogy, according to Madni [3], [4] is that of examining a precious stone such as a diamond. "As you hold the gem up to the light and rotate your hand, you get to view its different facets. The rays of light from each facet offer a unique insight about the diamonds clarity and cut" [3]. A reference model is much like a gem. Its facets correspond to different perspectives or views, while the rays of light correspond to the information and insights contained in each perspective view. A reference model is a collection of different perspectives. It offers a high-level view of the problem domain (space). The key characteristics of a reference model are: abstractions, relationships, and entities. A reference model is methodology-neutral and technology-agnostic [3] [4].

Thus, the CubeSat Reference Model is an abstract framework for understanding the relationships among the entities of the CubeSat environment. Even though it is at least three levels of abstraction away from any physical instantiation, it still provides valuable assistance to the Mission-specific CubeSat development teams.

Our use of the term Reference Model should not be confused with the use of the same term by the Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards (OASIS). OASIS uses to the term in the context of Service Oriented Architectures [5].

The term "Model as used in Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) is represented using a language such as Systems Modeling Language (SysML). Since we are interested in modeling a generic CubeSat mission domain, and not a specific mission, we qualify the model as a "Reference Model."
The CRM will be delivered by SSWG to Mission-specific CubeSat development teams to:
- Populate the model with their Mission Statement and Mission Objectives, their Measures of Effectiveness and Performance, and their Stakeholders and Stakeholder Concerns
- Develop their Use Cases, System and Subsystem requirements, and Validation and Verification approach; and
- Refine the Logical Architecture and develop the Physical Architecture.
The challenges [6] facing the development teams include the following:
- There is currently no agreed-upon process for developing a CubeSat Enterprise [7]
- To date, no Mission-specific CubeSat Enterprise has been modeled
- It is anticipated that different Mission-specific CubeSat development teams will bring different levels of engineering and development skill and experience to bear
- Budget constraints will continue to be a driver

Encouraging the various Mission-specific CubeSat development teams to adopt MBSE, Object Oriented System Engineering Methodology (OOSEM), and SysML and providing them a standard Reference Model for their development will boost the efficiency and productivity of less experienced teams without any negative impacts.

Previously, the SSWG demonstrated the ability to model behaviors, interface with commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) simulation tools, and carry out trade studies [8]. Currently, the team is building a reference CubeSat model for use by aerospace students in the classroom, and by mission teams building mission-specific CubeSats [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14].

In Section 1, we have introduced the SSWG CubeSat effort. Section 2 presents a more detailed look at the effort required to develop the CubeSat Reference Model, including a description of the Logical Architecture, and the organization of the model (particularly the requirements captured in the model). Section 3 identifies the effort required to develop a Mission-specific CubeSat model using the CRM as a foundation. Section 4 discusses the approach to conducting Validation and Verification of the CubeSat Reference Model, and compares that approach to the approach for conducting Verification and Validation of the Mission-specific CubeSat model. Section 5 presents conclusions and future work.

The CRM is intended to be used by university project teams designing space missions utilizing the CubeSat form-factor. The model is being developed assuming that the members of the team have an intermediate-level understanding of space mission analysis and design, Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), Systems Modeling Language (SysML), and that their work is being guided by subject matter experts. MBSE is the formalized application of modeling to support key systems engineering tasks for addressing requirements, design, analysis, and validation and verification.

Logical and Physical Architectures. The CRM provides the logical architecture of a CubeSat. The logical components, which are abstractions of physical components, symbolically execute system functions (i.e., without implementation constraints). The physical architecture defines physical components of the system including hardware, software, persistent data, and operational procedures. The CRM logical elements are intended to be reused as a starting point for a mission-specific CubeSat logical architecture, followed by the development of physical architecture from the logical architecture during CubeSat development. On the other hand, should the Mission-specific Team decide to adopt a different logical architecture, the CRM is sufficiently flexible to accommodate

CubeSat Domain and Enterprise. Figure 1 shows the CubeSat Domain, which consists of the CubeSat Mission Enterprise (with its two segments and various services), Stakeholders, External Environment, and External Constraints. The External Environment consists of the Space Environment and Earth Environment. The External Constraints include Licenses and Regulations. The CubeSat Mission Enterprise encompasses everything that involves the development, deployment, and operation of the CubeSat mission.
Figure 1. CubeSat Domain and Mission Enterprise

CubeSat Space Segment. The CubeSat Space Segment consists of one or more CubeSats along with their orbits and subsystems. The Space Segment includes designs, interfaces, and operations to comply with the requirements and constraints that are imposed by the External Environment, as well as those by other aspects of the mission such as the Transport, Launch, and Deploy Services. For example, a launch

has a pressure and vibration profile that constrains the design of the CubeSat. These requirements and constraints can be incorporated into a Transport, Launch, and Deploy Services model unique to the service providers.

CubeSat Ground Segment. The CubeSat Ground Segment consists of the CubeSat Mission Operations and one or more Ground Stations. Mission Operations includes the software, data, procedures, and personnel used to operate the CubeSat mission. Mission Operations activities include mission planning and scheduling, command and control of the CubeSat, control of the ground equipment, mission telemetry processing, and mission data processing and distribution. The Ground Station consists of the computers, network, communication equipment, and associated control infrastructure hosted in a ground facility. Communication equipment includes the space-ground antennas. The architecture accommodates a CubeSat project developing its own ground station or operating with an existing ground station that provides uplink and downlink services.

Model Organization. There are packages for the domain, enterprise, space and ground segments, and space and ground subsystems. The enterprise, segment, and subsystems packages contain behaviors, structures, validation, and verification packages.

Requirements. Requirements are organized by enterprise, space and ground segments, and space and ground subsystems packages. The enterprise package consists of mission needs, mission objectives, mission constraints, and mission requirements packages with model elements to establish the relationships to the stakeholder needs, objectives, constraints, and measures of effectiveness. Figure 4 shows model elements that help define lower-level requirements. The relationships between elements are illustrative not prescriptive. Segment requirements are derived from mission requirements and trace to mission use cases. Segment requirements trace to measures of performance which trace to measures of effectiveness. Subsystem requirements are derived from segment requirements and trace to segment use cases. Subsystem requirements trace to technical performance measures which trace to measures of performance and to measures of effectiveness.

Technical Measures. Technical measures provide the stakeholders insight into the definition and development of the technical solution. Measures of effectiveness, key performance parameters, measures of performance, and technical performance parameters as are technical measures. They are distinct from requirements, although performance and other requirements may be traced to them. They are incorporated into the CRM as block value properties. A technical measure can be measured and compared to a target value.

Functional and Non-Functional Requirements. Requirements can be classified as functional or non-functional. Functional requirements define the desired behaviors of the system and non-functional requirements define the overall qualities or attributes of the resulting system. Non-functional requirements (which include Quality Factors) place constraints on the product being developed, the development processes, or conformance with external regulations. Examples of non-functional requirements include safety, security, usability, reliability, and performance. However, as requirements are decomposed, the distinction between functional and non-functional requirements may disappear. For example, a top-level mission reliability requirement may lead to lower level requirements that identify where redundancy would be needed. The presence of redundancy requires redundancy management functions whose behaviors could be considered functional requirements. Whether a requirement is expressed as a functional or non-
functional requirement may depend on the level of detail to be included in the requirements document, the extent to which the application domain is understood, and the experience of the developers.

Although the CRM space and ground subsystems have been broadly defined, the mission teams may find it necessary to modify the subsystem definitions according to the allocated requirements.

The next step is to create the physical architecture from the logical architecture, and this is accomplished by determining the types of subsystem components that meet the functional and performance subsystem requirements. The CRM is basically a model of a model. That is, the CRM will be used by a mission-specific CubeSat team to design and develop their mission-specific CubeSat.
Validation confirms, by providing objective evidence, that the system, as-built (or as it will be built), satisfies the stakeholders' needs. That is, the right system has been (or will be) built.

Verification confirms, by providing objective evidence, that the system and all its elements perform their intended functions and satisfy the requirements allocated to them. That is, the system has been built right. Verification methods include inspection, analysis, demonstration, and test.

Stakeholders are individuals or organizations with an interest in the system. Typical stakeholders include users, operators, organization decision makers, parties to the agreement, regulatory bodies, developing agencies, support organizations, and society at large. They can also include interoperating and enabling systems.

Stakeholders have various interests in the CRM: Some are interested in the models themselves and others are interested in the missions that can be realized from the mission-specific instantiations of the model, and some are interested in both.
Stakeholders, Concerns, Viewpoints, and Views. ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2011 established the following terminology [15]:

- Stakeholders and Concerns: A concern could be manifest in many forms, such as in relation to one or more stakeholder needs, goals, expectations, responsibilities, requirements, design constraints, assumptions, dependencies, quality attributes, architecture decisions, risks or other issues pertaining to the system.
- Architecture Viewpoint: Work product establishing the conventions for the construction, interpretation and use of architecture views to frame specific system concerns
- Architecture View: Work product expressing the architecture of a system from the perspective of specific system concerns

Regulatory Agencies are stakeholders. Licenses and regulations, timelines, and procedures must be must be well understood and part of the CRM. In the U.S. the FCC regulates the radio frequencies, NASA provides orbital debris guidelines, and NOAA regulates remote sensing. The validation that the national stakeholders' regulations and guidelines have been properly instantiated, will consist of viewpoints into the CRM. The viewpoints include source regulations, guidelines, procedures, and timelines. Verification of compliance with the regulations and timelines will be the responsibility of the mission-specific CubeSat team. Their mission-specific CubeSat model will need viewpoints for the compliant model elements, licenses, and authorizations.
Cal Poly CubeSat Project is a stakeholder. The Cal Poly CubeSat Specification [16] specifies a CubeSat's physical, mechanical, electrical, testing, and operational requirements.

INCOSE and OMG are both stakeholders. They jointly developed SysML to support MBSE. An independent review team will validate that the CRM complies with accepted SysML modeling guidelines. OMG is responsible for establishing the CRM as a specification. OMG review and approval of the CRM will validate that the CRM is qualified to be a specification.

SSWG and University CubeSat Teams are both stakeholders since they are model users. The SSWG is a stakeholder since it is developing the model for use by the university team. A traditional pre-MBSE approach would be to negotiate a CRM requirements document and then to develop the model. In MBSE, the SSWG works with the university teams to define the model elements and relationships from the CubeSat domain and enterprise to the space and ground segments and subsystems.

As MBSE matures and continues to penetrate real world engineering practice, the concept of a reference model is an important development to facilitate transition of MBSE into real world practice [1], [17]. This paper has presented recent advances in developing a CubeSat Reference Model (CRM) in accord with MBSE specification. This paper discusses the specification, validation, and verification of the CRM. This activity is being pursued by a team comprising government, academia, and INCOSE SSWG. This activity is expected to continue into the foreseeable future resulting in further advances in MBSE [17], [18]. Future advances include the development of a library of reference models (for different domains and missions) that are metadata-tagged for easy retrieval.

Small satellites (>100kg) are becoming more prevalent with increasing mission types driving the complexity of the design. These missions range from earth imaging to technological demonstrations as well as educational uses within universities. The design and engineering of these satellites become more challenging with the miniature size, coupled subsystems and dynamic environments. One major issue of this architecture is the selection and verification of requirements. Model-based systems engineering is a powerful system engineering methodology providing engineers a model of the entire system model. This modeling environment can provide system design in the trade space as well as integrating disciplines together and allowing simulation. NASA Marshall Space Flight Center is currently working on a small satellite using an iodine fueled Hall thruster, called iSAT. This 12U satellite will be a technological demonstration of the use of a 200W Hall thruster in low earth orbit. Integrating the system models into SysML with the requirements and system architecture allowed for an analysis of the power system. A simulation of the power system was completed providing insight into the design.

SMALL satellites, which here are defined as satellites weighing less than 100kgs, are becoming more popular in use. These satellites can be seen as an answer to the "better, faster, cheaper" approach with the decrease in the size of technology. However, the size of these satellites increases some of the design difficulties. Marshall Space Flight Center is currently working on a small satellite, called iSAT, through the Space Technology Mission Directorate. It is a 12 unit CubeSat with a size of 8" x 8" x 12", being used as a platform for a technological demonstration of an iodine Hall thruster propulsion system. $ ^{1} $ This will be done by starting at around a 600km circular orbit and reducing down to a 300km circular orbit with a 200W thruster. SmallSats are typically constrained by volume, mass, and power, which limit their propulsive capability. With this demonstration, NASA can provide future satellites with a means of electric propulsion while meeting constraints. On the other hand, using electric propulsion places a greater emphasis on the

analysis of the electrical power system. The preliminary power model for the iSAT is currently modeled in LabView and Excel, which produces an open loop set of values. By shifting over to a model based systems engineering approach, the power profile can be modeled throughout the orbit. It also provides a platform that can leverage other powerful tools such as Satellite Toolkit and Matlab to simulate the satellite systems for a mission profile.

Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) is the formalized application of modeling to support system requirements, design, analysis, verification, and validation activities from concept design through realization $ ^{2} $ . MBSE grew out of the model based software engineering approaches (e.g. [UML]) developed to facilitate complex software developments. Systems Modeling Language (SysML), an extension of UML, allows the construction of system models encompassing not only hardware and software elements of a system, but also human operators and the system context including other systems. MBSE system models help keep all project activities (engineering, development, integration) consistent and track all the interfaces and dependencies in the system.

Within the context of model based design (MBD) of complex engineered systems, MBSE methods and tools are experiencing more application in system development as they allow a system to be designed, analyzed, implemented, and verified against system-level and high-fidelity multidisciplinary systems simulations $ ^{3} $ . In particular, MBSE is witnessing increasing applications in the fields of mechatronics $ ^{4} $ and real time embedded systems $ ^{5} $ . SysML is the most widely used MBSE tool $ ^{6} $ . SysML is a standardized general-purpose modeling language to describe systems including hardware, software, personnel, and processes. Many modeling tools support SysML since it is based on the widely used software modeling language Unified Modeling Language (UML $ ^{7} $ . SysML was developed as a domainindependent system-level modeling language providing a unified description of the functions and architectures of a system $ ^{8} $ . In an MBD context, SysML provides a means to integrate and organize the hierarchy of models necessary to describe all the aspects of the system. SysML models are compatible with most software models in UML, and they can integrate additional parts that are needed to build a high-level model of a physical system, since the models in the hierarchy may be heterogeneous both in terms of the portion of reality they describe and in terms of the particular tool used for describing it $ ^{9} $ . When used in a complex system application, the system architecture view is described in SysML and a continuous system dynamics view defined in various physical system models $ ^{10} $ .

SysML is a graphical modeling language that can be used to visualize and communicate the design of systems. It is developed and maintained by the Object Management Group and initiated by INCOSE. The language is structured using diagrams and blocks to specify, analyze, design, optimize, and verify complex systems including software, hardware, and information. $ ^{11} $ The following descriptions are of the blocks and diagrams mainly used in this project which is provided by A Practical Guide to SysML.
A package is a container for other model elements. Any model element is contained in exactly one container which can be used as model navigation $ ^{11} $

A block is the fundamental modular unit for describing system structure in SysML. It can define a type of logical or conceptual entity. They are often used to describe reusable components that can be used on many different systems. Block Definition Diagrams is a widely diagram used to define blocks in terms of their features and their structural relationships with other blocks within the system. $ ^{11} $

An activity diagram defines the actions used and the flow of input/output between them. They can be used to describe activities done by the system and execute behaviors. For this model, the use of the opaque behavior was widely used which can evaluate a mathematical expression $ ^{11} $

Requirements specify a capability or condition that must be satisfied, a function that a system must perform or a performance condition a system must achieve. The requirement diagram graphical represents the hierarchies of these requirements providing traceability and means to satisfy, verify, and refine them $ ^{1 1} $
State Machines are used to describe the state-dependent behavior of a block throughout a cycle. The transition between these states is represented in a state machine diagram $ ^{11} $

The purpose of this paper is to show the use of MBSE on small satellites by integrating models using SysML. The work was completed using NoMagic Cameo System Modeler using SysML. The integrated model simulates the mission to analyze the power requirements and the electrical power system for the iSAT. It transfers a previous analytical power model that used Excel into SysML. This model is currently open loop providing basic outputs to inputs. This integration into a new environment allows the model to provide a closed loop orbit simulation with regards to the power system along with the supporting diagrams. Because chemical propulsion systems weigh more and are larger, they are prohibitive to this scale. Many engineers are focusing towards the use of electric propulsion for maneuvering capabilities for small sats. By showing that the power cycle is feasible for use, electric propulsion could expand its use on spacecraft. Furthermore using iodine as a propellant would provide a greater venue for electric propulsion on small satellites. This work would lower the uncertainty and risk associated with the use of electric propulsion.

Previous work into the field of MBSE for small satellites has mainly been focused in industry. The INCOSE Space Systems Working Group (SSWG) was founded in 2007 and investigating the application towards CubeSats since 2011. The chair David Kaslow has focused on the modeling of the University of Michigan's RAX CubeSat. The working group along with others in the industry started out by modeling the framework and then moved on to the behavior modeling. The latest focus has been on the lifecycle phases and trade studies. The paper "Integrated ModelBased Systems Engineering (MBSE) Applied to the Simulation of a CubeSat Mission" used a SysML model in Magic Draw combining models from MATLAB and STK using Model Center and the MBSE Analyzer $ ^{12} $ . This model was used to analyze hardware and mission configurations. These trade studies focused on the power and communications systems. Because the RAX CubeSat was launched back in 2010, this work is mainly a case study exercise for the application of MBSE. Up until now, this has been the only work done with the focus of CubeSats. Research is lacking in the application of MBSE for small satellites and its use during the preliminary phase.

The power model was previously completed by the Rotorcraft Systems Engineering and Simulation Center at the University of Alabama in Huntsville providing all the equations used in this analysis $ ^{13} $ . These equations are used to calculate the power generated from the solar panels, the power drawn from all the components and the energy provided to the batteries. These calculations use constant values, single input values, look up values and arrays. For the implementation into SysML, the look up values and arrays are held constant and were implemented as instances with the calculations as opaque behaviors. To begin the analysis, the power generated from the solar panels is calculated using the following equation.
$$ P _ {g e n} = F l u x _ {S o l a r} * S C _ {R A W e f f} * S C _ {T E M P e f f} * I _ {d} * F _ {E} * A r e a * c o s \left(\theta_ {i}\right) $$

Equation (1) multiplies the solar flux, $ Flux_{Solar} $ , the raw and temperatures efficiencies for the solar cells, $ SC_{RAWeff},SC_{TEMPeff} $ , the inherent degradation, $ I_{d} $ , the eclipse factor, $ F_{E} $ , the solar panel area, Area, and the cosine of the angle of incident to the sun, $ \cos(\theta_{i}) $ . The solar flux, raw efficiency and the solar panel area are constants. The inherent degradation and MPPT efficiency are single input values. The temperature efficiency is a look up value and the eclipse factor and incidence angle are arrays. The next step is to find how much power is being drawn from each component. This is calculated using the following equation.
$$ P _ {d r a w n} = \sum N * I * V $$

Equation (2) multiplies the number of each component, N, by the current, I, and the voltage, V, of the component which are all single input values. These equations are used as the foundation to determine the amount of energy used

to charge the battery and used during the eclipse. After factoring efficiencies for the separate voltage converters and modes, the available energy to charge the battery can be found by the following.
$$ E _ {a v a l b a t t} = E _ {s c} * M P P T _ {e f f} - E _ {d r a w n} $$

The available battery energy, $ E_{avalbatt} $ , is found by multiplying the energy generated by the solar cells, $ E_{sc} $ , by the maximum peak power tracking efficiency and subtracting the energy drawn. The energy for the satellite and the battery depth of discharge can be found by the following.
$$ B _ {C S} = 1 0 0 * \frac {E _ {b a t t e r y} + E _ {a v a l b a t t}}{B _ {M a x}} $$

These equations will only provide instantaneous values for the spacecraft. Using a software like Excel, time steps could be added to provide a temporal element but it does not provide a usable simulation. For this, the power model was transferred into SysML in Cameo Systems Modeler.

In order to calculate the power of each component, extra consideration was taken to look up features of those components. The model was developed with the analysis and components in different packages, once again seen in the structure tree. Extra read structural feature actions were provided as a result. To take the avionics subsystem as an example, calculating the power for the flight computer requires two extra read structural feature actions to achieve the proper logic level in the structure tree to read the current and voltage values. As shown in figure 5, the read self action comes first. The diagram continues to the avionics subsystem read structural feature which is contained in the power tool package. To transfer to back to the system model package the diagram reads the computer structural feature which is under the avionics package. This transition is feasible because the computer is a part of the avionics subsystem which is then a part of the power tool. Now that the logic level is down to the component level, the current and power values can be read, feeding into the power opaque behavior yielding the power being drawn from the flight computer. Similar activity diagrams were built for each component. Instances were created for each component as the classifier with values for current, voltage and power mimicking the single input values. Then the subsystem's power draw can be calculated by summing up the components power. Figure 6 shows the activity diagram used to calculate the total power used for the avionic subsystem. Not unlike finding the power for each component, the subsystem structural feature is read in breaking off into the constituent parts and then the values. These values are then fed into
an opaque behavior summing them up yielding the subsystem power.

The next step in the analysis is to calculate the battery level shown in figure 8. The battery level opaque behavior models equation 3 in SysML yielding the battery level.

Finally, the last step in the calculations is to increase the simulated elapsed time. Once the time reaches a certain value, the simulation transitions into the eclipse activities, which is the same as the sun battery level without the energy generation, completing the simulation as seen in figure 3.
Ultimately to run the simulation, a simulation configuration diagram was created. The simulation configuration
Figure 7. Power draw calculations activity diagram

block used an instance of the power tool populated with the parameters as the execution target. Furthermore, a Time Series Chart was set as the user interface to plot the charge level against the mission elapsed time. The results of each simulation are saved and placed into a results package which can be used for additional analysis.

With the recent emergence of the Complex Systems Integration Lab at the University of Alabama in Huntsville, the integration of a previous system model into SysML has been a practical learning experience. While modeling the architecture and requirements was straight forward, simulating the power system was more nuanced. The first simulation completed was the stopwatch tutorial provided by NoMagic $ ^{15} $ . This introduced the use of read self, read structural feature, add structural feature, and opaque behaviors. Because of the
Figure 8. Battery level calculation activity diagram

simplistic nature of the tutorial, the analysis package was created separately from the system model package. The power tool package and block were then created, under which the analysis would be completed. It began with the power and energy generation activities. Moving forward a misunderstanding of the behavior of the read self action came clear. Since the component structural features were not under the same packages, the model was not able to read them. After consultation, the solution was found by associating the subsystems to the power tool block and increasing the read structural feature levels. Once the execution logic was figured out, the values for the equations were inputted. With slight discrepancies in the voltage converter modeling, the values are similar to the previous power model.

In regards to the iSAT mission, the SysML power model allows for further insight into their power system design. The results of the simulation display a need for further refinement in the power model. Currently, there is no duty cycle which rapidly drains the battery, as shown in figure 9.

Also without an initial battery charge, the satellite does not produce enough power to last during the eclipse. However, all of these issues can be addressed by manipulating values within the model, such as providing an initial battery level or changing the efficiency levels once component level testing is done. As a secondary payload, the power margins are tight due to the size constraint, but the SysML power simulation provides a powerful tool for the iSAT team at
Figure 9. Initial orbit battery energy results

Marshall Space Flight Center. In the same model, the power system can be analyzed beginning with orbit insertion and working through the mission profile. Moreover, if there is any change to the architecture it can be reflected in both the block definition diagram and the power system simulation. Near future work for this power model is a 15 orbit simulation to analyze the charge state of the batteries for a propulsive maneuver. It is also the plan of the Complex Systems Integration Lab to combine the power model with propulsion and attitude control models to provide higher fidelity through the inclusion of STK and Matlab with other diagrams.

Small satellites are becoming more viable and with this technological demonstration, they will be able to include a propulsive system. Modeling these systems in SysML can assist in the preliminary analysis of the design. This paper shows that the iSAT electrical power system can be modeled in SysML. It not only provides a graphical representation of the system but also provides a means for simulation in the same environment. This technology can be leveraged for a future mission to hopefully reduce the cost and unforeseen interactions.

Without him, this work might not have been possible. They would also like to acknowledge John Dankanich and Michael Selby from the iSAT team for the opportunity to work for this project. And lastly, the authors would like to the rest of the systems engineering department at the University of Alabama in Huntsville.

section: Integrating SysML and Value-Based Design with an NEA Scout Small Satellite Example
section_key: integrating sysml and value based design with an nea scout small satellite example
text: There has recently been a tremendous growth in the use of model-based systems engineering (MBSE) among different categories of practitioners including government, industry, and academia. MBSE aims at using a consistent system model that is updated throughout the system life cycle to form a digital twin, to enable improved decision-making. OMG's Systems Modeling Language (SysML) is one of the primary modeling languages used to model not only system hardware and software, but also the people and processes involved in system development. SysML is finding increased application in different sectors, and is gaining favor among practitioners for their modeling needs. Value-based design (VBD) mathematically represents the preference of the stakeholder in the form of a value model which can be maximized to determine the optimal system. This paper attempts to bring together the benefits of SysML and value modeling to enable more informed decisions. This is performed by integrating value models with SysML to evaluate and compare alternatives. The challenges to integrating the two approaches are discussed and an example of the NEA Scout cube satellite modeled in Cameo Enterprise Architecture with stakeholder preference represented mathematically in a value model is used to explore the topic.

section: Integrating SysML and Value-Based Design with an NEA Scout Small Satellite Example > I. Introduction
section_key: integrating sysml and value based design with an nea scout small satellite example / i introduction
text: LARGE-SCALE complex engineered systems (LSCES) are characterized by the extensive number of individuals participating in designing the system, the complex interactions between various disciplines, and the large amounts of money, time, and risk associated with each [1]. These LSCES often interact with other LSCES in order to fulfill their operational purpose, adding further to the complexity of these systems. LSCES generally tend towards the greater extremes in terms of size, cost, risk, and number of involved organizations and personnel. A complication of involving many organizations are the many decision-makers within those organizations. The flow of decisions in organizations generally follows a top-down approach, where decisions made at the top most level are communicated down the organizational hierarchy [2], [3]. The stakeholders at the top most level may be company CEOs or directors in case of industry or the generals at the highest level in case of the military. It is important that the preferences of these stakeholders are communicated in such a way that enables consistent decision making throughout the organization. If this occurs, then the decisions made by the decision-makers at the lower levels will be that which the top level stakeholders themselves would make. It is imperative to correctly capture and represent the preferences of the stakeholders in order to ensure that the designed system aligns with the desires of the stakeholders. Value-based design (VBD) is a new design philosophy aimed at representing preferences through meaningful mathematical models called value model [4], [5]. By representing preferences in value models some information that was previously communicated through requirements are now captured in an objective function. VBD has been increasingly gaining favor in the systems engineering (SE) community.

section: Integrating SysML and Value-Based Design with an NEA Scout Small Satellite Example > I. Introduction
section_key: integrating sysml and value based design with an nea scout small satellite example / i introduction
text: Another approach that has been progressively recognized in the past few decades is model-based systems engineering (MBSE). It is a new and improved method for enabling the design of systems using an integrated system model. The roots of MBSE lie in model-based software development which is based on incremental development. Similarly, traditional SE activities also follow serial development [6]. Models provide a means to represent the physical system in a way that assists in predicting the behaviors of the system and understanding the system. Models, in essence, represent a digital twin of the system in question, and design decisions can be based upon the response of the model to stimuli. They provide insights into different system states that may or may not have been predicted before. Thus, models, if used correctly, can be of tremendous help in the design of systems, especially LSCES where understanding the system is difficult. The Object Management Group's (OMG) Systems Modeling Language (SysML) and the SAE International Architecture Analysis and Description Language (AADL) are the two eminent MBSE languages. Literature has shown that of the two, SysML is used more widely [7]-[9]; however the language is constantly evolving.

section: Integrating SysML and Value-Based Design with an NEA Scout Small Satellite Example > I. Introduction
section_key: integrating sysml and value based design with an nea scout small satellite example / i introduction
text: Since both VBD and MBSE attempt at improving the design of LSCES, it is of interest to explore if the approaches can be used together for greater improvements. This paper integrates value models with SysML to study the advantages and challenges. NASA's Near-Earth Asteroid (NEA) Scout project was used as an example to demonstrate the integration. A model for the small satellite was created in Cameo Enterprise Architecture, a well-known tool for employing SysML. The value model was created using Matlab and then integrated with Cameo. The methodology section elaborates on the process followed and the challenges faced. A brief background about VBD and MBSE, the MBSE tools, as well as the Scout project is discussed in the following background section.

section: Integrating SysML and Value-Based Design with an NEA Scout Small Satellite Example > A. MBSE
section_key: integrating sysml and value based design with an nea scout small satellite example / a mbse
text: As per INCOSE, "Model-based systems engineering is the formalized application of modeling to support system requirements, design, analysis, verification, and validation beginning in the conceptual design phase and continuing throughout development and later life cycle phases" [10]. The models are stored in a central repository which enables the establishment of formal relationships between models. This translates to increased traceability of information related to the model throughout the system design process [11]. The primary object of MBSE is an integrated systems model that enables different views of the same model to facilitate better understanding of the system and its functions. The ability of multiple views could help to increase the involvement of stakeholders in the design process, which in turn could help the designers better understand the preferences of stakeholders. The other assumed advantages of MBSE over traditional document-centric SE approaches include support for incremental development, traceability, support for early Verification and Validation, and improved risk identification, among others.

section: Integrating SysML and Value-Based Design with an NEA Scout Small Satellite Example > B. SysML
section_key: integrating sysml and value based design with an nea scout small satellite example / b sysml
text: SysML was developed as an extension of the popular Unified Modeling Language (UML) belonging to the field of software engineering. The language was developed to support system engineering activities by developing models that could encompass not only system hardware and software elements, but also model the people and processes involved [12]. The representation of these system elements is supported by the nine different diagrams comprising SysML [13]. Eight of the nine diagrams fall under two categories, namely structure and behavior diagrams. The classification of the SysML diagrams is depicted by the flowchart in Fig. 1. SysML has been constantly evolving over the years. Its governing standards have been revised four times in the past ten years [12]. A detailed understanding of SysML can be found in [11], [13]. There also exist a wide variety of tools to support SysML [8] $ - $ [10]. In this paper, the model for the Scout from the NASA Scout project was created in Cameo Enterprise Architecture (Cameo), one of the widely used tools for SysML in both industry and academia [14].

section_key: integrating sysml and value based design with an nea scout small satellite example / c vbd
text: VBD is a new approach to SE that aims at capturing the true preferences of stakeholders by means of a single mathematical representation called a value model [4], [5]. The primary underlying ideology behind VBD is that a

section: Integrating SysML and Value-Based Design with an NEA Scout Small Satellite Example > C. VBD
section_key: integrating sysml and value based design with an nea scout small satellite example / c vbd
text: VBD is a new approach to SE that aims at capturing the mathematical representation called a value model [4], [5]. The single source of truth to represent the stakeholder's preference can be used to determine the best system. If the value model is formed correctly some of the preferences that were previously represented as requirements will become unnecessary as they will be represented in the value model. For example, a requirement for an electric car of a range of at least 200 miles could be eliminated if the desires concerning the attribute of range are effectively captured in the stakeholder's value model. This facilitates increased exploration of the design space which may result in a design that was initially disregarded due to the imposition of requirements. As another example, design in a profit-seeking organization may be driven by minimization of mass. This may happen because it is believed that the least mass will lead to the minimum cost, which in turn will drive the profit up. However, the organization likely does not care about mass, and in this case, the minimization of mass or cost act as surrogates for maximization of profit [15]. A correct value model would

text: represent profit directly, where mass may or may not be an attribute in the model. Design optimization in the context of VBD (specifically associated with the value-driven design method) is represented by Fig. 2 that shows the life cycle development of systems [16]. Value models are composed of attributes that represent the characteristics of the system. High level attributes are functions of lower level attributes and design variables. Design variables are the variables that can be altered by the designer to change the system. The value model has a singular unit which is usually monetary, allowing for direct comparisons between designs. The decomposition of the value model to the lowest levels of the design hierarchy enables improved consistency in decision-making as decision-makers at all levels are designing for a single objective that is desired by the stakeholder at the topmost level [17]. Past researchers have accommodated the inclusion of physics-based couplings to achieve system consistency in physics [18] $ ^{–} $ [20]. Previous works have also

section: Integrating SysML and Value-Based Design with an NEA Scout Small Satellite Example > D. NEA Scout
section_key: integrating sysml and value based design with an nea scout small satellite example / d nea scout
text: The NEA Scout is a cube satellite (CubeSat) being developed by NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC), Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), and NASA Langley Research Center. The CubeSat is proposed to fly as secondary payload on the Space Launch System (SLS) Exploration Mission 1 (EM-1) to analyze and study near-earth asteroids (NEAs). Asteroids falling within a distance of 1 AU from the earth will be targeted. The objective of the mission is to develop a system that can help fill in the knowledge gaps that exist about NEAs with an overall goal of possible human exploration of asteroids in the future. The satellite will execute a reconnaissance with the target and then perform high resolution imaging using an updated JPL OCO-3 Context Camera [24]. The expected mission duration is 2.5 years during which it will target a number of pre-identified targets to measure the physical properties of the asteroids to address certain key strategic knowledge gaps (SKGs). The satellite will be a standard 6U CubeSat with a maximum mass of 14 kg and will primarily employ commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) components [25]. The Scout proposes to employ solar sail propulsion. An overview of the mission is provided in Fig. 3 that shows the mission Concept of Operations (ConOps) [26]. A detailed description of the NEA Scout mission can be found in [25], [27], [28].
